units.la: CUm TOTIVS historicæ scriptionis, Vir clarissime, magna semper laus, magnáque apud omnes gentes commendatio fuit: tùm verò eius historiæ partis maxima prædicatio extat, quæ res antiquissimas tanquam primas Mundi huius origines tradit, ac comprehenditur. Quanquam enim quanto unumquodque à nostra memoria longius abest, & magis remotum apparet, tanto facilius à multis censeri fabulosum, & incer-
units.tr: Since the whole of historical writing, most distinguished sir, has always been greatly praised and widely recommended among all peoples, the greatest glory of that history is the part which deals with the most ancient matters, the first origins of this world. For although the further anything lies from our memory and the more remote it appears, the more easily many people are accustomed to judge it fabulous and uncertain,

units.la: ã 2 tum dici consueuit: tamen ubi vetustæ res à certissimis, & fide dignissimis autoribus prodita, & verissimis testimoniis semel co- probatæ fuerint, nihil est eiusmodi cognitione vel scitu iucundius, vel etiam ad vsum vitæ humanæ vtilius: imò quò quidque tãc vetustius fuerit, eò cömendatius hominibus est, ac venerabilius. Quid enim vel nobis singulis lætius esse solet, quàm ipsorum primorum nostræ natiuitatis incunabulorum recordatio, quàm primæ ætatis nostræ me- moria, quàm ipsius denique ortus nostri afsectus ac repræsentatio? Quæ eadem quin non de vno aliquo homine quantumuis exi- mio: sed de toto ipso terrarum orbe, de totius Mundi machina & vniuersitate tradǔtur ac docentur, certè sunt tam grata, vt nihil ea narratione sáctius, & eo acroamate suauius esse possit. Me quidem hæc ipsa tam an- tiqua Orbis Terrarum primordia ac monumenta perquirentem sic delectarunt: postquàm aute inueni, sic in admirationem ra-puerunt, ut ingenuè fatear nullum vnquàm studij aut cognitionis genus tantopere, quàmtum istud, mihi placuisse: Itaque lubens feci, ut hæc ipsa etiā aliis communicarem, ac proderem. Ex iis enim rectè perspectis & Dei gloria maiestásque splendidiùs elucescit, & hominum piorum fides nō solùm confirmatur: verumetiā impiorum & ἀσιων proteruia confutatur: atque ex infirmorū animis omnis de illis rebus, quæ inhærēt, dubitatio tollitur. Et certè quum ea, quæ de prima Mundi origine, & progressu in Dei verbo scribuntur, à profanis irrideri, ab Ethnicis hominibus negari ex eorū sanniis & scriptis intelligeremus. Illa ipsa non solùm ex Mose autore sacro, & vero totius istius Antiquitatis historico collegimus: sed etiam ex ipsismet Ethnicorum libris, ac profanorū vetesta traditione comprobauimus, asseruimúsque, ut omnino vera esse omnes fateri oporteat
units.tr: yet when ancient matters have been handed down by the most certain and trustworthy authors and have once been confirmed by the most reliable testimonies, nothing is more pleasant to know or to learn, or more useful for the conduct of human life. Indeed, the older a thing is, the more commendable and venerable it is to men. For what is usually more delightful to each of us than to recall the very cradle of our birth, the memory of our earliest age, or the very picture and impression of our own origin? And these matters, which are taught and handed down not about any one man, however outstanding, but about the whole globe itself and the mechanism and universe of the whole world, are certainly so pleasing that nothing can be more agreeable as a narrative or sweeter as a lecture. I myself, when I was searching out these most ancient beginnings and monuments of the lands of the world, was so delighted, and after I discovered them was so carried away with wonder, that I may frankly confess no kind of study or knowledge has ever pleased me so much as this one. So I gladly resolved to share these things with others and to publish them. For when these things are rightly understood, both the glory and majesty of God shine out more brightly, and the faith of pious men is not only strengthened but also the arrogance of the impious and [ἀσεβῶν] is refuted, and all doubt about those matters which cling to the weak minds is removed. And indeed, since we understood from their jeers and writings that what is written in God's Word about the first origin and progress of the world is mocked by profane men and denied by pagans, we have gathered those very things not only from Moses, the sacred author and true historian of all this antiquity, but have also confirmed them from the books of the pagans themselves and from profane ancient tradition, and have asserted them, so that everyone must admit they are wholly true,

units.la: ea, quæ de ijs rebus Dei verbo traduntur. In quo certè quidem cernitur admiranda planè Dei Providentia, & cura de genere humano, & de hac sua veritate inter homines conferuanda, qui tot etiam in illis Ethnicorum monumentis nostræ, id est, sue, sacræ, verèque Historiæ, quanuis vetustissimæ, vestigia, testimoniáq; extare etiamnum hodie voluerit. Sic enim omnes eas primas Orbis res gestas & Antiquitates adumbrarunt Ethnici, ut vnus illis duntaxat color, id est propria eorum (quos Moses commemorat) nomina desint, ut Moisasse videantur, sic earum memoriam retinuerunt, licèt longissimo illo temporis interuallo iam quasi detrita, & velut fumo obscuratam, ut magna lux veritatis facilè in eorum scriptis splendescat, imò perspicua eniteat. Quædam habent illi quidem, fateor, propter annos interpolata, & velut carie quadam exesa & obsoleta: sed tamen quæ nullo negotio possint ex Mofis libris, velut inducta & repetita tinctura, pristinum colorem, & natiuam faciem, formamq; primam induere, & recuperare. Præclarè enim Augustinus, Nulla falsa doctrina, ac scriptio est, ait, quæ non aliqua vera intermisceat, ac proinde quæ non primæ veritatis scintillas retineat. Id quod in Ethnicorum scriptis apparet. Eas verò scintillas colligere & magni laboris fuit, & iudicij. Verùm quod ait Xenophon, ὁ ἀκ τῶν πόνων μαλακὰ γίγνεται, id est, ex huiusmodi labore magna voluptas manat. Quod si cui curiosius quædam à nobis inuestigata, producta�q; videbuntur, hoc responsum habeat, In tam vetustis Mundi illius primi & iam euersi ruderibus multa obscura inesse, & exigua quidem illius veritatis vestigia: sed quæ sunt illius vestigia tamen. Nam quemadmodum in Corinthi urbis Græciæ quondam opulentissimæ, postquam à Romanis eversa fuit, etiam tenuissimis ruderibus ac ramentis, multa tamen & uti reliquiæ repertæ semper fuerunt: sic in istis etiam exiguis, & pene, ut multis videtur, obsoletis testimoniis, quæ apud Ethnicos restant, multa nihilominus & vera nostræ diuinæ historiæ monumenta sunt relicta, quæ nec fastidire, nec reicere, præsertim ad profanos homines (qui eam pernegant) reuincedos debuimus, aut volumus. Et quoniam hanc tam augustam & sacram primæ Mundi Ætatis historiam nude proponere religio nobis erat, addidimus ad eam ipsam eiusmodi interpretationes & quæstiones, quæ & pios in vera rerum istarum fide corroborarent, & scopum Mosis doctrinámque ex ipsis rebus salutarem demonstrarent.
units.tr: those things which are handed down about these matters in God's Word. In this one certainly sees the truly admirable Providence of God and his care for the human race, and his will that this truth of his should be preserved among men, since he wished that so many traces and testimonies of our history, that is, of his sacred and truly history, however ancient, should still survive today in those monuments of the pagans. For all the pagans have so sketched out those first deeds and antiquities of the world that only their colour is missing, namely the proper names (which Moses records), so that they seem to have been made in Moses' manner. They have preserved the memory of them, although over that very long interval of time it has been, as it were, worn away and darkened like smoke, so that the great light of truth shines easily in their writings, indeed gleams clearly. Some things in them, I admit, have been corrupted by the years and are, as it were, eaten away by a kind of rot and grown obsolete; yet these can, without any difficulty, from the books of Moses, as if by a re-applied and renewed dye, put on and recover their former colour, their native appearance and original form. For Augustine states it well: there is no false doctrine or writing, he says, that does not mix in some truth, and so does not retain some sparks of the first truth. This appears in the writings of the pagans. But to gather those sparks has required great labour and judgment. Yet what Xenophon says, ὁ ἀκ τῶν πόνων μαλακὰ γίγνεται [that is, great pleasure flows from such labour], is true. If anyone thinks that some of the things we have investigated and brought forward are too minute, let him have this answer: in the very ancient ruins of that first world, now overthrown, many things are obscure and there are only slight traces of its truth, but they are nonetheless traces of it. For just as in the city of Corinth, once the most wealthy city of Greece, after it was overthrown by the Romans, many remains were always found even among the slightest rubble and fragments, so also in these meagre and, as many think, almost obsolete testimonies that survive among the pagans, many true monuments of our divine history have nevertheless been left, which we ought not, and do not wish, to despise or reject, especially when we are contending with profane men who deny it. And since we thought it a matter of religious obligation to set forth this so august and sacred history of the first age of the world bare, we have added to it interpretations and questions of this kind, which both strengthen the pious in the true faith of these matters and demonstrate the purpose of Moses and the doctrine, salutary from the very facts themselves.

units.la: Vere enim Philo Iudæus lib. quæst. in Gen. Sicut cæci, inquit, tractant tantum ipsam corporum spissitudinem tactu, non decus colorum, non formas, non figuras, non aliud quicquam eximiæ qualitatis testitestimonium prębens: sic minus docti, & inertis animæ oculi nihil in historijs intrinsecus cernere possunt: nec ad considerandam mentis historicę sublimitatem conscendunt, maxime vbi ipsa narratio conscientiam arguit, & medelam suggerit. Hæc autem summam cum voluptate vtilitatem auditoribus prębebunt, eoqs magis, quemadmodum spero, nostrum hunc laborem commendabunt, quo & antiquiora, & salubriora omnia tota hac narratio continebit. Ergo (liceat enim mihi propter antiquitatem illud Virgilianum hoc loco vsurpare) volumus, Pandere res alta terra, & caligine tectas: & propter vtilitatem illud Horat. huic scriptioni pręfigere
units.tr: Indeed Philo the Jew truly says in the book of Questions on Genesis: "Just as the blind handle only the thickness of bodies by touch, and do not perceive the beauty of colours, the forms, the figures, or anything else of exceptional quality, so the eyes of the less learned and sluggish soul can discern nothing inwardly in the histories, nor do they rise to consider the sublimity of the historical mind, especially where the narrative itself accuses the conscience and suggests a remedy." These things, however, will offer the hearers the greatest utility together with delight, and so, as I hope, will commend this our labour all the more, since this whole narrative contains things both more ancient and more wholesome. Therefore (for I may here use that Virgilian phrase, because of its antiquity) "we wish to lay open deep things, and things hidden in darkness," and, for its usefulness, to prefix to this writing that line of Horace:

units.la: Porrò autem hanc meam operam atque historiā, Fuillati, vir Generose, tibi dedicare iamprídem apud me constitueram, multis quidem & grauibus aliis de causis, sed im-primis, tum quod te rerum istarum, imo totius sacrę veritatis, & cœlestis doctrinę (cuius hęc narratio pars est) vehementer amantem, & percupidum semper cognoscere: tum etiam quod quum multis beneficiis tibi sim deuinctus, æquum iudicaui aliquod meæ grati erga te animi testimonium publicum extare, vt si tecum reipsa propter rerum inopiam par facere non possem, saltem verbis & scriptis agnoscerem summa tua in me beneficia, eaque aliquo munusculo rependerem.
units.tr: Moreover, I had long since resolved in my own mind to dedicate this work and this history of mine to you, Fuillati, most generous sir, for many other weighty reasons, but chiefly because you are greatly devoted to these matters, indeed to the whole of sacred truth and heavenly doctrine (of which this narrative is a part), and are always most eager to know it; and also because, since I am bound to you by many kindnesses, I judged it right that some public testimony of my gratitude to you should exist, so that, if I could not repay you in fact because of my lack of means, I might at least acknowledge in words and writings your great kindnesses to me, and repay them with some small gift.

units.la: Accedit pietas illa tua insignis, in qua laude & gloria nemini, meo quidem iudicio, secundus cedere vel potes, vel debes. Sic enim in vera pietatis fide instructus es, vt ne summis quidem in ea cognitione ingeniis & Theologis cedas: Sic in eadem confirmatus vuis, vt nullæ te à vera Christi fide afflictiones quantumuis graues (quas plurimas iam perpessus es) vllo tempore auocare po-tuerint. tuerint: imo ne quidem tuum illud in propagando Dei regno maximum studium vlla unquam pericula retardarint, nedum (quod tamen plurimis euenit) exstinxerint. Sic sancte vitam ipse tua instituisti, vt omnibus sis virtutum omnium exemplar Christianarum. Et quanquam reliquos mortales magnae opes & diuitiae (quibus abundas) generisq; nobilitas, quae in te summa est, ad luxum, vitamque dissolutam incitare, ac pene etiam inuitos pertrahere solet: illa tamen ipsa eo magis te ad Deum colendum inuitarunt, quod vt illa esse optima Dei in te dona Christiane agnoscis, sic in eiusdem laudem studiose conuertis omnia. Sic denique totam familiam tuam pie, ac in Dei metu edoces, ac regis (quanquam illa est amplissima) vt mihi alter quidam & secundus Abrahamus amicus Dei, & Pater fidelium esse in his terris videaris. Itaque etiam magnam huic meo labori commendationem
units.tr: Add to this that outstanding piety of yours, in which, in my judgment, you can or ought to yield second place to no one in praise and glory. For you are so instructed in the true faith of piety that you give way to no one, not even to the greatest minds and theologians, in that knowledge. You are so confirmed in the same faith that no afflictions, however grievous (and you have already endured very many), could at any time call you away from the true faith of Christ. Indeed, your great zeal in spreading the kingdom of God has never been held back by any dangers, let alone extinguished, as happens to very many. You have so holily arranged your own life that you are an example of all Christian virtues to everyone. And although great riches and wealth (in which you abound) and the nobility of your family, which is supreme in you, are wont to stir other mortals to luxury and a dissolute life, and almost to drag them along even against their will, those very things have invited you all the more to worship God, since, as you acknowledge them to be the excellent gifts of God in you as a Christian, so you eagerly turn them all to his praise. Finally, you teach and rule your whole household in piety and in the fear of God (though it is a very large household), so that to me you seem to be, in these lands, another and second Abraham, the friend of God and father of the faithful. Therefore I think that this my labour will also gain great commendation among pious men from the naming of you in the frontispiece of this work.

units.tr: I think it will be well received by all the godly, as it appears under the dedication of your name on the title page of this work. I beg you, most excellent sir, to accept this gift of mine as kindly as it is offered to you by me with a candid and well-wishing heart, and to consider me yours for ever. Farewell.

units.la: De varijs M- undi, quæ vocantur, ætatibus, & quæ Ætas in hoc opere describatur.
units.tr: On the various so-called ages of the World, and which Age is described in this work.

units.la: VONIAM nobis propositum est primam ætatem huius conspicui Mundi à Deo cõditi, eiúsque vetustissimæ antiquitatem tùm ex ipsissimis S. Scriptura & limpidissimis fontibus haustas, tùm ex Ethnicorum etiam ipsorum monumentis investigatas, describere, (quæ res cum scitu iucundissima est: tum verò ad veram pietatis agnitionem, id est, tum nostræ damnationis, tum redemptionis causas explicandas, nosq; in fide confirmandos necessaria) primùm in quot ætates, distinctaq; secula tota Mundi huius durant.
units.tr: Since it is our purpose to describe the first age of this conspicuous World, created by God, and its most ancient antiquity, drawn both from the most authentic Holy Scripture and its clearest springs, and investigated also from the monuments of the Gentiles themselves (a matter which is most pleasant to know and, indeed, necessary for the true knowledge of piety, that is, for explaining both the causes of our damnation and of our redemption and for confirming us in faith), it seems first necessary to explain into how many ages, and what distinct centuries, the whole duration of this World is divided.

units.la: ratio diuidi soleat, videtur exponendum. Illud verò dignum est, quod obseruetur, penè quanis hominum ætate scriptores tum sacros, tum Ecclesiasticos, tum etiā Ethnicos, in certa quadam tempora digessisse totam illam seculorum, quibus Mundus iam suo seculo extiterat, seriem. Sed Profani in eo toto temporis spatio quatuor tantum ætates constituunt, nimirum ætatem Auream, quæ prima fuit: Argenteam, quæ secunda: Æneam, quæ tertia: Ferream denique, (Sic enim ex Danielis cap. 2. verf 32. vocant) quæ postrema est, quæ etiamnum hodie durat, & perpetuò (ut profani illi homines putant) quoque duratura est. Sic autem eas finiunt singulas, vt Aurea quidem ætas ab exordio Mundi ad Iouem usque fuerit: Argentea, à Iouis regno ad Heroum virorum præstantissimorum exortum, celebritatem, & frequentiam: Aenea, ab Heroibus illis (in quibus iustitia vis adhuc regnabat) usque ad Monarchiarum & Regum diuersorum (sub quibus iura polluta sunt, & regna instituta) in hoc terrarum Orbe constitutionem, ac distinctionem. Ab hoc denique tempore Ferrea ætas duret. Sic Hesiodus (à quo ceteri omnes postea sumpsere) in lib. 1. qui dicitur [Opera & Dies:] sic Virgilius lib. 1 Georg. Ouidius lib. 1. Metamorph. Diodorus Siculus, & alij horum vestigia secuti penè infiniti tum veteres, tum recentes scriptores. Verùm Moses, sacrique ac Diuini Prophetæ neququam has esse Mundi ætates annotant, vel sic eas tradunt. Nam si qua fuit ætas Aurea Mundi prima, illa breuissimo tempore certè quidem extitit, vtpote duntaxat ante peccatum Adami: reliquum autem Mundi tempus totum, quod secutum est plane ex Prophetis Ferreum, & Improbum seculum est dicendum, non Argenteu, non Aeneum. Nam quod est apud Danielem cap. 2. verf. 32. ad illud primu nascentis Mundi tempus minime pertinet, sed ad Monarchias innumerabilibus pene seculis post primam Aetatem Mundi introductas, e quibus prima, caeterarum comparatione nominatur Aurea, id est, ditior, & rerum omnium, ac praesertim auri abundantior reliquis, ac copiosior, ut apparet Dan. 2. 1. Caeteræ egentiores, & minus opulentæ fuere. Quid igitur? Insignes ac memorabiles rerum mutationes & velut ὑπογραφὰς observarunt, ac describerunt Prophetæ Dei, ex quibus diversus Mundi status, diversaque conditio, saltem quod ad Ecclesiam, distingui discernique potest: ex quibus Viri Ecclesiastici, id est posteri, sequentesque scriptores pÿ varias Mundi Aetates deinde definierunt. Nec tamen omnes eafdem, & ijsdem temporum punctis, & rebus gestis terminarunt: sed aliy aliter, & alias: atque adeo quidam, plures: quidam vero, eas pauciores nobis reliquerunt. Quidam enim duntaxat Quinque Mundi aetatis esse volunt: aliy Sex: aliy, Septem: aliy, Octo: aly etiam plures: prout cuique libuit hanc vel illam epochan, & rem memorabilem observare, eamque initium, vel finem alicuius Aetatis Mundi à se constitutã ponere. Quamobrem quum varij Scriptores Ecclesiastici Aetates Mundi explicare & distinguere voluerint, studuerintque, non semper tamen inter se consentiunt sed sæpè dissentiũt: quæ discordia tamen neminem offendere debet, quum esse debeat liberum cuiq; in ea re definienda animo. mi fui iudicium. Ergo Philo Judaeus, Africanus Christianus scriptor, & post eum Eusebius Pamphili, Hieronymus, Paulus Orosius, Beda, Addo Viennensis, Carolus Bovillus, Ioannes Funccius, Antonius Contius, & reliqui (qui Aetatas Mundi describunt) non ταυτὸν γεγραμμὲν semper sunt secuti. Caeterum Augustini potissimum sententiam recentiores ampletuntur & nos quoque hic, qui tum lib. 83. Quaest. cap. 58, & lib. 12 contra Faustum Manichaeum cap. 8. sex totius huius Mundi velut unius hominis, aetates constituit, quibus sit Mundus duraturus, quemadmodum sex Diebus idem hic Mundus primum conditus fuit. Septima vero aetate sit Mundi huius & quies, & plena instauratio per Christum, post illius universale iudicium futura. Verba vero Augustini sunt haec, cap. 8. lib. 12 contra Faustum Manichaeum, [SEX diebus in Genesi ait, consummavit Deus omnia opera sua, & septimo requievit. Sex aetatibus humanum genus hoc seculo per successiones temporum Dei opera insigniunt: quarum Prima est ab Adam usque ad Noe: Secunda a Noe usque ad Abraham: Tertia ab Abraham usque ad David: Quarta a David usque ad transmigrationem in Babyloniam: Quinta inde usque ad humilem adventum Domini nostri Iesu Christi: Sexta quae nunc agitur, donec Excelsus veniat ad Iudicium: Septima vero intelligitur in requie Sanctorum, non in hac vita, sed in alia.] Primam vero aetatem Mundi, ab Adamo ad Noachum id est diluvium scribit idem Augustinus lib. 15. de Civit. Dei, cap. 20. cōtinere, ex Latinorum codicum supputatione, annos bis mille ducentos sexaginta duos: ex Hebraeorum autem numero, mille fexcentos quinquaginta sex. Quae postrema ratiocinatio seu calculus verus est: itaque nos eum sequimur, non autem Latinum. Nam ab Adamo condito seu creato ad annum Diluuij seu generalis immersionis Orbis terrarum (quem annum hic Augustinus Noachum appellat, nimirum insignem illam calamitatem, quae sub eo contigit: non autem annum natiuitatis Noachi speCtàs) non plures anni, quàm mille sexcenti quinquaginta sex intercedunt. Nos vero vnū duntaxat addemus, fientq; anni prima Mundi Aetatis 1657, quoniam Aetas Mundi secunda non ab initio seu immissione diluuij: sed potius ab eius fins, & generis humani ex eo liberatione, id est, ab exitu Noachi ex Arca incipit, estque statuenda & sumenda. Habet vero totum hoc prima Mundi Aetatis spatium quattuor sectiones, seu ἐπχὰς insignes: quarum vnaquaeque sua capita, & res obseruatione dignas, ac singulares comprehendit.
units.tr: It is worth noting that almost every writer of every age, sacred, ecclesiastical and even Gentile, has arranged the whole succession of centuries during which the World has already existed into certain fixed periods. The profane writers, however, mark out only four ages in the whole span of time: the Golden Age, which was first; the Silver, which was second; the Bronze, which was third; and finally the Iron Age (for so they call it, from Daniel 2:32), which is the last, which still lasts today, and which will, as those profane men think, last forever. They define each of these ages thus: the Golden Age ran from the beginning of the World to Jupiter; the Silver from the reign of Jupiter to the rise, celebrity and abundance of the most outstanding heroic men; the Bronze from those heroes (in whom justice still reigned) to the establishment and division of monarchies and of various kings in this orb of the earth (under whom laws were corrupted and kingdoms instituted). Finally, the Iron Age lasts from this time onward. So Hesiod, from whom all the others afterwards took their lead, in the first book of the work called [Works and Days]; so Virgil in the first book of the Georgics; Ovid in the first book of the Metamorphoses; Diodorus Siculus; and almost endless other writers, ancient and recent, who followed their footsteps. But Moses and the holy and divine prophets do not note these as the ages of the World in vain, nor do they hand them down in this way. For if there was a first Golden Age of the World, it certainly existed for a very short time, namely only before the sin of Adam; and the whole remaining time of the World that followed must clearly, from the Prophets, be called an Iron and wicked age, not a Silver or a Bronze one. For what is in Daniel 2:32 does not pertain at all to that first time of the newly born World, but to the monarchies introduced almost countless centuries after the first age of the World, of which the first, in comparison with the others, is called Golden, that is, richer and more abundant in all things, and especially in gold, than the rest, and more copious; as appears from Daniel 2:1. The others were poorer and less wealthy. I formed my own judgment. Therefore Philo the Jew, the Christian writer Africanus, and after him Eusebius Pamphili, Jerome, Paulus Orosius, Bede, Adso of Vienne, Carolus Bovillus, Johannes Funccius, Antonius Contius, and the rest who describe the ages of the World, have not always followed the same written scheme. Yet the opinion of Augustine above all is embraced by more recent writers, and we too follow him here, who, in book 83 of the Questions, chapter 58, and in book 12 against Faustus the Manichaean, chapter 8, established six ages of the whole World, as if it were one man, during which the World will last, just as this same World was first created in six days. The seventh age, however, will be the rest and full restoration of this World through Christ, to come after its universal judgment. Augustine's own words, in chapter 8 of book 12 against Faustus the Manichaean, are these: "In Genesis it says that God completed all his works in six days, and rested on the seventh. By successions of time, the human race in this age marks God's works in six ages: the first is from Adam to Noah; the second from Noah to Abraham; the third from Abraham to David; the fourth from David to the transmigration into Babylon; the fifth from there to the humble coming of our Lord Jesus Christ; the sixth, which is now in progress, until the Most High comes to judgment. The seventh is understood as the rest of the Saints, not in this life but in another." Augustine likewise writes, in book 15 of the City of God, chapter 20, that the first age of the World, from Adam to Noah, that is to the flood, contains, according to the reckoning of the Latin codices, 2262 years, but according to the number of the Hebrews, 1656 years. This latter reckoning or calculation is the true one, so we follow it rather than the Latin. For from Adam, when he was made or created, to the year of the Flood, or the general immersion of the orb of the earth (which year Augustine here calls Noah, namely that notable calamity which happened under him, not the year of Noah's birth), not more than 1656 years intervene. We shall add only one year, so that the first age of the World becomes 1657 years, since the second age of the World does not begin from the beginning or outbreak of the flood, but rather from its end and the liberation of the human race from it, that is, from Noah's exit from the Ark; and it is to be fixed and taken from there. This whole span of the first age of the World has four sections, or notable epochs, each of which comprises its own chapters and matters worthy of observation and distinct treatment.

units.la: Ergo Sectio Prima huius Prima Aetatis Mundi completitur quicquid est ante peccatum Adami, id est à Mundi initio ad Peccatum ipsum ab Adamo primum perpetratum. Cōtinet autem totum illud spatium ad minus totos dies septem.
units.tr: Therefore the First Section of this First Age of the World includes whatever happened before the sin of Adam, that is, from the beginning of the World to the very sin first committed by Adam. That whole span contains at least seven days.

units.la: Secunda Sectio ea, quae S. Scriptura tradit contigisse ab Adami peccato vsque ad publicam Nominis Dei profanationem. Tempus autem hoc ab exordio Mundi computatum habet annos circiter ducentos triginta quinque.
units.tr: The Second Section comprises what Holy Scripture relates to have happened from the sin of Adam to the public profanation of the Name of God. This period, reckoned from the beginning of the World, amounts to about 235 years.

units.la: Tertia Sectio eiusdem primae aetatis Mundi durat ab illa Nominis Dei popularī & publica profanatione vsque ad annum, quo Diluuium vniuersale contigit. Habet autem annos ab initio creati Mundi 1656: A profanatione Nominis Dei annos mille quadringentos viginti vnum: A peccato primo Adami minus, quàm à creatione Mundi, aliquot diebus, vel annis, vel mensibus. Est enim incertum quando Adamus & Eua primum peccarunt.
units.tr: The Third Section of the same first age of the World lasts from that popular and public profanation of the Name of God until the year in which the universal Flood occurred. It has 1656 years from the beginning of the created World; from the profanation of the Name of God, 1421 years; and from the first sin of Adam it is less than the creation of the World by some days, or years, or months. For it is uncertain when Adam and Eve first sinned.

units.la: Quarta vero & vltima huius Aetatis sestio est Annus Diluuij. id est, ab immissis à Deo in vniuersum terrarum Orbem aquis ad exitum Noachi ex Arca, in qua toto tempore eluuionis istius iussu Dei subsitirat vnà cum vxore, filijs, nuribus, & cæteris Animatibus in eam ab ipsomet Deo introductis. Durat hoc spatium Annum duntaxat vnum. Atque hæc est totius futura disputationis nostræ summa partitio; & velut operis designatio, ædificiq́ frontispicium nostri, quod, Deo Optimo Maximo bene fauente, iam aggredimur, & ordimur, si prius Lectorem admonuerimus in vnaquaque Sectione hæc quattuor præcipua Capita à nobis distingui, statuiq́ nimirum Historica, Disputata, Vestigia relica, & Collecta, seu Porismata, quæ qualis tum Politicus, tum Ecclesiasticus Mundi status tunc fuerit, ostendent. Ergo quod sœlix sit, & faustum, & ad Dei gloriam, & Ecclesiæ ædificationem, & singulorum salutem, incipimus.
units.tr: The fourth and last section of this age is the year of the Flood: that is, the span from when God poured the waters over the whole orb of the earth until Noah left the Ark, in which, by God's command, he lived through the whole period of this deluge together with his wife, sons, daughters-in-law, and the other living creatures that God himself had brought into it. This span lasts only one year. And this is the summary division of the whole discussion we are about to undertake, and, as it were, the outline of the work and the frontispiece of our edifice, which, with God, the best and greatest, favouring us, we now begin and set in order—provided we first warn the reader that in each section we distinguish these four principal heads and set them down as follows: the Historical, the Disputed, the Remaining Traces, and the Collected or Porisms, which will show what the political and ecclesiastical state of the world then was. Therefore, that it may be happy and prosperous, and for the glory of God, the building up of the Church, and the salvation of each one, we begin.

units.la: LIBRI, SEV SECTIO- NIS PRIMAE PRIMAE MVNDI ÆTATIS, QVÆ EST Ab Exordio Mundi ad pri- mum Adami primi Ho- minis peccatum.
units.tr: BOOK, OR SECTION, OF THE FIRST AGE OF THE WORLD, WHICH RUNS FROM THE BEGINNING OF THE WORLD TO THE FIRST SIN OF ADAM, THE FIRST MAN.

units.la: CAPVT PRIMVM
units.tr: CHAPTER I

units.la: ¶ Continet Historica octo: Dies autem ad minus septem.
units.tr: ¶ This chapter contains eight historical matters, and the days number at least seven.

units.la: ABET Historia hæc, 1. Creationem Mundi. 2. Hominis. 3 Paradisi terrestris situm. 4. Arbores in eo duas. 5. Impositionem nominum. 6. Mulieris formationem. 7. Coniugij institutionem. 8. Statum primum Adami & Evæ.
units.tr: This history contains: (1) the creation of the world; (2) the creation of man; (3) the situation of the earthly paradise; (4) the two trees in it; (5) the giving of names; (6) the formation of the woman; (7) the institution of marriage; (8) the first state of Adam and Eve.

units.la: I. Dies Mundi. I. Mundi creatio.
units.tr: I. The days of the world. I. The creation of the world.

units.la: Ex nihilo Cœlum summum & Primum, id est, totum hunc visibilem Mundum ambitu suo concludens creatur: item & Terra, sed rudis, inanis, tenebrosa primum, & vacua. Hoc eodem die & Lumen quoque (sed posti cælum illud & terra conditam) producitur: quod Lumen totis quatuor prioribus diebus fuit vagum, nul. loque certo corpore, & loco comprehensum ferebatur supra terram quidem: sed tamen infra cælum illud primum creatum. Dies igitur a nocte post lumen productum per vices successivi distinctus est. Fuit autem ista dies primus ac natalis huius mundi, Gen. 1.1. Vocatur Dies Creationis.
units.tr: Out of nothing the highest and first heaven is created, that is, the whole of this visible world, enclosing it within its compass. Likewise the earth is created, but rough, empty, dark at first, and void. On this same day light is also produced (though after that heaven and earth were founded). This light, during the four earlier days, was wandering and was not held in any fixed body or place; it was carried over the earth, but still below that first heaven that had been created. So the day was distinguished from the night by a succession of alternating periods after the light was produced. This first day was the birthday of this world, Gen. 1.1. It is called the Day of Creation.

units.la: 2. Expansionis productio continetur, id est, eius loci, & spatij, quod interponeretur inter Aquas inferiores (quae sunt erant, cum ipso corpore Terræ) & Aquas sublimiores, (quae sunt erant, sursum elevata supra elementum & Orbem Terræ) easque secerneret. Hæc expansio etiam Cælum a Deo nominata est, quemadmodum & primum illud corpus seu cælum primo die creatum, quod primum Cælum [Cælum cælorum] dicitur. Patet autem hæc expansio latissime a superficie terræ usque ad illud summum & primum Mundi huius cælum & corpus, Gen. 1.6. Vocatur Dies Distinctionis.
units.tr: (2) The production of the expanse is described, that is, of the space and extent that was placed between the lower waters (which were, along with the body of the earth itself) and the higher waters (which were lifted up above the element and the globe of the earth), and that separated them. This expanse too was named Heaven by God, just as that first body or heaven created on the first day is called the first heaven [heaven of heavens]. This expanse extends very widely from the surface of the earth up to that highest and first heaven and body of this world, Gen. 1.6. It is called the Day of Distinction.

units.la: 3. Aquarum inferiorum in unum locum (qui Mare dictus est) collectio fit. Terra igitur emersit tunc ex aquis, & quæ eminens ex Aquis extitit [Arida] vocata est. Hæc vero illo eodem die Herbas & Arbores tum in usum Hominis & Animalium postea futurorum & creandorum, tum in ornatum Terræ ipsius, ex suo corpore produxit, Gen. 1.9. Vocantur hic, & sequentes dies, Dies ornatus: sed proprie iste Dies ornatus Terræ.
units.tr: (3) The lower waters are gathered into one place (called the sea). The earth then emerged from the waters, and what stood out above the waters was called dry land. On that same day it brought forth from its own body herbs and trees, both for the use of men and animals who were to come later and be created, and for the adornment of the earth itself, Gen. 1.9. These and the following days are called the Days of Adornment, but properly this is the Day of Adornment of the earth.

units.la: 4. Luminaria creata sunt in Expansione cœli (quæ secundo die fuerat condita) maiora duo, primum nêpe Sol, & Luna: deinde reliqua minora, quæ Astra, Stellæ, & Sidera vocantur, ut Diem & Noctem Mundo distribuerent, & lumen administrarent vicissitudine quadam perpetua. Ergo in Sole, Luna, cæterisque stellis Collectio Luminis primo die creati facta tunc à Deo fuit. Gen.1.14.
units.tr: (4) Lights were created in the expanse of heaven (which had been founded on the second day): two greater ones, namely the sun and the moon, and then the remaining lesser ones, which are called stars, constellations and heavenly bodies, so that they might divide day and night for the world and provide light in a certain perpetual alternation. Thus the gathering of light, which had been created on the first day, was then done by God in the sun, moon and the other stars. Gen. 1.14.

units.la: Vocatur Dies ornatus non Cæli primi, sed Expansionis, quæ sub eo est.
units.tr: It is called the Day of Adornment not of the first heaven, but of the expanse which lies beneath it.

units.la: 5. Aves, & Pisces creantur ex aquis: nimirum Aves quidem ex aquis superioribus, quæ sunt in expansione cœli: Pisces autem ex aquis inferioribus, quas Mare dicebantur. Additur hîs præceptum Dei de multiplicatione, & propagatione sui cuiusque generis ex coitu nempe Maris, & Fœmina, cuique generi Animalis factum in sua specie, Gen.1.20.
units.tr: (5) Birds and fishes are created out of the waters: birds indeed out of the upper waters, which are in the expanse of heaven, but fishes out of the lower waters, which were called the sea. To these is added God's command concerning multiplication and propagation of each kind, by the mating of male and female, each kind of animal being made in its own species, Gen. 1.20.

units.la: Dies ornatus Aquarum superiorum, & inferiorum, id est, Maris.
units.tr: The Day of Adornment of the upper and lower waters, that is, of the sea.

units.la: 6. Brutorum animantium e terra productio fit, Gen.1.24.
units.tr: (6) The production of the animals of the earth, the brute beasts, takes place, Gen. 1.24.

units.la: II. Creatio Hominis, velut totius huius boni ac domus Patrisfa- milias, & Domini.
units.tr: II. The Creation of Man, as the Chief of All This Good and the Lord's Household Steward.

units.la: Homo Mu eodem illo die sexto creatur à Deo. Corpus quidem eius sumptum est è limo seu pulvere terræ: Anima vero, quæ tota est immortalis, ex inspiratione, & flatu Dei ipsius in Hominem, id est, in corpus hominis iam conditum per faciem eiusdem hominis à Deo immissò. Hic Homo primus Mas a Deo conditus est, & Adam à rubore vocatus est, creatusque ad Dei ipsius imaginem, & quidem ex omni rerum in hoc visibili Mundo conditarum numero & genere solus, Dei autoris, & Prototypi sui tum agnoscendi, tum colendi gratia, Gen. 1. 26. 29, & 2 7. & ut istarum rerum omnium à Deo conditarum in hoc visibili Mundo dominus esset Homo, id est Adamus, & eius posteri, Gen. 1. 29, Psal. 8.
units.tr: Man was created by God on that same sixth day. His body was indeed taken from the slime or dust of the earth, but his soul, which is wholly immortal, was breathed into him by God himself, that is, into the body of the man already formed, by the breath of God sent through the face of that same man. This first man, the male, was created by God and called Adam from the red earth, and he was made alone, out of the whole number and kind of all things created in this visible world, in the image of God himself, so that he might acknowledge and worship God, his author and prototype (Gen. 1. 26, 29; and 2. 7). And so that man, that is Adam and his posterity, might be lord of all those things created by God in this visible world (Gen. 1. 29; Ps. 8).

units.la: Dies Perfectionis, & consummationis huius Mundi.
units.tr: The day of the perfection and completion of this world.

units.la: 7. Quievit Dominus Deus à toto suo opere, cui benedixit, id est, à totius Mundi huius fabrica, Gen. 1. 31, & 2. 2. Dies Sabbati, seu Quietis.
units.tr: 7. The Lord God rested from all his work, which he blessed, that is, from the whole construction of this world (Gen. 1. 31; 2. 2). The day of the Sabbath, or of rest.

units.la: III. Eden, seu Paradisus Terrestris.
units.tr: III. Eden, or the Earthly Paradise.

units.la: Hortum Deus in Edene regione parat, omni herbarum & arborum genere abundantissimum, ac copiosissimum. Horti autem illius situs, uti & regionis ipsius Edenis, erat ad Orientem ratione Deserti, in quo tunc scribebat Moses: & Iudea seu Terra promissa, cuius idem Moses rationem habuit, Gen. 2. 8, & 3. 10. 23. Non fuit autem tota regio Eden, Hortus: sed pars eius duntaxat.
units.tr: God prepared a garden in the region of Eden, most abundant and most richly stocked with every kind of herb and tree. The situation of that garden, as also of the region of Eden itself, lay to the east in relation to the desert in which Moses was then writing, and to the land of Judea, or the promised land, which Moses also took into account (Gen. 2. 8; 3. 10, 23). Yet the whole region of Eden was not the garden; it was only a part of it.

units.la: IIII. Arbores in eo duę Prae- cipuae conditae.
units.tr: IIII. The two principal trees were created in it.

units.la: Duae autem Arbores Praecipuas in eodem illo horto Deus plantas seu germinare fecit: Vnam, [Vitae] quae immortalis Adami posterorúmque eius in hoc Mundo status flatus, felicitatis, & durationis futuræ symbolum erat à Deo datum Adamo ac illius posteris, Genes. 2. 9. Apoc. 2. 7. Alteram [Scientiæ Boni & Mali] quæ symbolum fuit mali, & vitij in Adamo, & eius posteris futuri, seu inhabitaturi (si ex ea ederet, ac sua sorte & felicitate non contentus, Deo non obtemperaret.) Datum autem fuit Adamo hoc sacramentum à Deo, ut eum eiusq; posteros tentaret qua fide in se futuri erant, & ut eos cautiores, prudentioresq; faceret. Erat autem utraq; Arbor & conspectu incundissima, & esu suavissima, Gen. 2. 9. & 3. 6.
units.tr: Moreover, God caused two principal trees to be planted or to sprout in that same garden. The first, [of Life], which was given by God to Adam and his posterity as a symbol of their immortal state in this world, of felicity, and of future endurance, Gen. 2. 9; Rev. 2. 7. The second, [of the Knowledge of Good and Evil], which was a symbol of evil and vice in Adam and in his posterity who would dwell there (if he ate from it, and, not content with his lot and happiness, disobeyed God). This sacrament was given to Adam by God so that He might test him and his descendants, to see with what faith they would be toward Him, and so that He might make them more cautious and prudent. Both trees were most pleasing to the sight and most sweet to eat, Gen. 2. 9 and 3. 6.

units.la: Adamum à se recens alibi tamen conditum Deus die eodem sexto, quo eum creauerat, in eo Edenis Regionis Horto collocat, velut praestantissimo domicilio; ac totius huius Terræ solo optimo, incundissimo, ac fertilissimo: eumque Hortum Adamo & colendum, & custodiendum idem Deus tradit, quòd in eo Horto cum Adamo colloqui postea vellet, permisso ei cuiusvis alterius Herbæ & Arboris esu liberrimo pro animi voluntate: solius autem, & vnius Arboris Scientiæ Boni, & Mali interdictio, addita etiam ad sui interdicti confirmationem, & Adami posterorumque terrorem grauissima Mortis vtriusq; (id est, Animæ & Corporis) pœna, quam Adamus hanc Dei Legem violans, eiusq; posteritas erat sensura. Gen. 1. 29. & 2. 17. & 3. 2. & 3. 8. Rom. 6. 23, vti postea sensit.
units.tr: God, having just created Adam (though elsewhere), on the same sixth day on which He had made him, placed him in this garden of the region of Eden as in a most excellent dwelling, on the best, most pleasant and most fertile soil of this whole land; and the same God handed over this garden to Adam to be both cultivated and guarded, because He wished afterwards to converse with Adam in that garden. He granted him the completely free eating of every other herb and tree at his heart's pleasure, but only one tree, the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil, was forbidden; and to confirm this prohibition, and to strike terror into Adam and his posterity, the most grievous penalty of death of both kinds (that is, of soul and body) was added, which Adam, violating this law of God, and his posterity, were to feel. Gen. 1. 29; 2. 17; 3. 2 and 3. 8; Rom. 6. 23, as he afterwards felt.

units.la: V. Impositio Nominum.
units.tr: V. The Naming of Things.

units.la: Nomina rebus omnibus in hoc visibili Mundo conditis imposuit Adamus, velut earum Dominus, Deo sic iubente, volente, ac eas Adamo donante. Imponit autem ea nomina Adamus praesertim Animantibus Terrenis, & Caelestibus: qua Deus ipse coram Adamo statuerat, ut eum illa velut terrenum dominum suum agnoscerēt, & ex nomine sibi ab Adamo posito, datoque postea citata adessent, seq; coram eo ipsa per se se sistrent, id est, non vinculis constrictā, non vi coacta, vel opera hominum vlla adiuta, sed ipsa sponte sua sicque vnumquodq; Animal voci Adami & posterorum eius, velut Domini sui legitimi, & a Deo sibi constituti iussui parere, & spote obsequeretur. Gen. 2.19 & 6 19 Ps.8 Heb 2.8. Nomina vero rebus creatis imposuit Adamus cuiq; pro natura ipsius proprietate, vt nomē illud natura rei conueniret quā nouerat Adamus ipso naturali lumine (id est, quod sibi a prima natiuitate Deus infuderat, eratq; in eius posteris perm infurum) vtpote quum ea res omnes creatae in hominis vsum a Deo faste essent. Ergo earum singularū naturam, vim, soproprietatēsque nosse debebat Adamus, & illius posteri, vt iis commode, & in finem (ad quem singulae conditae erant) vterentur. 1.Tim 4. 3 4. Nam rei ignota nullus esse potest vsus, nullaue, quemadmodum habeat proprium verbum vetus, cupido.
units.tr: Adam imposed names on all the things created in this visible world, as their lord, since God so commanded and willed, and gave them over to Adam. Adam imposed these names chiefly on the earthly and heavenly animals, which God himself had placed before Adam so that they would recognise him as their earthly lord, and, once called by the name given to them by Adam (and afterwards given), would come before him and present themselves in his presence of their own accord: not bound with chains, not compelled by force, nor aided by any human effort, but spontaneously, so that each animal would obey the voice of Adam and of his posterity, as its lawful lord constituted by God, and would follow his command willingly. Gen. 2.19 & 6.19; Ps. 8; Heb. 2.8. Adam, however, gave to each created thing a name suited to its natural property, so that the name would agree with the nature of the thing, which Adam knew by the natural light itself (that is, the light God had infused into him from his first birth, and which was to remain in his posterity), since all created things had been made by God for human use. Therefore Adam ought to have known the nature, power and properties of each of them, and so his posterity too, so that they might use them fittingly and for the end for which each was created. 1 Tim. 4.3-4. For there can be no use of a thing that is unknown, nor, as the old saying has it, can desire attach itself to what has no proper name.

units.la: VI. Mulieris Formatio.
units.tr: VI. The Formation of the Woman.

units.la: Mulierem seu fœminam Hominem in Paradiso terrestri Deus creat post omnia creata. Creat autem eam ex vna Adami costa, in eseremq; istam vocat [Ifcham] nomine ab Isch (quod virum seu marem significat) deducto. Ergo Ischaest Virago, sic a Deo appellata, vt originis sua vel ipso nomine admoneretur. Hæc eadem [Eua] postea dictā est. Fœminam autem Hominem creauit Deus, quoniā inter omnia animalia condita nullum reperiebat, quod esset par, commodum, atque conueniens Adamo ad Dei ipsius imaginem cōditio, & auxilium illi esset, id est, cum quo consortium, colloquium Adamus haberet, vt de Dei cultu, & præcepto sibi dato communicaret, & cum quo de rerum natura agere & conferre ad Dei gloriam posset: denique ex quo prolem sibi similem susciperet Adamus. Ergo condita est Ischa, id est Mulier & ipsa ad Dei imaginem quoq; sicut & Adamus, qua eiusdem cognitionis Dei, & cultus ipsius, & felicitatis, ac dominationis in hic terris particeps, & capax esset, cuius & Adamus: & quæ eiusdem indolis, naturæ, sermonis, rationis, & ratiocinationis vsum haberet, cuius & vir seu Mas ille Homo iam conditus. Eam igitur condidit Deus, vt futuram Maris seu Viri Hominis sociam, & auxilium ad prolem suscipiendam aptum. Itaque ex latere seu costa Adami eam compegit ac fecit. Adamum autem, ne quem dolorem propter istam costæ detractionem sentiret, magno sopore Deus affecit, atq; consopiuit interea dum ei costam detrahit, eiusque locū postea carne replet, ac reficit. Genef. 1. 27. & 2. 21. 1. Timoth. 2. 13.
units.tr: God created the woman, or female human being, in the earthly paradise after all other creatures. He made her from one of Adam's ribs, and called her in Hebrew [אִשָּׁה], a name derived from [אִישׁ] (which means man or male). So Ishah is "woman," so called by God, so that her origin would be recalled by the very name. This same one was afterwards called [Eve]. God created the female human being because among all the animals he had made he found none that was equal, suitable, and fitting for Adam, who was made in God's own image, and who would be a help to him: that is, one with whom Adam could have companionship and conversation, to share with him about the worship of God and the command given to him, and with whom he could discuss and consider the nature of things to the glory of God; and finally, from whom Adam might have offspring like himself. Therefore Ishah, that is Woman, was also made in the image of God, just as Adam was, so that she might share in and be capable of the knowledge of God, his worship, and the happiness and dominion on this earth, as Adam was. She had the same disposition, nature, speech, reason, and power of reasoning as the man, or male human being, who had already been made. God therefore made her as the future companion of the male human being, and as a help suited to bearing offspring. So he fashioned and made her from Adam's side or rib. But lest Adam feel any pain from the removal of the rib, God put him into a deep sleep and lulled him while He took the rib away, and afterwards filled and restored its place with flesh. Gen. 1. 27. & 2. 21. 1 Tim. 2. 13.

units.la: VII. Matrimonij Institutio.
units.tr: VII. The Institution of Marriage.

units.la: Matrimonium ex quo propagatio generis humani, id est, Imaginis Dei in hac terris fieret, Deus ipse instituit inter duos tantum nempe Adamum, & Ischam, (quæ eadem Eua est) inter vtrumq; videlicet ad Dei Imaginem à se conditum, è quibus vnus esset Mas: Altera verò Fœmina. Quamobrem neque inter Hominem & Brutum Animal: neque inter duos Homines vtrumq; Marem, vel vtrumque Fœminam: neque inter plures, quàm duos & quidem Vnum Marem, & Alteram Fœminam: neque denique inter alios, quàm quos Deus coniunxit, matrimonium, aut propagatio generis humani, aut denique legitimus homini coitus esse potest. Gen. 1. 27. & 2. 22. Malach. 2. 15. 1. Cor. 7. 2. 3. 4 Coitum quidem esse inter Bruta Animantia iam præceperat, instituerat q; Deus die etiam quinta, videlicet ad speciei cuiusq; Animalis conseruationem, eique benedixerat. Genes. 1. 20. Verum Hominis ad suam Imaginem cōditi Deus sanctiorem, augustiorem, & aliam, quàm simplicis coitus naturalis (qualis est inter brutas pecudes) originem esse voluit. Itaque ad genus humanum conseruandum, præter coitum naturalem, Matrimonium quoque intercedere Deus voluit. Nam Mulierem à se ex ⟨Adami costa creatam Deus ipsemet ad ⟨Adamum confestim adduxit, illiq́ue eam in vxorem, & vnicum auxilium dedit Hominum ad Dei Imaginem eandem (ad quam ipse vterque Homo conditus iam erat) postea gignendorum (id est ad humani generis propagationem) Ergo ⟨Adamo eam tradidit in manum. Ergo vtrosque illos inter se ipsemet Deus coniunxit. Inde Coniugium, eiusque sanctissimū, atque arctissimum vinculum Adamo, Eua, & posteris eius institutum est, cuius Deus autor fuit, & conciliator primus, Gen. 2. 22. 23. Prov. 2. 17. Matt. 19. 8. Vnde qui vxorem nanciscitur, dicitur à Deo bonum accepisse. Pro.18.22. Huic autem coniugio & copu-la Maris & Fœminæ Hominis à se factâ Deus postea peculiarem benedictionem addidit, summum animorū affectum insecit, denique & perpetuam firmissimámq; societatem, adeo vt Coniux Patri & Matri præferri à coniuge debeat, & vtrŏque parens propter coniugem à coniuge deseri. Gen.1.28. & 2.23.24. Psal 45. Matth.19.5. Quod Vinculum, & quæ societas & benedictio etiamnum post peccatum postea permansit, ac permanet quoque hodie. Math.19.6. Rom.7. 1. 1.Corinth.7.11.
units.tr: God himself instituted marriage, so that the human race, that is, the image of God on this earth, might be propagated, between two only, namely Adam and Ischa (who is the same as Eve), that is, between the two whom he had created in his own image, of whom one was the male and the other the female. For this reason, marriage, or the propagation of the human race, or indeed any lawful intercourse for man, cannot exist between a man and a beast; nor between two men, or two women; nor between more than two, and indeed not between anyone other than one male and one female; nor finally between anyone other than those whom God has joined. Gen. 1. 27. and 2. 22. Malach. 2. 15. 1. Cor. 7. 2, 3, 4. Intercourse among the brute animals God had already ordained and instituted on the fifth day as well, namely for the preservation of each kind of animal, and he had blessed them for it. Gen. 1. 20. But God willed that the origin of man, who was made in his own image, should be holier, more august, and different from simple natural intercourse (such as that among the brute beasts). So, for preserving the human race, God willed that marriage should also come between, besides natural intercourse. For God himself brought the woman, created by him from the rib of Adam, straight to Adam, and gave her to him as wife and as the only help of men, to bear children (that is, for the propagation of the human race) in the same image of God in which both humans had already been created. Therefore he handed her over to Adam into his hand. Therefore God himself joined those two together. From this came marriage, and its most holy and most close bond, instituted for Adam, Eve, and their posterity, of which God was the author and first matchmaker. Gen. 2. 22, 23. Prov. 2. 17. Matt. 19. 8. Hence he who obtains a wife is said to have received a good thing from God. Prov. 18. 22. To this marriage and union of the male and female whom he had made, God afterwards added a special blessing, implanted the highest affection of minds, and finally a perpetual and most firm partnership, so much so that a wife ought to be preferred by her husband to father and mother, and the husband, for the sake of his wife, ought to leave each parent. Gen. 1. 28. and 2. 23, 24. Psal. 45. Matt. 19. 5. This bond, and this partnership and blessing, has remained even after sin, and remains today also. Matt. 19. 6. Rom. 7. 1. 1 Cor. 7. 11.

units.la: VIII. Status Hominis Vtriusque, id est Viri, & Mulieris in paradiso Edenico.
units.tr: VIII. The State of Each Human, that is of Man and Woman, in the Garden of Eden.

units.la: Statu autem vtriusque Hominis Primi, id est, Adami maris, & sscha (quæ eadem postea Eua est) fœmina in summa hic erat, quod vterque Dei veram, plenissimamque Imaginem (quanta natura humana Animalis & in his terris versans habere potuit) nastus erat. Erat autem sœlicissimus, ac perfectissimus hic status. Nihil enim sœlicius, ac perfectius Deo, Deiquê imagine esse potest. Etsi vero Dei imago in hominis anima præprie, verèque scita erat: cotinebat tamen hæc sœlicitas quattuor hæc Dei dona præcipua, Nempe, 1. Mentis seu Intelligentiæ humanæ perspicacitatem & cognitionem ex connatis ingenitisque notitiis rerum tum Diuinarum, velut Dei ipsius (quis & qualis esset, Viuum videlicet, immortalis, spiritus) & rerum ad Deum colendum necessariarū: tum etiā terrenarum rerū velut natura proprietatisq; rerum omnium in hoc visibili mūdo creatarū. 2. Habebat cordis seu voluntatis humane puritatē & rectitudinem. 3. Corporis copositiqué ipsius totius summā pulchritudinē, ac immortalitatē. 4. Dignitatem ac dominatum in omnia hæc visibilia à Deo condita. Erat igitur vterq; homo mente perspicax, corde purus, corpore immortalis, dignitate dominus. Omnia enim Homini Deus subiecerat: Hominem sibi duntaxat: vt esset Homo quidē totius huius Mundi Dominus vtilis, qui vocatur: Deus autem ipse eiusdem Mundi Dominus directus. Denique Deus ad se colendum dederat Homini & Legem, & sacramenta duo, nempe duas illas, quas diximus, Arbores: Legem autem hanc, nimirum vt sua sorte contentus Homo earum arborum altera abstineret, Gen. 1. 27. 29. & 2. 17. & 3. 3. & 5. 3. Quaue donis & Spiritualibus, & corporeis (quantum eius felicitas in his terris postulabat) praditus erat Homo vterque à Deo, quibus ysdem donis posteri quoque eorum postea donandi omnes erant, & haredes futuri.
units.tr: The state of each first human, that is, of Adam the male and Ischa (who is afterwards also Eve) the female, was here at its highest, in that each had been born with the true and most complete image of God (as far as human nature, an animal dwelling on this earth, could have). It was the most happy and most perfect state. For nothing can be happier or more perfect than God and the image of God. Although indeed the image of God was situated in the human soul properly and truly, this happiness still contained these four chief gifts of God: namely, 1. The keenness and knowledge of the human mind or understanding, drawn from innate and inborn notions both of divine things, such as God himself (who and what kind he is: living, immortal, spirit), and of the things necessary for worshipping God; and also of earthly things, such as the nature and properties of all things created in this visible world. 2. It had the purity and uprightness of the human heart or will. 3. The highest beauty and immortality of its body and its whole make-up. 4. Dignity and dominion over all these visible things created by God. Each man was therefore keen of mind, pure of heart, immortal in body, and lord in dignity. For God had subjected all things to man, and to man alone, so that man might be, indeed, the useful lord of the whole world, as it is called, while God himself was the direct lord of the same world. Finally, for worshipping himself, God had given to man both a law and two sacraments, namely those two trees we have mentioned; and this law was that man, content with his lot, should abstain from one of those trees. Gen. 1. 27, 29; 2. 17; 3. 3; 5. 3. Each of the two humans had been endowed by God with both spiritual and bodily gifts (as far as their happiness in this earth required), and their posterity too were all to be given these same gifts and to be heirs of them.

units.la: CAPVT II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: Disputata, & agitata quedam in his singulis capitibus octo.
units.tr: Several matters were disputed and discussed under each of these eight headings.

units.la: Multa
units.tr: Many

units.la: VLTA vero quærunt Scholastici in prima Mundi huius (quem conspicimus) historia, quæ apud eos extant tum in Lombardi lib. 2. Sentent. tum apud Thomam in Prima parte prima Summæ diftinct. 65, & fequentibus. Multa Philosophi & Platonici, & Ariftotelici, vt alios omittam. Nos vero neq; omnes eorum quæstiones (quæ da enim sunt prorsus inepte) persequemur neque etiam nullas. Ergo quæ præcipuæ, maximeque vtiles visæ sunt nobis, hæ sunt, & quidem in primo capite, quod est de Creatione Mundi, in qua quæritur:
units.tr: The Scholastics ask many questions about the first history of this world (the one we see). They are found in Lombard's Sentences, book 2, and in Thomas Aquinas, Summa, part 1, question 65 and following. The philosophers, both Platonists and Aristotelians, also raise many, to leave others aside. We, however, will pursue neither all of their questions (many of which are quite foolish) nor none. Those we have judged most important and most useful are these, in the first chapter, which is on the creation of the world. The question is:

units.la: Ad I. De Creatione Mundi.
units.tr: To I. On the Creation of the World.

units.la: Vtrum Cœli primo die conditi nomine Angelica natura contineatur. Visibilium enim & invisibilium Creator est unus Deus, Col. 1. 16. Quid fit, fuerit ve Mosi propositum ἐξ ἀπ tantum in hac historia defcribere, & conspicuum hunc Mundum nobis notum, in quo velut Dominus collocatus est Adamus, proponere Gen. 1. 13. de Angelis, eorumque creatione nequaquam agit in toto hoc capite vel libro Mosis. Vtrum omnia Dei opera uno duntaxat die condita sint re ipsa, vt putat Augustinus lib. 4. cap. 34. de Genesi ad literam, & lib. 15. de Ciuit. Dei: Ecclesiastici 16. 26, & 27: quæ diuersis tamen diebus innotuerint, & à Deo postea patefacta sint: an sex diebus omnia nempe singula, quæ admodum à Mose narrantur, suo die. Quum nihil fit allegoricum in hac Mundi conspicui creatione prima: sed naturaliter sint accipienda illa omnia, tanquam ab historico, quæ Moses in hac descriptione tradit, singula suis queque & diuersis diebus creata sunt, non autem simul omnia. Q. Vtrum primum cœlu, id est, primo die creatum sit illud ipsum, quod postea fuit ornatum à Deo stellis videlicet, quum Solem, & Lunam, & astra Deus condidit, Psal.19. R. Cœlum illud primum tanquam cortina quædam à Deo hominum oculis duntaxat obiectum est. facliunque ut curiositatem & visum eorum terminaret, Psal. 104.2. Itaque de eius Cœli ornatu nihil postea scribit Moses. Solem autem, Lunam, & stellas collocauit Deus in expansione, quæ infra illud primum Cœlum est usque ad aquas protensa. Ergo stellæ sunt expansionis illius ornatu, non supremi & primum conditi Cœli. Sol tamen, Luna, & Stellæ in ista Expansione sitæ dicuntur esse in cœlo, quoniam hæc ipsa Expansio Cœlum quoque nominatur. Sed primum illud Cœlum dicitur Cœlum cœlorum, Psal.115.16, & 148 4. Id quod etiam in extremo Dei iudicio concutietur, & cum Stridore prætheribit, ac renouabitur, vti & terra ipsa, & reliqua elementa, Luc.21.26, 2.Pet.3.10. Q. Quotuplex sit genus Aquarum illarum, quas expansio à se ipsis diuidit, & vtrum supra totam Expansionem sint Aquæ aliquæ. R. Diuidit quidem Expansio aquas cælestes (quas aereas vocant ex quibus sunt, fiuntque nubes, pluuia, tonitrua, grandines, ros, &c. huiusmodi, Pf. 147.8, & 148.4) a terrenis & marinis, quæ cum globo & corpore terra comprehenduntur, ac simul coniunguntur non tamen tota expansio intra vtrasque illas aquas comprehenditur, ac concluditur, vt nulla supra aëreas aquas sit & resset illius Expansionis pars & portio. Est enim illius expansionis supra aquas etiam cœlestes & aëreas partes aliqua,nimirum ea, ex qua Sol, Luna,& Stella extiterunt & in qua collocata fuerunt. Ex quo fit vt illius Expansionis longitudo & spatium totum etiam aquas cœlestes superet,sitque etiam supra eas expansum Gen 1.6.15. Expansio ergo continet interuallum aquas inter se separâs,& præterea illud spatium,in quo Stellæ,ac Planetæ mouentur, vel harent, certè collocantur.
units.tr: Whether the heavens created on the first day are included under the name of angelic nature. For the Creator of things visible and invisible is one God (Col. 1.16). Whether Moses intended, in this history, only to describe from the beginning [ἐξ ἀπ] and to set out this visible world known to us, in which Adam was placed as lord (Gen. 1.13), he does not deal at all with angels or their creation in this whole chapter or book of Moses. Whether all of God's works were created in fact on one day only, as Augustine thinks (De Genesi ad literam, bk 4, ch. 34; De Civitate Dei, bk 15; Ecclesiasticus 16.26–27), though they were made known on different days and afterwards revealed by God; or whether each of the things Moses narrates was created on its own day, six days in all. Since nothing in this first creation of the visible world is allegorical, but everything Moses relates in this description must be taken naturally, as a historian would take it, each thing was created on its own separate day, not all at once. Q. Whether the first heaven, that is, the heaven created on the first day, is the very one afterwards adorned by God with stars, when God made the sun, moon and stars (Ps. 19). A. That first heaven was set before men's eyes only like a curtain, and was made to bound their curiosity and sight (Ps. 104.2). So Moses writes nothing afterwards about the adornment of that heaven. God placed the sun, moon and stars in the expanse, which extends below that first heaven as far as the waters. The stars are therefore the ornament of that expanse, not of the highest, first-created heaven. Yet the sun, moon and stars set in this expanse are said to be in heaven, because this same expanse is also called heaven. But that first heaven is called the heaven of heavens (Ps. 115.16; 148.4). It will also be shaken at God's final judgement, and will pass away with a roar and be renewed, as will the earth itself and the other elements (Luke 21.26; 2 Pet. 3.10). Q. How many kinds of those waters are there, which the expanse separates from themselves, and whether there are any waters above the whole expanse. A. The expanse indeed divides the heavenly waters (which they call aerial, and from which clouds, rain, thunder, hail, dew and the like are made and come into being, Ps. 147.8; 148.4) from the earthly and marine waters, which are contained together with the globe and body of the earth. Yet the whole expanse is not contained and enclosed within those two kinds of water, so that no part or portion of that expanse lies above the aerial waters. For there is some part of that expanse above even the heavenly and aerial waters, namely that from which the sun, moon and stars arose and in which they were placed. Hence it follows that the length and entire extent of that expanse exceeds even the heavenly waters, and that it is stretched out above them (Gen. 1.6, 15). The expanse therefore contains the interval separating the waters from one another, and besides that the space in which the stars and planets move or are fixed.

units.la: Ad III. De Edene Regione.
units.tr: Ad III. Concerning the Region of Eden.

units.la: Quaritur Edene illa regio vbi fuerit,in cuius parte vna terrestris Hortus erat.Nec enim tota illa regio erat Hortus ille amœnissimus. Fuisse eam regionem sitam ad Orientem Mosi tunc in deserto Arabico scribenti versantiq. Huius autem regionis non simel sit mentio in Dei verbo,sed septim,vti 2.Reg.19.11, Isa.37.12, Ezech.27.11,12, vbi Eden & Carra ciuitas coniunguntur. Item Amosi 1 3 illa regio commemoratur, & nota fuit non tantum sacris Scriptoribus: verumetiam & prophanis,atque etiam aliis. Aethicus eam inter nobiles (quas famosas vocat) Orientis prouinciâ collocat & recenset,vbi Adonis pro Edonis, vitio librariorum scriptum est, quemadmodum rectè obseruauit Josias Simlerus vir eruditissimus. Stephanus in libro de Vrbib.Edana vrbis meminit (quæ ad Euphratem sita esset.) Hanc ex Edenis regionis nomine velut insignes fuisse reliquias quis dubitet, & idcirco sic appellatam? Apparet autem eam maioris Armeniæ pronunciam vel partem fuisse, & totam Mefopotamiam comprehendisse. Patuit usque ad Damascenam regionem, Amosi 1.5, Plinius lib.6.Histor.natur.cap.9. Armenia Maior Tigrim & Euphratem fluvios fundit, & initium Mesopotamia per duos amnes iturat facit. Hos autem eosdem fluvios tribuit hic Moses Edeni regioni. Mesopotamia vero etiam Armenia maiori tribuitur, olim autem Assyria, confusis & mutatis postea regionum illarum nominibus, uti & nunc. Nam illarum appellationum vestigia iam nulla extant.
units.tr: The question is where that region of Eden was, in one part of which the earthly Garden lay. For that whole region was not the most pleasant Garden itself. That region lay to the East, as Moses was writing in the Arabian desert where he then dwelt. Now mention of this region is made not just once in God's word but seven times, as in 2 Kings 19:11, Isa. 37:12, and Ezek. 27:11,12, where Eden and the city Carra are joined together. Likewise that region is recorded in Amos 1:3, and it was known not only to the sacred writers but also to profane writers and to others. Aethicus places it among the noble provinces of the East (which he calls famous) and lists it there, where "Adonis" has been written for "Edonis" through a copyist's error, as the very learned Josias Simlerus rightly observed. Stephanus, in his book on cities, mentions the city Edana, which was situated on the Euphrates. Who would doubt that this name is a notable remnant of the region of Eden, and so was named after it? It appears, moreover, that this was a province or part of Greater Armenia, and that it took in all of Mesopotamia. It extended as far as the region of Damascus (Amos 1:5); Pliny, Natural History, book 6, chapter 9: Greater Armenia pours forth the rivers Tigris and Euphrates, and by means of these two streams makes the beginning of Mesopotamia. Moses here assigns these same rivers to the region of Eden. Mesopotamia, however, is also assigned to Greater Armenia, while formerly it was Assyria; the names of those regions were confused and changed afterwards, as they are now too. For no traces of those former appellations survive at all.

units.la: Q. Quae sit regio Heuila, quam universam fluminen Pischon ex Edene regione, non autem ex Horto nascens, alluit, uti & Hortum ipsum Gen.2.10.11. Quid regio Chuz, quam Gichon fluvius (qui est fluvius ex Edene nascentis diurtius, & alueus seu rivus) alluit post irrigatum Hortum hunc terrestrem. Quid denique, & ubi Paradisus, in quo collocatus a Deo fuerat Adamus primus homo.
units.tr: Q. What is the region of Havilah, which the river Pishon, rising from the region of Eden and not from the Garden itself, winds through in its entirety, as in Gen. 2:10,11? What is the region of Cush, which the river Gihon waters after it has irrigated this earthly Garden (the Gihon being a branch or channel of the river rising from Eden)? And finally, what and where is the Paradise in which God placed Adam, the first man?

units.la: R. Primum observandum est quatuor illa flumina, quae recenseт Moses, fuisse unius & eiusdem, sive aquae, sive fluvii ex Edene regione nascentis diurtia seu brachia, quae diversa quoque nomina sortita sunt, quemadmodum apparet. Ex his enim unum Euphrates: alterum Chiddeket sive Tigris: tertium Geon: quartum Pischon nominatur. Orsus est autem Moses in istis quatuor brachiis eiusdem fluvii recensendis ordine retrogrado, non a capite fluvii istius vel vicinioribus capiti brachys, & diuortys: sed ab ys, quae remotiora erant, & vicinora tunc Mosi ista scribenti, & populo Israelitico, cui scribebat. Ergo facit Tigrim tertium brachium, & Euphratem quartum: qui tamen vterq; fluvius est fonti originis fluvii istius, a quo
units.tr: A. First it must be observed that the four rivers which Moses lists were of one and the same river: branches or arms of one river or stream rising in the region of Eden, which also received different names, as is evident. For of these, one is called Euphrates, another Hiddekel [חִדֶּקֶל] or Tigris, a third Gihon, and a fourth Pishon. Moses began his enumeration of these four arms of the same river in reverse order: not from the source of that river or from the arms and branches nearest its source, but from those that were more remote and nearer to Moses as he wrote, and to the Israelite people to whom he was writing. Therefore he makes the Tigris the third arm and the Euphrates the fourth; yet both of these rivers are from the source of that same river, from which…

units.la: Ex hac parte quatuor fluminum, unde scriptis cubi Heuila, Chuz etc. à quo deducûtur proximior. Fons autem, & ex eo fluuius emanàs in Edene regione (antequam se in dinortia illa quattuor diduceret) irrigabat, & quidē totum adhuc, & nondū diuisus in brachia, Hortum terrestrem: postquam autem totum illum Hortum irrigauerat, tunc se infra Hortum in quattuor illa flumina diuidebat. Ergo nequaquam Hortus ille extendendus est vsque ad ea terrarum loca, in quae illa quattuor flumina, seu dinortia feruntur, & labuntur. (nec enim Hortus terrestris terram Chuz, vel regionem Heuila complectebatur, vel tam late ex ea parte patebat, sed iam supra eum locum, id est ante vnius illius fluuij seu Aquae diductionem seu dinortia in illa regione Edene finiebatur) imò ne ipsa quidem Edene regio patebat in longitudinem tantum quantum cursus quattuor illorum fluminum, ex vno illo Paradisi fluuio derivatorū, & fluctuum. Cur igitur dicet quispiam, horum quattuor fluminum facta est à Mose mentio? Nimirum, vt intelligeretur quàm esset abundàs aquę, & copiosus vnus ille Paradisi terrestris fluuius, ex quo tot tamq; opulenta illa quattuor flumina posteà oriebantur, & fluebant, velut riui. (nec enim in toto terrarum orbe his quatuor maiora flumina sunt) ac proinde facile vel vnum illorum fluminum potuisse aqua sua elicibus ductis, & ab Adamo factis, totum illum Hortum terrestrem irrigare: Nomina autem & fluminum illorum, & quarundam regionum, quas illa alluunt, addita sunt à Mose, vt huic Historiæ tam antiquae fidem faceret, ac auctoritatem conciliaret, ne fabula quaedam esse censeretur. Secundo loco notandum est, Euphraten flumen, item & Tigrim varia nomina etiam eodem tempore apud diuersos populos sortitum esse. Nam qui hic à Mose dicitur Euphrates, idem ab aliys populis & Auxim, & Pixirates, & Oºnirra, & Aramalcha i. flumen regiũ distum est olim, uti docet Plinius lib. Hist. Natur cap. 26. Ammianus Marcell. libr. 23. Histor. [Et Marsias, ait, & Regium flumen Euphrates cunctis excellens.] Tigris etiam Pasitigris vocatus est, quem admodum Strabo lib. 15. & Plinius lib. 6. cap. 27. tradunt: & Basilius, ut idem Strabo scribit lib. 16. Sed & Pallacopa quoque nominatus, quemadmodum apparet ex Arriani libro de Expeditione Alexandri, lib. 7. Solinus cap. 40: [Primum, ait, pigre fluit Tigris, non cum suo nomine: at quũ fines Medorum inuectus est. Tigris dicitur.] Denique meminisse oportet tertio loco flumen Euphratem, item & Tigrim, & a diuersis Regibus. & diuersis in locis & temporibus, in alueos plures derivatum deductúmque fuisse: eorúmque alueorum inter se commissuras, seu confluenta varie dissecta à varijs, seu dirupta, ac diductá: denique oppleta, vastata, & immutata nomina alueorũ ipsorum varie, ut iam sit propterea vel difficile, vel valde nobis ignotum id, quod hic scribit Moses: erat autem illo seculo notissimum. Certè Herodotus lib. 5. scribit vel unum Gyndem (qui in iis locis est) in 360 alueos fuisse diductum. Plinius lib 6 Hist. Natur. cap. 20. ait, Euphratem diuisum sub Assyrijs à Semiramide, quod commemorat Pomponius Mela lib. 1. cap. 11: item à quodam Satrapa Babyloniorum in plures partes, ne infestaret Babyloniam: postea à Nicatore: ab Orchenis quoque, dum agros suos irrigant, vt ibidem Plinius cap 27. tradit: atque etiam scribit Arrianus libr 7 de Exped. Alexand. Babylonios deduxisse & deriuasse saepe diuersis temporibus Euphratem magnis fossis, magnoque labore in Pallacopam flumen. Denique & Traianus quoque fossas nouas parauit ad commutandum Euphratem pluribus in locis cum Tigre, vt tradit in eius vita Dion Historicus. Vide Ammianum Marcellin lib. 23 Hist. Quibus expositis, vt viam futuræ expositioni praemuniamus, probemusque istius rei explicationem esse perdifficilem, dicimus regionem Heuilam, quæ Pischone si imine infra Paradisum seu Hortum terrestrem alluitur, esse eam, quam Tigris (quum Pasitigris vocatur) alluit, & ambit ex vno latere, quæ Parapotamia quoque vocatur à Plinio lib. 6 cap 27. Hæc regio vicina est ad Meridiē Susiana prouincia, vt tradit Strabo lib 15. & Persidę inferior, & ad Mare seu Sinum Persicum pertingit. Ergo nobis est trans Tigrim Heuila. Hæc etiā & Palmetis, & oliua, pomisque, & arbustis nobilis est, vt ait idem ibidem Plinius. Imo Solinus cap. 40 scribit miram & ingentem esse in iis regionibus, quas ad Sinum Persicum Tigris (qui in Sinum Persicum defert Euphratem) alluit, & gemmarum & pretiosorum omnis generis lapidum vim, & copiam. In Sinu autem Persico, vicinisque illi regionibus & affusis, esse nascig̃ Aurum quoque optimum & experientia nauigatiog̃ Lusitanorum docet, & historia cuiusuis aetatis imo sibi etiā copiosissimum, & abundantissimum Aurum est: ibidem quoque & Vniones, & Gemmæ. & Bdellium: id quod de terra Heuila testatur quoq; Mosis. Quamobrem ista omnia propterea à vicinis illis regioni populis spernuntur,ut ait Plinius lib.6.cap 27, Aurum nempe & Gemmæ,propter copiam: quæ tamen duo reliquæ Orbis gentes plurimi faciunt. Idem de iis regionibus scribit Tertullianus in lib.de Cultu Mulierum. Ex iis enim Legati suo tempore ad Severum Imperatorem Romā venerant. Quæ omnia cum ipsa Mosis Historia, & Heuila terræ laude, & descriptione hic facta consentiunt. D. Stukhius amicus meus quedam in suis commentarijs in Periplum maris Erythrei de Heuila tradit: sed non tam ex sua quàm aliorum sententia. Heuila igitur est regio illa, quam Pasitigris alluit, nobis Trasti-gritana, a cuius finibus vsque ad Sur desertum Ægypto vicinum soboles Ismaelis (qui fuit filius Abrahami ex Agara ancilla) & posteritas habitauit postea per duodecim diuersa regna, familiasque latissimè divisa. Igitur posteritas Ismaelis eam incoluit, fratribus suis nimirum Israëlitis pene vndique oppositá. Ille enim latissimus terra tractus proximè & collimitaneè totum terræ promissæ Orientale Meridianum, & Occidētale latus claudit, adeò vt qui ex terra promissa exit ex iis tribus partibus, statim in terram Ismaelitarum ingrediatur. Atque ea est via, qua itur in Assyriam ex Ægypto per Sur desertum (quod, vt dixi, Ægypto, Marique rubro proximum est Exo.15.23,&17 8 Eius autem deserti Metropolis fuit Hagra, sita ad sinum Elaniticum, vt ait Plinius lib.6.cap.29:) ea, inquam, est via, qua itur ex Ægypto in Assyriam, nempe tractus ille totus quem Ismaelitæ occuparunt à Sur ad Heuila, nempe claudentes à latere trino Israëlitas suos fra. fratres. Hinc ÿdem Ifmaelitæ dicuntur habitasse coram fratribus suis videlicet Israelitis, quod eis ex Oriente, Meridie, & Occidente obiecti ac oppositi essent ratione regionis quam incoluerunt. Id quod apparet ex istis S. Scripturæ locis, Gen.16.7,& 21.21,& 25 18, 1.Sam.15. Hac igitur regio Heuila erat Orientalis Mosi. Etsi vero in Saba regione aurum est copiosum,ut est 1.Reg.10.11 :gemmæque plures reperiuntur, 2.Chron.9.9: optimum tamen aurum,optimæque gemmæ sunt ex ista Heuila, regione latissima, quæ ad Persicum vsque Sinum pertinet,& pertingit,claudit q; Ismaelitas ab Oriente, & quam Pischon qui & Pasitigris,alluit,vt dixi. Iam de regione Chuz,& Geone flumine dicamus. Chuz regio proculdubio à Chuzo filio Chami (qui fuit filius Noachi) dicta est,continet q; totum eum Syriæ tractum, quem Chuzi stirpi posteritas occupauit. Illa vero exteditur à flumine Euphrate ac Babylonia ad Meridiem,sub vel intra Ismaelitarũ regionem vsque ad Ægyptum ipsum seu Sinum Arabicum,qui & Mare Rubrum vocatur. Ergo regio Chuz fuit inferior quam Heuila, & toti Mari Meridionali vicinior ad Meridiem Mosi, seu Iudæa sita. Totus hic tractus terra Arabia postea dicta est, quæ & ipsa triplex constituta est,& distinctla,nimirū Deserta,Petræa,& Felix. Eadem & Æthiopia quoque cognominata ab incolarum nigro colore. Ergo hæc Æthiopia (quæ Chuz dicitur) est ea Æthiopia, quæ est Syris citra Ægyptum,& Mare Rubrum:non autem ea,quæ ÿsdem est trás Ægyptum in media Africa ad montes Abyssenos sita. Sed & duplicem quoq; Æthiopiam agnouit Homerus in Iliade vetus imprimis scriptor. Hoc verum esse, & eam regionem quae Chuz vocatur, esse eam Aethiopiam, quae Syris est cis Mare Rubrum probant hi S. Scripturae loci, Genes. 10.6,7, Exo. 2. 22, Num. 12, 2 Chron. 14 & 21 6, Hiere. 25 24 vbi ab Hieremia Arabes appellatur, qui Chuz dicuntur ab Ezechiele 30 9.
