Hic docet & persequitur late copiosèque primus Matthaeus Beroaldus tum lib 2. Chron. cap. ultimo, tum lib. 4. cap 6, & duplicem illam Aethiopiam distinxit: quaquam Flavius Iosephus Arabas & Aethiopas communi nomine Chuz dici generaliter scripserat, sed confuse. Confirmatur autem Beroaldi (ex quo postea certatim omnes mutuati sunt) sententia ex Plinij lib 5. Natur. Hist. cap. 11. & 12, Strabonis lib. 15. & 16, vbi agit de Syria traction Babylonys & Aegyptys vicino. Solini cap. 40 & Aethici libello, vbi hic Oceani Orientalis flumina recensens, Tigrim describit. Ergo latissima fuit Chuzeorum sedium regio, & terra hac, quae Chuz proprie dicta est: ac, vti dixi, eadem fuit magis, quam regio Ismaelitarum, Mosi Meridionalis (quanquam Ismaelitae saepe generaliter Arabum quoque nomine comprehenduntur) & Aegypto propinquior, tres illas Arabiae nempe continens supra a nobis commemoratas. Verum haec regio Chuz neque in Edene regione fuit, sed extra Edenem: neque Horti terrestris pars, sicut nec Hauila: sed fuit Syriae portio maxima ad Mare Rubrum, & Meridionale (quod Sinum Arabicum & Persicum interiacet) pertinens. Hac eadem toto latere vno nempe Orientali, a flumine Geone alluitur, vt hic tradit Mosis Moses Gen. 2. Alii asunt ab Euphratis brachio, alij Tigris. Nam Euphratem (postquam in Tigrim incidit confluxitque) suum nomen amittere, & in sinum Persicum à Tigri deferri Plinius, & ex eo Solinus in Polyhistore scribunt. Ergo verba hac Moses, Gen. 2. 13, [Nomen verò secundi Gichon is est, qui alluit vniuersam regionē Chuz] non sic accipiē, vt Gichon vel Geon ille omni ex parte & latere terram Chuzaorum circumplectatur & ambiat: sed vt ex vno duntaxat latere, nimirū Orientali ea alluat: quemadmodū flumen Pischō ex latere & plaga Occidentali duntaxat alluit & circundat terrā Heuila. Quamobrem istorū diuortiorū seu fluminum duorū ex eodē illo & vno fluuio (qui ex Edene regione nascebatur, & Hortum totum alluebat) defluentium ac dimanantium vnum, Arabas: alterum, terram Heuila perluebat. Ex quo iam apparet quod sit diuortium illud seu flumen, quod Gichon, vel Geon appellatur. Est autem pars & brachium totius illius aquæ (quæ ex Euphrate & Tigre iam commixtis inter se, & confluentibus in Abiadene regione, vti docet Ammianus Marcellinus lib. 23. Historia, conflatur, & sic coniuncta labitur) quod brachium ex duobus illis vicinius est nobis, & tamen à nonnullis etiam Euphrates ex ea parte dicitur: vti eiusdem aquæ brachium alterū quod est Orientale, id est magis vicinum India, nominatur quoque à nostris (qui nomina istorum diuortiorum propria ignorant) Tigris, qui Hanilam alluit. Ergo Euphrates Arabiam seu Chuzam regionem totā ex parte, quæ Mosi fuit Orientalis, claudit, alluitque. Plinius lib. 6. cap. 26. ait, [Ambitu vero Euphratis Nomades Arabia vsque ad deserta Syria compreheduntur: unde in Meridiem flecti eum dicimus, solitudines Palmyrenas relinquentem ]Hoc Arrianus lib. 7.expeditionis Alexandri probat. Strabo lib 15. videtur etiam eum fluvium quem alij Euphratem, vti dixi, Moses autem Geon nominat, Tigrim appellasse. Sic & Aethicus in descriptione Tigris fluminis: Eum enim ait per Aethiopiā id est Chuzæam regionem perlabi. Quin idem quoque Strabo refert quosdam existimasse omnia Syriæ flumina per meatus subterraneos ex lacubus Euphratis & Tigris profluere. Certe quum hæc duo eiusdem fluvij, & eiusdem aquæ brachia tàm diuersa situ, & regione fuerint, rectè Moses virique suum nomen & proprium seorsim tribuit, quale tunc fuit: male vero profani scriptores vtrumque illud brachium confuse sæpe vno & eodem vt diximus nomine appellant. Verùm Dionysius Alexandrinus docet incertum esse quo nomine illa brachia sint vocanda. Herodotus libr. 5. videtur Gyndem nominasse hoc ipsum flumen, quod Geon vocat hic Moses. Accedit enim Herodotus ad Mosem, vel ipso vocis sono. Marcellinus meminit etiam istius Gyndis fluminis. Porro Geon flumen & in Gallia quoque quoddam esse annotat Aethicus: & plerique Nilum vocant Geon. Est & Geon rivus seu fluviolus in Iudæa Hierosolymam illabens, qui & Siloë dicitur, vt nonnulli volunt ex 1.Reg.2.33. 2.Chron.32.30: de quo Geone scribit Epiphanius in epist. ad Ioannem Hierosolymitanum Episcopum se ex eo gustasse quum Hierosolymis esset. Sed hic Geon ad hunc locum non pertinet. Et hæc quidem est mea de istiu
units.tr: From this part of the four rivers, whence (as written) the land of Havilah, Cush, etc. are derived, the nearer one... The spring, however, and the river flowing from it in the region of Eden (before it divided into those four branches), watered the whole Garden of Earth while it had not yet been divided into branches. After it had watered that whole Garden, it then split below the Garden into those four rivers. Therefore that Garden must by no means be extended as far as the regions of the earth into which those four rivers, or branches, flow and fall. (For the earthly Garden did not embrace the land of Cush or the region of Havilah, nor did it extend so far on that side; rather, above that place, that is, before the river was divided into its branches, it was bounded within the region of Eden.) Indeed, not even the region of Eden extended in length as far as the course of those four rivers, which were derived and flowed from that single river of Paradise. Why, then, will someone ask, did Moses mention these four rivers? Surely so that it might be understood how abundant and copious was that one river of the earthly Paradise, from which those four great and rich rivers afterwards arose and flowed, like streams. (For in the whole world there are no rivers larger than these four.) Accordingly, even one of those rivers could easily have watered the whole earthly Garden, with its water drawn off by channels made by Adam. Moses added the names both of those rivers and of certain regions which they wash, so as to give credibility and authority to this very ancient history, lest it be thought to be some fable. In the second place, it must be noted that the Euphrates and likewise the Tigris received various names at the same time from different peoples. For what Moses here calls the Euphrates was also called, by other peoples, Auxis, Pixirates, Oninra, and Aramalcha, that is, "the royal river," as Pliny teaches in book 6 of his Natural History, chapter 26. Ammianus Marcellinus, book 23 of his Histories, says: [And the Marsyas, and the Euphrates, the royal river, surpassing all.] The Tigris too was called Pasitigris, as Strabo, book 15, and Pliny, book 6, chapter 27, relate; and Basilius (as Strabo also writes, book 16). But it was also called Pallacopas, as appears from Arrian's book on the expedition of Alexander, book 7. Solinus, chapter 40: [At first, he says, the Tigris flows sluggishly, without its own name; but when it has entered the borders of the Medes, it is called the Tigris.] Finally, in the third place, one must remember that the Euphrates, and likewise the Tigris, were diverted and led into several channels by different kings, in different places and times; and that the points where those channels met, or their confluences, were variously cut by different people, or broken and separated; and finally that those channels were filled up, laid waste and renamed in various ways. So it is now either difficult or quite unknown to us what Moses writes here, although it was very well known in that age. Herodotus, book 5, certainly writes that the Gyndes alone (which is in those parts) was divided into 360 channels. Pliny, book 6 of the Natural History, chapter 20, says that the Euphrates was divided under the Assyrians by Semiramis, as Pomponius Mela relates in book 1, chapter 11; likewise by a certain satrap of the Babylonians into several parts, so that it should not harm Babylonia; afterwards by Nicator; also by the Orchenes, while they irrigated their fields (as Pliny says in the same place, chapter 27). Arrian also writes, in book 7 of the Expedition of Alexander, that the Babylonians often at different times led off and diverted the Euphrates into the river Pallacopas by great ditches and great labour. Finally, Trajan too prepared new ditches to connect the Euphrates with the Tigris in several places, as the historian Dion relates in his life. See Ammianus Marcellinus, book 23 of the Histories. Having set out these things, so as to pave the way for the explanation to come, and to show that the explanation of this matter is extremely difficult, we say that the region of Havilah, which is washed below Paradise or the earthly Garden by the Pishon, is that which the Tigris (when it is called Pasitigris) washes and surrounds on one side. It is also called Parapotamia by Pliny, book 6, chapter 27. This region lies to the south, near the province of Susiana, as Strabo teaches in book 15, and lower Persia, and it reaches to the Sea or Persian Gulf. Therefore Havilah lies beyond the Tigris for us. It is also famous for palms, olives, fruits and shrubs, as Pliny says in the same place. Indeed Solinus, chapter 40, writes that in those regions which the Tigris washes as it reaches the Persian Gulf (for it carries the Euphrates into the Persian Gulf) there is a wonderful and great abundance of gems and precious stones of every kind. In the Persian Gulf, and in the regions near and bordering it, gold of the finest quality is also found, as the voyages of the Portuguese teach, and history of every age; indeed gold is there in the greatest plenty and abundance for them. There are also pearls, gems and bdellium there; and this is also attested of the land of Havilah by Moses. Therefore all these things are despised by the neighbouring peoples of that region, as Pliny says in book 6, chapter 27: gold and gems, on account of their abundance; yet the other two peoples of the world value them very highly. Tertullian writes the same about those regions in his book On the Apparel of Women, for envoys from them had come to the emperor Severus at Rome in his time. All these things agree both with Moses' own history and with the praise and description of the land of Havilah given here. My friend D. Stukhius, in his commentaries on the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, says some things about Havilah, but not so much from his own opinion as from that of others. Havilah, then, is that region which the Pasitigris washes, which we call Trastigritana; from its borders as far as the Shur desert, near Egypt, the offspring of Ishmael (who was the son of Abraham by Hagar the maidservant) and his posterity lived afterwards, divided into twelve different kingdoms and families, very widely spread. Therefore the posterity of Ishmael inhabited it, lying almost everywhere opposite their brothers, the Israelites. For that very wide tract of land borders closely and adjacently the whole eastern and southern and western side of the promised land, so that whoever leaves the promised land from those three sides immediately enters the land of the Ishmaelites. And this is the road by which one goes from Egypt into Assyria through the Shur desert (which, as I said, is near Egypt and the Red Sea; Exod. 15.23, and 17.8. The metropolis of that desert was Hagra, situated at the Elanitic Gulf, as Pliny says, book 6, chapter 29). That road, I say, by which one goes from Egypt into Assyria, namely that whole tract which the Ishmaelites occupied from Shur to Havilah, bordering on the Israelites their brothers on three sides. Hence the same Ishmaelites are said to have dwelt "before the face of their brothers," that is, the Israelites, because they were set against them and opposite to them on the east, south and west, by reason of the region which they inhabited. This appears from these passages of Holy Scripture: Gen. 16.7, and 21.21, and 25.18; 1 Sam. 15. Therefore this region Havilah was east of Moses. And although gold is abundant in the region of Sheba, as at 1 Kings 10.11, and gems are found in many places, 2 Chron. 9.9, yet the best gold and the best gems come from this Havilah, a very wide region which reaches to the Persian Gulf, and bounds the Ishmaelites on the east, and which the Pishon, which is also the Pasitigris, washes, as I said. Now let us speak of the region of Cush and the river Gihon. The region of Cush was without doubt named after Cush, the son of Ham (who was the son of Noah), and it embraces that whole tract of Syria which the posterity of Cush occupied. That region extends from the river Euphrates and Babylonia southward, under or within the region of the Ishmaelites, as far as Egypt itself or the Arabian Gulf, which is also called the Red Sea. Therefore the region of Cush lay lower than Havilah, and lay to the south of Moses, or Judaea, nearer to the whole southern sea. This whole tract was afterwards called Arabia, which itself is divided into three parts: the Desert, the Stony (Petraea), and the Happy (Felix). It was also called Ethiopia, from the black colour of its inhabitants. Therefore this Ethiopia (which is called Cush) is that Ethiopia which lies on the Syrian side of Egypt and the Red Sea; it is not that which is beyond Egypt in middle Africa, near the Abyssinian mountains. But Homer too, the most ancient writer, in the Iliad recognised a double Ethiopia. That this is true, and that the region called Cush is that Ethiopia which lies on the Syrian side of the Red Sea, is proved by these passages of Holy Scripture: Gen. 10.6, 7; Exod. 2.22; Num. 12; 2 Chron. 14 and 21.6; Jer. 25.24, where by Jeremiah they are called Arabs, who are called Cush by Ezekiel 30.9. Here Matthaeus Beroaldus, first of all, teaches and pursues the matter widely and copiously, both in the last chapter of book 2 of Chronicles and in book 4, chapter 6; and he distinguished that double Ethiopia, although Flavius Josephus had written in general terms, but confusedly, that Arabs and Ethiopians were generally called Cush by a common name. Moreover the opinion of Beroaldus (from whom afterwards everyone eagerly borrowed) is confirmed by Pliny's Natural History, book 5, chapters 11 and 12; by Strabo, books 15 and 16, where he treats of the tract of Syria near Babylon and Egypt; by Solinus, chapter 40; and by the little book of Aethicus, where, listing the rivers of the Eastern Ocean, he describes the Tigris. Therefore the region of the Cushites' settlements was very wide, and this land which is properly called Cush was, as I said, larger than the region of the Ishmaelites, to the south of Moses (although the Ishmaelites are often included generally under the name of Arabs), and nearer to Egypt, containing those three parts of Arabia which we mentioned above. But this region of Cush was neither in the region of Eden, but outside Eden, nor a part of the earthly Garden, any more than Havilah was; rather it was the greatest part of Syria, reaching to the Red Sea and to the south (which lies between the Arabian and Persian Gulfs). This same region is washed on one side, namely the eastern, by the river Gihon, as Moses here teaches, Gen. 2. Others say it is a branch of the Euphrates, others the Tigris. For Pliny, and after him Solinus in his Polyhistor, write that the Euphrates, after it falls into the Tigris and joins it, loses its own name and is carried by the Tigris into the Persian Gulf. Therefore these words of Moses, Gen. 2.13, [And the name of the second is Gihon; it is the one that waters the whole land of Cush], are not to be understood as meaning that Gihon or Geon encircles and surrounds the land of the Cushites on every side and every edge; rather, that it washes it on one side only, namely the eastern, just as the river Pishon washes and surrounds the land of Havilah on the western side and plague only. Accordingly, of those two branches or rivers which flowed out and streamed from that same single river (which rose in the region of Eden and watered the whole Garden), one watered Arabia, and the other the land of Havilah. From this it now appears what that branch or river is which is called Gihon or Geon. It is a part and branch of the whole water which is formed (as Ammianus Marcellinus teaches in book 23 of the Histories) when the Euphrates and Tigris have been mixed and joined together and meet in the region of Adiabene, and so joined flow on. This branch, which is nearer to us of the two, is sometimes also called the Euphrates on that side; and the other branch of the same water, which is on the east, that is, nearer to India, is also called the Tigris by our people (who do not know the proper names of these branches), the one which washes Havilah. Therefore the Euphrates encloses and washes Arabia, or the whole region of Cush, on the side which was east of Moses. Pliny, book 6, chapter 26, says: [In the circuit of the Euphrates the Nomads of Arabia are included, as far as the deserts of Syria; hence we say it bends to the south, leaving the Palmyrene wastes.] Arrian proves this in book 7 of the Expedition of Alexander. Strabo, book 15, seems to have called that river the Tigris which others call the Euphrates, as I said, but which Moses names Geon. So too Aethicus, in his description of the river Tigris: for he says that it flows through Ethiopia, that is, the region of Cush. Indeed, Strabo himself reports that some thought all the rivers of Syria flow through underground channels from the lakes of the Euphrates and Tigris. Certainly, since these two branches of the same river and the same water were so different in position and region, Moses rightly gave to each its own proper name, as was then the custom; but profane writers have often confusedly called both branches by one and the same name, as I have said. Yet Dionysius of Alexandria teaches that it is uncertain by what name those branches should be called. Herodotus, book 5, seems to have named this very river, which Moses here calls Geon, the Gyndes. For Herodotus approaches Moses, even by the very sound of the word. Marcellinus also mentions this river Gyndes. Moreover Aethicus notes that there is also a river Geon in Gaul; and most people call the Nile Geon. There is also a stream or small river Geon in Judaea, flowing into Jerusalem, which is also called Siloam, as some hold, from 1 Kings 2.33 and 2 Chron. 32.30. Epiphanius, in his letter to John, bishop of Jerusalem, writes about this Geon that he had tasted of it when he was at Jerusalem. But this Geon does not pertain to this place. And this, indeed, is my view concerning that matter.

units.la: {y} Nomades Arabia... istis locùs sententia. Hortus autem Terrestris vbi fuerit iam apparet, nimirum ad Orientem Iudæa & Terra promissa in Edene regione (quæ Armeniæ Maioris pars fuit) in ea nimirum Edenis parte, in qua fluuius ille (ex quo quatuor ista, quæ demonstrauì, diuortia fiunt) totus fluit, & nondum diuisus. Ergo erat Hortus supra diuulsiones istarum aquarum situs, Tigris, Euphratis, Geon & Pison: quemadmodum etiam Iosephus lib. 1. Antiquit. Iudaic. cap. 2. sentit & scribit. Verist autem hic Hortus, eiusque facies tota tum post peccatum primi hominis: tum post diluuiū vniuersale, quod sub Noacho contigit, nisi si qua illius vestigia, sed obscura, existēt ea, quæ dicemus. Nec verò in aere fuit, vt Scholastici existimant, Paradisus seu Hortus iste: ac propterea falsum est, quod ydem scribunt, in extremo totius Orbis incendio non esse eum locum igne, vt cætera loca, repurgandum. Q. Vbi Deus hominem primum videlicet Adamum considerit: Nam Ischam, id est primam Mulierem in Horto illo creatam fuisse ex ipso Mosis textu Gen. 2. apparet. R. Id nullo certo S. Scriptura testimonio posse demonstrari: nonnulli tamen volunt in Damasceno agro, qui Edeni regioni sit vicinus, Amosi 1, fuisse conditū: unde in Hortum Edenis translatum postea a Deo fuerit: Aliÿ in monte Moria, vbi & Templum Dei exstructum postea fuit, & Isaacus Deo oblatus: Aliÿ denique iuxta mare Rubrum, vbi terra ipsa colore naturali rubet. Erat autem Adamus recens conditus Rubeus, vnde dictus est Adamus. Q. Cur Adamus (cui ab arboribus fructus, & herba ex terra assatim absque vllo labore, sed sponte ferebatur ad vistlum) colebat hortum illum: item quomodo eum colebat, ac custodiebat. R Jucundioris dutaxat exercitationis, & quidem corporeæ gratiâ (nam Spiritualis eiusdē exercitatio tota in Dei potentia, sapientia, bonitatu, & Mundi huius creationis meditatione posita fuit) Adamus Hortum illum colebat. Erat enim Adam animalis, non Spiritualis homo (quales post Resurrectionem beneficio Christi ef-ficiemus) Ergo uti & cibo, & potu ad victum, corporisque sui sustentationem egebat: sic & somno seu quiete, & exercitatione seu labore quodam: (Diem enim propterea a nocte distinxerat Deus, Psal. 104. 22, 23, ad eiusdem corporis conservationem, 1. Cor. 15. 44.) Id quod in Adami posteris locum quoque habituru erat. Colebat autem eum Hortum Adamus ante peccatum, abs-que molestia fatigatione, tedio vllo, sed summa cum animi corporisque voluptate. Ergo vera est illa Augustini sententia, lib. 14. de Civitate Dei cap. 11: [Viuebat itaque homo secundum Deum in Paradiso & corporali, & Spiritali. Neque enim erat Paradisus corporalis propter corporis bona: & propter mentis, non erat spiritualis.] Itaque Adamus illic & bonis animi & bonis corporis fruebatur. Colebat vero Hortum elicibus seu riuis e fluuio, qui per hortum fluebat, in omnes, quascunque volebat, partes deductis, ut maiori copia & venustate Herbæ, Arboresve illæ crescerent, & conservarentur imprimis duæ illæ Arbores, nempe Arbor vitæ, & Arbor Scientiæ Boni, & Mali: Sed ut cætera quoque, quantum fieri per earum naturam poterat, crescerent, ac multiplicarentur. Porro Adamus fernaseruabat Hortum illum in ssu Dei, ne a beluis & bestiis facies ac decor eius, amœnitásve corrumperetur, nève in eum passim irruerent, & ingrederetur, quod is totus locus esset conslitutus Adamo & posteris eius velut Tempum Dei, in quo cum eo ipse colloqueretur, illisque Deus appareret: ac proinde velut sanctius quoddam domicilium erat conseruandum, atque ab eo tuendum, Exod. 3. 5, Jos. 5. 15. Vide Augustini lib. 8. de Genesi ad literam, cap. 10. {Q.} Cur in Ægypto, & ad Meridiem non fuerit potius collocatus Adamus, aut Hortus ipse à Deo positus, quum tota terra Ægypti sit irrigationibus, & exūdationibus seu deriuationibus naturalibus & anniuersarys ꝯilis feracissima, & fœcundissima absque labore hominum: & Ægyptus ipsa cum Horto illo Edenico comparetur. Genef. 12. 10. Strabo, Plinius, & Solinus testantur id, quod S. Scriptura docet, Fertilissimam fieri quotannis totam Ægyptum inundationibus Nili secundum tamen ab Horto Edenico locum illa habet. Primam autem fœcunditatis & iucunditatis laudem Hortus ipse Edenicus, Deo sic illi pro bona sua voluntate benedicente, semper obtinuit. Præterea cômodior fuit Adami habitatio in Oriente, & loco temperatiore, & primùm radiis Solis illustrato, quàm in Meridie, vbi maior est estus & serpentes frequentes. {Q.} Vtrum Adamus (quamuis non peccasset) fuerit tamen & ipse, & eius posteri, ex Horto isto & Paradiso terrestri in Cœlum supremum & Paradisum cœlestem postea transferendi, tanquam in meliorem vitam. {R.} Hoc non definit quidem pracisè S. Scriptura: tamen Adamum inexterminabilem ( vt loquitur Augustinus in libro de Agone Christiano ) & immortalem futurum fuisse, si non peccasset, docet verbum Dei Gen. 2. 17. quod idem de eius posteris est sentiendum. Praterea constat ex eodem Dei verbo, ( quicquid contra sentire videatur Augustinus lib. 9. de Genesi ad literam, cap. 16.) quod in Coelum e terris transferimur a Deo, & quod immortalis illius felicitatis quam in coelo consequimur fimus participes, totum esse speciale & proprium beneficium Christi pro nobis incarnati, id est naturam nostram humanam assumentis sibi vnientis: non autem esse conditionem humanam naturae datam. Nam quo natura nostra, id est humana cum ipso omnis boni fonte, i. cum ipsamet Deitate arctius in persona Christi, quam Adami communis est: eo maiores quoque Dei gratias, maiora dona, maiorimque felicitatem, & splendidiorem locum eadem natura nostra consecuta est a Deo sed per Christum, vt dixi. Quare si nostram naturam Christus Dei Filius non assumpsisset, neque eiusmodi dona consequeremur. Sic Deus incredibili sua potentia ex nostris tenebris lucem & ex peccatis bonum eduxit, vt docet Paulus 2. Corint. 4. 6. Et quod dicitur etiam & coelum, & terra, in illa (quae nobis per Christum parta est) beatiore felicitate, futura, verum quidem est: sed illud coelum & illa terra erit prorsus nova, neque duntaxat qualis primum fuit condita a Deo: neque dicitur eadem illa terra nova futura sedes & domicilium beatorum cum Christo collectorum. Q. Utrum omnes Adami posteri in eodem illo terreno seu Edenico Horto erant cotinendi, atque duntaxat habitaturi. R. Nequaquaquam. Nam dictum fuerat à Deo homini, [Replete terram] Gen.1.28. Et hac quidem satis. Iam ad Arbores, quæ erant in Horto, accedamus.
units.tr: Nomades Arabia... the meaning of these passages. Now it is clear where the Garden of Earthly Paradise was: to the east, in the land of Edom, that is, the Promised Land, in the region of Eden (which was part of Greater Armenia), and in that part of Eden where the river from which the four rivers I have described divide flows as a whole and is not yet divided. The Garden therefore lay above the point where these waters separate: Tigris, Euphrates, Gihon and Pishon. Josephus also holds and writes this, in Jewish Antiquities book 1, chapter 2. But this Garden, and its whole appearance, did not survive either after the sin of the first man or after the universal flood under Noah, except perhaps some traces, though obscure ones, which I will discuss. Nor was this Paradise or Garden in the air, as the Schoolmen think; so it is false that they also write that in the final burning of the whole world that place is not cleansed by fire as the other places are. Q. Where did God set the first man, namely Adam? For that Ischam, that is, the first woman, was created in that Garden is clear from the text of Moses itself, Genesis 2. R. This cannot be shown from any certain testimony of Holy Scripture. Yet some think he was made in the field of Damascus, which lies near the region of Eden, citing Amos 1; from there he was later carried by God into the Garden of Eden. Others say on Mount Moriah, where the Temple of God was later built and where Isaac was offered to God. Others, finally, say by the Red Sea, where the earth itself is reddish in its natural colour. Adam, newly made, was ruddy, and that is why he was called Adam. Q. Why did Adam (for whom fruit from the trees and herbs from the earth were provided in abundance, without any labour, growing of their own accord for his food) cultivate that garden; and likewise how did he cultivate and guard it? R. Adam cultivated that garden only for the sake of a more pleasant exercise, and indeed a bodily one. (His spiritual exercise lay wholly in meditating on the power, wisdom and goodness of God and on the creation of this world.) For Adam was an animal man, not a spiritual one, as we shall become after the Resurrection by the benefit of Christ. So he needed food and drink for sustenance and for the upkeep of his body, and likewise sleep or rest, and some exercise or labour. (For God had therefore distinguished the day from the night, Psalm 104:22-23, for the preservation of that same body; 1 Corinthians 15:44.) This would also have applied to Adam's descendants. Adam cultivated that garden before the sin without trouble, weariness or any boredom, but with the greatest delight of mind and body. So that saying of Augustine's is true, in City of God book 14, chapter 11: [So man lived according to God in Paradise, both bodily and spiritually. For Paradise was not bodily only because of the goods of the body, nor was it spiritual only because of the goods of the mind.] Thus Adam enjoyed both the goods of the mind and the goods of the body there. He cultivated the garden with channels, or streams drawn from the river that flowed through the garden, led into whatever parts he wished, so that those herbs and trees would grow with greater abundance and beauty and be kept; above all those two trees, namely the Tree of Life and the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil; and so that the rest also grew and multiplied as far as their nature allowed. Moreover Adam guarded that garden by the command of God, so that its appearance, its beauty and its pleasantness might not be spoiled by wild animals and beasts, nor might they wander in and enter at will; for that whole place was established for Adam and his descendants as a kind of Temple of God, in which God would speak with him and appear to them. So it had to be kept as a holier dwelling and protected by him, Exodus 3:5; Joshua 5:15. See Augustine, On the Literal Meaning of Genesis book 8, chapter 10. {Q.} Why was Adam, or the Garden itself, not placed by God in Egypt or to the south instead? For the whole land of Egypt is most fertile and fruitful without human labour, through natural irrigation, overflowing and channels, and every year; and Egypt itself is compared with that Garden of Eden, Genesis 12:10. Strabo, Pliny and Solinus bear witness to what Holy Scripture teaches, that all of Egypt is made fertile each year by the floods of the Nile; yet it holds second place to the Garden of Eden. But the Garden of Eden itself always held the first praise for fruitfulness and delight, since God so blessed it by his good will. Besides, Adam's dwelling was more convenient in the East, in a milder place, and lit first by the rays of the sun, than in the South, where the heat is greater and serpents are frequent. {Q.} Whether Adam, even if he had not sinned, and his descendants too, would afterwards have been carried from this Garden and earthly Paradise into the highest heaven and the heavenly Paradise, as into a better life. {R.} Holy Scripture does not state this precisely, yet the word of God in Genesis 2:17 teaches that Adam would have been imperishable (as Augustine says in his book On the Christian Struggle) and immortal had he not sinned; and the same must be understood of his descendants. Moreover it is clear from the same word of God (whatever Augustine, On the Literal Meaning of Genesis book 9, chapter 16, may seem to think to the contrary) that we are transferred from earth to heaven by God, and that we share in that immortal happiness which we obtain in heaven, is a special and proper benefit of Christ, who was made flesh for us, that is, who took our human nature and united it to himself; it is not a condition given to human nature. For the closer our nature, that is, human nature, is joined with the very source of all good, namely with Deity itself, in the person of Christ, than Adam's nature was, the greater the graces, the greater the gifts, the greater the happiness and the more splendid the place which this same nature of ours has obtained from God, but through Christ, as I have said. So if Christ, the Son of God, had not taken on our nature, we would not obtain such gifts. Thus God by his incredible power brought light out of our darkness and good out of our sins, as Paul teaches, 2 Corinthians 4:6. And it is true that heaven and earth are also said to be going to exist in that happier blessedness which has been won for us through Christ; but that heaven and that earth will be entirely new, and not merely such as they were first created by God. Nor is that same earth said to be going to be the new seat and dwelling of the blessed gathered together with Christ. Q. Whether all of Adam's descendants were to be confined to that same earthly or Edenic Garden, and were to dwell there alone. R. By no means. For God had said to man, [Fill the earth], Genesis 1:28. And so much for this. Now let us come to the trees that were in the Garden.

units.la: Ad IIII. De Arboribus.
units.tr: To Question IV. On the Trees.

units.la: Q. Si bonus erat fructus earum Arborum, Cur Deus prohibuit hominem eo fructu vesci. Sin malus, cur eas creauit? R. Bonus quidem erat earum Arborum fructus, ut est Gen.3.6, Prou.3.18. Verum Deus in eo periclitari voluit, quàm sibi obsequens suturum esset Adamus eiusque posteritas. Itaque fuerunt Arbores illæ futuri in Deum animi humani signum, & obedientiæ testimonium. Augustinus Serm. 34 in Lucam: [Si autem, inquit, debuit Deus aliquid subere, ut te (quod tibi expedit) sentires esse sub Domino, necessario ab aliquo prohibendum erat, non propter illius Arboris malitiam, sed propter tuam obedientiam. Non potuit Deus perfectius demonstrare quantum bonum esset obedientia, nisi quum prohibuisset ab ea re, quæ non erat mala: Ergo bonum est, sed nolo tangas.] Arbores autem istæ duæ fuerunt vere Arbores, non autem res quædam incorporeæ, & spirituales: sed corporeæ, & terrenæ, vtpote signa sacramentalia, sicuti docet idem Augustinus lib.13.Ciuit.Dei cap.21, & lib.8.cap.6.de Genesi ad literam. Q. Vbi, id est, in qua parte Horti, seu Paradisi sitæ erant Arbores illæ. R. In medio Horti, quemadmodum diserte Scriptum extat, Gen.3.3, Prou.3.18, Apoc.2.7. Q. Quomodo Deus, quum Adamo esu Arboris interdiceret, locutus est. R. Anxiè quidem de eo quærit Augustin. lib.8.de Genesi ad literam, tum cap.18, tum etiā 27. Dubitat enim utrum tam cito fuerit Adamus intelligens, quum recens adhuc creatus esset: utrum vtrum alia, quàm seipso, creatura egeret ad cognoscendam Dei voluntatem. Frustrà. Erat enim Adamus ab ipso sua creationis principio conditus à Deo sapiens, intelliges, & instructus: & quoniam Animalis fabulus erat, etiam aliis rebus & creaturis opus habuit, quibus Dei voluntas vel ei indicaretur, vel confirmaretur. Ergo Arboribus illis & sacramentis egebat Adam. Deum verò per seipsum & suam essentiam loquentem intelligere absque voce articulata idem non poterat. Ergo vocem sibi sinxit Deus (vti in monte Horebo, quū Legem suam dedit Exod 20. & sæpè alias) & quidem sonoram, & articulatam, qua cum homine primo loquebatur. Q. Vtrum Præceptum de non edendo fructu Arboris Scientia boni & mali vtriq; Homini, id est, Euæ & Adamo datum est primum à Deo. R. Augustinus lib.8. de Genesi ad literam, cap.17. ait, [Deus ordinatissimè præcepit, id est, præceptum hoc primum dedit Adamo seu viro] & quidem tunc soli, utpote quum nondum esset creata fœmina, ut per virum seu Adamum, postea idem hoc præceptum ad fœminam peruenirent. Quam disciplinam seruat & in Ecclesia Apostolus, dicens 1.Cor.14.35. [Siquid autem discere volint, domi viros suos interrogent mulieres.] Q. Vtrum nulli morbi in Adamo, & posteris eius futuri erant, si non peccasset Adamus. Videntur enim morbi inijs esse potuisse, quanuis immortales futuri erant. R. Arbor vitæ erat omnis morbi, omnisque calamitatis, infirmitatis, & ægritudinis ex Adamo, eiusque posteris à Deo ipso tollenda sacramentum, & aduersus eos praesentissimum remedium. Ipsius enim tum esus tum etiā solus aspectus ex fide morbos, & defectus omnes, ac dyscratiam ex Adami corpore fugasset, quemadmodū solus in Deserto Serpentis ænei aspectus ex fide tollebat aliorum serpentum venena, Num.21.9. Ioan.3 14. Sunt enim morbi & infirmitates praecursores mortis, & vexatio corporis, qua vtraq; tunc, id est absque peccato Adami, nulla futura erat, Psal 73.3, 1.Cor.15. 56. Jam de Nominum impositione agamus.
units.tr: Q. If the fruit of those trees was good, why did God forbid the man to eat of it? And if it was bad, why did he create the trees? R. The fruit of those trees was indeed good, as Genesis 3:6 and Proverbs 3:18 show. But God wished to test in it how obedient Adam and his posterity would be to him. So those trees were to be a sign of the human mind's submission to God and a witness to obedience. Augustine, Sermon 34 on Luke: "But if God had to make you subject, so that you would feel yourself to be under the Lord (which is for your good), he had necessarily to forbid you something. This was not because of the wickedness of that tree, but because of your obedience. God could not have shown more clearly how great a good obedience is than by forbidding a thing that was not evil. So it is good, but I do not want you to touch it." Those two trees were true trees, not some incorporeal and spiritual things, but bodily and earthly, as signs of a sacrament, as Augustine teaches in City of God 13.21 and in On the Literal Meaning of Genesis 8.6. Q. Where, that is, in which part of the garden or paradise, did those trees stand? R. In the middle of the garden, as Scripture clearly states at Genesis 3:3, Proverbs 3:18 and Revelation 2:7. Q. How did God speak to Adam when he forbade him to eat of the tree? R. Augustine anxiously asks this in On the Literal Meaning of Genesis 8, both in chapter 18 and also in chapter 27. He doubts whether Adam, though newly created, understood so quickly, and whether he needed some creature other than himself to know God's will. But the question is idle. Adam was made by God wise, intelligent and instructed from the very beginning of his creation; and since he was a speaking being, he also needed other things and creatures by which God's will could be either shown to him or confirmed. So Adam needed those trees and sacraments. But he could not understand God speaking through himself and his own essence without an articulated voice. So God formed a voice for him (as on Mount Horeb, when he gave his law, Exodus 20, and often elsewhere), a voice that was audible and articulated, by which he spoke with the first man. Q. Was the command not to eat the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil given by God first to both the man and the woman, that is, to Eve and Adam? R. Augustine, in On the Literal Meaning of Genesis 8, chapter 17, says: "God most orderly commanded; that is, he gave this command first to Adam or the man," and indeed then to him alone, since the woman had not yet been created, so that through the man, Adam, the same command would later reach the woman. The Apostle keeps this order also in the Church, saying in 1 Corinthians 14:35: "If they want to learn anything, let the women ask their own husbands at home." Q. Would there have been no diseases in Adam and his posterity if Adam had not sinned? For diseases seem likely to have been possible even though they would have been immortal. R. The tree of life was a sacrament, to be provided by God himself, of the removal of every disease, every calamity, every weakness and sickness from Adam and his posterity, and the most effective remedy against them. For its eating, or even the mere sight of it, in faith would have driven out diseases, all defects and every dyscrasia from Adam's body, just as in the wilderness the mere sight of the bronze serpent, in faith, removed the poison of other serpents (Numbers 21:9; John 3:14). For diseases and infirmities are forerunners of death, and the suffering of the body, which in that state, that is, without the sin of Adam, would have been absent (Psalm 73:3; 1 Corinthians 15:56). Now let us deal with the giving of names.

units.la: Ad V. De Nominum Impositione.
units.tr: V. On the Imposition of Names.

units.la: Q. Quando Adamus nomina imposuerit Animalibus. R. Quoniam rationem seriemque temporis, quo res vnaquaeque gesta est, sequitur Moses: & post nomina rebus imposita condita fuit mulier: Deus autem ab omni opere suo creando die septima quieuit, necessario colligitur nomina fuisse imposita Animalibus ab Adamo die sexto, id est, eo ipso die, quo creatus fuerat Adamus. Vide Augustinū lib 9.cap.1.de Genesi ad literam. Q. Quæ lingua nomen cuiq; Animali sit ab Adamo primum impositum. R. Augustinus lib.16. Ciuit. Dei, cap.11. scribit, & sentit Hebraea lingua fuisse nomen cuiusvis animalis nuncupatum ab Adamo, quòd ea lingua & prima omnium extiterit, id est, à principio Mundi: & in diuisione linguarum minimè corrupta fuerit, sed integra permanserit. Hæc Augustini sententia est, quam omnes sequuntur, & eam primâ Mundi linguam Hebræam ab Heber postea dictam fuisse volunt (quanquam postea eadem quoque Chananæa dicta est, Ifa.19.18) & sanctam. Eam autem prorsus incorruptam semper mansisse, ac talem (quali Adamus ipse utebatur) aly negant. Certè multa vocabula peregrina .i. tum Syriaca, tum Chaldæa, tum Persica irrepsisse in linguam Hebream (quæ & qualis nunc extat in libris sacris, nedum in communi Iudæorum colloquio & visu) certò certius est, & nemo vel pius vel eius lingua peritus diffitebitur, aut negauerit. Incorruptior tamen, quàm aliaulla, perstitit, ac Dei beneficio, perstat. Q. Vtrum rebus omnibus creatis in hoc visibili Mundo (nam Adamus cœlestibus, velut Angelis procul dubio nomen non dedit) imposuerit Adamus nomen. R. Præclarè docet Augustinus lib.3.de Genesi ad literam cap.11: Varia esse animantium genera, velut Volatilia, Reptilia, seu Aquatilia & Quadrupeda seu Iumenta: sed & hæc suas quoque species habent diuersas. Videtur autem, ac colligitur, ut nonnulli volunt, ex Gen.2.20. Adamum primum aquatilibus animantibus, id est, Piscibus nomen minimè dedisse. (Nam neque ad Adamum adducti fuisse Pisces dicuntur, neq; volatilium cœli, vel bestiarum agri nomine comprehenduntur, Gen.1.21.25. quibus duobus duntaxat animantium generibus videtur Adamus nomen dedisse.) Deinde neque plantis terræ, vel herbis, vel etiam arboribus videtur Adamus nomen imposuisse. Denique neque astris, seu stellis ipsis, vel cœlestibus qui dicuntur, orbibus. Ergo tot rerum genera non videtur Adamus proprijs nominibus appellasse, Gen 2.19.20. Et hæc est quorundam sententia. Verum
units.tr: Q. When did Adam give names to the animals? A. Because Moses follows the order and sequence of time in which each thing was done, and records that the woman was made after names had been given to things, and that God rested on the seventh day from all his work of creation, it is necessarily concluded that Adam gave names to the animals on the sixth day, that is, on the very day on which Adam himself was created. See Augustine, On Genesis according to the Letter, book 9, chapter 1. Q. Which language did Adam first use to name each animal? A. Augustine, The City of God, book 16, chapter 11, writes and holds that each animal was named by Adam in the Hebrew language, because that language was the first of all, that is, from the beginning of the world, and was not corrupted at the division of tongues but remained intact. This is Augustine's opinion, which everyone follows, and they hold that this first language of the world, Hebrew, was afterwards called the language of Heber (although it was later also called Canaanite, Isa. 19.18), and that it was holy. But that it remained wholly incorrupt, and was such as Adam himself used, others deny. Certainly it is more certain than anything that many foreign words, Syriac, Chaldean and Persian, crept into the Hebrew language (which now exists in the sacred books, and much more in the everyday speech and usage of the Jews), and no one, whether pious or skilled in that language, will deny or gainsay this. Yet it has persisted more incorrupt than any other, and by God's blessing it still persists. Q. Did Adam give a name to all created things in this visible world? (For he certainly gave no name to heavenly beings, such as the angels.) A. Augustine teaches admirably, On Genesis according to the Letter, book 3, chapter 11: there are various kinds of living things, such as flying creatures, creeping or aquatic creatures, and four-footed creatures or beasts; and these too have their various species. It seems, and is gathered, as some hold, from Gen. 2.20 that Adam did not at all give a name to the aquatic animals, that is, the fishes. (For the fishes are not said to have been brought to Adam, nor are they included under the name of the birds of heaven or the beasts of the field, Gen. 1.21, 25; it seems Adam gave names to these two kinds of animals only.) Then, it seems, Adam did not give a name to the plants of the earth, or to the herbs, or even to the trees. Finally, not to the stars themselves, or to the heavenly bodies called orbs. So it seems Adam did not call so many kinds of things by their proper names, Gen. 2.19, 20. And this is the view of some. But

units.la: .. Vide ut supra. Verùm quum omnia hæc in vsum hominis creata suissent, eisque omnibus, velut Dominus earum Homo dominaretur, Psalmo 8, Hebr. 2 8, Gene. 1.29, & 2. 16. certè & ys quoq; rerum generibus omnibus & singulis, velut feruis suis, & rebus sibi à Deo dicatis, nomen Adamus imposuit, vt ys ipse vteretur, etiam Sole ipso & Luna quemadmodum Iosua fecit, Iof. 10.12. & de ys cum vxore, & posteris suis Adamus loqui ad Dei gloriā posset. Quare verba illa Mosis [Indidit, Adam omnibus iumentis, & volatilibus cœlis, & omnibus bestijs agri] per synecdochen sunt explicanda, vt ex parte totum rerum creatarum omnium genus intelligatur ab Adamo nomen accepisse: Nam si hæc maiora nominauit Adamus, multo magis & illa minora velut herbas, arbores, quas facilius nosse poterat, quibusq; ad esumfuum quotidianum ipse frequentius vtebatur.
units.tr: .. See above. Since all these things were created for the use of man, and man, as their lord, ruled over all of them (Ps. 8; Heb. 2.8; Gen. 1.29 and 2.16), certainly Adam also gave names to all and each of the kinds of things, as to his servants and to things dedicated to him by God, so that he might use them, even the sun itself and the moon, as Joshua did (Josh. 10.12), and so that he, with his wife and his descendants, might speak of them to the glory of God. Therefore those words of Moses, [Adam gave names to all the cattle, and to the birds of the heaven, and to all the beasts of the field], are to be explained by synecdoche, so that from a part the whole genus of all created things is understood to have received names from Adam. For if Adam named the greater things, much more did he name the lesser, such as herbs and trees, which he could more easily know, and which he himself used more frequently for his daily food.

units.la: Q. Vtrum bestiæ fuerint in Hortum ipsum & terrestrem Paradisum ad Adamum adductæ, vt videret ecquod nomen cuique rerum speciei inderet, Gen 2 19, quum eundem Hortum Adamus Dei iussu sedulo custodiret, ne in eum bestiæ illæ ingrederentur? R. Adductæ quidem à Deo dicuntur ad Adamū bestiæ agri: sed locus non additur vbi illæ consisterint, aut vbi, interea dum nomen sortiuntur, subsederint, Vtrum foris extra Hortum: an potius in Hortum ipsum venerint, quem illo tam breui tempore, quo quaque bestia & animal nominabatur, non corruperunt. Erant enim tunc veluti & postea quæ ingressæ sunt iussu Dei in Arcam Noachi, placidissima omnia animantium, en utem petulantia, viti nunc sunt Gen.6.19. Vide A quætinnm lib. 3. de Genesi ad literam cap. 15. & 16, & lib. 9. cap. 14 & 12. Ego vero sentio postquam nomina bestijs Adamus imposuisset, iussum fuisse custodire Hortum, ne passim vel gregatim ille postea in eum introirent, & tantâ illius Horti venustatem atque amoenitatem corrumperent ac confunderent: non tamen vt nulla omnino, aut nunquâ in Hortum eum (Adamo nempe iubente, volente, vel accersente) bestiæ ingrederentur. Nam in eum ipsum Hortum postea Serpens introiit, & Euam tentauit, Gen. 3. 1. 2. His autem expositis, ad Creationem Mulieris accedamus.
units.tr: Q. Were the beasts brought into the garden itself, and the earthly Paradise, to Adam, so that he might see what name he would give to each kind of thing (Gen. 2.19), since Adam diligently guarded that same garden at God's command, lest those beasts should enter it? A. Beasts of the field are said to have been brought by God to Adam, but no place is added where they stayed, or where they settled while they received their names: whether outside the garden, or rather came into the garden itself, which in so short a time, while each beast and animal was being named, they did not corrupt. For they were then, as afterwards those who entered Noah's ark at God's command, all most gentle creatures, but now they are wanton and violent (Gen. 6.19). See Augustine, On Genesis according to the Letter, book 3, chapters 15 and 16, and book 9, chapters 14 and 12. I, however, think that after Adam had given names to the beasts, he was commanded to guard the garden, lest they should afterwards enter it at random or in herds and corrupt and confuse its great beauty and charm; yet not so that no beasts at all would ever enter that garden (Adam, of course, commanding, willing, or summoning them). For afterwards the serpent did enter that very garden and tempted Eve (Gen. 3.1, 2). Having set these things out, let us now come to the creation of the woman.

units.la: Ad VI. De Mulieris Creatione.
units.tr: Ch. VI. On the Creation of Woman

units.la: Quaeritur ex qua costarum parte, supremâne an infima, sumpta sit ea costa, ex qua Mulieris corpus à Deo cõpaclum est, ac cõpositum Gen. 2. 21. R. Rs ipsa docet ex inferioribus costis sumptam fuisse eam costa, seu costas, ex quibus Mulier condita fuit à Deo. Nam & costae habent Mulieres vna plures, quàm Viri: & inferiores virorum seu Marium costae appellantur Notha, quia breuiores sunt, & caro potius, quàm os, vel costa videntur esse. Costae, inquiunt Medici, quae à Graecis πλευραι dicuntur, in omnibus fere animantibus viginti quatuor sunt, ab vtroque scilicet latere duodecim. Septem priores longiores, Graecis γνάσσαι, Latinis vera & legitime dicuntur. Reliquae inferiores breuiores, & ad pectus haud pertinentes, quinque in quouis latere, νόθαι Graecè, Spuria Latinè nominantur. Ha ad septum trâfuerfum desinunt. Deque & Fuschius, vnde has transcripsimus, & Cornelius Celsus lib. 8. cap. 1. & Ioannes Fernelius lib. 1. Physiologia, cap. 3. Ex inferioribus vero costis sumpta est mulier, vt se dignitate inferiorem esse agnosceret suo viro, è cuius corpore desumpta fuit. Ex latere vero viri sumpta est ad ipsius Maris & fœmina coniunctionis vim commendandam, & vt socia sui viri esse intelligeretur. Augustinus lib. 9 de Genesi ad literam cap. 13. Petrus Lombard. lib. 2. Distinct. 18. cap. [Quum autem.] Q. Ex quo Mulier creata sit, vtrū à Deo ipso costa illa fuerit Adamo detracta, an ab Angelis. R. A Deo ipso. Nam quòd eam costam fuisse per Angelorum ministerium Adamo dormienti detractam putant nonnulli, vt ait Augustinus lib. 9. de Genesi ad liter. cap. 15, colorem non habet. Cur enim istud minùs Deo competit, & convenit, quàm ipsummet Deum è terra pulverem accepisse, ex quo primum Hominem creauit? Certè in hac prima rerum creatione nulla fuit, fuerúntve Angelorum partes, nec istius operis portio vlla ad eos deriuatur in S. Scriptura: nec alius, quàm vnus est cuiuslibet creaturæ seu parua, seu magna creator, nempe verus Deus. Vitanda tamen est hoc loco puerilis de Deo, & Dei manibus cogitatio, quemadmodum rectè monet Augustinus lib. 6. de Genesi ad literam cap. 12: Fœmina verò prima corpus à Deo creatum est ex illa costa, eo sexu, ea forma, & ea distinctione membrorum, qua fœmina nobis hodiè quoque notæ sunt. Hæc enim eadem fœmina postea peperit Cainum, & Abelem, & fœminas alias similes nostris, ex quibus postea procreatum est reliquum genus humanum, quemadmodum præclarè scribit lib. 9. eiusdem operis idem Augustinus cap. 11.
units.tr: Q. From which part of the ribs, the uppermost or the lowest, was the rib taken from which the body of the woman was fashioned and formed by God (Gen. 2:21)? A. The rabbis themselves teach that the rib, or ribs, from which God formed the woman were taken from the lower ribs. For women have one or more ribs more than men, and the lower ribs of men are called "spurious" [Notha], because they are shorter and seem to be flesh rather than bone or rib. Physicians say that the ribs, which the Greeks call pleurai [πλευραι], are in almost all animals twenty-four in number, twelve on each side. The seven upper ones, which the Greeks call gnassai [γνάσσαι], are rightly and lawfully called "true" in Latin. The remaining lower ones are shorter, do not reach the breast, and are called "bastard" [νόθαι] in Greek and "spurious" in Latin, five on each side. They end at the diaphragm. I have taken this from Fuchs, and likewise from Cornelius Celsus, book 8, chapter 1, and John Fernel, Physiology, book 1, chapter 3. The woman was taken from the lower ribs so that she would recognise that she was inferior in dignity to her husband, from whose body she was taken. But she was taken from the side of the man to commend the power of the union of male and female, and so that she might be understood to be his companion. See Augustine, On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, book 9, chapter 13, and Peter Lombard, Sentences, book 2, distinction 18, chapter "Quum autem". Q. From what was the woman created? Whether that rib was taken from Adam by God himself or by angels? A. By God himself. For the opinion of some, that this rib was taken from the sleeping Adam through the ministry of angels, as Augustine says in On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, book 9, chapter 15, has no plausibility. For why should this be less fitting to God than that God himself took dust from the earth, out of which he first created man? Certainly in this first creation of things there was no part, nor were there parts, for the angels, nor is any share of this work derived to them in Holy Scripture. There is no creator of any creature, whether small or great, other than the one true God. Yet at this point the childish notion of God and of God's hands must be avoided, as Augustine rightly warns in On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, book 6, chapter 12: the first woman's body was created by God from that rib, with that sex, that form, and that distinction of members by which women are known to us today. For this same woman afterwards bore Cain and Abel, and other women like ours, from whom the rest of the human race was afterwards produced, as Augustine himself writes admirably in book 9 of the same work, chapter 11.

units.la: Q. Vnde creata fit anima Mulieris, vtrum ex Adami costa, an in corpus Mulieris iam factum à Deo insufflata postea, quemadmodum & in Adamů ipsius virum. R. Placet Augustini lib. 10. cap. 1 de Genesi ad literam hac responsio, [Quoniam Deus omnes animas hominum nascentium facit, sicut primam: propterea Scriptura de aliis tacuit (vti & de anima Eua) quoniam posset, quod in una factum commemoratum est, etiam de ceteris prudenter intelligi.] Alioqui Scriptura non siluisset, si quid diuersum in Muliere factum in eo fuisset, quàm in viro Adamo. Ergo frustra se torquent in hac facili quæstione Scholastici soluenda. Q. Vbi creata sit Mulier prima. R. In horto Edenice, queadmodů ex ipso Moysis contextu satis apparet Gen. 2. 15. 21. Q. Quando creata, seu formata fuerit prima Mulier. R. Sexto die, & post Adamů conditű, & impositá animalibus nomina. Augustl. lib 6. Genesi ad liter. cap. 2. ait, [Neque enim sexto die factus est masculus, & accessu tepori facta est fœmina, sed fecit eum, inquit Moyses Gen. 11. Masculum, & Fœminam.] Idem cap. 5, & 6. Quòd si creari Mundus cepit, vt vult Augustinus in lib. Quaest. ex utroque Testamento mixtum cap. 106. in aquinoctio verno, prima die mensis Nisan primo die Pascha, seu vndecimo Calend mensis Aprilis, id est, xxii. Martij mensis nostri, Homo vterq; conditus fuerit die xxvii Martij. Verum non in aquinoctio verno, sed potius autumnali factus est Mundus, mense Septembri medio. Q. Vtrũ Mulier sit à Deo rerum hic creatarũ Domina constituta, viti & Adamus ipsius maritus. R. Quum ad Dei imaginem quemadmodum & vir ipsius Adamus, fuerit condita Mulier, illiusque imaginis pars quaedam sit, ac fuerit dominium illud in res creatas, Psal. 8. certe fuit Mulier Domina quoque rerum hic conditarum à Deo constituta, uti & Adamus: eiusdem felicitatis particeps quemadmodum & ille: atque etiam nunc est aeterna, 1. Pet. 3. 5. 6. & eorundem donorum κοινωνὸς, & capax quorum Mat. Vnde & Plato lib. 5. de Repub. & Basilius (ex quo suum Hexameron descripsit Ambrosius) Homil. 10. in Hexameron sentit in genere humano parem esse Maris & Foemina indolem: eorundem donorum & operum utrumque capacem: parémque denique naturam esse utriusque. Iam de Matrimonio primo agamus.
units.tr: Q. From what was the soul of the woman created: from Adam's rib, or breathed into the woman's body after it had been made by God, as into Adam, her husband? A. I approve of this answer of Augustine, On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, book 10, chapter 1: "Since God makes the souls of all men as they are born, as he made the first, Scripture has been silent about the others (as also about the soul of Eve), because what is recorded as done in one can be prudently understood also of the rest." Otherwise Scripture would not have been silent if anything different had been done in the woman from what was done in the man Adam. Therefore the Schoolmen labour in vain in solving this easy question. Q. Where was the first woman created? A. In the garden of Eden, as is sufficiently clear from the very context of Moses, Gen. 2:15, 21. Q. When was the first woman created or formed? A. On the sixth day, after Adam had been made and the names of the animals had been given. Augustine, On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, book 6, chapter 2, says: "For man was not made on the sixth day as a male, and then the woman was made by addition at a later time, but, as Moses says (Gen. 1:27), he made him male and female." The same in chapters 5 and 6. But if the world began to be created, as Augustine holds in Questions on Both Testaments, chapter 106, at the vernal equinox, on the first day of the month Nisan, the first day of Passover, or the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, that is, the 22nd of March in our calendar, then both humans were created on the 27th of March. But the world was made not at the vernal equinox but rather at the autumnal one, in the middle of September. Q. Whether the woman was appointed by God as lady of the created things here, as her husband Adam was. A. Since the woman, like her husband Adam, was created in the image of God, and is a certain part of that image, and that dominion over created things (Ps. 8) belonged to her, certainly the woman was also appointed by God as lady of the things created here, just as Adam was. She shares the same happiness as he does, and even now is eternally so (1 Pet. 3:5, 6), and is a partaker of the same gifts, and capable of them, which Matthew describes. Hence Plato, in book 5 of the Republic, and Basil (from whom Ambrose copied his Hexameron), in Homily 10 on the Hexameron, hold that in the human race the nature of male and female is equal, that each is capable of the same gifts and works, and that the nature of each is in the end the same. Now let us deal with the first marriage.

units.la: Ad VII. Matrimonij Institutio.
units.tr: On VII. The Institution of Marriage.

units.la: Q. Quando coniugium inter Adamum & Ischa (quae & Eua seu Chaua est) primum institutum fuerit, utrum die sexto, an septimo (est enim ex Pythagoreorum sententia numerus septenarius coniugij symbolum, utpote qui contineat quattuor velut Marem, & tria velut Foeminam) an oftavo potius die, vel sequentibus.
units.tr: Q. When was marriage first instituted between Adam and Ischa (who is also Eve or Chava): on the sixth day, or on the seventh (for according to the Pythagoreans the number seven is the symbol of marriage, since it contains four, as the male, and three, as the female), or rather on the eighth day, or on the days following?

units.la: R. Augustinus lib. 14. cap. 22. de Ciuit. Dei scribit Masculum & Foeminam homines fuisse, & quidem vere, inter quos à Deo coniugium institutum est primitus, ut nunc homines duo diuersi sexus videmus, & nouimus: neque ista Mosis verba esse allegorice interpretanda, ut Mas sit ratio hominis: foemina vero sit eiusdem cupiditas. Hoc enim sentire, ait, est magna absurditas. Verum lib. 6. cap. 3. de Genesi ad literam, idem tradit Coniugium inter Marem Adamum, & Ifcham seu Euam mulierem nequaquam eodem die institutum, quo utrumque creatum est, nempe die sexto, ut ibidem idem docet, cap. 2: sed neque septimo, id est, proximè sequentis verum die octavo, vel aliis aliquot ab utriusque creatione interiectis diebus. Etsi vero Moses Gen. 1. 28 statim post creationem hominis subjicit, [Et benedixit eis Dominus, & dixit, Crescite, & multiplicamini, &c.] tamen videtur feriis rerum gestarum, & narratarum Genes. toto capite secundo, & eiusdem cap. vers. 22. postulare, ut alio die fœmina creata fuerit, alio Coniugium institutum. Ergo per anticipationem scripsit Moses, quod tradit Genes. 1. 27, & 28. de Coniugio, ut totam historiam illam semel absoluteret, & uno velut orationis filo continuaret. Et certè quidem Eccles. 17. 5. 6. ubi Mulieris creatio narratur, ex communi, quæ tunc erat recepta, Iudæorum sententia, nulla coniugij, illiusve institutionis fit mentio. Ex quo apparet sic verba Moses Gen. 2. 22. ab illis populariter explicata fuisse, ut alio tempore condita prima fœmina fuerit, alio autem Coniugium inter eam & Adamum institutum sancitumque à Deo. Quam ego quoque sententiam ampliectQr. Ergo post septimum diem coniuges facti sunt Adamus & Eua. Q. Vtrum Adamus Ifcham vxorem suam in Paradiso seu Horto Edeno ante peccatum cognouerit? Atque utrum quæ inter eos eiusque posteros si non peccasset Adamus, copula carnalis erat futura, turpis esset. R. Patres, uti Basilius, Hieronymus, Ambrosius, & ex iis alij fere sic sentiunt: In Horto Edenico seu Paradiso Terrestri ante peccatum Hominis fuisse quiquidem inter Adamum & Euam Coniugium, & vinculum: non tamen coitum & nuptias. At vbi contra Pelagianos docet Augustinus, si Adamus minimè peccasset, futuros fuisse omnes hominis affectus, & actiones absq; turpitudine, sordibus, & spurcitie: quare & coitus quoque coniugalis tunc absque turpi cupiditate & peccato erat. Sic lib 9 de Genesi ad liter. cap. 3. & 9. Imo vero idem Augustinus lib. 14. cap. 23 de Ciuit. Dei, graviter eos reprehendit, qui putant homines Adamum & Euam inter se coituros non fuisse, nisi peccassent: [quasi vero, inquit, propter numerositatem sanctorum necessarium fuerit peccatum.] Ergo ante primum peccatum cupiditas, appetitúsque coitus, & copula carnalis in homine erat honestus, sanctus, omni turpitudine, etiam coram Deo ipso carens: poteráɵque inter Adamum & Euam esse, atq; inter eius posteros. Copulam verò illam carnalem inter Adamum & Euam fuisse etiam ante peccatum, qua causa vel ratio negare obsecro, suaserit? Certè nulla. Imò hac fortasse cogét fateri eam copulam ab ijs ante peccatum exercitâ fuisse, quòd dictum ijs in Paradiso seu Horto fuerat à Deo iam pracipiente, [Crescite, & multiplicamini.] Hoc enim ipsum verba hac sonant, vti coeat iam tum, id est etiam ante peccatū. Ergo accesserat Diuina autoritas, de quo tamē videtur ambigere Augustinus lib. 9. cap. 4. de Genesi ad literā. Quemadmodum igitur Adamus & Eua ederunt, biberunt, dormierunt ante peccatum: sic coierunt. Erant enim tunc omnes iste actiones & honestæ, & naturales. Q. Vtrum siceha vxor Adami conceperit Cainum ante peccatum. R.
units.tr: R. Augustine, in Book 14, chapter 22 of The City of God, writes that the man and the woman were truly men, and that marriage was first instituted by God between them, just as we now see and know two people of different sexes. He holds that these words of Moses are not to be interpreted allegorically, so that the man is reason and the woman is his desire, for to think this, he says, is a great absurdity. But in Book 6, chapter 3 of On Genesis according to the Letter, he hands down that marriage between the male Adam and Ischa or Eve the woman was by no means instituted on the same day on which both were created, namely the sixth day, as he teaches in the same place, chapter 2; nor on the seventh, that is, the day immediately following, but on the eighth day, or after some other days had passed since the creation of both. Yet although Moses, at Gen. 1:28, adds immediately after the creation of man, [And the Lord blessed them, and said, Increase and multiply, etc.], the order of the events done and narrated throughout Genesis chapter 2, and at Gen. 2:22, seems to require that the woman was created on one day and marriage instituted on another. Therefore Moses wrote by anticipation what he hands down about marriage at Gen. 1:27 and 28, so that he might complete that whole history at once and continue it along one thread of narrative. And certainly Ecclesiasticus 17:5, 6, where the creation of woman is narrated, makes no mention of marriage or its institution, following the common opinion of the Jews, which was then received. From this it appears that those words of Moses at Gen. 2:22 were explained by them in a popular way, so that the first woman was made at one time, and marriage between her and Adam was instituted and sanctioned by God at another. I too embrace this opinion. Therefore Adam and Eve became spouses after the seventh day. Q. Whether Adam knew his wife Ischa in Paradise, or the Garden of Eden, before the sin; and whether the carnal union that would have existed between them and their posterity had Adam not sinned would have been shameful. R. The Fathers, such as Basil, Jerome, Ambrose, and nearly the others from among them, think that before man's sin, in the Garden of Eden or the Earthly Paradise, there was marriage and a bond between Adam and Eve, but not intercourse and nuptials. But when Augustine teaches against the Pelagians that, had Adam not sinned, all human affections and actions would have been free of shame, filth and foulness, then conjugal intercourse also was without shameful desire and sin. So he says in Book 9, chapters 3 and 9, of On Genesis according to the Letter. Indeed the same Augustine, in Book 14, chapter 23 of The City of God, sharply rebukes those who think that Adam and Eve would not have come together had they not sinned: [as if, he says, sin were necessary because of the number of the saints]. Therefore before the first sin, the desire, the appetite for coition and the carnal union in man were honourable and holy, free from all foulness, even before God himself, and could have existed between Adam and Eve and among their posterity. But what cause or reason, I beg you, would persuade anyone to deny that this carnal union between Adam and Eve existed even before the sin? Surely none. Indeed this will perhaps compel us to admit that they practised that union before sin, since God had already said to them in Paradise or the Garden, [Increase and multiply.] For these very words sound as if they should already come together then, that is, even before sin. Therefore divine authority had been added, about which, however, Augustine seems uncertain, in Book 9, chapter 4 of On Genesis according to the Letter. Just as Adam and Eve ate, drank and slept before sin, so they came together, for all those actions were then both honourable and natural. Q. Whether Ischa, Adam's wife, conceived Cain before sin. R.

units.la: De eo nihil quicquam certi Statui potest, quanuis fateamur & concedamus Adamum, & Ifcham (qua & Eua) coysse ante peccatum. Nam quod Caini anni & caeterorum numerantur & sumuntur ab annis Adami, nihil probat, aut concludit. Probabilius tamen est nonfuisse conceptum Q. Virum si Adamus non peccasset, ipse ac Eua, & eius posteri tam Mares, quam Fœmina perpetuò fœcundi futuri fuissent & quauis ætate liberos potuissent gignere. R. Plane curiosum est hoc quærere, & temerariū definire. Illud modò statuatur, quodcunq; natura vel humana vel alterius cuiusquam iam vitium est, vel labes vel Sterilitas vel infirmitas, id omne ex peccato Adami profectum, ac infusum esse. Principio autem rerum nulla vitia vel extitisse, vel futura fuisse absque peccato. Q. Virum quisque cum propria vxore sic ante mortem tndustam coysset vt post a litum semel ab ea partū amplius eam cogniturus non fuerit, quum immortales futuri essent homines, & terra statim replenda videretur, si ex eodē Coniugio plures sœpiusq; liberi susciperentur. Nuc autem hominum quotidiana continuáque mortalitas dispendium interitus noua assiduaq; aliorū hominum procreatione, etiam ex eodem coniugio nascentium reparetur. R. Nec hoc ipsum ex Dei verbo definiri potest: etsi de eo nonnihil Augustinus lib 9. cap. 9 de Gen. ad liter. Certum tamen est tunc futuros fuisse compositos, & moderatos omnium hominum affectus, vt neq; lasciuia, neque salacitas, neque intemperies vlla in eorum coitu, vllaue actione futura fuerit. Sed ad statum primi Hominis, qualis fuerit ante peccatum, accedamus. Ad
units.tr: Nothing certain can be determined about this, although we grant and concede that Adam and Ischa (who is also Eve) came together before sin. For the fact that the years of Cain and the others are counted and reckoned from the years of Adam proves or concludes nothing. It is more probable, however, that she did not conceive. Q. Whether, had Adam not sinned, he himself, Eve and their posterity, both males and females, would have remained fruitful forever, and could have begotten children at any age. R. It is plainly a curious question and a rash thing to define. Let this only be laid down: whatever is now a defect of nature, whether in human beings or in anything else, whether a blemish, sterility or infirmity, all of it has come about and been poured in from the sin of Adam. But at the beginning of things, no defects either existed or would have existed without sin. Q. Whether a man who had come together with his own wife before death, in such a way that after she had once borne a child he would no longer know her, since men would have been immortal and the earth seemed to need filling at once, if children were born more often and in greater numbers from the same marriage. But now the daily and continual mortality of men is made good by the loss of others, through the new and constant procreation of other men, even those born from the same marriage. R. Nor can this itself be determined from the word of God, although Augustine says something about it in Book 9, chapter 9, of On Genesis according to the Letter. It is certain, however, that the affections of all men would then have been composed and moderated, so that neither wantonness, nor lust, nor any intemperance would have existed in their coition or in any of their actions. But let us come to the state of the first man, as it was before sin. To

units.la: Ad VIII. De Statu utriusque hominis.
units.tr: Chapter 8. On the State of Each Human Being.

units.la: Q. Vtrum Imago Dei in Adamo, id est, masculo, & Ischa, id est, muliere omnino par erat. R. De hoc ipso videtur Augustinus lib. 12. de Trinit. cap. 12 aliquid quaerere, sed non definire. P. Lombardus lib. 2 Sentent. Distinct. 32. cap. ultimo, de hoc disputat, qui hoc controuerfit, Vtrum omnium hominum anima creentur inter se aequales. Ego vero vt quid sentiam liberè promam, atque symbolum quoque & ipse de ea re meu conferam, Dico Maremquidem & Foeminam id esse, Adamum & Ischa ad eandem vnius & eiusdem Dei, nempe veri Imaginem conditos fuisse, Gen. 1 27: Eius tamen Imaginis radios, viuacitatem splendorem, aciem, & vim in Adamo, quàm in Ischa, .i. in Mare, quàm Foemina maiorem, efficaciorem, & potentiorem fuisse, vti in eodem corpore fortiter manuum est dextera. Ergo & per Maritum Vxor Dei praeceptum didicerat, etiam ante peccatum: & eam Satan per Serpentem potius quàm Adamum adortus & aggressus est, taquam infirmiorem: & prima peccauit Eua, non autem Adam, Gen. 3. 1. Tim. 2. 14. Nam & in Angelis quoque ipsis aliy alys à Deo conditi sunt excellentiores, quanquam omnes ab initio sua originis erant ad Dei imaginem, & eam quidè lucidiorem, quàm Homo, creati, Iob. 4. 18. Iud. ver 6. Hac autem distinctio, discrimenque in posteris Adami, id est, in genere humano postea fuisset observatum. Nam Mares quàm Foemina, viuidiores, viuaciores, atque Ϸασικώτεροι futuri erat. Q. Quid sibi vult Paulus, quum de primo Homine virôque loquens, qualis ante peccatum erat, ait eum fuisse eis ψυχὴν ζῶσαν, id est [animal viuens:] non autem eis πνεῦμα ζωοποιοῦν, id est [Spiritum viuificum.] I.Cor. 15.45. Anut hominis adhuc puri felicem illum statum deiceret. Nam id etiam ad Euam pertinet quanquam à Paulo dicitur de Adamo. Augustinum etiam ipsum vexauit haec quaestio, quemadmodum apparet ex eius libro Genesi ad literam cap. 19. & 25. Lib. 13 Ciuitate Dei cap. 23. Nonnulli existimarunt corpus Adami primum quidem factum fuisse animale: sed quum Adamus in Hortum Edenicum translatus est à Deo, conuersum fuisse in corpus spirituale, vt esset immortale: quam sententiam refutat idem Augustinus, eodem lib. 6. cap. 20, & 23: & certè quoque falsa est. Scholastici de hac eadem quaestione multa, velut Thomas, & Durandus in librum P. Lombardi sententiarum secundum, distinct. 19. Verum ibidem Lombardus ipse melius: Sic enim scribit, [In primo statu fuit corpus Hominis animale, id est, egens alimentis ciborum. Unde & Homo factus dicitur in animam viuentem, non spiritualem, id est, in animam corpus sensificantem, quod adhuc erat animale, non spirituale, quod egebat cibis, vt per animum viueret. Factus est ergo in animam viuentem, id est, vitam corpori dantem per sustentamenta ciborum. Et tunc erat corpus Hominis mortale, & immortale, quia poterat mori, & poterat non mori.] Ergo Adami caro etiam ante peccatum ita immortalis creata est, vt per alimoniam adiuuanda esset, quò mortis & doloris esset expers. Nam Adamus, vt & cetera animalia, ad corporis vitam cibis egebat. Itaque illi à Deo à Deo designatæ ad victum fuerant herbæ, & arborum fructus: & alia animalia quoque Anima viuens nominantur, etsi eorum vita non erat, vt Adami, immortalis Gen. 1. 24, 29. & 30. Ergo anima Adami præbebat eius corpori vitam per cibos, ijsque egebat ad sustentandum corpus, vti & somno ad concoquendum eos, & labore ad vires corporis illius tum recreandas, tum fouendas, vti & in ceteris animantibus. Erat tamen, si Deo obsequeretur Adamus, ettam immortalis corpore futurus, Dei beneficio: non autem ipsius anima, aut natura sua viribus, quemadmodum præclarè respondet Augustinus lib. 6. de Genesi ad liter. cap. 25: quicquid Thomas & Durandus disputent, & Lombardus habet lib. 2. Sententiarum distinct. 19. cap. 2. In animam viuentem dicitur factus esse primus Homo, non in Spiritum viuificantem, quoniam anima est quæ corpus viuificat, ne sit mortuum cadauer. Ergo ab ea iure denominationem sumit. Post resurrectionem præstantior erit vis illa viuifica, quam à Spiritu Dei corpus accipiet. Huius autem Dei beneficij, futuræque istius immortalitatis etiam in corpore, (Nam anima hominis, quoniam erat imago Dei, erat immortalis) Arbor vitæ erat Adamo signum & symbolum: at post Resurrectionem, vti ait Paulus, erit Homo in Spiritum viuificantem, nõ quod aliud ἔσται corpus, animamque aliam fit habiturus homo, quàm ea est, quam nunc habet. Sed anima Deo plena, illique indiuulsè coniuncta, perfectèque per Christiu tunc instaurata, nullis cibis & alimentis ad sustentandum corpus sibi adiunctum egebit: Verùm vi illa, petestate, & efficacitate (quâ immediatè à Deo accipiet, & qua Spiritus vocatur) se, corpusque suum potenter absque alio adminiculo sustinebit. Erit enim Deus tunc omnia in omnibus. Tanta igitur vis immediate tunc in animā à Deo infusa dicitur à Paulo [Spiritus vivificans] 1. Cor. 15.45. Anima vero qualis erat, estque cibis egēs etiam in primo Adamo nō quidem ad se, sed ad corpus suum tuendum, vocatur à Paulo [Anima viuens.] Vide Damascenum libro 4 Orthodoxæ fidei cap. 28.
units.tr: Q. Whether the image of God in Adam, that is, the male, and in Ischa, that is, the woman, was wholly equal. R. Augustine seems to inquire into this very question in On the Trinity 12.12, but he does not settle it. Peter Lombard, Sentences 2, distinction 32, last chapter, also discusses it, in the same question: whether the souls of all human beings are created equal. Now, to state my own view freely, and to offer my own opinion on the matter as well: I say that the man and the woman were both created in the image of the one and same God, that is, the true God (Gen. 1:27). Yet the rays of that image, its vitality, brilliance, keenness and power, were greater, more effective and more potent in Adam than in Ischa, that is, in the male than in the female, just as the right hand is stronger in the same body. Hence the wife had learned God's command through her husband, even before the fall; and Satan attacked and assailed her through the serpent rather than Adam, as the weaker one. Eve sinned first, not Adam (Gen. 3; 1 Tim. 2:14). For among the angels too, some were created by God more excellent than others, although all were from the beginning made in God's image, and indeed more brilliant than man (Job 4:18; Jude v. 6). This distinction and difference, moreover, was afterwards to be observed among the posterity of Adam, that is, in the human race. For males were to be more lively, more vigorous and more animal [ψυχικώτεροι] than females. Q. What does Paul mean when, speaking of the first man and husband as he was before the fall, he says that he was a living soul [ψυχὴν ζῶσαν], that is, [an animal living], and not a life-giving spirit [πνεῦμα ζωοποιοῦν], that is, [a quickening spirit] (1 Cor. 15:45)? Surely this would dislodge the happy state of man still in his innocence. For this applies also to Eve, although Paul speaks of Adam. Augustine himself was troubled by this question, as is clear from his Literal Commentary on Genesis, chapters 19 and 25, and from The City of God 13.23. Some have thought that Adam's body was at first made animal, but that when Adam was transferred by God into the Garden of Eden, it was changed into a spiritual body, so that it would be immortal. Augustine refutes this opinion in the same work, book 6, chapters 20 and 23; and indeed it is also false. The Schoolmen have said much about this same question, as Thomas and Durandus do on the second book of Peter Lombard's Sentences, distinction 19. But Lombard himself there says it better. For he writes thus: [In the first state the human body was animal, that is, needing food. Hence man is also said to have been made into a living soul, not a spiritual one, that is, into a soul that gives sensation to the body, which was still animal and not spiritual, and which needed food in order to live by its breath. He was therefore made into a living soul, that is, one giving life to the body through the sustenance of food. And at that time the human body was both mortal and immortal, because it could die and it could not die.] Therefore Adam's flesh was created immortal even before the fall in such a way that it had to be helped by nourishment, so that it would be free from death and pain. For Adam, like the other animals, needed food to sustain the life of his body. Accordingly, herbs and the fruit of trees were appointed by God as his food; and other animals too are called a living soul, although their life was not immortal, as Adam's was (Gen. 1:24, 29, 30). So Adam's soul supplied his body with life through food, and it needed food to sustain the body, as it also needed sleep to digest it and labour to refresh and cherish the strength of that body, as also in the other living creatures. Yet if Adam obeyed God, he would have been immortal in body too, by God's favour, not by the powers of his own soul or nature; as Augustine rightly answers in his Literal Commentary on Genesis 6.25, whatever Thomas and Durandus may argue, and whatever Lombard holds in Sentences 2, distinction 19, chapter 2. The first man is said to have been made into a living soul, not into a quickening spirit, because it is the soul that gives life to the body, so that it is not a dead corpse. Therefore it takes its name from the soul. After the resurrection that quickening power, which the body will receive from the Spirit of God, will be greater. But the Tree of Life was a sign and symbol for Adam of this favour of God and of that future immortality in the body as well (for the soul of man, since it was the image of God, was immortal). But after the resurrection, as Paul says, man will be a quickening spirit; not that man will have a different body [ἔσται] and a different soul from what he now has.
