Rather, the soul, full of God and inseparably joined to him, and then perfectly restored through Christ, will need no food to sustain the body joined to it. Instead, by that power, that efficacy, by which it will receive immediately from God and which is called Spirit, it will sustain itself and its body powerfully, without any other support. For God will then be all in all. Thus Paul calls the power poured immediately into the soul by God at that time [the quickening Spirit] (1 Cor. 15:45). But the soul, as it was and as it is, needing food even in the first Adam, not for itself but to preserve its body, is called by Paul [the living soul]. See Damascene, On the Orthodox Faith 4.28.

units.la: Q. Quomodo Homo corpus immortale habebat, si cibo sustentabatur. Nam corpus illud fame corrumpi non poterat: quamobrem cibo non egebat. Praeterea, si propter peccatum mortalis effectus est Homo, vtique ante peccatum non egebat talibus cibis. R. Vt intelligeret Homo se solo Dei beneficio, (quandiu Homo ipse pareret Deo) nō natura, id est, materiæ (qua ipsius corpus constabat, & unde desumptum fuerat) vt & potestate futurum immortalem, voluit Deus, vt Hominis corpus, sicut & caeterorum animātium, opus haberet cibis, & esca ad se tuendum. Id quod docet Augustinus lib. 13. Ciuit. Dei, cap. 23. lib. 3. Genesi ad liter. cap. 21: & confirmatur Gen. 1.29, 30. Quare corpus illud natura quidem mortale erat: sed Dei gratiâ & sustentatione futurum erat immortale. Itaque fame corrumpi poterat per se. Sic Christi corpus natura sua frangibile fuit, & corruptibile: Dei vero decreto fuit infrangibile & incorruptibile. Psal. 16, Exo. 12.46, Num 9.12, Ioan 19.36. Q. Si cibis egebat homo, vt & caetera animalia: quibus hac suam vitam sustentaret, & quum eosdem cibos homo ederet, quos animantia reliqua, cur non & hac quoque immortalia futura erant. R. Augustinus in lib. Quæst. Veteris & Novi Testamenti cap. 19. respondet, Arbor vita, medicina modo, in homine corruptionem omnem prohibebat, ac prohibitura fuerat: ex qua solus Homo edebat, non etiam reliqua animantia. Ergo illa non fuissent immortalia, sed solus Homo. Nam gustus arboris vitæ corruptionem corporis inhibebat: adeo quidem ut, si quemadmodum ibidem scribit Augustinus, post peccatum de eadem arbore illi concessum fuisset edere, Indissolubilis mansisset. Gen. 3. 22. Q. Virum in Adami corpore, quemadmodum nunc in nostris aliquid ante peccatum deperditum fuisset, quod cibis, & novo alimento sarciendum esset. R. De hoc ipso anxie Thomas in lib. 2. sentent. P. Lombardi dist. 19. Art. 1, & Durandus quaest. 2. N. 3, disputant. Certe deperditum aliquid fuisset, quod tamen nonnisi cibus plene in primo homine & ceteris restituisset. In aliis autem animantibus non item. Ergo hac mortalia, ille vero immortalis futurus erat. Nam corporis humani destructio futura non erat, quum ex eo quicquid esset deperditum, integre illi reponeretur. Cibus enim perfecte in alimentum convertebatur, & eadem mensura, vi concoctionis, restituebatur, qua oportebat, & prius in Homine erat.
units.tr: Q. How did man have an immortal body if he was sustained by food? For that body could not be corrupted by hunger, and so it had no need of food. Moreover, if man became mortal because of sin, then before sin he certainly did not need such foods. R. So that man might understand that he lived on by God's favour alone (as long as man himself obeyed God), and not by his nature, that is, by the matter of which his body consisted and from which it had been taken, God willed that man's body should, like that of the other animals, need food and nourishment to sustain itself, and so be immortal by power. This is taught by Augustine in The City of God 13.23 and in his Literal Commentary on Genesis 3.21, and is confirmed by Gen. 1:29, 30. Wherefore that body was indeed mortal by nature, but by God's grace and sustenance it was to be immortal. So it could by itself be corrupted by hunger. Thus Christ's body was by its nature breakable and corruptible, but by God's decree it was unbreakable and incorruptible (Ps. 16; Exod. 12:46; Num. 9:12; John 19:36). Q. If man needed food, as the other animals do, by which to sustain his life, and if man ate the same foods as the other living creatures, why would these not also be immortal? R. Augustine, in Questions on the Old and New Testament, chapter 19, answers that the Tree of Life, merely as a remedy, prevented and was to prevent all corruption in man. Only man ate from it, not the other living creatures. Therefore those others would not have been immortal, but only man. For tasting the Tree of Life checked the corruption of the body; indeed, as Augustine writes in the same place, if after the fall it had been permitted to man to eat of that tree, he would have remained indissoluble (Gen. 3:22). Q. Whether something was lost in Adam's body before the fall, as something is now lost in ours, which had to be made good by food and new nourishment. R. Thomas anxiously disputes this very question on the second book of Peter Lombard's Sentences, distinction 19, article 1, and Durandus on question 2, number 3. Surely something would have been lost, which nevertheless only food could fully restore in the first man and in the others; but in the other living creatures it was not so. Therefore these were mortal, but he was to be immortal. For the destruction of the human body was not going to happen, since whatever was lost from it would be fully replaced to him. For food was perfectly converted into nourishment, and by the power of digestion it was restored in the same measure as was needed and as had been in man before.

units.la: Q. Qua statura Adamus a Deo primum conditus est: Item & Ischa. R. Perfectissima, & consummatissima, adeo ut quicquid subsequentibus momentis & temporibus postea rebus inchoatis accedit, Deus rebus a se primum creatis indederit. Fuerunt quidem res primum creatæ rerum eiusdem generis postea gignendarum velut femina: sed erant ipsæ in se absolu-
units.tr: Q. In what stature was Adam first created by God? Likewise Eve? R. In the most perfect and most complete stature, so that whatever comes afterward, in the later moments and times, as things are begun, God had already given to the things he first created. The first-created things were, indeed, the seeds of the kinds of things to be produced later, as the woman is for the man. Yet they were in themselves most absolute-

units.la: D tissimè. Sic Augustinus lib.6.Gen.ad liter.cap.10, 11. Imò etiam idem lib. 13.cap.24. Ciuit. Dei, scribit ea primorum parentum corpora,ac proinde ceterorum, perperpetuò in iuuentutis flore fuisse permansura,id est, in eô vigore,in quo est adulta Hominum etas,seu virilis, Ephe 4 13 Reliqua pete ex Gregorij Niceni libro de Creatione Hominis,quae pertinent ad corpus hominis. Quae vero ad eiusdem Animam,ex nostrae Isagoges Christianae Tractatu De Homine.
units.tr: ly so. Thus Augustine, On Genesis according to the Letter, book 6, chapters 10 and 11. Indeed, in the same work, book 13, chapter 24, of The City of God, he writes that the bodies of the first parents, and therefore of all others, would remain forever in the flower of youth, that is, in that vigour in which the adult or manly age of men is. Ephe 4 13 For the rest, seek from Gregory of Nyssa's book On the Creation of Man, which concern the body of man. But what concerns its soul, from our Christian Isagoge, the treatise On Man.

units.la: CAPVT III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: Vestigia superioris Veritatis, & Historiae
units.tr: Traces of the Earlier Truth and History

units.la: ETVSTISSIMAE Rerum Historia, & ipsorum Mundi penè incunabulorum certe natalium (quae res est nobis antiquissima) vestigia, quae, magna Dei providentia, superfuncts, collectarum, praefari debeo. Nihil quidem esse Ethnicorum scriptorum testimonijs (quae huic veritati nostris .i. Sacris literis comprehensae consentiunt) admirabilius: nihil tamen à plerisque magis esse aut omnino neglectum, aut minus observatum, & annotatum. Cuius rei duplex ratio afferri potest:Vna, quòd res ista, quamquam verissima, dum ab ipsisinet profanis, fanis,& veri Dei ignaris hominibus recitantur,appellantur fabulæ,quemadmodum lib 1.Bibliotheca scribit & eas nominat Diodorus Siculus. Ex quo fit, ut tota hac prima mundi ætas ea,quæ sunt fabulosa, duntaxat completa ab ys censeatur. Falsò quidem: sed tamen quoniam vetustissimam hominum memoriam continet, (cui plerique non assentiuntur) idcirco ea & ignota, & difficilis,& fabulosa dicta est,ut docet Plato,illum tamen vbiq; sanctissimus studiosissimúsque inuestigator, custos,& patronus, vti tum 3.lib.de Leg.tũ in Timæo Dialogo. Altera neglecta tam vetustæ historiæ caussa est, Ipsamet eius Antiquitas, quæ facit vt à multis ignoretur:ac proinde minimè vera esse credatur. Præclarè enim Augustinus lib. 16.Ciuitate Dei cap.43. Hæc prima Mundi ætas velut infantia Mundi fuit: quam demergit oblivio, sicut deleta est diluuio. Præterea quotus quisq; est, qui suam recordetur infantiæ? Ergo nec Mundi primam infantiam norunt Homines: verùm suâ maximâ culpâ,vitioq;. Nam hoc pacto & Deum laude pulcherrimorum ipsius, quæ tunc extiterunt,operum fraudant: & seipsos vtilissima,& incundissima rerum notitia. Voluit tamen Deus etiam istarum,quàtumvis à nostro seculo remotarum rerum,vestigia etiam apud ipsosmet homines Verbi ipsius contemptores extare ad sua veritatis confirmationem , & hominum ipsorum arguendum stuporem ab ipsismet hominibus. Ergo etiam in hac ipsa prima Mundi historia euenit, quod habet proverbium vetus, σφὸς ἀλλὰ ἀλλ' ἀλλος,id est,vt Sapiés doceatur vnum ab altero: & per manus tam necessaria cognitio primùm traderetur, post autem etiam literis mãdaretur ac consigna-retur, ne prorsus tādem perireт ex hominum memoria. Atque huius veritatis tam augusta, tamq; conformia Dei verbo vestigia, & Ethnicorum testimonia collegerunt quedā ante nos nonnulli, velut Lactantius septem libris: Eusebius de Praeparatione Evangelica: Augustinus varie, sed imprimis in libris de Civitate Dei: Cyrillus in libris contra Julianum: Theodoritus in libello περὶ ἑλληνικῶν παδημάτων. Denique nostro hoc seculo doctissimè Philippus Marneus-Plessieus in libro De Veritate Christiana. Nos vero quanquam fortasse non Pindarica diligentia & interpretatione nostra addemus: quia tamen id instituti nostri ratio policitationes requirit, breviter ista eadem veritatis huius antiquissima vestigia colligemus, & recitabimus ex Ethnicis ipsis, illa quidem e multis pauca, & tantum ea, quae ante Christi Domini nostri adventum, fidemque Evangelicam inter Gentes propagatam in libris infidelium hominum extat, quo certius appareat illa Ethnicorum Dicta ex ipsa vetustissima traditione inter eos populariter recepta emanasse, & eos cum Divina veritate, quam sequimur consensisse. Caeterum saepe contenti fuimus locos ipsos autorum notasse: verba vero eorum non transcripsimus, quoniam id fuisset infinitum: & ea ipsa potest per se quisq; apud ipsos Autores perlegere. Quadam tamen describimus.
units.tr: I must first say something about the traces of the most ancient history, and of the very beginnings of the world's birth, which is for us the most ancient matter. By the great providence of God, some of these traces have survived, and I shall gather them. Nothing is more remarkable than the testimonies of the non-Christian writers, which agree with this truth as it is contained in our Sacred Letters. Yet most people have either neglected or paid less attention to them and noted them less. There are two reasons for this. The first is that these matters, though most true, when they are recounted by the profane, the godless, and men ignorant of the true God, are called fables, as Diodorus Siculus calls them in the first book of his Library. As a result, this whole first age of the world is regarded as consisting only of fabulous things, though falsely. Yet because it contains the most ancient memory of mankind, which many do not accept, it has therefore been called unknown, difficult, and fabulous, as Plato teaches. Plato, however, everywhere remains the most holy, most diligent investigator, guardian, and patron of it, both in the third book of the Laws and in the Timaeus dialogue. The second reason this ancient history is neglected is its very antiquity, which causes many to be ignorant of it, and so to think it not true at all. Augustine, in the sixteenth book of the City of God, chapter 43, puts it well: this first age of the world was as it were the infancy of the world, which oblivion submerges just as the Flood destroyed it. Moreover, how few people are there who remember their own infancy? So men do not know the first infancy of the world, but this is through their own great fault and vice. For in this way they defraud God of the praise of his most beautiful works, which then existed, and they defraud themselves of the most useful and pleasant knowledge of things. Yet God willed that traces of these matters, however far removed they are from our age, should also survive among men themselves, even among those who despise the Word of God, both to confirm his truth and to convict men of their own stupidity, drawn from men themselves. So in this first history of the world also there happens what the old proverb says, one man learns from another [σοφὸς ἀλλ᾽ ἄλλος], that is, that the wise is taught by one another. Thus this necessary knowledge was first handed down by hand, and afterwards committed to writing and sealed, lest at last it perish utterly from human memory. Several men before us have gathered these traces of truth, so august and so agreeing with the Word of God, together with the testimonies of the Gentiles. Among them are Lactantius in seven books, Eusebius in his Preparation for the Gospel, Augustine in various places, but chiefly in the books of the City of God, Cyril in his books against Julian, and Theodoret in his little book on the Greek remedies. Finally, in our own century, Philippe du Plessis Mornay has done this most learnedly in his book On the Christian Truth. As for me, though perhaps I shall not add anything with Pindaric diligence and interpretation, nevertheless, since the plan of my undertaking requires it, I shall briefly gather and recite these same most ancient traces of this truth, drawn from the Gentiles themselves. I shall give a few from many, and only those which exist in the books of unbelievers from before the coming of our Lord Christ and the spread of the Evangelical faith among the nations. This will make it clearer that those sayings of the Gentiles flowed from the most ancient tradition generally received among them, and that they agree with the divine truth which we follow. Otherwise, I have often been content merely to note the places of the authors themselves, and I have not transcribed their words, since that would have been endless. Anyone can read them through in the authors themselves. Still, some I shall describe.

units.la: Ad I. De Mundi Creatione.
units.tr: I. On the Creation of the World.

units.la: AIT igitur Moses, [DEVS] Deum esse, eum, qui haec omnia produxerit, docet Trismegistus auctor tor vetustissimus in Pimandro, Dialogo primo. Moses ait tenebras fuisse super faciem Abyssi: Trismegistus se vidisse, & extuisse umbram quandam horrendam, quae in rebus producendis demigrabat in humidam naturam. Moses docet omnia potenti Dei verbo facta: Trismegistus, Verbum illud, quod Mundum fecit, esse verbum lucens, omnia illuminans, germen mentis Divinae, Filius Dei. Ait Moses, Spiritus Dei fovebat molem aquarum: Trismegistus ait, Verbum vocis suae sono fouisse humidam illam naturam, illiusque adstitisse. Moses denique ait, Et Deus dixit, [Crescite, & multiplicamini:] Trismegistus scribit, [Extemplo Verbo sancto Deus clamavit, Pullulate, adolescite, propagate universa germina, & opera mea.] Quid igitur magis esse potest conforme Mosi, & verbo Dei? Linus Poeta vetustissimus Graecus, ut est apud Diogenem Laertium, initio libri primi de Vitis Philosophorum, sic scripsit, [Tempus erat, quo cuncta simul sunt condita quondam] Orpheus in Argonautis, & Hesiodus in Theogonia Mundum coepisse, & ex quodam Chao a Deo factum fuisse diserte tradunt. Imo etiam idem Orpheus versibus scripsit librum περὶ κοσμοποιίας, id est, De Creatione Mundi. Nonne vero haec sunt verissima nostrae veritatis vestigia, quae etiam apud Ethnicos apparent? Empedocles idem quoque docuit. Plato tum in Protagora, tum in Politico, tum in Timaeo quoque, Mundum & factum non aeternum, & quidem a Deo absque circuitione docet. Id quod Plutarchus quoque diligens eius lector observavit, & in Psychogonia annotavit. Platonici vero omnes, aut Varro, idem sentiunt. Nam tradunt Mundum aliquando coepisse, non autem aeternum esse. Imo ipsemet Varro Historia à Creatione Mundi ad primam Olympiadem contexuerat. Stoici Philosophi & ipsi Ethnici idem probarunt. Ovidius lib.
units.tr: Moses therefore says that God is God, the one who produced all these things. Trismegistus, the author, the most ancient, in Pimander, first dialogue, teaches this. Moses says that darkness was over the face of the abyss; Trismegistus says that he saw and beheld a certain horrible shadow, which in the production of things passed over into the moist nature. Moses teaches that all things were made by the powerful word of God; Trismegistus says that the Word which made the world is a shining word, illuminating all things, the offspring of the divine mind, the Son of God. Moses says, The Spirit of God brooded over the mass of waters; Trismegistus says that the Word warmed that moist nature with the sound of its voice and stood beside it. Moses finally says, And God said, [Increase and multiply]; Trismegistus writes, [Immediately God cried out to the holy Word: Sprout, grow up, propagate all the germs and my works.] What therefore can be more in accord with Moses and the word of God? Linus, the most ancient Greek poet, as found in Diogenes Laertius at the beginning of the first book of the Lives of the Philosophers, wrote thus: [There was a time when all things were created together once.] Orpheus in the Argonautica and Hesiod in the Theogony plainly report that the world began and was made by God out of a certain Chaos. Indeed the same Orpheus wrote a book in verse, peri kosmopoiias [περὶ κοσμοποιίας], that is, On the Creation of the World. Are not these the most true traces of our truth, which appear even among the heathen? Empedocles taught the same. Plato, in the Protagoras, in the Politicus and also in the Timaeus, teaches that the world was made, not eternal, and indeed made by God without any circuity. Plutarch, a diligent reader of Plato, observed this too and noted it in the Psychogony. Indeed all the Platonists, or Varro, hold the same view. For they hand down that the world once began and is not eternal. Indeed Varro himself composed a history from the creation of the world to the first Olympiad. The Stoic philosophers and the heathen themselves likewise proved the same.

units.la: 1. Metamorphoseos, ex Hesiodi, & Anaxagora sententia, nonne manifestissime Mundum à Deo aliquando conditum ac formatum canit, docetque quum ait,
units.tr: Ovid, in the first book of the Metamorphoses, following the opinion of Hesiod and Anaxagoras, does he not most clearly sing that the world was once created and formed by God, when he says:

units.la: [Ante mare, & terras, & quod tegit omnia, caelu, Vnus erat toto natura vultus in Orbe, Quem dixere Chaos, rudis indigestaque moles. Hanc Deus & melior litem natura diremit. Nam caelo terras, & terris abscidit undas. Quae postquam euoluit, caecoque exemit acervo, Dissociata locis concordi pace ligavit.] Seneca de vita Beata cap. 31. Item lib. 1. Quaest. naturalium. Cyrillus ex Ethnicis scriptoribus idem confirmat lib. 2 contra Iulian. & Eusebius lib. 9. cap. 4. de Praeparatione Euangelica. Lactantius quoque Firmianus ex Sibyllinis versibus lib. 1. Diuinarum Institutionum cap. 6. hoc ipsum demonstrat.
units.tr: "Before sea and lands, and the sky that covers all things, there was one face of nature across the whole orb, which they called Chaos: a rough and undigested mass. God, and a better nature, divided this strife. For he parted the heaven from the earth, and the earth from the waters. And when he had unrolled these and taken them from the blind heap, he bound them, separated in place, in harmonious peace." Seneca, On the Happy Life, ch. 31; likewise Natural Questions, book 1. Cyril, drawing on the heathen writers, confirms the same in book 2 against Julian, and Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel, book 9, ch. 4. Lactantius Firmianus also demonstrates this very thing from the Sibylline verses, Divine Institutes, book 1, ch. 6.

units.la: Ἀλλὰ Θεὸς μόνος εἷς ταυτὸν τὸ πάντα ποιήσας Οὐρανὸν, ἡλίον τε, σελήνην, ἀστέρας, ἢ δὲ Σελήνην, Καρπορόφον γαῖαν τε, ἀλλὰ ὑδάτων οἰδματα πάντα. Id est,
units.tr: [But God alone is one, who made all things: the heaven, the sun, the moon, the stars, and the earth bearing fruit, and all the swellings of the waters.] (Ἀλλὰ Θεὸς μόνος εἷς ταυτὸν τὸ πάντα ποιήσας Οὐρανὸν, ἡλίον τε, σελήνην, ἀστέρας, ἢ δὲ Σελήνην, Καρπορόφον γαῖαν τε, ἀλλὰ ὑδάτων οἰδματα πάντα.)

units.la: Est Deus & summusque, unusque: Hic omnia fecit Et caelum, & Solem, Lunamque, & Sydera caeli, Frugiferam Terramque, & vasti littora Ponti.
units.tr: God is, and highest, and one: he made all these things, the heaven, the sun, the moon, and the stars of heaven, the fruitful earth, and the shores of the vast sea.

units.la: Idem Lactant. lib. 7. cap. 7. Ex quibus pene infinitis Ethnicorum testimonijs Deum Mundum hunc condidisse apparet.
units.tr: The same Lactantius in the seventh book, chapter 7. From almost endless testimonies of the Gentiles it is clear that God created this world.

units.la: CREAVIT INITIO] Trismegistus in Pi-
units.tr: HE CREATED IN THE BEGINNING

units.la: Pimand. Dialogo II. confutat eos, qui negant Deum aliquando potuisse efficere hunc Mundum. Plutarchus in Psychogonia reprehendit Heraclitum, qui Mundũ hunc, neque à Deo, neque ab Homine potuisse vnquam fieri contendebat. Etsi vero Philosophi non concedunt ex nihilo factum esse hunc Mundum: tamen ydem & factum esse, & quidem in tempore, eoque certo non antem eum ab æterno cœpisse fatentur. Imo de eo consensu pene Mortalium omnium fuit, Mundum hunc existendi principium seu initium habuisse quemadmodum tradit Diodorus Siculus lib. I.cap. I. Itaque Plato tũ in Protagora, vti dixi, tum in Politico, tum in Timæo disertè docet Mundum in tempore productum fuisse. Quin vero idem Diodorus Siculus à bello Troiano ad sua tempora tradit intercessisse tantum Annos 1138. At Lactantius lib. 4. cap. 6. scribit à Propheta Mose ad bellum Troianum, non plus quàm 900. annos interuenisse, ac fluxisse. Porro à Mundi principio vsque ad Mosem extinctum seu mortuum, sunt, vt apparet ex Dei verbo, anni 2553. Summa ergo iam ista tota collecta efficit annos 4591, qui fluxerunt à Creatione Mundi ad Diodori Siculi, qui vixit sub finem imperij Augusti, ætatem ex ipsorummet Ethnicorum testimonio. Quæ secutus Macrobius lib. I. Saturnal. minimè vetustam esse ait huius Mundi ætatem. Cæterum de Creatione Mundi hæc sunt quoque apud eos vestigia, quòd in Mundi materia definienda ipsi variant. Nam materiam Mundi censuerunt nonnulli Ethnici Philosophi rudem primùm & informem cui tenebræ insidebant: eamq; etiam nominarunt Chaos, vt Hesiodus, Anaxagoras, Ouidius. Alij eam materiam maluerunt esse terram, vti veteres quoque plerique Philosophi, quemadmodum scribit Plutarchus, quâ barbarè Moth, Græce ὕλην, id est limum (a quo ὕλη per inuersionem literarum factum est vocabulum) vocabant, ex quo limo nata sunt, ortâque omnia. Quod quàm parum à Creatione abest? Verùm recte Plesseius in lib. de Veritate Christiana cap. 10. Recte inquam, argumentatur ei, qui Mundum conditum à Deo fatetur, esse necesse, vt ex nihilo, non autè ex precedente materia vlla factum agnoscat, ac concedat. Alioqui progressus fiet in infinitum. Quod ipsum antea Tertullianus contra Hermogenem seu Materiarios docuerat. Sic ex nihilo creatum esse Mundum apparet. Imo Sibylla apud Lactantium, libro 4. capite 6. Deum vocat κτισὴν, id est, Creatorem disserte, non tantum δημιουργὸν, id est, Exornatorem Mundi.
units.tr: Trismegistus, in Pimander, Dialogue II, refutes those who deny that God could ever have made this world. Plutarch, in the Psychogony, rebukes Heraclitus, who maintained that this world could never have been made either by God or by man. Although the philosophers do not concede that this world was made out of nothing, they nevertheless confess that it was made, and indeed in time, and at a definite moment, and that it did not begin from eternity. Indeed there was almost universal agreement among all mortals that this world had a beginning or origin of existence, as Diodorus Siculus relates in book I, chapter I. Thus Plato, as I said, clearly teaches in the Protagoras, in the Politicus and in the Timaeus that the world was produced in time. Diodorus Siculus also relates that only 1138 years passed from the Trojan War to his own times. But Lactantius, book 4, chapter 6, writes that from the Prophet Moses to the Trojan War no more than 900 years intervened and elapsed. Moreover, from the beginning of the world to the death of Moses there are, as appears from the word of God, 2553 years. The sum of all these, therefore, makes 4591 years that elapsed from the Creation of the world to Diodorus Siculus, who lived at the end of the reign of Augustus, by the testimony of the pagans themselves. Following these figures, Macrobius, book I, Saturnalia, says that the age of this world is by no means very ancient. Furthermore, there are also traces among them of the Creation of the world, in that they disagree among themselves in defining the matter of the world. For some pagan philosophers held that the matter of the world was at first crude and formless, and over it lay darkness; and they called it Chaos, as Hesiod, Anaxagoras and Ovid did. Others preferred that this matter be earth, as did many of the ancient philosophers too, as Plutarch writes, which they called in barbarian fashion Moth, in Greek hyle, that is, mud (from which the word hyle came by transposition of letters), and from this mud, they said, all things were born and arose. How little does this differ from Creation? But Plessis rightly argues, in his book On the Truth of Christianity, chapter 10, rightly I say, that for one who confesses that the world was made by God, it must be acknowledged and conceded that it was made out of nothing, and not out of any preceding matter. Otherwise there would be an infinite regress. Tertullian had taught this earlier against Hermogenes, or the Materialists. Thus it is clear that the world was created out of nothing. Indeed the Sibyl, in Lactantius, book 4, chapter 6, calls God ktisēn [κτισὴν], that is, Creator, clearly, and not merely dēmiourgon [δημιουργὸν], that is, Fashioner of the world.

units.la: OMNIA] Aristoteles in lib. de Mundo ait, Νὸς αὐτὸς ὅλῳ πάντων, & eadem Mens cuiq;, rerum generi dat motum. Idem in lib. de Admiral. Audition. scribit, Mare olim tegebat totam terram, verùm Deus terra partem discooperuit in vsum hominum. Id quod etiamsunte eum dixerat Trismegistus in Pimandro. Animalia omnia primùm ex terra & aqua emanasse scripsit Euripides, & post eum Diodorus Sicul. eamq; fuisse veterum Philosophorum sententiam tradit Plutarchus lib. 1. de Placitis Philosoph. cap. 2. Horatius, [Quum prorepserunt primis animalia terris] Quae omnia cum Historia Sacra consentiunt. Illa enim docet omnia Animalia vel ex aquis, vel è terra orta fuisse Dei
units.tr: ALL THINGS Aristotle, in the book On the World, says: "Mind itself through the whole of all things" [Νοῦς αὐτὸς ὅλῳ πάντων], and the same Mind gives motion to each kind of thing. In the book On Admirable Hearings, he likewise writes that the sea once covered the whole earth, but God uncovered part of the land for the use of men. This Trismegistus also said in Pimander. Euripides wrote that all animals first emanated from earth and water, and after him Diodorus Siculus did so, and Plutarch, book 1 of On the Opinions of the Philosophers, chapter 2, relates that this was the opinion of the ancient philosophers. Horace says: "When living creatures crept forth onto the first lands." All of these agree with Sacred History, for that teaches that all animals arose either from the waters or from the earth by the command and precept of God. The pagans too hold and teach this same thing. What greater trace of our truth could be required? Aratus, in the Phaenomena, writes that the Sun, Moon and the other heavenly stars were made to be signs for us, and for the distinction of days and seasons. Thales of Miletus said that the night precedes the day in the artificial reckoning, that is, the day is the lit part, as Plutarch says in the Table Talk. The Druids taught the same, as Gaius Julius Caesar recorded in book 6 of his Commentaries on the Gallic War: "Thus the Gauls counted time so that the night came before the day." Do not these things agree plainly with Sacred Scripture?

units.la: {a} Aristoteles, Ouidius: marginal references, partly cut off at the foot of the page. Dsi iussu, & præcepto. Hoc idem & isti quoq; Ethnici sentiunt & docent. Ecquod igitur nostra veritatis vestigium maius requiri potest? Solem, Lunam, & reliqua cœli sydera condita fuisse, vt essent nobis in signa, & dierum & temporum distinctionem, scribit Aratus in Phænomenis. Noctem die artificiali, id est, lucente priorem dixit Thales Milefius, vt ait Plutarchus in Conuiuio. Idem Druydæ docuerunt, quemadmodum Caius Iulius Cæsar lib. 6. Comment. Belli Gall. memoriæ prodidit, Itaque sic tempora numerabant Galli, vt diem nox præcederet. Hæc vero nonne plane cum Sacra Scriptura consentiunt?
units.tr: {a} Aristotle, Ovid: marginal references, partly cut off at the foot of the page. By the command and precept of God. The Gentiles too perceive and teach this same thing. What greater trace of our truth can be sought? That the Sun, the Moon and the other heavenly stars were created to be signs for us, and for the distinction of days and seasons, Aratus writes in his Phaenomena. Thales of Miletus said that night comes before day in the artificial reckoning, that is, the lit day, as Plutarch reports in the Symposium. The Druids taught the same, as Gaius Julius Caesar recorded in book 6 of his Commentaries on the Gallic War: "And so the Gauls reckoned time in such a way that the night came before the day." Do not these things agree plainly with Holy Scripture?

units.la: TERVERBVM] Trifmegistus in Pimandro, Dial. 5. ait, [Mundum hunc Verbo, nō manibus fabricatum est opifex Deus.] Hoc autem Verbum idem Trif. Dial. 1. ait esse Intelligentiam seu Sapientiam æternam, quæ est etiam Filius Dei primogenitus, & mera eius voluntate, non coitu ab eo genitus. Orpheus citante Cyrillo, lib. 1. contra Iulian. in Cosmogonia sic scripsit,
units.tr: THE WORD. Trismegistus in Pimander, Dialogue 5, says: "God the Maker fashioned this world by the Word, not by hands." Moreover, the same Trismegistus, in Dialogue 1, says that this Word is eternal Intelligence or Wisdom, which is also the firstborn Son of God, begotten of him by his pure will, not by intercourse. Orpheus, as cited by Cyril in book 1 against Julian, wrote thus in the Cosmogony:

units.la: [Cœlum adiuro te Dei magni sapiens opus: Vocem adiuro te Patris, quā locutus est primū Pater, Quum Mundum vniuersum suis firmauit consilijs.] Idem in Argonautis sapius repetit. Lactantius lib. 4. cap. 6. ex Sibylla citat hos versus in eandem plane sententiam, consentientésq;, cū veritate superius explicata.
units.tr: "I adjure you by heaven, the wise work of the great God; I adjure you by the voice of the Father, with which the Father first spoke, when he established the whole world by his counsels." He repeats the same thing often in the Argonautica. Lactantius, book 4, chapter 6, cites from the Sibyl these verses to the same effect, agreeing with the truth explained above.

units.la: Πάντα τεύχον κτίσιν, ὅσις γλυκὺ πνεῦμα ἀπαστ Κάτθετο, χ' ἡμῆτε ... θεῶν πάντων ἐποιησε. Αὐτὸν εἰ ὄντα θεὸς πιστοῖς ἀνδρῶσι γεραίρειν. Αὐτὸς σὺν γίνωσκει θεὸν θεῶ ὁμὸν ἐοντα. Id est, Hunc(vitam qui dat cunctis,essq; omniū alumnus, Cuncta creans) cunctis prefecit Regibus ille. Hunc cunctis Sanctis venerandum prabet eundem. Hunc agnosce Deum,natúmque Dei Patris esse. Ergo etiam huius veritatis vestigia tam magna inEthnicorum scriptis extant, vt eos, si illam negent, ex illis confutemus.
units.tr: Panta teuchon ktisin, hosis glykys pneuma apasi / Katthete, ch' hēmeteron ... theōn pantōn epoiēse. Auton ei onta theon pistoi andrasin gerairein. Auton sy gignōske theon theō homoion eonta. Translation: "He who gives life to all things, and is the nourisher of all, creating all things, he set over all kings. Him let all the holy venerate, and let them make him known. Recognise him as God, and the Son of God the Father." Therefore, the traces of this truth are so great in the writings of the pagans that, if they deny it, we may refute them from those very writings.

units.la: Ad II. De Creatione Hominis.
units.tr: Ad II. On the Creation of Man.

units.la: EX LIMO SEV PVLVERE Terra] Creatum Hominem ex limo seu pulvere Terra docet Moses, eundemq; esse vocatum Adamum. Hominem ex limo terra primùm conditum fuisse Abydenus, & Alexander prodiderunt, vt refert Eusebius lib.9.cap. 4.de Praeparatione Euangel. Idem ipsum ex veterum Ethnicorum sententia Diodorus Sicul.lib. I I :ad cuius confirmationem affert exemplum ranarum,quae ex limo terra,Nilo recedente,in Aegypto nascuntur. Hunc ipsum hominem ex limo terra a Deo ipso factum vocatum fuisse Adamum, vetustas etiam ex profano suo oraculo intellexit,cuius hic est versus apud Iustinum Martyrem.
units.tr: OUT OF THE CLAY OR DUST OF THE EARTH: Moses teaches that man was created out of the clay or dust of the earth, and that this man was called Adam. Abydenus and Alexander also reported that man was first made out of earth, as Eusebius relates in book 9, chapter 4 of his Preparation for the Gospel. Diodorus Siculus, in book 1, gives the same account from the opinion of the ancient pagans, and to confirm it he cites the example of the frogs that are born in Egypt from the mud of the earth when the Nile recedes. Antiquity also understood, from its own pagan oracle, that this man made by God from the clay of the earth was called Adam. The line is found in Justin Martyr:

units.la: Οὓς ἀεχ̀ρον πλάσας ἀνθρώπους, Ἀδὰμ δὲ καλέσας, Id est,
units.tr: Who first fashioned man and called him Adam [Οὓς ἀεχ̀ρον πλάσας ἀνθρώπους, Ἀδὰμ δὲ καλέσας]

units.la: Qui primum finxit hominem, Adamq; vocauit. Ex quo apparet, & ex eorum scriptis colligitur, & hominem ex terra conditum, & primum fuisse vocatum Adamum: quae sunt certissima nostrae veritatis testimonia. Quid verò nomen Ischa(quo nominata est prima foemina, & vxor Adami) nónne apparet in voce [Isis,] quam Aegyptij retinuerunt, magnámque,& antiantiquissimam Deam esse voluerũt omnium parentem? Ipsis autem pro Isla ex Ischa Latini, & Graeci peßimè postea pronunciarunt, & descripserunt. Ergo ut Ischa est vxor Adami in Dei verbo: sic ex veteri Aegyptiorum traditione Ipsis fuit vxor Osiridis, quam Latini Osiridem appellant, Aegyptiaca ad suum idioma mollientes, & transferentes. Adam nomen extat in vita Alexandri apud Plutarchum: Sic enim regina Cariæ vocata est, quæ fuit vetus memoria illius nominis, & vocis reliquia. Alius autem versus etiam apud Lactantium lib. 2. cap. 12 ex Sibyllis extat, hic nempe,
units.tr: Who first fashioned man and called him Adam. From this it appears, and is gathered from their own writings, that man was made from earth and that the first man was called Adam. These are the most certain witnesses to our truth. And does not the name Ischa, by which the first woman and wife of Adam was called, appear in the word Isis, which the Egyptians retained, and which they wanted to be the great and most ancient goddess, the mother of all? Later the Latins and Greeks very badly pronounced and wrote Isis in place of Ischa. So, just as Ischa is the wife of Adam in the word of God, so in the old tradition of the Egyptians Isis was the wife of Osiris, whom the Latins call Osiris, softening and transferring the Egyptian form to their own idiom. The name Adam also occurs in the life of Alexander in Plutarch: a queen of Caria was so called, which is a remnant of the old memory and of the word. Another line is also found in Lactantius, book 2, chapter 12, taken from the Sibyls, namely:

units.la: Ἀνθρωπος πεπλασθεὶς θεῷ πλασματος ἐν αὐτοῖς.
units.tr: Man, formed by the handiwork of God among them. [Ἀνθρωπος πεπλασθεὶς θεῷ πλασματος ἐν αὐτοῖς.]

units.la: Vbi Dei manibus formatum hominem aperte dicitur. Huic consentit qui multis postea seculis secutus est Ovidius, lib. 1. Metamorph. & ipse quoque Ethnicus:
units.tr: Here the man formed by the hands of God is plainly spoken of. Ovid, who followed many centuries later, agrees with this, and he too was a pagan. In book 1 of the Metamorphoses he says:

units.la: [Siue recens tellus, seductaque nuper ab alto Aethere cognati retinebat semina cæli, Quam satus Iapeto mixtam fluuialibus undis Finxit in effigiem moderantum cuncta Deorum.
units.tr: Whether the new earth, recently separated from the high aether, still kept the seeds of the kindred heaven, which the son of Iapetus, mixing it with river water, fashioned into the likeness of the gods who govern all things.

units.la: Horatius Flaccus lib. 1. Carm. od. 16 idem docet Prometheum ex limo formasse hominem. Idem quoq; Diodorus Siculus, lib. 1. Bibliothecæ. Ergo ex limo terræ conditum à Deo hominem etiam ex ipsismet profanis scriptoribus intelligimus, qui illa veterum vetustatis illibata vestigia retinuerunt, literisq; prodiderunt. Porro cur, id est, in quem finem conditus sit Homo his verbis consentientes Mosi tradit Trismegistus in Pimandro Dialogo 3. [Generatio hominis, ait (sequuta est omnium animalium ortum) ad diuinorum operum cognitionem: ad imperandum omnibus quæ cœlo tegunturq; ad bonorum
units.tr: Horace, in book 1 of the Carmina, ode 16, teaches the same, that Prometheus formed man from clay. Diodorus Siculus, in book 1 of his Library, says the same. Therefore we learn from the profane writers themselves that man was made by God from the clay of the earth, for they preserved and set down in writing these untouched vestiges of the most ancient antiquity. Further, why, that is, to what end, man was made, Trismegistus hands down in agreement with the words of Moses, in the third dialogue of the Pimander: "The generation of man," he says, "followed the origin of all animals, for the knowledge of the divine works; for ruling over all things that are covered by heaven; for the discernment of good things;

units.la: [Note in small type at the foot, not legible in full.] discretionem: ad incrementum & propagationem generis sui: ad coelestium Deorum discursum suscipiendum: ad varium bonorum, & artium artificium inveniendum.] Cicero lib. 1. de legibus, & in Somnio Scipionis. lib. quoque 2. de Natura Deorum idem docet. Seneca huic consentiens in lib. de Vita Beata: Ut Deo serviret conditus homo est, ait. Quid cum Dei verbo convenientius scribi, dicive potuit? Certe nihil. Ovidius quoque lib. 1. Metamorphoseos,
units.tr: [Note in small type at the foot, not legible in full.] for the increase and propagation of his own kind; for undertaking the course of the heavenly gods; for discovering the various craftsmanship of good things and arts."] Cicero, in book 1 of the De Legibus and in the Somnium Scipionis, and also in book 2 of the De Natura Deorum, teaches the same. Seneca, agreeing with this, says in the De Vita Beata: "Man was made to serve God." What could have been written or said more in agreement with the word of God? Certainly nothing. Ovid too, in book 1 of the Metamorphoses:

units.la: [Os hominis sublime dedit, caelumque videre jussit, & erectos ad sydera tollere vultus.] Hæc nonne sunt certissima sacra veritatis vestigia?
units.tr: He gave man a lofty face, and bade him look upon heaven and raise his upright gaze to the stars. Are these not the most certain sacred vestiges of the truth?

units.la: AD IMAGINEM DEI] Trismegistus scribit penè ex verbis Mosis in Pimandro dial. 1, [Hominem creavit Deus sibi similem.] Itaque ait idem Dial. 10. eiusdem operis, Non est terrenus brutis similis Homo, sed Deo. Supra ex Ovidio idem demonstrarunt, dum dixit, [Finxit in effigiem moderantum cuncta Deorum.] Verum apud Lactantium lib. 2. cap. 10. difertissime Sibylla in Dei persona loquens, scribit
units.tr: TO THE IMAGE OF GOD: Trismegistus writes almost in the words of Moses, in the first dialogue of the Pimander: "God created man like himself." So too the same author says in the tenth dialogue of the same work: "Man is not earthly like the beasts, but divine." Above, Ovid showed the same thing when he said: "He fashioned him in the likeness of the gods who govern all things." But in Lactantius, book 2, chapter 10, the Sibyl speaks most eloquently in the person of God and writes:

units.la: Εἰκὼν ἐς ἀνθρώπου ἐμὴ λόγον ὀρθὸν ἔχουσα, Id est, Est Homo imago mei felici predita mente. Et cap. 11. extat aliud oraculum Sibyllæ in eandem sententiam. Plato appellat formam hominis εἰκόνα, & θεοείκελον, id est, conformem Deo, & ad Dei imaginem expressum. Sed ante Platonem Archytas Tarentinus scripserat (sicut Iamblicus prodidit memoria in lib. de Setta Pythagoreor.) à Deo fuisse imaginem sui impressam Homini, eámque omnis cognitionis, rationisque fuisse capacem. Sic enim, id est, talem eam Deus fecerat. Cicero ex libris Platonis de leg. & ipse lib. 1. de leg. sic ait, [Animal hoc prouidum, sagax, multiplex, acutum, memor, plenum rationis, & consilij, quem vocamus Hominem, praclara quadam conditione generatum est à supremo Deo. Solum est enim ex tot animantium generibus, atque naturis, particeps rationis, & cogitationis, cuius cetera sunt omnia expertia. Quid est autem, non dicam in homine, sed in omni coelo, & terra, ratione diuinius?] Reliqua veritatis ipsius vestigia persequi est supervacaneum, ne dicam infinitum, quum nihil sit hac Ethnicorum hominum sententia magis tritum, Hominem in his terris esse Dei ipsius Imaginem.
units.tr: Man is an image of me, possessing right reason [Εἰκὼν ἐς ἀνθρώπου ἐμὴ λόγον ὀρθὸν ἔχουσα], that is, a man is my image, endowed with a happy mind. In chapter 11 of the same book there is another oracle of the Sibyl to the same effect. Plato calls the form of man an image and godlike, that is, conformed to God and expressed after the image of God. But before Plato, Archytas of Tarentum had written (as Iamblichus reports from memory in his book On the Life of the Pythagoreans) that the image of himself was impressed by God on man, and that man was capable of all knowledge and reason, for God had made him such. Cicero, from the books of Plato on the laws, and also in book 1 of his De Legibus, says: "This provident, sagacious, versatile, keen, mindful animal, full of reason and counsel, whom we call man, was born under a singular condition from the supreme God. For he alone, of so many kinds and natures of living things, shares in reason and thought, while all the others lack them. What is there, I will not say in man, but in the whole heaven and earth, more divine than reason?" To pursue the remaining vestiges of this truth would be superfluous, not to say endless, since nothing is more commonplace than this opinion of the pagan men that man on these earth is the very image of God.

units.la: Ad III. De Horto Edenico seu Paradiso.
units.tr: Ad III. On the Garden of Eden, or Paradise

units.la: De Horto Edenico, seu Paradiso (quis autem id existimaret?) extant etiam certissima apud eosdem Scriptores testimonia, & vestigia, quanquam sunt infidelia. Ac primum de nomine ipso Edenico seu Paradiso, esse, & notare delitiarum Hortum (quod vox ipsa Hebraea Gheden significat. Est enim Gheden voluptas, ac delitia) constat. Nam & Chaldaei, & Persae, quemadmodum scribit Xenophon in libris de Pædia Cyri, & Expeditione Cyri, vocant Pardeis, quod Graeci παράδεισον dixerunt (deducto a Pardeis vocabulo) Latini vero à Graecis mutuati nominant Paradisum. Est autem Paradisus omnis locus amœnissimus, & voluptatis plenissimus, ut etiam ᾱ. Gellius definit, quem etiam Vinaria dici à Latinis putat, lib. 2. Noctium Attic. cap. 20. Ex quo fit, ut Beatorum post hanc vitam sedes illa felicissima, Paradisus in Dei verbo passim nominetur, Luc.23.44, 2.Cor.12.4, Apo.2.7. Hæc autem omnia ad nomen Hebraum Gheden alludunt, cuius significanem referunt, ac retinent: Imo vox ipsa Graca ἡδονὴ, quæ voluptatem significat, ab Hebræa deducta videtur Eden. Unde & Adonis sive Edonis regio (quæ Edene est) sed vitiose à peregrinis Græcis pronuntiata Edonis, & Adonis, pro Edenis, vel Edene. Sibylla etiam apud Lactant. huius Horti delitiosi, id est, Edenici & Paradisi diserte meminit, lib. 2. cap. 12. hæc versibus, ubi de primis parentibus agitur.
units.tr: Concerning the Garden of Eden, or Paradise (but who would have thought it?), there are also very certain testimonies and traces among the same writers, although they are unfaithful ones. And first, it is established that the name itself, Eden or Paradise, means and denotes a garden of delights (which is what the Hebrew word itself, Gheden, signifies; for Gheden means pleasure and delight). For both the Chaldeans and the Persians, as Xenophon writes in his books on the education of Cyrus and on the expedition of Cyrus, call it Pardeis, which the Greeks called παράδεισος (derived from the word Pardeis), and the Latins, borrowing from the Greeks, call it Paradisus. Paradise is any place most pleasant and full of delight, as Gellius also defines it, who thinks the Latins also call it Vinaria, in book 2 of the Attic Nights, chapter 20. Hence it is that that most happy abode of the blessed after this life is everywhere in God's word called Paradise: Luke 23:43, 2 Cor. 12:4, Rev. 2:7. All these names allude to the Hebrew name Gheden, and they keep and refer to its meaning. Indeed the Greek word itself, ἡδονή, which signifies pleasure, seems to be derived from the Hebrew Eden. Hence also the region of Adonis or Edonis (which is Edene), though wrongly pronounced Edonis and Adonis by foreign Greeks, instead of Edenis or Edene. The Sibyl too, in Lactantius, book 2, chapter 12, expressly mentions this delightful garden, that is, of Eden and Paradise, in these verses, where the first parents are discussed.

units.la: Οἱ δὲ Θεὸν πμῶντες ἀλλὰ ἱερὸν ἀλλὰ ἑνακίνη
units.tr: Οἱ δὲ Θεὸν πμῶντες ἀλλὰ ἱερὸν ἀλλὰ ἑνακίνη [Those who honour God, the true and the eternal one]

units.la: Ζωὴν κλήρου οὐδὲν τὸν αἰῶνα ἀχαρίστως αὐτοί
units.tr: Ζωὴν κλήρου οὐδὲν τὸν αἰῶνα ἀχαρίστως αὐτοί [Having obtained life as an allotted portion for eternity]

units.la: Οἰκοῦντες ἀμφὶ Δία ἔνδον ἐνθάδε ἀνάλυσ κήπον, Id est,
units.tr: Οἰκοῦντες ἀμφὶ Δία ἔνδον ἐνθάδε ἀνάλυσ κήπον, That is, [dwelling here together in the garden that flourishes]

units.la: Ergo Deum venerantes, verumque, æternumque, Æternam nactii vitam quoque sorte fuissent, Frondentem ut colerent Paradisi tunc simul hortu.
units.tr: Therefore, worshipping God, who is true and eternal, they would have obtained eternal life too by lot, to tend together the flourishing garden of Paradise, then.

units.la: Quid magis simile Divinæ veritati dici aut scribi potest? His etiam, etsi longa manu, videtur accedere & illud, quod Homerus ex veterum traditione, de campi Elysiis scribit, id est, felicissimo quodam huius Orbis loco, & quidem in extremis finibus orbis sito, in quo beatissime boni, pïque homines vixerunt, lib. 5. Odyss. & ex Homero postea alii, tum Poetæ, tum Philosophi sumpserunt. Porro Adonis Horti, & Horti Hesperidum tam celebres Ethnicorum scriptis quidpiam quoque his simile, atque aliquod illius Horti vestigium fuisse censeri possunt: de quibus Plinius lib. Hist. Naturalis 19. cap. 4. Præsertim verò Adonis, qui dicti sunt, Horti, fuerunt hic ipsæ Hortus Edenicus. Præclarè enim in Æthico annotat Simlerus, [Adonis] pro
units.tr: What could be said or written that is more like the divine truth? To these, though from a distant hand, there seems also to be added that which Homer, from ancient tradition, writes about the Elysian Fields, that is, a certain most fortunate place on this earth, and indeed one situated at the furthest edges of the world, where the most blessed and pious men lived (Odyssey, book 4); and afterwards others, both poets and philosophers, took this from Homer. Further, the gardens of Adonis and the gardens of the Hesperides, so famous in the writings of the pagans, can also be judged to have been something similar to this, and some trace of that Garden: concerning which Pliny, Natural History, book 19, chapter 4. Especially the so-called gardens of Adonis were here the very Garden of Eden. For Simler rightly notes in his Aethicus that [Adonis] was written in place of [Eden], the region or province there, as we said above; whence those early writers, ignorant of the truth, called the gardens of Adonis, from the Greek word ἀδονίς, the gardens of the region of Eden. Though some want a certain Adonis, a king, who was named thus from the name of that region.

units.la: [Edenis] regionem seu prouinciam illic scriptam esse, & nos supra diximus: Unde [Adonis] à Græca voce ἀδονὶς, Horti pro Edenis regionis horti dixerunt veteres illi, sftius veritatis ignari: quanquâ ydem quendam ᾿Adonin Regem esse volunt, qui ex illius Regionis nomine sic appellatus fuerit. Et hæc quidem de Horto. Verum de Edene regione, illiúsque fertilitate & facunditate (quanquam alio nomine, nempe tum Mesopotamia, tum Mattiana regionis appellatione, quas vtrasque regiones Edene complexa est) etiam hæc vestigia supersunt. Moses scribit quattuor flumina ex Edene fluere, velut quattuor diuersa eiusdem aqua brachia, & diuortia. Herodotus lib. 5. qui est Terpsichore, ait in Armenia (quæ generaliter sumpta, vti fit ab Herodoto, Edenem quoq; regionem, comprehendit) quattuor flumina oriri, quorum vnum sit Tigris, alter Euphrates, tertium etiâ Tigris, quartum Gyndes. Strabo lib. 16. Geographiæ, quattuor item flumina recenset ijsdem in locis, velut ex eodem fonte & monte manantia, nimirum Euphratem, Tigrim, Basilium & Aboraram. Mutata quidem sunt, fateor, nomina (quid enim vetustas temporis nō mutet?) sed quid Mosi in re ipsa magis simile? Vberrimum autem & facundissimum fuisse totum eum Edenis regionis tractum apparet ex Mose. Dionysius Alexandrinus idem hoc plani docet. Nam in libro de Situ Orbis nihil Mesopotamia, & Mattiana regionibus (quæ sunt inter se vicinæ, & Edenis regionis partes erant) in omni fructuum, ac pomorum præsertim genere feracius scribit. Strabo de Mesopotamia eodem lib. 16. Geograph. ait, [Regio facunda est, & maximè pascendis bobus idonea, fert quæ semper virent, & aroma amomum.] De eodem Plinius lib 6. Hist. Natur. cap. 26, & 27. Porro de Euphrate flumine, ut facile agros certo anni tempore irriget, terrasq; velut Nilus, impinguat, & facilius tamen cohibeatur, vide & Strabonem lib. 16. & Plinium loco iam citato, Solinum, Ptolemeum, & Ammian. Marcellin. lib. 14. Historia. Et hæc quidem sunt Edenis regionis, Edeniciq; Horti vestigia, pauca quidem ex multis: verum aly plura colligent. Præterea enim quædam iam exposuimus de ea, in quæstionibus etiam ex Ethnicis. Nos enim breuitate, quam qui maximè gaudemus: & digitum ad fontes intendere duntaxat volumus, non autem ipsam Lectorum sitim explere, ne cuiquam industriæ, & laboris sui laudem præriperemus.
units.tr: And these, indeed, are about the Garden. But concerning the region of Eden, and its fertility and abundance (though under another name, namely both Mesopotamia and the region called Mattiana, both of which regions Eden embraced), there are also these traces remaining. Moses writes that four rivers flow out of Eden, like four different arms and branches of the same water. Herodotus, book 5, which is Terpsichore, says that four rivers rise in Armenia (which, taken in general, as Herodotus uses it, also includes the region of Eden): one is the Tigris, another the Euphrates, a third again the Tigris, and the fourth the Gyndes. Strabo, book 16 of the Geography, likewise lists four rivers in the same places, as if flowing from the same spring and mountain: namely the Euphrates, the Tigris, the Basilius and the Aborras. The names, I admit, have changed (for what does the passage of time not change?), but what is more like Moses in the matter itself? That the whole tract of the region of Eden was very rich and fertile appears from Moses. Dionysius of Alexandria teaches the same thing clearly: in his book on the Description of the World he writes that nothing is more fruitful in every kind of produce and fruit, especially fruit, than Mesopotamia and the region of Mattiana (which are neighbours to each other, and were parts of the region of Eden). Strabo, in the same book 16 of the Geography, says of Mesopotamia: [it is a fertile region, and especially suitable for pasturing oxen; it bears things that are always green, and the aromatic amomum]. Pliny, Natural History, book 6, chapters 26 and 27, writes of the same. Concerning the river Euphrates, how it easily irrigates the fields at a certain season of the year and fattens the lands like the Nile, but yet is more easily restrained, see also Strabo, book 16, and Pliny in the place already cited, Solinus, Ptolemy, and Ammianus Marcellinus, book 14 of the History. And these, indeed, are the traces of the region of Eden and of the Garden of Eden, few indeed out of many; but others will gather more. For I have already explained some things about it, and also among the questions from the pagans. For we, who most of all delight in brevity, wish only to point the finger at the sources, and not to satisfy the readers' thirst itself, lest we snatch away from anyone the praise of his own diligence and labour.

units.la: Ad IIII. De duabus Arboribus Paradisi, seu Horti.
units.tr: Chapter IV. On the Two Trees of Paradise, or of the Garden.

units.la: Duas Arbores in Paradiso collocatas à Deo fuisse scribit Moses, alterius quarum vsus interdictus Hominis fuerat, quo Dei interdicto violato per nimiam hominis tum superbiam, tum auiditatem cupiditatemq;, malum omne genus, & calamitas in Mundum irrepsit. Huius ipsius veritatis vestigium est, quod Timon Poeta in Syllis scripsit, vt refert Diogenes Laërtius, Πάντων μὲν σεφάνα κακῶν ἔκθυμία ἐσίν,
units.tr: Moses writes that God placed two trees in Paradise. The use of one of them was forbidden to man. When God's prohibition was violated, through man's excessive pride and also his greed and lust, every kind of evil and calamity crept into the world. A trace of this very truth is what the poet Timon wrote in his Silloi, as Diogenes Laertius reports: "The desire of all wicked things is the first cause" [Πάντων μὲν σεφάνα κακῶν ἔκθυμία ἐσίν].

units.la: [Omnium scelerum, ac vitiorum concupiscentia prima causa est.] Sed & illud eiusdem veritatis testimonium maius & clarius, quod ex Sibylla profert Lact. lib. 2. cap. 12
units.tr: [Desire for every crime and vice is the first cause.] But there is also a greater and clearer testimony to the same truth, which Lactantius (Institutes, book 2, chapter 12) cites from the Sibyl:

units.la: Ἀ᾿ν᾿θρώπου πνεῦμα ἀνάθεσις εἰς ἀντὶς, Οὔτε πλάνησιν ὑπὸς ἀλίως ἀπὸ μοῖραν ἀνῄδειν. Τῆς θανάτου γνῶσιν τε λαβεῖν ἀγαθὸς τι, κακὸν τι. I.
units.tr: "The breath of man was given over to ... nor did they know the wandering from the path. To gain knowledge of death is something good and something evil." [Ἀ᾿ν᾿θρώπου πνεῦμα ἀνάθεσις εἰς ἀντὶς, Οὔτε πλάνησιν ὑπὸς ἀλίως ἀπὸ μοῖραν ἀνῄδειν. Τῆς θανάτου γνῶσιν τε λαβεῖν ἀγαθὸς τι, κακὸν τι.]

units.la: Nam s hominē Deus ipse manu plasmauerat: atq; Deceptus serpens sortem suasit adire (hunc Mortis, nottiuang, vaser reliq; malig;.
units.tr: For God himself had formed man with his own hand, and the deceiving serpent persuaded him to approach the lot of death ... (of death, of ... and the rest of the evil).

units.la: Hæc vero ex ipso Mose descripta quis non dixerit? Denique quid illud de Pandora muliere, & eius pixide figmentum Poëtarū (per quam omne mali miseriæ, snorbi, mortisque genus primum in Mundum inuectū esse scribunt, vti Hesiodus lib. 1. Oper. & Dier.) aliud sibi vult: aut unde traslatum, nisi ex obscuris stium veritatis vestigiis, vti postea dicetur.
units.tr: Who would not say that these things were taken from Moses himself? Finally, what does that poetic fiction about the woman Pandora and her box mean otherwise? The poets write that through it every kind of evil, misery, sorrow and death was first let loose into the world, as Hesiod says in his Works and Days, book 1. Where else could it have been borrowed from, except from the obscure traces of this truth, as will be said later?

units.la: Ad V. De Nominum Impositione.
units.tr: Chapter V. On the Imposition of Names.

units.la: Cæterum Nomina rebus ab Homine, velut earum Domino fuisse imposita scribit Moses, pro eiusque rei natura. Huius veritatis scintillæ ac vestigia hæc extant: Primum, quod Atheneus lib 6. Dipnosophist. ex Cratete Poëta in bestiis scribit futurum fuisse tempus, quā res omnes, suis nominibus ab Homine citate, velut pisces bestiæ, & c adfuissent praslò slatim Homini, illisque pro nutu paruissent. Legat locum illum qui volet. Cicero lib. 1. de Inuent. in Præmio ait, Magnum quendā, & sapientem virum olim fuisse, qui res nominibus primùs notauerit, docuerítque sensa animi ex his exprimere. Plinius lib. 7. Natur. Hist. cap. 6. ait semper apud Assyrios literas fuisse. Sunt autem ad Orientem siti, vbi habitabat Adam. Quòd si literæ, ergo & nomina primi habuerunt, si ess, vocabula: verum & ab ijs ad alios linguam, & vocabula quoque emanasse, vti & literas, quibus scribuntur, verum est, & cum Mose, velut veritatis vestigium, consentit. Plato in Cratylo Dialogo, tomo 1. totus in eo est, ut doceat Ζomina rebus fuisse primum imposita, velut earum ἀνλωματα, & similitudines earum naturam exprimentes. Denique concludit his verbis, Δnλοτόn ὁ Δεμιυ & ... [Greek text] ... [Nimirum qui primus nomina imposuit, qualem existimabat esse rerum naturam, talia & imponebat nomina, ut diximus.] Quid restat, nisi ut eundem Adamum appellet? Haec vero quam sunt omnia maxima veritatis nostra testimonia, vestigiaq;
units.tr: Moses writes that names were imposed on things by man, as their lord, according to the nature of each thing. These sparks and traces of this truth survive: first, Athenaeus (book 6 of the Deipnosophists) writes, from the poet Crates in his work on beasts, that there was a time when all things, called by their names by man, such as fishes and beasts, were present at once to man and obeyed his nod. Let whoever wishes read that passage. Cicero, in the preface to book 1 of On Invention, says that long ago there was a great and wise man who first marked things with names and taught people to express the feelings of the mind by these. Pliny, Natural History book 7, chapter 6, says that writing has always existed among the Assyrians. They live to the East, where Adam dwelt. But if letters existed, then the first men also had names and words. And that words and language, as well as the letters by which they are written, passed from them to others is true, and agrees with Moses as a trace of the truth. Plato in the dialogue Cratylus (vol. 1) is wholly concerned to show that names were first imposed on things as their images, expressing their nature by resemblance. Finally he concludes with these words: [Δηλοῖ ὁ Δημιουργός] ... [Clearly, he who first imposed names, judging what the nature of things was, imposed names accordingly, as we have said.] What remains, except that he should call this very Adam? How very great all these testimonies and traces of our truth are ...

units.la: Ad VI. De Mulieris Formatione.
units.tr: Ad VI. De Mulieris Formatione.

units.la: Mulierem ex mare homine dormiente, & ex eius costa desumptam scribit Moses. Huius veritatis vestigium extat apud Trismegistum in Pimand. Dial. 1. & alys, dum ait Hominem primum a Deo factum fuisse Marem, & Foeminam simul, vbi & de vigilia hominis quoque agitur. Plato in Conuiuio ex eadem doctrina vult primum Homines fuisse duplicis sexus, nimirum Mares, & Foeminas simul, & in vno eodemq; corpore, Androgynos, propterea nominatos: quos Deus postea in Mares, & Foeminas seorsim diuisit, secreueritque, quales hodie manent. Hesiodus Pandoram, quae prima in humano genere foemina fuit, & a viro conditam, & hominis speciem efformatam fuisse contendit lib.
units.tr: Moses writes that woman was taken from the sleeping man, from his rib. A trace of this truth survives in Trismegistus in the Pimander, Dialogue 1, and elsewhere, where he says that man was first made by God as male and female together, and there he also treats of man's sleep. In the Symposium Plato, from the same teaching, holds that the first human beings were of a double sex, namely males and females together in one and the same body, and for this reason called androgynes. God afterwards divided them into males and females separately and set them apart, and so they remain today. Hesiod, in the first book of the Works and Days, maintains that Pandora, who was the first woman in the human race, was fashioned by a man and formed in the likeness of a human being.

units.la: 1. Operum & Dierum. Ouidius lib. 1. Metamorphos. tradit eandem esse & Maris Hominis, & foeminae originem ginem, nimirum è terra. Sed hîs omnibus maius testimonium reddat, nimirum natura ipsa. Nam illius costa viri, unde fœmina sumpta est, damnū etiamnum hodie apparet in Maribus, qui (quemadmodum Medici docent) habent veras costas minus una quàm mulieres. Quod ipsum quoque ad fœtus maiorem capacitatem, viterive faciliorem gestationem commodè mulieribus accidisse docent. Denique lib. 5. de Repub. Plato huius veritatis de creatione fœminæ hominis vestigium retinēs, ait, Mulieres ad eadem prorsus studia, officia, munìaque natas, & natura aptas (Nam sunt eiusdem Dei imago) ad quæ & viri ipsi sunt, excepto coitus usu & discrimine, propterquod illæ Mulieres, hi verò Mares & viri sunt, & vocantur. Idem Aristoteles lib. 2. de Generat. Animal. tradit.
units.tr: Ovid, in the first book of the Metamorphoses, teaches that the origin of man and woman is the same, namely earth. But nature itself gives a greater witness than all these. For the loss of that rib of the man from which the woman was taken still appears today in males, who (as physicians teach) have one rib fewer than women. The physicians also teach that this fits well with women's greater capacity for bearing offspring and their easier carrying of the foetus. Finally, in the fifth book of the Republic, Plato, retaining a trace of this truth about the creation of woman, says: women are born for exactly the same pursuits, duties and offices, and are by nature fitted for them (for they are the image of the same God), as men are, except in the use of intercourse and in the distinction, on account of which the women are called women and the men are called men. Aristotle also teaches the same in the second book of the On the Generation of Animals.

units.la: Ad VII. Coniugij institutio.
units.tr: Ad VII. On the Institution of Marriage

units.la: Coniugium à Deo inter Marem unum, & Fœminā unam Homines institutū fuisse scribit Moses, ut essent duo in carne una. Huius veritatis vestigium perspicuum fuit inter Profanos, non tantum quod illi scripsérunt Coniugia esse à natura, ac proinde à Deo (Nam illi Deum appellant Naturam) verumetiā, quòd suis Coniugijs Deum aliquem præesse, aliy Iunonem, aliy Venerem, aliy Iovem ipsum senserūt: & non nisi magnis religionum suarū cæremonijs semper adhibitis, matrimonia contrahebant. Nam adhibebant flamea, & cereos: imo sacerdotes quoq; ipsos Deorum suorum, ex sententia Platonis, ad ea accersebant. Deum enim Coniugij præsertim inter homines autorem esse agnoscebant. Itaque prius quam uxores ducerent, sacrificabant, & auguria capiebant: quae si non fuerant bona, ab eiusmodi uxore, & nuptiis abstinebant, quod eas, Deo autore earum nolente, facere non liceret. Terentius in Pherm. Act. 4. Scena 4. Quod vero Brutorum inter se copulam vocat Matrimonium quoque Plutarchus in libello de naturali parentum affectu, per Metaphoram tantum ab eo dictum est: non quod Deum agnoscerent illi etiam infideles homines perinde copulationis Brutorum inter se autorem, ac principem, atque eius matrimonij, quod est inter Homines. Ergo etiam Plato lib. 5. de Rep. vult sacra, hymnos sacros, dies festos in coniugijs intervenire, sine quibus matrimonium nullum fiat inter homines. Imo idem lib. 6. de Leg. iubet, ut sponsus, & sponsa sobrij inter se prima nocte nuptiarum coeant, & conveniant, nimirum ut Deo placeant, a quo, ait, proles fructuosa coniugij sit expectandus. Quod vero marem hominem cum foemina homine coire oporteat, non autem marem cum mare, foeminam cum foemina, docuit eadem vetustas, ex sacra nostraq; veritatis reliquijs, qua superfuerunt.
units.tr: Moses writes that marriage was instituted by God between one man and one woman, so that they should be two in one flesh. A clear trace of this truth existed among the profane writers. They wrote that marriages are from nature, and therefore from God (for they call God Nature), and moreover they believed that some god presided over their marriages: some Juno, some Venus, some Jupiter himself. They never contracted marriages without great ceremonies of their religions. They used torches and wax candles, and indeed they summoned to these rites the priests of their gods, according to Plato's opinion. For they acknowledged God as the author of marriage, especially among men. So before they took wives, they sacrificed and took auspices; and if these were not favourable, they abstained from such a wife and from the wedding, because it was not lawful to do so when God, the author, was unwilling. Terence, in the Phormio, Act 4, Scene 4. As for Plutarch calling the union of brutes with one another "marriage" in his little book On Natural Affection of Parents, he said this only metaphorically; not because those unbelieving men acknowledged God as the author and prince of the copulation of brutes in the same way as of the marriage that is between men. So Plato too, in the fifth book of the Republic, wants sacred rites, sacred hymns and festival days to attend marriages, without which no marriage among men would be made. Indeed the same Plato, in the sixth book of the Laws, orders that bride and groom, sober, should come together and lie together on the first night of the wedding, namely so that they may please God, from whom, he says, fruitful offspring of the marriage is to be expected. That a man should couple with a woman, and not a man with a man or a woman with a woman, the same antiquity taught from the remnants of our sacred truth that survived.

units.la: Nam idem Plato lib. 1. de Legibus, [Greek text] [intelligendum est eam esse naturalem voluptatem, quum foemina masculo copulatur ad generationem.] Quum vero Masculi cum masculis, aut foemina cum foeminis copulantur illam esse praeter naturam, & summum eorum, qui hoc primi auf sunt, facinus ex foeda voluptatu
units.tr: For the same Plato, in the first book of the Laws, [it must be understood that this is natural pleasure, when a woman is joined with a man for the sake of generation.] But when males are joined with males, or females with females, that is against nature, and the greatest crime of those who first did it arises from a foul intemperance of pleasure.

units.la: [Greek text] tis intemperie natum.] Praterea lib.8.eiusdem operis ait hanc esse Ⅳatura legem, quæ ante Laij Thebanorum regis tempora posita sit, [Ne mascul o, fœmineve Venerem commisc ere fas sit, id est, ne Masculus cum masculo, Fœmina cum fœmina misceatur, & coeat.] Denique, quod Vir & Vxor una Caro fiunt per Coniugiu, scripsit etiam ex veteri traditione Plutarchus in Erotico seu Amatario Dialogo. Amor enim ille, nempe coniugalis (de quo diserte illic loquitur Plutarchus) ait, animas coniugum colliquat, ut iam neq; velint duo esse, neque duo se esse censeant. Eodem pertinet quod in Conivio ait Plato, per coitum, præsertim coniugalem, fieri ex Masculo, & Fœmina velut unicum hominem, unicámque carnem, quales primùm erat Androgyni. Denique scribit Horatius in Arte Poetica fuisse primùm boni, prudentisque Legislatoris, qualis fuit Orpheus, imprimis [Concubitu prohibere vago, dare iura maritis.] Sic igitur Coniugium & honestum imprimis esse, & à Deo institutum vita etiam Ethnici ipsi veritatis nostra vestigia sequentes, & retinentes exististimarunt, & cœlibatui prætulerunt. Ad VIII. De Statu vtriusq; hominis. DE Statu primo, ac felici vtriusq; hominis apud eosdem extant quoque vestigia quamplurima. Et primùm quidem de hoc, nempe homines fuisse primum animo, & corpore prorsus immortales. Mors enim per peccatum est ingressa in Mundum. Idem enim scribit Trismegistus in Pimandro Dial.12. videlicet Hominem Dei capacem factum fuisse, consortémque naturæ Diuina. Itaque & animam, & corpus habebat, ait, im-mortale. Secundo loco, dicitur homo tunc paruisse Deo, Hortum Paradisum coluisse. Sic supra ex Sibylla citante Lactantio, lib. 2. cap. 12: [Frondentem vt colerent Paradisi tunc simul Hortum.] Plato etiam in Theeteto, Hominis summam felicitatem & praestantiam tunc fuisse, ait, quum similis Deo esset, insteque vivebat: atque etiamnum hodie talem eum fieri debere, vt felix, & beatus viuat. Sed & homo tunc rebus omnibus dominabatur, cum bestijs versabatur. Hoc ipsum in Politico Dialogo Plato ex veteri traditione commemorauit. Idem Cicero lib. 2 de Natura Deorum, Deus, ait, Hominem finxit, & ornauit, quem voluit esse rerum omnium principem. Hominis ergo causa omnia in hoc Mundo esse facta docuerunt ex vestigijs veritatis Stoici ante Christi in has terras aduentum, quemadmodum scribit Lactantius lib. 7. cap. 7. Docuerunt Iurisconsulti, vti Brutus, ait Cicero. Sed quid cum ista veritate magis consentit, quam quod his versibus ait Ouid. lib. 1. Metamorphosis, citatque Lactantius:
units.tr: [...]tis intemperie natum.] Moreover, in the eighth book of the same work he says that this is the law of nature, which was laid down before the time of Laius, king of the Thebans: [that it is not right for a man or a woman to commit love with the same sex, that is, that a male should not mingle and couple with a male, or a female with a female.] Finally, that man and wife become one flesh through marriage, Plutarch also wrote, from ancient tradition, in his Erotikos or Dialogue on Love. For that love, namely the conjugal love (of which Plutarch speaks plainly there), he says, melts together the souls of the spouses, so that they no longer wish to be two, nor think themselves two. To the same point belongs what Plato says in the Symposium, that through coition, especially conjugal, a male and a female become as it were one single man and one single flesh, such as the androgynes were at first. Finally, Horace in the Art of Poetry writes that it was first the task of a good and wise lawgiver, such as Orpheus was, above all to restrain people from wandering lust and to give laws to husbands. Thus, marriage was regarded as honourable above all and instituted by God, even by the pagans who followed and retained traces of our truth, and they preferred it to celibacy. Ad VIII. On the State of Each Human Being. Concerning the first and happy state of both human beings, there are also very many traces among the same writers. And first, of this: that human beings were at first altogether immortal in soul and body. For death entered the world through sin. Trismegistus writes the same in the Pimander, Dialogue 12, namely that man was made capable of God and a partner of the divine nature. Therefore, he says, he had a soul and a body that were immortal. Second, it is said that man then obeyed God and tended the garden of Paradise. So above, from the Sibyl as quoted by Lactantius, book 2, chapter 12: [to tend the Paradise garden then in leaf.] Plato too, in the Theaetetus, says that the highest happiness and excellence of man was then, when he was like God and lived in his company; and that even now he ought to become such, if he is to live happily and blessedly. But man then also had dominion over all things and lived among the beasts. Plato recalled this very thing in the Politicus, from ancient tradition. Cicero likewise, in the second book of On the Nature of the Gods: God, he says, fashioned and adorned man, whom he willed to be the prince of all things. The Stoics, before Christ's coming to this earth, taught from the traces of truth that all things in this world were made for the sake of man, as Lactantius writes in book 7, chapter 7. The jurists taught it too, as Brutus, says Cicero. But what agrees with this truth more than what Ovid says in these verses in the first book of the Metamorphoses, which Lactantius also quotes:

units.la: [Sanctius his animal, mentisque capacius alta Deerat adhuc, & quod dominari in cetera posset, Natus Homo est.] Plato vero luculentissime in Politico, Tom. 2. vti dixi. Scribit enim in Prima, Aureaque illa Mundi aetate, qua intemperies hominum nondum erat, Homines intrepide cum bestijs fuisse versatos, colloquutos, & his omnibus tanquam adiumentis, ad philosophandum vsos, id est ad Deum contemplandum: atque in eum, ait finem alij cum aliis, & cum bestijs versabantur. Ex quo fit, vt idem lib. 1. de Leg. appellet ex veteri traditione Hominem[Diuinum miraculum, & opus, itémque μικεγκοσμὶν,] nimirum ex illa prima ortus sui conditione consideratum. Denique nihil tunc, id est, in eo primo hominis statu, seu ætate in toto mundo erat confusum, vel perturbatum, nec in cœlo, nec in terra. Omnia homini è terra sponte nascebantur, ius, pietas, reltúmque vigebat in Homine, quæ eadem veritas etiam in illis ipsis autoribus Ethnicis extat. Plato enim in eodem Politico sic ait, [Sub Saturni regno] id est, prima illa Hominis, & Mundi ætate adhuc pura, [cœli revolutiones erant, sponte omnia nascebantur è terra, quod ei stellarum conuersioni, quæ nunc est, minimè quadrat, sed superiori pottus coeur niebat. Tunc sanè toti illi circuitui Princeps inuigilabat summa curâ Deus. Tunc nihil erat ferum, neque alia alias se vorabant animantes: aberat bellum penitus, & seditio. Deus homines pascebat, ipse erat eorum pastor, & custos, quemadmodum homines nunc, quorum natura diuinior, caeterarum animantium genera pascunt. Deo igitur sic regente, ciuitatum constitutiones nulla erant.] Ergo & scelus omne tunc aberat, uti & Hesiodus lib. 1. Operū & Dier. & ex eo describit Ouid. lib. 1. Metamorph.
units.tr: [A holier creature, more capable of lofty thought and able to rule the rest, was still lacking, and man was born.] Plato, however, most splendidly in the Politicus, as I have said. For he writes that in that first, golden age of the world, when the corruption of men did not yet exist, men lived fearlessly among the beasts, conversed with them, and used them all as aids to philosophising, that is, to contemplating God; and to this end, he says, some lived with others and with the beasts. From this it follows that the same Plato, in the first book of the Laws, calls man, according to ancient tradition, [a divine wonder and work, and a microcosm,] that is, considered in his first condition of origin. Finally, nothing then, that is, in that first state or age of man, was confused or disordered in the whole world, neither in heaven nor on earth. Everything grew spontaneously for man from the earth; justice, piety and what is right flourished in man. This same truth is also found in those very pagan authors. For Plato in the same Politicus speaks thus: [under the reign of Saturn,] that is, in that first age of man and the world, still pure, [the revolutions of heaven were such that everything grew spontaneously from the earth, which does not at all fit the present arrangement of the stars, but the earlier one.] Then indeed God, the Prince, kept watch over that whole circuit with the greatest care. [Then nothing was savage, nor did animals devour one another; war and sedition were entirely absent. God fed men himself, he was their shepherd and guardian, just as men now, whose nature is more divine, feed the other kinds of animals. Therefore, with God thus ruling, there were no constitutions of cities.] So all wickedness was then absent too, as Hesiod in the first book of the Works and Days, and Ovid in the first book of the Metamorphoses, following him, describes.

units.la: [Aurea prima sata est ætas, quæ vindice nullo, Sponte sua, sine lege, fidem, rectúmque colebat. Pœna, metúsque aberant.] Denique vt veteres omnes Philosophi sensere, prodente Lactant. lib. 2. cap. 11, Mundi initio neque hyems, neque æstas, id est, vis nimia frigoris, aut æstus erat, hominésve ledès: sed perpetua quedam cœli temperies, & ver aquabile rebus creandis, fouendisque apti[simum. Et hæc quidem tot sot sunt prisca veritatis & nostra de primo & felici Hominis conditi statu vestigia ex profanis scriptoribus à nobis ad ᵃᵈᵉᵘˢ, & Verbo Dei incredulos homines arguendos comprimendosq; collecta, & descripta.
units.tr: The golden age was first born, which, with no avenger, of its own accord and without law, kept faith and uprightness. Punishment and fear were absent.] Finally, as all the ancient philosophers have held, as Lactantius reports in book 2, chapter 11, at the beginning of the world there was neither winter nor summer, that is, no excessive cold or heat, and nothing that harmed men; instead there was a constant mildness of the sky and an even spring, most suited to creating and nourishing living things. These many traces of the ancient truth about man's first and happy condition, once created, have been gathered and set down by us from profane writers, so that they may be used to refute unbelieving men with the Word of God.

units.la: CAPUT IIII.
units.tr: CAPUT IIII.

units.la: Collectanea ex superioribus, vbi de statu mundi Politico, & Ecclesiastico agitur, quis tunc vterque fuerit.
units.tr: A collection from the above, where the political and ecclesiastical state of the world is discussed, and what each was at that time.

units.la: OLLECTANEA, quæ dicuntur à nobis, eò pertinet, vt ex superioribus intelligamus, ac colligamus, tum ecquis Politicus, tum etiā ecquis Ecclesiasticus mundi Status tunc fuerit, id est, toto eo (quod Adami peccatum antecesserit) tempore. Et quidem is Politicus status (qui Magistratuum leges, & urbes continetur) fuit, vt Magistratus quidem mundi totius esset vterq; Homo, Primus, & quidem summus, is, qui masculus erat: inferiore vero loco, Mulier. Videtur enim in eo superior fuisse Mas quam fœmina: quòd Homo mas à Deo ipso didicerat discebatque, itemque acceperat, & accipiebat, quod postea fœminam docebat ipse, eique communicabat. In omnia vero Animantia imò in universum mundum, vterque ius habebat par, non sanum tamen aut crudele imperium: sed vt tutor, & eorum clemens Dominus: quo vtebantur neque ad curiositatem, neque ad libidinem turpem quam carebat vterq; homo. Leges istius regiminis erant, Dei ipsius praecepta, & sana tunc reliqueque ad illorum obsequium composita Hominis utriusque voluntas, omni vitio carens & iniustitia, sed benigna, & iusta. Ciuitates tunc quoque nullae erant aedificatae: sed neq; eas exstrui fuisset necesse, quin omni metu homines, qua a se, & qua a beluis prorsus vacarent. Metus autem & terror est, fuitque vrbium aedificandarum primaria quemadmodum demonstrabimus, inter homines causa. Et haec quidem de Politico illius seculi Statu.
