Ecclesiastici autem Status (qui in hisce quattuor versatur, nempe Dei verbo, eius Ministro, sacramentis, & loco) erat eiusmodi Verbum Dei, quod Adamo, ac proinde Ischa (quae & Eua) eius uxori innotuerat, a Deo ipso illi revelatum, minimè autem scriptum erat. Continebat autem primum Historiam Creationis totius huius Mundi, imprimisq; ipsius hominis. Deinde ius, & imperium Homini concessum a Deo in hanc rerum universitatem. Denique futurum utriusque Hominis, ac totius generis humani felicem conditionem, ac immortalitatem, si Deo Homines illi duo paruissent, seque in suo semper ordine continuisset. Huius verbi a Deo revelati Minister erat Adamus uxori: ac proinde caeteri Mares foeminis, & Mariti suis uxoribus, & Parentes liberis. Ministri, & Concionatores eiusdē Dei verbi erant futuri eodem modo. Sacramenta vero, quae illi Dei verbo promissionique fuerant a Deo adiuncta, recensentur duo: nimirum v. num, Arbor vitæ: alterum, Arbor Scientiæ boni, & mali, quæ postrema edere à Deo vetitum erat ad Adam, addita gravissima pœna, quo migis timerent. Eam autem Arborem duntaxat cernere oculis, & manu tangere poterant. Nec enim id illis fuerat interdictum, vt ei nec vescéi priore Arbore, id est, Arbore vitæ. Denique locus Ecclesiæ fuit, & futura quidem ipsius Dei cum Adam, & posteris eius collocutionis Hortus. Ergo velut Templum, Mundi totius sacratum, & peculiare, Paradisus ille, sive Hortus Edenicus erat. Futura autem parentum cum liberis, & Maritorum cum vxoribus de eodem Dei Verbo communicationis, locus fuit mutua conuersatio, domesticum que consortium. Nulla tunc pecorum sacrificia Deo fiebant, vel futura erant, quoniam hæc sunt, fuerúntve futura Christi passionis symbola, quæ tunc, id est, si homo non peccasset, nulla sutura erat. Laudu autem, gratiarúmque actiones Deo canebant primi homines, eiusque posteri futuri eundem Deo cultum obtulissent, & nomen Domini invocabant, vti & Dei sui, & parentis benignissimi. Et hæc quidem de primo illo, quod Adami peccatum præcessit, tempore.
units.tr: This collection, which we are making, aims at this: that from what has gone before we may understand and gather what the political and also the ecclesiastical state of the world was at that time, that is, throughout the whole period that preceded Adam's sin. The political state (which is contained in the laws of magistrates and in cities) was as follows. Both the first human beings were magistrates of the whole world, and the man, who was male, was the chief and highest of them; the woman held the lower place. For the male seems to have been superior to the female in this, that the man had learned from God himself, and was learning, and had received and was receiving, what he himself afterwards taught the woman and shared with her. Over all animals, indeed over the whole world, each had equal right, yet not a harsh or cruel rule, but that of a guardian and a gentle lord over them; and they used it neither for idle curiosity nor for shameful lust, from which both human beings were free. The laws of this government were the precepts of God himself, and the will of each human being, sound and composed in obedience to those precepts, free of every vice and injustice, but kindly and just. No cities had yet been built; nor was there any need to build them, since people were entirely free from fear, both of one another and of wild beasts. Fear and terror, however, are, as we shall show, the chief cause of building cities among men. So much concerning the political state of that age. The ecclesiastical state (which consists of these four things: the Word of God, its minister, the sacraments, and the place) was of the following kind. The Word of God, which had been made known to Adam, and so to Ischa (who is also Eve), his wife, was revealed to them by God himself and was in no way written down. It contained, first, the history of the creation of this whole world, and especially of man himself; next, the right and dominion over this whole created order granted to man by God; and finally, the future happy condition and immortality of both human beings and of the whole human race, should those two obey God and keep themselves always in their proper order. The minister of this word revealed by God was Adam, to his wife; and so the other men were to be ministers to their wives, and husbands to their wives, and parents to their children. Ministers and preachers of the same Word of God were to be such in the same way. The sacraments, which were joined by God to that word and promise, are counted as two: namely, the Tree of Life, and the other, the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil, which Adam was forbidden by God to eat from the latter, with the most severe penalty added, so that they would fear the more. They were allowed only to look at that tree and to touch it with their hands. For it was not forbidden to them to eat of the former tree, that is, the Tree of Life. Finally, the place of the Church was the garden, which was to be the place of God's own future conversation with Adam and his posterity. Therefore that Paradise, or the Edenic Garden, was like a temple, consecrated and set apart over the whole world. The mutual communication of the same Word of God, which was to take place between parents and children and between husbands and wives, was to happen in their daily dealings and in their domestic fellowship. At that time no sacrifices of cattle were offered to God, nor were they to be offered, since these are, or were to be, symbols of Christ's passion, which would have had no place then, that is, had man not sinned. The first human beings sang praises and thanksgivings to God, and their descendants would have offered the same worship to God and called upon the name of the Lord, as of their God and most kind Father. So much concerning that first time, before Adam's sin.

units.la: LIBER
units.tr: BOOK

units.la: ROPOSITVM est nobis in hac Sectione completi breuiter ea, quae ab Hominis Peccato ad publicam, & popularem Nominis Dei Profanationem contigerunt, prout ea Sacra Dei Scriptura tradit. Illa vero sunt varia, & multiplicia (Nam crescente & adolescente Mundo, crescit quoque Historia Mundi) numero septemdecim capita sunt, è quibus est
units.tr: It is our purpose in this section to set out briefly the events that occurred from man's sin to the public and popular profanation of the name of God, as the holy Scripture of God relates them. These events are various and manifold (for as the world grows and matures, its history grows too), and there are seventeen chapters, of which the first is:

units.la: I. Peccatum Primum Primorum Hominum.
units.tr: I. The First Sin of the First Men.

units.la: Adamus, & Ifcha vxor Adami (quæ & Eua) primi Hominum, & adhuc in Mundo soli, nondum propagato genere humano, liberè, prudentes, scientes & volentes mandatum Dei de non edendo fructu Arboris Scientiæ boni, & mali transgredimur, Satanæ astu (qui per Serpentis tunc pulcherrimi vaferrimique omnium Animalium os, ac ministerium eos allocutus est) mendacióque persuasi, prima quidem Ifcha à Serpente, postea verò Adamum per Ifcham vxorem suam. Vterque verò nempe Adamus, & Ifcha primum peccât ex magna infidelitate, vtpote Verbum Dei, id est, tum promissiones, tum minas sibi à Deo ipso factas negligentes, & minimè verae esse existimantes: magna item animi in Deum ipsum ingratitudine, beneficia Dei in se plus quàm in cæteras animantes præstantissima spernetes, suaque originis & conditionis oblitii: Sed ex immani quoque superbia, ordinem & locum tam honorificum inter omnia huius Mundi opera à Deo sibi datum ac concessum deferentes, & abijcientes. Præterea ex intolerabili perfidia locum Domini sui, id est, Dei ipsius regnum occupantes: Deinde Sacrilegio se non vltrò quidem, sed tamen sponte, libereq; animi consensu Diabolo, carnisq;, id est, voluntatis suæ Deo rebellis, & repugnantis, libidini & potestati (contradicente etiam tunc propria eorum conscientia, rationeq;) in perpetuū vendentes ac subijcientes, & Deo sese substrahentes, ac suffurantes Domino suo & vero nempe, Gen. 3 2.Cor. xi.3, 1.Timoth.2.14, Roman.7.14, Ioan.8.44, 1.Ioan.3.8, Apoc.12.9, & 20.2. Ergo infinita fuerunt in hoc vno peccato vitia & peccata.
units.tr: Adam and Ischa, the wife of Adam (also called Eve), the first of men, and as yet alone in the world, since the human race had not yet been propagated, freely, knowingly, wittingly and willingly transgressed God's command not to eat the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. They were persuaded by the cunning of Satan, who addressed them through the mouth and agency of the serpent, then the most beautiful and craftiest of all the animals, and by his lies: first Ischa was persuaded by the serpent, and then Adam was persuaded through Ischa, his wife. Both Adam and Ischa first sinned out of great unbelief, namely by neglecting the Word of God, that is, both the promises and the threats made to them by God himself, and by judging them not to be true at all. Likewise they sinned out of great ingratitude of mind towards God himself, scorning the benefits God had bestowed on them, far more excellent than on the other living creatures, and forgetting their origin and condition. But they also sinned out of monstrous pride, rejecting and casting off the so honourable rank and place among all the works of this world that God had given and granted them. Besides this, out of intolerable treachery, they seized the place of their Lord, that is, God's own kingdom. Then by sacrilege they gave themselves over and subjected themselves to the Devil, and to the flesh (that is, to the lust and power of their own will, which was rebellious and resistant against God), not indeed unwillingly but still of their own accord and with free consent of mind, for ever, their own conscience and reason also then contradicting this; and they withdrew and stole themselves away from God, their Lord and true Lord. Therefore infinite were the vices and sins in this one sin.

units.la: II. Poena Peccati Hominum.
units.tr: II. The Punishment of Human Sin.

units.la: TAM Nefarium & immane Hominis vtriusq; Spontaneumque peccatum & sceleu,quanuis non vltraneum, grauissima in omnes peccati istius actores, auto- resque primum: post autem in vniuersum quoque huno Mundum Hominí subiectum poena à Deo ipso secuta, pronuntiatáque est tum generalis,tum Specialis: omnis tamen iustissima. Generalis quidem in vtrumque Hominem,nempe Adamum, & Ischam (quæ & Eua) ao communis poena, duplex secuta est, videlicet primùm turpitudinis ipsius sua suique sceleris,ac iam nullitatis ob Deum offensum,nuditatisque agnitio: deinde Mors tum animi,tum corporis impositta,futuráque postea vtrique:unde & morbi,& infirmitates(qua ad mortem deducunt,hominisque compositionem dissoluunt)secuta, & peccata nata sunt ex illa defectione prima à Deo nata, & imaginis Dei in vtróque Homine summa labefactatio, id est, Tenebræ in mente: rebellio in corde, Gen.3 7.19, Psal.73 4, Rom.5.12,& 6.24.Apoc. 12.9. Hæc poena communis fuit vtrique Homini. Peculiaris vero poena, quæ Adamo seu viro & Mascule addita est,& ipsa quoque fuit duplex. Primùm nempe labor,Viri, & Maris præsertim, perpetuus & anxius in victu querendo, quum antea esset illi è terra in promptu sine labore, & in parato vberrimus, Gen.2. 23. Deinde etiam in eo ipso labore Maledictio Dei, nempe quod nequaquam vel semper,vel pro spe, vel pro enolestia grauitate fructuosum sit homini labor suus,Gē. 3.17.19, 2.Thef.3.10, 1.Thef.5.14, Psal.128.2. Pœna quoq; peculiaris Ifcha(qua eadem Eua)duplex fuit imposita, videlicet Primum, illius Subiectio sub Marito,ac proinde iuris in res omnes prioris(quod illa habebat) imminutio quædam, ratiocinationisq; etiam ipsius damnum: Deinde labor in partu, vexatioq; mulieris maxima, & ineredibilis, quòd hominem dum parit, pariat Dei hostem & aduersarium, ipsius mulieris culpâ, effectum, Gen. 3.16, Ioan. 16.21, Isaia 37.3. Et hæc quidem pœna Hominis fuit. At Serpenti(cuius ministerio vsus est Satan ad impellendum Adamum in peccatum) pœna quoque & ipsi duplex indicta est: Primum nempe Maledictio Dei eum secuta est grauissima. Nam pra cæteris Animantibus Serpenti laboriosissima vita est, incessus abiectus, & laboriosus, visusq; difficilis, asper, & inuucundus: imo etiam reliquis Animalibus iam exosus est serpens, velut venenatum & fœtidum etiam alijs animalibus. Deinde perpetuæ illi cum homine inimicitiæ intercedunt: Caput enim serpentis petunt homines, vt eum prorsus extinguant: Serpens autem calcaneum hominis petit, vt hominem vulneret, & deiciat humi, Gen. 3.14, Psal. 58.4, & 91.13, Act. 28.4, Isa 65.25. In reliquum autem Mundum vniuersum etiam Peccati hominis pœna extitit, ac effusa est, velut in hereditatem ipsi à Deo destinatam, & rem hominis. Ac quidem in eos, qui ex vtroq; illo Homine postea nasciturî erant, homines, pœna eadem transiit, quæ in primis illis Hominibus omnium hominum parentibus supra descripta fuit. Nam quum totum genus humanum futurum repræsentarent primi illi homines, (id est, & Mascalos, & Fœminas futuras) ex iis duobus Creatus primum in posteros omnes eorum & singulos, id est, in omnes & singulos homines, culpaque transgressa est: ex Creatu corruptio eorum in animo & corpore: ex corruptione pœna quoque in eosdem instlë, velut ob propria iam labem secuta est. Qua tria Peccatum Originale vocantur, quod ex Parentibus transit in liberos. Unde dicuntur Homines illi duo postea, id est, post peccatum suum generasse homines ad suam, non autem ad Dei imaginem, Gen. 5. 3, 1. Corinth. 15. 49, Rom. 5. 12, Ephes. 2. 3. In reliquas autem Mundi huius partes pœna eiusdem hominum peccati effusa est granissima, quoniam hominis gratia conditus fuerat, vt dixi, hic Mundus, illique velut domus & familia propria, datus a Deo. Ergo totus hic Mundus, eiusq; partes omnes & singulæ ob peccatum istud hominis vanitati, Deique maledictioni subditæ, & quidem ex eo tempore fuerunt, vt neque priores (quas a Deo acceperant) vires retineant, neque pulchritudinem vsumque tantum hemini prabeant. Præterea in malitio, id est, occasione peccandi; & rerum abusu positum est totus hic Mundus, malitia hominis depravatus, Gen. 3. 17. 18, Rom. 8. 20, 1. Ioan. 5. 19. Diabolo denique ipsi (qui fuit istius peccati princeps, & autor, suasorque Hominibus Gen. 3, 1. Ioan. 3. 8.) pœna imposita quoque est, eáque maxima, quæ comprehensa est his verbis: [Pœnè inimicitias inter te, & semen Mulieris, & conteret caput tuum,] vti postea docebitur.
units.tr: So shameful, so monstrous, and so deliberate was the sin and crime of both human beings, though not beyond forgiveness, that God himself pronounced upon all the perpetrators and authors of that sin, first, and then upon the whole world made subject to man, a punishment that was both general and specific, yet entirely just. The general punishment, falling on both human beings, Adam and Ischa (who is also Eve), came in two parts: first, the recognition of their own shame and of their wrongdoing, a sense of their own nakedness and of having lost their standing before God, who had been offended; then death, both of soul and of body, laid upon them and destined to come upon them afterward. From this came diseases and sicknesses that lead to death and dissolve the human frame, and sins were born from that first defection, which God had brought about. There was also the great overthrow of the image of God in both human beings, that is, darkness in the mind and rebellion in the heart (Gen. 3:7, 19; Ps. 73:4; Rom. 5:12; 6:24; Rev. 12:9). This general punishment fell on both alike. The punishment peculiar to Adam, or to the man and male, was also twofold. First, labor, perpetual and anxious, especially for the man and the male, in seeking food, whereas before, the earth had supplied him abundantly and ready without labor (Gen. 2:23). Then, in that very labor, the curse of God: that man's toil is by no means always or regularly fruitful, nor fruitful in proportion to hope or to the weight of his troubles (Gen. 3:17, 19; 2 Thess. 3:10; 1 Thess. 5:14; Ps. 128:2). The punishment peculiar to Ischa (who is the same Eve) was also twofold, namely: first, her subjection under her husband, and therefore a certain diminishment of the rights over all things that she had before, along with a loss even of her reasoning; then, labor in childbirth and the greatest and incredible suffering of the woman, because, through the woman's own fault, the man she bears, while she bears him, becomes God's enemy and adversary (Gen. 3:16; John 16:21; Isa. 37:3). This was the punishment of the man. But for the serpent (through whose service Satan made use to drive Adam into sin) a twofold punishment was also decreed: first, the curse of God fell upon it most heavily. For of all living creatures the serpent has the most toilsome life, its movement is abject and laborious, its sight is poor, harsh and unpleasant; indeed, even among the other animals the serpent is now hateful, as something poisonous and foul to them. Then, a perpetual enmity was set between it and man: for men aim at the serpent's head, so as utterly to destroy it, while the serpent aims at man's heel, so as to wound him and throw him to the ground (Gen. 3:14; Ps. 58:4; 91:13; Acts 28:4; Isa. 65:25). The punishment of man's sin also extended and spread over the whole rest of the world, as if it were an inheritance and property destined for man by God. And indeed, the same punishment that was described above in the first human beings, the parents of all men, passed on to those human beings who were to be born afterward from both of them. For since those first human beings were to represent the whole human race (that is, both the males and the females who would come after them), the guilt of their transgression passed first from the two of them to all their descendants, to each and every human being; from the guilt came their corruption in soul and body; and from the corruption a punishment followed and was fixed upon the same persons, as on account of their own already existing stain. These three things are called original sin, which passes from parents to children. Hence those two human beings are said to have begotten afterward, that is, after their sin, human beings in their own likeness and not in the image of God (Gen. 5:3; 1 Cor. 15:49; Rom. 5:12; Eph. 2:3). Upon the remaining parts of this world, too, the punishment of this same human sin was poured out most heavily, since this world had been made for man's sake, as I have said, and was given by God to him as his own house and household. Therefore the whole of this world, and all its parts, singly and together, were subjected because of man's sin to futility and to God's curse, and from that time on they neither keep the powers they had received from God, nor offer man anything but beauty and use. Moreover, the whole world is placed under the abuse of things and under the occasion for sinning, having been corrupted by man's wickedness (Gen. 3:17, 18; Rom. 8:20; 1 John 5:19). Finally, a punishment was also laid upon the Devil himself, who was the prince and author of this sin and the persuader of the human beings (Gen. 3:1; 1 John 3:8), and it was the greatest, contained in these words: [I will put enmity between you and the seed of the woman, and it shall bruise your head], as will be shown afterward.

units.la: 3. Promissio Messiæ, seu Seruatoris futuri.
units.tr: 3. The promise of the Messiah, or of the future Saviour.

units.la: DEVS tamen spem saluti Hominibus etiam post peccatum reliquam fecit. Namqs futurum Seruatorem ex Semine Mulieris statim pollicitus est, nempe qui caput Serpentis, ac proinde Diaboli (cuius Serpes minister fuerat) contereret, ac illius regnum, & virtutem minueret, ac prorsus tandem euerteret, tolleret, ac concul carct, Gen. 3. 15, Apoc. 12. 9, & 20. 2, Mat. 25 41
units.tr: God, however, left hope of salvation for humankind even after the sin. For he at once promised a future Saviour from the seed of the woman, namely one who would crush the head of the Serpent, and therefore of the Devil (whose minister the serpent had been), and would diminish his kingdom and power, and finally utterly overthrow, remove and shatter it, Gen. 3:15, Rev. 12:9, and 20:2, Matt. 25:41.

units.la: Is autem fuit Christus, ex femine Maria Virginis & Mulieris sine femine viri, natus, qui toti quidem generi humano datus est à Deo Seruator sufficienter: ys tamen solis efficaciter, & efficienter, & re ipsa, qui hoc remedium à Deo sibi gratuiter oblatum acceptant, & vera certâque fide ampleCtuntur, & recipiunt. Hi autem sunt soli fideles, & Electi Dei Mat. 26. 28, Actu. 13. 48. Porrò hunc generis humani Seruatorem, non tantum Hominem ex femine mulieris esse, & fieri oportuit: verumetiam Deum, vt caput istius veteris Serpentis, id est, Diaboli vires, potestatem ac regnum immensum euertere posset, Isa. 7. 14. Mat. 1. 23, Rom. 1. 2. 3. Nulla enim vis nisi vere Diuina, tanti tamque robusti hostis (qualis is fuit, qui hominem vtrumque, & quidem purum, viuidum integrámque Dei imaginem ad huc gestantem detexit) regnum, & potestatem proftrare, & vincere certè quidem quibat. Non vis humana, quam iam superarat Satan: non Angelica, quoniam & ipsemet Diabolus est Angelus, natura praestantissimus, Apoc. 5. 5, & 12. 9. 10. Ergo & Homo & Deus suturum erat hic Hominum Seruator, ex mente Dei, & vera intelligentia huius Dei promissionis misericordissimae erga homines [Poenam inimicitias (o Serpens) inter te, & inter Mulierem hanc: similiter inter Semen tuum, & Semen Mulieris: ipsum conteret tibi caput, & tu conteres ei calcaneum, Genef 3.15, 1.Pet. 5.8.] Huius autem Dei gratuita plane, & ex summa Dei benignitate & φιλανθρωπία profecta, Tit 3.4. promissionis triplex est effectum. Primum quidem generale, quod omnium hominū (quatenus sunt femen mulieris) commune est, nempe, Generale dissidium inter homines & serpentes, Num 21.6, 1.Cor.10.9. hominumque maior vis & ad nocendum serpenti potestas, quam serpentis animalis ad nocendum homini, Ecclesiastic.39. 35. Secundum est peculiare fidelium hominum (qui sunt Christi, id est, illius Seruatoris promissi membra) videlicet vires illis à Deo per Christum & Seruatore illum concessae, ad vincendum etiam nunc ex parte diabolum, Rom 16.20, 1.Cor.15.57, 1.Ioan.5.4. Tertium denique effectum est, Proprium unius & solius illius Seruatoris seu Christi tunc veturi, ac futuri hominis nimirū Plena de serpente illo victoria, & totius regni ipsius abolitio, euersio, & internecio ab ipso Christo, seu semine Mulieris futuro facienda tunc, & quidem per seipsum, Mat.4.11, Ioan.14.30, 1.Cor.15 54:quae ab eo iam facta est in se: In nobis autem fit, ac impletur quotidie.
units.tr: This was Christ, born of Mary the Virgin, a woman without a man's seed, who was given by God as a Saviour sufficiently for the whole human race, but efficaciously, effectively and in fact only for those who accept this remedy freely offered to them by God and embrace and receive it with true and certain faith. These alone are the faithful and the elect of God, Matt. 26:28, Acts 13:48. Moreover, it was necessary that this Saviour of the human race should be not only a man born of a woman, but also God, so that he might overthrow the head of that old serpent, that is, the power, authority and vast kingdom of the Devil, Isa. 7:14, Matt. 1:23, Rom. 1:2-3. For no power other than truly divine could cast down and conquer the kingdom and authority of so great and so strong an enemy (such as he was, who had deceived the man, who was both pure and alive and still bore the whole image of God). Human power could not, since Satan had already overcome it; nor angelic power, since the Devil himself is an angel, most excellent in nature, Rev. 5:5, 12:9-10. Therefore the Saviour of men was to be both man and God, according to the mind of God and the true understanding of this most merciful promise of God towards men: [I will put enmity (O Serpent) between you and this woman; likewise between your seed and the seed of the woman; he shall crush your head, and you shall bruise his heel, Gen. 3:15, 1 Pet. 5:8.] The effect of this promise, which is entirely gratuitous and springs from the great kindness of God and his love of mankind [φιλανθρωπία], Titus 3:4, is threefold. The first is general, common to all men (insofar as they are the seed of the woman): namely a general enmity between men and serpents, Num. 21:6, 1 Cor. 10:9, and the greater strength and power of men to harm the serpent than the serpent has to harm man, Ecclus. 39:35. The second is peculiar to the faithful (who are Christ's, that is, members of that promised Saviour): namely the strength granted to them by God through Christ the Saviour to overcome the devil, even now in part, Rom. 16:20, 1 Cor. 15:57, 1 John 5:4. Finally, the third effect is proper to that one and only Saviour, Christ, the man who was to come in the future: namely the full victory over that serpent, and the abolition, overthrow and complete destruction of his whole kingdom, to be accomplished then by Christ himself, the future seed of the woman, and indeed by himself, Matt. 4:11, John 14:30, 1 Cor. 15:54; which he has already accomplished in himself, but which is done and fulfilled in us daily.

units.la: IIII. Mutatum nomen Mulieri Primae.
units.tr: IIII. The Name of the First Woman Is Changed.

units.la: ISCHAE vero (quae erat Adami vxor, sicque prius ante peccatum vocabatur Ischa, id est, Virago.) Adamus nomen post peccatum immutauit, & pro Ischa [Chauam] appellauit: quod vocabulum [Eua] conuersum fuit, etiam ab ipsismet Apostolis. Sic autem eam nominauit, à spe suscipienda ex ea postea prolis & soboliis, id est, propagandi generis humani, Gen.3.21, 1.Tim.2.13, 2.Cor.11.3. quo ipso nomine voluit Euam uxoris sua dolorem, & animi mœrorem de suo peccato maledictione & doloribus partum lenire ac consolari (ne absorberetur) utpote sapiens maritus, [Chauam] vocans eam, id est, hominum futurorum fontem & Matrem potius quam [Motam] vel [Maueiam] id est, mortis generis humani caussam, & autorem, propterea quod Deus ipse consolatus Euam fuerat, quum dixisset, [Et Semen Mulieris conteret caput Serpentis.] Ergo eam Adamus Chauam appellauit, attendens ad Dei promissionem, cum de nascituro ex ea femine generaliter totius generis humani: tum peculiariter de Semine illo, hominum nempe Seruatore, seu Christo ex eadem futuro. Nam ex Eua & Adami semine natus est multis post seculis Christus, Luc 3.38. non ex coitu quidem viri, sed tamen ex utriusque stirpe, videlicet ex Virgine Maria.
units.tr: Eve, however (who was Adam's wife, and who before the sin was therefore called Ischa, that is, Virago), was renamed by Adam after the sin: he called her Chava instead of Ischa, a name which was also rendered as Eve, even by the Apostles themselves. He named her thus from the hope that, through her, offspring and progeny, that is, the propagation of the human race, would afterwards be obtained (Gen. 3:21; 1 Tim. 2:13; 2 Cor. 11:3). By this very name he wished to soothe and console his wife Eve for the grief and sorrow of mind that her sin had brought upon her, and for the pains of childbirth that came as a curse (so that she would not be overwhelmed); as a wise husband he called her Chava, that is, the fountain and mother of the future generations of men, rather than Motah or Maveiah, that is, the cause and author of the death of the human race. He did this because God himself had consoled Eve when he said, "And the Seed of the Woman shall bruise the head of the Serpent." Adam therefore called her Chava, looking to God's promise, which concerned the seed to be born from her in general for the whole human race, and in particular concerned that Seed, the Saviour of men, that is, Christ, who was to come from her. For Christ was born many ages later from the seed of Eve and Adam (Luke 3:38), not indeed by the union of a man, but nevertheless from the stock of both, namely from the Virgin Mary.

units.la: V. Vestitutus Hominum Primus & Unde, & Quis.
units.tr: V. The First Clothing of Human Beings: Whence and by Whom

units.la: VESTIVIT postea Deus Hominem utrumque, duabus de causis. Primum, quoniam utrumque hominem pudebat cum in universum sua nuditatis: tum precipue eorum membrorum, quae in utroque genitalia sunt, id est, quae ad generationem hominum peccatorum, & Deo iam exosorum postea futuram erant destinata. Hac cernebat uterque ille homo Mas nimirum & foemina mina in se, & nuda, & prater cetera maxime pudenda propter peccati sui effectum, id est, propter suam sobolem, quam sciebat esse Deo iam maledictâ: & propter motum, & affectum, qui in illis membris & primùm, & maxime turpis, & immoderatus iam sentiebatur. Nam antequam ea operiret, perceptu ab viroq; homine fuerat statim post peccatum. Hic motus Libido nominatur, Gen. 3.7 & 9 22.23, 1.Corinth.12.23. Quamobrem eas sui corporis partes velut indecoras iam texerat ipse uterque Homo ficulneis foliis, etiam ante accepta nimirum à Deo vestimenta, quibus reliquas sui corporis partes, & membra operirent. Deinde vestiuit Deus Hominem propter iniurias cœli, quas & tunc sensit, & postea sensurus erat. sentiúntque homines propter sua peccata iam molestissimas, Isa.32 2, Psal. 107.29, Deuter.28.23. Vestes autem eas conficit Deus, & cótexuit ex pellibus animalium à se videlicet occisorum. Nam eas pelles ydem bestiys mortuis Deus ipse detraxit, bestiasq; aliquas excoriauit, Gen.3.21, Mat.25.36. Ex quo apparet Vestitum iam esse partem unâ quandam præcipuam vitius hominis, 1.Tim. 6.8. Porrò Deus tunicas pelliceas, id est, ex pellibus mortuorum animalium potius, quam ficulneas, id est, ex foliis ficuum vel aliarum arborum contexuit, atque iis Hominem utrumque vestiuit, ac induit: Primùm, ut hoc suo vestitu assiduè admoneretur Homo uterque de sua conditione misera iam ac mortali effecta, immò etiam sese in media ipsa morte, & pellibus mortuarum bestiarum, quantumvis vivum, versari tamen agnoscere. Ergo viderunt Homines sese in illis pellibus adhuc fœtidis ac recentibus esse, velut in sepulcro, & ijs involuti velut impedimentis quibusdam. Deinde ea se habere aduersus cœli iniurias intellexerūt (quibus iam obnoxij propter peccatum facti erant) velut munimenta necessaria. Proinde hoc tam tristi spectaculo (quod vbique ficum circumgestabant, atque etiamnum homines pene emores gestant) & ipsi Homines primi, & eorum posteri terrerentur. Denique, vt poenam mortis sibi denunciatam homo iam tunc ex parte animo sentiret, apprehenderet, ac postea meminisset semper, Iobi 4. 19. Iac. 5. 2. dum se vestitum cernit.
units.tr: God afterwards clothed each of the two human beings, and he did so for two reasons. First, because each of them was ashamed of their nakedness in general, and especially of those parts of the body that are the genitals in each, that is, the parts destined to be the means of generating a sinful people who would afterwards be hateful to God. Each of these two, the male and the woman, naked in herself, and, beyond all other parts, most shameful because of the effect of their sin, that is, because of their offspring, which they knew was already accursed by God, and because of the impulse and desire which in those members was felt to be the first and most shameful and now immoderate. For before he covered them, the man had perceived this impulse immediately after the sin. This impulse is called lust (Gen. 3.7, 9, 22, 23; 1 Cor. 12.23). Therefore each of them had already covered those parts of the body as unseemly with fig leaves, even before receiving from God the garments with which they would cover the remaining parts of their bodies and limbs. Then God clothed the man because of the injuries of the sky, which he already felt and would feel still more afterwards; and men now feel them, most troublesome on account of their sins (Isa. 32.2; Ps. 107.29; Deut. 28.23). God himself made these garments and wove them from the skins of animals, namely of those he had himself killed. For God himself stripped those skins from the dead beasts, and flayed some of the beasts (Gen. 3.21; Matt. 25.36). From this it appears that clothing is already one of the chief marks of human wretchedness (1 Tim. 6.8). Moreover, God wove tunics of skin, that is, from the skins of dead animals, rather than fig leaves, that is, from the leaves of figs or other trees, and with these he clothed and dressed both the man and the woman. First, so that by this clothing each of the two human beings would be constantly reminded of their wretched condition, now made mortal, and would even acknowledge that, although alive, they dwell in the very midst of death, wrapped in the skins of dead beasts. Thus men saw that they were in those skins, still foul and fresh, as in a sepulchre, and wrapped in them as in certain shackles. Then they understood that these skins were necessary protections against the injuries of the sky, to which they had become subject through sin. Accordingly, by this very sad spectacle (for they carried the fig leaves everywhere, and men still almost always carry the dead about), the first human beings and their descendants were terrified. Finally, so that the man might even then partly feel in his mind the punishment of death pronounced upon him, grasp it, and always remember it whenever he sees himself clothed (Job 4.19; James 5.2).

units.la: VI. Eiectio Adami & Euæ, post pecca- tum suum, ex Horto Edenico.
units.tr: VI. The expulsion of Adam and Eve from the Garden of Eden after their sin.

units.la: CAETERVM Deus Adamum & Euam priùs à se contra cœli iniuriam, & ad tegendam eorum nuditatem post peccatum vestitos, ex Horto tamen Edenico non manu leniter educit, sed vi & terrore ijs inesso eiecit, & expellit, Gen 3. 23. 24. Fugerunt igitur illi velut iam furea, aut sceleratí, qui metu, conscientiaque perpetrati grandis alicuius maleficij pauidi, perterriti, & trepidantes, ex eo loco, vbi deliquerunt, eripiunt se ac fugiunt. Priùs tamen Deus eos increpauit, & quàm falsa essent, ac fuisset Diaboli promissa, quàmque stulta & perfida Hominum ipsorum in se parentem infidelitas ironica oratione (vt eosdem vehementius, atque acrius compungeret) docuit Gen. 3. 22. vt saltem v I nunc malo iam accepto, & illi, & reliqui Homines sapiant, nec in posterum vllis Satanæ quantumvis se beneuolum fingentis verbis, aut promissis credant: Dei vero verbum nunquam relinquat, aut abjiciant, 2.Cor. 11.13.14, Ephes.6.11, Jac.4 7. Verum ne in eundem illum Hortum postea ipsi ipsi Homines denuo ingredirentur: aut statim posteri eorum (antequam ipsius horti Edenici deleta facies esset) eundem adirent, Deus ad Horti illius Orientem, & in anteriore illius parte Cherubinos plures velut in statione collocauit, qui Homines aditu seu ingressu in eum prohiberent, ac impedirêt, ne ab iis excoleretur, aut eius amœnitas ab iis spectaretur: sed ut desertum, incultus, & horridus locus fieret, & a beluis paulatim vastaretur. Denique mucronem flammei, aut fulgidi gladij in quamuis partem circumuolitantis, & se mitantis, ac vertentis in ipso horto collocauit Deus ad terrorem, quò viam hominibus omnibus, ad Arborem vitæ, eiusque fructum decerpendum, & edendum (ne fierent hic immortales) præcluderet, & immani metu obiecto eos ab ingressu impediret, Gen.3.24. Psal.35.6, & 78.49.
units.tr: Moreover, God did not lead Adam and Eve gently by the hand out of the Garden of Eden, though he had first clothed them after the sin against heaven's injunction and to cover their nakedness. Instead he drove them out and expelled them with force and the terror that was inherent in them (Gen. 3:23, 24). So they fled like thieves or criminals, fearful and terrified by the dread and the guilty conscience of some great wrong they had committed, and they tore themselves away from the place where they had sinned and fled from it. Yet God first rebuked them, and taught them, in an ironical speech (to sting them more sharply and keenly), how false the devil's promises were, and how foolish and treacherous was the unbelief of these humans against their own parent (Gen. 3:22). His purpose was that they, and the rest of mankind, might at least now, with the evil already received, grow wise, and never again believe any words or promises of Satan, however kindly he pretends to be. They should never abandon or cast off God's word (2 Cor. 11:13, 14; Eph. 6:11; James 4:7). But lest the humans themselves should later enter that same garden again, or their descendants should go there before the face of the Garden of Eden had been destroyed, God set several cherubim as sentries at the east of that garden and in its front part. They were to keep humans from entering it and to prevent them from tending it or enjoying its beauty, so that the place would become deserted, uncultivated and rough, and gradually be laid waste by wild beasts. Finally, God placed in the garden itself a flaming, gleaming sword, flashing and turning in every direction, to terrify people and to block for all humans the way to the tree of life and to the eating of its fruit (lest they become immortal here), and by fearsome dread to keep them from entering (Gen. 3:24; Ps. 35:6; Ps. 78:49).

units.la: VII. Propagatio prima Generis humani.
units.tr: VII. The First Propagation of the Human Race.

units.la: PRIMA vero Generis Humani Propagatio (nec enim propter peccatum homines infœcundi facti sunt) facta est ab Adamo, & Eua ex iusto, legitimo coniugio, nempe susceptò primum ex Eua, ac prognato Caino, deinde Abele seu Hebele, tertio Setho post occisum a fratre Caino Abelem. Gen.4.1, & 5.3. Genuit autem & Adamus, & Eua uxor eius, et coæua seu æqualis Sethum, anno ætatis centesimo trigesimo. Caeterum hi (uti & quicunque post peccatum primum ab
units.tr: The first propagation of the human race (for men did not become infertile on account of sin) was made by Adam and Eve from a lawful, legitimate marriage: first Eve conceived and bore Cain, then Abel or Hebel, and third Seth, after Abel had been killed by his brother Cain (Gen. 4.1; 5.3). Adam and his wife Eve also begot Seth, who was coeval with them, or of the same age, in the hundred and thirtieth year of their life. Moreover, these (as also all who were born after the first sin

units.la: Adamo & Eua commissum, vel ab ijs ipsis, vel ab eorum posteris nati sunt, post ea homines) illi inquam geniti natiq; sunt non ad veram illam Dei imaginem (quam primum Adamus a Deo ipso habuerat) sed ad Adami & suorum parentum imaginem duntaxat, in quibus magnam partem iam illa pura & prior imago Dei per peccatum deleta est, fuerátque, qualis etiamnum hodie in hominibus restat, nempe fœdata, cōmaculata, deformis, & penè tota exstincta. Quod enim est Gen. 5.3: [Et genuit Adam filium ad imaginem suam, & secundum similitudinem suam,] non modo ad Adamū: verum ad omnes omnino, qui liberos naturali modo procreant homines in vniuersum, & quouis tempore, pertinet. Eos enim procreant, sibi similes, ac proinde coram Deo reos & peccatores, quales ipsi sunt, qui sunt eorum parentes, 1.Cor.15.49, Iob 14.4, & 25.4, Isa.64.6, Ephes.2.3. Quo vero aetatis suæ anno, ac tempore Adamus & Eua Cainū, & Abelem procrearint, non apparet ex sacra Scriptura.
units.tr: committed by Adam and Eve, whether by them or by their descendants), those men, I say, were begotten and born not to that true image of God (which Adam had first received from God himself), but only to the image of Adam and of their parents, in whom for the most part that pure and original image of God was destroyed by sin, and which remains in men even today, namely defiled, stained, deformed, and almost wholly extinguished. For Gen. 5.3, "And Adam begat a son in his own image, and after his likeness," pertains not only to Adam but to all men in general who procreate children in the natural way, at any time whatever. For they beget children like themselves, and therefore guilty and sinners before God, just as they themselves are who are their parents (1 Cor. 15.49; Job 14.4; 25.4; Isa. 64.6; Eph. 2.3). But in what year of his life Adam and Eve begot Cain and Abel does not appear from Holy Scripture.

units.la: CAPUT VIII. Artes Primæ Hominum, id est, ab Hominibus primum inventæ, exercitæ, & institutæ.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII. The First Arts of Men, that is, those first invented, practised and instituted by men.

units.la: ARTES vero, quas primas, & primi quidem Homines, exercuerunt, fuerunt hæ duæ, nempe Agricultura, qua terra colebatur: & Pastoritia, qua pecudes pascebatur, & alebatur, Gen.3.23, & 4.2. Nam Adamus ipse fuit Agricola, & post eum Cainus: Sed & Noachus quoque, Mundo postea renouato, Gen.9.20. 20. Abel vero fuit pastor, & custos gregis & pecoris. Ergo haec sunt artes duae primae, & imprimis naturales. Reliquae vero postea sunt inventae, & magis ad quaestum & splendorem, & cupiditates explendas, quam ad naturam, vitaeque huius sustentationem, & necessitatem, sed vitae naturalem comparatam, ac proinde nominatur [Artificia] & [Quaestus] & ad χρηματιστικὴν potius quam φυσικὴν τεχνὴν referuntur. Porro ex his artibus institutis apparet, quàm, fuerit immutata prima illa honestaque hominum conditio, qui ut victum haberent, inserviebant iam terrae, ex qua sumpti fuerat, quaeque antea sponte omnia profundebat largissime illis, qui item Pecoribus, id est, bestiis brutisque animantibus (quae ad ipsorum obsequium, & servitium antea condita fuerant) obsequi, famulariaque cogerentur, ac cogantur, mutata nempe tam horribiliter & miserè propter hominum peccatum, vice rerum, ut qui Dominus omnium earum prius fuerat, Homo, servus omnium nunc sit, & evaserit, 1. Cor. 9. 7, Ioan. 10. 5, Job. 14.
units.tr: The first arts that the first men practised were these two: agriculture, by which the earth was cultivated, and pastoral farming, by which flocks and herds were tended and fed (Gen. 3.23; 4.2). For Adam himself was a farmer, and after him Cain; and Noah too, after the world was renewed (Gen. 9.20). Abel was a shepherd and keeper of the flock and herd. So these are the two first arts, and above all natural ones. The rest were invented later and serve more for gain, show and the satisfying of desires than for nature and the sustaining and necessities of this life, although they supply a natural living. For this reason they are called [crafts] and [trades] and are reckoned as belonging to the [chrematistic] rather than the [physical] art. Moreover, from these institutions of arts it is clear how greatly that first and honourable condition of men was changed. In order to have a living, they were now obliged to serve the earth from which they had been taken, which before had poured out everything abundantly and freely for them. Likewise they were compelled, and are still compelled, to obey and serve the animals, that is, the beasts and brute creatures, which had earlier been appointed for their obedience and service. Because of human sin, this change of conditions has been so terrible and wretched that man, who was first lord of all these creatures, is now and has become the servant of all (1 Cor. 9.7; John 10.5; Job 14).

units.la: IX. Sacrificium Primum Hominum Memorabile.
units.tr: IX. The First Memorable Sacrifice of Men.

units.la: SACRIFICIVM primum memorabile fuit illud, quod eodem tempore à Caino, & Abele fratribus oblatum est Deo (ut refert Moses) à Caino quidem ex fructibus terrae. Nam is eos obtulit, velut sua opera, laboris, & artis benedictionem, & primitias: verum Abel obtulit ex pecore, non solum velut sua artis fructum, sed etiam velut sacrificium, ex futuri passurique Christi & Seruatoris promissi, quem apprehenderat fide, certáque notitia & expectatione. Ergo ex grege suo sacrificium obtulit Deo Abel, velut mortis Christi typum. Q́uamobrem ad hanc Abelis oblationem respexit Deus potius quàm ad illa Caini. Respexisse autem Deus ad Abelem visus est manifeste aliquo visibili signo (quod ipsi quoque Caino apparuit) ostenso & patefacto Gen.4.3.4, Heb.11.4. Non videtur quidem fuisse illud primum omnium sacrificium, quod Deo fuerit oblatum ab hominibus post peccatū, quum multum temporis interposituū fuisse, & effluxise dicatur,etiam à natiuitate vtriusque,nimirum Caini,& Abelis (nedum à tempore primi peccati primorū hominum) vsque ad hanc oblationem,sed fuit primum sacrificium memorabile. Denique Adamus toto illo praecedente hoc sacrificium spatio, non vixit absq; eo, vt Deo sacrificaret ipse,eúmque aliquibus publicis ritibus publice ex ipsius voluntate & reuelatione coleret. Verum hoc sacrificium primum ex omnibus etiam antegressis habuit manifesta & conspicua diuini fauoris & acceptationis signa & testimonia, quibus anteriora illa caruerunt. Caeterum in eo sacrificio,vel alijs,non ex omni genere pecudum etiam tum Abel obtulit Deo,vel offerre potuit:sed ex ijs tantùm animalibus,quae Deus ipse iam ad sacrificia sua designarat: quoniā distinctio inter Munda,& Immunda Animalia, tum quod ad victum hominum, tum etiam quod ad sacrificandum & Christum ac Seruatorem illum (purissimam hostiā futuram) repraesentandum iam tum innotuerat hominibus,ex Dei reuelatione,fuerâive ab eo explicata,vt
units.tr: The first sacrifice worth remembering is the one that Cain and Abel, the brothers, offered to God at the same time, as Moses reports. Cain offered fruits of the earth, as a sign of his work, the blessing of his labour and skill, and as first fruits. Abel, however, offered from his flock, not only as a product of his skill but also as a sacrifice, looking to the future suffering Christ and Saviour, whom he had grasped by faith, with sure knowledge and expectation. So Abel offered a sacrifice to God from his flock as a type of the death of Christ. For this reason God regarded Abel's offering rather than Cain's. God was plainly seen to regard Abel by some visible sign, which was also shown and made known to Cain himself (Gen. 4:3-4; Heb. 11:4). Indeed this does not seem to have been the very first sacrifice offered to God by men after the sin, since a considerable time is said to have passed, and to have run out, even from the birth of both Cain and Abel (let alone from the time of the first sin of the first men) until this offering. But it was the first sacrifice worth remembering. Adam, moreover, during all the time before this sacrifice, did not live without offering sacrifice to God himself and worshipping him with certain public rites, by God's own will and revelation. Yet this first sacrifice, unlike all those that went before it, had clear and visible signs and testimonies of God's favour and acceptance, which the earlier ones lacked. In that sacrifice, or in others, Abel did not offer to God, or was not able to offer, from every kind of animal, but only from those animals that God himself had already designated for his sacrifices. For the distinction between clean and unclean animals, both as regards human food and as regards sacrificing and representing that Christ and Saviour (who was to be the purest victim), was already known to men from God's revelation, or had been explained by him, as appears from Gen. 7:2. Concerning the time of this sacrifice, when it was offered to God by both of them, the word of God also says nothing.

units.la: appáapparet Gen.7.2. De tempore autem huius Sacrificij nihil definit quoque Dei verbum, quàdo ab utroq; fuerit oblatum Deo.
units.tr: As appears from Gen. 7:2. Nor does the word of God define anything about the time of this sacrifice, when it was offered to God by both.

units.la: X. Maleficium primum Publicum perpe- tratum in Mundo post peccatum primum.
units.tr: X. The First Public Crime Committed in the World after the First Sin.

units.la: TORRO maleficium, quod primum post peccatum primorum parentum publicè commissum est, fuit Homicidium, aut potiùs Fratricidium. Nam Cainus maior natu fratrem suum Abelem natu minorem ex invidia illius sibi à Deo prælati, occidit vi, & quidem per insidias, & in solitudine, blandiùs eum verbis in agrû, & seorsum semotis a arbitris pertrahens, Genef.4.8, 1. Ioan.3.12, Iude 1. Ergo quemadmodum Satà in ipso Homine imaginem Dei internam priùs corruperat: sic Cainus ex ipso Mundo toto illam Imaginem totam expulit, hominem occidens, & ex hoc mundo fratrem tollens. Quod fuit grauissimum in proximum scelus, horribilissimumq; aliis hominibus spectaculum: uti à Satana suasum Adamo facinus, fuit in Deum maximum. Adami verò & Eue ingens luctus, & mœror hic fuit: tristissimúmque furoris humanæ mentis, & imprimis vindictæ, atque invidiæ exemplum, & effectum. Nam mens hominis effreni vitæ sui per peccatum primorum parentum cotracti impetu percita & agitata, nec Deū timet, nec sibi ipsa parcit, nec aliis, tam est præceps, insana, amens, & furiosa, desperataq;. Huius autem sceleris in corde humano fons fuit, & primùm quidem Invidentia melioris alienæ conditionis, quàm suæ: Deinde animus & cupido vindicta. Quemadmodum autem Homicidium fuit primù ab hominibus in primo mundo perpetratū publicè maleficium seu crimen: sic quoq; Mundo postea renouato primum grauissima pœna fuit à Deo prohibitum, & interdictum, Gen 9.6. Porrò publica quoq; pœna fuit à Deo punitum hoc Caini sceleu, post ademptam illi omnem excusationem, factique fui defensionem. Nam excusationem omnem Caino Deus adimit, quae esse potuit duplex, nempe vel quòd nō fuisset munus oblatio; sua æquali fauore, quàm fratris Abelis à Deo dignata: vel quòd propter hunc Dei fauorem, in contemptum fratris sui natu minoris venturus esset. Verum quòd nō esset à Deo dignatus Cainus æquali fauore, quàm Abel, fuit ipsiusmet Caini culpa, quandoquidem pœna, vel premium à Deo pro ratione fidei & operis cuiusque manat, & decernitur, Gen.4.7 Rom 2.6, Psal.62.13, Heb 11.4. Quòd autem propterea contemptum sui à fratre minore metuebat idem Cainus, frustra. Nam mãsisset illi semper subiectus Abel frater, vtpote minor natu, nec propter eum Dei fauorem ius & prærogatiuam suam Cainus amisisset: eratque ius, & ordo Politicus à donis cœlestibus distinguendus, non vtraque hæc confundenda, Gen. 4.7, Deut. 21.15. & deinceps. Sequitur iam istius Maleficij Caini publica pœna à Deo inflicta.
units.tr: Truly, the first crime committed publicly after the sin of the first parents was murder, or rather fratricide. For Cain, the elder, killed his brother Abel, the younger, out of envy at the favour God had shown him. He killed him by force, indeed by treachery, and in a lonely place, luring him with soft words into the field and away from witnesses (Gen. 4:8; 1 John 3:12; Jude 1). Just as Satan had first corrupted the inner image of God in man himself, so Cain, by killing a man and removing a brother from this world, drove that whole image out of the entire world. It was the gravest crime against a neighbour, and the most horrible spectacle for other men, just as the deed that Satan persuaded Adam to commit was the greatest against God. For Adam and Eve this was a great grief and sorrow; and it was the saddest example and result of the fury of the human mind, and above all of revenge and envy. For the mind of man, stirred and driven by the unbridled impulse of life that was contracted through the sin of the first parents, fears neither God, nor spares itself, nor others; so headlong, mad, witless, furious and desperate is it. The source of this crime in the human heart was first the envy of another's condition, which was better than one's own, and then the spirit and desire for vengeance. Just as murder was the first public crime or offence committed by men in the first world, so too, when the world was later renewed, it was the first most grievous punishment forbidden and prohibited by God (Gen. 9:6). Moreover, this crime of Cain was also punished by God with a public penalty, after every excuse and defence of his deed had been taken from him. For God removed from Cain every excuse he could have had, and there could have been two: either that his offering had not been honoured by God with the same favour as that of his brother Abel, or that because of this favour of God he would have come to despise his younger brother. But that Cain was not honoured by God with the same favour as Abel was Cain's own fault, since punishment or reward flows from God and is decreed according to the quality of each man's faith and work (Gen. 4:7; Rom. 2:6; Ps. 62:13; Heb. 11:4). As for Cain's fear that he would be despised by his younger brother, that too was in vain. For Abel would always have remained subject to him as his elder brother, nor would Cain have lost his right and precedence because of God's favour to Abel; and political right and order are to be distinguished from heavenly gifts, not confused with them (Gen. 4:7; Deut. 21:15 and following). There follows now the public punishment of this crime of Cain, inflicted by God.

units.la: XI. Excommunicatio Prima, Pœnaque prima publica publici criminis à Deo imposita.
units.tr: XI. The First Excommunication, and the First Public Punishment of a Public Crime Imposed by God

units.la: POENA vero publica, quæ Primæ Primo illi & publico mdeficto Caini, ac proinde Hominum post peccatum à Deo imponitur, est duplex, Animi quidem seu conscientiæ ratione, Excommunicatio à facie Dei, ex fidelium cœtu & Ecclesia, quũ erro fit Cainus: Corporis autem seu Politiæ rejectu, primum Maledictio eius etiam in ipsa terra, & quidem maior, quàm communis illa, quæ ad omnes homines generaliter propter peccatum pertinet. Deinde odium reliquorum hominum in Cainum, & perpetuus ipsius Caini ab ijsdem sibi metus, terror, & trepidatio. Unde erro, & vagus toto reliquo vitæ tempore præ trepidatione illa & metu talionis fuit, fugitque sæpe cœtus hominum Cainus, Gen.4. 12.16.17. Porrò quum à toto eo tractu eiectus & extorris, sit factus Cainus in quo erat, habitabat Adamus, atque ubi promissio de futuro Messia sonabat, ubi Deus ex ipsius verbo invocabatur, ubi Sacramenta & sacrificia fiebat, erantve: ubi denique collecta tunc erat Ecclesia Dei, non autem alibi, dubitari non poterat, quin Eiectio Caini ex eiusmodi loco à Deo facta, fuerit vera Excommunicatio, qualis nunc fit ex Dei verbo in Ecclesia Christiana, 1 Cor.5 4.5.9.11, 2.Thef.3.14,
units.tr: The public punishment, which God imposed on Cain for his first public crime and therefore on humankind after sin, is twofold. As regards the soul or conscience, it is excommunication from the face of God, from the assembly of the faithful and from the Church, since Cain became a wanderer. As regards the body or civil life, it is first his curse upon the earth itself, a greater curse than the common one that applies generally to all men because of sin. Then comes the hatred of other men toward Cain, and Cain's constant fear, terror and trembling before them. Hence he was a wanderer and a vagabond for the rest of his life, from that trembling and fear of retaliation, and Cain often fled from the company of men (Gen. 4.12, 16, 17). Moreover, since Cain was cast out and banished from that whole region, he was driven from the place where Adam dwelt, where the promise of the future Messiah resounded, where God was called upon through his word, where sacraments and sacrifices were performed, and where the Church of God was then gathered, and nowhere else. It could not be doubted that Cain's expulsion from such a place by God was a true excommunication, of the kind that now takes place in the Christian Church by the Word of God (1 Cor. 5.4, 5, 9, 11; 2 Thess. 3.14).

units.la: 2 Ioan 10. Ioan 9.22. Unde verba hæc [A facie Iehouæ] significant non tantum à consortio iucundissimo Adami patris fuisse expulsum, Gen 4.16: verumetiam ex toto Dei cultu, piorum cœtu, verbíque ipsius auditione, & congressu Ecclesiæ privatum eum fuisse demonstrant. Ex quo euenit ut & Cainus ipsemet enaserit, minseritque postea impœnitens, & impius, eiusque posteritas contemptrix Divini numinis, & ignara Verbi ipsius extiterit, ac tandem corruptissima sua culpa Tamen nequis propterea existimaret sese posse lege Talionis Cainum ipsum Homicidà interficere, Deus signum in Caino posuit, quo eum à vi hominum seruaret, ac tueretur.
units.tr: 2 John 10; John 9.22. Hence these words [From the face of Jehovah] signify not only that he was expelled from the most pleasant company of his father Adam (Gen. 4.16), but also show that he was deprived of the whole worship of God, of the assembly of the pious, of the hearing of the Word and of fellowship with the Church. As a result, Cain himself lived on and afterwards remained impenitent and impious, and his posterity became contemptuous of the divine majesty and ignorant of his Word, and at last, through their own most corrupt guilt. Yet lest anyone should think that on that account he could kill Cain himself by the law of retaliation, God set a sign upon Cain by which he kept and protected him from the violence of men.

units.la: XII. Urbs Prima in Mundo condita.
units.tr: XII. The First City Built in the World.

units.la: VRBEM autem condidit postea Cainus, (illa vero fuit urbs prima omnium condita in orbe terrarum) in qua velut in munitione & praesidio tutus a pavore illo Panico, quo agitabatur, & metu hominum esset, & habitaret, saltem ad tempus, Gen. 4. 17. Illam autem de nomine primogeniti sui Enochi seu Canochi nominavit Enochiam seu Canochiam. Nam Cainus sibi semper ab hominibus metuebat, ne lege Talionis ab iis interficeretur. Quamvis enim signum in eo fuisset à Deo positum ne eum quisquam occideret, ille tamen conscientia furiys, & terrore perpetuo agitabatur velut Orestes quidam. Ergo urbem aedificauit id est coetum hominum collegit, & munitiones muros, & portas (quibus se suosque claudsaret, & seruaret) exstruxit, in quam se recipiebat, ibique continebat tantisper dum licebat per intermittentem ipsius morbum ac furorem. Nam habuit Cainus horribiles mentis furores ipsum vexantes & exstimulantes à tempore occisi fratris, qui eum per interualla dilucida immaniter & ad tempus corripiebant, & postea intermittebant tamen. Ergo tempore istius furoris sui vagabatur, fugiebat, errabatque Cainus per deserta, sese ex hominum coetu in deserta subducens, substrahénsque, horrendo, tristique cum eiulatu, & misero caeteris hominibus ira Dei in scelaratos spectaculo. Quum autem furor ille remittebat, tempore illo interualloque dilucido quiescentis furoris, Cainus cum ceteris hominibus versabatur, & in illam sese vrbem à se edificatam recipiebat. Quamobrem animi in Caino pauitatio, trepidatio, terrorque fuit potissima vrbis primæ in Orbe terrarum ædificandæ causa, quæ non vt tristis carcer, sed vt valida munitio Caini, & reliquos homines clauderet, & ab aliorum fortiorum publicis priuatisque iniurijs prohiberet, ac tutos redderet, Psal. 107 36, & 147.13. Hoc Caini ædificium, & exemplum postea aliy mortales sunt imitati, non tantum vt sese ab aliorum hominum insidijs, rapinis, & violentia tutos præstarent: sed etiam ab ipsarum bestiarum vi, & iniurijs.
units.tr: Cain afterwards built a city (and that was the first city ever built on the earth), in which, as in a fortress and stronghold, he might be safe from that Panic terror by which he was driven, and dwell, at least for a time, secure from the fear of men (Gen. 4:17). He named it Enochia or Canochia after his firstborn son Enoch or Canoch. For Cain always feared men, lest they should kill him by the law of retaliation. For although God had set a sign on him that no one should kill him, he was nevertheless driven by a conscience of furies and by perpetual terror, like a sort of Orestes. So he built a city, that is, he gathered a company of men, and raised walls and gates (by which he might shut himself and his people in and keep them safe), and he retreated into it and remained there for as long as his intermittent sickness and madness allowed. For from the time of his brother's murder Cain had dreadful furies of mind that tormented and goaded him; they seized him fiercely for periods, and then at intervals they ceased. So during the time of his fit he wandered, fled and roamed through the deserts, withdrawing from the company of men into the wilderness, with a horrible and mournful howling, a pitiable spectacle to other men of God's anger against the wicked. But when that fury abated, in the lucid interval of the quieted madness, Cain mixed again with other men and retreated into that city he had built. Therefore the trembling, dread and terror in Cain's soul was the chief cause for building the first city in the world. It was meant not as a grim prison but as a strong fortress for Cain, to shut in the other men and to keep them from the public and private wrongs of stronger men, and to make them safe (Ps. 107:36; 147:13). Later mortals imitated this building and example of Cain's, not only to secure themselves against the snares, robberies and violence of other men, but also against the force and injuries of the wild beasts themselves.

units.la: XIII. Propagatio familiæ Caini, postquam occisum Abelem, in diuersas appella- tiones, autores, & Distinctio.
units.tr: XIII. The propagation of Cain's family after Abel was killed: its various names, authors, and distinctions.

units.la: ETSI vero dignum erat Cainum post interfectum fratrem, qui interneciione prosternitur, æternoque, & animi & corporis exitio periret, & infœcundum maneret, Deus tamen naturâ benignissimus, genus humanum multiplicare ex illo primo Adami femine, ordine naturali, cupiens, & ipsum Cainum superstitem esse, & ex eodem illo magnam postea sobolem nasci voluit. Ergo plures familiæ ex Caino post occisum à se Abelem propagatæ sunt, & quidem antequam Sethus nasceretur, ex quo Setho demum piorum familiæ sunt prognatæ. Hanc autem generationem et am ex ipso Caino multiplicationem naturalem Deus esse, & fieri voluit, ut vim istius sue vocis & benedictionis Hominibus primis facta[Crescite, & Multiplicamini] Gen. 1. 28, quanta quamque immota esset, ostenderet: atque ut dona etiam illa quae nobis naturaliter eveniunt, atque dantur, qualis procreatio feminis, & a Deo esse, & ex mera eius benignitate, non ex hominum meritis, vel viribus etiam naturalibus proficisci omnes intelligant Gen 3. 2. Sunt ergo hae familiae ante natum Adamo Sethum (si modo, quod puto, Moses in hac sacra historia contexenda secutus est ordinem temporis) ex Caino post occisum Abelem natae, numero octo, nimirum prima familia Chanoci: 2. Hiradi: 3. Mechuiaelis: 4. Methuaselis: 5. Lamechi: 6. Iabalis: 7. Iubalis. 8. Tubalcaini. Nam Naamah soror Tubalcaini non constituit familiam, Gen. 4. 17. 18 & deinceps. Ergo tot diversarum familiarum capita, tamque numerosa soboles iam ex Caino improbo natae erant, antequam pij in terris propagarentur, imo nascerentur, ut & quod pij velli postea fuerint inter homines prope sit miraculum, certe summum Dei Opt. Max. beneficium meritoque gratuitum: & quod etiam Mundus hic totus, id est homines omnes tam scelerati postea extiterint, mirum non sit, quum improbi & impij homines Mundum hunc & diu iam obtinuissent, & mirabiliter corrupissent, priusquam pij in terra vlli multiplicarentur. Verum hic peccati, corruptaq, ac pene deleta Dei imaginis in homine verum fructus, veraq, poena certe fuit, Psal. 12. 1. 9, Hab. 1. 1. 2, & seq.
units.tr: Although it was fitting that Cain, after killing his brother, should be struck down by the punishment of death and perish in both soul and body, and remain without offspring, God, being most kind by nature, wished the human race to be multiplied from that first seed of Adam by the natural order, and wished Cain himself to survive and a great posterity to be born from him afterwards. So several families were propagated from Cain after he had killed Abel, and indeed before Seth was born, from whom the families of the pious were at last descended. God willed that this generation, this natural multiplication even from Cain himself, should take place, in order to show how great and how unchanging was the force of his word and blessing spoken to the first men, "Be fruitful and multiply" (Gen. 1. 28); and so that all might understand that those gifts which come to us naturally and are given, such as the begetting of offspring, come from God and from his mere kindness, not from human merits or even natural powers (Gen. 3. 2). Therefore these families, born from Cain after Abel's death and before Adam begot Seth (if indeed, as I think, Moses followed the order of time in weaving together this sacred history), number eight: (1) the first family, that of Enoch; (2) that of Irad; (3) that of Mehujael; (4) that of Methushael; (5) that of Lamech; (6) that of Jabal; (7) that of Jubal; (8) that of Tubal-cain. For Naamah, the sister of Tubal-cain, did not found a family (Gen. 4. 17, 18 and following). So many heads of different families, and so numerous a progeny, had already been born from wicked Cain before the pious were propagated on earth, indeed before they were born. Thus it is hardly a miracle that the pious were afterwards few among men, and certainly it was a supreme benefit of God Almighty, rightly given freely. And it is no wonder that this whole world, that is, all men, became so wicked afterwards, since wicked and impious men had already long held this world and corrupted it wonderfully, before any of the pious were multiplied on the earth. Yet this was indeed the true fruit of sin, and the true punishment, by which the image of God in man was corrupted and nearly destroyed (Ps. 12. 1, 9; Hab. 1. 1, 2 and following).

units.la: XIIII. Bigamia Prima, seu Coniugij Prima
units.tr: XIV. The First Bigamy, or the First Marriage

units.la: Prima violatio, & corruptela in Mun- do, & a quo.
units.tr: The first violation and corruption in the world, and by whom.

units.la: BIGAMIA prima, seu prima instituti à Deo coingy Gen. 2.24, corruptela facta est, & cepta a Lamecho filio Mathusaelis ex stirpe Caini, homine non tantum lasciuo, mulieroso, & libidinoso: verumetiam superbo, saevo, & truculento. Id quod ipsum cum ambabus suis vxoribus colloquium, mineaque ijs facta (quales à Moße describuntur) ostendunt, Gen.4.19.23. ✱Antea enim homines vxore vnica contenti erant. Verum ille nouus Præcepti Dei violator non tantum audax & temerarius fuit: sed etiam seuus ferox, & sanguinarius, vt à quo spiritu ingenioq; tentata primum, & postea inducta fuerit (celerum, & peccandi publica licentia, audaciaque appareat, nempe truculento, fero, & immani. Nam qui in Deum vel primus ipse rebellat, vel alios ad rebellandum docet, ac format, is est perdita vir audacia, proiectiq; pudoris, & immanis natura, vti in Caino, Lamecho isto, Pharaone, Saule cernitur. Porro ex istis maleficiorum gradibus & incrementis facile colligitur, quomodo paulatim postea communis illa, & popularis omnium Hominum corruptio in Mundum inuaserit, aggressa sit, grassata sit, planeq; tandem peruicerit, & obtinuerit.
units.tr: The first bigamy, or the first corruption of the marriage instituted by God (Gen. 2.24), began with Lamech, son of Methushael, of the stock of Cain. He was a man not only lascivious, given to women and lustful, but also proud, cruel and savage. His own conversation with his two wives and the threats he made to them, as Moses describes them, show this (Gen. 4.19, 23). ✱For before this, men were content with one wife. But that new violator of God's precept was not only bold and reckless. He was also fierce, ferocious and bloodthirsty. The spirit and mind by which he was first tempted, and afterwards drawn on, appear from the speed, the public licence and the audacity of his sinning, which were savage, fierce and monstrous. For whoever first rebels against God himself, or teaches and forms others to rebel, is a man of lost audacity, with his shame cast off and a monstrous nature, as is seen in Cain, this Lamech, Pharaoh and Saul. Moreover, from these degrees and increases of wickedness it is easily gathered how that common and popular corruption of all men later crept gradually into the world, attacked it, spread through it, and at last wholly prevailed and held sway.

units.la: XV. Pastoritiæ Artis Incrementum, & Expolitio.
units.tr: XV. The Growth and Refinement of the Pastoral Art.

units.la: ARS Pastoritia (quæ per Abelem primum instituta fuerat) Abele occiso, vel (quia Cainus & Adamus erant agricolæ) intermissa: vel in odium Abelis à posteris Caini (qui soli supererant) reiečta, repudiataque ad tempus, quæ tamen postea vrgente necessitate (id est, ipsorum hominum usu sic monente) fuit repetita, resumptáque ab ipsismet Caini posteris: imò etiam ab ijsdem auĉta, expolita, & in certum perpetuúmque vitæ genus propter tum vitłum humanum (qui bestijs partim constabat) tum etiam lucrum (quod ex ys percipiebatur) instituta, formatáque certis regulis, observationibus, & pecorum cuiusq; generis distinctionibus. Neque enim omnia pecora uno modo, uno vićtu & pabulo, eodem tecto & caula pascuntur, curantur, recipiuntur. Ergo Iabal filius Lamechi artem istam tanquam intermortuam restituit, distinxitque magna industria species pecudum, & greges animalium, quæ sub cura & pastura hominis ali possunt, vt vnumquodque genus commodè, & pro sua natura pasceretur, & haberetur. Denique quoniam hæc ars perutilem quandam hominum curam, & pecoris ipsius perpetuam custodiam desiderat, vixit ipse primus in Mapalibus, tugurijs, & tentoriis sub dio: & suis posteris idem vitæ genus & exemplum instituit, ac reliquit. Itaque homines isti extra vrbes (quas superiores posteri Caini ad patris imitationem incolebant) vixerunt, sparsi per agros apertos, & sub dio habitarunt, sequentes ipsi greges pecorum suorum, & armentorum a se distributos, eósque in optima queque pabula producētes. Qua ratione, vitaque instituto sućtum est, vt desertæ & incultæ terræ partes primùm paulatim inuiserentur, & habitabitarentur ab hominibus: deinde vt genus humanū sese per orbem terrarum sensim diffunderet, ac longius progrederetur, & dilataret, Gen.4.20, & 31.40, Psal. 106.13. Talis fuit postea gens, & vita Rechabitarum, (vt est Hieremiæ 35.7, 2.Reg.10.15) & Nomadum.
units.tr: The pastoral art (which had been founded first by Abel) was, after Abel was killed, either interrupted (since Cain and Adam were farmers), or, from hatred of Abel, rejected and repudiated for a time by the descendants of Cain (who alone survived). Yet later, when necessity pressed (that is, when human practice itself so advised), it was taken up again and resumed by the very descendants of Cain; indeed it was further enlarged and refined by them, and established as a fixed and permanent way of life, both on account of human sustenance (which consisted partly of beasts) and of the gain that was derived from them, and it was shaped by fixed rules, observances, and distinctions of each kind of livestock. For not all cattle are pastured, tended, and housed in one way, with one feed and fodder, under the same roof and fold. So Jabal, son of Lamech, restored this art as if it had died out, and with great industry distinguished the species of cattle and the herds of animals which can be kept under human care and pasturage, so that each kind might be fed and kept conveniently and according to its nature. Finally, since this art requires a most useful care by people and a constant guarding of the flock itself, he himself was the first to live in huts, cottages and tents under the open sky; and he established and left the same way of life and example to his descendants. Thus these men lived outside the cities (which the older descendants of Cain inhabited in imitation of their father), scattered over open fields and dwelling under the open sky, following their own flocks and herds, which they had divided among themselves, and leading them to the best pastures. By this method and way of life it came about that the deserted and uncultivated parts of the earth were gradually entered and inhabited by men; then that the human race spread itself gradually across the world and advanced and extended further, Gen. 4.20, and 31.40, Ps. 106.13. Such was afterwards the nation and way of life of the Rechabites (as in Jer. 35.7, 2 Kings 10.15) and of the nomads.

units.la: XVI. Artium aliarum inuentio, & pri- mum quidem Artis Musicæ.
units.tr: XVI. The invention of the other arts, and first of the art of music.

units.la: MVSICA quoq; fuit eadem pene ætate, certè paulò post inuenta, non quæ vocalis (est enim hæc naturalis) sed quæ organica est, & prior quam vocalis in vsu. Postquam enim homines Caini posteri artes vitæ suo necessarias, nimirum Agriculturam, & Pastoritiam, reperijssent, vel saltem instituissent, excolerenartes eas postea magna, solertique industria, & mentis præclara vivacitate pepererunt, quæ voluptatem eis, delectationémque animi maximam afferebat. Eas autem Musica Organica completitur. Ergo Iubal filius Lamechi dicti, & frater Iabalu (qui antea Pastoritiam Artem auxerat, & docuerat) Musicam, Citharam, organicaq; Musices instrumenta commentus est, & excogitavit eorumque sonore & modulatè ad percipiendam voluptatem aurium & animi tractandorum & pulsandorum artem tum primùm ipse inuenit, tum posteris suis tradidit ac reliquit, Gen.4.21. Postea verò Vocalem Musicam repertam esse ex Organica non dubito. Ex quo apparet artis Musices inter Mortales vsum, ac institutionem esse antiquissimam, atque
units.tr: Music was also of almost the same age, and was certainly invented a little later. I do not mean vocal music, for that is natural, but instrumental music, which came into use before vocal. For after the posterity of Cain had discovered, or at least established, the arts necessary for life, namely agriculture and herding, they cultivated these arts and later, by great and skilful industry and a remarkable liveliness of mind, brought them to perfection. These arts gave them the greatest pleasure and delight of mind, and instrumental music completes them. Therefore Jubal, son of the Lamech mentioned above and brother of Jabal (who had earlier advanced and taught the art of herding), devised the lyre, the cithara and the instruments of instrumental music. He himself was the first to discover the art of producing their sounds melodiously, so as to give delight to the ears and to move and stir the soul, and he handed it down and left it to his descendants, Gen. 4.21. I do not doubt that vocal music was afterwards discovered from instrumental music. From this it appears that the use and institution of the art of music among mortals is very ancient, and

units.la: G ab ipso cepisse penè Mundi exordio quò detestabiliores sunt qui ea Arte tam nobili abutuntur. Porrò Homines primi ist ius seculi fuisse voluptarios, & molles, ex hoc eorum ingenio, & inuento apparet.
units.tr: that it took its origin almost from the very beginning of the world, so much more detestable are those who abuse so noble an art. Moreover, that the first men of this age were given to pleasure and soft living appears from their character and from this invention.

units.la: XVII. Artis Ferrariæ, & Æraria Inuentio.
units.tr: XVII. The invention of the art of the smith and of the bronze-worker.

units.la: FERRARIA vero, & eÆraria ars inuenta quoque est a posteris Caini penè eodem tempore, nempe a Tubalcaino filio quoque & ipso Lamechi ex Tzilla secunda eius uxore, seu potius prioris uxoris videlicet Hadæ pellice. Nam Tubalcainus primùm & ferrum atque æs in terra primus ipse dignouit, & posteros suos dignoscere in terra venis docuit: deinde opera instrumentáque cuiusuis generis ex ferro, & are illo cudere, & fabricari, quæ ad usum hominū, vel abusum etiam postea translata sunt, monstrauit. Quamobrem, artem ipsam Metalla fundendi, tractandi, fabricandi, ducendique malleo, & sub incude ferri, & æris primus habuit iste Tubalcainus, alijsque postea tradidit, Gen. 4 22. Quæ res & industria magnum Dei donum fuit, cum erga ipsum Tubalem Cainum: tum etiam erga totum genus humanum, quum vita hæc nostra eiusmodi instrumentorum, & ferramentorum usu ad terram colendam, ad ædificandum, ad scindendum, ad pugnādum omnino egeat, Exod. 36: & latè postea propagata est, & in diuersas partes, artes, species. & officinas distributa, partitáque à posteris. Porrò ex istius artis inuentione videntur homines postea fauores, & ad eadem mutuā, mutua propensiores, truculentiorefque factli, quum ferrum & arma iam in manu, & in promptu habere coepissent ad sese mutuo iugulandos, & offendendos. Vnde apparet quibus occasionibus, nempe propter beneficia Dei in homines collata, item quibus sensim ac paulatim gradibus tota illa Caini familia misere, ac omnino sese corruperit, & ferociop, superbiorque fuerit, atque etiá in Deum ipsum contumeliosa euaserit, adeo vt tandem etiam nomen ipsum & numen Dei (quod antea sacrosanctum habitum fuerat) blasphemare, nihil facere, & aspernari auderet. Hinc totius Mundi corruptela, & omnium hominum depravatio postea contigit, eaq; immedicabilis. Caeterum, quandoquidem Mosem existimamus sequi seriem & ordinem temporis rerum gestarum in hac Sacra historia describenda) haec omnia Mundo contigerunt ante natum Adamo Sethum, ac proinde ante annum ipsius Adami, seu Mundi conditi centesimum trigesimum, Gen. 5. 3. Fuerunt autem istae contemptu blasphematiq; à Cainicis postea diuini numinis causa, & praeparationes miserrimae, & indignissimae. Verum à nato Setho, vt postea dicetur, ad publicam Nominis Dei Profanationem intercedunt anni 105. Ergo tota haec summa collecta efficit annos 235.
units.tr: The art of working iron and bronze was also invented by the posterity of Cain at almost the same time, namely by Tubalcain, likewise a son of Lamech, born of Zillah, his second wife, or rather of Adah, his first wife's concubine. For Tubalcain was the first to recognise iron and bronze in the earth, and taught his descendants to recognise them by their veins in the ground. Then he showed how to forge and fashion from that iron and bronze tools and implements of every kind, which were afterwards put to the use of men, or even to their abuse. Therefore Tubalcain himself first had the art of melting, working and fashioning metals, of drawing them out with the hammer and of shaping iron and bronze on the anvil, and he later passed it on to others, Gen. 4.22. This skill was a great gift of God, both to Tubal-cain himself and to the whole human race, since our life altogether needs the use of such instruments and iron tools for tilling the earth, for building, for cutting and for fighting, Exod. 36. It was later widely spread, and distributed and divided by its descendants into various parts, arts, kinds and workshops. Moreover, from the invention of this art men seem afterwards to have become more savage, fiercer and more inclined to these things, since they had begun to have iron and weapons already in hand and ready to cut one another's throats and to strike one another down. From this it appears by what occasions, namely because of the benefits God had conferred on men, and by what gradual steps that whole family of Cain became wretched and utterly corrupt, and grew more fierce and proud, and even became insolent toward God himself, so that at last it dared to blaspheme the very name and divine majesty of God, which had been held sacred before, to make nothing of it and to despise it. Hence came the corruption of the whole world and the depravity of all men, which was incurable. Moreover, since we think Moses follows the order and sequence of time of the events in describing this sacred history, all these things happened to the world before Seth was born to Adam, and therefore before the hundred and thirtieth year of Adam himself, or of the world since its creation, Gen. 5.3. These contempts and blasphemies were afterwards committed by the Cainites, and were most wretched and most unworthy preparations for the divine majesty. But from the birth of Seth, as will be said later, there intervene 105 years until the public profanation of the name of God. Therefore this whole sum, when collected, makes 235 years.

units.la: CAPVT II.
units.tr: Chapter II.

units.la: Disputata, & agitata quedam in his singulis capitibus septemdecim.
