units.tr: Certain matters disputed and discussed under each of the seventeen chapters.

units.la: THAEC quidem sunt illius aetatis historica: Verum in ijs multa disputantur, quae nos, Deo bene favente, iam ad singula capita accommodabimus, ne quid vel obscurum, vel confusum, vel dubium in tam sacra historia saltem moderatis ingenijs relinquatur.
units.tr: These are the historical facts of that age. But many questions are debated in them, which, God willing, we shall now address under the individual chapters, so that nothing obscure, confused or doubtful is left in so sacred a history, at least for moderate minds.

units.la: Ad I. De Primo peccato Primorum Hominum.
units.tr: On I. The First Sin of the First Men.

units.la: Quaeritur igitur, Cur Deus hominem fecerit ad imaginem suam, qui peccare posset, ac non potius qui peccare non posset, neque labi, neque deficere. R. Vitio depravati potuit Adam, item & Eva, quoniam ex nihilo facti erant. Itaque, Dy non erant. Nam etsi de terra iam facta pulvere finxit Deus hominem, eadem tamen terra, omnisque terrena materies omnino de nihilo est: imo Animam etiam de nihilo factam, ac proinde creatam dedit Deus corpori, quum factus est Homo. Ergo excepto eo, quem Pater genuit de seipso, (Est autem Verbum, per quod omnia sunt facta) omnis alia natura & creatura facta est a Deo de nihilo, ac propterea obnoxia vanitati, id est, defectioni, lapsuique a summo bono ac proinde qua peccare posset natura, & conditione sua, nisi speciali quadam gratia a Deo confirmaretur. Sic Augustinus lib. 14. Civit Dei, cap. 11: Ergo ut esset Homo arbor mala, contra naturam illius factus est. Nam nonnisi sua voluntatis vitio (quod contra naturam procul dubio est) utique malus fieret Homo: sed vitio depravari nisi ex nihilo facta, natura non poterat, ait idem cap. 3. Ac per hoc habet Homo a Deo ut sit quaedam dam natura, quatenus ab eo factus est: Vt autem ab eo, à quo factus erat, deficeret, ex eo est, quod ex nihilo factus est. Q. Vtrum pertypbatu fuerit Dei consilium de immortalitate & felicitate hominis, dum homines peccant. R. Quum Deus Hominem peccaturum esse & praescisset, & decrevisset, Homo peccando non compulit Deum mutare, quod semel statuerat: Imò Deus praesciendo utrumque praevenit. Nam praevidit hominem quem ipse bonum creaverat, malum suturum esse: & bonum quoque praevidit, quod sic etiam de illo erat ipse facturus. Augustinus lib. 14. cap. 11. Civit. Dei, & lib. Enchirid. ad Laurent. cap. 100. Vide eundem Augustinum lib. 11 de Genesi ad liter. cap. 4. 5. 7. & Petrum Lombardum, libr. 2. Sentent. Distinct. 23.
units.tr: The question is therefore asked: why did God make man in his own image, a being who could sin, rather than one who could not sin, nor fall, nor fail? Answer: Adam, and Eve likewise, could be corrupted by sin, because they had been made out of nothing. For before they were made they were nothing. Even though God formed man from earth already made into dust, that earth, and all earthly matter, is wholly from nothing. Indeed God gave the soul also, made from nothing and therefore created, to the body when man was made. Therefore, apart from the one whom the Father begot from himself (and he is the Word, through whom all things were made), every other nature and creature was made by God out of nothing, and so is subject to vanity, that is, to defection and falling away from the highest good. By its own nature and condition it could therefore sin, unless it were confirmed by a special grace from God. So Augustine, On the City of God, book 14, chapter 11: "Therefore man was made, as a tree, contrary to his nature to be bad. For man could become bad only through a fault of his own will, which is certainly contrary to nature; but a nature made out of nothing could not be corrupted by a fault," says the same author, chapter 3. Thus man has from God that he is a certain nature, insofar as he was made by him; but that he could fall away from him by whom he was made comes from the fact that he was made out of nothing. Question: whether God's plan for the immortality and happiness of man was thrown into confusion when men sinned. Answer: since God both foreknew and decreed that man would sin, man by sinning did not force God to change what he had once decided. Rather, by foreknowing, God anticipated both outcomes. For he foresaw that man, whom he had created good, would become evil; and he also foresaw the good that he himself would do with him in this way. Augustine, City of God, book 14, chapter 11, and Enchiridion to Laurentius, chapter 100. See also Augustine, On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, book 11, chapters 4, 5 and 7, and Peter Lombard, Sentences, book 2, distinction 23.

units.la: Q. Vtrum mala hominum voluntas praecesserit eorum peccatum, id est, factum eorum, & manducationem fructus interdicti. R. Etsi & voluntas mala, quam homines habuerunt, & factum ipsum ex Satana suggestione fuit: tamen ut ad malum opus perveniretur, praecessit hominum mala voluntas opus ipsum (seu esum vetiti fructus. In occulto igitur mali esse coeperunt, ut in apertam inobedientiam laberentur. Nec enim, ut praeclarè respondet Augustinus lib. 14 Civit. Dei, cap. 13. Malum illud opus factum est, (id est, illa transgressio eventit, videlicet ut cibo prohibito vescerentur) nisi ab iis, qui mali iam erant. Vt autem esset arbor mala, contra naturam eam factum est, in qua primùm à Deo fuerant conditi. Porrò mala istius hominum voluntatis initium quod potuit esse, nisi superbia? ait Augustinus. Spontaneum igitur fuit ille hominum appetitus, & def- ctus quoniam si voluntas eorum in amore superioris immutabilis boni id est. Dei (a quo illustrabatur, ut videret: & accendebatur, ut amaret) stabilis permansisset, non inde ad sibi placendum auersa fuisset, & ex hoc tenebresceret, & frigesceret. Itaque neque tua verum dixisse serpentem crederet: neque Adamus ipse Dei mandato praponeret uxoris voluntatem. Porro mala voluntas prima (quoniam omnia mala opera praecessit in homine) defectus potius fuit quidam ab opere Dei, ad sua opera: quam opus vllum. Et ideo mala, quia secundum se, non secundum Deum erat, ut eorum operum malorum tanquam fructuum voluntas ipsa esset velut arbor mala. Detrahitur porro malum, inquit Augustinus lib. 14 cap. 11 Ciuit. Dei, non aliqua natura, (quae accesserat) vel vlla eius essentia, quae peccat, parte subtracta. Sed ea, quae vitiata & depravata fuerat, sanata, atque correcta. Arbitrium igitur voluntatis tunc est vere liberum, quum vitijs peccatisque non seruit. Tale datum est Adamo primum a Deo, quod amissum proprio vitio, nisi a quo dari potuit reddi non potest. Inde quippe liberator est Deus, unde saluator. Q. Ecquod peccati genus homines primi primum peccando admiserunt. R. Augustinus lib. 14 de Ciuit. Dei cap. 12, & 13 Superbiam: Ait enim [Initium omnis peccati superbia est]. Quid est autem Superbia, nisi peruersa celsitudinis appetitus? Peruersa enim celsitudo est, deserto eo, cui debet animus inhaerere pr acipio sibi quodammodo fieri, atque esse principium. Hoc fit quum sibi nimis placet homo: Sibi vero ita placet, quum ab illo Bono immutabili deficit, quod ei magis placere debuit, quàm ipse sibi.] Relicto igitur Deo esse in semetipso, id est, sibi placere non tam est nihil esse, sed nihilo propinquare. Bonum est quidè sursum habere cor, sed non ad seipsum, quod est superbia: sed ad Dominum, quod est obedientia. Est igitur aliquid humilitatis miro modo, quod sursum facit cor: & est aliquid elationis, quod deorsum facit cor. Ipsum quippe extolli, deyci est. Idem Augusti lib. 11. cap. 5, & 15. de Gen. ad liter. Sequuntur quoque hoc ipsum Scholastici, & Lombard. lib 2. Sentent. Dist 22. Alij & vere quoque infidelitatem huius hominum superbiæ fontem ac radicē fuisse scribunt & sentiunt.
units.tr: Question: whether the evil will of men came before their sin, that is, their deed, the eating of the forbidden fruit. Answer: although both the evil will which men had and the deed itself came from the suggestion of Satan, nevertheless, for the evil deed to come about, the evil will of men preceded the deed itself, that is, the eating of the forbidden fruit. Thus they began to be evil in secret, before they fell into open disobedience. For, as Augustine answers well in City of God, book 14, chapter 13: that evil deed, that transgression, that they ate the forbidden food, came about only from those who were already evil. But the tree became evil, contrary to nature, in the state in which they had first been created by God. Moreover, what could be the beginning of the evil of this human will, if not pride? says Augustine. That desire and defect of men was therefore voluntary; for if their will had remained steadfast in love of the higher, unchangeable good, that is God, by whom it was illuminated so that it could see and by whom it was kindled so that it could love, it would not have been turned away to please itself, and from this grown dark and cold. And so they would not have believed the serpent that he spoke the truth, nor would Adam himself have preferred his wife's will to God's command. Moreover, the first evil will (since it preceded all evil works in man) was rather a certain defection from God's work to one's own works than any work at all. And it was evil because it was evil in itself, not according to God; so that the will itself, like the root of these evil works as their fruits, was like an evil tree. Furthermore, evil is not removed, says Augustine, City of God, book 14, chapter 11, by taking away some nature (which had been added) or any essence of that which sins; rather, what had been corrupted and depraved is healed and corrected. The free choice of the will is therefore truly free when it is not enslaved to vices and sins. Such freedom was first given to Adam by God, and, once lost through his own fault, it cannot be restored except by him who could give it. Indeed, God is our liberator for the same reason that he is our saviour. Question: what kind of sin did the first men commit first when they sinned? Answer: Augustine, City of God, book 14, chapters 12 and 13: pride. For he says: "The beginning of all sin is pride." But what is pride, except a perverse desire for height? For it is a perverse height when a man, abandoning him to whom his soul ought to cling, wishes in a way to become and be the source of himself. This happens when a man is too pleased with himself. He is pleased with himself when he falls away from that unchangeable Good, which ought to have pleased him more than himself. Therefore to be in oneself, having abandoned God, that is, to please oneself, is not merely to be nothing, but to draw near to nothing. It is good to lift the heart upward, but not to oneself, which is pride, rather to the Lord, which is obedience. There is therefore a certain humility which lifts the heart upward in a wonderful way, and there is a certain haughtiness which casts the heart downward. For to be exalted in oneself is to be cast down. Augustine, the same, On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, book 11, chapters 5 and 15. The Scholastics also follow this, and Lombard, Sentences, book 2, distinction 22. Others also write and hold that unbelief truly was the fount and root of this pride of men.

units.la: Q. An propter esum unius arboris Pomi debuerit Deus tantum, tamque asperè irasci hominibus illis.
units.tr: Question: whether God ought to have been so great and so harsh in anger against those men merely because they ate the fruit of one tree.

units.la: R. Augustinus lib 14. Ciuit. Dei, cap. 12. caussam huius Dei iræ, & quidem verissimam sic exponit: Non ideo, ait, quis debet existimare leue ac parum fuisse illud primorum Hominum commissum, quia in esca factum est, non quidem mala, nec noxia, nisi quia prohibita (nec enim quicquam mali Deus in illo tanta felicitatis Paradiso crearet, atque plantaret) sed obedientia commendata est in præcepto, qua virtus in creatura rationali mater quodammodo est omnium, custosque virtutum.
units.tr: Answer: Augustine, City of God, book 14, chapter 12, explains the cause of this anger of God, and indeed the truest cause, thus: "One ought not to think that the sin committed by the first men was slight and minor because it was a matter of food, not in itself evil or harmful, but only because it was forbidden. For God would not have created and planted anything evil in that Paradise of such happiness. Rather, obedience was commended in the precept, which is in a rational creature in a way the mother and guardian of all the virtues."

units.la: Hoc itaque de vno cibi genere non edendo, vbi aliorum tanta copia subiacebat, tam leue præceptum ad observandum: tam breue ad memoria retinendum, vbi præsertim nondum voluntati cupiditas resistebat (quod de pœna transgressionis postea subsecutum est) tanto maiore iniustitia violatum est, quantò citiore posset observantia custodiri. Hac Augustinus, & recte. Ergo non propter pretium Pomi ab Adamo gustati, sed propter immanem ✠Adami rebellionem sic ei fuit ιratum Deus. Q. Cur Serpente animali potissimum vsus est Satan ad primos homines, sed Euam imprimis decipiendam. R. P. Lombardus lib. 2. Sentent. dist. 21. cap. 2. ait, Ne Diaboli fraus ab homine perciperetur, in alienâ, non in suâ forma Satan tentare hominem voluit. Serpentem autem Animal ex omnibus delegit, tum quia rationali creaturæ omnis irrationalis subiecta erat: tum quia per solum Serpentem id facere a Deo permissum est Diabolus, non autem per Columbæ formâ, quod fortasse maluisset, vt melius fraudem subesse in Satanæ verbis Homo ex eo, quod serpens loquebatur, subolfaceret: & clarius ipsius tentatoris, id est Diaboli natura, per columbrum illum tortuosis anfractibus mobilem, ac proinde magis operi ipsi congruum, significaretur. ait ✠August. lib. 14 Ciuit. Dei, cap. 11, & libr. 11. Genef. ad liter. cap. 12. At verò S. Scriptura ait Diabolum idcirco delegisse vnum hoc Animal, nempe Serpentem, quòd omnium animalium λόγων erat Serpens astutissimus, Gen. 3. 1. Addunt verò nonnulli etiâ Homini tunc familiarissimum, vti Josephus lib 3. Ant. Judaic. cap. 3. Porrò de duplici Serpentis prudentia vide Epiphanium lib. 1. De Haref. tomo 3. haresi 37. contra Ophitas, quæ ex ea, quam primum habebat, reliqua est. Fuit igitur Animal hoc omnium astutissimum, ac proinde à Diabolo deleǝtum. Q. Vtrum verba Serpentis fuerint ipsiusmet Serpentis, an potius Diaboli? R. ✠Augustinus lib 11. Genef. ad liter. cap. 27. ostendit Serpentem, dum cum Eua loqueretur, neq; intellexisse quid diceret: neque animam rationalem habuisse. Ergo Diabolum ipsum per Serpentem fuisse locutum, quemadmodum per Phanaticos & Energumenos etiam homines sæpe loquitur. Itaq; Satan Serpente velut instrumento vsus est, quo deciperet Hominem. Alia vero ratio est Asinæ Balaami, quæ locuta est ipsa quidem, non Angelus Domini per eam, quoniam Asinæ isti vox humana & articulata à Deo concessa ad tempus fuit, Num. 22.28, 2.Pet. 2.16: quod idem à Diabolo in Serpente fieri non poterat. Porrò Deus pro voce sibilum tantum Serpenti reliquit: & pro verbis illis lenibus, quibus Euam persuasit, venenum et sub lingua posuit, vt est Psal. 140.4. Rom. 3.13, & annotat Iosephus lib. 1. cap. 3. Antiquitat. Iudaic.
units.tr: Therefore, concerning the single kind of food not to be eaten, when there was such an abundance of the others at hand, a precept so slight to observe and so short to remember, especially when desire did not yet resist the will (which followed afterwards as the punishment of transgression), was violated with all the greater injustice, the more easily it could have been kept. Thus Augustine, and rightly. Therefore God was angry with Adam not because of the price of the fruit he tasted, but because of Adam's enormous rebellion. Question: why did Satan use the animal serpent in particular to deceive the first men, and above all to deceive Eve. Answer: Peter Lombard, Sentences, book 2, distinction 21, chapter 2, says: so that the fraud of the devil would not be perceived by man, Satan wished to tempt man not in his own form but in another's. He chose the serpent from all animals, both because every irrational creature was subject to the rational creature, and because God permitted the devil to do this only through the serpent, not through the form of a dove, which he would perhaps have preferred; so that man might sniff out the deceit more readily in Satan's words from the fact that the serpent was speaking, and so that the nature of the tempter himself, that is the devil, might be more clearly signified by that creature, moving in twisting coils and therefore better suited to the work itself. So says Augustine, City of God, book 14, chapter 11, and On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, book 11, chapter 12. But Holy Scripture says that the devil chose this one animal, the serpent, because the serpent was the most cunning of all animals [φρονιμώτατος], Genesis 3:1. Some add that it was also very familiar to man at that time, as Josephus says, Jewish Antiquities, book 1, chapter 3. Moreover, on the twofold wisdom of the serpent, see Epiphanius, Against Heresies, book 1, vol. 3, heresy 37, against the Ophites, which remains from the wisdom it first possessed. This animal was therefore the most cunning of all, and so was chosen by the devil.

units.la: Q. Ecquod genus serpentis fuerit, per quod Satan tentauit primos homines.
units.tr: Q. What kind of serpent was it through which Satan tempted the first humans?

units.la: R. Multa quidem sunt Serpentum supra ventrem nunc repentium genera: ex eorum vero numero & genere fuit is, quo Satan vsus est in decipienda Eua, Gen. 3.14. Itaq; non ex genere anguium ille erat, qui in aquis viuunt: non ex alatorum Serpentum numero, quoniam illi non repunt supra ventrem suum: Sed ex terrenis Serpentibus, id est, flexuosis, & in terra de terra puluere viuentibus. Hunc autem ex Colubrorum, quos vocamus, genere fuisse scribit Augustinus lib. 14 cap. 11. Ciuit. Dei. Idem & Basilius in Hexamero: Alij viperam potius: Denique non desunt, qui etiam aliud genus fuisse existimant. Id autem praecise non definit S Scriptura. Is tamen Serpens flexuosus iam, & terrenus fuit. Nec verum est quod scribit Iosephus, Pedes quos antea habebant, Serpentibus à Deo fuisse ademptos in pœnam, vt supra ventrem serpant. Nullum enim membrum ys demptum a Deo dicitur. Q. Ecquod Pomi genus fuerit, quod hominibus esse interdixerat Deus. R. Sed nec hoc ipsum definit S. Scriptura. Ergo curiosi homines varie sese torserunt in eo, sed frustra, desiguando. Nam alij putat id Pomi genus fuisse malum Persicum, quod in Oriente (vbi peccarunt Adamus) hodie est letale & venenosum, si edatur, licet nobis in Occidente sit suauis cibus. Alij Malum Cottoneum seu Cydonium fuisse malunt, quod genus Pomi Dioscorides vocat μῆλον ἀλλᾶ̈νον, id est, verum Malum, & præ cateris germanum. Est autem iam nobis omnino gustu ingratum. Alij Malum aureum, quod & esu suaue, & aspectu iucundum est. Non desinunt denique, qui illud Cerasum, vel Pirum vulgare fuisse dicant. Verum quorsum ista tam incerta? Q. Quandiu in statu illo suo felici permanserint homines primi, & quando peccarint. R. De hoc etiam ipso (quod tamen ex Dei verbo decidi non potest) anxiè homines, imprimis autem R. Abbini Hebræorum inter se digladiantur. Alij igitur volunt Adamum statim, postquam conditus fuit, cecidisse nempe sub vesperum eius diei, quo factus est. Alij post sex demum horas, quàm creatus est à Deo. Alij post diem totum naturalem elapsum. Irenæus lib. 4. scribit Adamu & Euam ea ipsa die, qua creati fuerant, edisse ex fructu vetita arboris: ac proinde eo ipso die, quo nati sunt, peccarunt, ac perierunt, ait. Denique nonnulli censent, quod quemadmodum Christus in suo ministerio fuit per tres annos & semestre: sic Adamum tanto temporis spatio in illo suo
units.tr: There are indeed many kinds of serpents that now crawl upon their belly, and the serpent that Satan used to deceive Eve (Gen. 3.14) was one of them. It was not one of the water snakes, nor one of the winged serpents, since those do not creep upon their belly. It was an earthly serpent, that is, one that winds its way along and lives on the earth, in the dust of the ground. Augustine writes (City of God, bk. 14, ch. 11) that it was of the kind we call colubers, and Basil says the same in his Hexaemeron. Others think it was rather a viper, and there are some who think it was of yet another kind. Holy Scripture does not define this precisely. In any case, that serpent already crept along and was an earthly creature. Nor is it true what Josephus writes, that the feet the serpents once had were taken away from them by God as punishment, so that they creep upon their belly. For nowhere is it said that any member was taken away by God. Q. What kind of fruit was it that God had forbidden men to eat? R. Holy Scripture does not define this either. So curious people have tormented themselves in various ways over it, but in vain, since they are guessing. For some think that fruit was the Persian apple, which in the East (where Adam sinned) is today deadly and poisonous if eaten, although for us in the West it is a pleasant food. Others prefer that it was the quince, which Dioscorides calls [μῆλον ἀλλᾶ̈νον], that is, the true apple and the most genuine of all. Yet it is now altogether unpleasant to taste. Others say it was the golden apple, which is both sweet to eat and pleasing to look at. Finally, there are those who say it was the cherry or the common pear. But why these matters so uncertain? Q. How long the first men remained in that happy state of theirs, and when they sinned. R. Men, and above all the rabbis of the Hebrews, wrangle anxiously among themselves about this very question, which nonetheless cannot be settled from the Word of God. Some therefore hold that Adam fell at once, right after he had been created, namely at evening of the same day on which he was made. Others, only after six hours from the time he was created by God. Others, after a full natural day had passed. Irenaeus (bk. 4) writes that Adam and Eve ate of the fruit of the forbidden tree on the very day on which they had been created, and so, he says, on the same day they were born they sinned and perished. Finally, some judge that just as Christ was in his ministry for three years and a half, so Adam remained with Eve and lived in that happy state of his for a like span of time.

units.la: — suo felici statu cum Eua perdurasse, & vixisse. Verùm ἀδηλα ista relinquamus ἀδηλα. Sunt enim incomperta nobis, nec iuuant etiam cognita. Certè Irenæus lib. 5. adversus Hæreses putat Adamum à Deo vespere reprehensum fuisse. Alij tamen aliter hæc verba Mosis [Ad ventum diei] interpretantur. Math. Beroaldus lib. 1. cap 7 Chronici putat Adamum in Autumno defecisse a Deo, uti in Autumno creatus fuerat, quoniâ eo tempore poma & fructus arborum sunt maturi. Ex his autem edens ex ligno, in Deum peccaunt. Sed uti dixi, hæc ἀδηλα sinamus. Illa potius explicemus, quæ utilitatem & ædificationem afferunt.
units.tr: — But let us leave these unclear matters [ἀδηλα] alone. For they are unknown to us, and even if they were known they would not help us. Certainly Irenaeus, in his book Against Heresies (bk. 5), thinks that Adam was rebuked by God in the evening. Others, however, interpret these words of Moses [At the breeze of the day] differently. Mathias Beroaldus (bk. 1, ch. 7 of his Chronicle) thinks that Adam fell away from God in autumn, the season in which he had been created, since at that time the fruits and produce of the trees are ripe. Eating from the tree at that time, they sinned against God. But, as I said, let us leave these unclear matters alone. Let us rather explain those points which bring profit and edification.

units.la: Q. Cur à Deo data lex vlla fuerit Adamo, quem huius Mundi Dominum, Regem, & liberù Moderatorem constituerat.
units.tr: Q. Why any law was given by God to Adam, whom he had appointed lord of this world, its king and free ruler.

units.la: R. Augustinus lib. Quæst. ex veteri Testam. cap. 4 In secunda parte Tomi 4. sic scribit, [Quàuis in Mundo Dominus positus esset Adam, quia non vtique ex se, sed à Deo id accepit, debuit huius rei & accepti ab alio imperij significationem ex lege accipere, ut ipse, qui dominus videretur, per legem illi subiectus esset, qui ei hanc dederat potestatem, ne dominatio tanta extolleret Adamum, & immemor fieret Dei conditoris sui.]
units.tr: A. Augustine, in Questions on the Old Testament, chapter 4, in the second part of volume 4, writes thus: [Although Adam was placed as lord over the world, since he had this not from himself but received it from God, he ought to learn the meaning of this rule, and of the authority he had received from another, from a law, so that he who seemed to be lord would be subject through the law to him who had given him this power, lest such great dominion should lift Adam up and make him forget God his creator.]

units.la: Q. Cur igitur Deus hominibus à primordio Legem sua (qualem postea per Mosem in monte Horebo dedit) nö præscripsit, ac promulgauit.
units.tr: Q. Why then did God not prescribe and promulgate his law to humans from the beginning, such as he later gave through Moses on Mount Horeb?

units.la: R. In prima illa Lege seu primordiali, quæ data fuit Adamo à Deo omnia ipsius Legis (quæ per Mosem postea fusius & apertius prolata est) femina & præcepta breuiter & compendiosè inerant quemadmodum docet Tertullianus & Gregorius Magnus, & Lombardus lib. 2. Sentent. Dist. 21. cap.4. Verum illam describi, & latius declarari, præfertim illo primo creationis tempore, nihil fuit necesse, vt ait Augustinus in 1 parte Quæst. Veteris & Novi Testamenti, cap.4. Primum, quia recens adhuc erat Lex illa, & in ipsa natura inserta erat Creatoris notitia. Deinde quia de malo non erat docendus aut commonefaciendus Adamus, quod ab eo prorsus ignorari Deus volebat: Atqui Lex malorum & vitiorum meminit, quæ prohibet. Denique, quia si primi Homines eam unicam Dei Legem sibi primum in Paradiso terrestri datam observassent, nullis aliis præceptis, legeque alia egebant. Nam sponte & natura in Dei obsequium ferebantur. At ubi lex illa naturalis evanuit, impressa consuetudine peccandi, tunc oportuit Decalogum Legem manifestari, vt eam in Iudæis omnes audirent: non quod penitus obliterata in conscientiis hominum esset: sed quod maxima eius autoritas perierat. Quanuis enim & Diluuio Peccatum vindicatum fuisset. & Sodoma & Gomorrha fuerant subuersa in monumentum pœnarum peccati debitarum: tamen obliuio exempla ista deleuerat ex hominibus, ac proinde Legem scribi, darique à Deo oportuit. Et hæc quidem de Primo primorum Hominum peccato, hactenus. Iam videamus quæ de pœna Peccati istius quari, ac disputari soleant.
units.tr: A. In that first law, or primordial law, which God gave to Adam, all the substance and precepts of that law (which was later set out more fully and clearly through Moses) were present briefly and concisely, as Tertullian, Gregory the Great, and Lombard, in book 2 of the Sentences, distinction 21, chapter 4, teach. But to write it down and declare it more widely was not necessary, especially at that first time of creation, as Augustine says in part 1 of his Questions on the Old and New Testaments, chapter 4. First, because that law was still fresh, and the knowledge of the Creator was implanted in nature itself. Second, because Adam did not need to be taught or warned about evil, since God wanted him to be wholly ignorant of it. Yet the law that forbids mentions evils and vices. Finally, if the first humans had kept that single law of God given to them first in the earthly paradise, they would have needed no other precepts or other law. For by their own will and nature they were inclined to obey God. But when that natural law faded away, and the habit of sinning had taken hold, then it was necessary for the Decalogue to be made known as law, so that all would hear it among the Jews. This was not because it had been wholly erased from the consciences of men, but because its great authority had perished. For although sin had been punished by the Flood, and Sodom and Gomorrah had been overthrown as a memorial of the punishments that sin deserves, nevertheless forgetfulness had wiped those examples from men, and so the law had to be written and given by God. So much for the first sin of the first humans. Now let us see what is commonly asked and disputed about the punishment of this sin.

units.la: Ad II. De Pœna Primi hominū peccati.
units.tr: On the second question: the punishment of the first human sin.

units.la: Q. Vtrum omnis imago Dei fuerit in Homine per peccatum abolita. R. Nequaquam, sed magna partem tantum deleta. Nam alioqui homines iam non homines forent, sed bruta, & ἄλογα prorsus animalia. Et quod Psal. 49. 20. nonnulli homines dicuntur similes brutis animantibus, illud κατὰ τ duntaxat intelligendum est, nempe quatenus de futura melioriq; illa vita (quam hanc sequitur) nihil cogitant, toti sunt huic terrae affixi: non autem ἀπλῶς & simpliciter. Augustinus lib. 14. Ciuit. Dei, cap. 13, [Nec sic defecit homo, ait, vt omnino nihil esset: sed vt inclinatus ad seipsum minus esset, quàm erat, quia ei qui summè est, inhaerebat. Nam homo plus appetendo, minus fuit, qui dum sibi sufficere delegit, ab illo, qui ei verè sufficit, defecit.] De quo ipso idem Augustin. lib. 12. de Trinit. cap 8, & 9. Atque huius nostrae sententiae confirmatio est, quod S. Scriptura docet, In nobis imaginem Dei dutaxat renouari per Christum, ac proinde non omnino exstinctam, sublatamque fuisse: non autem prorsus creari, quasi amplius nulla in nobis esset. Sic Paulus Ephes. 4. 23, Colos. 3. 10. Sic Pauli secutus Augustinus lib. 7. Genes. ad liter. cap. 24 & 25.
units.tr: Q. Was the whole image of God in man abolished by sin? A. By no means; it was only partly destroyed. Otherwise men would no longer be men but beasts, creatures wholly without reason [ἄλογα]. And where Psalm 49:20 says that some men are like the beasts that perish, this must be understood only in a certain respect [κατὰ τι], namely insofar as they think nothing of that future and better life which follows this one, and are wholly fixed to this earth; not simply [ἁπλῶς] and absolutely. Augustine, De civitate Dei, book 14, chapter 13: [Man did not so fall, he says, that he became altogether nothing; but being turned in upon himself he became less than he was, because he no longer clung to Him who is supremely, and in the highest sense, being. For by desiring more, man became less; and when he chose to be sufficient to himself, he fell away from Him who truly suffices him.] On this same matter Augustine says the same in On the Trinity, book 12, chapters 8 and 9. And the confirmation of our view is that Holy Scripture teaches that the image of God in us is only renewed through Christ, and therefore was not wholly extinguished and taken away, nor utterly created anew, as though there were no longer any of it in us. So Paul, Ephesians 4:23 and Colossians 3:10. Augustine, following Paul, says the same in The Literal Meaning of Genesis, book 7, chapters 24 and 25.

units.la: Q. Cur a Deo velut peccatrix punita est Eua quum seducta fuisse, deceptáque a Serpente dicatur. R. Non dicitur Eua a Serpente seducta, tanquam ignoraret quid ageret ipsa, aut quid illi Serpens offerret, tunc enim esset excusabilis. Sed quod eam primam velut imbecilliorem Diabolus per Serpentem aggressus est, ac tentauit, illique prudens & sciens, libenterque prima est assensa Eua: in quo est inexcusabilis reddita. Sic initium mali a Foemina fuisse scribitur, Eccles. 25. 33. Sic a Paulo, Adam non seductus, sed Eua seducta dicitur, 1. Timoth. 2. 14. Sic Augustinus lib. 1. de peccatorum Meritis cap. 16. interpretatur. Ergo si Seducei sumpseris pro non Experiri verum id, quod alius tibi pollicetur, vterq; nempe Adam & Eua seduƈti sunt, quo significato Paulus accipit Galat. 6.
units.tr: Q. Why is Eve punished by God as a sinner, when she is said to have been seduced and deceived by the Serpent? A. Eve is not said to have been seduced by the Serpent as though she did not know what she was doing or what the Serpent was offering her; for in that case she would be excusable. Rather, the Devil attacked and tempted her first, as the weaker one, through the Serpent, and Eve assented to him knowingly and willingly, and so she was made inexcusable in this. In the same way, Ecclesiasticus 25:33 writes that sin began with the woman. Likewise Paul says that Adam was not seduced, but Eve was seduced, 1 Timothy 2:14. Augustine so interprets it in On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins, book 1, chapter 16. Therefore, if you take "to be seduced" to mean not to test by experience what another promises you, then both Adam and Eve were seduced, and in this sense Paul uses the word in Galatians 6.

units.la: 3. Verum si [seducti] intellexeris, alicuius colloquio frui, & verba ipsius audire, quibus decipieris & falleris, id est, falsa tibi dicuntur, a Serpente sola Eua seducta est, non autem Adamus. Illa enim sola Diaboli per serpentem loquentis verba suis auribus hausit, excepit, & induit: quae ad maritum uti & pomum ipsum a se decerpti postea detulit. Ergo Eua a Serpente: Adamus autem ab ipsa Eua, non, autem a Serpente audiuit ea verba Diaboli, quae Mosi narrat cap. 3 Genesis. Sic igitur, eoque sensu exaudiendum est, quod [sola Eua] seducta dicitur, non etiam Adamus seductus, vt appareret Gen. 3. 13. Sic Augustinus lib. 14. Ciuit. Dei, cap. 11, & lib. 11. cap. 42. Genes. ad litter. Lombardus lib.
units.tr: 3. But if you understand "seduced" to mean enjoying someone's conversation and hearing his words, by which you are deceived and misled, that is, when false things are said to you, then Eve alone was seduced by the Serpent, and not Adam. For she alone took in, received, and welcomed into her ears the words of the Devil speaking through the serpent; and afterwards she carried them to her husband, together with the fruit she had plucked. So Eve heard from the Serpent, but Adam heard those words of the Devil, which Moses recounts in Genesis 3, from Eve herself, and not from the Serpent. Therefore it must be understood in this sense, that "Eve alone" is said to have been seduced, and Adam was not seduced as well, as appears from Genesis 3:13. So Augustine, City of God, book 14, chapters 11; and The Literal Meaning of Genesis, book 11, chapter 42. Lombard

units.la: 2 Sentent. Dist. 22. cap. 5.
units.tr: The Sentences, book 2, distinction 22, chapter 5.

units.la: Q. Vtrum Eua foemina plus, & grauius peccarit, quam vir ipsius Adamus.
units.tr: Q. Whether the woman Eve sinned more and more gravely than her husband Adam.

units.la: R. Si temporis ratio habeatur, peccauit Eua grauius, quam Adamus: quoniam & prima peccauit, & Adamo viro suo incitamentum fuit ad peccandum, ad quem & fructu Arboris vetita detulit, & verba Serpentis promissionesque retulit, quem denique & suauitate & pulchritudine fructus seu pomi perswasit, vt ipse quoque de eo ederet. Sin vero ratio conditionis ac personae spectetur, peccauit grauius Adam quam Eua, vtpote qui & primus imaginem Dei, & plus habuisset, & ipse Dei mandatu, ne ex eo fructu gustasset, accepisset, poenamq; futura inde sibi mortis ipsis auribus suis ex Deo ipso audiuisset, eamque ipse vxori suae Eua antea significasset, & declarasset. Sic Augustinus lib. 14. Ciuit. Dei, cap. cap. 11. ait Adamum magis sciuisse id, quod faceret, esse peccatum, quàm Eua scinerit. Et idem quoque lib. 11 Genes. ad liter. cap. 42. Quod verò idem scribit, [Credendum esse illum virum sua fœmina, vni vnum, hominem hominum, coniugem coniugi, ad Dei legem transgredien-dam, non tanquam verum loquenti credidisse seductum, sed sociali necessitudine paruisse:] quódque ex eo colligit P. Lombardus lib. 2. Sentent. Dist. 22. cap. 5: Amicabilis tantùm benevolentia Adamum peccasse, falsum est. Nam & infidelis, & superbus fuit Ada-mus, vti & Eua: neque ab eadem culpa vel peccato excusari poterat. Q. Cur partus dolores pro pœna Mulieri imponuntur a Deo, Gen. 3.16, quum Paulus affirmet Mulierem seruari dia tñs tixvoyoviaς, id est, liberos gignendo, 1. Tim. 2.15? R. Non partus, liberorumque procreatio pro pœna Mulieri a Deo data est: sed immensi illi labores, cruciatus vteri ac dolores partus, quas Græci ὠδίνας vocant, sunt Pœna peccati Mulieris. Nam Mulier alioquin erat etiam in terrestri Paradiso, & statu innocentiæ, paritura iuxta illud, [Crescite, & multiplicamini,] sed absque vllo dolore. Nunc verò post peccatum, quia dum Mulier hominem parit, hostem Dei sua culpa profert in lucem (qui sit nempe Deo contradicturus, iam & filius ira Dei, Rom. 8 7, Ephes. 2.3.) idcirco summos cruciatus & dolores Mulier sentit, quales ne in morte pene perferuntur, Ioan. 16.21. Ergo non tixvoyoviα, sed ὠδίνα sunt Pœna, eáque in hoc Mundo grauissima, peccati Mulieris. Vide Augustinum lib. 11 cap. 37. Genesi ad literam. Q. Ecquis primus verba Dei immutauerit, ac salfificauerit, Euáne, an Serpens? R. Eua prima videtur minas illas Dei certissimas (nempe Genef. 2. 17. [Q hodie comedetis ex eo certe moriendo moriemini] tabefactasse, & substitutâ dubitatione, aut dubitandi formulâ pro voce certitudinis dedisse occasionem Serpenti seu Diabolo vlterius pergendi. Dixit enim mulier, referens verba Dei, tanquam de euentu eorum dubitás, [Ne comedatis ex isto, ne moriamini] Gen 3.
units.tr: A. If the order of time is considered, Eve sinned more gravely than Adam, since she sinned first, and she was an incitement to her husband Adam to sin. To him she brought the forbidden fruit of the tree, reported the words and promises of the Serpent, and at last persuaded him by the sweetness and beauty of the fruit to eat of it too. But if the consideration is of condition and person, Adam sinned more gravely than Eve, since he was the first to bear the image of God, and had more, and since he had received from God's own command not to eat of that fruit, and had heard from God himself with his own ears the punishment of death that would follow, and he himself had previously made this known and declared it to his wife Eve. So Augustine, City of God, book 14, chapter 11, says that Adam knew better than Eve that what he was doing was sin. Likewise in The Literal Meaning of Genesis, book 11, chapter 42, he writes that we must believe that this man, one with his wife, one human being with another human being, a spouse with his spouse, did not believe her as one speaking the truth, when she was breaking God's law, and so was not seduced; but he yielded out of the necessity of partnership. From this Peter Lombard concludes, in The Sentences, book 2, distinction 22, chapter 5, that Adam sinned only out of friendly goodwill. This is false. For Adam was both unbelieving and proud, as Eve was, and he could not be excused from the same guilt or sin. Q. Why does God impose the pains of childbirth on the woman as punishment, Genesis 3:16, since Paul affirms that the woman is saved through childbearing [διὰ τῆς τεκνογονίας], that is, by bearing children, 1 Timothy 2:15? A. The bearing and procreation of children was not given to the woman as punishment by God; rather, those immense labours, the torments of the womb and the pains of birth, which the Greeks call birth pangs [ὠδίνας], are the punishment of the woman's sin. For otherwise the woman would have been in the earthly Paradise and in the state of innocence, and would have borne children according to the words "Increase and multiply," but without any pain. But now, after sin, since in bringing forth a man the woman by her own fault brings into the light an enemy of God (who is to oppose God, and is already a child of wrath, Romans 8:7, Ephesians 2:3), therefore the woman feels the greatest torments and pains, such as are not endured even in death, John 16:21. Therefore it is not childbearing [τεκνογονία] but birth pangs [ὠδίνα] that are the punishment of the woman's sin, and in this world the heaviest. See Augustine, The Literal Meaning of Genesis, book 11, chapter 37. Q. Who first altered and falsified the words of God, Eve or the Serpent? A. Eve seems first to have weakened those most certain threats of God (namely Genesis 2:17, "On the day you eat of it, certainly dying you shall die"), and by substituting doubt, or a form of doubting, for the language of certainty, she gave the Serpent or Devil an occasion to go further. For the woman, reporting God's words, spoke as though doubting their outcome: "Lest you eat of it, lest you die," Genesis 3.

units.la: 3. Itaque vulgaris versio habet, [ne forte moriamini.] Lombardus lib. 2. Sentent. Dist. 21. cap. 3: [Attende, ait, ordinem, ac progressum humanæ perditionis. Primò Deus dixerat, Q uacunque die comedetis ex eo, morte moriemini. Deinde Mulier dixit, Ne forte moriamini. Nouissimè Serpens dixit, Nequaquam moriemini. Deus affirmauit: Mulier quasi ambigendo illud dixit: Diabolus negauit.] Q ue ergo dubitauit, ab affirmante recessit, & negauti appropinquauit. Q uod si Mulier restituisset Diabolo, Diabolus ab ea fugisset, ut est apud Iacob. Epist. cap. 4. 7. Q. Q uid verba haec in poena Serpentis significent, [Et tu conteres Mulieris semini calcaneum] Gen. 3. 15. R. Poenam hus verbis afflictionem q describi certum est, quam Serpens, quantum potest, infert hominibus, ut suam in eos inimicitiam, odiumq; etiamnum hodie testetur. Ergo Serpens homines præsertim in pede, & calcaneo punit & vulnerat, ut corruant & cadant. Est enim ista pedis Hominis & calcanei (quæ membra totum corpus reliquum ferunt, & sustentant) læsio, vulneratio, apprehensióque signum voluntatis Serpentis nobis infestæ, & antagonistæ nostri nos deicere, ac frangere cupientis. Sic
units.tr: 3. Accordingly the common version has "lest perhaps you die." Lombard, The Sentences, book 2, distinction 21, chapter 3: [Notice, he says, the order and progress of human ruin. First God had said, "On whatever day you eat of it, you shall die the death." Then the woman said, "Lest perhaps you die." Last of all the Serpent said, "By no means shall you die." God affirmed; the woman spoke as if doubting; the Devil denied.] Therefore she who doubted moved away from the one affirming and drew near to the one denying. But if the woman had resisted the Devil, the Devil would have fled from her, as is found in James 4:7. Q. What do these words mean as the punishment of the Serpent: "And you shall bruise the heel of the woman's seed," Genesis 3:15? A. It is certain that these words describe the affliction which the Serpent, as far as it can, inflicts on men, and by which it still today shows its enmity and hatred against them. So the Serpent punishes and wounds men especially in the foot and heel, so that they stumble and fall. For this injury, wound, and seizing of the foot and heel of a man (members which carry and support the rest of the body) is a sign of the will of the Serpent, hostile to us and our antagonist, who desires to throw us down and break us. So

units.la: Iacobus dicitur apprehendisse calcaneum fratris sui Esau, Gen.25.26. Sic Danid calcaneum ab hoste domestico in se publicatu esse scribit, Psal. 41.10, Ioan. 13, 18, Psal. 56.7. Sic Daniel.2.41 quum Monarchia quarta deturbatur à Christo, pedes eius ab eo inuadi dicuntur. Est enim formidolosus hostis & gladiator, qui primum omnium inuadit pedes. Superiores autem corporis nostri partes attingere Serpens non potuit, quia iam à Deo fuisset sic deiectus, vt humi perpetuò serperet, seque minime iam attollere facile posset, Gen. 3.14. Inferiores autem partes potest. In summa, qua colluctatio & pugna inter Hominem & Serpentem futura esset, & nunc perpetua durat, declaratur his verbis. Ἔχ-am homo petit caput ipsum Serpentis animalis (taquam fontem vitæ illius) vt illud conterat, sicque Serpentem necet, & exstinguat. Serpens autem animal petit calcaneum hominis (qui est fundamentum corporis totius) vt eum feriat, sicque hominem deiciat, & tandem occidat. Ergo maior ab homine serpenti plaga infligitur, quam homini à serpente. Quæ quum anagogice ad fideles, & Satana (cuius fuit Serpens ille typus) referuntur certe quanuis, ratione naturæ Satan, vtpote angelus, & Princeps aëris sit fortior homine, & contra eum de loco superiore pugnet, Ephe.2.2, & 6.12: tamen homo fidelis, quia Spiritus Christi sit per fide participes, fortior est Satana, ratione istius Dei in fe gratia, eumque iam à Christo sub pedes suos contritum, & fractum ligant ydem fideles, vincunt, & superant, vt est Psal.91, Math.12.29, Rom.16.20: vt iam letaliter Homini nocere Satan non posset. Cur pra-
units.tr: Jacob is said to have seized the heel of his brother Esau, Gen. 25.26. So David writes that the heel was attacked by a domestic enemy, Ps. 41.10, John 13.18, Ps. 56.7. So too Daniel 2.41, when the fourth monarchy is overthrown by Christ, its feet are said to be attacked by him. For he is a fearsome enemy and gladiator, who attacks the feet first of all. But the serpent could not reach the upper parts of our body, because it had already been cast down by God so that it would crawl on the ground forever and could no longer easily raise itself, Gen. 3.14. It can, however, reach the lower parts. In sum, the struggle and fight that would be between man and serpent, and which still lasts, is declared in these words. Enmity [ἔχθρα]: man aims at the head of the serpent-animal (as at the fountain of its life), so that he may crush it and thereby kill and extinguish the serpent. The serpent-animal, however, aims at the heel of man (which is the foundation of the whole body), so that it may strike him, bring him down and at last kill him. Therefore a greater blow is inflicted by man on the serpent than by the serpent on man. Although these things are referred anagogically to the faithful and to Satan (whose type that serpent was), certainly, by the nature of things, Satan as an angel and prince of the air is stronger than man and fights against him from a higher place, Eph. 2.2 and 6.12. Nevertheless the faithful man, because through faith he participates in the Spirit of Christ, is stronger than Satan by reason of God's grace in him. The same faithful bind, conquer and overcome him, now crushed and broken under their feet by Christ, as in Ps. 91, Matt. 12.29, Rom. 16.20, so that Satan can no longer mortally harm man. Why

units.la: H termissa est pœna Diaboli, dum Deus peccatum Hominis punires, quum Diabolus fuerit verus peccati illius autor & suasor, Apoc. 12. 9. R. Quoniam de Diabolo nulla mentio facta fuerat à Mose, idcirco pœna Diaboli ab eodem est prætermissa. Praterea quemadmodum recte monet Augustinus Genesi ad liter. lib. 11. cap. 36, quod supplicium in Serpentem Animal à Deo fuit pronuntiatum, etsi primum quidem in ipsum Serpentum genus quadrat vere, & naturaliter: typicè tamen & figuratè convenit etiam in Diabolum, cuius fuit instrumentum Serpens. Itaque Deus Serpentem non interrogat, cur id fecerit, quod egerat, quoniam sciebat Deus Serpentem id minimè operatum esse per se, & in sua natura, ac voluntate: sed Diaboli de illo potius per illum, & in illo seduxisse homines. Quâobrem id, quod Serpenti dicitur, ait idem Augustinus, & ad eum, qui per Serpentem operatus est, utique refertur. Ergo illud ipsum, quod Semen mulieris conterit caput Serpentis, quum ad Diabolum accommodatur, ostendit Christum (verum semen mulieris, & quidem solius) vires, & regnum Satanæ evertere ac conterere, & pios omnes, quatenus illi incorporantur Eph. 3. 6, idem posse per fidem, & Christi Spiritum, contra quem ne portæ quidem omnes inferi quicquam valent, ac possunt. Mat. 16. 18.
units.tr: the punishment of the Devil was passed over when God punished man's sin, since the Devil was the true author and instigator of that sin, Apoc. 12.9? A. Because Moses made no mention of the Devil, the punishment of the Devil was therefore omitted by him. Moreover, as Augustine rightly observes (Genesis literally, book 11, chapter 36), the penalty pronounced by God against the serpent-animal, although in the first place it truly and naturally fits the serpent kind itself, nevertheless also fits typically and figuratively the Devil, whose instrument the serpent was. Thus God does not question the serpent as to why it did what it had done, since God knew that the serpent had not done this of itself, by its own nature and will, but that the Devil had seduced men through it and in it. Wherefore what is said to the serpent, says the same Augustine, is referred to him who acted through the serpent. Therefore that very thing, that the seed of the woman crushes the head of the serpent, when applied to the Devil, shows that Christ (the true seed of the woman, and indeed the only one) overturns and crushes the powers and kingdom of Satan, and that all the pious, insofar as they are incorporated into him, Eph. 3.6, can do the same through faith and the Spirit of Christ, against whom not even all the gates of hell prevail or can prevail, Matt. 16.18.

units.la: Q. Cur à primis illius parentibus & culpa, & pœna primi istius eorum peccati transiit, transitque in singulos homines, id est, in eorum posteros. R. Quoniam Adamus & Eva totum genus humanum repræsentabant, promissionesque, uti & minas, non sibi solis, sed & posteris quoque suis vel saluti vel exitio futuras acceperant,
units.tr: Q. Why did the guilt and punishment of this first sin pass from its first parents, and pass into each single man, that is, into their posterity? A. Because Adam and Eve represented the whole human race, and had received promises, and also threats, which were to be for salvation or ruin not only for themselves alone but for their posterity too,

units.la: Q. Mark at the left margin of the first paragraph: marginal note marks "Q." and "R." as printed in the text. perant, idq; ipsi intelligebant. Ergo his duobus, qui fuerunt reliqui generis humani totius fons, corruentibus, corruit quoque totum genus humanum: ijs reis coram Deo effectis, reum quoque redditum fuit totum genus humanum: ijs pœnæ obnoxijs tota quoq; natura & massa humana eidem pœnæ facta est obnoxia. Neque enim alium ex peccatore, quam peccator nasci potest: nec rivus alium ex fœtido fonte, quam fœtidum fluit, Iob. 14. 4, Iac. 3. 12. Vnde à Paulo omnes & singuli homines dicuntur peccasse in Adamo, id est, rei primum coram Deo reddíti esse: Deinde ex eodem illo participes pœnæ facti, Rom. 5. 12, Psal. 14. 1, & 51. 7. Quare non tantum pœna, sed & culpa ex Adamo in posteros transit: ac primum quidem culpa, postea pœna, ne immerentes eam pœnam ferre posteri videantur: quæ duo peccatum originale nominantur. Ergo ex corruptis parentibus nati sunt, ac nascuntur (& quidem æquissima lege & naturali) liberi corrupti, & peccatores. Vide Lombard. lib. 2. Sententi. Distinct. 30, & 31. per totum.
units.tr: and they understood this themselves. Therefore, since these two, who were the whole source of the rest of the human race, fell, the whole human race fell with them: when they were made guilty before God, the whole human race was also made guilty; when they became liable to that punishment, the whole nature and mass of humanity was also made liable to the same punishment. For no one can be born of a sinner other than a sinner, nor does a stream flow from a foul spring other than foul, Job 14.4, James 3.12. Whence Paul says that all and each man sinned in Adam, that is, were first made guilty before God, and then were made sharers in the same punishment, Rom. 5.12, Ps. 14.1, and 51.7. Wherefore not only punishment but also guilt passes from Adam to posterity: first guilt, indeed, and afterwards punishment, lest the posterity seem to bear that punishment undeservedly, though innocent. These two are called original sin. Therefore children have been born, and are born, from corrupt parents, and by a most just and natural law they are corrupt and sinners. See Lombard, Sentences, book 2, distinctions 30 and 31, throughout.

units.la: Q. Cur in Bruta Animantia, reliquásque Mundi huius partes transfiit quoque huius primi peccati effectum, & pœna? R. Quanquam neque Bruta animantia peccarunt proprie, neque etiam reliqua huius Mundi partes, utpote ἄλογα: tamen quoniam sunt res hominum peccatorum, & pars destinata data, ijs à Deo familiæ, effectum quoque peccati & hominum in Dei rebellionis sentiunt. Nam in crimine præsertim læsæ Maiestatis non solum criminis autor, sed & liberi eius, & tota rei consanguinei, hominis familia punitur. Ex quo evenit, ut, quemadmodum ait Paulus Rom. 8. 19. res creata sint vanitati subiecta, non sua sponte, sed propter hominem, qui subiecit eam illi vanitati. Quare rectè & merito illa quoque peccati effectum sentiunt. His autem explicatis, accedamus ad tertium caput, quod continet promissionem futuri Messiæ factam primis Hominibus post eorum peccatum.
units.tr: Q. Why did the effect and punishment of this first sin pass also into brute animals and the other parts of this world? A. Although brute animals did not sin properly, nor did the other parts of this world, being without reason [ἄλογα], nevertheless, since they are things belonging to sinful men, and were given by God as a destined part of their household, they too feel the effect of sin and of men's rebellion against God. For in the crime especially of treason, not only the author of the crime but also his children and all the kin of the guilty man, that is, his household, are punished. Hence it happens that, as Paul says, Rom. 8.19, the creatures were subjected to vanity, not of their own will but because of man, who subjected them to that vanity. Wherefore they rightly and deservedly also feel the effect of sin. Having explained these things, let us proceed to the third chapter, which contains the promise of the future Messiah made to the first men after their sin.

units.la: Ad III. Promissio Messiæ post peccatum.
units.tr: On the third point: the promise of the Messiah after the sin.

units.la: Quæritur, Utrum hæc verba Dei, [Et semen Mulieris conteret caput Serpentis, Gen. 3. 15.] promissionem de futuro Mundi Seruatore & Messia Christo contineant. R. Dubitari non potest quin hæc Dei verba tunc fuerint, atque adeò etiamnum sint, hodie magna non tantum Eua, sed & Adami quoque, & omnium hominum contra Serpentem, & Serpentis impulsorem Diabolum consolatio & victoria. At illa nequaquam eiusmodi esse possunt, nisi propter aliquem, qui non modò sit ipse superior viribus, quam Homo: sed etiam quàm Diabolus, cuius caput conterit, Matth. 12. 29. Nam nec inferior Diabolo, nec par ei tantum eum vinceret. Ergo fortior eo sit oportet quicunque eum per se vincit. Atqui Diabolus est natura Angelus: Quare Angelica natura potentiorem esse oportet eum, qui Diaboli regnum fit euersurus, & veteris illius Serpentis caput contriturus. Iam vero sola Diuina natura est maior quàm Angelica. Quamobrem Deus sit necesse est ille de quo promissio tam excellens sit hoc loco. Sed & Homo quoque sit oportet, quoniam est Semen Mulieris. Ergo u primitiur his verbis, qui & Deus & Homo futurus erat, vnus & idem vna persona. Iam vero qui est eiusmodi,non solùm ipse potest & viribus, & æquitate caussæ (vtpote in natura humana plenè satisfaciens Deo pro natura humana peccato Heb.2 14. 16) vincere Satanam victorem Hominis:sed etiam aliys hominibus vires sumministrare (quatenus fide sibi coniunguntur,suique Spiritus fiunt participes) ad superandum eundem seu Satanam,seu Diabolum. Porrò qui talis est (nimirum & pro hominibus Deo plenè satisfaciens, & vires illis ad conterendum caput istius Serpētis suggerens)proculdubio is & Messias,& Mediator,& Seruator noster est, Rom.16.20, Ephe.4. 16. Ex quo fit, vt illis Dei verbis & promissione verum Messias hominibus fuerit demonstratus: hominum salutis,& cum Deo reconciliationis fundamentum, & caussa explicata: denique plena consolatio isdem proposita:ac proinde Dei Filius Dominus noster Iesus Christus fuit his verbis promissus. Hinc verò consentit,aut potius hanc nostram sententiam confirmat hoc distum Ioannis Apoc. 13.8. Christum esse illum Dei Agnum, qui mactatus fuit iam inde à iactis Mundi fundamentis, Item Augustinus lib. Quæst. Veteris & Noui Testamenti cap.3.sub finem: [Priores,inquit,ergo omnes, quotquot fidem habuerunt vnius Dei (quam Saluator prædicauit) iure Christiani dicendi sunt. Ab initio enim Saluator venturus promissus est. Vnde Ioannes in Apoc.ait, Agnus,qui occisus est à constitutione Mundi.] Eodem pertinet,quod tractat, disputátque idem Augustinus lib.2.de Gratia contra Pelagium,cap.26 & 27: & est apud Ioannem 8.58. Q. Quid significent hæc verba, [Semen Mulieris.] R. Nonnulli existimant de solo Christo ea esse intelligenda, quoniam vnus ille ex solius Mulieris femine, absque coitu viri & masculi conceptus est. Nam ex Maria Virgine natus est Christus, Math. 1, Luc. 1, quicquid impij & impostores Turcae ad eleuandam tanti miraculi fidem, mentiantur multos esse inter se ex Virginibus foeminis, & absque femine virili natos. Alij eadam hac verba ad omnes in vniuersum homines extendunt. Alij denique ad solos fideles & electos Dei. Certe proprie & per se ad vnum & solum Christum ea pertinent: communicatiue vero ad alios homines, & quidem omnes, quatenus de capite Serpentis animalis conterendo literaliter sumuntur: ad solos autem fideles, quatenus eadem illa verba anagogice de Diaboli veteris Serpentis regno euertendo dicuntur, & intelliguntur. Nam omnes homines Christo communicant, quatenus homo est: soli autem fideles eidem communicant, quatenus Christus est & Messias. Porro ex eo apparet etiam Semen humanum (ex quo, vti ex Semine mulieris Homines naturaliter procreantur) in his verbis [Semen Mulieris] generaliter contineri: sed quia mulier a Serpente decepta ipsa fuerat, idcirco in eius consolationem dixit Dominus [Semen Mulieris.] Item Christum (cuius beneficio homines alij hoc habent) solium mulieris, non etiam viri Semen futurum fuisse ex his Dei verbis facillime, verissimeque colligitur & efficitur. Q. Cur statim addita facta fuit a Deo promissio de Messia: non autem in longum tempus dilata, postquam nempe poenam sui peccati homines sensissent. R. Deus quemadmodum iustus est, ita & misericors, Exod. 34. 6. 7: imo & Hominum faufautor & ϕιλάνθρωπος, Tit.3.4 Ose 11.4. Ergo vti quâ iustus, pœnam hominibus statim post eorum peccatum denuntiauit:ita, quâ Misericors, consolationem, ac salutem seu liberationem ab ipsa miseria promisit, & fore declarauit. Quare summa quadam in genus humanum charitate Messiam illum,si est Filium suum ipse promisit hominibus, etsi hostibus & inimicis suis, Ioan.3.16, Rom.5.8, Cur Deus homines peccatores seruare voluit,ac redimere: Diabolos autem peccatores noluit. Gregorius Magnus lib.4. Moralium,cap.9. sic scribit, [Est adhuc aliud propter quod & perditus homo reparari debuit, & superbiens Spiritus seu Angelus reparari non possit, quia nimirum Angelus suâ malitiâ cecidit: Hominem vero alienâ prostrauit.] Verum Lombardus lib.2.Sentent. dist.21.cap.5.& 6.magis perspicuè hoc ipsum, atque his verbis, [Homo,quia aliquâ licet medicam,cadendi occasionem habuit, idcirco per gratiâ iuuari potuit ad veniam, vt qui per alium ceciderat, per alium erigeretur. Qui ergo incitatorem habuit ad malum, non sinistrè reparatorem habuit ad bonum. Diabolus vero, quia sine alicuius tētatione peccauit,per alium,vt surgeret,iuuari non debuit:nec per se potuit. & ideo irremediabile peccatum eius extitit.] Et hæc vera sunt. Iam venio ad quartum caput, quod est de mutato nomine foeminae hominis seu uxoris Adami.
units.tr: Question: Whether these words of God, [And the seed of the woman shall bruise the head of the serpent, Gen. 3. 15.], contain a promise of the future Saviour of the world and the Messiah Christ. A. It cannot be doubted that these words of God were spoken at that time, and so are still, today, a great comfort and victory not only for Eve but also for Adam and for all men against the Serpent and the Devil who prompted the Serpent. But these words could not be of this kind unless they refer to someone who is not only stronger than man but also stronger than the Devil, whose head he crushes (Matt. 12. 29). For one who was weaker than the Devil, or equal to him, would not conquer him by himself. Therefore whoever conquers him by his own power must be stronger than he. But the Devil is by nature an angel. Hence the one who is to overthrow the Devil's kingdom and crush the head of that old Serpent must be stronger than the angelic nature. Now only the divine nature is greater than the angelic. Therefore the one of whom this so excellent promise speaks must be God. But he must also be man, since he is the Seed of the Woman. Thus by these words is foreshadowed one who was to be both God and man, one and the same person. Now he who is of this kind not only can, by his power and by the justice of his cause (since, in human nature, he fully satisfied God for the sin of human nature, Heb. 2. 14. 16), conquer Satan, the conqueror of man, but also can supply strength to other men (insofar as they are joined to him by faith and become partakers of his Spirit) to overcome the same Satan, or the Devil. Moreover, one who is such (namely, one who fully satisfies God on behalf of men and supplies them with strength to crush the head of that Serpent) is without doubt our Messiah, our Mediator and our Saviour (Rom. 16. 20; Eph. 4. 16). From this it follows that by those words of God and that promise the true Messiah was shown to men: the foundation of human salvation and of reconciliation with God, and the cause of this was explained; and finally a full consolation was set before them. Accordingly, our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, was promised by these words. Moreover, this is confirmed by the saying of John in Revelation 13. 8, that Christ is that Lamb of God who has been slain from the foundation of the world. Likewise Augustine, in his book Questions on the Old and New Testament, chapter 3, near the end: [Therefore, he says, all the earlier men who had faith in the one God (whom the Saviour preached) are rightly to be called Christians. For from the beginning the Saviour was promised as the one who would come. Hence John says in the Apocalypse, the Lamb who was slain from the foundation of the world.] To the same point belongs what Augustine discusses and argues in book 2 of On Grace, against Pelagius, chapters 26 and 27; and see John 8. 58. Q. What do the words [seed of the woman] mean? A. Some think that they are to be understood of Christ alone, since he alone was conceived from the seed of a woman alone, without intercourse of a man and a male. For Christ was born of the Virgin Mary (Matt. 1; Luke 1), whatever the impious and impostor Turks may lie, to lessen the faith in so great a miracle, that many were born of virgin women without male seed. Others extend these words to all men in general. Others finally refer them only to the faithful and elect of God. Certainly they properly and in themselves pertain to the one Christ alone; but by communication they pertain to other men, and indeed to all, insofar as they are taken literally, of crushing the head of the animal Serpent; but to the faithful alone, insofar as the same words are said and understood allegorically, of overthrowing the kingdom of the Devil, the old Serpent. For all men share in Christ insofar as he is man; but only the faithful share in him insofar as he is Christ and Messiah. Further, from this it also appears that the human seed (from which, as from the seed of a woman, men are naturally produced) is generally contained in the words [seed of the woman]; but because the woman had been deceived by the Serpent herself, therefore the Lord said [seed of the woman] for her consolation. Likewise, it is most easily and most truly inferred and established from these words of God that Christ (by whose benefit other men have this) was to be the seed of a woman only, and not also of a man. Q. Why was the promise about the Messiah given at once, and not deferred for a long time, after men had felt the punishment for their sin? A. God is just, and so also merciful (Exod. 34. 6, 7); indeed he is a friend of men [φιλάνθρωπος] (Titus 3. 4; Hos. 11. 4). Therefore, just as in his justice he announced punishment to men immediately after their sin, so, in his mercy, he promised and declared consolation and salvation, or deliverance from that very misery. Hence, out of a certain supreme love for the human race, he himself promised to men that Messiah, who is his Son, though they were his enemies and foes (John 3. 16; Rom. 5. 8). Why did God wish to save and redeem sinful men, but did not wish to save the sinful Devils? Gregory the Great, in book 4 of the Morals, chapter 9, writes thus: [There is yet another reason why fallen man ought to be restored, while the proud spirit, or angel, cannot be restored: namely, that the angel fell by his own malice, but man was cast down by another's.] But Lombard, in book 2 of the Sentences, distinction 21, chapters 5 and 6, states the same thing more clearly, in these words: [Man, although he had an occasion to fall, yet had a remedy, and so could be helped by grace to forgiveness; so that he who had fallen through another might be raised up through another. Therefore he who had an inciter to evil did not lack a restorer to good. But the Devil, since he sinned without any temptation from another, ought not to be helped to rise through another, nor could he be helped by himself; and therefore his sin remained irremediable.] And these things are true. Now I come to the fourth chapter, which concerns the changed name of the first woman, that is, the wife of Adam.

units.la: Ad IIII. Mutatio nominis Mulie- ris Primae.
units.tr: On the Fourth Point: The Changing of the First Woman's Name

units.la: AC primùm quaritur, Cur Adamus uxoris suae nomen mutauit? R. Vt immutata eius conditio, & dispar a superiore intelligeretur. Prius enim Ischa tanquam par marito, id est, Virissa vocatur, uti maritus ipsius Isch, id est, Vir, dicebatur, Gen. 2.23. tanquam foemina sicut nomine, ita potestate viro par esset, & aequalis. Sed iam postquam per peccatum viro subiecta fuit foemina seu uxor, illique iam non par, sed subdita Gen 4.16. nomen illi immutatum fuit, & pro [Ischa] vocata est [Chaua] id est Eua, quemadmodum Graece conuertit Paulus 1.Tim.2.13. ex communi receptaq; iam inter Iudaeos ipsos Graece loquentes terminatione & sententia. Dicitur autem diserte Adamus, non autem Deus, hoc nomen uxori suae, velut illius iam caput & Dominus impositisse, Gen.4.20, 1.Cor.11.3. Fuit enim Dominorum nomen rebus sibi subditis imponere, Gen.2.19 quemadmodum antea docuimus. Q. Quid vox [Chaua] seu Eua significat. R. Cur sic nominata fuerit Homo foemina a marito, diximus supra in Historia. Quid vox haec significet, nunc est explicandum a nobis. Chaua, ut omnes Hebraice eruditi norunt, significat Viuentem, quod omnium hominum futurorum mater esset Eua futura: & ut luctu illum uxoris, quod posteris suis mortis causa extitisset, minueret Adamus. Ergo qne [Mota] seu [Maueta] id est, causa mortis ex ipsius peccato dici potuit: ex ipse futura ex ea prolis, & Dei benedictionis, Eua potius fuit appellata. Miror autem quid Philoni Iudaeo venerit in mentem, ut in libro de Nominibus Hebraicis scriberet, Euam [Ua] vel [calamitatem] notare. Cui Iosephus perspicue lib. 1.cap.2. Antiquitat. Iudaic. contradicit, & recte.
units.tr: First, it is asked: why did Adam change the name of his wife? Answer: so that her changed condition would be understood as different from her former one. For earlier she was called Ischa, as a companion to her husband, that is, Virissa, just as her husband Isch, that is, Man, was called, Gen. 2.23. As a woman she was equal to him in name and in power. But after, through sin, the woman or wife became subject to her husband and no longer his equal but his subordinate, Gen. 4.16, her name was changed, and instead of Ischa she was called Chava, that is, Eve, as Paul translates it into Greek, 1 Tim. 2.13, following the ending and sense already common and accepted among the Jews themselves who spoke Greek. But it is stated explicitly that Adam, not God, gave this name to his wife, as her head and lord, Gen. 4.20; 1 Cor. 11.3. For it was the mark of a lord to give names to the things subject to him, Gen. 2.19, as we taught earlier. Q. What does the word Chava or Eve mean? A. How the woman was named by her husband, we explained above in the history. What this word means must now be explained by us. Chava, as all learned in Hebrew know, means Living, because Eve was to be the mother of all men to come; and Adam, to lessen his grief at his wife, who had become the cause of death for his descendants, [Mota] or [Maueta], that is, cause of death, could be said from her sin. Rather, Eve was so called from the offspring to come from her, and from God's blessing. I wonder, however, what came into the mind of the Jew Philo, that he wrote in his book on Hebrew names that Eve [Ua] or [calamity] signifies. Josephus clearly contradicts him, Antiquities of the Jews, book 1, chapter 2, and rightly so.

units.la: Q. Quando sic ab Adamo Homo fœmina seu vxor nominata fuerit, Vtrum ante ipsius Eua peccatum, an demum postquam defecit à Deo, & eius voluntas maritò subdita à Deo fuit. R. Nonnulli existimant Mulierem sic etiam ante peccatum fuisse vocatam (in quibus est Iosephus lib. 1.cap.2. Antiquitat. Iudaic.) & Ischam dictam propter dignitatem illius supra cetera animantia: Euam vero seu Chauam proprio nomine. Tamen ex Genef. 4.20. videtur verius colligi posse, eam id nominis demum postquam peccauit, fortitam fuisse, nec ante lapsum suum fuisse binomiam: sed tunc Ischam duntaxat dictam, Gen. 2.23. Postea vero Chanam solùm. Q. Num superbior fuerit ista mulieris appellatio, quam par esset, dum Chaua, id est, Viuens, nullo addito epitheto, & distinctione nominatur ista mulier. R. Dum Viuens appellatur Mulier & Chaua, eiusmodi nomen illi tribuitur, ut futura ex ea benedictionis, posteritatis, ac sobolis spes, promissio Dei refricaretur illi, & ex ipso suo nomine ad consolationem proponeretur, & obuersaretur ante oculos, Hebr. 12.9: non autem ut causa ipsa primaria vitæ posteris esse suis Eua agnosceretur, & censeretur (cuius vitæ sunt vtérque Parens causa duntaxat instrumentalis) non item vt essentiatrix futurorum postea Hominum statueretur. Hoc enim est proprium unius Dei. Itaque non est appellata eo vocabulo, quod thema & originem cum voce & nomine Iehoua (quod unius Dei peculiare est) communem haberet: sed quod cum animantibus eandem vocis radicem apud Hebræos retinet. Animal enim ab Hebraïs voce [Chaial,] quæ ab eodem verbo derivata est, appellatur. Iam vero de quinto capite, in quo primus Hominum Vestitus continetur agamus.
units.tr: Q. When was the woman or wife named by Adam in this way: before Eve's sin, or only after she fell from God and her will, subject to her husband, was subjected by God? A. Some think the woman was called this even before sin (among them is Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews, book 1, chapter 2), and that she was called Ischa because of her dignity above the other living creatures, but Eve or Chava by her proper name. Yet from Gen. 4.20 it seems more truly to be gathered that she received this name only after she sinned, and that before her fall she was not called by two names, but only Ischa, Gen. 2.23, and afterwards only Chava. Q. Is this name of the woman more proud than it should be, since she is named Chava, that is, Living, without any added epithet and without distinction? A. When the woman is called Living and Chava, this name is given to her so that the promise of God concerning the future blessing, posterity, and offspring from her might be renewed for her and set before her as a consolation from her very name and kept before her eyes, Heb. 12.9. It was not, however, so that she would be acknowledged and reckoned as the primary cause of life for her descendants (both parents are only the instrumental cause of life), nor so that she would be established as the one who gives being to men who would come afterward. For this belongs to God alone. She was not named with that word because it had a root and origin in common with the name Jehovah, which is peculiar to the one God, but because among the Hebrews it keeps the same word root as the word for animals. For the Hebrews call animal [Chaial], which is derived from the same verb. Now let us deal with the fifth chapter, in which the first clothing of men is treated.

units.la: Ad V. De Vestitutus Hominum Primus.
units.tr: On the Fifth Point: The First Clothing of Men

units.la: Quaritur, Cur homines sua nuditatis post peccatum puduit, cuius eos ante peccatum non pudebat, neque aliud membrum in se, quàm Dei opus, id est, à Deo ipso recens factum cernerent? Augustinus lib. 11 Gen. ad liter cap 34. scribit, Deus no permisit homines ante peccatum suum aduertere nuditatem suam, eorum intentionem in superna suspollens, nisi quum possent peccatum pudendum in membris motum pœnalis membrorum lege sensissent. Quod ipsum fusius lib 14. Ciuit Dei, cap. 16, & 17 explicas, sic ait, [Secur scriptum est Gen. 2.25, Nudi erant, & non confundebantur homines, non quod eis sua nuditas esset incognita: sed turpis nuditas non erat, quia nondum libido membra illa præter arbitrium commouebat: nondum ad hominis inobedientiam redarguendam sua inobedientia caro quodammodo testimonium perhibebat. Cognouerunt ergo quia nudi erant, nudati scilicet ea gratia, quà fiebat vt nuditas corporis nulla eos peccati lege menti eorum repugnante, confunderet. Proinde confusi inobedientia carnis sue, tanquam teste pœna inobedientiæ suæ,confuerunt folia fici,& fecerunt sibi campestria, id est, succinctloria genitalium. ] Hactenus ille. Quare non puduit homines illos primos,quatenus membra sui corporis omnia, Dei esse opus agnoscebant: sed quatenus in iis motum iam aliquem turpem,& suæ conscientiæ reliquis scintillis adversantem senserunt. Id quod primum in membris genitalibus suis manifestè perceperunt: (atque hic motus libido venerea nominatur, ut vult idem Augustinus) ac proinde primum ea membra ipsimet homines, quantum potuerunt, texerunt, uti & nunc tegunt quoque: imo natura quoque ipsa postea texit obiectis illis corporis parti ac inductis densis pilis, ut apparet 1.Cor.12.23. Deinde etiam in cæteris corporis sui membris nudis ydem viderunt quiddam propter suam iam infirmitatem & imbecillitatem Dei imagini indecorum, fragile, caducum, ac minus, quam in aliis animantibus etiam brutis (quæ natura pilosa tunc erat) robustum & firmum: Id quod ipsum in se quoque esse pœnam peccati sui primi illi homines cognouerunt. Sic enim fuerunt ipsos cernentes nudos affectos, ut solent affici homines nudi sub oculis aliorum hominum: & talis affectio & pudor de Peccati pœna erat Gen.3.7, Iob.1.21. At hæc omnia nec erant in homine ante peccatum, nec ab eo quoque sentiebantur: ac proinde ante peccatum eos sua nuditatis non pudebat. Q. Cur Deus ipse Homines vestiebit, eos autem ipsos sibi reliqui corporis vestimenta,& integumenta, (quemadmodum Genitalium membrorum iam fecerant) quærere non finit: aut nudos in perpetuum esse non permisit & voluit? R. Etsi Iosephus lib.3. Antiquitat. Iudaic. non memi nit vestimentorum à Deo primis hominibus confectorum: verbum tamen Dei diserte eos à Deo ipso post peccatum vestitos fuisse docet, Gen. 3 21. Quare Deus eos ipse vestiuit, idq; summa in hominnes benignitatis argumentum fuit. Primùm,ne iniurys & tempestatibus cœli, quæ propter peccatum futura erant, suntque maximæ & tristissimæ, essent obnoxij absque vllo integumento & propugnaculo. Ergo Deus iys vestimenta tanquam tecta quædam, vt inquit Plato, & præsidia dedit aduersus tot mortis pericula, quæ è cœlo profluunt, & irruunt vbique in homines. Ea verò tecta sunt vestimenta, quæ commode secum circumgestarent, quorumque obiectu tutiores essent, ne statim nimio algore, vel æstu illi, eorumque posteri perirent. In quo incredibilis elucet, vt dixi, Dei in homines (qui recens ipsum offenderant, seque eius hostes præbuerat) φιλανθρωπια. Deinde Deus ipse homines post eorum peccatum vestimentis operuit, tanquam eos iam cernere nolens, & opus in ys suum (quod ab ipsismet erat corruptum & depravatum) obtegens. Nam labefactato per peccatum corporis humani & robore, & valetudine, & firmitate, iam non videtur hoc ipsum corpus esse digna Imaginis Dei theca. Ergo fuit quodammodo tota ea theca occultanda, nisi in ys partibus, quibus necessario ad huius vitæ humanæ functiones assiduas egemus, quales sunt oculi, aures, nares, manus, os. Caterum, eadem illa Dei immensa in hominem etiam sibi hostem, bonitas, caussa est, cur Deus hominem post peccatum noluerit permanere nudum id est, tam afflictum, & sibi ipsi alysque aspectu fœdum & indecorum. Cur autè Deus Ada-
units.tr: It is asked: why were men ashamed of their nakedness after the sin, when they had not been ashamed of it before, and when they saw in themselves no member other than God's work, that is, one just made by God himself? Augustine, in book 11 of the Literal Commentary on Genesis, chapter 34, writes that God did not permit men before their sin to notice their nakedness, keeping their attention fixed on higher things, until they could feel the shameful movement in their members through the penal law of the members. He explains this more fully in book 14 of The City of God, chapters 16 and 17, and says: [Scripture says, Gen. 2.25, They were naked, and were not ashamed. Not that their nakedness was unknown to them, but their nakedness was not shameful, because lust did not yet move those members against their will; their flesh, disobedient to them, did not yet bear witness to the disobedience of man. They knew therefore that they were naked, stripped, that is, by that grace through which the nakedness of the body, with no law of sin resisting their mind, did not cause them shame. Accordingly, confused by the disobedience of their flesh, as the penalty of their disobedience acting as a witness, they sewed fig leaves together and made themselves aprons, that is, loincloths for the genitals.] Thus far he. Why were those first men not ashamed insofar as they recognised that all the members of their body were God's work, but insofar as they felt in them some shameful movement, opposed to the remaining sparks of their conscience? This they first clearly perceived in their genital members, and this movement is called venereal desire, as the same Augustine holds. Accordingly, men themselves first covered those members as well as they could, as they still do; indeed nature itself later covered that part of the body with thick hair, as appears from 1 Cor. 12.23. Then also in their other naked members they saw something unbecoming to the image of God, frail, perishable, and weaker and less sturdy than in other living creatures, even the brutes (which at that time were naturally hairy), because of their now-present weakness and feebleness. The first men knew that this too was a punishment of their first sin. For they felt, seeing themselves naked, as men usually feel when naked before the eyes of other men; and such feeling and shame were a punishment of sin, Gen. 3.7; Job 1.21. But none of this was in man before sin, nor was it felt by him; accordingly, before sin they were not ashamed of their nakedness. Q. Why did God himself clothe men, and not allow them to seek for themselves coverings and garments for the rest of the body, as they had already done for the genital members, nor did he permit or will that they remain naked forever? A. Although Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews, book 3, does not mention the garments made by God for the first men, the word of God clearly teaches that after sin they were clothed by God himself, Gen. 3.21. So God clothed them himself, and this was a supreme sign of his goodness toward men.
