First, so that they would not be exposed without any covering or shelter to the injuries and storms of the sky, which were to come because of sin, and which are very great and most sorrowful. Therefore God gave them garments as coverings, as Plato says, and as protection against so many dangers of death, which flow from the sky and rush upon men everywhere. These garments were coverings which they could conveniently carry about with them, and by whose cover they would be safer, so that they and their descendants would not perish at once from excessive cold or heat. In this, as I have said, the incredible philanthropy [φιλανθρωπία] of God toward men, who had recently offended him and had made themselves his enemies, shines forth. Then God himself covered men with garments after their sin, as if unwilling to look upon them any longer, and concealing his work in them, which had been corrupted and depraved by themselves. For with the strength, health, and firmness of the human body weakened by sin, this body no longer seems a worthy case for the image of God. Therefore that whole case had in some measure to be hidden, except in those parts which we necessarily need for the constant functions of this human life, such as the eyes, ears, nostrils, hands, and mouth. Moreover, that same immense goodness of God, even toward man who had become his enemy, is the reason why God after sin would not allow man to remain naked, that is, so wretched, and so unsightly and shameful to himself and to others in appearance. But why God clothed Adam

units.la: Adamum & Euam non fuerit ipsos sibi quærere aliarum quoque corporis sui partium vestimenta, ratio est. Quod quum illa ex pellibus vel pilis animalium essent conficienda & sumenda, non fuissent ausi primi homines statim post Peccatum, animalia attingere, quæ iam sibi refractaria, truculenta, & inobedientia experiebantur. Præterea quum antea Deus non subiecisset homini Animantia in eum usum, Homo attentare ea in hunc quoque usum non potuit, nec debuit, ut ea excoriaret, & occideret, nisi hoc exemplo suo & in hominem beneficio Deus docuisset tacite se idem illud concedere hominibus in posterum, ut animalium pellibus & pilis se vestirent ac proinde ea interficere in eum usum possent, quemadmodum & ad edendum seu vescendum. Hoc enim Dei factum fuit Lex subiectionis, impositu cateris animantibus: & benigna iuris in eadem animantia concessio Homini, licet peccatori, facta de novo a Deo. Male tamen ex eo concluditur feliciorem hominis conditionem ergo post ipsius peccatum extitisse. Id quod putat Iosephus: Fuit enim felicius non vestiri, quam vestiri.
units.tr: The reason why Adam and Eve did not themselves seek clothing for their other body parts is this. Since such clothing had to be made and taken from the skins or hides of animals, the first men did not dare, immediately after the Fall, to touch animals, which they now found to be unyielding, fierce, and disobedient. Moreover, since God had not previously made animals subject to man for that use, man could not and ought not to have attempted to flay and kill them for that purpose, unless God by this example, and for man's benefit, had silently taught that he would grant the same thing to men in future: that they might clothe themselves with the skins and hides of animals, and so might kill them for that use, just as they might kill them for eating. For this act of God was a law of subjection imposed on the other living creatures, and a kindly grant of right over those same creatures, made anew by God to man, even though he was a sinner. Yet it is wrongly concluded from this that man's condition became happier after his sin. Josephus thought so: "It was happier not to be clothed than to be clothed."

units.la: Q. Utrum Deus ipse animalia quædam, ex quorum pellibus vestes pelliceas faceret, occidit, quæ postea excoriarit: an nevas quasdam pelles ipse creavit, non ex ullis animalibus detraxerit, quas ipse met in vestimenta contulerit?
units.tr: Q. Did God himself kill certain animals, from whose skins he then made fur garments, and afterwards flayed them? Or did he himself create certain new skins, not stripped from any animals, and put them to use as clothing?

units.la: R. Sine ipse Deus per se, sive per Angelos beatos vestes illas pelliceas confecerit, ac parærit, perinde est. Per se enim facere videtur qui per alium facit. Certe pellibus recentibus & omnino scorteis, & adhuc fœtidis Hominem vtrumque statim Deus involuit postquam eorum lapsum, tanquam mortis odorem seu potius putorem naribus eorum obiceret, & eos his vestibus, tanquam ordinario quodam sepulcro, concluderet ac integeret, ut quæ fœditas & pavor mortis esset tam ex his exemplis discerent homines isti. Eas autem pelles nequaquam novas ex nihilo, vel ex terra Deus creavit: sed eas animalibus à se interfectis (saltem tunc mortuis) detraxit, quibus ipsis statim homines induit. Ergo hac ratione Deus homini & mortis terrorem incussit (quum fœditatem, horrorem, miseriam⁕ cadaveris illi in animalibus istis occisis proponeret) & usum, iusque novum in Animalia concessit. Itaque hoc Dei exemplo, (quod fuit velut præceptum à Deo datum Homini) admoniti postea homines animalibus, eorumque pellibus sunt usi ad eum, & vestitum suum, tanquam cibis in eum finem creatis, & sibi à Deo benigne traditis, & concessis, 1. Tim. 4 3. Q. Cur ex pellibus Animalium potius, quam ex foliis arborum, velut ficus, Palma Christi, qua vocatur Cucurbita terrestris contextis (quod sine cade fieret) vestimenta fecit Deus hominibus. R. Hieronymus lib. 1. Epistolarum, Epist. de Vita Pauli Eremitæ, scribit Paulum ipsum Monachum vestem duntaxat ex foliis palmarum contextis, & inter se cosutis habuisse, quam Antonius Monachus postea gestauerit: non autem vestem ex pellibus animalium. Nam ait idem Hieronymus, [Cibum, & vestimentum et Palma præbebat.] Verum dubium de caussis Deus ex istis foliis vestimenta homini nō confecit: Primum, quod huiusmodi materia nō erat ad prohibendas diuturnas cœli iniurias satis firma & robusta. Itaque solidiore fuit opus, ac duriore, qualis fuit qua ex pelli-bus bus animalium nondum expolitis, & pilo nudatis texebatur. Hoc autem vestis pellicea genus rude, impolitū, & ἀπηχνον Iulius Cæsar lib. 6. Comment. de Bello Gall. Rhenones appellat, Germanica voce. Deinde, vt hoc exemplo suo Deus ostenderet Hominibus licere, & quidem ex ipsius beneficio, vti animalibus brutis ad vestitum, & ad victum. Nam absque hoc novo Dei beneficio neque potuissent, neque ansi fuissent homines ijs in eum finem vti, ea que vllo prorsus modo attrectare.
units.tr: R. Whether God himself made and prepared those fur garments, or did so through the blessed Angels, makes no difference. For one who acts through another seems to act himself. Certainly God at once clothed both humans in fresh hides, indeed entirely flayed and still foul-smelling. He held the smell of death, or rather its stench, before their noses, and enclosed and covered them in these garments as in a kind of ordinary tomb, so that these people might learn from such examples the foulness and dread of death. But God did not create these skins at all from nothing or from the earth. Rather, he stripped them from animals he had himself killed (dead at least by then), and with these he immediately clothed the men. So by this means God struck terror of death into man, since he set before him the foulness, horror, and misery of a corpse in these slaughtered animals, and he granted man a new use of and right over the animals. Therefore, admonished by this example of God (which was, as it were, a command given by God to man), men afterwards used animals and their skins for clothing, just as for food, which were created for that end and graciously handed over and granted to them by God. (1 Tim. 4:3) Q. Why did God make clothing for men from animal skins rather than from leaves of trees, such as the fig, or the Palma Christi (called the earthly gourd), woven together, which could have been done without killing anything? R. Jerome, in book 1 of his Letters, in the Life of Paul the Hermit, writes that Paul the monk had only a garment woven and sewn together from palm leaves, which Antony the monk later wore, and not a garment of animal skins. For Jerome says in the same place: [He was given food and clothing by the palm tree.] But there is doubt about the reasons why God did not make clothing for man from those leaves. First, such material was not firm and strong enough to ward off the long-lasting injuries of the sky. So the work had to be more solid and harder, such as that woven from the skins of animals not yet dressed and stripped of hair. Julius Caesar, in book 6 of his Commentaries on the Gallic War, calls this rough, unpolished kind of fur garment [ἀπηχνον], in the German word "Rhenones." Second, so that by this example God might show men that it was lawful, and indeed by his own kindness, to use brute animals for clothing and for food. For without this new benefit of God, men would neither have been able nor dared to use animals for that purpose, nor to touch them in any way at all.

units.la: Q. Vtrum primi Homines post peccatum (nam ante peccatum solis herbis & fructibus arborum vtebātur) & ante Diluuium carnes animalium comederint. R. Grauis quæstio, & festu non modo iucunda, sed etiam propter Manichæos hæreticos, & Pythagoreos Philosophos (qui carnes animalium edendas esse negant) necessaria. Certe, quanuis de ea non habeamus expressum in Dei verbo testimonium, facit tamen rationum, quæ proferuntur, vis & momentum, vt fateamur desendamusque veram esse eorum sententiam, qui existimant homines statim post peccatum carnem Animalium comedisse. Prima verò huius rei ratio est, quòd quum ad vestimenta sibi conficienda homines statim post peccatum seu lapsum suum, atque ante Diluuium Animalia occiderent, eaque excoriarent, id est, pelles ijs detraherent, Gen 3. non fuerunt animalium à se interfectorum carnes inutiliter perire, præsertim eas, quibus vesci commodè, id est, & cum valetudine, & cum voluptate poterāt, quales sunt carnes Agnina, Ouina, Vitulina, Bouina, Capreolorum, & catera huiusmodi. Deinde ante Diluuium, & statim post peccatum (saltem grandiore iam facto Abele) Homines pastores fuerunt, & greges pecudum, & armenta pecoru aluerunt, Gen 4. Quorsum vero? An tatium vt lacte ex illis vesceretur 1.Cor. 9.7:non etiam eorundem carne, si vellent ? Quorsum enim tantus pecorum numerus ab vno homine pasceretur? Praeterea non omnia animalia lac habent. Ergo & vt lacte, & vt carne animalium, quae pascebant, vterentur, Pastoritiam artem excoluerunt primi Homines ante Diluuium. Tertia ratio est, quod statim post peccatum, & ante Diluuium homines Animalia Deo sacrificarunt: Ergo ex animalium carne ederunt Nam ex quo Animalium genere Deo sacrificabant homines, ex eodem edebant quoque Deut.14.12, Leuit.7. (excepto postea, sed peculiari praecepto, holocausto tantum) Ex quo factum est, vt sub Lege Dei sacrificates homines ex suis sacrificijs, .i. carne sacrificata, seu ex Animalium à se oblatorum parte vescerentur quoque, & quidem in medio Dei templo, & iussu Dei, Leu.3.6, 7, Deu.12. Vnde illud est Athenaei lib.1.Dipnosoph. ex Epicharmo vetustissimo Poeta, ἐκ τῶν θυσιῶν ἀοίνυ, id est, Ex sacrificio conuiuia manasse. Sed & mundorū atque immundorum animalium distinctio, quae fuit ante Diluuium, & ad victum & ad sacrificium similiter pertinuit, vt scirent homines quibus animantibus vesci, & sacrificare Deo possent. Atque hac caussa est cur in Diluuio Deus etiam animalia Bruta exstinxit, nempe quòd ea Deus concesserat hominibus ad victum. Itaque quum Deus homines deleret, & ea quoque necauit, quae hominum vitae sustentandae necessaria erant: & quum homines restituit Mundo, eisdem quoque animalia ve-lut no
units.tr: Q. Did the first men after the sin (for before the sin they used only herbs and the fruits of trees) and before the Flood eat the flesh of animals? R. This is a grave question, and one not only pleasant to examine but also necessary because of the Manichaean heretics and the Pythagorean philosophers, who deny that the flesh of animals should be eaten. Certainly, although we have no explicit testimony on this in God's word, the force and weight of the arguments put forward make us admit and defend as true the opinion of those who think men ate the flesh of animals immediately after the sin. The first reason for this is that, since men killed animals and flayed them, that is, stripped their skins off, to make clothing for themselves immediately after their sin or fall, and before the Flood (Gen. 3), the flesh of the animals they had slain should not have been allowed to perish uselessly. This is especially so for those flesh meats which they could eat conveniently, that is, both healthily and with pleasure: such as lamb, mutton, veal, beef, venison, and others of that kind. Second, before the Flood, and immediately after the fall (at least when Abel had grown older), men were shepherds and fed flocks and herds (Gen. 4). But to what end? Was it so that they might feed only on the milk (1 Cor. 9:7), and not also on their flesh, if they wished? For why would one man feed such a great number of animals? Moreover, not all animals give milk. Therefore the first men cultivated the pastoral art both to make use of the milk and of the flesh of the animals they tended, before the Flood. The third reason is that immediately after the fall, and before the Flood, men sacrificed animals to God. Therefore they ate the flesh of animals. For from whatever kind of animal men sacrificed to God, from the same kind they also ate (Deut. 14:12; Lev. 7), except later, under a special precept, in the case of the burnt offering alone. From this it came about that under God's law the priests who offered sacrifices ate from their sacrifices, that is, from the sacrificed flesh, or from the part of the animals they had offered; and they did so in the very midst of God's temple and by God's command (Lev. 3:6–7; Deut. 12). Hence that saying of Athenaeus, in book 1 of the Deipnosophists, from the very ancient poet Epicharmus: [ἐκ τῶν θυσιῶν ἀοίνυ], that is, banquets arose from sacrifices. But also the distinction between clean and unclean animals, which existed before the Flood, applied similarly to both food and sacrifice, so that men might know which animals they could eat and sacrifice to God. This is also the reason why God in the Flood destroyed even the brute animals: namely, because God had granted them to men for food. So when God destroyed men, he also slew those things which were necessary for sustaining human life. And when he restored men to the world, he gave the same animals back to them, as if

units.la: . lut noua reddidit, & ius, vt prius, in eadem illa conceffit. Denique non fuit post peccatum & ante diluuium puriōr hominum vita, quàm esset sub Euangelio, & Apostolorum D. N. Iesu Christi tempore. At Apostoli carnes animalium etiam ex Dei præcepto comederunt Act.10.13. Cur non igitur primi homines illi, qui ante diluuionem vixerunt? Verum obstat, quod id diuerte factum esse nusquam tradit S. Scriptura. Sed neq; eadem memoria prodidit eosdem illos homines illo tempore vixisse frumēto, bibisse aquā. Ergo frumento (quod ex terra cultura tunc nascebatur) homines illos vi&ita- tasse, vel aquam bibisse minimè credendum est. Cur igitur erant agricolæ Adamus, & Cainus? Sed & obiicitur Gen.9.3. vbi post eluuionem Mundi vniuersalem primum videntur Animalia fuisse Homini à Deo incibum concessa. Respondeo verò non tunc primum ea homini in vitium fuisse data: sed illic repeti, aut potius confirmari (nempe quia nouus quodammodo videbatur ille Mundus restitutus) ius vetus, quod iam hominibus tribuerat Deus. Simile exemplū extat Gen.8.21.22, videlicet de futuro Mundi in posterum ordine eodem, qui in priore Mundo, id est, ante aquarum diluuionem fuerat. Quid si dixero amplificatam fuisse Gen.9.3. Dei concessionem de esu Animalium à Deo prius factam, additaq; illi fuisse reptilia, quales sunt Pisces, & Aues pleraq;, & testudines, quibus antea vesci non solebant homines, vtpote animantibus à terra (in qua ipsi habitant) cognatoq;, sibi elemento secretis, & velut in alio quodam Orbe habitatibus? In summa, sic sentio homines ante eluuionem carne vesci & potuisse, & solitos fuisse. Et hæc de Primo vestitu Primorum hominum. Nunc de eorundem eiectione ex Edenico Paradiso.
units.tr: new, and granted the right over them as before. Finally, between the sin and the Flood, human life was no purer than it was under the Gospel and at the time of the Apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ. Yet the Apostles also ate the flesh of animals by God's command (Acts 10:13). Why then not those first men who lived before the Flood? Indeed, the Scripture nowhere records the opposite. Yet neither does the same record tell us that those same men at that time lived on grain and drank water. Therefore it must by no means be believed that those men fed on grain (which then grew from cultivated ground) or drank water. Why then were Adam and Cain farmers? But Gen. 9:3 is also raised as an objection, where after the universal flood animals seem to have been granted to man as food for the first time. I answer that they were not given to man for food for the first time then. Rather, the old right which God had already granted to men was repeated there, or rather confirmed (namely because that world seemed in a way to be restored as new). A similar example is found in Gen. 8:21–22, concerning the future order of the world, which would be the same as the order in the earlier world, that is, before the flood of waters. What if I say that God's earlier grant of the eating of animals was enlarged in Gen. 9:3, and that reptiles were added to it, such as fish, most birds, and turtles, which men were not accustomed to eat before, since they are animals separated from the earth on which men live, kindred to their own element, and living as it were in another world? In sum, I think that before the flood men both could eat flesh and were accustomed to do so. And these things are said about the first clothing of the first men. Now about their expulsion from the Paradise of Eden.

units.la: Ad VI. Eiectio Primorum Hominum ex Paradiso.
units.tr: To the Sixth. The Expulsion of the First Men from Paradise.

units.la: Queritur, Cur Deus hominem (quem & iam punierat, & ex Horto eiciebat) irridet etiam amare, Gen. 3.22, [Ecce homo euasit sicut unus e nobis] quū afflictio non sit afflictio danda, & cumulanda, Psal. 69 26, & 109.16. Resp. Oportuit Hominem serio pungi, & de suo peccato admoneri, illiusque mendacia Satanæ (a quo se decipi passus erat) detegi. Pœna ergo a Deo prius inflicta Homini, fuit admonitio de foeditate & gravitate peccati ab ipso perpetrati. Irrisio vero, & συμπαθὲς iste, qui fuit additum [Ecce Homo euasit, &c.] fuit manifesta mendacij Satanæ demonstratio, quæ tunc Hominibus facta est a Deo. Vim autem & pondus maius habuit hæc Dei oratio hominem irridentis. Nam hac ratione magis stupidum, & superbum illum Adamum perstrinxit Deus, & pupugit. Verum sicut a Deo dictum fuit Adamo reo [Ecce homo:] sic innocenti Christo, peccatum Adami expianti dictum est a Pilato, postquam eum irrisum Pilatus flagellis pene excoriasset, [Ecce Homo] Ioan. 19.9. Q. Quando eiecti fuerint primi homines post sum peccatum? R. Incertum est. Eodem tamen die eiectos fuisse, quo peccarunt, verisimile est, ne si post peccatum in eo Horto diu remansissent, de fructu Arboris vitæ maducarent. Ergo statim depulsi sunt ex eo loco Gen 3.22. Q. Quam in mundi partem à Deo deducti sunt primi illi Homines ex Edenico horto eiecti? R. Nonnulli putant in Damascenam regionem, ex cuius terra & solo, aiunt, desumptus fuerat. Ait enim Moses Gen.3.23, dimissum à Deo fuisse Adamum in eam terram, ex qua desumptus fuerat. Verum quis eos ista docuit, Nimirum Adamum in Damascena regione fuisse conditum à Deo, & ex illius terra humo, solo, seu pulvere desumptum? Deinde quod generaliter dixit Moses de terra ab homine colenda, restringunt isti ad certi loci solum & terram. Alii in terram Cananeam deductum à Deo Adamum malunt, propterea quod, aiunt, in urbe Hebrone mortuus esset Adamus. Sed quis hoc illis revelavit? aut unde hoc habet? Quid igitur? ex ipso Mose Gen 3.24 apparet Adamum & Euam ex Edenico Paradiso expulsos, à Deo collocatos fuisse in Orientali Mundi regione, & anteriore istius Horti parte. Quae prima igitur Mundi plaga ab hominibus habitata, cultaque fuit, ea fuit Oriens Orbis terrarum. Q. Cur Deus ad custodiendum hortum, arcendosque ab eo homines omnes constituit Cherubinos, id est, Spiritus ignota homini facie potius, quam Angelos, id est Spiritus nota & familiari homini facie & vultu? R. Ut magis omnes homines terreret Deus, Angelos & Spiritus eiusmodi vultu illic ad prohibendum aditum Horti collocavit, id est, forma ignota, horribili, & tremenda. Nam si Spiritus facie & forma hominibus nota fuissent in Horti constituti, non sic, nec tantum homines perterrefecissent. Q. Utrum etiam pecudes ab aditu Horti Cherubini illi post Hominis peccatum prohibuerunt? R. Incertum quidem est: non puto tamen Cherubin prohibuisse pecudes, quominus in Hortum ingrederentur, eumque conculcarent, & velut prophanarent, etsi illius aditus hominibus interdictus erat. Et hac quidem hactenus. Nunc ad caput 7. historiae veniamus, quod est de prima generis humani propagatione.
units.tr: The question is raised why God, who had already punished man and was driving him out of the garden, also mocks him with the words, "Behold, the man has become as one of us" (Gen. 3.22), since affliction should not be added to affliction (Ps. 69.26; 109.16). Answer: it was necessary that man be seriously stung and reminded of his own sin, and that the lies of Satan, by whom he had allowed himself to be deceived, be exposed. The punishment God first inflicted on man was therefore a warning about the foulness and gravity of the sin he had committed. The mockery and this show of sympathy [συμπαθὲς], which was added in the words "Behold, the man has become," etc., was a clear demonstration of the falsehood of Satan, which God then made known to men. This speech of God mocking man had greater force and weight, for in this way God struck and pricked the more stupid and proud Adam. Indeed, just as God said "Behold the man" to the guilty Adam, so Pilate said "Behold the Man" (John 19.5) to the innocent Christ, who was making expiation for Adam's sin, after Pilate had nearly flayed him with whips when he had been mocked. Q. When were the first men expelled after their sin? A. It is uncertain. Yet it is likely that they were driven out on the same day on which they sinned, lest, had they remained a long time in that garden after the sin, they might have eaten of the fruit of the tree of life. Therefore they were at once thrust out of that place (Gen. 3.22). Q. To what part of the world were those first men led by God when they were expelled from the garden of Eden? A. Some think into the region of Damascus, from whose earth and soil, they say, Adam had been taken. For Moses says (Gen. 3.23) that God sent Adam into the land from which he had been taken. But who taught them that Adam was formed by God in the region of Damascus and taken from the earth, soil, or dust of that land? Then they restrict to one particular place and land what Moses said generally about the land to be tilled by man. Others prefer that Adam was led by God into the land of Canaan, because, they say, Adam died in the city of Hebron. But who revealed this to them, or where do they have it from? What then? From Moses himself (Gen. 3.24) it appears that Adam and Eve, expelled from the Paradise of Eden, were placed by God in the eastern region of the world and in the outer part of that garden. Therefore the first quarter of the world inhabited and cultivated by men was the East of the earth. Q. Why did God appoint Cherubim, that is, spirits with a face unknown to man, rather than angels, that is, spirits with a face and countenance known and familiar to man, to guard the garden and keep all men away from it? A. So that God might terrify all men more, he placed angels and spirits of that kind there to block the entrance to the garden, that is, in an unknown, dreadful and awful form. For if the spirits had been set in the garden with a face and form known to men, they would not have terrified men in this way or to this extent. Q. Did those Cherubim also keep cattle away from the entrance of the garden after man's sin? A. It is indeed uncertain; I do not think, however, that the Cherubim kept the cattle from entering the garden and trampling it and, as it were, defiling it, although entry was forbidden to men. And so much for this. Now let us come to chapter 7 of the history, which concerns the first propagation of the human race.

units.la: Ad VII. Propagatio prima Generis Humani.
units.tr: To the Seventh. The First Propagation of the Human Race.

units.la: Quaeritur, Quo aetatis anno, aut quo primum tempore seu die Adamus cognoverit vxorem suam, vtrum in Paradiso Edenico, an postquam ex eo fuit eiectus? Vtrum ante peccatum, an demum post peccatum. R. De Setho quidem Adami filio, quo aetatis Adami anno suscepti ab eo ex Eua fuerit, commemorat, agiiq; S. Scriptura Gen. 5. 3. De aliis autem (velut Caino & Abele) eius filijs nihil traditur. Potuisse quidem Adamum in Edenico horto, & ante peccatum cognoscere vxorem suam, anteà demonstratum est à nobis: imo etiam fortasse cognovit. Verum vtrum in eo loco, & eo tempore, id est, antequam peccasset, conceptus fuerit Cainus, ex Dei verbo nequaquam apparet. Alij quidem aiunt, alij vero negant. Ego vero eorum accedo sententiae, qui volunt demum post peccatum, & eiectum ex Edenico Paradiso Adamum & Euam Cainum fuisse conceptu.
units.tr: It is asked in what year of his life, or at what first time or day, Adam knew his wife: whether in the Paradise of Eden or after he was cast out of it; whether before the sin or only after the sin. A. Holy Scripture records that Seth, the son of Adam, was begotten by him from Eve in the year of Adam's life (Gen. 5.3), but nothing is handed down about the others, such as Cain and Abel. That Adam could indeed have known his wife in the garden of Eden and before the sin has been shown by us earlier; indeed perhaps he did know her. But whether Cain was conceived in that place and at that time, that is, before he sinned, does not appear at all from God's word. Some say so, others deny it. I, for my part, agree with those who hold that Adam and Eve conceived Cain only after the sin and after Adam had been expelled from the Paradise of Eden.

units.la: Q. Vtrum ante Cainum alij liberi Adamo nati sint, sed mortui, & non superstites. R. Nec hoc ipsum tradit S. Scriptura, nec verisimile est alios ante ipsum fuisse suscepto s. Idcirco enim eum Cainum Eua mater nominauit quòd is primus ex se natus esset,eúmque sibi Deus primùm dedisset seu concessisset, Gen 4.5 adeo vt in ipso Caini nomine notetur Eua desiderium de suscipiendo ex se saltem aliquo:quem quum Eua Deus esset post longam ipsius exspectationem largitus,eum Caini ex Dei in se beneficio vocauit Eua. Ex quo colligi potest satis diu Adamum & Euam simul absq; liberis vixisse:neque Cainum illis statim atque è Paradiso eiecti sunt natú,ac procreatú fuisse. Q. Cur Cainus, Abel, & Seth sic nominantur à suis parentibus Adamo, & Eua? R. Cainus dictus est à beneficio Dei quod eum primum suscepisset primi homines, & acquisissent, seu potius possedissent à Deo,sibi concessum, Genes.4.1 Ergo in eo primùm senserút vim illius Dei benedictionis [Crescite,& multiplicamini:] Euáque se primùm in eo vidit verè Chauam & matrè. Ergo sese consolata est mirificè. Nam læta de partu suo,etiam in ipso Caini nomine notauit potius Dei beneficium, quàm partus sui dolores. Imò docet hæc appellatio filios omnes,quos ex coniugio suscepimus,esse Dei donum. Verùm in Abele aliud est obseruandum. Nam [Abel] dictus est, id est,luctus, vel quodam spiritu prophetico, quasi qui postea magnum vtrique parenti suo luctú, & mœrorem ob immaturâ mortem esset allaturus:vel quòd in secundo partu maiores,quàm in primo,dolores Eua sensisset. Id quod omnes mulieres nunc quoq; experiuntur: nam in secundo , tertióque puerperio grauiùs affliguntur, quàm in primo. Itaque à sensu doloris istius tristissimi, quem experta erat,Eua in hoc secundo partu & filio suo addendo,eum Abelem nominauit, Gen.4.2,id est,fi-
units.tr: Q. Whether other children were born to Adam before Cain, but died and did not survive? A. Holy Scripture does not hand this down, nor is it likely that others were begotten before him. For this reason Eve his mother named him Cain, because he was the first born from her, and because God had first given or granted him to her, (Gen. 4.1) so that in the very name of Cain Eve's longing to bear at least some offspring is marked; and since God had granted him to Eve after her long expectation, Eve called him Cain as a sign of God's kindness to her. From this it can be gathered that Adam and Eve lived together for quite a long time without children, and that Cain was not born and begotten as soon as they had been expelled from Paradise. Q. Why are Cain, Abel and Seth so named by their parents Adam and Eve? A. Cain was so called from the blessing of God, because the first men had got and acquired him, or rather had been granted him and possessed him from God (Gen. 4.1). So in him they first felt the force of that blessing of God, "Increase and multiply," and in him Eve first saw herself truly becoming a mother. So she was wonderfully comforted. For, glad of her child, she marked in the very name of Cain God's kindness rather than the pains of her childbirth. Indeed this name teaches that all the children we have from marriage are God's gift. But in the name of Abel something else must be noted. For Abel was so called, that is, "mourning," either by a certain prophetic spirit, as if he was going to bring great grief and sorrow to both his parents by his untimely death; or because Eve felt greater pains in the second birth than in the first. This is something all women still experience now, for in the second and third childbirth they suffer more grievously than in the first. Therefore, from the sense of that most sad pain which she had experienced, Eve, in bearing this second child and adding him to her son, named him Abel (Gen. 4.2), that is, the son of grief.

units.la: lium doloris. Porrò Sethus dictus est, quasi Repositus & restitutus. Quum enim hic loco filij Abel iam occisi esset Adamo & Eua a Deo substitutus, & velut redditus, repositúsque, vocatus est a Parentibus seipsos consolantibus, & Dei beneficium in se agnoscentibus, [Sethus] .i. Restitutus, a quo est tota quæ postea secuta est, Dei Ecclesia in Mundo propagata Gen. 5.3. 4.5. & deinceps. Augustin. lib. 15. Ciuit. Dei, cap. 17: [Quum ergo esset Adam, ait, utriúsque generis pater (id est, & cuius series ad terrenam, & cuius series ad cœlestem pertinet ciuitatem) occiso Abele (atque in eius interfectione commendato mirabili Sacramento) fulti sunt duo Patres singulorum generum, Cain & Seth: in quorum filys, quos commemorari oportebat, duarum illarum ciuitatum in genere mortalium euidentius indicia clarere coeperunt.] Ergo Cain improborum societatis Pater est, qui terrenam quoque condidit ciuitatem. Seth verò, qui Resurrectio, ait Augustinus, interpretatur, Ecclesia Dei, bonorúmque societatis est stirps & pater, qui Enos chum procreauit eum, qui in cœlum à Deo raptus est. Nam qui verè sunt Ecclesia Dei, cum Christo resurrexerint necesse est, vt in cœlum rapiantur. Q. Vtrum praeter hos tres, alios liberos Adamus & Eua fuscepierint, masculos vel fœminas: an hos tres solum? R. Vtrum inter Abelem & Cainum alii qui liberi internati sint Adamo, & interpositi: itemque Vtrum post eos alij sint ab eodem ex Eua procreati, nõ deffinit S. Scriptura. Philo tamen Iudæus in Biblicis Antiquitat. sic scribit, [Initio Mundi Adam genuit tres filios, & vnam filiam, nempe Cain, Noaba, Abel, &.
units.tr: Moreover Seth was so called as if "appointed in place of" and "restored." For when Abel, now slain, was replaced by God as a substitute for Adam and Eve, and as if given back and set in his place, he was called by his parents, who were comforting themselves and acknowledging God's kindness toward them, [Seth], that is, "Restored." From him comes the whole Church of God that afterwards was propagated in the world (Gen. 5.3; 4.5 and following). Augustine, City of God, book 15, chapter 17: [Since therefore Adam was the father of both kinds (that is, of both the series belonging to the earthly city and that belonging to the heavenly city), when Abel was slain—and in his killing a wonderful sacrament was commended—two fathers of the individual kinds, Cain and Seth, were supported; and in their sons, whom it was fitting to record, the signs of the two cities in the human race began to shine more clearly.] Therefore Cain is the father of the fellowship of the wicked, who also founded the earthly city. Seth, however, who, Augustine says, is interpreted as "Resurrection," is the stock and father of the Church of God and of the fellowship of the good, who begat Enos, the one who was taken up into heaven by God. For those who truly are the Church of God must rise with Christ so that they may be caught up into heaven. Q. Whether Adam and Eve had other children, sons or daughters, besides these three, or only these three? A. Holy Scripture does not determine whether other children were born to Adam between Abel and Cain and placed between them, nor whether after them others were begotten by him from Eve. Yet the Jewish writer Philo, in his Biblical Antiquities, writes thus: [In the beginning of the world Adam begat three sons and one daughter, namely Cain, Noaba, Abel, &c.

units.la: & Hebrew Ecclesia ... & Seth. Et vixit Adam postquam genuit Seth annos D. CC. & genuit filios duodecim, & filias octo. Et hæc sunt nomina virorum, Aelisfeel, Suris, Aelamiel, Brabal, Naat, Harama, Zafam, Maathal, & Anath. Et hæ filiæ eius, Phua, Ielias, Arebica, Siphatecia, Sabaasin.] Qui locus Philonis plane corruptus est: nam nec duodecim masculorum nomina habet, nec octo foeminarum. Praeterea in numero annorum vitæ Adami post natum Sethum, mendum est. Nisi forte eos tatum liberos Adami nominauit Philo, quorum appellationes ex veteri traditione superexerant, nō autem omnes. Certè nec Cainus ducere uxorē potuisset, nec Sethus, si Adamus alios nullos liberos omninò suscepisset, quàm quos recitat Moses. Nullas enim fœminas commemorat: quas ex eo tamen nasci oportuit, ut & Cainus, & Sethus matrimonium contraherent. Nec enim ex Caini stirpe duxit uxorem Sethus: sed ex familia ipsa Adami, sororem nempe suam. Nam Gen 6.2, damnantur y py, qui ex Caini familia coniuges sibi acceperunt. Abel quoque nullam familiam reliquisse videtur, nec vllos ex se liberos. Sethus enim in Abelis occisi, & absque liberis mortui locum à Deo substitutus, datusque Adamo fuit. Unde Sethus dictus est. Siqui enim ex Abelis interfecti stirpe filij remansisset, eum Adamo repræsentasset, & eius locum tenuisset, non autem Sethus minor eius frater. Deinde in familia Abelis Deus constituisset Ecclesiam suam, quum Abel primum piorum & Electorum Dei exemplum à Christo ipso statuatur, & iustus appelletur Math. 22.35: non autem in Sethi familia. Id quod tamen contigit, factum fuit. Ergo plures nati sunt Adamo filij quàm tres isti, quos enumerat Moses. Id quod etiam contendit Augustin. lib. 15. Ciuit. Dei, cap. 15. Q. Quid hac Moses de Setho ab Adamo creato loquentis verba significat Gen. 5. 3: [Genuit Adamus filium in imagine sua, secundum similitudinem suam.] R. Nonnulli sic ea explicant, vt velint ea pertinere ad formam externam, velut oris venustatem, quae fuit in Adamo, & illam compositionem, constitutionemque corporis pulcherrimam, quam Adamus a Deo conditus constabat, quam repraesentarit ad vnum Sethum. Quasi nempe neque Cainus, neque Abel tam formosi fuisset, & similes Adamo patri, quam erat hic Sethus, ex quo Deus postea fecit ac progenuit Ecclesiam suam. Verum quum eadem phrasis sit vsus supra Moses Gen. 1. 27, & 5. 1: quae ad externam formam corporisve lineamenta pertinere non poterit, certè neque etiam hoc loco sic est explicanda. Significat igitur μορφὴν illam, quam Philip. 2. vocat Paulus internam, à qua res quaeque naturam sortitur. Ergo quum post peccatum Homines nascantur peccatores, vtpote ex hominibus peccatoribus, quae in homine iam restat natura non est integra illa, incorrupta, lucidaque Dei imago, ad quam Adamus ipse primus homo fuerat conditus: sed est deformata ista, & pene deleta, quam Homo, id est, ipse adeo Adamus post peccatum à se perpetratum reliquam habuit Colos. 3. 10. Ergo Adamus genuit Sethum filium suum ad imaginem tātum suam, id est, qualem (summo quidem Dei beneficio) retinuerat post offensam suam (nimirū ne esset brutum pecus) & quam habent post peccatū omnes homines Ioan. 1. 9. (Hanc autem dat Christus omni homini venienti & nascenti in hunc Mundum) non autem ad imaginem illā primam & incorruptam Dei, quam Adamus ante lapsum habuerat, Sethum genuit. Q. Cur demum, quum de Setho agitur, dixit Moses Adamum genuisse filium ad imaginem suam: non etiam de Caino, & Abele idem scripsit, qui tamen propter peccatum, & post peccatum Adami nō perfectiorem Dei imaginem portabant, quàm Sethus. R. Hoc quidem verum est, & ex ipsa Caini vita & factis apparuit. Sed quoniam intra centum illos & triginta annos, post quos à creatione Adami natus est Sethus, malitia hominum manifestè apparuit, & tunc Dei imaginis labefactatio in hominibus populariter cernebatur, denique tristissima peccati Adami effecta diffundebantur in Mundum: idcirco dixit Moses Sethum, & eos, qui post illud tempus ex Adamo peccatore nascebantur, ab eo perspicuè genitos fuisse ad suam, non autem ad Dei ipsius imaginem, ac similitudinem. Q. Quinetiam ut melius clariusq; tanta hominum corruptio ex prioris statu cum eo, in quo iam post peccatum sumus, comparatione intelligeretur, priusquam Moses id de Setho, & aliis posteā natis diceret, breviter & expressè priorem illam hominis conditionem repetyt, & commemorauit, in qua primum à Deo fuerat conditus, Gen. 5. 1. 2. Q. Quamobrem quū tanta iam labefactata Dei in homine imaginis signa extarent, scripsit Moses tunc in posteris & filijs Adami non eam aut tantam (quantam prius Adamus ipse habebat) remansisse Dei similitudinem: sed eam duntaxat, quā post peccatum, Dei benignitate, retinuerat. Deinde hoc ipsum quoque eo maxime loco commemorasse videtur Moses, ut quum de Setho patre, & fonte futurae in Mundo Ecclesiae affurus esset, intelligeret & ipsemet Sethus, & eius posteri, scilicet quòd tales sint, sola Dei gratia existere, quoniam natura essent, & sint, sicut ceteri homines, corrupti, filii irae, & iam in Adamo, deleta Dei imagine, maledicti, Eph. 2. 3. Ergo ut electio illa Ecclesiae, quae sit ex Adami posteris, perspiceretur, & agnoscatur etiamnù hodie esse gratuita, & ex sola Dei misericordia & electione, Deut. 6, Rom. 9, Malach. 1, de prima Ecclesiae origine, & distinctione dicturus Moses, ostendit eos ipsos (ex quibus & primum constituta est, & nunc restat Ecclesia) esse natura ceteris mortalibus pares, nempe deformes mente, corruptos, miseros, & damnatos. Q. Virum in primo illo seculo anni sterilitatis erant in foeminis Anni quinquaginta vel paulo post, quemadmodum nunc, ut post eos annos foeminae concipere non possent, Luc 1. 36. R. Apparet Euam illo seculo concepisse anno aetatis suae 130. (fuit enim coeva Adamo viro suo) nec id miraculo factum dicitur, (quemadmodum de Sara uxore Abrahami, Gen. 18. 10, & 21. 1. narratur) sed tanquam ordine naturae & communi lege caeterarum Mulierum. Praeterea satis intelligi potest ex aliis liberis, qui eo tempore suscepti sunt ex aliis mulieribus, illas etiam post centum aetatis suae annos concepisse. Quare qui anni iam sunt post diluvium steriles foeminis, idem ante diluvium erant ipsdem foecundi. Sed postquam Deus vitam hominum coarctavit, ut appareat Gen. 6: sic etiam tempus foeminis ad concipiendum breviùs, quàm antea, dedit. Et hæc quidem de prima generis humani propagatione. Accedamus ad primas hominum artes, & videamus ecquæ fuerint.
units.tr: & Hebrew Ecclesia ... and Seth. And Adam lived after he begat Seth 800 years, and he begat twelve sons and eight daughters. And these are the names of the men: Aelisfeel, Suris, Aelamiel, Brabal, Naat, Harama, Zafam, Maathal, and Anath. And these were his daughters: Phua, Ielias, Arebica, Siphatecia, Sabaasin.] This passage of Philo is plainly corrupt: it gives neither the names of twelve sons nor those of eight daughters. Moreover, there is a fault in the number of years of Adam's life after the birth of Seth. Unless perhaps Philo named only those children of Adam whose names had survived in old tradition, and not all of them. Certainly Cain could not have taken a wife, nor Seth, if Adam had never had any children besides those that Moses recites. For Moses mentions no daughters, and yet daughters must have been born, so that both Cain and Seth could contract marriage. Nor did Seth take his wife from the stock of Cain, but from Adam's own family, that is, his own sister. For Gen. 6.2 condemns those of Cain's family whom they took as wives for themselves, the sons of God [בני האלהים]. Abel also seems to have left no family and no children of his own. For Seth was given to Adam by God in place of the slain Abel, who died without children, and that is why he was called Seth. For if any son had remained of the stock of Abel who was slain, he would have represented Adam and held his place, and not his younger brother Seth. Again, God would have established his Church in the family of Abel, since Abel is set forth by Christ himself as the first example of the pious and elect of God, and is called righteous (Matt. 23.35); but not in the family of Seth. Yet what did happen, happened. Therefore more sons were born to Adam than those three whom Moses lists. Augustine also maintains this, De civitate Dei 15, ch. 15. Q. What is the meaning of Moses' words about Seth, when he speaks of Adam begetting him after his creation: Gen. 5. 3: [Adam begat a son in his own image, after his likeness.] R. Some explain these words so as to refer them to outward form, such as the beauty of countenance that was in Adam, and that most beautiful composition and constitution of body with which Adam was made by God, which he is said to have passed on to Seth alone. As if neither Cain nor Abel had been so handsome and so like Adam their father as Seth, from whom God afterwards made and brought forth his Church. But since Moses used the same phrase above (Gen. 1.27; 5.1), which cannot refer to outward form or bodily features, it certainly must not be explained in that way here either. It therefore means that form [μορφήν] which Paul in Phil. 2 calls inward, from which each thing receives its nature. Therefore, since after the sin men are born sinners, being born of sinful men, the nature that remains in man is not that whole, incorrupt and bright image of God to which Adam the first man himself was made, but is that deformed and almost obliterated image which Man, that is, Adam himself, retained after the sin he committed (Col. 3.10). Therefore Adam begat his son Seth only in his own image, that is, such as (by the great kindness of God) he had kept after his offence, lest he should be a mere brute beast, and such as all men have after the sin (John 1.9; this light Christ gives to every man who comes and is born into this world), and not in that first and incorrupt image of God which Adam had before the fall. Q. Why, when speaking of Seth, did Moses at last say that Adam begat a son in his own image, and did not write the same of Cain and Abel, who nevertheless, because of the sin and the sin of Adam, bore no more perfect image of God than Seth did? R. This is indeed true, and it appeared from Cain's own life and deeds. But since within those hundred and thirty years, after which Seth was born from the creation of Adam, the wickedness of men was openly evident, and then the weakening of the image of God in men was plainly seen by all, and finally the most grievous effects of Adam's sin were spreading through the world, for this reason Moses said that Seth, and those who after that time were born from Adam the sinner, were clearly begotten by him in his own image, and not in the image and likeness of God himself. Q. Moreover, so that so great a corruption of men might be better and more clearly understood by comparison of their earlier state with that in which we now are after the sin, before Moses said this of Seth and the others born afterwards, he briefly and expressly repeated and recalled that first condition of man in which he was first made by God (Gen. 5.1, 2). Q. Why then, since such great signs of the weakening of God's image in man were already visible, did Moses write that in the posterity and sons of Adam the likeness of God did not remain in the same degree or as great as Adam himself had it before, but only that which he had retained after the sin by God's goodness? Moreover, Moses seems to have recalled this very point in this place especially, so that when he was about to speak of Seth the father, and the source of the Church to be in the world, Seth himself and his posterity might understand that they are such only by the sole grace of God, since by nature they were, and are, like other men, corrupt, children of wrath, and already cursed in Adam, the image of God having been effaced (Eph. 2.3). Therefore, so that that election of the Church, which is from the posterity of Adam, might be seen and acknowledged even today to be gratuitous, and to come from the sole mercy and election of God (Deut. 6; Rom. 9; Mal. 1), Moses, about to speak of the first origin and distinction of the Church, shows that those very persons from whom it was first established and from whom the Church now remains, are by nature equal to other mortals, namely deformed in mind, corrupt, wretched and damned. Q. Whether in that first age there were barren years for women, when they were about fifty or a little later, as now, so that after those years women could not conceive (Luke 1.36)? R. It appears that Eve conceived in that age in her 130th year of life (for she was contemporary with Adam her husband), and this is not said to have been done by a miracle (as is related of Sarah, the wife of Abraham, Gen. 18.10 and 21.1), but by the ordinary course of nature and the common law of other women. Moreover, it can be sufficiently understood from the other children who were born at that time from other women, that they too conceived after their hundredth year. Hence the years which are now barren for women after the flood were equally fruitful for the same women before the flood. But after God shortened the life of men, as appears in Gen. 6, so he also gave women a shorter time for conceiving than before. And these things concerning the first propagation of the human race. Let us come to the first arts of men, and see what they were.

units.la: Ad VIII. Primæ Hominum Artes.
units.tr: Chapter VIII. The First Arts of Men.

units.la: Queritur, Cur has primum & potissimum Artes nimirum Agriculturam, & Pastoritiam primi illi homines post peccatum exercuerunt, non autem alias, quæ postea tamen inventæ, & in usu fuere inter mortales, atque adeo nunc sunt. R. Eas artes præcipuè à primis hominibus post peccatum excultas fuisse dico, ex quibus victum sibi, eumque naturalem & necessarium: non autem superfluum, sumptuosum, & cupeditas compararent. Ergo Agriculturam, ex qua & frumentum, & terræ fructus etiam ex arboribus perciperent, didicerunt Gen. 4. 1. Agricultura enim nomen extendo non tantum ad ipsam arvorum culturam, nempe arationem & sationem, ut inde fruges proveniât: sed etiam ad arborum curā, ut inde fructus homines perciperent. Audierat namque Adamus ex Dei ipsius ore post peccatum suum Gen. 3. 17: [ Maledicta esto terra propter te, cum molestia comedito ex ea omnibus diebus vitæ tuæ. ] Id quod ad omnem provenientem, qui ex terra fit, generaliter pertinet. Quare Agricultura hoc loco & Hortensem (quæ in herbis & arboribus colendis posita est) & Agriculturam (quæ proprie dicta est sitaque in arvis serendis) complectitur. Hanc igitur artem excoluerunt Homines illi primi, ut & frumentum, & triticum, & arborum fructus, herbasque ad victum utiles, uti dixi, haberent. Verum & Pastoritiam quoque (quæ & in minoribus, & maioribus pecudibus pascendis versatur) ut inde carnes ad victum sibi necessarias haberent semper in parato. Quare quum hae artes dua victum eiusmodi, id est, naturalem & necessarium hominibus praebeat, primae quoque omnium & Dei beneficio cognitae, & exculte fuerunt. Sic Abrahamus utramq; exercuit, Gen. 21. Sic Isaacus, Gen. 26. Reliquae ve- ro, quae ad delicatum hominum cultum & victum pertinent, postea sunt reperte, atque ab omnibus probata, & usurpata. Q., Quomodo ista hominum seruitus ac vilis status in pascendo pecore conveniat cum Psal. 8. [Omnia subiecisti sub pedibus eius.] Turpe enim videtur ut homines pecorum domini, illis tamen seruiant, sintque additi, quales sunt tamen dum ea pascunt, curant, & sequuntur. R. Haec tam abiecta conditio, ut rebus sibi prius subditus Homo iam post suum in Deum peccatum subiciatur, Homini competit, & quidem merito. Nam Homo deserendo Deum a quo dominatum illum habebat, & seipsum perdidit, & dominium suum. Ergo iam pecudum seruus est, qui dominus earum antea fuerat, Psal. 49.21, & tam abiecte deiectus a Deo. Per Christu vero in illius dominatus partem (quantum quidem ad huius vitae usum est opus) tamen in his terris restitutus est homo, idq; ipsum declarat Psal. 8.5, Heb. 2.8: non autem in plenum illud, quod antea possidebat ius, ac dominium. Quamobrem, aequum est hominem, quatenus peccator est, & primae o- riginis sua defertor, Dei contemptor, seruire pecudibus ipsis brutis, Gen. 31.40.41, & ys subiici, quatenus de ys curam propter suum ipsius victum habet. Q. Cur primi homines eas solas Artes duas tenuerunt, & excoluerunt: reliquas autem non item, quales quæ Ferrariæ sunt, ædificatoriæ, Musicæ, quemadmodum tamen postea in hac prima Mundi ætate, & ante Diluvium factum est Gen. 5. Quia nondum isti postremi artibus egebant. Ergo seriys, & omnino necessariis huic vitæ rebus primum Homines animum intenderunt, postea vero aliis, quum iis egere, aut iis delectari coeperunt. Nam verum est illud,
units.tr: It is asked why the first men, after the sin, practised chiefly these two arts, agriculture and herding, and not the others, which were invented later and have been in use among mortals, and so are in use now. I answer that the first men after the sin cultivated chiefly those arts by which they could acquire for themselves a livelihood that was natural and necessary, and not one that was superfluous, costly and self-indulgent. So they learned agriculture, by which they gained both grain and the fruits of the earth, including fruit from trees (Gen. 4.1). For I extend the word agriculture not only to the tilling of fields, namely ploughing and sowing so that crops may come up, but also to the care of trees, so that men may gather fruit from them. For Adam had heard from God's own mouth after his sin (Gen. 3.17): "Cursed is the ground for your sake; in toil shall you eat of it all the days of your life." This applies in general to everything that comes up from the earth. Hence agriculture here embraces both gardening, which consists in cultivating herbs and trees, and husbandry proper, which is set in sowing the fields. Those first men therefore cultivated this art, so that they might have, as I said, both grain and wheat, the fruits of trees, and herbs useful for food. They also practised herding, which concerns the pasturing of both smaller and larger livestock, so that they would always have meat ready for their necessary food. Since these two arts supply men with food of this kind, that is natural and necessary, they were the first of all to be known and cultivated, by the gift of God. So Abraham practised both (Gen. 21), and so did Isaac (Gen. 26). The remaining arts, which concern the refined culture and food of men, were discovered later and were approved and adopted by all. Q. How does this servitude and lowly condition of men in pasturing livestock agree with Psalm 8: "You have put all things under his feet"? For it seems shameful that men, who are lords of the flocks, should yet serve them, and be made like them, as they are while they feed, tend and follow them. A. This very abject condition, by which man, who was first made lord of things, is now, after his sin against God, made subject to them, is fitting for man, and rightly so. For in forsaking God, from whom he had that dominion, man lost both himself and his lordship. So he who had been lord of the beasts is now their slave (Ps. 49.21), and has been cast down so abjectly by God. Yet through Christ, man has been restored in this earthly life, as far as the needs of this life require, to a part of that dominion; and Psalm 8.5 and Hebrews 2.8 declare this itself. But he has not been restored to the full right and dominion that he once possessed. Therefore it is fitting that man, insofar as he is a sinner, a deserter of his original state and a despiser of God, should serve the brute beasts themselves (Gen. 31.40-41), and be subject to them, insofar as he has care of them for his own livelihood. Q. Why did the first men hold and cultivate only these two arts, and not the others, such as smithing, building and music, which were nonetheless practised afterwards in this first age of the world and before the Flood (Gen. 5)? A. Because those later men did not yet need the arts. So the first men directed their minds first to the more serious things, and things wholly necessary for this life, and only afterwards began to take up other things when they needed them or began to delight in them. For that saying is true: [Labour gave wretched men their wit, and each man's fortune, by pressing hard, taught him what to bring against his troubles.]

units.la: [Et labor ingenium miseris dedit, & sua quemque, adversus quæ, inferre fortuna premendo.]
units.tr: And toil gave wit to wretched men, and each man's own fortune, pressing hard, drove them to contrive against its hardships.

units.la: Labor enim omnia vincit improbus, & duris urgens in rebus egestas. Ergo quæ primam hominum ætatem sublevabant Artes, ea prima sunt procurata, & in pretio habita. Ad nonum vero caput Historicum, quod est de Primo hominum Sacrificio in his terris, veniamus.
units.tr: For relentless toil conquers all, and need that presses in hard circumstances. Therefore the arts that relieved the early life of men were the first to be pursued and held in esteem. Now let us come to the ninth chapter, the historical one, which is concerning the first sacrifice of men upon this earth.

units.la: Ad VIIII, seu IX. Primum Homi- num Sacrificium.
units.tr: To the Ninth, or IX: The First Sacrifice of Men.

units.la: Quaeritur, Utrum vero Deo prius fuerit ab hominibus sacrificatum post eorum peccatum, quam Idolis, vel Diabolo, cui primi illi duo Parentes fidem contra Dei verbum adhibuerant. R. Prius vero Deo fuit sacrificatum, quam Idolis ac Diabolo. Prius enim vera religio fuit, viguitque: postea vero Idololatria recepta est & introducta (quemadmodum & quidem vere docent Tertullianus & Lactantius) quae fuit pura sincere que Religionis corrupta, & κακοζηλία. Nec enim peccans homo, aut post peccatum agnitionem Dei prersus amisit,sed eum in se iratum sensit Gen. 3 8. unde se ab eo abscondit. Porrò Epiphanius affirmat toto illo primo Mundi seculo, quod aquarum diluuionem praecessit,nullum inter homines fuisse idolorū cultum. Hoc enim malum demum post diluuium natum est: Diabolum autem, aut Serpentem, à quo deceptus fuerat Homo,nequaquam pro Deo suo agnouit, vel coluit:sed verum duntaxat Deum, cui tamen instinctu Diaboli non paruit. Q. Unde homines primum cognouerunt esse sacrificandum Deo. R. Ex ipsomet Deo, id illis post eorum peccatum reuelante. Ratio est, Primum quòd nulla vnquam ἐϑελοθρησκεία Deo placuit, gratâ ve fuit Colos. 2. 23, Deut. 12.8, Math. 15.9: sed is demum cultus, quem ipsemet Deus sibi instituisset, ac poposcisset. Deinde, quòd dicitur Abel per fidem sacrificasse Hebr. 11.4. Ergo ex Dei mandato. Quicquid enim fit absque fide, peccatum est, Rom. 14.23. Fides autem absque precedente & praeunte Dei verbo esse nullo modo potest, Hebr. 11.1, Isa. 1.12. Ergo quum ex fide sacrificarint primi parentes post peccatum, eorúmque posteri, fueritque hic cultus Deo gratus, praeceptum de Sacrificando habuerint necesse est. Nec verò Deus celauit homines mysterium salutis eorū futura, quam ijs ipsis post eorum peccatū promiserat his verbis, [Et Semen mulieris conteret caput Serpentis] Promittere autem eam,& eandem explicare, fuit eiusdem Dei misericordiæ. Eius autem promissionis explicatio in praecepto de Sacrificando, & sacrificiorum declaratione, quid nempe significarent, quidve repraesentarent, posita fuit. Q. Cur alia, & priora hominum sacrificia ficia, velut Adami (nec enim fuit, tandiu ante Abelis & Caini oblationem vixit. Adamus post peccatum suum absque eo, quin Deo sacrificarit) non commemorat Moses, sed primum hoc Caini, & Abelis. Q. Quoniam hoc primum in signe quidpiam, ac notatu dignum habuit, quod non fuit in prioribus sacrificiis. Siquis tamen hoc fuisse primum omnium sacrificium voluerit, quod sit ab hominibus oblatum Deo, non repugnabo, quemadmodum contra Julian. lib. 3. scribit Cyrillus: Sin alia praecessisse malit, eius sententiam ipse probabo.
units.tr: Question: Did men offer sacrifice to the true God before they offered it to idols or to the Devil, after their sin, the Devil being the one whom those first two parents trusted against the word of God? Answer: Sacrifice was offered to God first, before idols and the Devil. For true religion came first and flourished. Afterwards idolatry was received and introduced (as Tertullian and Lactantius rightly teach), a corruption of pure and sincere religion and a kind of perverse zeal [κακοζηλία]. For man, sinning, did not wholly lose the knowledge of God after his sin, but he felt God angry with him (Gen. 3:8), and so hid himself from him. Moreover, Epiphanius affirms that throughout that whole first age of the world, which came before the flood of waters, there was no worship of idols among men, for this evil arose only after the flood. Nor did men ever recognise or worship the Devil or the Serpent, by whom man had been deceived, as their God. They worshipped only the true God, though at the Devil's prompting they did not obey him. Nec enim peccans homo ... non paruit. Question: How did men first come to know that sacrifice must be offered to God? Answer: From God himself, who revealed it to them after their sin. The reason is this. First, no self-chosen worship [ἐθελοθρησκεία] ever pleased God or was acceptable to him (Col. 2:23; Deut. 12:8; Matt. 15:9), but only that worship which God himself had instituted and demanded. Second, it is said that Abel offered sacrifice by faith (Heb. 11:4), and therefore by God's command. For whatever is done without faith is sin (Rom. 14:23), and faith cannot exist at all without the prior word of God (Heb. 11:1; Isa. 1:12). Therefore, since the first parents and their posterity offered sacrifice in faith after the fall, and this worship was pleasing to God, they must have had a command concerning sacrifice. Nor did God hide from men the mystery of their future salvation, which he had promised them after their sin in these words: [And the seed of the woman shall bruise the head of the serpent]. To promise this and to explain it belonged to the same mercy of God. The explanation of this promise was set out in the command concerning sacrifice, and in the declaration of the sacrifices, namely what they signified and what they represented. Question: Why does Moses not mention other and earlier sacrifices of men, such as Adam's (for Adam lived long before the offering of Abel and Cain, and after his sin he surely sacrificed to God), but mentions only this first one of Cain and Abel? Answer: Because this first one had something remarkable and worth noting that was not in the earlier sacrifices. Yet if anyone wishes this to have been the first of all sacrifices offered to God by men, I shall not object, as Cyril writes against Julian in book 3. But if he prefers that others came before it, I shall myself defend his opinion.

units.la: Cur Abelis oblatio fuit Deo gratior, quam oblatio Caini, quae vterq; primitias, saltem munus suae artis offerret, & magis innoxia fuisse videatur oblatio Caini, utpote quae sanguinis effusione carnerit, quam Abelis, quae cruenta fuit. R. Varia in eo variè sentiunt. Nonnulli ex Hebr. 11.4. existimant Abelis munus fuisse Deo gratius, quia fuit maioris pretij, nimirum ex primogenitis gregis. Caini vero oblatio fuit tantum ex fructibus terrae. Verum pinguedine pecudum, aut pretio rerum minime Deus per se delectatur, Psal 50, 1. Sam, 15.22. Alij censent idcirco placuisse Deo sacrificium Abelis, quod ex primogenitis gregis sui obtulisset, id est, ex primis animalium suorum fœtibus. Cainus vero fructus quidem, sed non primos & optimos dedisset Deo. Sic Cyrillus lib. 10. contra Julian sect. 6. At vero propter fidem, non propter rem ipsam oblatam dicitur Abelis sacrificium acceptum fuisse Deo. Q. Quaerem alij volunt gratius fuisse hoc munus Abelis, quia Deo magis placuit, quam Caini. Placuit vero propter fidem, quam Dei promissionibus habuit Abel, praesertim tim illi, quae erat de futuro Messia & eodem ex genere humano extituro, iuxta illud [Et Semen mulieris conteret caput Serpentis.[ Quūn igitur ille spectaret hanc Dei promissionem, totusque ex ea penderet, maiore & zelo & studio, & animo sinceriore sacrificauit Deo, quam frater ipsius Cainus. Itaque & sacrificium illud obtulit Deo, quod magis Christum illum futurum repraesentabat, nempe pecudem obtulit iugulatam, & cuius adipem cremauit, quod sacrificium peccatorum coram Deo per eundem Christum abolitionem significabat, Leuit. 3. Ergo in Christum promissum respexit Abel, ac proinde fidem iustificantem habuit, quae nos, nostraq; omnia Deo grata efficit, Rom. 5. Hac autem eadem caruit Cainus, contentus obtulisse Deo, ut supremo suo Regi, terrae suae fructus, quae terrae fruges erant, siue flores siue similia, siue poma arborū. Etsi vero sacrificia a Deo postea instituta, & sale, & similia (quae est ex tritico) Dei iussu fuerunt cōsperfa, & fruges habebant, Numer. 6, & Mincha, quae Deo offerebatur, omnis ex frugibus erat oleo & thure aspersis: repraesentatio tamen Christi fuit potissima in ipsa victima, seu pecude iugulata, & igne postea cremata, qualem Abel obtulit. Denique quod affertur sacrificium Caini fuisse magis innoxium, vtpote quod erat incruentum, ex hominum, scriptorumq; profanorum opinione dicitur, non ex ipsa rei veritate. Nullum enim sacrificij genus Deo gratius fuit, quam Expiatorium peccatorum. Atqui illud semper cruentum fuit, Hebr. 9.22. Verum ut concludam, Dico rationem cur Abelis sacrificiū fuerit gratum Deo, fuisse, solam eius fidem de Christo. Dequo tamen anxiè & variè disputat, imò ambigit Cyrillus lib. 10. contra Iulian. sect 10, vti dixi. Q. Quo-modo Deus ostendit Abelis sacrificium esse sibi gratius, quàm Caini? R. Aliquo visibili signo id testatum est, quod etiam Cainus ipse percepit. Itaque propterea accensa est ira Caini in fratrem, Genes. 4. 4. 5. Ergo Heb. 11. 4. dicitur testimonium ipse Deus perhibuisse de illa muneris sibi ab Abele oblati acceptatione, & muneris Caini reiectione. Q. Quod ipsum quoque sentit Augustinus lib. 15. Ciuit. Dei, cap. 7. Siue vero ignis de cœlo descendit, qui sacrificium Abelis consumpserit (quèadmodum & in primo Aaronis sacrificio euenit, Leuit. 9. 24. & Elia Propheta sacrificante coram populo factum est, 1. Reg. 18. 36) sine quidpiam aliud tunc extiterit à Deo, unde ista munerum distinctio aperte ab utroque sacrificante deprehenderetur, dici non potest. Visibile tamen signum ac testimonium istius acceptationis fuisse negari non debet. Q. Quid Cainus & Abel, eorumq; sacrificia nobis hodie demonstrant? R. Augustinus toto lib. 15. Ciuit. Dei, sed in primis cap. 5. & 17, ostendit in Caino & Abele (qui ex primo homine Adamo fuerunt procreati primi) duarum, quæ in hoc Mundo cernuntur, Ciuitatū fundamenta describi & proponi: quarū una Terrena est nimirum ea, quæ à Caino fratricida exordium habuit, atque in eius posteris continuauit, Ioan. 3. 12, Gen. 4. & 5. Altera, Cœlestis, & Spiritualis, quæ est Ecclesia Dei, cuius primum exemplum est Abel, Math. 23. 35. Sed quoniam Abel sine successore mortuus est, à fratre suo Caino interfectus, ab eo non est propagata hæc Dei Ciuitas & Ecclesia, sed à Setho, qui pro Abele defuncto substitutus est à Deo, & in cuius Sethi posteris mansit Ecclesia Dei. Hinc verò etiam intelligitur, qualis sit conditio utriusque Ciuitatis in his terris, nimirum vt Dei & Cœlestis Ciuitas à terrena affligatur, ac persecutionem patiatur, quemadmodum Abel à Caino, Isaac ab Esauo, Gal. 4. 29. Porrò sacrificium seu munus Caini, & Cainum ipse repræsentat nobis quale sit ingenium hypocritarum, & dona quæ offerunt Deo, nempe velle quidem eos videri cæteris sanctiores, & tamen non esse. Abel autem, & eius munus ostedit verè piorum animum esse, vt vera fide Deum vnum quærát, & in eo acquiescant. Ergo non sunt contenti videri ab hominibus boni, sed reipsa tales esse studeant. Verùm ad decimum caput historiæ venio.
units.tr: Why was Abel's offering more pleasing to God than Cain's? Both offered, at least, a gift from their labour, the first fruits, and Cain's offering seems the more harmless, since it involved no shedding of blood, whereas Abel's was bloody. Answer: Writers differ on this in various ways. Some, relying on Heb. 11:4, think Abel's gift was more pleasing to God because it was of greater value, namely from the firstborn of his flock, whereas Cain's offering was only from the fruits of the earth. But God is not delighted in itself by the fat of beasts or by the price of things (Ps. 50; 1 Sam. 15:22). Others judge that God was pleased with Abel's sacrifice because he offered from the firstlings of his flock, that is, the first young of his animals, while Cain gave fruits indeed, but not the first and best ones. So Cyril, in book 10 against Julian, section 6. But Abel's sacrifice is said to have been accepted by God on account of his faith, not on account of the thing offered. Others want Abel's gift to have been more pleasing because it pleased God more than Cain's did. It pleased him, however, because of the faith Abel had in God's promises, especially the promise concerning the future Messiah, who would arise from the human race, according to that word: [And the seed of the woman shall bruise the head of the serpent]. Since Abel looked to this promise of God and depended wholly on it, he sacrificed to God with greater zeal, eagerness and a sincerer mind than his brother Cain. And so he offered to God that sacrifice which more truly represented the Christ who was to come: he offered a slaughtered beast, whose fat he burned, a sacrifice which signified the abolition of sins before God through that same Christ (Lev. 3). Therefore Abel looked to the promised Christ, and so had the justifying faith which makes us and all that we do pleasing to God (Rom. 5). Cain lacked this faith, being content to offer to God, as to his supreme King, the fruits of his land, which were the crops of the earth, whether flowers or similar things, or the fruit of trees. Although the sacrifices instituted by God later, with salt and similar things (and the meal offering, which is made of wheat), were sprinkled at God's command and had fruits (Num. 6), and the meal offering offered to God was made entirely of fruits sprinkled with oil and frankincense, nevertheless the representation of Christ lay chiefly in the victim itself, the slaughtered beast afterwards burned with fire, such as Abel offered. Finally, the claim that Cain's sacrifice was more harmless, as it was bloodless, is made according to the opinion of men and of profane writers, not according to the truth of the matter. For no kind of sacrifice was more pleasing to God than the sacrifice of atonement for sins, and that always involved blood (Heb. 9:22). But to conclude: I say that the reason Abel's sacrifice was pleasing to God was his faith alone concerning Christ. Yet Cyril disputes this anxiously and in various ways, indeed he hesitates, in book 10 against Julian, section 10, as I have said. Question: How did God show that Abel's sacrifice was more pleasing to him than Cain's? Answer: It was attested by some visible sign, which Cain himself also perceived. That is why Cain's anger was kindled against his brother (Gen. 4:4-5). So Heb. 11:4 says that God himself bore witness to his acceptance of the gift offered by Abel and his rejection of Cain's gift. Augustine also thinks this, in book 15 of The City of God, chapter 7. Whether fire came down from heaven and consumed Abel's sacrifice (as also happened at Aaron's first sacrifice, Lev. 9:24, and when the prophet Elijah sacrificed before the people, 1 Kings 18:36), or whether something else then appeared from God by which this distinction of the gifts was plainly perceived by each of the sacrificers, cannot be said. Yet it must not be denied that there was a visible sign and testimony of that acceptance. Question: What do Cain and Abel and their sacrifices show us today? Answer: Augustine, throughout book 15 of The City of God, but especially chapters 5 and 17, shows that in Cain and Abel, who were the first children of the first man Adam, are described and set forth the foundations of the two cities seen in this world. One is earthly, namely that which began with Cain the murderer and continued in his posterity (John 3:12; Gen. 4 and 5). The other is heavenly and spiritual, which is the Church of God, whose first example is Abel (Matt. 23:35). But since Abel died without a successor, killed by his brother Cain, this City of God and Church was not propagated from him but from Seth, whom God appointed in place of the dead Abel, and in whose posterity the Church of God remained. From this it is also understood what the condition of each city is on this earth: namely that the heavenly City of God is afflicted by the earthly one and suffers persecution, just as Abel suffered from Cain and Isaac from Esau (Gal. 4:29). Moreover, Cain's sacrifice or gift, and Cain himself, show us what kind of disposition hypocrites have, and the gifts they offer to God: they wish indeed to seem holier than others, and yet are not so. But Abel and his gift show that the mind of those who are truly pious is such that they seek the one God with true faith and rest in him. Therefore they are not content to seem good to men, but strive to be so in fact. But I now come to the tenth chapter of the history.

units.la: Ad X. Maleficium primum Publicū post primum peccatum admissum.
units.tr: Chapter X. The first public crime committed after the first sin.

units.la: Quaritur, Quando perpetratum est à Caino illud fratricidium Abelis? R. Multo quidem tempore post peccatum primum Adami, vt docet S. Scriptura, Gen. 4. 3. Sed tamen ante annum 130. ex Adami seu Mundi conditi, vt apparet Gen. 5. 3. Philo Iudæus in Antiquitat. Biblic. scribit Cainum fuisse quindecim annorum, qui Abelem fratrem suum occidit. Id quod mihi facile non suaserit. Nec enim solet homines adhuc ea ætate arare terram, quam tamen arabat Cainus ante id fratricidium à se perpetratū. Quare tempus huius cadis à Caino commissæ incertum est, nec potest à nobis dessiniri. Q. Quomodo Cainus fratrem suum occiderit, quum nondum ullis enses, ullaue ferramenta essent: imo nec Ars ipsa Ferraria (quae enses & gladios cudit) adhuc inuenta, quemadmodum apparet Gen. 4. 22. R. Siue lapide, siue ossibus animalium mortuorum aliquibus repertis, (vt Sampson Philistinos caeciderit, Iudic. 15. 16) siue pugno fratrem Abelem occiderit, perinde est: occidit tamen. Prima vero inter homines arma, fuerunt vngues & pugni, postea lapides, deinde fustes, postremò enses, quos homines fabricarunt in suam cædem. Horat. lib. 1. Serm. Sat. 3. Quum prorepserunt primis animalia terris, Mutu, & turpe pecus, gladem atq; cubilia propter Vnguibus, & pugnis, dein fustibus, atque ita porrò Pugnabant armis, quae post fabricauerat vsus.
units.tr: Question: When was that murder of Abel committed by Cain? Answer: Long after the first sin of Adam, as Holy Scripture teaches, Gen. 4.3. Yet it was before the year 130 from Adam, or from the creation of the world, as appears from Gen. 5.3. Philo the Jew, in his Biblical Antiquities, writes that Cain was fifteen years old when he killed his brother Abel. That does not easily persuade me. Men of that age do not usually plough the land, yet Cain was ploughing before the murder he committed. The time of this slaying by Cain is therefore uncertain and cannot be fixed by us. Q. How did Cain kill his brother, since there were as yet no swords or iron tools? Indeed the art of smithing, which forges swords and blades, had not yet been discovered, as appears from Gen. 4.22. R. Whether he struck him with a stone, or with the bones of dead animals found somewhere (as Samson struck down the Philistines, Judg. 15.16), or killed his brother Abel with his fist, it makes no difference: he killed him all the same. The first weapons among men were nails and fists, afterwards stones, then clubs, and lastly swords, which men fashioned for their own slaughter. Horace, Satires, book 1, satire 3: "When the living creatures crept forth upon the first lands, a dumb and ugly herd, they fought for mates and lairs with nails and fists, then with clubs, and so on; they fought with the arms that later use had invented."

units.la: Ergo quocunq; modo & instrumento tale facinus comiserit Cainus interfecit, & quidem perfidè fratrem suum, priùs à se verbis lenibus & blandis deceptum, ac in agros seu solitudinem pertractum, vt sine teste eum scelerate ingularet. Q. Cur Cainum interrogat Deus vbi esset frater eius? R. Non ignarus factî Deus, sic Cainum interrogat: sed vt eum & perfrictæ frontis, & proiecti pudoris, & audacissimum, ac nefarium hominem esse argueret, qui repugnante conscientia ausus est negare Deo factum, aut coram eo tergiuersari.
units.tr: Therefore, by whatever means and instrument Cain committed such a deed, he killed him, and indeed treacherously: he had first deceived his brother with gentle and flattering words and led him out into the fields or the wilderness, so that he might wickedly stab him without a witness. Q. Why does God ask Cain where his brother is? R. God was not ignorant of the deed, but asks Cain thus to show that he was a man of brazen face, shameless, and most bold and wicked, who, though his conscience resisted, dared to deny the deed to God or to evade him to his face.

units.la: Quaobrem se quoque impœnitentem probauit Cainus, & hominem perditum, & hypocritam summum, qui Deo crimen suum non fuerit confessus, quem vt pungeret Deus, & sceleris sui conuinceret, sic interrogat, [Vbi est Abel frater tuus?] Gen. 4. 9. Porrò Josephus lib.
units.tr: Wherefore Cain also proved himself unrepentant, a lost man, and a supreme hypocrite, who did not confess his crime to God. To prick him and convict him of his sin, God asks him thus: [Where is Abel your brother?] Gen. 4.9. Moreover Josephus, in book 1 [sic].

units.la: Antiquit. Judaic. cap. 4. scribit Cainum postquam fratrem suum Abelem nefarië, ac proditorie occidisset, occultasse cadaver eius, quasi lateret Deum: ac propterea fuisse sic a Deo interrogatum, ne putaret Cainum se celasse Deum. Scribit vero idem Josephus eundem Cainum fuisse hominem tota vita rapacem, avarum, inuidum, ac propterea men suraruum (quibus homines deciperet) inuentorem. Sive vero hæc vetus Judæorum traditio fuit, siue commentum R. Abbinicum, certe Cainus fuit, vt apparet, summus hypocrita, vir impœnitens, & sceleratissimus. Q. Cur in secunda Legis Diuinæ Tabula, vbi hominum peccata in homines describuntur, præceptū [Nō occides] non ponitur primo loco, quū homicidium sit primū scelus, ac maleficiū ab homine in hominem publicè perpetratū. R. Quoniam sanctieda fuit Lege Dei primum paterna autoritas, quæ natura præcedit, vtpote Dei in his terris imago. Imò etiam patris sui cum Adami præceptum suumque erga eum officium primum violauit Cainus in occidēdo fratre. Ergo præceptum de honorandis parentibus in secunda illa Legis Tabula primum collocatum est, & quidem merito. Secundum autem præceptum est, De Homicidio: Tertium de Adulterio. Nam prius homo occisus fuit, quàm Lex coniugiū à Lamecho violaretur. Viuebant enim adhuc homines continenter, & absque lasciuia. Vrde κρόνος ζωή, i. Saturnia vita, id est continens à libidine & crapula diƈta apud Horatium, est Vita antiquissima: & Cœna, Vitaque Deorū, id est, tenuis & frugalis, quemadmodum præclarè obseruauit ac collegit D. Gulielmus Stukius in Quast. ConConuiualibus, lib.1. qualis solet esse piorum hominum continentia. Sed de capite vndecimo, in quo poena isti[?] Caini sceleris continetur, iam agamus.
units.tr: Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews, chapter 4, writes that after Cain had wickedly and treacherously killed his brother Abel, he hid the corpse, as if God could not see; and therefore he was questioned by God, lest he think Cain had hidden himself from God. The same Josephus writes that this Cain was a man greedy all his life, rapacious and envious, and for that reason the inventor of false weights and measures, with which men might deceive one another. Whether this is an old tradition of the Jews or a rabbinical invention, Cain was clearly a supreme hypocrite, an unrepentant man, and most wicked. Q. Why, in the second table of the divine Law, where the sins of men against men are described, is the precept [You shall not kill] not placed first, since homicide is the first crime, and the wrong committed publicly by man against man? R. Because paternal authority, which precedes by nature as the image of God on earth, had to be placed first in God's Law. Indeed Cain, in killing his brother, also first violated the command given to his father Adam and his first duty toward him. Therefore the precept on honouring parents is placed first in that second table of the Law, and rightly so. The second precept is On Murder, and the third On Adultery, for man was killed before Lamech violated the marriage bond. For people still lived continently and without lust. Hence κρόνος ζωή, that is, Saturnian life, a life free from lust and gluttony, is in Horace the most ancient life; and the supper and life of the gods, that is, slight and frugal, as the pious Wilhelm Stucki carefully observed and collected in his Convivial Questions, book 1, is the sort of continence that pious men usually practise. But let us now deal with the eleventh chapter, in which the punishment for Cain's crime is set out.

units.la: Ad XI. Excommunicatio Prima: ac Pœ- na Maleficij primi post peccatum Adami.
units.tr: Chapter XI. The first excommunication, and the punishment of the first crime after the sin of Adam.

units.la: Quaeritur, Cur Adamus vel Deus ipse Cainum non punierit morte statim, quum Deus hanc Legem homicidio sanciuerit Gen.9.6, [Qui effuderit sanguinem hominis, sanguis eius per hominem effunditor.] R. Adamus non puniuit filium suum Cainum morte, (licet esset illius Magistratus, uti Iuda Tamara nurus sua, Gen.38.24) tum propter amorem paternum, tum etiam propter paucitatem hominum, quæ tunc erat in toto terrarum Orbe. Solus enim ipse mas cum Caino reliquit, occiso Abele.
