Ne igitur Caino interfecto Adamus solus omnino ad gignendos homines, & propagandum genus humanum superesset, reliquit Adamus Cainum superstitem, nec eum occidit velut Magistratus. Deus vero Cainum non sustulit, sed grauissimis, ut apparet, pœnis propter illam cædem fratris affecit, atque in exeplum aliis quamdiutissime in hoc Mundo reliquit, & statuit, ut ceteri terrerentur, neve tale quidpiam ipsi committerent. Atque hæc causa est non statim sublati Caini. Q. Cur Deus signum Caino impositum, quem puniebat ipse, ne quis eum interficeret, quum ipsius pœna satis terrere cæteros à tali facinore potuerit, Gen.4. 15. R. Quoniam effrenis est hominum licentia, & furiosus impetus, desperataq; audacia: Ergo ne[?] quis hominum Cainum occideret, vel in vindictam interfecti ab eo Abelis: vel quapiam alia mala voluntate, signum & notam istam Dominus ei apposuit, impressitq;. Voluit enim eum in caeterorum mortalium metum seruari. Praeterea nec eam poenam per priuatos exigi priuata autoritate Deus voluit. Ergo fuit hoc signum velut interdictio à Deo facta priuatis, ne sua ipsi autoritate in quenquam vendicarent, aut vendicent maleficia hominum. Quemadmodum autem Cainus ipse nõ sapuerat, seque a peccando non abstinuerat, exemplo patris sui Adami, & tristissima illius poenae: sic nec homines alij sapientiores futuri erant, propter poenam impositam Caino, ne eum necarent, nisi Deus aliquo speciali signo caeteros admonuisset, & deterruisset ab eode trucidando & iugulando. Ecquod autem fuerit istud signum, non aliter, aut aliud videtur explicare S. Scriptura, quam fuisse eiulatus miros, furores, & vagam Caini fugam, ac per agros errorem, dum stimulis & furiys sua conscientia palam agitaretur, & se detestaretur. Id quod non quidem semper faciebat ille: sed nonnunquam, vti furiosi homines nunc quoque facere solent, interpositis nimirum interuallis, & spatijs aliquibus dilucidis. Alij hoc signum putat fuisse perpetuum corporis tremorem, & trepidationem, quae in Caino apparuerit. Alij notam quandā à Deo in Caini fronte inustam, & impressam, ex qua dignosceretur à caeteris hominibus. Ego vero in mea illa sententia & interpretatione persto. Q. Quis fuerit ille Caini error, & vagatio, quae cū poena illa continuata fuit, & propter quam vrbem primus, in qua viueret, condidisse dicatur, Gen.4.12.13.14.17. R.
units.tr: Question: Why did Adam, or God himself, not punish Cain with death at once, since God sanctioned this law against homicide, Gen. 9.6, [Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed]? R. Adam did not punish his son Cain with death, although he was his magistrate, just as Judah did not punish his daughter-in-law Tamar, Gen. 38.24. He spared him partly out of paternal love, and partly because of the small number of men then in the whole world. For with Cain alone, Abel having been killed, only Adam himself, the male, was left. So that Adam should not be left wholly alone to beget men and propagate the human race if Cain were killed, Adam left Cain alive and did not kill him as a magistrate would. God did not take Cain away either, but, as appears, punished him for that murder of his brother with the gravest penalties, and left him in this world for a very long time as an example to others, so that others would be terrified and would not commit such a thing themselves. This is the reason Cain was not at once taken away. Q. Why did God set a sign on Cain, whom he himself punished, so that no one would kill him, since his punishment could have sufficiently deterred others from such a crime? Gen. 4.15. R. Because the licence of men is unbridled, their impulse furious and their audacity desperate. Therefore, lest any man should kill Cain, either in vengeance for Abel, who had been slain by him, or from some other evil intent, the Lord set and impressed that sign and mark upon him. For he wished Cain to be preserved as a fear to other mortals. Moreover, God did not want this punishment to be exacted by private persons on their own authority. The sign was therefore, as it were, a prohibition laid by God on private persons, that they should not by their own authority take vengeance on anyone, or avenge men's crimes. But just as Cain himself had not been wise, nor had he restrained himself from sinning by the example of his father Adam and the most sorrowful punishment of that example, so other men would not be wiser on account of the penalty laid on Cain, that they should not kill him, unless God by some special sign had warned the others and deterred them from butchering and slaughtering him. What that sign was, Holy Scripture seems to explain in no other way than that it was Cain's strange wailing, his frenzy, and his wandering flight, roaming through the fields, while his conscience openly goaded and drove him with furies and he loathed himself. Indeed he did not always do this, but sometimes, as furious men are wont to do even now, with intervals and some lucid spaces in between. Others think the sign was the constant trembling and trepidation of body that appeared in Cain. Others think it was a mark branded and impressed by God on Cain's forehead, by which he might be distinguished from other men. But I persist in my own opinion and interpretation. Q. What was that error and wandering of Cain, which continued along with that punishment, and on account of which he is said to have built the first city in which he lived, Gen. 4.12-14, 17? R.

units.la: Non sic vagus fuit, & erro Cainus, vt semper hominũ societatem fugeret, atque per agros, & deserta miserè flebiliterque detestans suum factum, & iram Dei cohorrens erraret: sed tunc solùm quum furore, & furys sceleris à se perpetrati conscientia eius corriperetur, & agitaretur: quod, vti dixi, per dilucida temporum interualla fiebat, illique accidebat. Ergo velut hominis à Deo æterna morti damnati tunc effigies quædam Cainus erat, cæteris mortalibus horribilis, & ipsimet Caino intolerabilis. Ergo planè miserabilis erat omnibus hominibus Cainus, vt nemo eum miseriorẽ vellet. Q uũ autem cessauerat, aut interquieuerat ille furor, & conscientia stimulus, & flagellum tunc sese in hominum societatem aliorũ quietus recipiebat, cum ijs erat, & versabatur & in vrbe manebat, quam primus ipse exedificarat. Sic Saul ad tempus furore, post neglectum Dei mandatũ sæpè corripiebatur 1.Sam. 16.14. Sic Nabugadnezer, post profanatũ à se, & euersum Dei templum superbus mania agitatus est, ac per septennium in syluis erro & vagus in pœnâ sceleris habitauit, fuitque, Dan.4.27. Sic Orestes occisa matre: sic Oedipus occiso patre furys agitati ac perciti, per dilucida tamen interualla sese tempore furoris à cœtu hominum subducebant, & tunc vagi erronesq; per deserta furiosi vagabantur. Sic Bellerophon quoque in campis Cilicie errabat furiosus
units.tr: Cain was not so wandering and erratic that he always fled human company and wandered through fields and deserts, miserably and tearfully detesting his deed and shrinking from the wrath of God. He was like this only at the times when the fury and frenzy of his crime, which he had committed, seized and drove his conscience. As I said, this happened during clear intervals of time, and it came upon him in those intervals. So Cain was then a kind of image of a man condemned by God to eternal death, dreadful to other mortals and intolerable even to himself. Cain was plainly pitiable to all men, so that no one wished to be near him. But when that frenzy and the goad of conscience had ceased, or had lulled for a while, he returned quietly into human society. He lived among others, dwelt with them, and remained in the city which he himself had been the first to build. So Saul was often seized by a frenzy for a time after he neglected the command of God (1 Sam. 16.14). So Nebuchadnezzar, proud after he had profaned and overthrown the temple of God, was driven about on his walls and for seven years wandered and roamed in the woods as punishment for his crime (Dan. 4.27). So Orestes, after killing his mother, and Oedipus, after killing his father, were driven and stirred up by furies; yet during clear intervals they withdrew from the company of men in the time of their madness, and then, as madmen, wandered and roamed through the deserts. So too Bellerophon, mad, wandered in the plains of Cilicia,

units.la: Ipse suum cor edens, hominum vestigia vitans, quemadmodum ait Homerus. Denique sic olim in Gallia Rex Carolus, nomine Sextus, Dei iudicio punitus scribitur. In summa, Cainus tamen nõ legitur propterea pœnituisse: sed de pœna tantum sua conqueflus. Quod etiam annotat Iosephus lib 1.cap 4. Antiquitat. Quid sit [Facies Iehoua,] à qua se expulsum conqueritur. Cainus, Gen. 4.14. & 16. Notanda sunt Caini verba. Non enim simpliciter, ait, dum me exulem & vagum facis, Eycis ac expellis me à facie Adami patris mei, vel matris Eua (quod quidem tam erat per se durum, & in tanta terra vastitate moestum, ac in pecudum iam ferarum ferocia tata periculosissimum:) sed inquit, [Expulisti me à facie tua, Domine.] Et postea addit, [Egressus est Cainus à facie Iehoua.] Ergo plus quiddam dicit & significat, quam si suauissimo illo vultus paterni aspectu solum priuari se coquereretur: vel se in magna iam manifestaq; pericula expositum à Deo esse expostularet. Imo exclamat, Maior est mea pœna, quam ut eam sustinere possim. Genes. 4.13. Praterea quomodo dicitur Cainus egressus à facie Iehoua, quum Deus sit vbiq;, vbiq; clare videant ac spectent eius oculi homines, & hominum facta, Psal. 139. 7. Amos 9.1, Heb. 4.13? Cur in eo vno loco, vbi prius cum patre suo Adamo & matre Eua habitabat, dicit esse faciem Iehoua, à quo quum expellatur, coqueritur se eici non à facie & conspectu parentum, vt dixi, sed Dei ipsius? Putauitne Cainus Deum. Deique potentiā vni cuidam orbis gleba & loco ascriptā, quum pœnam ab eo sibi impositam ipse vbique sentiret, & circumgestaret? Certè ista non cohærent & melius de infinita ac vbique sparsa Dei potentia, & præsentia sensit Cainus, quam vt Deum per se vno quodam loco circunscriptum ac conclusum esse indicaret. Quid igitur hic vocat [Faciem Iehoua?] Cornelius Bertramus olim collega meus, Vir in Hebraeus, siquis alius, eruditissimus, in libello, quem scripsit, verè aureo, De Politia Iudaica, cap. 2. praeclare verèque sensit, & docet (cui propterea ego quoque assentior) Faciem Iehoua hic notare certum locum, in quo Dei iussu, sacra, sacrificia, cultusq; Dei externus a Deo ipso praescriptus exerceretur, ac fieret. Ex quo quum expelleretur a Deo Cainus, dicit se eici a facie Iehoua. Est enim cum ex tota S. Scriptura, tum ex Iona cap. 2, & Leuitico, Numeris, & Deuteronomio certissimum, ac notissimum locum eum, in quo erat Dei Arca vel Templum (quoniam illic externus Dei cultus a Deo mandatus agebatur) dici κατ' ἐξοχὴν faciem Dei: & eos agere, laetari, iurare, stare coram Deo, Deiq; facie, qui illo in loco erant, vbi Deus externè colebatur. Ex quo fit, vt proculdubio ista Caini expulsio a facie Iehoua significet Excommunicationem a Sacris, quam Deus pro poena istius fratricidij Caino imposuit & inflixit, quae certè quidem est grauissima poena, & prima Excommunicatio, quae fulminata est in homines. Haec autem est testis irae Dei in peccatum, & poenae illius aeternae ac tristissimae, quae in damnatos parata est typus, & praeludium, Matth. 25. Haec illustrior in ista Caini excommunicatione fuit, quòd in eo perpetuò, totoq; vitae illius tempore duraverit. Q. In qua Mundi regione Cainus habitaverit, quum esset expulsus a facie Iehoua. R. S. Scriptura, Gen. 4. 16, ait ad Orientem Edenis eum habitasse, non tamen cum patre Adamo. Sed progressus est ulterius ad Solem orientem Cainus, & versus extremam Indiam, quae nunc vocatur. Ex quo apparet primas illas Orbis partes nimirum Orientales, fuisse ab hominibus cultas, & habitatas: postea vero alias. Quonam autem diserte in loco versatus sit Cainus, quaesitum est. Iosephus lib. 1. Antiquit. Iudaic. cap. 4. sic scribit: [Multam vero peragrans terram cum uxore sua Cain, collocatur in loco, qui Naida nuncupatur, ibique moratus est: in quo et etiam filii nati sunt.] Lib. 1. Chron. 5. 9. fit mentio populi Nodabi, qui fuit Agarenus, & in Arabia habitavit. Sed ille populus in Oriente nequaquam fuit, & ad hunc locum non pertinet. Illud vero potius facit ad huc locum, nempe quod apud Plinium lib. 6. Natur. Hist. cap. 20. inter extremos Indos [Nobunda] populi nominantur, qui verisimilius a Nob dicti videntur, vel potius Nod Hebraeo. (facilius enim est mutatio literae d, in b, praesertim peregrinis hominibus, & Hebraicè nescientibus) Nod vero dicta est terra illa ob errorem & demigrationem Caini in eam post occisum fratrem, Gen. 4. Hanc autem Nod Hebraea vocem LXX. Interpretes Naiada nuncuparunt, & Graece converterunt. Verum alij existimant Nod apud Moysem non proprij cuiusdam loci nomen esse, sed appellatiuum & generale pro quavis regione, in qua quis errat & vagatur. Ego tamen iudico Nod certa regionis in Oriente & in India sita appellationem esse, quae sic a Caino, eiusque posteris propter errorem patris nominaretur. Unde & Nodūba populi, uti dixi, quos Plinius Nobundas vocat. Quomodo Cainus in certa quadam Orbis regione habitasse dicatur Gen. 4. 16: imo etiam in certa urbe, verf. 17, qui iussu est a Deo esse vagus & erro, verf. 12. Non
units.tr: "devouring his own heart, avoiding the footsteps of men," as Homer says. In short, King Charles, named the Sixth, is recorded to have been punished in Gaul by the judgment of God in this way. In sum, it is not read that Cain repented on this account; he only complained about his punishment. Josephus also notes this in Antiquities, book 1, chapter 4. What is meant by "the face of Jehovah," from which he complains he was cast out (Gen. 4.14 and 16)? The words of Cain must be noted. For he does not simply say, "Since you make me an exile and a wanderer, you cast and drive me out from the face of my father Adam or my mother Eve" (which in itself was harsh enough, and in so vast a waste of land sorrowful, and, amid the fierceness of the beasts, very dangerous). He says instead, "You have driven me from your face, O Lord" (Gen. 4.14). And afterwards he adds, "Cain went out from the face of Jehovah" (Gen. 4.16). He therefore says and signifies something more than if he were only lamenting that he was deprived of that most sweet sight of his father's countenance, or complaining that he was exposed by God to clear and great dangers. Indeed he cries out, "My punishment is greater than I can bear" (Gen. 4.13). Moreover, how is it said that Cain went out from the face of Jehovah, since God is everywhere, and his eyes see clearly everywhere and behold men and their deeds (Ps. 139.7; Amos 9.1; Heb. 4.13)? Why, in that one place where he had earlier lived with his father Adam and mother Eve, does he say there is the face of Jehovah, from which, when he is expelled, he complains that he is cast out not from the face and sight of his parents, as I said, but from the very face of God? Did Cain think that God and his power were attached and assigned to some clod of earth and place, since he felt and carried about the punishment imposed on him by God everywhere? Certainly these ideas do not cohere; Cain judged more rightly of the infinite and everywhere spread power and presence of God than to suppose that God is confined and enclosed in one particular place. What, then, does "the face of Jehovah" mean here? Cornelius Bertram, formerly my colleague, a man most learned in Hebrew, as learned as any, in his truly golden little book On the Jewish Polity, chapter 2, rightly and admirably judged and taught (and so I too agree with him) that "the face of Jehovah" here denotes a certain place in which, by God's command, sacred rites, sacrifices, and the external worship of God prescribed by God himself were performed and carried out. When Cain was thrust out by God, he says he is cast out from the face of Jehovah. For it is most certain and most well known, both from all of Holy Scripture and from Jonah chapter 2, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy, that the place in which the Ark of God or the Temple stood (since there the external worship commanded by God was carried on) is called the face of God par excellence [κατ' ἐξοχὴν], and that those who were in that place where God was worshipped outwardly act, rejoice, swear, and stand before God and the face of God. From this it follows that, without doubt, this expulsion of Cain from the face of Jehovah signifies excommunication from the sacred rites, which God imposed and inflicted on Cain as punishment for this fratricide. This is certainly a most grievous punishment, and the first excommunication ever hurled against men. It is a witness of God's wrath against sin and of that eternal and most sorrowful punishment prepared for the damned, and a type and foretaste of it (Matt. 25). In this excommunication of Cain, this was the more evident, that it lasted continually, throughout the whole time of his life.

units.la: R. Non perpetuò & semper erro fuit Cainus,uti dixim{us:}sed tunc tantum quum conscientiæ,& nefarij illius fratricidij à se perpetrati furys & stimulus percelleretur,& agitaretur (qualem hoc nostro seculo vidimus ipsi virum quidem doctissimū sed quia Christum abnegauerat, sic æstro conscientiæ percitum, nomine Nicolaum Cruartum. Ille enim sic nonnunquam vagabatur furore & metu iudicij Dei exanimatus.) Ergo quum quies erat ab eo furore, Cainus & prudenter se gerebat, & quietus erat, & terram colebat, & in vrbe a se condita habitabat,certámque illam Mundi regionem tenebat. Nec tamen quum Cainus vagabatur, errabat per totum terrarum orbem,velut Ifis, seu Io illa Ouidy & Aeschyli Poetarum: sed in Nod regione duntaxat. Sed hæc hactenus. Accedamus ad caput duodecimum Historiæ.
units.tr: Reply. Cain was not a fugitive and a wanderer perpetually and at all times, as I said, but only when he was struck by the fury and goad of conscience over that wicked murder of his brother which he had committed (as we ourselves saw in our own age, a man indeed most learned, but because he had denied Christ, thus driven by the gadfly of conscience, named Nicolaus Cruartus. For he sometimes wandered about in this way, lifeless from the frenzy and fear of God's judgment.) Therefore, when he was at rest from that frenzy, Cain also conducted himself prudently, was quiet, tilled the land, and lived in a city he had founded, and he kept to that particular region of the world. Nor, when Cain was wandering, did he roam through the whole globe, like Isis, or that Io of the poets Ovid and Aeschylus, but only in the land of Nod. But so much for this. Let us proceed to the twelfth chapter of the History.

units.la: Ad XII. Vrbs Prima in Mundo condita.
units.tr: Chapter XII. The First City Built in the World.

units.la: Quaeritur, Cur Cainus condidit vrbem Gen.4.17. R. Iosephus lib.1. Antiquitat.Iudaic.cap.4.scribit ob eam causam conditam esse primùm à Caino vrbem, quòd ille bestiarū in se impetum formidaret, nempe ne ab ys dilaniaretur,aut alio aliquo modo periret,& occideretur. Vtrumq; certè verissimum est, primam huius prima vrbis à Caino ædificandæ, potissimamq; causam fuisse ipsius metum tum ab hominibus ipsis, tum à ferís & bestiis ne ab ys interficeretur. Quü enim (eum accusante conscientia) semper trepidus esset,nec pœnam illam à Deo impositā pro emendatione haberet, sed pro perpetuo supplicio,& animi cruciatu (nec enim vnquā verè pœnituit, & ad Deum conuersus est Cainus) remedium sibi quæsiuit ipse contra istos sua conscientia terrores,qui eum vexabant. Itaque se muro circuncinxit, & conclusit,velut carcere voluntario: mœnia & turres ad vim irruentium prohibendam addidit: portas ad se custodiendum adiunxit: & quantum potuit, metum illum à furore & vi hominū & bestiarum sibi ademit. Ergo pauor conscientiæ & metus: non affectus humani generis sparsi colligendi prima præcipuaq;, vrbis condendæ caussa Caino fuit. Nam sine isto carcere & munitione eodem tempore viuebat Adamus pater eius etiam in medio orbe terrarum vacuo, & deserto: nec sibi à feris & beluis ( quas omnes & cicures & sibi subditas antea expertus erat, & tamen iam sentiebat sibi rebelles ) tale quicquam metuebat, quoniam careb-at Adamus ys conscientia terroribus , quibus Cainus vexabatur. Et quidem de genere humano (quæ sua erat posteritas)colligendo nō minus sollicitus fuit Adamus, quàn Cainus iste: verum propterea oppida nō exstruxit Adamus, nec homines in ea tanquam in custodias coniecit. Q. Cur sibi Cainus metuebat vel ab hominibus,vel à feris,quum haberet signū sibi à Deo impositum,ne quis eum caderet,vel occideret, Gen.4 15, ac proinde promissionem Dei certam cerneret de sua salute tuta futura? R. Cainus,quū vrbem edificare cogitaret, imò edificaret, non speculabat verba vel promissionem Dei de se tuto futuro:sed solos conscientiæ & mentis suæ terrores attedebat, quibus percitus se in isto munimento condiderat, aut potius abdiderat. Ex quo apparet etiam Caini infidelitas,qui Dei promissionem neqnaneque aquam fecerit tanti, ut se per eam solam tutum fore speraret, absque aliquo alio præsidio. Ergo suum illud præsidium in urbe tutius indicavit, perfectque, prout quinque. Quamobrem 1.Ioan.3.12, Cainus dicitur fuisse à Malo illo, nec inter Dei filios unquam recenseretur. Augustinus quoque lib.15.Ciuit.Dei,cap.7 ostendit eundem fuisse cōtumacem in Deum ipsum.Cui sententia accedit etiā Iosephus lib.1.cap.4. Antiquit. Iudaic. Scio quidem media iusta nostræ incolumitatis conseruanda nequaquam esse spernenda. (Nam Dauid arma capit, & insidias hostibus struit, de quibus vincendis habebat Dei promissum, 2.Sam.5.19) Verum Cainus iste nec eo animo fecit,quo Dauid:nec dubitare de sua incolumitate post signum à Deo acceptū desiuit.
units.tr: Question: Why did Cain build a city? Gen. 4.17. Answer: Josephus, in book 1, chapter 4 of the Jewish Antiquities, writes that Cain first built a city for this reason: he dreaded attacks from wild beasts, namely that he might be torn apart by them, or otherwise perish and be killed. Both are certainly most true. The first and chief cause for Cain's building this first city was his fear, both of men themselves and of wild beasts, lest he be killed by them. For since he was always trembling, his conscience accusing him, and since he did not regard the punishment laid on him by God as a cure but as a lasting torment and anguish of mind (for he never truly repented, and Cain did not turn to God), he sought for himself a remedy against those terrors of conscience that tormented him. So he surrounded himself with a wall and shut himself in, as in a voluntary prison. He added walls and towers to keep off the force of attackers, he added gates to guard himself, and as far as he could he took from himself the fear of the violence of men and beasts. So fear and dread of conscience, not any desire to gather the scattered human race, was the first and chief reason Cain had for founding a city. For without such a prison and fortification, his father Adam lived at the same time, even in the middle of the empty and desolate world. Nor did Adam fear anything of this kind from wild beasts, which he had found both tame and subject to himself, though he already sensed them rebelling against him; Adam lacked those terrors of conscience by which Cain was vexed. Indeed Adam was no less anxious than Cain about gathering the human race, which was his own offspring; yet Adam did not build towns, nor herd men into them as into prisons. Question: Why did Cain fear either men or wild beasts, since he had the sign God had set on him, that no one should strike or kill him (Gen. 4.15), and so could see God's promise of his safety as certain? Answer: When Cain was planning to build a city, indeed while he was building it, he did not look to God's words or promise that he would be safe. He attended only to the terrors of his conscience and mind, by which he was driven to hide himself in this fortification, or rather to shut himself away. From this appears Cain's unbelief: he did not value God's promise so highly as to hope to be safe by it alone, without any other protection. Therefore he judged that his protection lay more securely in the city, and he completed it, as ... Wherefore Cain is said to have been of that Evil One (1 John 3.12), and was never counted among the sons of God. Augustine also, in book 15 of The City of God, chapter 7, shows that he was obstinate against God himself, and Josephus, in book 1, chapter 4 of the Jewish Antiquities, agrees with this opinion. I know indeed that the means of preserving our safety are by no means to be despised (for David takes up arms and lays ambushes for his enemies, whom he had God's promise to conquer, 2 Sam. 5.19). But Cain did not act in the same spirit as David, nor did he cease to doubt his safety after he had received the sign from God.

units.la: Q. Vbi sita fuerit urbs hæc prima,quæ à Caino ædificata est. R. Quū ab eo tempore tota terræ facies per Diluuium fuerit immutata: deinde,quum tot gentium migrationes facta terminos nationum regionumq; confuderint, difficile omnino est locum & situm primæ illius urbis certò describere, vel commemorare. Tamen eam in Oriente fuisse, & quidem ab Edene regione remotissimo apparet. Qua regio ea esse videtur, quæ nunc Cambalu ab Historicis nominatur, in extremis Indiæ trans Imaum montem sita finibus, ubi etiamnum hodie sunt amplissima oppida & urbes. Si quis tamen aliter iudicat,& sentit, is suo iudicio per me fruatur, licet. Stephanus mihi adstipulatur:nam in libro de vrbibus,[Heniochia,ait,est regio ad Caucasum mōtem,] qui idem est Imaus. Vox autem ista Heniochia veteris istius nominis quædam sunt reliquiæ. Q. Vtrum unicam duntaxat Vrbem per totam vitam condiderit Cainus. R. Aliarũ non meminit S.Scriptura,quam vnius huius,quam ex nomine Henoch primogeniti fui, saltem filij, Henochiam vocauit, Gen.4.17: cuius, vti dixi,vestigia quaedã & nominis,& res videntur adhuc extare in India. Nam huius quada pars & prouincia à posteris vocitata est Heniochia,vt ait & Strabo,& Stephanus in lib.de Vrbib. Caterum Philo Iudaeus in Bíblicis Antiquit sic scribit, [Ex eo coepit Cain aedificare ciuitates,quousque conderet septem. Et haec sunt nomina ciuitatum: Nomen prime ciuitatis secundum nomen filij sui Enoch: Nomen autem secunda ciuitatis, Maich: tertia,Jared:quarta,Tehe: quinta nomen, Iesca:nomen sexta,Celet:& nomè septima,Iebbat.] Et haec quidem Philo,quibus paria non habet Iosephus tamen.
units.tr: Question: Where was this first city, which Cain built, situated? Answer: Since then the whole face of the earth has been changed by the Flood, and since the many migrations of peoples have confused the boundaries of nations and regions, it is altogether difficult to describe or record with certainty the place and site of that first city. Yet it clearly lay in the East, and indeed in a region very remote from Eden. That region seems to be the one now called Cambalu by the historians, lying at the farthest borders of India beyond Mount Imaus, where even today there are very large towns and cities. If anyone judges and thinks otherwise, let him enjoy his own opinion by my leave. Stephanus supports me, for in his book on cities he says: [Henioch-ia is a region near Mount Caucasus], which is the same as Imaus. This word Henioch-ia is some remnant of that old name. Question: Did Cain build only one city during his whole life? Answer: Scripture makes no mention of others, only of this one, which he called Henochia after the name of his firstborn, or at least his son Enoch (Gen. 4.17). Some traces of its name and of the thing itself, as I have said, seem still to survive in India. For a part and province of that region was later called Heniochia by its descendants, as Strabo says, and Stephanus in his book on cities. But Philo the Jew, in his Biblical Antiquities, writes thus: [From then on Cain began to build cities, until he founded seven. And these are the names of the cities: the first city, after the name of his son Enoch; the second city, Maich; the third, Jared; the fourth, Tehe; the fifth, Iesca; the sixth, Celet; and the seventh, Iebbat.] Thus Philo; Josephus has nothing like this.

units.la: Q. Quomodo Cainus ciuitatem condere potuit, aut cui condidit, quum tunc temporis homines tam pauci numero fuerint? R. Hanc quaestionem monet Augustinum in Quaest.in Genef.cap 1.quam sic idem definit, & soluit,cuius ego sententiae subscribo suffragorq,[An ideo,ait,quaestio est,(id est dubitatio) quoniam,qui leguntʻ,putant solos tunc fuisse homines,quos diuina Scriptura commemorat: nec aduertunt eos,qui prius sunt conditi,duos:vel etiam eos,quos genuerunt tandiu viuisse,vt multos gignerent. Non enim & Adam eos solos genuit,quorum nomina leguntur:quum de illo Scriptura loquens ita concludat, quod genuerit filios & filias.Gen.5.4. Proinde quum illi multo pluribus vixerint annis,quàm Israelita in Aegypto fuerunt, quis non videat quàm multi homines nasci potuerunt, unde illa ciuitas impleretur, si Hebrai multò minore tempore ita multiplicari potuerunt?] Ergo Cainus eam ciuitatem condidit tum multiplicato iam suo fœminæ tum posteris ex se futuris de habitatione mature prospiciens & cogitans. Et certè Philo Iudæus eodé, quo superius, libro, scribit Cainum suscepisse ex vxore sua sex liberos partim mares, partim fœminas, quorum nomina recitasse, vti vxoris Caini, quam vult fuisse Themech: quæ eadem est, quæ Themis illa Dea antiquissima Profanorum hominum. Q. Vtrum Chanoch, vel Henoch, vt alij vertunt, fuerit primogenitus Caini. R. Id sentire videtur Philo, & Iosephus. Et quum tam præclarum opus suum, nimirum vrbem à se primam conditam, ex illius nomine vocarit Cainus, non est incredibile eum fuisse Caini primogenitum. Tamen diserte ex Dei verbo colligi id nequaquam potest. Nec enim qui primi nominatur omnes sunt primogeniti. Porrò [Chanoch] Hebraïs est Eruditus Latinis, & Græcis, siue ex voto, vt talis esset: sic eum appellauit Cainus pater: siue ostendes qualem eum esse oportere, erudituʼ suo exemplo in Dei metu: quam nominis interpretationem prætermisit Philo in nominibus Hebraicis. Sed ad caput tertium & decimum accedamus, in quo describitur propagatio familiæ Caini post Abelem fratrem à se occisum.
units.tr: Question: How could Cain build a city, or for whom did he build it, since there were so few people at that time? Answer: Augustine raises this question in his Questions on Genesis, chapter 1, and he himself defines and resolves it in this way; I subscribe to his opinion and support it: [Is the question, he says, (that is, the doubt) because those who read think that the only men then were those Divine Scripture mentions? They do not notice that there were two first created, or even that those they begot lived so long that they produced many. For Adam did not beget only those whose names are read, since Scripture, speaking of him, concludes that he begot sons and daughters (Gen. 5.4). Therefore, since they lived for much longer than the Israelites were in Egypt, who does not see how many men could have been born, enough to fill that city, if the Hebrews could multiply in far less time?] So Cain built that city when his wife's family had already multiplied, and with his future descendants in mind, providing early for a dwelling. And indeed Philo the Jew, in the same book as above, writes that Cain had six children by his wife, some males and some females, and he recites their names, as well as the name of Cain's wife, whom he says was Themech, the same as Themis, that most ancient goddess of the profane peoples. Question: Was Chanoch, or Henoch, as others render it, the firstborn of Cain? Answer: Philo and Josephus seem to think so. And since Cain named his fine work, the first city he founded, after his son, it is not incredible that this son was Cain's firstborn. Yet this cannot be clearly gathered from God's word. For not everyone who is named first is a firstborn. Moreover, Chanoch means "trained" in Hebrew, and "educated" in Latin and Greek; either because Cain his father wished him to be such, and so called him, or because he would show by his own example how he ought to be trained in the fear of God. Philo has omitted this explanation of the name among his Hebrew names. But let us come to the third chapter, in which the propagation of Cain's family after his brother Abel, whom he had killed, is described.

units.la: Ad XIII. Propagatio Caini familiæ.
units.tr: Chapter 13. The Propagation of Cain's Family

units.la: Quaeritur, Cur Deus multiplicauerit genus & familiam Caini, quum ille esset tam impurus: cur non potius cum sine liberis suscepto mori voluerit Gen. 4. 17
units.tr: Question: Why did God multiply the race and family of Cain, since he was so wicked? Why did he not rather want Cain to die without offspring? Gen. 4. 17

units.la: R. Deus natura non tantum bonus, verumetiam benignus & clemens benefacit omnibus, id est tam malis quam bonis, vt est Mat 5.45.46. Ergo eadem caussa genus Caini, quantumuis mali, multiplicauit & accreuit. Praterea quum in genere dixisset cuiuis rerum generi Deus, [Crescite & multiplicamini] oportuit genus quoque humanum hanc Dei benedictionem sentire, ac proinde crescere sine ex bonis siue ex malis homines nascerentur. Gignunt enim mali liberos, non quidem quatenus mali sunt, sed quatenus homines, vt ait Augustinus contra Iulianum. Q. Cur tot homines ex Caino improbo nati sunt, & ipsi quoque improbi, minimeque Dei Ecclesia, prius quam Sethus nasceretur, vel Sethi posteri vlli in quibus tamen fuit Ecclesia Dei, quum hos prius, quam illos nasci ac propagari oporteret, vt boni piique mores prius, quam mali in Mundo, atque inter homines obtinerent florerentve Gen.4 & 5 R. Quandoquidem homines natiua bonitatem, quam a Deo primum acceperant, non seruarunt: sed magna sua culpa in improbitatem & prauitatem conuerterunt, aequum fuit vt tales nascerentur, & multiplicarentur homines, quales ipsi seipsos effecerant. Quare improbi & mali homines primum post peccatum extiterunt, non autem recti probiue, quales iam nasci natura nulli possunt, vt effectum sua illius in Deum nefaria rebellionis homines ipsi perciperent ac viderent. Tale igitur multiplicatum est genus humanum (& quidem sic postulante Dei iustitia, & poena peccato imposita) quale se reddiderat, nimirum nefarium & sceleratu, non modo malum. Quod autem postea Deus Sethum virum bonum dedit Mundo, ex quo propagata est ipsius Ecclesia, id fia, id preter ordinem nature humane iam corrupta factum est, singularissima videlicet Dei Opt. Max. in genus humanum misericordia, ne totum genus hominum periret, non modo hic diluuio, quod secutum est: sed etiā post hanc vitam æterno exitio, quod sceleratis in futuro seculo infertur. Vt igitur Deus ostenderet Ecclesiam suam, quæ in his terris est, non naturā, sed gratiâ nasci, & esse Ecclesiam, voluit primùm Caini filios existere, id est, homines tales, quales seipsos per peccatum suum effecěre, vt quæ appareret in aliis hominibus probitas, & emendatio vitæ, illa non naturæ hominum, non Legi genituræ: sed soli Dei gratia tribueretur. Q. Cur multi ex Caini, & Sethi dissimillimarum tamen stirpiū & generum posteris fuerunt, vel moribus, vel nomine similes, & quidem nomine plures, vt habet vetus versio nominum: vt autem recens, & eruditior, saltem hi tres fuere inter se cognomines, nempe Hanoch filium improbi Caini, Gen. 4. 17: & Hanoch filius Ieredi, ex familia Sethi pÿ, Gen. 5. 18: itē Metuschael filius Iradi, ex familia Caini, Gen 4: 18, & Metuschelah filius pÿ Hanochi Gen. 5. 21. Denique Lemech bigamus, filius Metuschaelis, ex stirpe Caini, Gen. 4. 19: & Lemech pius & pater Noachi filius Metuschelah pÿ ex genere Sethi, Gen. 5. 26. Moribus autem longè plures Sethi posteri fuerunt similes posteris Caini, qui vnà cum illis propterea diluuio perierunt.
units.tr: Answer: God, who is good by nature, and not merely good but kind and merciful, does good to all, that is, to bad and good alike, as Matt. 5. 45, 46 says. Therefore the same cause multiplied and increased the race of Cain, however wicked it was. Moreover, since God had said in general to every kind of thing, [Increase and multiply] it was fitting that the human race also should feel this blessing of God, and so men should be born and multiply whether from good or from bad stock. For the wicked beget children, not indeed insofar as they are wicked, but insofar as they are human, as Augustine says against Julian. Question: Why were so many men born from the wicked Cain, and were themselves wicked, and in no way the Church of God, before Seth was born; or why were there any descendants of Seth, in whom nevertheless the Church of God was, when it was fitting that these should be born and spread before those, just as good and pious morals should prevail and flourish in the world and among men before bad ones? Gen. 4 and 5. Answer: Since men did not keep the native goodness they had first received from God, but by their great fault turned it into wickedness and depravity, it was right that men should be born and multiply such as they had made themselves. Therefore wicked and evil men first appeared after the sin, and not upright and good men, such as by nature no one can now be born, so that men themselves might perceive and see the effect of their impious rebellion against God. Thus the human race was multiplied in such a way (and indeed God's justice and the punishment imposed on sin demanded it) as it had made itself: namely, impious and criminal, not merely evil. But that God afterwards gave Seth, a good man, to the world, from whom his Church was propagated, this came about contrary to the order of human nature, now corrupted, by the most singular mercy of God the Best and Greatest towards the human race, so that the whole race of men might not perish, not only in the flood that followed, but also after this life by the eternal destruction that is inflicted on the wicked in the future age. So, that God might show that his Church, which is on this earth, is born not by nature but by grace, and is the Church, he willed first that the sons of Cain should exist, that is, men such as they had made themselves by their sin; so that whatever uprightness and amendment of life appeared in other men would be ascribed not to the nature of men or to the Law of birth, but to the grace of God alone. Question: Why were there many among the descendants of Cain and of Seth, though of most unlike stocks and races, who were similar either in morals or in name, and indeed more were similar in name, as the old version of the names has it; but according to the recent and more learned version, at least these three were namesakes of one another: namely, Hanoch, son of wicked Cain, Gen. 4. 17; and Hanoch, son of Jared, from the family of Seth, a pious man, Gen. 5. 18; likewise Methushael, son of Irad, from the family of Cain, Gen. 4. 18, and Methuselah, son of pious Hanoch, Gen. 5. 21. Finally, Lamech the bigamist, son of Methushael, from the stock of Cain, Gen. 4. 19; and Lamech the pious, father of Noah, son of Methuselah the pious, from the race of Seth, Gen. 5. 26. But in morals there were far more descendants of Seth like the descendants of Cain, who therefore perished together with them in the flood.

units.la: R. Q uod moribus corruptissimis fuerunt plerique, Sethi pÿ posteri, similesq, posteris impÿ Caini, factum est ex communi lege nascendi, & ex conditione pœna, cui post peccatum genus humanum vniuersum est obnoxium, nimirum vt ex peccatoribus (quales iam natura sunt omnes & singuli homines Eph. 2. 3) peccatores nascantur, Iob. 14. Ergo iam nascuntur omnes homines natura corrupti, filij irae Dei, vitiosi, Psal. 51. 7. Ex quo fit, ut quia posteri Sethi erant homines, essent quoq; natura mali & depravati, atque hoc in ijs naturalis vitiositas & manstt, & aulla est, in quibus eam Deus suo Spiritu S. non correxit, compressitve. Inde illa morum similitudo pravorum in posteris dissimillimorum Patrum nempe Sethi, & Caini. Porro nominum similitudo nihil habet incomodi. Constat enim iisdem duntaxat literis & syllabis: non autem moribus iisdem, quum qui ex Sethi prosapia fuerunt, cognomines posteris Caini fuerint pissimi: illi vero Cainiani pessimi, & Numinis contemptores. Ac fortasse ad nominum ipsorum significationem attendebant py Parentes, dum filijs suis haec nomina, quae impij sibi vsurparat, imponebant, non autem ad illos Caini liberos, qui eadem appellatione fuerant nominati. Ergo miseriam huius vitae eiusmodi vocibus designabant etiam py Patres in vocandis sic filijs suis. nam Hanoch seu Chanoch significat eruditu: Metuschael vel Metusehalah, mortem suam vel exitum suum a Deo postulantem potius, quam in his terris diuturnam vitam: Lemech, pauperem, afflictum, & vexatu, vt docet Philo in nominibus Hebraicis, & ipsa themati ratio id probat lingua Hebraea peritis. Porro non fuerit fortasse iniucundum ea, quae de Caini generationibus observat Augustinus, hoc loco transcribere. Is enim lib. 15. Ciuit. Dei, cap. 17. sic ait, [Hucusque porrecta sunt omnes generationes Caini, quae sunt omnes ab Adam octo (annumerato ipso Adamo)
units.tr: Answer: That most of the descendants of pious Seth were of most corrupt morals, and like the descendants of impious Cain, happened by the common law of being born and by the condition of the punishment to which the whole human race has been subject since the sin: namely, that sinners (as all and each of men are now by nature, Eph. 2. 3) should be born from sinners, Job 14. Therefore all men are now born corrupt by nature, children of the wrath of God, sinful, Ps. 51. 7. From this it follows that, because the descendants of Seth were men, they were also evil and depraved by nature; and this natural sinfulness remained in them, and there is no one in whom God has not corrected or restrained it by his Holy Spirit. Hence that similarity of wicked morals among the descendants of the most unlike fathers, namely Seth and Cain. Moreover, the similarity of names has no inconvenience. For it consists only in the same letters and syllables, not in the same morals, since those who were from the stock of Seth, though namesakes of the descendants of Cain, were most pious, while those were most wicked Cainites and despisers of the Divine Majesty. And perhaps the pious parents paid attention to the meaning of the names themselves when they imposed on their sons these names, which the impious had usurped for themselves, and not to those children of Cain who had been called by the same appellation. Therefore the pious fathers also, in naming their sons so, signified by such words the misery of this life. For Hanoch or Chanoch means instructed; Methushael or Methusehalah means one who asks God for his death or departure rather than a long life on this earth; Lamech means poor, afflicted and vexed, as Philo teaches in his book on Hebrew names, and the very reason of the theme proves it to those skilled in the Hebrew language. Moreover, it will perhaps not be unwelcome to transcribe here what Augustine observes about the generations of Cain. For he, in book 15 of the City of God, chapter 17, speaks thus: [Thus far have been set out all the generations of Cain, which are eight from Adam (counting Adam himself),

units.la: py ... (footnote text as printed in the margin, not legible enough to transcribe) dámo)septem vsque ad Lamech,qui duarum maritu̅ vxoru̅ fuit: & oƈtaua est generatio in filijs eius,in quibus cōmemoratur & fœmina. Vbi eleganter significatu̅ est terrenam ciuitatem vsque insui finem carnales habituram generationes, quæ marium fœminarumq; coniunƈtione proueniunt. Sicut autem Cain, qui interpretatur Possessio, terrena conditor ciuitatis,& filius eius (in cuius nomine condita est) Enoch, qui interpretatur Dedicatio,indicat istam ciuitatem & initium,& finem habere terrenum,vbi nihil speratur amplius,quàm quod in hoc seculo cerni potest. Sic Seth interpretatur Resurrećtio,&c.] Q. Cur Deus Caini posteros tam indufrios esse voluit, vt artium non modò ad vićtum necessariarum,verumetiam ad voluptatem comparatarū autores,inuentoresque essent,præsertim quū iis Dei donis in se collatis superbierint postea,& Deum ipsum contempserint. R. Quoniam Deus beneficus est,etiam hæc dona sua tam egregia in homines istos improbos contulit,vt eos magis redderet inexcusabiles. Sed dona hæc fuerunt terrena duntaxat,& tēporalia:non autem spiritualia & salutaria. Hæc enim postrema familiæ Sethi,id est, Ecclesia sua Deus reseruauit, quemadmodū demostrabitur postea. Fuerunt autem homines isti posteri Caini seculū hoc duntaxat, vitamq; terrenam diligētes terreni,& carnales:ac proinde in iis quoq; rebus & artibus terrenis vehementer industry, iuxta illud Christi, [Filij huius seculi prudentiores sunt filijs lucis in suo genere, Luc.16.8 ] Sic Ethnicis regibus Deus largitus est Monarchias huius mundi, non autem Dauidi,vel suæ Ecclesiæ. Nam meliora dona filijs suis,vti filys Sethi,(qualis est Fides, Pietas, Prophetia) Deus dat:minora vero alys,vti posterù istis Caini artes tantum terrenas. Sed iam de capite 14. tractandum.
units.tr: ... seven up to Lamech, who was the husband of two wives; and the eighth generation is in his sons, among whom a woman is also mentioned. Here it is elegantly signified that the earthly city will have carnal generations, which come about by the union of males and females, until the end of the world. Just as Cain, who is interpreted Possession, the earthly founder of the city, and his son (in whose name the city was founded) Enoch, who is interpreted Dedication, indicate that this city has an earthly beginning and end, where nothing is hoped for beyond what can be seen in this age, so Seth is interpreted Resurrection, etc.] Question: Why did God want the descendants of Cain to be so industrious that they were the authors and inventors of arts not only necessary for living but also devised for pleasure, especially since they afterwards grew proud of those gifts of God conferred on them and despised God himself? Answer: Since God is beneficent, he also bestowed these gifts of his, so remarkable, on those wicked men, so as to make them more inexcusable. But these gifts were only earthly and temporal, not spiritual and saving. For these last things God reserved for the family of Seth, that is, for his Church, as will be shown afterwards. Now those men, the descendants of Cain, loved this age only and this earthly life, and were earthly and carnal; and therefore they were also very diligent in those earthly things and arts, according to that saying of Christ, [The sons of this age are wiser in their own kind than the sons of light, Luke 16. 8.] So God granted to the heathen kings the monarchies of this world, but not to David or to his Church. For God gives better gifts to his own sons, such as faith, piety and prophecy, to the sons of Seth; but lesser ones to others, such as the merely earthly arts to the descendants of Cain. But now we must treat of chapter 14.

units.la: Ad XIIII. Bigamia Prima, seu prima Coniugij violatio.
units.tr: Chapter XIV. The First Bigamy, or the First Violation of Marriage.

units.la: Quaeritur, quid hac Lamechi Bigamia fuit, Gen.4 19. R. Fœdissima puritatis vinculi, coniugalis ac Matrimonij corruptela, eaq; prima & publica. Nam ante Lamechum istum instituntio coiugij, qualem Deus primum præscripserat, vt Vnu duntaxat uni adhareret, sanctè fuerat semper observata. Hac autem impurum iste, lascivus, libidinosus, superbus, & mulierosus homo primus violavit, & reliquis mortalibus ad eam violandam dux & exemplū fuit. Itaque scribit Philo Judæus in Antiquit. Biblic. [Ceperunt postea habitatores terræ exemplum hoc secuti etiam violare uxores alienas, eásque contaminare, nimirum unusquisque proximi sui uxorem.] Sic nimirū paulatim crescebat vis peccati, hominumq; immanis libido, audacia, & impudentia, præsertim in Caini familia. Quemadmodū igitur Cainus primus homicidiū perpetrauit: sic iste Lamechus ex eius stirpe primū stupri admisit, sed postea & sequenti tempore. Ex quo fit, vt in secunda Legis Divinæ Tabula præceptum [Non mœchaberis] ordine ac proximè sequatur illud, [Non occides] vti hæc vitia publicè & consequenter ab hominibus perpetrata sunt. Illud antè Non mœchaberis, vti & illud Non occides, mentibus hominū ex primæua lucis reliquis inhærebat, & & insculpta erat, Rom. 2. 14: hominesq; inexcusabiles reddebant. Q. Cur tàtopere Bigamia in Lamecho isto damnatur, quum Iacobus Patriarcha, Dauid, & alij pleriq; viri sancti multas simul vxores habuerint, retinuerintque, Gen 30, 2. Sam. 3. 2. 3. R. Quoniam tum primus iste tato scelerys fenestram patefecit, aliisque suo exemplo praeiuit: tum etiam quod sola libidine, & turpi impetu & carnis lasciuia impulsus, id fecit: Illi verò non vitist fœda libidine, sed ad promissionem Dei de futura feminis sui numerosa prole, & benedictione respicientes, duxerunt habuerunt q; simul vxores plures, quemadmodū scribit Augustinus. Et tamen etiam illud ipsum in Patribus illis, quantumuis alioqui piis, dànat Malachias Propheta cap. 2. 15. Q. Cur & quorsum Lamechus iste tam truculentus fuit, & apud mulierculas de suo furore in eum, cui trafceretur: & de futura sui vindicta tam iactabundè gloriatur, aut concionatur, Gen. 4. 23. R. Videtur sic minitabundus inter mulierculas fuisse Lamechus iste, quòd suis illis vxoribus metum sui inycere voluit, quas se contrarius & fas retinere, teste propria conscientia, sciebat, ne quid ille nimirū in eum tentarent, & aggrederentur: sed vt metu illo perculse eum timeret, ac vererentur. Itaq; minatur grauissimam fore pœnam, si quisquam ipsum occiderit, longéque duriorem, quàm si quispiam Cainū volens & ex professo interfecerit, quam pœnā Cainica pœna septuplo maiorem fore Deus ipse pronūtiauerat Gen. 4. 15, & 24. Ergo trux iste videri voluit, tum quòd omnes improbi (qualis Lamechus iste fuit) sint feroces, & natura superbi: tū quòd sibi à suis vxoribus vti dixi, metuebat. Et fortasse iam iurgia inter istas uxores suas domestica (quae in Bigamia sunt, plurima & ordinaria) senserat Lamechus. Quanquam autem amor muliebris dicatur emollire hominum crudele, & ferum ingenium, vti Polyphemi ferociā lenit amor Galatea: tamen non fuit mitior, quod esset mulierosus, iste Lamechus. Q. Vtrum Lamechus iste Cainum, qui erat e suis maioribus, occidit. R. Hoc quidem non nulli censent, quod tamen nusquam ex Dei verbo poterit probari. Certe ex hac Lamechi oratione apparet & tunc Cainū adhuc vixisse: & poenam Caini posteris eius notā fuisse. Haec autem omnia, meo iudicio, contigerunt ante natum Sethum, quia Moses sequitur ordinem, seriemq; temporis, & historia: ac proinde ante annos 130. à Mundo primum condito, Gen. 5. 3. Sed de capite XV. iam agamus.
units.tr: Question: What was the significance of this bigamy of Lamech, Gen. 4:19? Answer: It was the most shameful corruption of the bond of purity, of marriage, and a first and public one. For before Lamech, the institution of marriage as God first prescribed it, that one man should cling to one woman alone, had always been kept sacredly. But this impure, wanton, lustful, proud and womanizing man was the first to violate it, and he became the leader and example for the rest of mortals in violating it. So Philo the Jew writes in the Biblical Antiquities: [Afterwards the inhabitants of the earth, following this example, also began to violate the wives of others and defile them, each man indeed the wife of his neighbour.] Thus the power of sin and the monstrous lust, boldness and shamelessness of men gradually grew, especially in the family of Cain. Just as Cain first committed murder, so Lamech of his line first committed fornication, and later in the following time. From this it follows that in the second table of the divine law the precept [You shall not commit adultery] comes directly after [You shall not kill], just as these sins were committed publicly and in succession by men. The earlier prohibition, You shall not commit adultery, as also You shall not kill, clung to men's minds from the remnant of primeval light, and was engraved there, Rom. 2:14, and made men inexcusable. Q. Why is bigamy so strongly condemned in this Lamech, when the patriarch Jacob, David and many other holy men had and kept several wives at once, Gen. 30:2; 2 Sam. 3:2-3? A. Because this first man opened the door to so great a crime and went before others by his example; and also because he was driven only by lust, a shameful impulse and carnal wantonness. Those men, however, did not act out of foul lust, but looked to God's promise of a numerous offspring from their seed and to the blessing, as Augustine writes. And yet the prophet Malachi, ch. 2:15, condemns even that practice in those fathers, however otherwise pious. Q. Why and to what end was this Lamech so fierce, and why does he boast and brag so arrogantly among his women about his rage against the man who wounded him and about the vengeance he would take in future, Gen. 4:23? A. Lamech seems to have been threatening among the women so that he might strike fear into his wives, whom he knew, by his own conscience, he was holding back contrary to right; he wanted them to fear and dread him, lest they should try anything against him and attack him. So he threatens that the penalty will be most severe if anyone kills him, and far harsher than if someone killed Cain willingly and deliberately; God himself had declared that the penalty for Cain would be seven times greater, Gen. 4:15, 24. So this brute wished to appear fierce, both because all the wicked, such as Lamech was, are proud and fierce by nature, and because, as I said, he feared his wives. Perhaps Lamech had already noticed the domestic quarrels among his wives, which are numerous and ordinary in bigamy. Although love for a woman is said to soften the cruel and savage nature of men, as the love of Galatea softened the ferocity of Polyphemus, this Lamech was not any gentler for being a womanizer. Q. Did this Lamech kill Cain, who was one of his ancestors? A. Some hold this, but it can never be proved from the word of God. Certainly from Lamech's speech it appears that Cain was still alive then, and that the punishment on Cain was known to his descendants. In my judgment all these things happened before Seth was born, since Moses follows the order and sequence of time and of the history, and so they took place before the year 130 from the creation of the world, Gen. 5:3. But now let us turn to chapter XV.

units.la: Ad XV. Pastoritiae artis Incrementum.
units.tr: Chapter XV. The Growth of the Art of Herding.

units.la: Queritur, Cur Pastoritia ars potius aucta, exculta, fuerit, quam Agricultura, quum & Agricultura quoq; ipsa variam rerum cognitionem habeat, & varias partes. R. Primum Pastoritia seu Pecuariam artem differre ab Agricultura praeclare docet M. Varro lib. 1. cap. 2. Re Rustica his verbis, [Quare tota pastio, quae coniungitur à plerisque cū Agricultura, magis ad Pastorem, quam ad Agricolam pertinere videtur. Quocirca Principes, qui utrique rei praeponuntur, vocabulis quoque sunt diuersi, quod unus vocatur Villicus, alter Magister pecoris.] Deinde plures esse partes Agriculturae, i. disciplinae agrorum bene colendorum docet, traditque idem Varro, easque ostendit esse quatuor, vt est cap. 4. lib. 1. eiusdem operis. Cur tamen potius auctha, distinctaque fuerit ars Pastoritia, quàm Agricultura, ratio hæc mihi videtur esse, nempe, Quod quum post mortem Abelis (qui fuit Pecuarius seu Pastor) à Caino occisi fuisset vel in odiu Abelis, vel quoniam Adamus, & Cainus (cuius sola posteritas restabat) erant Agricolæ, non Pastores, ars Pastoritia fuisset intermissa: tamen postea repetita fuit à posteris Caini, idque suadente hominum & necessitate, & cõmoditate. Et necessitate quidem, quoniam carne Animalium homines vescebantur post peccatum: Commoditate vero, propterea quòd magnum inde, i. ex ea pastione lucrü faciebant. Quod verü esse probat Plinius lib. 18. cap. 3. Natural. Hist. qui scribit diu ex solis pecoribus inter homines vectigal fuisse. Vnde, i. à pecude pecunia quoque dicta est, quemadmodum etiam tradit Varro. Ergo lucri quoque sui causa homines, posteri Caini, Pastoritiam artem repetiuerunt, eámque potissimum auxerunt, & eam in disciplinam habuerunt, statuerunt q; Artem aliquâ potius, quàm in Agricultura, quoniam, vt docet idem Varro lib. 1. de re Rust. plures partes ea cura habet, quàm Agricultura. Habet enim primũ nouem, id est, ter ternas: Agricultura verò solùm quatuor. Earum autem nouem partium pars vnaquæque partes quoque habet nouenas, quarũ in pecore parando necessariæ quatuor: altera in pascendo totidem: vna cõmunis. Ita fiunt omnes Pecuariæ artis partes minimùm octoginta & vna, & quidem necessariæ, nec parue. Hæc Varro. Ex quibus apparet quàm diligenter tractãda, cognoscenda, tradendáve sit ac fuerit hæc Ars, utq; distribuenda in suas species, quod fecit Iabal filius Lamechi, Gen. 4. 20. Imo etiam pecoris pascendi gratia, novum vitæ genus à suis Maioribus, nêpe Caini prioribus filijs (qui in vrbibus habitabat) diuersum Iabal secutus est, ac instituit, nimirum vt sub Papilionibus, Mapalibus seu Tugurijs ac tentorijs sequendi transferendi q; pecoris gratia habitarêt homines. Quod idem postea Abrahamus fecit, & Iacobus Patriarcha, Gen. 31. 40 & 47. 3; & Rechabita verè pecuarijs illis similes, Ierem. 35. Imò præclariorê visam esse Pastoritiā, quàm Agriculturam, apparet ex eo, quod, vt Varro scribit, veteres vocabant Pecuariā artem Primam, & Incentiuam: Hanc autem Agricultura, Posteriorem, & succentiuam. Ergo Pastoritia meritò, sic vsu suadente, priùs exculta est. Q. Quinā fuerint isti Iabalis posteri, qui in Tentorijs pascendi pecoris gratiā habitabant, fuerúntque Nomades & vagi, vtrum Scytha, an Afri? R. Nec ý Afri erát, nec Scytha ý, quos nouit Orbis, habuitque post Dilunium. Nam posteri omnes Caini illa terrarum eluuione fuerunt extincti. Verùm hoc vitæ genus (quod hic commemoratur, estq; eiusmodi, vt pascendi sequendiq; cômodius pecoris gratiā, homines sub papilionibus habitêt, nec certas sedes habeant) hoc, inquam, vitæ genus à Iabale primùm institutū secuti sunt eius posteri: & ys deletis atque orbe renouato ý, qui & in Scythia maximè Asiatica (quæ pertinet ad Orientem) & in Africa habendi tuendiq; pecoris gratiā in Magalibus, curribus, & tentorijs postea vixerūt totū suæ vitæ spatium. Ac quidem ý Scytha, qui sic vitam suâ instituerũt, dicti sunt Hamaxobij. Afri verò, qui sic palantes pecudes pascebãtur, appellati sunt No· mades: ex veteri nepe eius vita memoria, quæ à Iabale primũ instituta, deinde à filys Noachi retenta fuerat, & culta postea diluuiũ. Q. Cur hoc Iabalis inuentũ à Mose laudatur, ac commemoratur, quod miserrimum & laboriosissimum, & plane homine indignũ vitæ genus continere videtur, vtpote in quo homines mancipia & viles perpetuique serui pecudum euadant, vagi fiant: quodque etiam nonnulle gentes exosæ fuerunt, tanquam humanæ societati contrarium, velut Aegyptij, Gen 46. 34: & Persæ, vt in Cyropædia tradit Xenophon. R. Ipsa quidem hominũ seruitus, & occupatio tam affixa additǽque pecudibus, est pœna peccati. Pecudes enim homini inseruire debent (cuius causa sunt conditæ) non autem homo pecudibus. Nec enim pecudũ gratiâ natus est homo. Iudustria verò scientiáque huius cura & pecorũ pastionis rectè tractanda, & gerenda in tanta humani ingenij cecitate, & tanta tamen huius rerũ generis vtilitate, est profectò dono Dei Opt. Max. & ars maximè laudanda. Q uare quicquid est in ea re, vel arte laboris, tedij, difficultatis totum id est finctum peccati, Gen.31.40: quicquid autem in eadem est industriæ, ingenij, vtilitatis, est pulcherrimum munus Dei. Ex quo fit, vt hoc ipsum à Mose iure & laudetur, & commemoretur. Q. Vtrum hoc vaga & pecuaria vitæ genus sit à Christianis hominibus vllo pacto sequendum, quũ qui illud amplectuntur, sint ἀπόλιδες, id est, sine certa vlla ciuitate. Id quod inter Dei maledictiones recensetur, Deut.28.52, Psal.109.10. R. Quum Abrahamus, Isaacus, & Iacobus Dei serui hanc vitae rationem amplexi fuerint, non esset à viro Christiano aliena, damnandáve hæc vita, Gen. 21, & 31.40. Nam pro vel regionis ratio ac cōmoditas suadet, vel mores hominum (inter quos versamur) nos mouent, vel agricole Statarij, vel pecuarij vagi, vel certi loci & vrbis ciues & incolæ, vel contrà palantes viuere & esse possumus, modò Deum verū verè & ex ipsius verbo in quouis vitæ genere colamus. Nihil enim interest statariā, an eiusmodi palantem vitam degamus, modo ne simus Σπολιάς, vel odio humani generis, vel temerè per Orbē terrarum discursandi animo, quod est agrestiū vel dissoluti hominis: non autem humani mansuetiq. Et hæc de capite xv. dicta sunto. Verum ad xvi. accedamus.
units.tr: Question: Why was the art of herding rather than agriculture developed and cultivated, when agriculture too has a wide range of knowledge and various parts? Answer: First, Marcus Varro clearly teaches in book 1, ch. 2, of his Rustic Matters, that herding or the art of keeping livestock differs from agriculture, in these words: [Wherefore the whole pasturage, which many join with agriculture, seems to belong more to the herdsman than to the farmer. Hence the chiefs who are set over each of these have different names as well: one is called the overseer, the other the master of the flock.] Then he teaches that agriculture has several parts, that is, the discipline of cultivating fields well, and Varro shows that there are four of them, as in ch. 4 of book 1 of the same work. Why, however, the art of herding was rather developed and distinguished than agriculture seems to me to be explained as follows: after the death of Abel, who was the herdsman or shepherd, slain by Cain, either out of hatred for Abel or because Adam and Cain (whose posterity alone remained) were farmers and not herdsmen, the art of herding was interrupted. Afterwards, however, it was taken up again by the descendants of Cain, urged on both by necessity and by convenience. By necessity, since men fed on the flesh of animals after the fall; by convenience, because they made a great profit from that pasturage. That this is true Pliny proves in book 18, ch. 3, of his Natural History, where he writes that for a long time revenue among men came from livestock alone. Hence money too was named from cattle (pecus), as Varro also teaches. So the descendants of Cain took up the art of herding again for the sake of gain too, developed it above all, made it a discipline, and established it as an art rather than as agriculture, since, as Varro teaches in book 1 of On Rustic Matters, that care has more parts than agriculture: it has nine, that is, three times three; agriculture has only four. Each of those nine parts in turn has nine parts, of which four are needed for acquiring livestock, the same number for pasturing them, and one is common to both. Thus the parts of the art of herding come to at least eighty-one, and these are necessary and not small. So Varro. From this it appears how carefully this art must be studied, learned and handed down, and how it was distributed into its kinds, as Jabal, son of Lamech, did, Gen. 4:20. Indeed, for the sake of pasturing livestock, Jabal followed and established a new way of life, different from that of his ancestors, namely of Cain's earlier sons, who lived in cities: men were to live in tents, booths, huts and pavilions, moving with and following their flocks. Abraham later did the same, and the patriarch Jacob, Gen. 31:40; 47:3, and the Rechabites, who were truly like those herdsmen, Jer. 35. That herding seemed more distinguished than agriculture appears from the fact that, as Varro writes, the ancients called the art of herding the first and the incentive art, but agriculture the later and the subsequent art. So herding was rightly developed first, as experience advised. Q. Who were the descendants of Jabal who lived in tents for the sake of pasturing livestock, and were nomads and wanderers? Were they Scythians or Africans? A. They were neither Africans nor those Scythians known to the world, nor did they exist after the Flood. For all the descendants of Cain perished in that flood of waters. But this way of life, which is mentioned here and is of such a kind that men live in tents and have no fixed dwelling in order to pasture and follow livestock more conveniently, this way of life, I say, was first established by Jabal, and his descendants followed it. After those people were destroyed and the world renewed, others lived this life their whole lives long, in the great Asiatic Scythia (which lies toward the East) and in Africa, in huts, wagons and tents for the sake of keeping and tending livestock. Those Scythians who ordered their lives in this way were called Hamaxobii, while the Africans who pastured their roving flocks in this way were called Nomads, from the ancient memory of that way of life, first established by Jabal, then kept by the sons of Noah and afterwards cultivated after the Flood. Q. Why does Moses praise and record this invention of Jabal, when it seems to be a most wretched and laborious way of life, altogether unworthy of man, in which men become slaves and menials and perpetual servants of cattle, and become wanderers? Some nations also hated it as contrary to human society, such as the Egyptians, Gen. 46:34, and the Persians, as Xenophon relates in the Cyropaedia. A. Indeed the servitude and occupation of men, so bound up with and added to cattle, is itself a punishment for sin. For cattle ought to serve man (for whose sake they were created), not man cattle. Man was not born for the sake of cattle. But the industry and skill of tending and properly managing the pasturing of flocks, given such great human blindness yet such great usefulness of these things, is certainly a gift of God, the Best and Greatest, and a most praiseworthy art. Therefore whatever labour, tedium or difficulty there is in that art is the fruit of sin, Gen. 31:40; but whatever diligence, skill and usefulness there is in it is a most beautiful gift of God. So it comes about that Moses rightly praises and records this. Q. Is this wandering and pastoral way of life to be followed by Christians in any way, since those who embrace it are [ἀπόλιδες], that is, without any fixed city, which is counted among God's curses, Deut. 28:52; Ps. 109:10? A. Since Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the servants of God, embraced this way of life, it was not alien to a Christian man, nor is this life to be condemned, Gen. 21; 31:40. For whether the nature and convenience of the region persuades us, or the customs of the people among whom we live move us, we can live either as settled farmers or as wandering herdsmen, or as citizens and residents of a particular place and city, or conversely as wanderers, provided we worship the true God truly and according to his own word in whatever way of life we live. For it makes no difference whether we live a settled life or a wandering one of this kind, provided we are not [ἄπολις], either out of hatred for the human race or out of a rash desire to roam the world, which belongs to the wild or dissolute man, not to the civil and gentle one. And let these things be said about chapter XV. Let us now proceed to chapter XVI.

units.la: Ad XVI. Artis Musicæ Inuentio.
units.tr: Chapter XVI. The Invention of the Art of Music.

units.la: Queritur, Cur Deus voluit Musicam statim, atq; ab ipso penè Mundi initio & exordio inueniri ab hominibus? Gen. 4.21. R. Primùm, vt suam in genus humanum quanuis perditū & per se miserum benignitatem testaretur Deus. Præclarè enim Augustinus lib. 22. Ciuit. Dei, cap. 24. [Præter artes, ait, & bene viuendi, & ad immortalem perueniendi fœlicitatem (quæ virtutes vocantur, & solâ Dei gratiâ, quæ in Christo est, filijs promissionis regni, donantur) nónne humano ingenio tot, tātæque artes sunt inuentæ, & exercitæ partim necessariæ, partim voluntariæ (aliy voluptariæ) vt tam excellens vis mentis atq; rationis, in his etiā rebus (quæ superfluæ, imò periculosas, perniciosasque appetit) quantum bonum habeat in natura, vnde ista potuit vel inuenire, vel discere, vel exercere, testetur? Vestimentorum & adificiorum ad opera quàm mirabilia, quam stupeda industria humana peruenit? quò in agriculturà quò in nauigatione profecerit: quæ in fabricatione quorùmque vasorum, vel etiam statuarum, & pisturarū varietate excogitauerit? &c.] Deinde vt hac ratione etiam ad pietatem suique cultum ardetius homines excitaret. Quod enim ad suam voluptatem ho- mines conuerterunt, hoc est, Musica instrumenta, id ipsum Deus in externo suo cultu adhiberi etiam tunc volebat, vti postea sub Lege ab eo data factu ac præceptū est, Psal. 149, & 150: quò magis accenderet homines etiam ex istis rebus externis ad se colendum, & ad publicos cœtus sacros seu Ecclesiasticos, vbi adorabatur, frequentandū. Denique vt eodem libentius conuenirēt homines. Musica igitur vsi sunt primi homines psalledo, instrumentaq; pulsando, vt seipsos obleCtaret. Deus autem eam artem statim inueniri voluit, vt hoc quoq; rerū genere homines ad laudes Dei canedas vterentur. Porrò hic ordo fuit artium ab hominibus excusarū ac repertarum, vt in iis primum inueniendis, exercendis, excolendisq; studium & operam suam ponerent, quæ ad vičtum humanum erant omnino necessaria, qualis est Agricultura, & Pastoritia. Postea in iis excogitandis laborarent, quæ ad Dei cultum adhibitæ sunt, erantque ad hominū delectationem coparatæ, qualis est Musica. Denique in iis reperiēdis sudarent, quæ ad hominū tuitionem, defensionem, & commoditatem erat necessaria, qualis ferraria ars, fabrilis seu mechanica. Sed & illud quoque dici potest, Musicam summā Dei prouidentiā inter primas artes inuentā, idque à Caini posteris viris industriis, vt ingenij eorũ ferocitas huius artis Musices beneficio & suauitate leniretur, ac quodammodo molliretur. Caeterum Artes ista omnes reperta sustulerunt animos hominum, atque arrogātes effecerunt, vt magis contumaces in Deū, sua tamen culpa & ingratitudine, euaderent: Nam de eorundem hominum, qui harū artium inuentores extitēre, pietate & fide in Deum, aut Dei metu nihil traditur à Mose, neque etiā à Philone in Antiquit Bibl. neque à Josepho lib.1. Antiquit.Iudaic.cap.4. qui tamen hac commemorant. Ergo Caini posterorum ingeniū quidem, sed carnale: industria, sed terrena his rationibus commendatur: nō autem pietas, fides, aut probitas Nec enim in istis hominibus fuit Ecclefia Dei, sed in posteris Sethi, de quibus postea. Q. Vtrum ex cœli, Astrorumque motu homines Musicam didicerint, vt vult Plato: an ex ferrariarum officinarū & operarum in illis ferrum in numerū tundentium, tinnitu & sono numeroso, qui percipitur auribus, quemadmodum sensit Pythagoras, vt Macrobius in Comment. in lib. M. Ciceronis de Somnio Scipionis refert. R. Primum, Platonis sententia, vt ait Plautus, est ΛΙΕΣΤ ΛΙΕΣΩΝ id est, nuga nugerrima. Q uomodo enim, aut vbi vnquam homines cōcentum illum cœlorum in terris audiuerūt? Secundo loco, opinio Pythagoræ falsa est: nam Musica priùs inuenta est, quàm ars fabrilis aut ferraria. Q uāobrem ex huius numeroso tinnitu & sono illa reperiri non potuit. Q uid igitur? Q uum essent Caini posteri, qui hæ artes pepererūt homines plane terreni, & voluptarij, industrij tamen, (vtpote qui semina primi illius vigoris adhuc retinerēt, quem hominū ingenijs Deus Deus indiderat)istas omnes artes facilè excogitarunt. Primùm quidem eas,quæ victui erât necessariæ: postea verò voluptarias, magnis tamen ingenij viribus[cõnixi, tamen libidini carnis immersi,vt apparet. Vetustissimam autem fuisse artem Musicam præsertim Organicam(nec enim de illa,quæ vocalis est, .i. fit hominum voce modulata certis partibus, hic agitur) satis intelligi potest ex antiquissima historia Arionis,qui Musicus fuit,de quo & Herodotus,& Ouidius in Fast. & A.Gellius scripserunt. Cur ars Nauigatoria, Mercatura,& Tinctura,aliæque artes vel lucrosæ,vel obleƈtantes animũ,non sunt prius ab hominibus tentatæ & excogitatæ,quàm musica,præsertim Organica? Propterea quod homines nondum eo tempore tam auari erant,quàm fuêre postea,minimèque tam lucro dediti, quàm nunc sunt:atque nondum pecunia & opum splendor tantus tunc repertus erat, quantum postea: Idcirco eæ artes, quæ tota lucri caussa cõparatæ sunt, & exercentur(qualis est nauigatoria,mercatura & similes) minimè quæsierunt primi illius seculi homines:sed has tãtum,quæ victûi necessarium, & voluptatem præberent. Caeteras verò artes,quas χρυσασικὰς , id est,lucratiuas vocant, postea etas inuenit,quû auaritia ad lucra maiora inuestigãda homines impulisset.Tinctura verò & pictura,quanquâ sunt voluptariæ artes, nõdum tamen fuerunt reperta, quòd quæ ex iis capitur voluptas, non tam naturalis est,quàm quæ ex arte Musica: quódque ad Dei cultum tunc non erant,vt hæc,necessariæ,& adhibenda. units.tr: The question is asked: why did God will that music be discovered by men immediately, almost from the very beginning and origin of the world? Gen. 4.21. I answer: first, so that God might bear witness to his kindness toward the human race, though it was lost and miserable in itself. For Augustine says excellently in book 22 of The City of God, chapter 24: [Besides the arts of living well and of attaining immortal happiness (which are called virtues, and are given to the children of the promise of the kingdom by the grace of God alone, which is in Christ), have not so many and so great arts been invented and practised by human genius, some necessary and some voluntary (others pleasurable), so that such an excellent power of mind and reason shows how much good it has in its nature, even in those things which are superfluous, indeed dangerous and destructive, from which it could have found, learned or practised these arts? To what marvellous heights has human industry come in making clothes and buildings, with what astonishing skill has it advanced in agriculture and in navigation, and what varieties of vessels, and even of statues and paintings, has it devised? etc.] Second, so that by this means men might be stirred more eagerly to piety and to the worship of him. For what men turned to their own pleasure, namely musical instruments, God wished to be used even then in his external worship, as was afterwards made and commanded under the Law given by him, Psalm 149 and 150, so that he might kindle men more by these external things to worship him, and to frequent the public sacred or ecclesiastical assemblies where he was adored. Finally, so that men might gather together more willingly. The first men therefore used music, singing psalms and striking instruments, so that they might delight themselves. God, however, willed that this art be discovered at once, so that men might use this kind of thing also for singing the praises of God. Moreover, this was the order of the arts devised and discovered by men: that they should first put their study and effort into discovering, practising and cultivating those arts which were absolutely necessary for human life, such as agriculture and herding. Afterwards they should labour at devising those which were employed in the worship of God and were prepared for human delight, such as music. Finally they should toil at discovering those which were necessary for human protection, defence and convenience, such as the art of the smith, the mechanical or metalworking art. But it can also be said that music was invented among the first arts by the highest providence of God, and that this was done by the industrious men of the posterity of Cain, so that the fierceness of their minds might be softened and in some measure tempered by the benefit and sweetness of this art of music. Otherwise, all these arts, once discovered, lifted up men's minds and made them arrogant, so that they became more stubborn against God, through their own fault and ingratitude. For nothing is recorded by Moses, nor by Philo in the Antiquities of the Bible, nor by Josephus in book 1 of the Jewish Antiquities, chapter 4, concerning the piety and faith in God, or the fear of God, of those men who were the inventors of these arts, although they do record these things. Therefore the talent of Cain's posterity, but a carnal talent, and their industry, but an earthly industry, are commended by these accounts; but not their piety, faith or uprightness. For the Church of God was not among those men, but among the posterity of Seth, of whom more later. Q. Whether men learned music from the motion of the heavens and the stars, as Plato holds, or from the workshops of the smiths and from the workmen beating iron into rhythm, whose ringing and rhythmic sound is perceived by the ears, as Pythagoras thought, as Macrobius reports in his Commentary on Cicero's book on the Dream of Scipio. A. First, Plato's opinion, as Plautus says, is a trifle of trifles [ΛΗΡΟΣ ΛΗΡΩΝ], that is, the most trifling nonsense. For how or when did men ever hear that harmony of the heavens on earth? Second, Pythagoras' opinion is false, for music was discovered before the smith's art or metalworking. Therefore music could not have been found from the rhythmic ringing and sound of these. What then? Since the posterity of Cain, who produced these arts, were entirely earthly and pleasure-loving men, yet industrious (inasmuch as they still retained the seeds of that first vigour which God had implanted in the minds of men), they devised all these arts with ease. First, indeed, those which were necessary for life; afterwards, however, the pleasurable ones, striving with the great strength of their genius, yet immersed in the lust of the flesh, as is evident. That music, especially the instrumental kind (for here we are not speaking of that which is vocal, that is, shaped by the human voice in certain measures), was a very ancient art can be sufficiently understood from the most ancient story of Arion, who was a musician, about whom Herodotus, Ovid in the Fasti, and Aulus Gellius have written. Why were navigation, commerce, dyeing and the other arts, either profitable or pleasing to the mind, not attempted and devised by men before music, especially instrumental music? Because at that time men were not yet as greedy as they later became, nor so given to gain as they now are; nor had the splendour of money and wealth yet been discovered to the great extent it was later. Therefore those arts which are designed and practised entirely for the sake of gain (such as navigation, commerce and similar things) were hardly sought by the men of that first age, but only those which supplied what was necessary for life and gave pleasure. The arts which they call chrysasic [χρυσασικάς], that is, lucrative, the later age invented, when avarice had driven men to seek greater gains. Dyeing and painting, although they are arts of pleasure, had not yet been discovered, because the pleasure derived from them is not as natural as that from the art of music, and because at that time they were not needed or to be employed for the worship of God, as music was. Now Noah is thought to have been the first to have established and learned the art of navigation, by the command of God, when he constructed that most fruitful ark, and steered it through the submersion of the world, so that he himself with his children and the animals placed in it might not perish. And so much for chapter 16 of this history. Now let us proceed to chapter 17, which is also the last.

units.tr: Here the Latin text contains a stray mark, and the author is simply finishing the discussion: Noah builds that most fruitful ark and steers it through the flood of the world, so that he himself, with his children and the animals placed in it, might not perish. And this is what I wanted to say about chapter 16 of this history. Now let us proceed to chapter 17, which is also the last.

units.la: Ad XVII. Artis Ferrariae, & Æraria Inventio.
units.tr: On the Invention of the Smith's Craft and of Bronze Working
