units.la: Quaeritur, Cur ex una Lamechi hominis truculenti & libidinosi, vitiosiq; familia tot, támque industriy novarum artium non modò artifices, sed & inventores extiterint. R. Ut Deus offenderet etiam ea, quae homines habent, naturalia ingenij ornamenta, non pro meritis habere: sed ex mera ipsius gratia accipere, quemadmodum apparet in Befelele, & Ooliabo, Exod. 36. 1.2. iuxta illud, [Omne bonum est supernè à Patre luminum] Iac. 1.17. Ergo vires etiá ingenij, quantumvis naturales, sunt mera Dei in homines dona. Quid enim habent, quod non acceperunt? Quod si acceperunt, cur de iis gloriantur ipsi, & totam eorum donorum laudem cur non acceptam suo autori ferunt? 1.Cor.4.7. Deinde ex iis apparet, magnam eius corruptionis, quae postea totum Mundum inuasit, partem ex una hac eadem Lamechi seuissimi & spurcissimi hominis familia & gente olim emanasse, & ortam esse, quin una illa, primas lucri artes, prima voluptatis incentiua, prima ferocia & audacia exequende instrumenta porrexerit hominibus, dum Pastoritia artis incrementum, musicam, & Ferrariam artes excogitauit. Ergo ab illis Lamechi posteris tanquam ex primo fonte dimanarunt postea hac hæc vitia, nimirum Avaritia, Libido, Sævitia ac Audacia, quæ in aliós mortales postea fuerunt propagata. Refert enim ille, quanquam profanus, scribit, nimirum Tibullus lib. I. Elegia 10. Quis fuit, horrendos primus qui protulit enses? Quàm ferrum, & verè ferreus ille fuit? Tunc cædes hominum generi, tunc prælia nata, Tunc breviór dira mortis aperta via est.
units.tr: Question: Why did so many and such industrious makers of new arts, not only craftsmen but inventors, arise from the one family of Lamech, a savage and lustful man, and a wicked family? Answer: so that God might show that even the natural gifts of talent that men have are not something they possess by merit, but something they receive from his pure grace, as appears in Bezalel and Oholiab, Exod. 36:1-2, according to the saying, "Every good gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights," James 1:17. Therefore even the powers of talent, however natural they may be, are pure gifts of God to men. For what do they have that they have not received? And if they have received it, why do they boast of these things, and why do they not ascribe all the praise of these gifts, as received, to their author? 1 Cor. 4:7. Further, from these things it appears that a great part of that corruption which afterwards invaded the whole world came from this one family and race of the most cruel and filthy man Lamech, and arose there. For this family, which first devised the arts of gain, the first incitements to pleasure, and the first tools for carrying out ferocity and audacity, provided these to men, while it devised the growth of the pastoral art, music, and the smith's art. Therefore from those posterity of Lamech, as from a first spring, these vices flowed afterwards, namely avarice, lust, cruelty and audacity, which were later propagated among other mortals. These vices, the pagan writer Tibullus also reports and describes, book 1, elegy 10: Who was the first to bring forth the dreadful sword? How truly iron was that man! Then slaughter of men was born for the human race, then battles, then the short and dreadful way to death was opened.

units.la: In summa illa Christi sententia quonis tempore vera fuit, Filii huius sæculi prudentiores sunt, & magis industrii in hac vita, quàm lucis seu Dei filii & servi, Luc. 16. 8. Verùm ut multa de istorum hominum, Caini nempe & Lamechi posterorum inductoria, ingenij vivacitate, & viribus narrantur: sic nihil de eorundem in Deum pietate & fide extat. Imò propter hæc ipsa dona ydem isti Deum primi contempserunt, & contemnendi exempla aliis fuerunt, inductaque postea publica nominis Dei Profanatione.
units.tr: In that saying of Christ, it has always been true that "the sons of this age are wiser and more shrewd in their dealings than the sons of light," Luke 16:8. But although many things are told of the cleverness and the powers of these men, namely of Cain and the descendants of Lamech who were the inventors, nothing of their piety or faith toward God is extant. Indeed, because of these very gifts, those same men despised God first, and became examples of contempt for others, and afterwards led to the public profanation of the name of God.

units.la: Q. Utrum Æs & ferrum è terra visceribus eruere noverint homines, ante Ferraria artis inventum: an Tubalcainus simul & metalla ista, eorumque venas dignoscere homines docuerit: & agnita eruere, ac effodere: denique erutā, & è terra effossa malleo cotundere, igne subigere, atque ex iis ita præparatis varia opera fabrilia facere, monstraverit.
units.tr: Question: Did men know how to dig copper and iron out of the bowels of the earth before the invention of the smith's art, or did Tubal-cain teach men both these metals and how to recognise their veins, and, once they were recognised, to dig them out and extract them, and finally to show how the extracted ore, dug out of the earth, could be beaten with a hammer, subdued by fire, and worked from these prepared materials into various metal works?

units.la: R. Omnia hæc docuit homines Tubalcainus, & quidem primus: non solum autem opera quædam & ferramenta ex iis, id est, ex ære & ferro iam inventis cudere ad hominum usum (velut agricultura, & ædificationem) necessaria. Nam & eorum, si qui prius metalla ista reperissent, facta fuisset mentio: & quū aut Moses Gen. 4. 22. de Tubalcaino, [qui erudiuit omnem fabrum ararium & ferrarium,] hoc sibi vult, quamlibet harum artium partem (est autem earum pars maxima in terra venis ea metalla primum dignoscere, & agnita effodere) esse hominis illius inuentum. In summa, hic est Tubalcainus, qui à Latinis & profanis postea [Vulcanus] contractiore vocabulo ex veteri illa traditione, quâ hic scribit Moses, fuit dictus, estque ab ijs faber, & fabrorum, artifex, ipsius ferrariæ autor, & parens appellatus, cuius vxor nominatur Venus, quæ hic Nΐoema, id est, Venusta seu voluptas, vt vult Augustin. lib 15. Ciuit. Dei, cap. 20. à Mose vocatur. Q. Cur ille Tubalcainus vocatus est, non autem simpliciter Tubal, vt fratres eius dicebatur Iabal, & Iubal: nō Iabalcainus, vel Iubalcainus. R. Sic nominatus est ille, nō tantum vt ab alijs hominibus distinguueretur, quorum nomen fuit Tubal (velut inter posteros Iapheti fuit alius Tubal Gen. 10.2) verumetiam vt in eo, tanquam viro quodam egregio & industrio, memoriam nomenque Caini primi fuit parentia & familiæ autoris parentes renouarent. Ex quo appareret Tubalcainū (vti quoq; conseruata est per tot posteā secula istius viri & appellatio, & memoria) pro magno celebrique viro & suo iam tempore, & posteà habitu, cultúmque fuisse: de quo sic Iosephus lib. 1. Antiquit. Iudaic. cap. 4. [Tubalcain, qui Lamecho ex altera vxore natus est, cunctos fortitudine excelluit.] Philo Iudæus Tubal & Tobal interpretatur [Conuersiu, seu aptus ad omnia. Alij verò quasi [Orbis possessione dignus.] sic nempe cæteris mortalibus admirabile fuit istius artis inuentum, quod tamen Aristoteles lib. 1. Politico-
units.tr: Answer: Tubal-cain taught men all these things, and indeed he was the first to do so. Yet he did not only forge certain works and tools from these, that is, from the bronze and iron already discovered, necessary for human use (such as for farming and building). For if anyone had discovered these metals earlier, mention would have been made of him. And when Moses in Gen. 4:22 speaks of Tubal-cain, who taught every craftsman in bronze and iron, he means that each part of these arts (and the greatest part of them is to recognise these metals first in the veins of the earth, and once recognised, to dig them out) was that man's invention. In sum, this is Tubal-cain, who was later called by the Latins and pagans Vulcan, by a shorter name, from that old tradition in which Moses writes of him. He is called by them the smith, the craftsman of smiths, the author and parent of the smith's art itself, and his wife is named Venus, who is called by Moses Naamah, that is, lovely or pleasure, as Augustine says in book 15 of The City of God, chapter 20. Question: Why was he called Tubal-cain, and not simply Tubal, as his brothers were called Jabal and Jubal, and not Jabal-cain or Jubal-cain? Answer: He was so named not only to distinguish him from other men whose name was Tubal (for among the descendants of Japheth there was another Tubal, Gen. 10:2), but also so that in him, as in a certain outstanding and industrious man, the parents of the first Cain, the founder of the family, might renew the memory and name of Cain. From this it appears that Tubal-cain (since the appellation and memory of this man have been preserved through so many ages afterwards) was regarded and held in high honour as a great and famous man, both in his own time and later. On this, Josephus writes thus in book 1 of the Jewish Antiquities, chapter 4: "Tubal-cain, who was born to Lamech by another wife, surpassed everyone in strength." Philo the Jew interprets Tubal and Tobal as "conversion, or fit for everything." Others, as if it meant "worthy of possessing the world." Thus this invention of the art, though admirable to other mortals, Aristotle in book 1 of his Politics counts among the most sordid arts.

units.la: {¦} litte coliticorum, inter sordidissimas artes recenset. Fortasse vero, quia cadis & homicidij, quod primus Cainus perpetrarat, primus instrumenta repererat, nempe ferramenta & enses, Cainus quoque ex primi hominis fratricidae nomine per ignominiam cognominatus est, non solum Tubal. Ego vero honoris ergo impositum illi Caini cognomen potius exististimauerim, quasi vir esset egregius: atque inde non simpliciter Tubal, sed Tubalcainus appellatus est. Q. Cur in libris Chronicorum, vbi Adami prosapia recensetur, istorum hominum (nempe totius familiae Caini) tam industriorum, & qui tam necessarias artes vitae humanae excogitarat, nulla tamen fit mentio.
units.tr: Perhaps, however, because Cain, who first committed murder and killing, was also the first to devise instruments, namely tools and swords, Cain too was surnamed in disgrace after the name of the first murderer, not Tubal alone. But I would rather think that the surname Cain was given to him as an honour, as if he were an outstanding man, and that from this he was called not simply Tubal but Tubal-cain. Question: Why, in the books of Chronicles, where the line of Adam is recounted, is no mention made of these men, namely the whole family of Cain, so industrious, and who devised such necessary arts for human life?

units.la: R. Tum quòd tota gens ista diluuio periit: sola autem Sethi soboles seruata fuit, & superstes, non quidè tota, sed ex ea persona solum oëlo, ex quibus postea propagatum est totum genus humanum, Gen. 8. 16, 1. Pet. 3. 20: tum quòd institutum erat eorum librorum, qui Chronica dicuntur, non totam Adami prosapiam describere, sed eam duntaxat, ex qua Israëlita, & Dei Ecclesia nata est. Q. Quamobrem posteri Caini in eo Catalogo, qui non essent de Ecclesia, fuerunt praetermissi. Q. Quid hominibus ex istius arariae & ferrariae Artis inuentione accidërit, vel accesserit.
units.tr: Answer: Partly because that whole race perished in the Flood, and only the offspring of Seth was preserved and survived, not entirely, but only one line of eight persons, from whom the whole human race was afterwards propagated (Gen. 8:16; 1 Pet. 3:20). Partly because it was the plan of those books which are called Chronicles not to describe the whole line of Adam, but only that from which the Israelites and the Church of God were born. Question: Why were the descendants of Cain passed over in that catalogue, since they were not of the Church? Question: What happened or came to men from the invention of this art of the plough and the smith?

units.la: R. Magnus certè quidem est, fuit tunc temporis in omnibus vitae humanae partibus istius artis vtriusque vsus ad arandum, ad aedificandum, ad secandum (nam primi cuneis, non ferro scindebant fissile lignum, quemadmodum scribit Virgil. lib. 1. Georgic.) & ad alia postea opera, velut ad nauigandum, ad quidpiam compingendum, ad pugnandum, & aduersus alios tuendum vel armis indutis, vel ense striŽlo. Porro de vsu ferri, &, quae ex eo percipitur, cōmo‑ ditate, vide Plinium lib. 34. hist. Natur. cap. 14. Magnus tamen abusus earundem illarum artium postea quoque inter mortales secutus est, dum his ferramentis sese mutuò inuadunt, iugulant, vulnerant, bella parant, & gerunt. Id quod non artibus tamen istis proprie: sed hominum malitia est tribuendū, sicut idem Tibull. lib. 1 eleg. 10. testatur hisce versibus, de repertore ferri agens:
units.tr: Answer: Its importance is certainly great. At that time in all parts of human life there was use of this art, both for ploughing, building, and cutting (for at first they split wood with wedges, not with iron, as Virgil writes in book 1 of the Georgics), and afterwards for other works, such as navigation, joining things together, fighting, and defending against others, either with armour on or with a drawn sword. Moreover, on the use of iron and the advantage that is gained from it, see Pliny, book 34 of the Natural History, chapter 14. Nevertheless, a great abuse of these same arts has afterwards followed among mortals, since with these tools they attack, slay, and wound one another, and prepare and wage wars. This, however, is to be attributed not to the arts themselves, but to the malice of men, as Tibullus also testifies in book 1, elegy 10, in these verses, speaking of the discoverer of iron:

units.la: ‒At miser iste nihil meruit: nos ad mala nostra Vertimus in seuas quod dedit ille feras.
units.tr: But that wretch deserved nothing: we turned to our own evils what he gave to savage beasts.

units.la: Diuitiis hoc vitium est auri: nec bella fuerunt, Faginus adstabat quum scyphus ante dapes.
units.tr: This vice belongs to the riches of gold: there were no wars when the beechwood cup stood before the feast.

units.la: Plinius metallum ferri optimū vita, pessimumque instrumentum esse scribit. Denique tunc quoq;, Idola fabricari esse coepta ait Philo Iudaeus in Bibl. Antiquit. quoniam homines ea ex aere & ferro tunc cuderunt, ait: quae tamen primum post Diluuium, etate Thara patre Abrahami, inuenta fuisse vult, scribitque Epiphanius in Panario. Et dubia quidem haͤtenus.
units.tr: Pliny writes that iron is the best metal for life and the worst for tools. Indeed, Philo the Jew says in his Biblical Antiquities that at that time too idols began to be made, since men then forged them from bronze and iron; yet he holds that these were first invented after the Flood, in the time of Terah, the father of Abraham, as Epiphanius writes in the Panarion. But these things are doubtful so far.

units.la: CAPVT III.
units.tr: Chapter III.

units.la: Vestigia superioris historię, & veritatis.
units.tr: The traces of the earlier history, and of the truth.

units.la: AD I. PECCATVM HOMINIS.
units.tr: Concerning the first sin of man.

units.la: VPERIORIS autem veritatis eaque etiam inter ipsos profanos vestigia extent, explicemus, quo & homines irrisores & ὑπαίχλοι seu potiùs Athei refellantur: & pÿ timentesque Dei in fide confirmentur. Ac primum. mūm ex Ethnicorum,qui Christi aduentum praece-ßerunt, (quorum duntaxat, etsi non omnium, testimonia quærimus: Esset enim infinitum omnia colligere) libri, scriptisque apparet, Hominem quidem,quatenus Dei opus est,esse bonum: eundem autem suâ culpâ & malù, & miserum effectum. Ergo à Deo bonus erat Homo: à se verò faCtus est nequam,prauus & malus. Trismegistus in Pimândro,quemadmodum ait, rubigo nequaquâ est ab artifice:sic neq; sunt à Creatore sordes. & lutum seu vitiû,quod est in nobis. Plato in Polit.editione H. Stephani,pag. 273. Tom. 2.scribit hominem suâ culpâ à prima sua sœlicitate, & prima Mundi ætatis curriculo excidisse. Aristoteles primam illam hominis creationem speCtàs,lib. 2. Ethic. putat hominis voluntatem esse fuisseq; à natura velut Tabulâ abrasam à Deo sactam, quæ vitio vel virtute (prout ipsa voluerit,seque inclinauerit) prædita fuerit,ac fiat. Sed & Platone & Aristotele antiquior Homerus, & ipse quoque Ethnicus lib. 1. Odyssea sic scribit,
units.tr: Next we shall set out the traces of that earlier truth, which are found even among the profane themselves, so that both the mockers and the hypaichloi, or rather the atheists [ὑπαίχλοι], may be refuted, and those who fear God may be confirmed in the faith. First, from the books and writings of the heathen who came before the coming of Christ, we find (I seek only the testimonies of some of them, since it would be endless to collect them all) that man, insofar as he is God's work, is good, but by his own fault he has become evil and wretched. So man was good by God's hand, but by his own doing he became worthless, depraved and bad. Trismegistus in the Pimander says: just as rust does not come from the craftsman, so filth and mud, or the defect in us, do not come from the Creator. Plato, in the Politicus (Stephanus's edition, p. 273, vol. 2), writes that man, through his own fault, fell from his first happiness and from the first course of the world's age. Aristotle, looking at that first creation of man in the second book of the Ethics, thinks that man's will was, as it were, a tablet wiped clean by nature and made by God, which becomes endowed with vice or virtue according as the man himself wishes and inclines himself. But Homer, older than both Plato and Aristotle, and himself a heathen, writes thus in the first book of the Odyssey:

units.la: Ω" πότοι,οἷον δή νυ θεὸς βεβροτοὶ αἰπόωντα.
units.tr: Ὢ πόποι, οἷον δή νυ θεοὺς βροτοὶ αἰτιόωνται. [Oh, how strangely mortals blame the gods!]

units.la: Ἐξ ἡμῶν γὰρ φασὶ κακ' ἔμμεναι. οἱ δὲ ἠ αὐτοὶ
units.tr: Ἐξ ἡμέων γάρ φασι κάκ' ἔμμεναι, οἱ δὲ καὶ αὐτοὶ [They say that evils come from us, but they themselves]

units.la: Σφῆσιν ἀτασθαλίησιν ὑπὲρ μόρον ἄλγε' ἔχουσι.
units.tr: σφῇσιν ἀτασθαλίῃσιν ὑπὲρ μόρον ἄλγε' ἔχουσιν. [by their own recklessness bring griefs upon themselves beyond their fate.]

units.la: [Papæ,quàm sanè mortales homines nos deos accusât. A nobis enim aiunt mala esse. At illi ipsi Suis stultitiĩs,præter fatum, miserias & angores sibi accessunt.] Hierocles denîq;,qui in vetustissima illa Pythagoræ carmina,quæ vocatur Aurea, cōmentarios scripsit, vetus sanè autor, & Stoicus: [ Homo, ait, à scipso propriâque voluntate proclivis est ad malum sequendum,& bonum deserendum.] Quemadmodum & illud quoque vetus & Menandri, & Terentij Poëtarū Comicorum, [Proclive est hominis ingenium à labore ad libidinem.] Deinde addit idē Hierocles. [Ne blasphememus interea, dicentes Deum esse autorem nostrorum criminum. Contrà vero, cuasiet Homo malus propria voluntate, & quum peccauimus, id egimus, quod erat in nobis: non autē id, quod erat Dei in nobis.] Hæc ille ex vetustissima Stoicorum secta, quà profitebatur. Et hæc quidem ostendunt id quod S. Scriptura docet, Hominem iam malū essectū esse, sed suo vitio & culpa: quatenus verò Dei opificium erat, fuisse bonum. Prætermitto enim Plotini, magni Platonici, infinitas in eā rem sententias, quas ex Enneadibus eius varijs in locis collegit accuratissimè Philippus Plesseius in opere De Veritate Christiana cap. 17. quod is autor post Christum passum aliquot seculis vixerit. Hoc igitur ipsum quod suprà diximus, confirmat quoque idem Trismeg. in Pimand. docetq; Dial. 4 Malorum caussam à nobis esse, extráque Deus culpam. Itaque cap. 6. irridet eos, qui hominem volunt esse bonum. Nam solus Deus bonus est, non homo, non Mundus hic, neque boni caussa, ait idem cap. seu dial. 10. Itaque à solo Deo lumen esse in homine: in homine verò iam meras esse tenebras: ac proinde regenerandum hominem esse, vt Deum cognoscat, atque ad eum accedat. Id quod in hymno de regeneratione cap. 13. eiusdē operis copiosius tradit idem Trismegistus. Porro quæ fuerit prima in homine ipso peccandi & bonam illam naturā, quam à Deo acceperat, amittendi caussa, vdem illi Ethnici ex vestigijs veritatis sacra pingūt vel describunt, certè saltem adumbrāt. Est autem, fuitque, aiunt, ambitio hominis superbiaq, dum vult homo Deo similis esse: dum eius opera imitaris dum nimium seipsum diligit: dum corpus suum, & quæ ex eo voluptates sentiuntur, amat plus æquo. Amor enim corporis fuit illi causa mortis, ait idē Trismegist. in Pimand. cap. 1. vbi etiam hæc extant, & si quibusdam fabulis (aliu Satana) obscurata, tamen vera veritatis nostræ testimonia: [Hominem, ait, sibi similem procreauit Deus, atque ei, tanquam filio suo, congratulatus est. Pulcher enim erat, patrisq; sui ferebat imaginē. Deus enim reuera propria forma delectat°, opera sua omnia vsui concessit humano. Homo autem quum considerasset in tempore suo omnium creationem, ipse quoque fabricare voluit, unde a contemplatione Patris ad Spheram generationis delapsus est, &c.] Hierocles, [Ambitio, inquit, est nobis lethalis, atque hoc malum a nobis ipsi habemus, quum a Deo defecimus.] Sed quæ fuerit homini externa peccandi causa ab ipsa illis Ethnicis explicatur quoque, quo magis etiam ex iis ipsis constet de nostra veritate. Fuit autem illa causa Serpens a Demone impulsus, qui primum per fœminam peccatum in Mundu, ex esu pomi seu malis (quod primi homines vetiti fuerant attingere) introduxit, Gen. 3. De quibus singulis vestigia veritatis, quæ restat, expendamus. Ac primum quidē a Serpente deceptos fuisse primos mortales aperte scripserat Sibylla, cuius versus extat apud Lactant. lib. 2. Institut. Christianarū, cap. 12. quos nos Græcos iam citauimus, & quorum hic est sensus, Ipse suis hominem m inibus Deus edidit, illum Dccepit Serpens, dans nosse bonumq, malumq,
units.tr: [How truly mortals accuse the gods! For they say evils come from us; yet they themselves, by their own folly, add miseries and anguish beyond what fate has assigned.] Finally, Hierocles, who wrote commentaries on those very ancient Pythagorean verses called the Golden Verses, was certainly an ancient author and a Stoic. He says: "Man, of himself and by his own will, is prone to follow evil and to abandon good." Like the old saying also found in the comic poets Menander and Terence: "Man's nature is prone to lust rather than to labour." Hierocles then adds: "Let us not blaspheme in the meantime by saying that God is the author of our crimes. On the contrary, since man is evil by his own will, when we have sinned we have done what was in us, not what was of God in us." Thus he spoke, from the most ancient sect of the Stoics, to which he belonged. These things show what Holy Scripture teaches, that man has already become evil, but by his own vice and fault; yet insofar as he was God's handiwork, he was good. For I pass over the countless opinions on this matter of Plotinus, the great Platonist, which Philip Du Plessis has most carefully gathered from various places in his Enneads, in his work On the Christian Truth, chapter 17, although that author lived some centuries after Christ's passion. Trismegistus, in the Pimander, confirms this very thing we have said above, and teaches in the fourth dialogue that the cause of evils is in us, and God is free of blame. So in chapter 6 he mocks those who want man to be good. For God alone is good, not man, not this world, nor for the sake of goodness, says the same author in chapter or dialogue 10. Therefore light is in man only from God, while in man himself there is now only pure darkness; and consequently man must be regenerated so that he may know God and come to him. Trismegistus sets out this same thing more fully in the hymn on regeneration, chapter 13 of the same work. Furthermore, these heathen, from traces of the truth, depict or describe, or at least sketch, the sacred account of what was the first cause in man himself of sinning and of losing that good nature which he had received from God. They say that it is, and was, the ambition and pride of man, while he wishes to be like God, while he imitates his works, while he loves himself too much, while he loves his body and the pleasures felt through it more than is right. For love of the body was his cause of death, says Trismegistus in the Pimander, chapter 1, where these things also appear, although they are obscured by some fables (as if about Satan), yet they are true testimonies of our truth: "God created man like himself and rejoiced in him as his own son. For he was beautiful and bore the image of his father. God indeed delights in his own form, and he gave all his works over to human use. But man, when he had considered in his own time the creation of all things, wished to make things himself too, and so he fell from the contemplation of the Father to the sphere of generation," and so on. Hierocles: "Ambition, he says, is deadly to us, and we have this evil from ourselves, when we have fallen away from God." But what the external cause of man's sinning was is also explained by these same heathen, so that the truth of our account may be established even from their own writings. That cause was the serpent, driven on by a demon, who first brought sin into the world through the woman, by eating the apple or fruit which the first humans had been forbidden to touch (Gen. 3). Let us weigh each of these points, and the traces of the truth that remain. First, the Sibyl had plainly written that the first mortals were deceived by the serpent; her verse is found in Lactantius, Divine Institutes, book 2, chapter 12. We have already cited it in Greek, and its sense is this: "God himself made man with his own hands; the serpent deceived him, giving him the knowledge of good and evil."

units.la: Eundem vero Serpentem à Cacodæmone fuisse ad idoperis suscitatum, docuit dixitque Pherecydes Syrus, quem eundem appellat ὀφιογενῆ, ὑφιόυσον, quemadmodum tradit Origenes contra Celsum, à quo esse scripsit ille idem Therecydes, & quidè consentienter veritati, quicquid est malorum in hoc Mundo. Quomodo verò cum muliere prima, quæ decepit, loqui Serpens ille potuerit idiomate humano, docet etiâ ex Ethnicis ipsis Cyrillus lib. 3. contra Iulian. sect. 2. nempe insitictu Satanæ id factum, quandoquidem Magorum (qui sunt famuli duntaxat Diaboli) vi, & incantationibus multa belua & nunc loquuntur, & olim sunt locuta (ut prætermittam Asinam Balaami, quæ Dei iussu locuta est, de qua est, Numer. 22. 27) velut Equus Achillis, Argo navis, Quercus & Columba in Dodonæa sylua, flumen Caustii Pythagoram salutavit, Arbor Vlmus Apollonium Philosophum, & Iovis Taurus in Rhodo insula. Sed nonne Pica & Gracchulus nostra verba discunt, & loquuntur? Porrò à fœmina, nō autem à mare initiū mali & peccati ortum esse tradiderunt Homerus, & Hesiodus. Ac Homerus quidè lib. Iliad. 19. Nam quòd ibi Aten quandam fœminam canit omnibus nobis mortalibus fuisse noxiam & perniciosam, proculdubio alludit ad omnium nostrum parentem Euam, (quæ primum peccauit) idque ex reliquis veritatis, de qua Homerus quidpiam inaudiuerat. Ait enim, Πρὲσ3ε Διὸς 3υγάτηρ Ἀτη, ἥ πάντας ἀᾶτεν Οὐλομένην.
units.tr: Pherecydes the Syrian taught and said that this same serpent was stirred up to do this work by a evil demon, whom he calls ophiogenē and ophiousos [ὀφιογενῆ, ὑφιόυσον], as Origen relates against Celsus; and the same Pherecydes wrote that all the evils in this world come from him, which indeed agrees with the truth. How that serpent could speak in human language to the first woman whom it deceived, Cyril also teaches from the heathen themselves, in the third book against Julian, section 2: namely, that this happened by the instigation of Satan, since by the power and incantations of the magi (who are merely servants of the devil) many beasts both now speak and formerly have spoken. (I pass over the ass of Balaam, which spoke by God's command, Numbers 22:27.) So the horse of Achilles, the ship Argo, the oak and the dove in the Dodonian grove, the river Caustius greeted Pythagoras, the elm tree spoke to the philosopher Apollonius, and the bull of Jupiter on the island of Rhodes. But do not magpies and jackdaws learn our words and speak them? Moreover, Homer and Hesiod have handed down that the beginning of evil and sin arose from a woman, not from a man. Homer, in the nineteenth book of the Iliad, sings that a certain woman, Ate, was harmful and destructive to all of us mortals; without doubt he alludes to Eve, the parent of us all, who first sinned, and he took this from the remaining truth, of which Homer had heard something. For he says:

units.la: [Filia primâ Iovis, quæq; omnes perdidit, Atè Perniciosa.] Quid quod ibidem Homerus alterius fabulæ integumento eandem historiâ attingit, dum ait
units.tr: Πρέσβιστη Διὸς θυγάτηρ Ἀτη, ἥ πάντας ἀᾶται Οὐλομένη [Ate, the eldest daughter of Zeus, who deludes all, the accursed one.]

units.la: ait Iouem omnium mortalium sapientissimum tamen à Iunone uxore sua olim deceptum fuisse? Et hæc quidem de initio malorum, quódque à fœmina ceperit, & per eam hominum prudentissimus deceptus sit, tradit Homerus. Hesiodus verò lib. 1. Oper. & Dier. idem quidem sentit & scribit, sed diuersis verbis, aliáve fabula confictâ ex veteri traditione. Nam ait, [A Pandora muliere (quæ omnium fœminarū & formosissima & prima condita à Dys fuerat) mala omnia in Orbem terrarum sparsa fuisse,] quanquam & Palæphatus de Fabulosis narrationibus, & Placiades Fulgentius libr. 2. Mythologic. aliter interpretantur Pādoram, dum ad nostram veritatem non attendunt. At verò Hesiodus nobiscum facit, ex cuius carmine, quod nos cōtendimus, ostendetur facilè.
units.tr: What of the fact that in the same place Homer, under the covering of another fable, touches on the same history, when he says that Jove, the wisest of all mortals, was once deceived by his wife Juno? Homer tells that evils began and came through a woman, and that through her the most prudent of men was deceived. Hesiod, in the first book of the Works and Days, thinks and writes the same thing, but in different words, or with a fable invented from the old tradition. For he says that all evils were spread over the world by Pandora, a woman (who was the most beautiful of all women and was first made by Dys). Although Palaephatus, in his book On Fabulous Narratives, and Fulgentius the Planciad, in the second book of his Mythologies, interpret Pandora differently, since they do not attend to our truth, Hesiod agrees with us, and from his poem, which we maintain, it will easily be shown.

units.la: Ἀλλὰ γυνὴ χείρεσι πίθος μέγα πωμὰ ἀφελῶσα Ἐοχέδας, ἀνδράσιν δ' ἐμήσατο κήδεα λυγρά.
units.tr: But the woman, lifting the great lid of the jar with her hands, scattered woes and grievous cares among men. [Ἀλλὰ γυνὴ χείρεσι πίθος μέγα πωμὰ ἀφελῶσα Ἐοχέδας, ἀνδράσιν δ' ἐμήσατο κήδεα λυγρά.]

units.la: [Námq; prius vixêre homines, verum absq; labore, Absque malis, morbóque graui tristíque senecta. At Mulier rapto de poclo tegmine sparsit Omne mali genus, & morbos, curasque molestas.]
units.tr: Before this, men lived without toil, without evils, without grievous sickness or wretched old age. But the woman, lifting the cover from the jar, scattered every kind of evil, and diseases, and troublesome cares.

units.la: Itaque Mulierem ex ira Iouis natâ, & χαλὸν χαλὸν appellauit idem in Θεογονίᾳ, vt lib. 3. contra Iulian. scribit Cyrillus in principio libri. Non desunt etiam qui [væ] ab Eua velint deductum per metathesin literarū. Hinc quoque illud est Platonis lib. 10. de Legib. Mulieres esse mortalium superstitiosissimas, vtpote quæ sunt natura valde imbecillis. Itaque fœmina potius quàm marem aggressus est serpens, vt eam falleret. Deniq; quod in esu pomi dicitur perpetratum primū hoc hominum scelus, nónne videtur cum eo consentire, quod de malis aureis scribunt Poeta, qua ne homines attingerent pernigilem draconem iys a dijs appositum volunt, vt draco iste homines,ne ex iys ederent, prohiberet. Et hac de primo nostra veritatis capite,& illius reliquijs, quales in Ethnicis scriptis extant.
units.tr: Therefore Hesiod, in his Theogony, called the woman, born from the anger of Jove, "evil, evil" [κακὸν κακόν], as Cyril writes at the beginning of the third book against Julian. Nor are there lacking those who want the word "woe" [vae] derived from Eve by a transposition of letters. Hence also comes that saying of Plato in the tenth book of the Laws, that women are the most superstitious of mortals, since by nature they are very weak. So the serpent attacked the woman rather than the man, in order to deceive her. Finally, the first crime of men, which is said to have been committed in eating the fruit, seems to agree with what the poets write about the golden apples, which they say the gods set beside a sleepless dragon so that the dragon would keep men from touching them and eating them. And this is enough about the first chapter of our truth, and its remnants, as they appear in heathen writings.

units.la: Ad II. Pœna peccati Hominum.
units.tr: Concerning the Second: the Punishment of Men's Sin.

units.la: Nunc de secundo dicamus, in quo Pœna peccati, id est, triftiffima Miseria, atque non modo ipsorum hominum ruina calamitasque cötinetur, verumetiam totius huius Mundi. Quod ipsum vt melius ex Ethnicorum hominum scriptis intelligatur, conferamus ea, quæ tradunt illi de prima & pura adhuc hominum ætate (quæ Aurea vocat) cum iis, quæ de Ferrea scribunt idem, in quam homines post peccatum inciderunt. Nec enim dubitari potest, quin Aurea illius ætatis ænigmate felicem illam vitam defignarint, quam homines ante peccatum vixerunt. Ætatis vero ferrea nomine eam, quæ iam post offensum à primis hominibus Deü omnes experimur. Auream autem ætatem Seculum Saturni nominant. Præclarè enim Plato in Cratylo, [Nempe equidem arbitror, ait, Hefiodü Auream ætatem appellare, non quæ aurea quidem effet natura, atque auro cöstaret: sed bonam & præclaram fignificaffe. Cui rei argumentum mihi est, quòd ætatem nostram Ferream nominarit.] Ergo idem in Polit. Plato hoc idem tempus & Saturni seculum & aureum dici tradit, cuius summam omnibus in rebus felicitatem describit. Nam ait omnia tunc sponte homini e terra nata: ipsos homines tunc fuisse immortales, aut ex seipsis renouatos.: cœli quoque temperiem tunc optimam. Sed ante Platonem Hesiodus lib. 1. Operum & Dierum sic scripserat: Χρύσεον μὲν ἀθάνατα γένεϑ᾽ μεσόπων ἀνθρώπων Οἱ μὲν ὅτι Κρόνου ἦσαν, ὅτ᾽ ὑρανῷ ἐυβασιλεῦον. Ὥρςε ϑεοὶ δ᾽ ἴζωον ἀκήδεα ϑυμὸν ἔχοντες, &c.
units.tr: Now let us speak of the second point, in which is contained the punishment of sin, that is, the most wretched misery, and the ruin and calamity not only of men themselves but of this whole world. So that this may be better understood from the writings of the heathen, let us compare what they say about the first and pure age of men (which they call golden) with what they write about the iron age into which men fell after sin. For there can be no doubt that the golden age was a riddle designating that happy life which men lived before sin. By the name of the iron age they mean that which we all now experience, since God was offended by the first men. Now they call the golden age the Age of Saturn. Plato in the Cratylus puts it well: "I suppose, he says, that Hesiod calls it the golden age not because its nature was golden or made of gold, but because he meant it to be good and excellent. The proof of this for me is that he called our age iron." Then Plato, in the Politicus, likewise teaches that the same time is called both the age of Saturn and the golden age, and he describes its sum of happiness in all things. For he says that then everything grew of its own accord from the earth for men, that men themselves were then immortal or renewed from themselves, and that the temperature of the heavens was then the best. But before Plato, Hesiod in the first book of the Works and Days had written thus: [Χρύσεον μὲν ἀθάνατα γένεϑ᾽ μεσόπων ἀνθρώπων Οἱ μὲν ὅτι Κρόνου ἦσαν, ὅτ᾽ ὑρανῷ ἐυβασιλεῦον. Ὥρςε ϑεοὶ δ᾽ ἴζωον ἀκήδεα ϑυμὸν ἔχοντες, &c.]

units.la: Id quod pulcherrimè Ouidius lib. 1. Metamorph. non tam imitatus, quàm conuertisse, & expressisse videtur his versibus: [Aurea prima sata est ætas, quæ vindice nullo Sponte sua sine lege fidem, rectúmque colebat. Nondum precipites cingebant oppida fossæ: Non galea, non ensis erat, sine militis usu. Ipsa quoque immunis, rastróque intacta, nec villis Saucia vomeribus per se dabat omnia tellus, Contentique cibis, nullo egente, creatis, Arboreos fructus, montanáque fraga legebant. Ver erat æternum, placidíque, tepentibus auris, Mulcebant Zephyri natos sine semine flores. Atque etiam fruges tellus inarata ferebat.]
units.tr: Ovid in the first book of the Metamorphoses seems to have not so much imitated as turned into verse and expressed this same thing in these lines: "The first age was the golden one, which, with no avenger, kept faith and right of its own accord, without law. Not yet were towns surrounded by steep ditches; there was no helmet, no sword, nor any use of soldiers. The earth too, untouched and unbroken by the rake, unwounded by plough-blades, gave everything of itself; and men, content with the food produced without need, gathered the fruits of the trees and the strawberries of the mountains. It was an eternal spring, and gentle zephyrs with mild breezes caressed flowers born without seed. Even unploughed, the earth bore grain."

units.la: Quibus consentiunt ea, quæ Virgilius, reliquiq; vetustissimi Poëtæ tum Græci, tum Latini de Saturni seculo tradiderunt: quæ nos, breuitatis gratiâ, minimè ex illis in hunc locum transcribemus. Sed postquam homo peccauit, mutata est aurea illius conditio & ætas in Ferreā, summa felicitas in summam miseriam & infelicitatem conuersa, qualem etiā ipsimet Ethnici declarant, adeo vt Sibylla scripserit metuendum esse, imò tempus fore, quo Deus vniuersum genus humanum deleat è terra, quemadmodum extant varij illius de ea re versus apud Lactantium in libro De Ira Dei. Ergo Hesiodus Ferrei istius Hominum seculi infelicitatem & poenam ostendit, quae secuta est hominum mutatos mores, id est peccatum ab iis in Deum Creatorem suum perfidissime admissum, idque congruenter verbo Dei. Imo idem tradit tantam hominum miseriam (qualis nunc est) non repente extitisse, quod verum est, sed per quosdam gradus, & temporum aetates, momenta, & successiones succrevisse: in quibus tamen intermiscet quaedam tum ipse, tum alii de fabulis, quoniam veritas ipsa lucida, qualis est in verbo Dei, semper a suis umbris (quae solas Ethnici habuerunt) differt. Illa enim sunt interpolatio & obscuratio veritatis. Ait igitur Hesiodus eiusdem operis lib. I. his verbis,
units.tr: What Virgil and the other most ancient poets, both Greek and Latin, have handed down about the age of Saturn agrees with these things; for the sake of brevity we shall not copy them out here. But after man sinned, that golden condition and age was changed into an iron one, the highest happiness turned into the highest misery and unhappiness, as the heathen themselves declare. So much so that the Sibyl wrote that there was to be fear, indeed that a time would come when God would destroy the whole human race from the earth; various verses of hers on this matter are found in Lactantius in his book On the Anger of God. Therefore Hesiod shows the unhappiness and punishment of this iron age of men, which followed the change of their morals, that is, the sin which they committed most faithlessly against God their Creator, and this agrees with the Word of God. Indeed, the same writer teaches that so great a misery of men (such as now exists) did not arise suddenly, which is true, but grew up by certain steps and ages, moments and successions of time. Yet in this both he and others mix in some fables, since the truth itself, bright as it is in the Word of God, always differs from its shadows, which alone the heathen had. For those are an interpolation and obscuring of the truth. Hesiod therefore says in the first book of the same work, in these words:

units.la: Νῦν γὰρ δὴ γένος- δὲ σιδήρεον εἰς ἔσται ἦμαρ Παύονται κάματός, ἡ ὀίπυος, νὺξ δὲ τ νύκτωρ Φθειρόμενοι. χαλεπῆς δεοὶ Διὸς ὤσπερ ἀμνυμένε. &c.
units.tr: [Νῦν γὰρ δὴ γένος- δὲ σιδήρεον εἰς ἔσται ἦμαρ Παύονται κάματός, ἡ ὀίπυος, νὺξ δὲ τ νύκτωρ Φθειρόμενοι. χαλεπῆς δεοὶ Διὸς ὤσπερ ἀμνυμένε. &c.] For now indeed is the iron race; by day they shall never cease from toil and sorrow, and by night they shall be destroyed, and the gods shall give them hard cares, as Zeus swears.

units.la: Ergo post peccatum statim immutata sunt rerum vices, ipsaque huius Mundi facies & felicitas amissa, quam aetatem Iovi tribuunt. Nondum tamen summa erat mundi corruptio & calamitas, quae sequentibus temporibus propter successrescentia multiplicataque hominum peccata demum exorta est. Ergo de Iove illi scribunt sub eo fuisse, non sub Saturno initium miserae illius conditionis, quae propter hominum peccatum iniecta est in Mundum: de quo sic Virgil. lib. I. Georgic. his versibus:
units.tr: Therefore, immediately after sin, the order of things was changed, and the very face and happiness of this world was lost, which they ascribe to the age of Jove. Yet the complete corruption and calamity of the world had not yet come; that came at last in later times, through the multiplied and increasing sins of men. So they write that under Jove, not under Saturn, began that wretched condition which, because of man's sin, was cast upon the world. Virgil speaks of this in the first book of the Georgics in these lines:

units.la: Ante Iovem nulli subigebant arva coloni, Nec signare quidem, aut partiri limite campum Fas erat: in medio quaerebant, ipsaque Tellus Omnia liberius, nullo poscente, ferebat, Ille malum virus serpentibus addidit atris, Prædarique lupos iussit pontúmque moueri, Mellaque decussit foliys,&c.] Essi Lactant.lib.5. cap.5.aliter ista interpretatur. Ergo crescente hominum malitia (postquam semel esse coepit) tandem omne genus vt peccati, sic miseria in Mundum irrupit. Vnde Ferrea,id est,miserrima hominū atas nata est, propter quam immissum est a Deo postea diluuium, vti ex eisdem Ethnicus dicetur. Caeterum de ista ætate Ferrea, quanta & scelera, & scelerum supplicia pepererit, sic Onid.lib.1.Metamorph. -De duro est vltima ferro.
units.tr: "Before Jove, no farmers tilled the fields, nor was it lawful to mark or divide the land with boundaries; they sought their goods in common, and the earth itself bore everything more freely, with no one asking. He added the evil poison to the black serpents, ordered the wolves to prey, and the sea to be stirred, and shook the honey from the leaves," etc. Lactantius, book five, chapter five, interprets these things differently. Therefore, as human wickedness grew (once it had begun), at last every kind of misery as well as of sin burst into the world. Hence the Iron age, that is, the most wretched age of men, arose, on account of which God afterwards sent the flood, as the same heathen writer will say. As for that iron age, how many crimes and punishments for crimes it brought forth, Ovid describes in the first book of the Metamorphoses: "The last age is of hard iron."

units.la: [Protinus irrupit vena peioris in aurumOmne nefas,fugere pudor,verúmque,fidésque:In quorum subiere locum fraudésque,dolique, Insidiaeque,& vis,& amor sceleratus habendi: Vuiitur ex rapto,non hospes ab hospite tutus,&c.]
units.tr: "Straightway there burst forth from the vein of a worse metal every wickedness: modesty and truth and faith fled. In their place came frauds and tricks, plots and violence, and accursed love of possession. Sailors spread their sails to the winds, and the guest was no longer safe from the host, etc."

units.la: Ergo & miseria quoque,nempe poena peccatorum istorum subsecuta sunt, quas lib.6.Aeneid.describit Virgilius. Nam iam inter nos & post peccatum est
units.tr: Therefore misery too, namely the punishment of those sins, followed, which Virgil describes in the sixth book of the Aeneid. For now, among us and after sin, is

units.la: [Luctus,& vltrices posuere cubilia curæ, Pallentesque habitant morbi,tristisque senectus: Et metus,& malesuada fames,& turpis egestas.]
units.tr: "Grief, and avenging cares have made their home, pale diseases dwell there, and sad old age; fear, and evil-counselling hunger, and shameful want."

units.la: Extat libellus Gracus inscriptione[Axiochus,]in quo humana vitæ calamitates commemorantur,qui Platoni tribuitur(certè est autoris & Ethnici,& vetustissimi) ex quo quanta sit hominum iam, id est,post peccatum miseria & infelicitas,apparet in quauis ætate,sexu,vita genere,adeo vt tandem concludatur vitam hanc hominis,id est,in his terris esse magnū & arumnosum malum. Legat illum libellum (est enim utilissimus) qui volet. Extitit Philosophus ante M. Tull. Ciceronem quidâ ut ipse Tusc. 1. testatur, nomine Hegesias, qui propter eiusmodi tantasque miserias, quibus haec vita obnoxia est, diceret, docereτque Optimum esse vel omnino non nasci, vel statim mori. Alcidamus idem docuit. Denique Thracum (fuerunt autem illi Europae gens nobilissima) mos is fuit, ut scribit Herodotus lib. 3. & Valerius Maximus lib. 2. ut in hominum nativitate lugerent foetum circumstantes: in morte vero hominum laetarentur, quod natiuitas esset malorum initium: mors vero finis. Cui sententia in Ctesiphonte astipulatur Euripides, his verbis, [Nam nos decebat coetus celebrantes, domi Lugere, ubi esset aliquis in lucem editus, Humana vita varia reputantes mala. At, qui labores morte finiisset graues, Omnes amicos laude, & laetitia exequi.)
units.tr: There is a Greek booklet with the title Axiochus, in which the calamities of human life are recounted, which is ascribed to Plato (it is certainly by a heathen author, and a very ancient one). From it one sees how great is the misery and unhappiness of men now, that is, after sin, at every age, sex and way of life, so that at last it is concluded that this life of man, that is, on this earth, is a great and troublesome evil. Let whoever wishes read that little book, for it is very useful. Before Cicero, as he himself testifies in the first Tusculan Disputation, there was a philosopher named Hegesias, who, because of such great miseries to which this life is subject, used to say and teach that it is best either not to be born at all or to die at once. Alcidamas taught the same. Finally, the custom of the Thracians (who were a most noble people of Europe), as Herodotus writes in the third book and Valerius Maximus in the second, was that at a man's birth those standing around mourned the newborn, but at his death they rejoiced, because birth was the beginning of evils and death the end. Euripides agrees with this opinion in the Cresphontes, in these words: "It behoved us, gathering together, to mourn at home when someone was born into the light, reckoning up the varied evils of human life; but whoever had finished his grievous labours by death, all friends should follow him with praise and joy."

units.la: Quin & Homerus quoque quem citat Plutarch sic ait, [Haud quidquam est miserum magis, aerumnosius atq; Est hominum in terris, quae spirant, quaeq; vagantur.
units.tr: Indeed Homer too, whom Plutarch cites, says: Nothing is more wretched or full of woe than all the men who breathe and wander upon the earth.

units.la: Et haec quidem in genere poenam peccati in hominibus extitisse, & extare ostendunt, atque inde infusam tnuniversum hunc Mundum calamitatem summam. Peculiariter vero Masculum in excolenda terra: Mulierem in partu: serpentem in victu maledictum esse idem illi Ethnici etiam testantur. Nam post peccatum & mutatam propterea Mundi huius primâ conditionem (quod sub Ioue contigisse volunt), Prima enim aetas & felix sub Saturno fuit) etsi forte idem fuit Saturnus & Iupiter, sed diuersa ei idem hominis conditio diuersis nominibus ab ijs notata est: vel Ionis nomine Cainũ illi proculdubio significant. Tost mutatam, inquã, ob scelus hominum primâ huius Mundi totius conditionem. post additum serpentibus venenũ, vt ait Virgilius, vita hominum miserrima fuit, & in quarendo e terra vitlu laboriofissima. Ergo prima illorum occupatio in terra aranda colendáque extitit, vt idem Virgilius ait lib. 1. Georgicorum: ---[Nam Iuppiter iste
units.tr: These things show that punishment for sin has come upon men in general and still remains, and that the greatest calamity has been poured out upon this whole world. Particularly, the heathen themselves also bear witness that the man was cursed in tilling the earth, the woman in childbirth, and the serpent in its food. For after sin, and the consequent change of the first condition of this world (which they say happened under Jupiter, since the first and happy age was under Saturn), although perhaps Saturn and Jupiter were the same, and the same condition of man was marked by different names, they undoubtedly signify Cain by the name of Janus. After the change of the first condition of the whole world through the wickedness of men, and after poison was added to the serpents, as Virgil says, the life of men became most miserable, and in seeking food from the earth most laborious. Therefore their first occupation was the ploughing and tilling of the land, as Virgil says in the first book of the Georgics: For Jupiter himself

units.la: Et passim riuis currentia vina repressit:
units.tr: And held back the rivers' running wine everywhere,

units.la: Vt varias vsus meditando extunderet artes, Paulatim & sulcis frumenti quaereret herbam.]
units.tr: So that by thinking he might sharpen various arts through use, and little by little seek the grain's herb in the furrows.

units.la: Eodé pertinet quod tantopere agriculturâ à vetustate ydem Ethnici laudant. Imo Cato Maior & Censorius docebat habere se eam pro oblectamento potius, quam in fructu. Philopœmenes quum esset Princeps Achaorum, ea tamen summè delestabatur, quemadmodum in eorum vitis scribit Plutarchus: Item Laertes rex pater Vlyssis, vt vult Homer. tamen, vt in Axiocho scribit Plato, etiam illa vita est & laborum, & molestiarũ plena, & durum ac miserum omnino, sed primum vitæ genus. Id quod etiam docet Horatius lib. 1. Epist. Ad Mæcenatem [Quinque dies] de Mena loquens. Mulieres autem in parũ summos dolores experiri ac tolerare cum ipsa rerum experientia docet, quæ quotidiè cernitur: tum illud Euripidis, [Decies mori mallem, quam parere vel semel,] ait apud eum fœmina. Vnde ὡς ἴνας dicti summi dolores à Græcis, quales in partu sentiunt mulieres: & illud quoque Homeri, quod non Homerum ipsum, sed Homericâ quandam potius poëtriâ, quæ iam puerpera fuisset, scripsisse putat Plutarchus in libello περὶ τῆς φιλοσοφίας, tam est nempe verum, Quū labor, atque dolor partus, & acuta & amara Tela graues feriunt uteros, quúmque Ilithyia Iunonis nata accurrunt mala multa ferentes.]
units.tr: To the same point belongs what the same heathen praise so highly about agriculture from antiquity. Indeed Cato the Elder and Censor used to teach that he regarded it as a delight rather than a source of profit. Philopoemen, when he was prince of the Achaeans, nevertheless took great pleasure in it, as Plutarch writes in his Lives. Likewise Laertes, the king and father of Ulysses, as Homer tells, and yet, as Plato writes in the Axiochus, that life too is full of toil and trouble, and altogether hard and wretched, though it is the first kind of life. Horatius also teaches this in the first book of the Epistles, to Maecenas, speaking of Mena: [Five days...]. That women experience and endure the greatest pains in childbirth, experience itself teaches, which is seen every day. Then there is that saying of Euripides, spoken by a woman in him: "I would rather die ten times than give birth once." Hence the Greeks call the greatest pains, such as women feel in childbirth, [ὠδῖνες]. And that verse of Homer, which Plutarch thinks was written not by Homer himself but by some Homeric poetess who had already been a mother, in his little work On Philosophy [περὶ τῆς φιλοσοφίας], is certainly true: "When the labour and pain of childbirth, sharp and bitter darts, strike the heavy womb, and Ilithyia, daughter of Juno, comes running, bringing many woes."

units.la: Quanquam verò in Conuiuio recte Plato ait, Η δ' ἀνδρὸς ἡ γυναικὸς συνουσίας, τόκος ἔσται. Εἰ δὲ δεῖον τὸ ᾱ ... [Ex mulieris iane & viri cogressu partus exiit. Est autem hoc diuinum opus, & in animali mortali immortale hoc est, Conceptio videlicet, & Generatio.] Tamen immensos esse mulierum parturientium dolores negari non potest. Quam fuisse poenam peculiarem mulieris scribit, docetque S. Scriptura. De Serpente, & quātas cum homine exerceat inimicitias, vtq; illum fugiat, vulneret tamen, notum est, quam ut dici possit, vel debeat: de quo luculeter Plinius lib. 11. Natural. Histor. Lucanus lib. 9. Pharsalidos. Et primum quidē Animal (quod ab hominibus fuerit occisum) volunt fuisse Serpentem, quem à tumore Pythonem appellarunt, & sagittis confossum ab Apolline peritissimo sagittario. Nec verò his obstat, quòd Phylli & Marsi vt scribit Plinius lib. 28. cap. 3. à serpentibus non laeduntur Id enim fit Magicis & Satanicis incantationibus. Sed & quòd nonnulli populi vescuntur quoq; serpentibus, vt Cădei in Aethiopico sinu, quemadmodum idem tradit libr. 6. cap. 29: & de Americanis populis scriptores Hispani, non officit huic sententiae. Hi enim, qui ibi serpentes appellantur, quoq; homines isti edunt, non sunt proprie serpentes, sed potius anguillae quaedam terrenae, vel aquae, fille venenoque carentes (quod tamen men habent serpentes omnes) quæ propter forma, corporifque similitudinem Serpentes nominantur: Ergo non serpentes, sed anguilla dici debuerunt illa animalia. Sunt enim illa innoxia hominibus: at Serpentes sunt semper noxij, venenatique, quos esse homines absque mortis periculo non possunt. Quod vero Iulianus Apostata contendebat Serpentem ab hominibus velut benefastorem, (vtpote qui cognitione boni & mali ss dedisset) potius amādum, quàm odio prosequendum, aut maledicendū, refutat luculenter Cyrillus lib. 3. contra Iulian. fest. 4.
units.tr: Although Plato rightly says in the Symposium: "The union of man and woman is procreation" [Ἡ δ' ἀνδρὸς καὶ γυναικὸς συνουσία τόκος ἐστίν]. "Indeed the union of woman and man is birth. Yet this is a divine work, and in a mortal creature this conception and generation is something immortal." Nevertheless, it cannot be denied that the pains of women in labour are immense. That this was a special punishment for women, Holy Scripture writes and teaches. About the serpent, and how great enmity it carries on against man, and how it flees him yet wounds him, is known too well to be said, or to need saying; Plinius writes about this splendidly in the eleventh book of his Natural History, and Lucan in the ninth book of the Pharsalia. And they hold that the first animal (which was killed by men) was the serpent, which they named Python from its swelling, and which was pierced with arrows by Apollo, the most skilled archer. Nor does it stand against this that the Phylli and the Marsi, as Plinius writes in the twenty-eighth book, chapter three, are not harmed by serpents. For this happens through magical and satanic incantations. Nor does it weaken this view that some peoples also eat serpents, such as the Cadei in the Ethiopian gulf, as the same author relates in the sixth book, chapter twenty-nine, and that Spanish writers tell of the American peoples. For those creatures that are there called serpents, which these men also eat, are not properly serpents but rather certain earthly or watery eels, which are without poison (which, however, all serpents have), and they are called serpents because of their shape and bodily likeness. So those animals should have been called eels, not serpents. For these are harmless to men, whereas serpents are always harmful and poisonous, and men cannot be near them without danger of death. As for Julian the Apostate, who maintained that the serpent should be loved rather than hated or cursed, as though it were a benefactor to men (since it gave them the knowledge of good and evil), Cyril refutes this splendidly in the third book against Julian, the fourth fragment.

units.la: Ad III. Promissio Messiæ.
units.tr: On the Third Point: The Promise of the Messiah.

units.la: Verum ad tertium caput nostræ historiæ veniamus, in quo promissio futuri Messiæ (qui Deus & homo suturus esset) continetur. Huius autem, tam, vt videtur, Christianorum duntaxat propriæ, & Ethnicis ignotæ historiæ, & cognitionis vestigia tamen apud eosdem illos Ethnicos extant plurima, qualia sunt hæc, quæ proponemus breuiter, etsi nos omnia colligere (ne cuiquam suæ industriæ laudem eriperemus) minimè studuimus. Ergo docent illi, Primum, Quod post lapsum hominis, casumque vniuersi Mundi, Deus illius administrationem curámque, magnâ suâ misericordiâ, & bonitate, nō abiecit. Id quod scripsit disertè Plato in Politico, Tomo 2. operum, his verbis, [Itaque Deus ille huius ordinis parens, & autor cernens Mundum in tātas angustias (propter hominum nempe ἀπιξίαν, quæ superuenerat) conieētum, sollicitus ne tumultu tam turbulento fluctuans dissolueretur, & in locum dissimilitudinis infinitum mergeretur, rursum Mundi gubernacula repetit, & ijs sollicitè insidet, agrotasque atque dissolutas Mundi partes, & quasi luxatas ad pristinum circuitu reuocatas ornat, atque emendat: ipsumq; proinde à seni & mortis iniuria vendicat.] Deinde, aiunt Deum hoc ipsum sola bonitate sua impulsum fecisse. Id quod Trismegistus docet, citante Lactantio lib. 4. Institut. Christ. cap. 7, Αἰτία τούτου, ἡ ἡ Θεοῦ ἀγαθὴ ἕλκυσις. Verum modum quoque addit idem Trismegistus, per quem bonus Deus huic Mundo ruenti succurrit, & subuenit. Adiungit enim, ἡ Θεὸν ποιήνεκεν, ἐ τὸ ὄνομα ἐν Σωτῆρα ἀνθρώπῳ σώσαι λαλῆσαι, id est, [Causa huius rei est boni Dei voluntas, qua Deum produxit (nempe filium suum) cuius nomen humano ore proferri non potest,] quem & Sapientiam Dei, & Sanctum vocat ibidem idem Trismegistus. Hic igitur est, fuitque modus seruandi Mundi, ac imprimis hominum qui perierant & omnino, & vniuersi, Quod Deus Pater Filium (quem ab aeterno progenuerat, cuiusque nomen est ineffabile) produxerit, ac promiserit hominibus post eorum ruinam. Is enim Filius est, qui homines perditos statim & ab initio seruauit, seruat ac solum seruabit, quem etiam Sibylla & verum Deum esse, & ab hominibus venerandum, & caeterorum Deorum, id est, piorum & fidelium hominum rectorem (Id enim [Dij] nomen significat apud veteres Philosophos, vt ex Pythagora aureis versibus apparet) ac gubernatorem testantur, quarum hi versus extant apud Lactantium lib. 4. quem iam citauimus, capite 6. Πανταφυγὴν κτίσιν, ὅσις γλυκὺ πνεῦμα ἅπαντ Κάτθετο, χ' ἡγητῆς Θεῶν πάντων ἐποίησε
units.tr: Now let us come to the third head of our history, in which the promise of the future Messiah (who was to be both God and man) is contained. Traces of this history, which seems to belong peculiarly to Christians and to be unknown to the Gentiles, nevertheless survive in great abundance among those same Gentiles. Such are the following, which we shall set out briefly, though we have deliberately not tried to gather everything, so as not to rob anyone of the credit for his own industry. Those writers teach, first, that after the fall of man and the ruin of the whole world, God, in his great mercy and goodness, did not abandon its governance and care. Plato states this plainly in the Politicus, volume 2 of his works, in these words: [So that god, the parent and author of this order, seeing the world thrown into such straits (namely because of the lack of mankind's wisdom that had come upon it), anxiously feared lest it be dissolved and plunged into the boundless region of dissimilarity by so violent a tumult; he therefore took up the reins of the world again, and sits over it with care, restoring and correcting its sick and dissolved parts, which had been as it were dislocated, bringing them back to their former circuit; and so he rescues it from the injury of old age and death.] Next, they say that God was moved to do this by his goodness alone. Trismegistus teaches this, as Lactantius cites him in Institutes 4, chapter 7: [The cause of this is the good attraction of God] [Αἰτία τούτου, ἡ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἀγαθὴ ἕλξις]. Trismegistus also adds the means by which the good God came to the aid and succour of this falling world. For he adds: [The cause of this thing is the good will of God, by which he brought forth (namely his Son), whose name cannot be uttered by human mouth] [Θεὸς ποιήσας ... ὄνομα ... σωτῆρα ἀνθρώπων σῶσαι]; this same Trismegistus calls him the Wisdom of God and the Holy One in the same place. This, then, was and is the way of preserving the world, and above all of the men who had perished, both wholly and as a whole: that God the Father produced the Son (whom he had begotten from eternity, and whose name is ineffable) and promised him to men after their ruin. For this is the Son who saved lost men at once and from the beginning, who saves them now, and who alone will save them. The Sibyl also testifies that he is the true God, to be worshipped by men, and the ruler and governor of the other gods, that is, of the pious and faithful men (for [Dii] is the name these ancient philosophers gave to them, as appears from Pythagoras' Golden Verses). Her verses are extant in Lactantius, book 4, which we have already cited, chapter 6: [Created the whole universe, who breathed sweet spirit into all things, and made him the leader of all the gods] [Πανταφυγὴν κτίσιν, ὅσις γλυκὺ πνεῦμα ἅπαντ' ...]

units.la: Αυτὸν ἐδωκε Θεὸς πνσοῖς ἀνθρώποις γεγέρμεν, Αυτὸν σὺν γίνωσκε Θεὸν θεὸς υἱὸν ἑοντα.
units.tr: [God gave him to mortal men to be their guide, that they might know him as God, being God's son] [Αυτὸν ἐδωκε Θεὸς πνσοῖς ἀνθρώποις γεγέρμεν, Αυτὸν σὺν γίνωσκε Θεὸν θεὸς υἱὸν ἑοντα.]

units.la: [Constituit Deus hunc cunctorum námque piorum Rectorem, qui cuncta creat, nutritque, foveatque, Quíque homini suauem voluit concedere mentem. Hunc Deus a cunctis iussit reclis honorari: Ergo Deum hunc agnosce tuum, quia Filius est Dei.]
units.tr: [God appointed this one as ruler of all the pious; he creates all things, nourishes and cherishes them, and he willed to grant a sweet mind to man. God commanded that he be honoured by all upright men. Therefore acknowledge this one as your God, because he is the Son of God.]

units.la: Sed & eundem (qui Dei Filius, & Deus erat, & aeternus) fore tamen Θνητὸν κατὰ σαρκὰ, i. mortalem & hominem secundum carnem, eadem Sibylla Ethnicorum prophetissa praedixerant, quarum versus refert Lactantius lib. 4. cap. 13. Ex quibus omnibus colligitur hactenus prophanos cum Mose consentire, quod ex obscuris quidem, sed tamen ex veritate sacra superstitibus reliquis & vestigys intellexerint Deum posse hominum peccatum succurrisse & ys ipsis hominibus, & toti mundo ruenti, hoc nimirum pacto, quod Filium suum ys promiserit, & eundem piorum rectorem, i. Ecclesiae principem & caput constituerit, per quem omnia iam condita fuerant & sustinetur: & qui postea homo futurus erat, ut homines a suis peccatis liberaret. Praeclara vero est illa Augustini aduersus Porphyrium disputatio lib. 10. Cinit. Dei, cap. 22, 23, & 32, nempe prophanos ipsos ex oraculis suis, testes ipsomet Porphyrio, iam pridem audiuisse, & didicisse etiam ante natum Christum opus sibi, ac cunctis mortalibus esse Mediatorem & conciliatorem apud Deum, qui Mediator hominum, hominumque animas a vitiis ipse per se purgaret. Nam neque per Teletas & sacrificia, quae Lunae vel Soli facerent, neque per alia sacrificia proprie peccata purgari:sed per eos dntaxat, qui sunt totius rerum natura principia. Quos idem Augustinus ex ipsorummet profanorum sententia docet esse Deum Patrem & Filium. Sic enim cap.23.scribit: [Dicit etiā Porphyrius diuinis(id est, Delphicis & profanis)oraculis, fuisse responsum nos no purgari Lunae teletis atq; Solis: vt hinc ostenderetur nullorum Deorum teletis (id est sacrificijs) hominem posse purgari. Cuius enim teleta purgant, si Lunae Solisue non purgant, quos inter Deos praecipuos habent? Denique eodem dicit oraculo expressum, Principia posse purgare, ne forte (quum distiu esset non purgare teletas Solis & Lunae) alicuius alterius Dei de turba valere ad purgandum teleta crederentur. Quae autem dicat Principia, tanquam Platonicus, nominus. Dicit enim Deum Patrem, & Deum Filium, quem Graece appellat Paternum Intellectum, & Paternam Mentem: De Spiritu enim sancto aut nihil, aut non aperte aliquid dicit.] At cap.24. addit idem Augustinus.
units.tr: But the same Sibyl, the prophetess of the Gentiles, had also foretold that he who was the Son of God and God, and eternal, would nevertheless become mortal according to the flesh, that is, a man in the flesh. Lactantius cites her verses in Institutes 4, chapter 13. From all these things it is gathered that the profane writers, so far, agree with Moses. From the obscure remnants of sacred truth that survived among them, they understood that God could come to the aid of sinful men, and of the whole falling world, in this way: that he promised his Son to them, and appointed him as the leader of the pious, that is, as prince and head of the Church, through whom all things had already been created and are sustained, and who was afterwards to become man so that he might free men from their sins. Augustine's disputation against Porphyry in book 10 of the City of God, chapters 22, 23 and 32, is truly excellent. It shows that the profane writers themselves, from their own oracles (Porphyry being the witness), had long since heard and learned, even before Christ was born, that there was need of a Mediator and reconciler with God for themselves and for all mortals; this Mediator of men would himself cleanse the souls of men from their vices. For sins are not purged by the rites and sacrifices that are made to the Moon or the Sun, nor by any other sacrifices, but only by those who are the first principles of the whole nature of things. Augustine shows, from the very opinion of the profane writers, that these are God the Father and God the Son. For in chapter 23 he writes thus: [Porphyry also says that the divine oracles (that is, the Delphic and profane ones) gave the answer that we are not purified by the rites of the Moon and the Sun, so that it might be shown that no rites of any gods (that is, sacrifices) can purify a man. For if the rites of a god do not purify, whom do they hold as the chief gods, if not the Moon and the Sun? Finally, the same oracle is said to have declared that Principles can purify, lest perhaps (since it was clear that the rites of the Sun and Moon do not purify) it be believed that the rites of some other god from the crowd had power to purify. But what he calls Principles, he names as a Platonist. For he speaks of God the Father and God the Son, whom he calls in Greek the Paternal Intellect and the Paternal Mind. Concerning the Holy Spirit he says either nothing or nothing clearly.] In chapter 24 Augustine adds this:

units.la: [Sed subditus Porphyrius inuidis potestatibus (utpote qui erat idololatra, & persecutoribus Ecclesiae Imperatoribus, nempe Diocletiano & Maximiano fauebat) noluit intelligere Dominum Iesum Christum esse principium, cuius incarnatione purgamur. Eum enim in ipsa carne contempsit quam propter sacrificium nostra purgationis assumpsit. Sed is solus peccata nostra potuit soluere moriendo, quia & mortuus est, & non pro suo peccato. Principium ergo (quod se esse dicit Christus, Ioan.8.25) suscepta anima & carne, & animam credentium mundat, & carnem. Propterea ergo nobis per Mediatorem praestita est gratia, vt peccati carne pol-luti, luti, carnis peccati similitudine mudaremur.] Id quod idem Augustinus eodem lib. 10. cap. 32. fusius quoque persequitur. At quem malitiose negat Porphyrius Iesum Christum esse nostrarum animarum, & peccatorum purgatorem & conciliatorē apud Deum Patrem, eundem tamen Sibylla iapridem ante Christi ipsius in carnum aduentu agnouerat, & ingenuè fuerat confessa esse talē in Acrostichide illa, cuius meminit Tullius in libr. de Diuinat. (quod prima versuum litera Iesum Christum continent) Huius autem particulam tantum ad refutandam ac reiciendam Porphyrij cōtumaciam ex ipsis illius Prophetis proferemus, uti est à Ioanne Lango conuersa, extátque in fine operum seu historia Nicephori Callisti: I [Iudicij metuet sudans præsagia tellus: E Et Rex aternum magno descendet Olympo, S Sublimis carnem, mundumq; vt iudicet omnem. V Vnum suspicient numen prauiqué, bonique, S Summum supremo cum sanctis tempore mundi. C Carnifer ille homines iudex inquiret in omnes. H Horrida terra vias cœli, spinaque tenebunt. R Reijcient simulacra viri, gazamque repostam. I Ille domos cæcas, & Ditis claustra refringet. S Sanctior à mortis iam nexu libera lucem T Turba hominū cernet, sceleratos flamma cremabit V Vltrix perpetuum mala qua quisque patrauit S Sontica, suppressitque diu, producet in auras.]
units.tr: [But Porphyry, subject to the hostile powers (since he was an idolater and favoured the emperors who persecuted the Church, namely Diocletian and Maximian), refused to acknowledge that the Lord Jesus Christ is the Principle by whose incarnation we are purged. For he despised him in that very flesh which he assumed for the sacrifice of our purification. But he alone could loose our sins by dying, because he both died and did not die for his own sin. Therefore the Principle (which Christ says he is, John 8:25), having taken on soul and flesh, cleanses the soul and flesh of believers. Hence grace has been granted to us through the Mediator, so that we who were polluted by the flesh of sin might be cleansed by the likeness of sinful flesh.] Augustine pursues the same point more fully in the same book 10, chapter 32. But Porphyry maliciously denies that Jesus Christ is the purifier and reconciler of our souls and sins before God the Father. Yet the Sibyl had long before the coming of Christ in the flesh recognised him as such, and had openly confessed him to be so in that acrostic, which Cicero mentions in his book On Divination, because the first letters of its verses spell Jesus Christ. To refute and reject the obstinacy of Porphyry, we will quote only a part of it from the Sibyl's own prophecies, as it has been translated by John Lang, and it stands at the end of the works or history of Nicephorus Callistus: [The earth, sweating, will dread the omens of judgement. And the King shall descend from mighty Olympus, / exalted in flesh, to judge the whole world. / One God shall the good and the wicked behold at the last time of the world. / That hangman shall question all men as judge. / The dreadful earth and the thorns shall hold the ways of heaven. / Men shall cast away their idols and their hidden treasure. / He shall break open the blind houses and the prison of Dis. / The holier throng of men, now freed from the bond of death, shall see the light. / The avenging flame shall burn the wicked. / The sins each man has committed, and long kept hidden, he shall bring out into the light.]

units.la: Ex quibus omnibus perspicuè colligitur etiam eum per quem mundus hic, & homines à suis peccatis purgandi erant, atque adeo sunt, esse IESVM CHRI- N 2 STVM Filium DEI, Regem aeternum, idque cum effecturum, quoniam humanam carnem assumpturus erat, & in eadem passurum, ac tandem Mundum iudicaturum. Quae omnia cum Mosis doctrina, seu veritate Divina, velut eiusdem vestigia plane consentiunt. Verum qui Ethnici suis illis Prophetis (sic enim Sibyllas nominaverim, quemadmodum Paulus Cretensem Epimenidem Prophetam appellat, Tit. 1. 12.) non attenderunt, in diverticula varia discessere ex his veritatis vestigijs, quae inter eos tamen retenta fuerant, digressi. Ergo in universum omnes Ethnici fatentur quidem nobis apud Deum purgatione, & conciliatione opus esse, quoniam is nobis propter peccata nostra meritò sit infensus, ac iratus. Verum in modo variant. Alij enim teletas & sacrificia, sacramentalia, i. opera externa constituunt esse verissimas illius animorum nostrorum purgationis apud Deum causas. Sic enim ex quorundam veterum Philosophorum traditione homo portentosa religionis Iamblicus in lib. de mysteriis scripsit. Alij eam animorum nostrorum purgationem apud Deum in sola animi pietate interna statuunt, uti Plato ipse, & ex eo Platonici: sed & alicubi quoque Trismegistus, ut docent Macrobius, & Lactant. Ille in Somno Scipionis, hic in lib. 2. Institut. Christian. cap. 15. Alij per Angelos seu Daemonas eam in nobis fieri malunt, eosque duntaxat bonos, quos Deus hominibus post eorum peccatum custodes apposuit, velut Hesiod. lib. 1. Operum, & Dierum, his verbis,
units.tr: From all of these it is clearly gathered that the one through whom this world and men were to be cleansed of their sins, and so have been cleansed, is Jesus Christ, the Son of God, an eternal King. He would effect this because he was going to take on human flesh, suffer in it, and at last judge the world. All of these things agree plainly with the teaching of Moses, or divine truth, as its traces. But the heathen, who did not heed their prophets (I shall call the Sibyls such, just as Paul calls the Cretan Epimenides a prophet, Titus 1:12), turned aside into various byways, departing from these traces of truth, which nevertheless remained among them. So in general all the heathen admit that we need purification and reconciliation before God, since he is rightly angry and hostile to us because of our sins. But they differ about the manner. Some hold that rites, sacrifices, and sacramental acts, that is, external works, are the truest causes of that purification of our souls before God. Thus Iamblichus, in his book on the mysteries, wrote in a portentous manner of religion, following the tradition of certain ancient philosophers. Others place this purification of our souls before God in inward piety of soul alone, as Plato himself did, and the Platonists after him; and also Trismegistus somewhere, as Macrobius and Lactantius teach: the former in the Dream of Scipio, the latter in book 2 of the Divine Institutes, chapter 15. Others prefer that this takes place in us through angels or demons, and only the good ones, whom God assigned to men as guardians after their sin, as Hesiod says in book 1 of the Works and Days, in these words:

units.la: Τεὶς γὰρ μυρίοι εἰσὶν ἐπὶ χθονὶ πτυλβοτείρῃ
units.tr: For thrice ten thousand are upon the bounteous earth [Τρὶς γὰρ μυρίοι εἰσὶν ἐπὶ χθονὶ πουλυβοτείρῃ]

units.la: Ἀσάι ατοι ζηνὸς φύλακες θνητῶν ἀνθρώπων. Alij aliam purgationis animam nostram rationem comenti sunt, velut Persæ, quemadmodum scribit Agathias lib. 2. de Bello Pers. Illi enim anniuersarium festû olim instituerunt, quod vocabant Vitiorum in homine Interitum. Indi, vt tradunt Historici Hispani, Indi inquam recens reperti aiunt, Deum offensum non placari sacrificijs, nec se ab Aquanis, id est, Dæmonis sibi infestì potestate, & manu saua propter ea eripi. In summa, fuerunt infinita pene dinerticula inter ipsos Ethnicos, qui nõ attendentes is primeuæ veritatis vestigijs (quæ Deus inter eos restare voluit) sed qui ea retinuerunt, vti demonstrauimus, plane nobiscũ, & cum Mose consentiũt. Et hæc quidé de tertio capite, & illius reliquijs hactenus. Accedo ad quintum, quod est de primo vestitu hominis. Nam quartũ à nobis prætermittetur, vbi Mulieris nomẽ à viro suo, nimirũ Adamo, mutatum fuisse docetur, vti diximus, quòd illius pauca inter Ethnicos vestigia, imò nulla reperimus.
units.tr: immortal guardians of Zeus over mortal men [Ἀθάνατοι ... Διὸς φύλακες θνητῶν ἀνθρώπων]. Others have devised other ways of purifying our souls, as the Persians did, as Agathias writes in book 2 of his history of the Persian war. For they once instituted an annual festival, which they called the Destruction of Vices in Man. The Indians, as the Spanish historians report, the recently discovered Indians I say, declare that God when offended is not appeased by sacrifices, nor is one snatched from the power of the Aquani, that is, the demon hostile to him, by a cruel hand for that reason. In sum, there were almost infinite byways among the heathen themselves, who, not heeding the traces of the first truth (which God wished to remain among them), but holding to those that they kept, as we have shown, agree plainly with us and with Moses. And these things, concerning the third chapter and its remnants, are enough for now. I come to the fifth, which concerns the first clothing of man. For the fourth will be passed over by us, where it is taught that the woman's name was changed by her husband, namely Adam, as we said, because we find few traces of this among the heathen, indeed none.

units.la: Ad V. Primus Hominum Vestitus.
units.tr: To Chapter V. The First Clothing of Man.

units.la: Nuditatem homini iam turpem esse, ac præsertim in pudendis (quæ vocantur) testatur S. Scriptura, postquam ab illa morum innocentia deflexit homo, in qua primùm conditus fuerat: & eum primum pellibus vestitum fuisse eadem illa testatur. Hæc vero etiam ex manifestissimis vestigijs (quæ in Ethnicorum hominum scriptis passim extant) colligi quoque possunt. Ac primum quidem totius corporis nostri nuditatem esse rem aspectu fœdam, imprimisque genitalium membrorum intuitum, idq; ex communi natura sensu, ac populorum omnium confensu docet Herodotus in Clio, .i. lib.1.his verbis: [Apud Lydos,ait,& fere apud cateros quoq; barbaros(.i. homines)magno probro eft etiam virum, nedum mulierem,confpici nudum.] Id quod etiā apud Gracos obtinuiffe ad fua vfq; tempora docet Plato,lib. 5.de Rep. Ergo apud omne mortalium genus ea res, id eft,nuditas corporis,turpis,velut natura voce,habita eft: Homerus, qui vtroque illo fcriptore longe fuit antiquior,idem teftatur Odyf.lib.6. Nam de veftimentis in genere loquens,ait,
units.tr: Holy Scripture testifies that nakedness is now shameful for man, especially in the parts that are called private, since man turned away from that innocence of conduct in which he was first created; and the same Scripture testifies that he was first clothed in skins. These things can also be gathered from the clearest traces, which are found everywhere in the writings of the heathen. And first, that the nakedness of the whole body is an ugly sight, and especially the sight of the genital organs, Herodotus teaches in the first book of his Clio, in these words: [Among the Lydians, he says, and nearly among the other barbarians too, it is a great disgrace even for a man, let alone a woman, to be seen naked.] That this also prevailed among the Greeks down to his own time, Plato teaches in book 5 of the Republic. Therefore among every kind of mortal that thing, that is, the nakedness of the body, has been regarded as shameful, as if by the voice of nature. Homer, who was far older than both of those writers, bears witness to the same in the Odyssey, book 6. For speaking of clothing in general, he says,

units.la: Εκ γαρ τοι τυτων φατης ανθρωπους αναλαινει [Ex his fama viris bona contigit omnibus effe.]
units.tr: For from these things a good report comes to men [Ἐκ γάρ τοι τούτων φάτις ἀνθρώπους ἀναλαμβάνει].

units.la: Itaque negat idem Ulyffem naufragum,& quanuis afflictiffimu,quia nudus erat, aufum fefe Nauficaa primum oftendere,velin vrbem Phaacum abfque veftimentis profici fci. Et quum primum nudus ad mulieres ille acceffiffet, mulieres illa,ait idem Homerus,ex communi natura voce
units.tr: So the same poet says that Ulysses, shipwrecked and most afflicted though he was, because he was naked, did not dare to show himself first to Nausicaa, and that he would not go into the city of the Phaeacians without clothes. And when he first came naked to the women, those women, the same Homer says, by the common voice of nature
