units.la: Τρεσαν δ' αλλυδις αλλη δη νιονας πρεχεσας, [Diffugere illac atque hac per littora fparfa.] Deinde quantumlibet incitatus a filia regis Nauficaa, vt in vrbe accederet, refpondet Ulyffes, Αιδεομαι γαρ Τυυνικ, κεγην ευπολιομ ιοι ... Nam pudet effe Me nudum,quanquam pulcris accedo puellis.]
units.tr: fled here and there, scattering along the shore [Τρέσαν δ᾽ ἄλλυδις ἄλλη δὴ νῦν ... πρέχεσθαι]. Then, however much Ulysses was urged by the king's daughter Nausicaa to approach in the city, he answers, "For I am ashamed, maiden, ... [Αἰδέομαι γὰρ τοῦνεκα, κούρη ...]: For I am ashamed to be naked, though I approach beautiful girls."

units.la: Cur vero? Nifi quia Natura ipfa docet id effe iam homini inhoneftum. Age vero,etiam vetuftiffima hominum traditione fcribit Athenaeus lib.1. Dipnofophist. [Cura fuit & veteribus vt veftem decenter colligeret, ac eos irriderent,a quibus hoc negligeretur. Plato in Theateto illos, qui nefciunt ingenue apteq; veftem induere, nec deorum vitam ait posse celebrare.] Denique vestem etiam ad eruditionem quidpiam conferre tradit ex Hermippo, & Aristarcho idem Athenæus: adeo ut malint homines etiam crudis animalium pellibus, quatumvis ferarum, aut ꝗ ysdem impoli is tegi, quàm nudi esse, & sic cospici ac incedere. Ex quo fit ut M. Tullius lib. 1. de Officijs ex eo ipso Cynicos Philosophos consutet, qui neque nuditatem esse obscœnam censebant, neque alia pleraq;, quæ verecundia repugnant: [Nos autem naturam, inquit Tullius, sequamur, & ab omni (quod abhorret ab ipsa oculorum, aurium̅que approbatione) fugiamus. Scenicorum quidem mos tantam habet verecundiam, ut in Scenam sine subligaculo prodeat nemo. Verentur enim, nʼ si quo casu evenerit, ut corporis partes quaedam aperiantur, aspiciantur non decore.] Quamobrem idem eodem libro postea sic concludit, [Cynicorum ratio tota est ejicienda: est enim inimica verecundiæ, sine qua nihil rectum, esse potest, nihil honestum.] Pugnat igitur ipsa natura cum eiusmodi hominum Nuditatem probantium opinione, etiam testibus ipsi met Ethnicis, quorum antiquissimum, ac naturale iudicium sic refert Augustinus, lib. 14. Ciuit. Dei, cap. 17. [Porro Campestria Latinum quidem verbum est, sed ex eo dictum, quod iuuenes, qui nudi exercebantur in campo, pudenda operiebant: Vnde qui ita succincti sunt, Campestratos vulgus appellat. Ex hoc omnes gentes (quoniam ab illa stirpe nempe libidinis ac vitiosorum hominum procreatæ sunt) vsque adeo tenet insitum, pudenda velare, ut quidam Barbari illas corporis partes nec in balneis nudas habeant: sed cum earum tegumentis latuant.] Atq; hic pudor,naturalisque tum totius corporis,tum pudendorum nuditatis verecundia est illius veritatis (quam tradit Moses) amplissimum testimonium,ac vestigium. Nec obstat,quod inter Indos Gymnosophistæ Philosophi viuebant nudi. Nam, vt ait ibidem Augustinus,adhibet genitalibus tegumenta. Praterea nec in eo probandi sunt,vti nec hodie Adamitæ Monachi:nec Lacedamonij, Cretensefve luctatores, de quibus Plato lib. 5 .de Repub. quod nudi conspiciebantur. Abhorret enim hoc tam sœdum spectaculum natura & communis sensus. Imo vero syluestres homines (quia vestimentorum vsu carent propter solitudinem,in qua procul ab alijs hominibus versantur) Deus ipse pilis grandioribus vestiuit, vt eorū nuditatem obtegeret. De quibus ýsdem hoc traditum est,vt explorarum,eos breuioris & imbecillioris vitæ esse, quòd nudi viuant,& cœli grauissimis iniurijs pateant. Itaq; malè Plutarchus in libro de Connubialibus præceptis Herodotum reprehendit,qui dixerat,Mulierem vnà cum veste pudorem quodammodo exuere. Nuditas enim reddit homines & impudentes, & inuerecundos. Caterum eius quoq; ipsius (quod addit Moses)nempe primum hominum vestitum fuisse crudas pelles Animalibus detractas, vestigia sunt, Primùm id, quod scribit Hesiodus lib.2.Oper.& Dier.rusticos naturali vestitu vsos suo tempore solis pellibus animalium sese cooperuisse,quas nec pilis spoliabant,nec adornabant:sed quales erant bestijs detractæ, easdem induebant. Hæc sunt Poëta verba: Ἀ̓νρι δ̓ ἐ̓ πρωτ̓ ... ἔ̓ ... ἐ̓γ...
units.tr: But why? Unless because Nature herself teaches that this is already dishonourable for man. Come now, Athenaeus in book 1 of the Deipnosophists also writes from the most ancient tradition of mankind. "It was a concern even for the ancients to wear clothing decently, and they mocked those by whom this was neglected." Plato in the Theaetetus says that those who do not know how to put on clothing nobly and fittingly cannot celebrate the life of the gods. Finally, Athenaeus says, from Hermippus and Aristarchus, that clothing also contributes something to culture; so that men would rather be covered even with raw hides of animals, however wild, or with any such rough skins, than be naked and so be seen and walk about. From this it follows that Marcus Tullius in book 1 of the Offices refutes the Cynic philosophers from this very point, who thought that nakedness was not obscene, nor many other things that conflict with modesty: "Let us, however," says Tullius, "follow nature, and flee from everything that offends the approval of our eyes and ears. The custom of the stage has such great modesty that no one comes onto the stage without a loincloth. For they fear that if by chance some parts of the body should be exposed, they would be looked at without grace." Therefore the same author, in the same book, afterwards concludes thus: "The whole system of the Cynics is to be rejected, for it is hostile to modesty, without which nothing can be right, nothing honourable." Thus nature itself contradicts the opinion of those who approve such nakedness of men, even by the testimony of the heathen themselves; and Augustine, in book 14 of the City of God, chapter 17, reports their most ancient and natural judgment as follows. "Moreover, Campestria is a Latin word, but it is named from this: young men who exercised naked in the field covered their private parts; hence those who are so girded are called campestrati by the common people." From this the whole race of men (since they were born from that stock of lust and of wicked men) holds so deeply ingrained the custom of covering the private parts, that some barbarians do not even have those parts bare in the baths, but keep them hidden with coverings. And this shame, the natural modesty of both the whole body and the nakedness of the private parts, is a very ample testimony and trace of that truth which Moses teaches. Nor does it count against this that among the Indians the Gymnosophist philosophers lived naked. For, as Augustine says in the same place, they use coverings for the genitals. Besides, they should not be approved in this, any more than the Adamite monks today; nor the Lacedaemonian or Cretan wrestlers, of whom Plato in book 5 of the Republic says that they were seen naked. For this so shameful a spectacle is abhorrent to nature and to common sense. Indeed, God himself clothed the wild men, who because of their solitude, living far from other men, lack the use of clothing, with thicker hair, so as to cover their nakedness. Of these same men it is recorded, as explorers report, that because they live naked and are exposed to the most severe injuries of the sky, they have shorter and weaker lives. And so Plutarch wrongly rebukes Herodotus in his book on the precepts of marriage, who had said that a woman in some measure lays aside modesty along with her clothing. For nakedness makes men both shameless and immodest. But as for the other point that Moses adds, namely that the first clothing of men was raw skins stripped from animals, there are traces of it. First, what Hesiod writes in book 2 of the Works and Days, that the rustics in his time, using their natural clothing, covered themselves only with the skins of animals, which they neither stripped of hair nor adorned, but wore as they were stripped from the beasts. These are the poet's words: [Ἀνρι δ᾽ ἐ πρωτ᾽ ... ἐ ... ἐγ...]
