units.la: Πεφυτογονέων δ᾽ Εειξων (ὑτότην κρύος ἄειο͂ς ἐλθη), Δείγματα συρ ῥάτ|ην ρεύρῳ βοός, ὅρῳ ὃ᾽ ἢ γώτῳ Τ᾽ ἐ᾽ ἀμφιβάλλῃ ἀλένην.
units.tr: Hesiod, when the cold comes on, tells how to shelter the body: wrap the shoulders in the hide of an ox [Πεφυτογονέων δ᾽ Εειξων (ὑτότην κρύος ἄειο͂ς ἐλθη), Δείγματα συρ ῥάτ|ην ρεύρῳ βοός, ὅρῳ ὃ᾽ ἢ γώτῳ Τ᾽ ἐ᾽ ἀμφιβάλλῃ ἀλένην].

units.la: [Calceus in pede fit ex corio crudoque, bubulcoque, Et cory pilos intra componito densos.
units.tr: [A shoe is to be made for the foot from raw leather and ox-hide, and the thick hair is to be set inside the hide.

units.la: Sic quum frigus erit, primorum sumito pelles Hædorum, neruoque boni quas consue firmo, Imponásque tuo, pluuiali tempore, collo.]
units.tr: So when the cold comes, take the skins of the first kids, sew them with strong sinew, and put them on your back in the rainy season.]

units.la: Deinde quod tradit Iulius Cæsar lib. 6. Commentar. de Bello Gall. loquens de omnibus Germanis, qua fuit gens latissima populosissimáque, cuius vestitus erat naturalis, non artificialis: purus, & simplex, non pretiosus, & adornatus [Pellibus] ait, aut [paruis renonum tegumentis vtuntur, magna corporis parte nuda.] Est autem [Reno] pellis cruda, & pecudi recens detracta, non expolita, quales exuuiæ pecudum: cuius etiam meminit Varro lib. 4. de lingua Latina. Hanc putat esse vocem Gallicam Iosephus Scaliger in eum Varronis locum: Isidorus autem lib. 19. Etymologiarum, Germanicam.
units.tr: Then there is what Julius Caesar, in the sixth book of his Commentaries on the Gallic War, records about all the Germans, a very wide and populous nation, whose clothing was natural rather than manufactured, plain and simple rather than costly and adorned. He says they wear [skins], or [small coverings of hide], leaving a large part of the body bare. A [reno] is a raw hide, taken fresh from the beast, not dressed, like the cast skins of animals. Varro also mentions it in the fourth book of his work on the Latin language. Joseph Scaliger, on that passage of Varro, thinks it is a Gallic word; Isidore, in the nineteenth book of his Etymologies, calls it Germanic.

units.la: Quod si pilis sunt oues, renones erunt pelles ouium, aut his similium aliarum parvarum pecudum, quales Capræ, hædi, arietes, ex quarum pellibus vestes & tegumenta fieri præcipit quoq; Hesiodus, vti demonstrauit & sibi Germani, quemadmodum docet Cæsar, vestimenta naturaliter conficiebant. Ex quibus apparet retentam fuisse ab hominibus memoriâ primi illius sui vestitus, qualem ipsis induit Deus post eorum peccatum. Atque huic sententiæ suffragatur Plato, qui in Politico scribit Vestimentum primo repertum fuisse ex eo Rerum genere, quod ille ⟨Greek⟩ appellat, & quod ait fuisse ⟨Greek⟩, ⟨Greek⟩ .i. primigenium, simplex, incompositum, & nullius scientiæ opus & artificium. Fuisse vero summi cuiusdã ac prestantissimi ingenij & viri, docet idem in Protagora, rationem Vestimentorum & Calceamentorum confuendorum inuenisse. Id quod ex eo postea Tullius quoque Tusculano primo descripsit. Caeterum postea & artificia, & pretia vestimentis accesserunt, ut monstrat Plinius lib.8. Natur. Hist. cap.48. Sed prima fuerunt simplicissima, qualia ea, quæ commemorat Moses à Deo primùm Adamo data fuisse: Denique quemadmodum lingua & idiomate: sic genere ipso vestitus, gentes ipsæ inter se distingui cœpere, sicut ex Herodoto colligitur, lib.1.2 4.5. Alia enim postea fuit Ionica vestis, alia Dorica, alia Aegyptiaca, alia Persica, alia Carica, alia Thebana, alia Graeca, alia Romana: sed primum omnes uno modo vestiebantur, eóque simplicissimo. Et hæc quidem sunt pulcherrima eius, quam ex Dei verbo tuemur, veritatis vestigia. Verum ut illa magis magisque adhuc confirmetur, etiam illud ostendamus esse verum, quod diximus, nempe animalium carne vsos fuisse homines statim post peccatum, & post primam illam, innocentémque mundi ætatem finitam. Cuius rei quoq; hæc extant apud Ethnicos quoque scriptores vestigia. Primùm, quòd ipsi magno inter se firmoq; consensu hoc tradiderunt, nempe toto Saturni seculo, vel aurea, quæ vocant, Mundi ætate (quæ fuit illa innoxia, & peccatiū hominum precedens ætas) Homines esu carnium abstinuisse. Hic enim Saturnus fuit Adam ille adhuc purus, & rum,& nondum peccator. Ergo sub Saturno nulli homines carnem animalium comedebant,testibus ipsismet gentilibus seu Ethnicis. Virgilius lib.2.Georgic.
units.tr: If sheep have wool, then the renones will be sheepskins, or those of other small animals like these, such as goats, kids and rams, from whose skins Hesiod also prescribes making garments and coverings. As Caesar teaches, the Germans, too, made their clothing naturally in this way. From this it appears that men kept in memory that first clothing of theirs, of the kind God gave them after their sin. Plato supports this view when he writes in the Statesman that clothing was first discovered among the kind of things he calls [...], which he says were [...], that is, primeval, simple, unworked, and the product of no skill or craft. In the Protagoras, the same Plato teaches that the art of sewing garments and shoes was invented by a man of supreme and outstanding genius. Cicero later described this too in the first book of the Tusculan Disputations. Afterwards, however, both craftsmanship and price were added to clothing, as Pliny shows in the eighth book of his Natural History, chapter 48. But the first clothing was most simple, like the garments Moses records were first given by God to Adam. Finally, just as with language and dialect, so with clothing itself the nations began to be distinguished from one another, as is gathered from Herodotus, book 1, 2, 4, 5. For later there was one dress of the Ionians, another of the Dorians, another Egyptian, another Persian, another Carian, another Theban, another Greek, another Roman; but at first everyone dressed in one way, and that the simplest. These are the most beautiful traces of the truth we hold from the word of God. But so that they may be confirmed more and more, let us also show that what we have said is true: that men ate the flesh of animals straight after sin, once that first, innocent age of the world had ended. Traces of this too are found among the Gentile writers. First, they handed this down with great and firm agreement: that throughout the whole age of Saturn, or what they call the golden age of the world (which was that innocent age before men's sins), men abstained from eating flesh. For this Saturn was that Adam, still pure and upright and not yet a sinner. So under Saturn no men ate the flesh of animals, as the Gentiles themselves bear witness. Virgil, in the second book of the Georgics:

units.la: [Ante etiam sceptrum Distai regis, & ante Impia quàm casis gens est epulata tuuencis, Aureus hanc vitam in terris Saturnus agebat.
units.tr: [Before the sceptre of King Dis, and before a people had feasted on impious oxen, the golden Saturn lived this life on earth.

units.la: Nec dum etiam audierant inslari classica: necdum Impositos duris crepitare incudibus enses.] Hæc eadem sententia confirmatur autoritate Platonis,lib.6 de Leg. vbi docet primos homines etiam sacrificijs cruentis caruisse: & carnium Animalium esu abstinuisse, omnibusq; rebus ἐμψύχοις, i. animatis:sola vero ἀλυ-χα, quæ vocat,esitauisse. Ergo primus & naturalis hominum nodum peccatorum vitium erat is,quem describit Moses,& cuius vestigium Ouidius lib.15.Metamorphos.expressit: Pythagorici autem,sed frustra,in vsum reuocare etiam post peccatum studuerunt. Sic igitur Ouidius:
units.tr: Nor had they yet heard the trumpets sound, nor the swords, forged on hard anvils, clang.] The same view is confirmed by the authority of Plato, in the sixth book of the Laws, where he teaches that the first men also went without bloody sacrifices and abstained from eating the flesh of animals, and that they ate only what he calls [...], that is, what has no soul, while all living things were spared. So the first and natural vice of men, the source of their sins, was the one Moses describes, and of which Ovid in the fifteenth book of the Metamorphoses expressed a trace. The Pythagoreans, however, tried in vain to bring it back into use even after sin. So Ovid says:

units.la: [Parcite mortales dapibus temerare nefandis Corpora:sunt fruges,sunt deducentia ramos Pondere poma suo:tumidaque in vitibus vuæ: Sunt herba dulces,sunt quæ mitescere flamma, Mollirique queant.]
units.tr: [Mortals, spare your bodies from defiling with unholy feasts. There are grains, there are apples bending the branches with their weight, and swelling grapes on the vines. There are sweet herbs, and things that can be softened and made tender by fire.]

units.la: Deinde fatentur idem Ethnici primum hominum vitum fuisse, quod ad cibum quidem, fruges terræ, i. ea quæ terra sponte producebat:quod ad potum autem meram aquam. Id quod tradit Ouidius lib.1. eiusd.operis.Verum ante Ouidii Euripides,cuius versus Græci extant apud A.Gellium, lib.7. Νοῦ. Attic.cap.16. Horum vero ista est sententia: [Nam quid, praeter duo, est opus mortalibus, Nempe frugibus terra, ac aqua potu leni: Quae nobis obuia sunt, ac data, ut nos alant?]
units.tr: Next, the same Gentiles admit that the first men's food was the fruits of the earth, that is, what the earth produced of its own accord, and their drink was plain water. Ovid says this in the first book of the same work. Yet before Ovid, Euripides, whose Greek verses survive in Aulus Gellius, book 7 of the Attic Nights, chapter 16, said: [For what, apart from two things, do mortals need: grain from the earth, and water for gentle drink? These are before us and given to us, to nourish us.]

units.la: Plane cum iis consentiunt quae vetustissimus Poëta Teleclides scripsit in Amphictyonibus, & refert Athenaeus lib. 6. Dipnosoph. tot nempe nostrae veritatis vestigia restant. Demum docent idem, postquam Pandora malum in mundum innexisset, & prima illa aetas aurea esse desijsset, homines & sacrificia ex animalium carnibus obtulisse Deo: & ex ijsdem carnibus edere quoque coepisse: quae omnia cum Mose consentiunt. Nec enim ante peccatum hominis animalia fuerunt oblata Deo: post peccatum autem, fuerunt, & carnes eorum quoque comesae. Quod ipsum dicimus in Ethnicorum quoque scriptis inueniri. Id primum ex ijs Athenionis Poëta vetustissimi versib° apparet, qui extat apud Athenaeum lib. 14. Dipnosof. etsi quadam fabulosa, velut in vestigijs veritatis fieri solet, admiscet. Sic igitur Athenion: [Minime stultus, vel fatuus vir quidam fuit, Primus qui hostiam maclauit, & carnem assauit: Visa tunc forte est, quam humana, illa suauior.
units.tr: Indeed they agree with what the very ancient poet Teleclides wrote in the Amphictyons, which Athenaeus reports in the sixth book of the Deipnosophists. So many traces of our truth remain. Lastly, they teach the same: after Pandora had let loose evil into the world and that first golden age had ceased, men offered sacrifices to God from the flesh of animals, and began to eat that same flesh. All of this agrees with Moses. For before man's sin animals were not offered to God; but after sin, they were both offered and their flesh was eaten. We say this same thing is found in the writings of the Gentiles too. It appears first from those verses of the very ancient poet Athenion, which survive in Athenaeus, book 14 of the Deipnosophists, though he mixes in some fable, as usually happens with traces of truth. So Athenion says: [No fool or simpleton was that man who first slaughtered a victim and roasted its flesh. The meat then seemed, by chance, more pleasant than human flesh.]

units.la: Itaque exinde mactatas pecudes assauerunt, & ederunt homines.] Id quod, quemadmodū dixi, statim post aneam aetatem seu lapsum hominum in ferrea aetate euenit. Id testificante quoque Germanico Caesare, cuius haec sunt carmina:
units.tr: And so from that time men roasted and ate the slaughtered cattle.] As I said, this happened right after the brazen age, or the fall of men into the iron age. The same is attested by Germanicus Caesar, whose verses are these:

units.la: [Aurea sed postquam proles terris data, nec iam Semina virtutis vitijs diuersa resistunt, Ferrique inuento mens est laetata metallo, Palluit & Taurus mensas assuetus aratro.] Idem Empedocles scripsit hoc versu
units.tr: [But after the golden race was given to the earth, and the seeds of virtue no longer stood against the vices, and the mind rejoiced in the invention of iron, the bull, used to the plough, turned pale at the tables.] Empedocles wrote the same in this verse:

units.la: Ἐωμὸν ἐρὰ δόντας μαχαίρην Διὸς Ἀθηνᾶ ... [illegible, ~20 letters]
units.tr: [Raw flesh ... with the knife of Zeus and Athena ...] [illegible, about twenty letters]

units.la: Diuum aspergentes altaria cæde calenti.
units.tr: Sprinkling the altars of the gods with hot slaughter.

units.la: Consentit cum hac sententia quod ex veteri traditione scribit Plinius lib.7. Natur.hist.cap.56. Hiperbium Martis Dei filium, item & Promętheum (qui duo fuerunt vetustissimi homines) & animalia, & Bouem (cuius caro editur) occidisse: imo ignem ab eodem Promętheo raptum, & excitatum testatur Hefiodus libro 1. Oper.& Dier.vt bouis à se occisi, & Iouì oblati ac sacrificati carnes concoqueret, & ederet. Sed hæc fabulis obscurata sunt. Eò tamen summa redit, quo nempe tempore animalia Deo maclari ab hominibus in sacrificiū cœperūt: eodem tempore carnes animalium ab hominibus edi cœpisse. Nec enim homines formidarunt, aut nefas putarunt comedere ac vescì ijs ipsis rebus, quas offerebant, ac sacrificabant Deo. Quæ cum Dei verbo conueniunt: ac proinde vera sunt. Nec tamen propterea verum quod refert Diodorus Siculus lib.1. Bibliothec. cap.1. & ex eo Plutarchus, Orat.1. de Esu carnium, Primos homines aurea illa ætate carnibus non vixisse, quod tunc nihil terra produceret, cœlum suum cursum non conficeret, neq; frugibus ferendis idonea tempestates anni essent distributæ. Itaque tunc durissima, ait, esset, miserrimaque hominum vita. Id quod repugnat cum ipsi rerum veritati (fuit enim in prima Mundi ætate, & ante hominum peccatum perbeata eorum vita, & fœlicissimus totius huius Mundi status) tum omnium Philosophorum calculo comprobata diuini Platonis sententia in Timæo, quam iam exposuimus. Sed hæc satis. Ergo ad caput Historiæ septimum, quod est de prima generis humani propagatione, veniamus. Nam sextū, quod continet hominum & seƈtionem ex Horto Edenico, superiore disputatione breuiter, & velut per compendium complexi sumus.
units.tr: With this view agrees what Pliny, in the seventh book of his Natural History, chapter 56, writes from ancient tradition: that Hyperbius, son of the god Mars, and also Prometheus (who were two very ancient men), killed animals and an ox (whose flesh is eaten). Indeed, Hesiod in the first book of the Works and Days testifies that Prometheus stole fire and kindled it so that he might cook and eat the flesh of the ox he had killed and offered and sacrificed to Jupiter. But these things have been obscured by fables. Still, the sum comes to this: at the time when animals began to be slaughtered by men as sacrifices to God, at that same time men began to eat the flesh of animals. For men did not fear or think it wrong to eat and feed on the very things they offered and sacrificed to God. These things agree with the word of God and are therefore true. Yet it does not follow that what Diodorus Siculus reports in the first book of his Library, chapter 1, and Plutarch after him in the first oration On Eating Flesh, is true: that the first men did not live on meat in that golden age, because the earth then produced nothing, the sky did not complete its course, and the seasons of the year were not arranged for bearing fruit. So their life then, he says, was very hard and most wretched. This contradicts both the truth of the matter (for in the first age of the world, before man's sin, their life was most blessed and the state of this whole world most happy) and the divine opinion of Plato in the Timaeus, which we have already set out, approved by the verdict of all philosophers. But enough of this. Now let us come to the seventh chapter of the History, which concerns the first propagation of the human race. For the sixth, which contains the account of the Garden of Eden, we have already briefly summed up in the earlier discussion, as it were in summary.

units.la: Ad VII. Prima Generis Humani Propagatio.
units.tr: On the Chapter VII: The First Propagation of the Human Race.

units.la: Caterum de ista hominum prima Multiplicatione dicturi, & quandam illius apud Ethnicos scriptores vestigia supersint, inuestigaturi, explicaturique, duo quaedam omnino necessaria premittimus, tanquam futura disquisitionis lucem ac fundamenta: è quibus primum est sumptum ex Genes. 6. 4: nempe Posteros Caini, ac Cainum ipsum (qui ante Diluuium vixerunt) esse potentes illos, industrios, & claros viros qui à seculo, omnique hominum memoria celebres notique fuerunt, & per totum terrarum orbem, etiam post diluuium laude insignes, quique fuerunt praestantissimis nominibus (velut Saturni, Iouis, Mercurij, Vulcani, Dionysij, & similibus) etiam inter Ethnicos ipsos (qui Mosis scripta non legerant) praedicati, ac rerum gestarum fama celebrati ac commendati. Postquam enim Moses eos Caini posteros recitasset, addidit, [Isti sunt potentissimi homines, qui à seculo vel olim fuerunt viri nominis,] .i. celebres, & fama noti inter omnes mortales, etiam post ipsorum mortem, atque adeo ipso adhuc Mosis seculo, & quum illa memoriae literisque proderet. Hoc primum est, ex quo perspicuè intelligitur eos, quos posteritas, & Mosis ætas,
units.tr: But before I speak of this first multiplication of mankind, and investigate and explain the traces of it that survive among the pagan writers, I set down two points that are wholly necessary, as a light and foundation for the coming inquiry. The first is taken from Genesis 6:4: that the posterity of Cain, and Cain himself (who lived before the Flood), were those mighty, industrious and famous men who from the earliest age and in all human memory were celebrated and known, who even after the Flood were distinguished by praise throughout the whole orb of the earth, who were proclaimed by the most excellent names (such as Saturn, Jupiter, Mercury, Vulcan, Dionysius and similar ones) even among the pagans themselves, who had not read the writings of Moses, and who were celebrated and commended for the fame of their deeds. For after Moses had recited those descendants of Cain, he added: [These are the mighty men who were from of old, the men of renown], that is, famous and known by repute among all mortals, even after their death, and indeed even in Moses' own age, when it was handed down by memory and writing. This is the first point, from which it is clearly understood that those whom posterity and the age of Moses

units.la: (Text at the foot of the page is cut off by the scan edge.) tas, & sequens quoq; postea seculum magnificè celebrauit, coluit pro suminis viris, fortissimis Heroibus, imò etiam pro Diis habuit, fuisse posteros Caini, qui Diluuium praecesserunt. Ii autem sunt, quos Ethnici, vti monui, dixerunt Saturnos, Iones, Mercurios, Vulcanos, alysque eiusmodi nominibus appellarunt, vt ex eorum scriptis apparebit. Illi enim, etsi pro Diis ab Ethnicis culti sunt, homines tamen, & quidem mortales fuerunt: sed qui propter artes egregias à se primum inuentas, immensaque illa dona in totu genus humanum à se primis collata innotuerant hominibus, & apud posteros in admiratione fuerant, huiusmodi appellationibus donati celebrati sunt. Id quod mecum sentit M. Tullius lib.
units.tr: (The text at the foot of the page is cut off by the edge of the scan.) and the age that followed afterwards magnificently celebrated and worshipped as great men, the bravest heroes, and even regarded as gods, were the posterity of Cain who preceded the Flood. These are the ones whom the pagans, as I have said, called Saturns, Joves, Mercuries, Vulcans, and named with names of this kind, as will appear from their writings. For although they were worshipped as gods by the pagans, they were nonetheless men, and indeed mortal; but because of the outstanding arts first invented by them, and the immense benefits conferred by them on the whole human race, they became known to the first men, were held in admiration by posterity, and were honoured and celebrated with appellations of this kind. Marcus Tullius agrees with me in this, in book

units.la: 1. Tusculan. Quaest. & Varro in libris Rerum Diuin. testante Augustino lib. 4. Ciuit. Dei, cap. 27. & lib. 6. cap. 6. Sed imprimis id docet verum esse idem Varro, eodem lib. 4. Ciuit. Dei, cap. 24. Secundum verò, quod tanquam praemunitionem quandam praemittendum iudico, est Nimirum illas siue Graecas, siue Latinas Κρονος, Διὸς, Ερμῆς, Ἡφαιστος, Διονυσος, i. Saturni, Iouis, Mercurij, Vulcani, Dionysij, & similium appellationes multis quidem datas & communicatas fuisse (prout videlicet vnaquaeq; gens quempiam vel sua originis autorem, vel suum benefactorem, vel primum sibi notum virum strenuum & industrium celebrare, & immortalem posteritati reddere voluit, studuitque) Vnum tamen fuisse, cui primum, & ab antiquissimo tempore hoc nomen vel Saturni, vel Iouis, vel Mercurij, &c. impositum fuit: ad cuius similitudinem alij (& quidem illi primo & antiquissimo longè aetate posteriores) Saturni, aut Iones, aut Mercurij, &c. postea fuerint nominati. Quod idem de mulierum Dearum, quae vocantur, nominibus est sentiendū. Ergo plures reperientur, qui & diuersis temporibus, & à diuersis gentibus, & [Saturni, & Iones, & Vulcani] fuerunt vocati: omnes tamen nomen ex admiratione illius (qui primus eo nomine dictus est) sortiti, ac consecuti. Ex quo fit, vt in Ethnicorum libris multos dici Saturnos reperias, multos item Iones, &c. inter quos tamen vnus est vetustissimus, ex cuius laude & celebritate nomen illud alij sibi desumpserunt, vel impositum habuerunt. Id quod locupletissimè ex Cicerone probatur. Ille enim lib. 3. de Natura Deorum plures Iones, & Saturnos, & Mercurios, & Soles, & Vulcanos in diuersis nationibus, varisq; temporibus recenset. Verùm ex his vnum semper antiquissimum, & ceteris priorem, imò primum omnium sic dictum demonstrat. Confirmat nostram sententiam M. Varro doctissimus (quemadmodū Augustinus testatur lib. 19. Ciuit. Dei, cap. 22) Romanorum, qui alios Deos, ac proinde Saturnos, & Mercurios, & Iones Politicos: alios Naturales: alios Fabulosos seu Poeticos, in libris Rerum Diuin. scripsit. Confirmat Diodorus Siculus, qui lib. 1 Biblioth. cap. 2, & lib. 5. cap. 1. eiusdē operis ostendit alios fuisse Aegyptiorum Iones, Mercurios, Vulcanos, quales Osiris, Orus, Tiphæus: alios verò Græcorum. Confirmat Eusebius lib. 1. de Præparat. Euang. cap. 7, & lib. 2. cap. 2. 3. 4. & 5. Vbi ex vetustissimorum scriptorum profanorum monumentis probat in vnaquaque gente, velut Phœnicum, Atlaticorum, Phrygum (præter Aegyptios & Græcos) Cretensium suos Iones fuisse, Saturnos, &c. Confirmat denique idem hoc autor grauissimus Arnobius lib 4. contra Gentiles. Quid enim Xenophontem in Aequinoctiis, qua inscribitur: & frat. Ioannem Viterb. suffraganeos mihi asciscam, qui licet à nonnullis reijciantur, verum tamen in eo, quod iam dico, sentiunt? Ex quibus efficitur, nemini mirum videri debere si quedā hic ad Saturnum, & Iouem, & similes accómodemus, qui non omnibus iis, qui [Saturni, Ioues, vel Mercurij] &c. dicti sunt, conueniunt. Nos enim hic de primis illis dicturi sumus, qui [Ioues, & Saturni] &c. vocati sunt, quiq; sunt celebres & potentes illi viri, qui à seculo, i. statim ab ipso Mundi initio fuerūt viri commendati posteris, & fama semper postea celebrati, (quemadmodum testatur Moses, etiam post diluuium, etsi ante diluuium illi vixerunt) inter Ethnicos, & inuniuerso terrarum Orbe. M.T. Cicero in lib. de Leg. ait quosdā Deos semper pro Dijs habitos fuisse ex infinita quadam hominum memoria: alios vero fuisse Adscriptitios, quos in cœlum merita in vnamquamq; gentem vocarunt. Id quod etiam Augustinus obseruauit, lib. 8. cap. 5. Ciuit. Dei. Nam vt ait Pausanias lib. 8. Dij postea sape sunt ex hominibus nati. Plato in Apologia Socratis. Sed his expositis iam doceamus, ecquæ sunt vere & prima hominum seu generis humani propagationis (qualem describit Moses) vestigia seu reliquiæ. Ait igitur ille Primum fuisse Adamum & Euā: ex quibus natus sit primogenitus Cainus: post Abelus. Sed ex Abele nulli posteri fuerunt, superstites. Caino vero plures nati sunt tum filij, tum nepotes, tū abnepotes & posteri, viri insignes, celebres, & industrij numero
units.tr: 1. Tusculan Questions, and Varro in his books of Divine Things, as Augustine testifies in City of God book 4, chapter 27, and book 6, chapter 6. But above all Varro himself, in the same book 4 of City of God, chapter 24, shows that this is true. The second point, which I judge must be put forward as a kind of preliminary defence, is this: those names, whether Greek or Latin, Cronos, Zeus, Hermes, Hephaestus, Dionysus [Κρονος, Διὸς, Ερμῆς, Ἡφαιστος, Διονυσος], that is, the names of Saturn, Jupiter, Mercury, Vulcan, Dionysius and similar ones, were indeed given to and shared by many. Each nation wished to honour someone as its founder, its benefactor, or the first vigorous and industrious man known to it, and to make him immortal to posterity, and it strove to do so. Yet there was one to whom this name, of Saturn or Jupiter or Mercury and so on, was first given, from the most ancient time; after his likeness others, and indeed those far later in age than that first and most ancient one, were afterwards named Saturns, or Joves, or Mercuries, and so on. The same is to be understood of the names of the goddesses, as they are called. Therefore more will be found who were called by different names at different times and by different peoples, [Saturns, Joves and Vulcans]; yet all of them obtained and acquired the name from admiration for the one who was first so called. From this it comes about that in the books of the pagans you will find many called Saturns, and likewise many Joves, and so on, among whom, however, one is the most ancient, from whose praise and renown the others took that name for themselves or had it bestowed upon them. This is most fully proved from Cicero. For in book 3 of On the Nature of the Gods he enumerates many Joves, Saturns, Mercuries, Suns and Vulcans among different nations and at different times; yet he shows that among these one is always the most ancient, earlier than all the others, indeed the first of all so called. Our view is confirmed by Marcus Varro, the most learned of the Romans (as Augustine testifies in City of God book 19, chapter 22), who in his books of Divine Things wrote that some gods, and therefore some Saturns, Mercuries and Joves, are political, others natural, others fabulous or poetic. Diodorus Siculus confirms it, who in book 1 of his Library, chapter 2, and book 5, chapter 1, of the same work shows that some Joves, Mercuries and Vulcans were Egyptian, such as Osiris, Horus and Typhon, but others were Greek. Eusebius confirms it in book 1 of his Preparation for the Gospel, chapter 7, and book 2, chapters 2, 3, 4 and 5, where, from the records of the most ancient profane writers, he proves that in each nation, such as the Phoenicians, the Atlantians, the Phrygians (besides the Egyptians and Greeks) and the Cretans, there were their own Joves, Saturns and so on. Finally, the weighty author Arnobius confirms the same in book 4 against the Gentiles. For what shall I say of Xenophon in the work that is entitled Aequinoctia, and of brother John of Viterbo, whom I take as my suffragans? Although some reject them, they nevertheless agree with me in what I now say. From this it follows that no one should think it strange if here I apply some things to Saturn, and Jupiter, and similar ones, which do not suit all those who were called Saturns, Joves or Mercuries and so on. For here we shall speak of those first ones who were called Joves and Saturns, who were those famous and mighty men who, from the age, that is from the very beginning of the world, were commended to posterity and afterwards always celebrated by fame (as Moses testifies, even after the Flood, although they lived before it), among the pagans and throughout the whole orb of the earth. Marcus Tullius Cicero in his book On the Laws says that some gods have always been held to be gods from an infinite memory of men, while others were added, whom their merits raised to heaven in each nation. Augustine also observed this, City of God book 8, chapter 5. For, as Pausanias says in book 8, gods were often afterwards born of men; Plato says the same in the Apology of Socrates. But these things having been set out, let us now show what are the true and first traces or remains of the propagation of mankind or the human race, such as Moses describes. He says, then, that first there were Adam and Eve, from whom was born the firstborn Cain, and after him Abel. But from Abel no posterity survived. Cain, however, had many children, both sons and grandsons, great-grandsons and descendants, men notable, famous and industrious, in number

units.la: {•} Ex Xenophontem: in Aequinoc. quæ inscribitur. decem, si Noemam filiam Tubalcaini his annumeres, ut Moses fecit. Quod si his decem, Adamum & Euam addideris, fient omnes numero duodecim, qui proculdubio sunt duodecim illi Dij antiquissimi, & maiorum gentium Dij ab Ethnicis appellati: inter quos dua sunt fœmina nimirum Eua & Noema, id est Rhea, siue Terra, mater Deorum omnium, & Venus. Decem autem sunt mares, nempe reliqui, Adamus, Cainus, Lamechus, Iabal, Iubal, Tubalcain, & cateri, quos recitat Moses ibidem: Id est, Saturnus, Iupiter, Mercurius, Apollo, & Vulcanus, quemadmodum ab Ethnicis nominantur. Idem isti sunt, quos profana antiquitas deos Samothracu, deos Cabiros, i. deos vocat arcanos, & cateris (qui postea in deorum numerum collocati sunt) angustiores habitos. Et quidem hæc in genere dicta sunto. Iam quedam sunt specialiter declaranda: ut vera esse, etiam ex ipsismet Ethnicorum monumentis, intelligantur, quæ scribit Moses. Dico igitur Adamum Mosis, esse eum ipsum, quem posteritas verbi Dei ignara & contemptrix Latine quidem vocauit Saturnum, Græce vero Κρόνον. Veterem, non nouum Cainum Mosis, esse antiquissimum Ethnicorum Latinorum Iouem, Græcorum Ζῆνα, vel Δία, non autem recentem quendam, aut unius duntaxat gentis cognominem Iouem. Saturnum igitur hunc, qui primus Orbi innotuit, esse Adamu, etiā testibus Ethnicis, ex his colligas, quod Saturnus iste dicitur Saturnus, à voce lingua Hebræa, quæ primum omnibus mortalibus communis fuit. Vox autem illa est verbum [Satar,] quod latitare, seu occultare significat. Fuit autem hoc nomen vestigium fugæ & latitationis à Deo, quam molitus litus est Adamus post suum peccatum, ut est Gen. 3. 8. Nonnulli vero malunt Saturnum à Satione diƈtũ, quoniam, vt scribit Arnobius ex Ethnicorũ arcanis lib. 4. Sationibus præerat. Quod etsi verum fuit, tamen Saturnus à Satione deriuari non potest, quum in Saturno [Sa] syllaba sit lóga:in satione vero breuis. Saturnus, aiunt aly, diƈtum est, quòd sationibus inter Ethnicos præerat, vtpote qui primâ rerum serendarum, terræ excolendæ, & agriculturæ rationem inuenîsset, caterosque docuisset. Quod de vno Adamo verè dici potest Gen. 3. 17, & 23. Nam fuit primus in Mundo agricola, & Sator rerum & hominum. Quòd Saturnus cœli ipsius filius, vtpote ex nullo superiore homine genitus, dicitur creditúrque ab Ethnicis, Cicero lib. 3. de Nat. Deor. Adamus autem Dei filius vocatur, Luc. 3. 38. quoniam à Deo immediatè creatus est, non ex alio homine natus, nónne nostræ veritatis vestigia sunt? Quòd Saturnus nominatur Κρόνος, vt ait Plato in Cratylo, velut Χρόνος, ἀ.æternus, & ab omni huius mundi æno existens: (est enim Adamus coœuus & contemporaneus Mundo ratione ortus sui.) Quòd sub solo Saturno seculum aureum, ac primam Mundi ætatem fuisse consêntiunt omnes Ethnici, nónne hac proculdubio demonstrant hunc Saturnum fuisse verũ Adamum, sub quo tum ætas prima Mundi, tum aurea fuit, vt diximus, ante illius peccatum? Quòd Saturnus primus in orbe terrarum imperium tenuit, nonne idem fecit primus Adamus, tum iure Creationis, tum priuilegio ætatis, quum esset omnium hominũ primus Parens? Quòd Saturnus fuit maritus Ῥhææ seu Cybeles, quæ eadem mater Deorũ, id est, hominum (qui primi ingenio & industria praestantes fuerunt) dicitur. Imo eadem & Pandora quoq; nominatur, ut ait Diodorus Sicul. lib. 4. cap. 5. Bibliotb. & mater Iouis, ut scribit Euseb. lib. 2. cap. 3. Praeparat. Euangel. quae mala omnia in Mundum, ut docuimus, inuexit: nonne pro nobis ista faciunt? Est enim haec Rhea seu Pandora Eua uxor Adami primi hominis. Denique quod Saturno veteres Ethnici aperto capite, quemadmodum tradit Plutarchus in Rom. Quaest. 11. sacrificabant, nostram veritatem confirmat, ut veraci, & caeteris sanctiori Deo. Fuit enim Adamus Caino filio, eiusq; posteris lege religiosior, ac sanctior. Et haec quidem ex Ethnicorum monumentis descripta declarat eundem fuisse veterem illum eorum Saturnum, & Adamum nostrum primum hominem: quae proculdubio sunt illustria, & optima nostra veritatis vestigia, quemadmodum apud eosdem extant. Caeterum, plura quoque vestigia sunt, maioraque ea, ex quibus probatur vetustissimum seu antiquissimum Ethnicorum Iouem fuisse eum ipsum, quem S. Scriptura vocat Cainum, veluti, quod Iuppiter ille, ut scribit Plato in Euthydemo, cognominatur ἐρκεῖος, καὶ φρατρίου Septorum, urbium, & tribuum, consociationisque hominum praeses. Vt autem tradit Pausanias lib. 1. etiam πολιεύς, quod urbium curam habeat. Quae plane conueniunt Caino primi Adami filio, quia primus (ut ait S. Scriptura) urbes condidit, societatemque hominum in unum locum congregavit. Sed & idem Iupiter dicitur [Sabazius,] vel, ut Graci homines pronuntiant [Sabazius,] quemadmodum ex ipsorummet profanorum literis ostendit Clemens in Protreptico. Eusebius lib. 4. de Præparat. Euangel. & Arnobius cōtra Gentes, lib. 5. Est autem Sabaisius vel Sabazius Iupiter, Tremens, Trepidus, à nomine Hebraeo [Sabats] quod tremorem & infirmitatem (quæ accidit ob gladij percussionem) significat. Quid autem melius Cainum demonstrare potest, qui propter occisum fratrem toto vita tempore & Trepidus, & Pallens fuit? Quod autem ad nomen ζεὺς attinet, quo nominatur à Græcis: à Pythagora verò vetustissimo Philosopho, ζάν, ut scribit ex Porphyrio Cyrillus lib. 20. contra Iulian. sect. 4. videtur ea vox ex voce Cain male & sono peregrino pronuntiata fluxisse: vel saltem ex imitatione Adami vocantis uxorem suam Chaua, .i. Vitam, & futura propagationis generis humani fontem, fuisse nomen ζωὴς impositum huic homini à suis posteris in ipsius velut auctoris sui honorem & commendationem? Ac quidem facile fuit ex Cain Chaua facere peregrinis hominibus id est, non Hebraeis. Chaua autem idem est atque ζωὴς, & ζωὴ, id est, Vita, & vitæ seu viuendi principiū dans aliis. Ergo ut grata Caini posteritati testaretur futuris seculis hunc originis suæ parentem Cainum esse eum, à quo post Saturnum, primumque hominem, satum esset genus humanum, ζῶνα eum vocauit, quod idem est atq; Chaua. Et certè hoc verū est. Nam ex duobus Adami liberis (nimirum Abele & Caino) Abele sine liberis vlis mortuo seu interempto, solus Cain extitit, superstesque mansit, à quo genus humanū postea propagaretur. Itaque fuit Cainus seu Chaua, seu ζωὴς, id est, viuentiū Pater. Quanquā aliy malunt vocabulum ζεὺς, pro Δεὺς (à quo postea fit genitiuus Διὸς,) substitutum esse facili
units.tr: Out of Xenophon, in the dialogue entitled Aequinoctium? Ten, if you count Noema, the daughter of Tubalcain, among them, as Moses does. If you add Adam and Eve to these ten, you get twelve in all. These are without doubt the twelve most ancient gods, the greater gods whom the Gentiles called the gods of the nations. Among them are two women, Eve and Noema, that is, Rhea or Earth, the mother of all the gods, and Venus. The ten men are the rest: Adam, Cain, Lamech, Jabal, Jubal, Tubalcain and the others whom Moses recites in the same place. That is, they are Saturn, Jupiter, Mercury, Apollo and Vulcan, as the Gentiles name them. These are the same ones whom profane antiquity called the Samothracian gods, the Cabiri, that is, the hidden gods, and it regarded the others (who were later placed among the gods) as lesser. These things have been said in general. Now certain points must be set out specifically, so that it may be understood that what Moses writes is true, even from the monuments of the Gentiles themselves. I say, then, that the Adam of Moses is the very one whom a posterity ignorant of and contemptuous of the Word of God called Saturn in Latin and Kronos [Κρόνον] in Greek. The ancient Cain of Moses is the most ancient Jupiter of the Latin Gentiles, Zēna [Ζῆνα] or Dia [Δία] in the Greeks, and not some recent Jupiter, or one who bore the name only of a single nation. That this Saturn, who was the first to become known to the world, is Adam, you may gather even from the testimony of the Gentiles, from this: that this Saturn is called Saturn from a word of the Hebrew language, which was first common to all mortals. That word is the verb Satar [סתר], which means to lie hidden or to conceal oneself. This name was the trace of the flight and hiding from God which Adam devised after his sin, as in Gen. 3. 8, which is the first man. Some prefer to derive Saturn from Satio (sowing), because, as Arnobius writes from the secret teachings of the Gentiles (book 4), he presided over sowings. Even if this were true, Saturn still cannot be derived from satio, since in Saturn the syllable Sa is long, but in satio it is short. Others say that Saturn was so named because among the Gentiles he presided over sowings, since he was the first to discover the method of sowing things, of tilling the earth and of agriculture, and taught the rest. This can truly be said of Adam alone, Gen. 3. 17 and 23. For he was the first farmer in the world, and the sower of things and of men. That Saturn is said and believed by the Gentiles to be the son of heaven itself, as one born of no earlier man, Cicero says (book 3, On the Nature of the Gods). But Adam is called the son of God, Luke 3. 38, because he was created immediately by God and was not born of another man. Are these not traces of our truth? That Saturn is called Kronos [Κρόνος], as Plato says in the Cratylus, as if Chronos [Χρόνος], that is, eternal, and existing from every age of this world (for Adam was coeval and contemporary with the world by reason of his origin). That all the Gentiles agree that the golden age and the first age of the world existed under Saturn alone: do these not undoubtedly show that this Saturn was the true Adam, under whom there was both the first age of the world and the golden age, as we have said, before his sin? That Saturn first held empire over the earth: did not the first Adam do the same, both by the right of creation and by the privilege of age, since he was the first parent of all men? That Saturn was the husband of Rhea or Cybele, who is said to be the same mother of the gods, that is, of men (who were the first to excel in talent and industry). She is even called Pandora too, as Diodorus Siculus says (book 4, ch. 5, Bibliotheca), and the mother of Jupiter, as Eusebius writes (book 2, ch. 3, Praeparatio Evangelica). She introduced all evils into the world, as we have shown. Do these things not favour us? For this Rhea or Pandora is Eve, the wife of the first man. Finally, that the ancient Gentiles sacrificed to Saturn with his head uncovered, as Plutarch relates (Roman Questions 11), confirms our truth, as that of the true and holier God over the others. For Adam was more religious and holier by law than his son Cain and Cain's posterity. These things, drawn from the monuments of the Gentiles, show that their old Saturn was the same as our Adam, the first man. These are without doubt illustrious and excellent traces of our truth, just as they are found among those same peoples. Moreover, there are also more traces, and greater ones, from which it is proved that the most ancient and first Jupiter of the Gentiles was the very one whom Holy Scripture calls Cain. For instance, that this Jupiter, as Plato writes in the Euthydemus, is called herkeios [ἐρκεῖος] and phratrios [φρατρίου], the president of enclosures, of cities, of tribes and of the association of men. And as Pausanias relates (book 1), he is also poleus [πολιεύς], because he has care of cities. These agree plainly with Cain, the first son of the first Adam, since he was the first (as Holy Scripture says) to build cities and to gather human society into one place. But this same Jupiter is also called Sabazius, or, as the Greeks pronounce it, Sabaisius, as Clement shows in the Protrepticus from the profane writings themselves; so too Eusebius (book 4, Praeparatio Evangelica) and Arnobius (Against the Gentiles, book 5). Sabaisius or Sabazius is Jupiter the Trembler, the Trembling one, from the Hebrew name Sabats [Sabats], which signifies trembling and weakness (which comes from a blow of the sword). What better could show Cain, who, because he had killed his brother, was trembling and pale all his life? As for the name zeus [ζεὺς], by which he is named by the Greeks: from Pythagoras, the most ancient philosopher, who called him zan [ζάν], as Cyril writes from Porphyry (book 20, Against Julian, sect. 4), that word seems to have arisen from the word Cain, badly pronounced with a foreign sound. Or at least, is it not possible that the name zōē [ζωὴ] was given to this man by his posterity, in honour and commendation of him as their originator, by imitation of Adam, who called his wife Chava, that is, Life, the source of future propagation of the human race? And indeed it was easy to make Cain into Chava for foreigners, that is, for non-Hebrews. Now Chava is the same as zōēs [ζωῆς] and zōē [ζωή], that is, Life, and the giver of life, or the principle of living, to others. Therefore, so that Cain's posterity might bear witness to future ages that this Cain, after Saturn and the first man, was the parent of their origin, from whom the human race was born, they called him zēna [ζῆνα], which is the same as Chava. And certainly this is true. For of the two sons of Adam (namely Abel and Cain), Abel died without children, slain, and only Cain remained alive, and from him the human race was afterwards propagated. Thus Cain was Chava, or zōēs, that is, the father of the living. Although others prefer that the word zeus [ζεὺς] was substituted for Deus [Δεὺς] (from which the genitive Dios [Διὸς] is later formed) by an easy...

units.la: {y} Lib. 4 de Præparat. vsitatáque harum literarum ζ, in δ contráque com mutatione, quemadmodum in Cratylo scribit Plato. Δεὺς autem vel à rigando, vt vult Phornutus in lib.de nominibus Deorum, dicitur, quòd omnia irriget: vel vt alij (quorũ verior est sententia) à metu, quòd hic Iupiter & homo metũ sui omnibus incusserit, ne quisquâ eum attingeret: quod Caino optimè cõuenit, vt est, Gen. 4.15. Plato tamen in Cratylo putat in declinatione huius vocis anomala (quum dicatur N. ζεὺς, G. Διὸς) contineri hanc sententiâ, hunc hominem esse generis humani stirpem, δ' ὃν ἄλλοι ζῶσι, nempe per quem, & ex quo reliqui mortales propagati sunt, & viuunt. Et hæc quidem de nomine ζεὺς, ex ipsorum Ethnicorũ scriptis prolata satis ostendunt Iouem hunc eorum antiquissimũ esse Cainum Mosis. Verùm quoniâ ea res ad damnandam Idololatriam pertinet, eiusque originem explicandam (vt intelligatur eos omnes, quos Ethnici & Idololatræ pro diis primos & communiter coluerunt, fuisse mortales homines, atque adeo ex impura Caini stirpe: Alios enim peculiares Deos & Iones & Saturnos, & primorum illorũ nomine diẝos, quos quaq; gens postea sibi asciuit) huius meæ sententiæ aliquot alias rationes addam praeterea, quo fit confirmatior, veriórque censeatur: Ea verò sumuntur ex comparatione tum personæ, tum rerum, quæ à Caino, & ab isto antiquo Ioue gesta dicuntur ab ipsismet Ethnicis, & imprimis Poëtis. Nam vt lib 1.cap. 11.ait Lactantius, [Vera sunt quæ loquuntur Poëtæ: sed obtentu aliquo, speciéque velata] Ergo fabulas veritati admiscuerunt Ethnici Poëtæ impulsi Spiritu Satanæ, partim vt veritas rerum, verbiq, Diuini certitudo nutare, & obliteraretur, partim, vt his fallacijs,& deorum suorum exemplis redderentur homines ad omne scelus & flagitiũ audaciores, vti Lactantius docet lib.2.cap.15.& ex eo Augustin.lib. 2.Ciuit.Dei,cap.22. Verùm ad cõparationem Caini, & veteris illius Iouis Ethnicorum,veniamus. Cainus fuit primogenitus Adami: Iuppiter ille primogenitus Saturni illius antiquissimi, quem fuisse Adamũ antea declarauimus. Cainus patrem suum Adamum spe successionis,praeterquàm ex seipso,priuauit,dum Abelem fratrem suum occidit: Iuppiter ille Saturnum patrem castrasse,Titanas expulisse dicitur,ne quis alium,praeter se vnum, illi succederet. Quod Plato in Eutyphrone Dialogo commemorat. Vnde Iuppiter iste & ἀλάσωρ, & πελαμναι&, id est,homo sanguinarius dictus est,vt tradit Lactant.ex ipsis Ethnicus lib.1. Cainus secundus fuit, qui tum propter aetatem,tum propter autoritatem, Orbis huius totius princeps habitus est. Adamus autem primus fuit: Iuppiter ille secundus dicitur toti mundo imperasse patre suo Saturno expulso. Cainus fuit primus in Orbe homicida, & propterea à Patre Adamo exul,& in Oriente sedes habuit: Iuppiter ille primus homicida,malorũ & scelerum publicè perpetrandorũ reliquis mortalibus autor,quiq; propterea vt scribit Arnobius, ex Ethnicis homicidio colebatur: & vt tradit Lactant.lib.1.cap.28. Cicero libr.3. de Nat.Deor. in Oriente habuit imperium. Cainus primus sacrificasse Deo commemoratur,& propterea Abelem fratrem occidisse: Iuppiter ille dicitur primus cœlo sacrificium fecisse, Lactant.lib.1. & propterea Prometheo germano & consanguineo suo iratus, eum Caucaso clauis affixisse, & feris dilaniandũ exposuisse. Cainus liberos & nepotes habuit, qui fuerunt Artium inuentores: Iuppiter ille plures liberos, & Higginus cap.155. & Diodorus Siculus lib.1.cap.2. asserunt, qui Artes mortalibus repererunt, velut Mercurium, qui pastionem: Apollinem, qui Musicam: Vulcanũ, qui artem ferrariā inuenit. In Caini familia primũm veri Dei nomen blasphemari cœpit, & ipsum cultum deprauari: Ab isto Ioue tradunt Ethnici primum ritus voluntarij Dei cultus, id est, idololatria inuentos, eundemque postea pro Deo cultum ibi esse, Laactant lib.1.cap. 22. vbi & postquam fuisset sepultus. Nam vt & Clemens Alexandrinus, & Cyrillus lib.10. contra Iulian. & Augustin. lib.18. Ciuit. Dei, cap.3. ibi primum fuerunt falsorum deorum templa, vbi eorum sepulcra cernebantur. Id quod in impurissimo illo Mahumete, & illius, qua dicitur Mecha, verum apparet. Primus Phlegous Ioui diuinos honores tribuit, quicunq; ille fit ex posteris Caini, vt ait Augustinus. Sepulcrum autem Iouis istius non est in Creta insula, sed in Oriente. Nam Iouis Cretensis, & lõgè isto Ioue posterioris (quem Enhemerus, & ex eo Ennius descripsit, vt ait Laactantius lib.1.) atas, vita, res gesta, & sepulcrum est in Creta: sed non huius antiquissimi Iouis. Cainus denique sororem vxorē habuit, quā Philo Iudæus vocat Themech: Iuppiter ipse sororem vxorem habuit, quam alij Themen esse volunt, alij Iunonem. Illud verò etiā cum Dei verbo plane consentit, quod Trifmegistus scribit in Pimandro, Hominem, postquam peccasset, & in seipso ae-quie. quicunque set, desisse procreare liberos ad Dei imaginem. Et hac quidem satis sunt de hoc historia capite, satisfaciunt ostendunt inter Ethnicos rei quidem ipsius veritatem mansisse: nomina vero solum, magno astu Satana, immutata tandem fuisse. Ergo ad reliqua pergamus.
units.tr: {y} Lib. 4 de Præparat. The letters ζ and δ were commonly interchanged, as Plato writes in the Cratylus. Δεύς (Deus) is said to derive either from rigando, "watering", as Phornutus holds in his book on the names of the gods, because he waters all things; or, as others hold (and this is the more probable view), from metus, "fear", because this Jupiter, being a man, struck fear into everyone so that no one would touch him. That fits Cain very well, as Gen. 4.15 shows. Plato in the Cratylus thinks that the irregular declension of this word (nominative ζεύς, genitive Διός) contains the idea that this man is the stock of the human race [δ' ὃν ἄλλοι ζῶσι], namely the one through whom and from whom the rest of mortals were propagated and live. These points about the name ζεύς, drawn from the writings of the Gentiles themselves, sufficiently show that this Jupiter, the most ancient of theirs, is Moses' Cain. But since this matter bears on condemning idolatry and explaining its origin (so that it may be understood that all those whom the Gentiles and idolaters first and commonly worshipped as gods were mortal men, and therefore of the impure stock of Cain, for the other peculiar gods, the Ions and Saturns, and the dioes named after those first ones, were adopted later by every nation), I will add some further arguments for my view, so that it may be held more firmly and more truly. These are drawn from comparing both the person and the deeds attributed to Cain and to this ancient Jupiter by the Gentiles themselves, and especially by their poets. For, as Lactantius says in book 1, chapter 11: [What the poets say is true, but veiled by some pretence and appearance.] So the Gentile poets, moved by the Spirit of Satan, mixed fables with the truth, partly so that the truth of the facts and the certainty of the divine Word might totter and be obliterated, and partly so that, through these deceptions and the examples of their gods, men would be made bolder in every crime and wickedness, as Lactantius teaches in book 2, chapter 15, and Augustine after him in City of God book 2, chapter 22. But let us come to the comparison of Cain and that old Jupiter of the Gentiles. Cain was the firstborn of Adam; that Jupiter was the firstborn of that most ancient Saturn, whom we have already shown to be Adam. Cain deprived his father Adam of any hope of succession other than through himself, when he killed his brother Abel; that Jupiter is said to have castrated his father Saturn and driven out the Titans, so that no one but himself would succeed him. Plato recounts this in the dialogue Euthyphro. Hence this Jupiter was called both ἀλάστωρ and πελαμναῖος, that is, a bloodthirsty man, as Lactantius reports from the Gentiles themselves, book 1. Cain was the second man, who was regarded as the prince of the whole world both by his age and by his authority; Adam was the first. That second Jupiter is said to have ruled the whole world after his father Saturn was driven out. Cain was the first murderer in the world, and therefore an exile from his father Adam, and he had his seat in the East; that first Jupiter was the murderer, the author of evils and of crimes committed publicly among other mortals, and for this reason, as Arnobius writes, he was worshipped among the Gentiles with murder; and as Lactantius reports in book 1, chapter 28, and Cicero in On the Nature of the Gods book 3, he held his dominion in the East. Cain is recorded as the first to offer sacrifice to God, and for that reason he killed his brother Abel; that Jupiter is said to have been the first to make sacrifice to heaven (Lactantius, book 1), and for that reason, angry at Prometheus, his brother and kinsman, he fastened him to the Caucasus with nails and exposed him to be torn by wild beasts. Cain had sons and grandsons who were the inventors of the arts; that Jupiter had many sons, and Hyginus, chapter 155, and Diodorus Siculus, book 1, chapter 2, state that they discovered the arts for mortals, such as Mercury, who discovered herding; Apollo, who discovered music; and Vulcan, who invented the art of the smith. In Cain's family the name of the true God first began to be blasphemed and worship itself corrupted. From that Jupiter the Gentiles report that the first rites of voluntary worship of God, that is, idolatry, were invented, and that he himself was worshipped as God there even after he had been buried (Lactantius, book 1, chapter 22). For Clement of Alexandria, Cyril in book 10 against Julian, and Augustine in City of God book 18, chapter 3 (as they also do), say that the first temples of false gods were there, where their tombs could be seen. This appears to be true in that most impure Mahomet and in the place called Mecca. The first to give divine honours to Jupiter was Phlegous, whoever he was among the descendants of Cain, as Augustine says. But the tomb of this Jupiter is not in the island of Crete but in the East. For the Cretan Jupiter, whose age, life, and deeds, and tomb are in Crete (a Jupiter much later than this one, described by Euhemerus and after him by Ennius, as Lactantius says in book 1), is not this most ancient Jupiter. Finally, Cain had his sister as his wife, whom Philo the Jew calls Themech; Jupiter himself had his sister as his wife, whom some want to be Themis, others Juno. Indeed, that also agrees plainly with the word of God, what Trismegistus writes in the Pimander: that man, after he had sinned and been left to himself, ceased to beget children in the image of God. These things are enough about this chapter of history; they show that among the Gentiles the reality of the matter itself remained, but that only the names were changed, by the great cunning of Satan. So let us proceed to the rest.

units.la: Ad VIII. Artes Primæ hominum, & quæ postea reperta.
units.tr: On the Eighth Point: The First Arts of Humankind, and Those Discovered Afterwards.

units.la: Sequitur Artium, quæ inter mortales prima reperta sunt, vsumque habuerunt, enumeratio. Hanc autem in vniuersum quatuor recenset Moses, nempe primam, Agricultura: Secundam, Pastoritia artem, cui magna postea incrementa accesserint, additaq; fuerint per Iabalem filium Lamechi: Tertiam, Musicam organicā, quæ vocatur: Quartam, Aerariam, & Ferrariā artem. Sed quæ huius veritatis vestigia supersint, inter Ethnicos, videamus. Multi quidem de harū, quæ iam commemoraui, & aliarum quoque artium inuentione, multa tradiderunt, vt Plinius lib. 7. Nat. Hist. cap. 56. Ante Plinium Aristoteles, & varij varijs in locis: post Plinium Solinus: post Solinum etiam longo postea tempore Polydorus Virgilius. Sed hi omnes in recentioribus autoribus penè substiterunt, nimirum ijs, qui à primis (quos Moses nominat) vel immediatè, vel longa etiam annorum serie per posteros eas artes didicerant, quæ postea vnicuidam dūtaxat genti communicarunt, veluti Græcis, vel Ægyptijs: non autem eas toti terrarum Orbi primi tradiderunt, quod fecerunt ij, quos recitat S. Scriptura. Verum nos non quærimus qui primi
units.tr: Next comes the list of the arts that were the first discovered among mortals and came into use. Moses in general recounts four of them: first, agriculture; second, the art of herding, to which great developments were later added through Jabal, son of Lamech; third, what is called instrumental music; fourth, the arts of bronze and iron. Let us now see what traces of this truth survive among the Ethnics. Many writers have handed down much about the discovery of these arts I have just mentioned and of others as well, as Pliny does in book 7 of the Natural History, chapter 56. Before Pliny, Aristotle and various others in various places; after Pliny, Solinus; and after Solinus, long afterwards, Polydore Vergil. But all of these have almost remained with more recent authors, namely those who learned these arts either directly from the first men (whom Moses names) or through a long succession of years from their descendants, and who afterwards communicated them to one nation only, such as the Greeks or the Egyptians. They did not, however, hand them down first to the whole orb of the earth, which is what those whom Holy Scripture recounts did. But we are not asking who among the first mortals taught the arts to the Greeks or the Gauls alone (for that history is altogether recent), but who first discovered them for the whole human race. Moses designates and names these men. Therefore, as I have said, let us examine the remaining traces of this truth that are among the Ethnics, and investigate them from their writings.

units.la: mortales Graecos, vel Gallos solum eas artes docuerunt (est enim haec omnino recens historia) sed qui toti ipsi generi humano eas invenerunt primi. Hos autem designat, & nominat Moses. Ergo huius veritatis, uti dixi, quae sunt apud Ethnicos reliqua vestigia scrutemur, & ex eorum scriptis invenstigemus. Artium quidem sit abijs varia distributio, ut quae prima ab hominibus reperta & exercita fuerint, demonstrent. Plato in Sophista vult Artium in universum esse duo genera: Aut enim in quaerenda possidendave re aliqua necessaria versatur hominum ars & industria, & κτητικὴ nominatur: aut in eadem efficienda & producenda, quae ποιητικὴ ab eode vocatur. In Philebo Artes aliter distributit: Vult enim eas aut esse ἐπιστήμας ⟨?⟩ aut circa πραξιν & θεωρὴν hominum versari. Idem in Politico aliter quoque. Sed tandem eo res redit, ut eas artes primum ab hominibus (Dei munere & concessione) repertas sentiat, quibus res ad hanc vitam necessarie quaeruntur, qualis est victus, & cultus. Itaque idem in Politico totidem verbis, & consentienter Sacra Scriptura scribit,
units.tr: Indeed, there is a varied division of the arts, so as to show which were the first to be discovered and practised by men. Plato in the Sophist holds that there are two general kinds of arts: for human skill and industry are concerned either with seeking out or possessing some necessary thing, and this is called acquisitive (κτητικὴ); or with bringing about and producing the same, which he calls productive (ποιητικὴ). In the Philebus he divides the arts differently: he holds that they are either sciences [ἐπιστήμαι] or are concerned with the practice and contemplation of men. The same man does this differently again in the Statesman. But in the end the matter comes to this: he thinks that the arts first discovered by men (by God's gift and grant) were those by which the things necessary for this life are sought, such as food and clothing. Accordingly, the same Plato in the Statesman, in almost the same words and in agreement with Holy Scripture, writes

units.la: [Quae vero de hominibus contigerunt (post peccatum in Deum) & breviora sunt, & magis instituto nostro conveniunt. Quum eius enim Daemonis (i. Dei) cuius veluti pastoris & domini praesidio homines tenebantur, providentia destituti: & animalia multa (quae suapte natura immania fuerant) efferata iterum esse nt, infirmi homines & custodia orbati ab illis belluis passim dilaniabantur. Atqui tellus haud ultra victum sponte suppeditabat: parandi vero industria nondum inventa, quia nulla necessitas illos ante coegerat. Propter has causas, in summum discrimen, atque penuriam illorum redacta res sunt. Quocirca dona illa, quae olim a Dijs tributa hominibus commemorantur, ob necessariam disciplinam, & institutionem data fuerunt. A Prometheo quidem, ignis: Artes autem a Vulcano, ipsiusque coniuge, eiusdem artis socia: Semina quoque, & terrae cultus ab alijs. Omnia summatim vitae hominum adminicula tunc, deorum beneficio, sunt comparata, quum homines (propter ipsorum intemperiem, ut docuit Plato) deorum providentia deseruissent, & iam ipsos oporteret sui & aledi, & propagandi curam gerere.] Hæc vir ille penè Moisans, & Christianizans. Ex quibus hæc tria manifestè colliguntur: Primum eos, qui primi artes humano generi necessarias pepererunt, pro dijs, & quidem primis & vetustissimis, habitos. Secundum, Eas artes prius inventas, quae ad nos alendos, & tuendos omnino sunt necessariae, qualis est proculdubio Agricultura, & Pastoritia. Ea enim dua imprimis alimenta nobis praebent. Tertium, Inventas esse eas artes demum quidem postquam Deus homines propter eorum intemperiem abiecisset, i. post peccatum hominis: statim autem postquam homines se desertos & destitutos prioribus illis in se Dei beneficijs agnoverunt, & senserunt. Necessitas enim seu egestas artes invenit, ut recte ait Publius Maro: --- [Labor omnia vincit Improbus, & duris urgens in rebus egestas.]
units.tr: [What happened to men after sin against God is briefer and better suited to our purpose. For when men were deprived of the providence of that Daemon (that is, God), under whose protection and as whose shepherd and lord they had been held, and when many animals (which by their own nature had been savage) became wild again, weak men, deprived of guardianship, were torn apart on every side by those beasts. And yet the earth no longer supplied food of its own accord, and the diligence of preparing it had not yet been discovered, since no necessity had yet compelled them. For these reasons the situation was reduced to the greatest danger and want. Hence those gifts which are recorded as having once been granted to men by the gods were given for the sake of necessary training and instruction. Fire indeed came from Prometheus; the arts came from Vulcan and his wife, a partner in the same craft; seeds and the cultivation of the land came from others. All the means of human life in summary were then provided by the benefit of the gods, when men, through their own intemperance (as Plato taught), had been forsaken by the providence of the gods, and it was now fitting that they should take care of their own sustenance, preservation and propagation.] Thus that man, almost a Mosaist and a Christianizer, speaks. From these points three things are clearly gathered. First, that those who first invented the arts necessary to the human race were regarded as gods, and indeed as the first and most ancient. Second, that the arts which are absolutely necessary for feeding and preserving us were invented earlier, such as undoubtedly agriculture and herding; for these two above all provide us with food. Third, that these arts were invented only after God had cast men away on account of their intemperance, that is, after the sin of man; and immediately after men recognised and felt that they had been abandoned and deprived of those earlier benefits of God toward them. For necessity or want invented the arts, as Publius Maro rightly says: "Relentless toil conquers all things, and pressing want in hard circumstances."

units.la: Et ex eo Manilius: [Et labor ingenium miseris dedit, & sua quemque Adiugilare sibi iussit fortuna premendo.]
units.tr: And from this Manilius says: "Toil gave wit to the wretched, and fortune, pressing hard, ordered each one to shift for himself."

units.la: Quamobrem ex Platonis Ethnici sententia, Primi. ab hominibus artes sunt inuenta, quæ propter peccatum suum quærere victum labore, atque sudore vultus sui cogerentur, & a Deo damnati essent. Deinde, Ea primum artes reperta, quæ victum illum summinístrarét, .i. cibos corpori alendo necessarios: quales sunt fruges terræ, & frumenta, ex quibus panis fit: fructus mansuetí, non autem agrestes arborum: & Carnes beluarum edulium. Ab hac eadem sententia non procul dissidet Aristoteles. Nam lib. 1. Politicor. cap. 5. postquam partitus est omnem victus quærendi curam & χρηματιστικὴν in κτῆσιν & χρηματιστικὴν, id est, in rationem eam, quæ per se victus comparatur, vel lucrum quæritur, ex quo postea contrahendo cōmutandóve cibos quærimus, ostendit eas artes (quibus victus per se & naturaliter quæritur, habetúrve) esse & primas & naturales, & prius in vsu inter homines fuisse, inter quas Agriculturam, & Pastoritiam artem imprimis idem Aristoteles recensét. Est enim, vt ait Plato in Eutyphrone, Agriculturæ præcipuum opus ἡ ἐκ τῆς γῆς ζοφὴ, vt è terra alimentum, victúmque præbeat. Vult quidem Aristoteles huius artis, per quā naturaliter victus paratur, esse quinque species, nempe Nομαδικὸν, Γεωργικὸν, Λῃστικὸν, Ἀλιευτικὸν, Θηρευτικὸν, Pastoritiam artem, Agriculturam, Prædatorium, Piscatorium, & Venatorium: è quibus Prædatorium quidem etiam laudat, & Venatoriá prefert ceteris quatuor vitæ generibus, quoniam fit copiosior, & latius se extendat, quàm reliquæ (Est enim & in paludibus, & lacubus, & fluuijs, & mari, & fyluis, & mótibus, locis apertis, & tectis, deniq; vbiq; mari & terra & in aëre quoque venari possumus.) Verum Agricul-
units.tr: Therefore, according to the opinion of the Ethnic Plato, the arts were discovered first by men who, because of their sin, were compelled to seek their food by labour and the sweat of their face, and had been condemned by God. Next, the first arts discovered were those that supplied that food, that is, the foods necessary to nourish the body: such as the fruits of the earth and grain from which bread is made; cultivated fruits rather than the wild fruits of trees; and the flesh of beasts for eating. Aristotle does not far depart from this same opinion. For in book 1 of the Politics, chapter 5, after dividing all the care of seeking food into acquisition [κτῆσις] and the art of getting wealth [χρηματιστικὴ], that is, into that reasoning by which food is procured for itself, or gain is sought, from which afterwards we seek food by contracting or exchanging, he shows that those arts by which food is sought and obtained naturally and in itself are both the first and the natural ones, and that they were in use among men earlier; among these Aristotle above all names agriculture and the art of herding. For, as Plato says in the Euthyphro, the chief work of agriculture is "the nourishment from the earth" [ἡ ἐκ τῆς γῆς τροφή], so that it may provide food and sustenance from the earth. Aristotle indeed holds that there are five kinds of the art by which food is naturally prepared: namely, the nomadic [Νομαδικὸν], the agricultural [Γεωργικὸν], the predatory [Λῃστικὸν], the fishing [Ἀλιευτικὸν] and the hunting [Θηρευτικὸν]; that is, herding, agriculture, plunder, fishing and hunting. Of these he indeed praises the predatory and prefers hunting to the other four ways of life, because it is more abundant and extends more widely than the rest (for we can hunt in marshes, lakes, rivers, the sea, woods, mountains, open and enclosed places, and finally everywhere, on sea and land, and even in the air). Yet he counts agriculture and herding among the first arts. And so far indeed that man agrees with the truth itself, insofar as he admits that the use of agriculture, by which life is had, is natural and was discovered at the earliest time.

units.la: suram, turam, & Pastoritiam inter primas artes enumerat. Et hactenus quidem ille cum ipsa veritate consentit, quatenus vsum agriculturæ, vt ex ea vitius habeatur, & naturalem & primo tempore repertum esse confitetur. In reliquis ecquæ fit Ethnicorum hominum cum .
units.tr: ture, and he lists agriculture and herding among the first arts. And so far indeed that man agrees with the truth itself, insofar as he admits that the use of agriculture, by which life is had, is natural and was discovered at the earliest time. In the rest, let us weigh how far the Ethnic men agree with Moses.

units.la: Mosæ concordia, perpendamus. Agricultura facit Moses & primam omnium inuentam ac exercitam, & ab Adamo primo homine. Quid Ethnici? Varro lib. 1. cap. 4. de Re Rustica scribit Agriculturæ eadem fuisse initia, quæ Mundi ipsius. Quamobrem antiquissima sit oportet. Et quod idem scribit cap. 2. Pastoritiam vitæ esse incentiuam, Agricolarum vero succentiuam, quod homines primis temporibus Pastoritia vitam agerent, quum neque scirent arare terra, aut ferere arbores, aut putare. Ergo ab his posteà susceptam Agriculturam, quod homines, vt ait idem lib. 2. cap. 1. vinerent primi ex his rebus, quæ inuiolata ferro vltro ferret terra: ex hac vita descendisse homines in secundam, nempe in Agriculturam: quum, inquam, hæc scribit Varro, non ex sua, sed ex Dicæarchi, & Aristotelis Stagyrita sententia loquitur. Atqui Aristoteles ipse Agriculturam eo, quem citaui, libro 1. Politic. cap. 5. Primam recenset, licet, vt inconstas, postea variet. Deinde rerum naturam hac Aristotelis de nata posterius Agricultura sententiam plane refutat. Nam prius est, semperque fuit, vesci pane (quæ agricultura sumministrat) quam carnes animalium (quia Pastoritia præbet.) Ergo Agricultura naturâ prior est, quàm Pastoritia. De Agricultura vero primo Inuentore acerba & vexata est inter ipsos Ethnicos digladiatio, quoniam à Mose recessserunt: & particularum eius artis apud quasdam duntaxat gentes monstratores (qui longis seculis fuerunt Adamo primo eius parente posteriores) pro primo tamen fumut. Ergo eorum alij aiunt Cererem esse terra frugum inuentricem, sed Graecis. Itaque ut ait ex Platone in Cratylo Cicero lib. 3. de Nat. Deor. dicam Cererem Ἀνυντῆς, quasi ϑὴρ μυντῆς, quod eos docuerit alimenta ex terra colligere. Quo vero primum tempore hoc beneficium ab Adamo ipso, et Adamique posteris longe antea Mundo communicatum, illa Graecis hominibus cotulerit, tradit Augustinus lib. 18. Ciuit. Dei, cap. 6. nempe regnante Argo in Peloponnesso (qui ex Aegypto eo, uti et Ceres illa, venerat) posquam primi posteri Adami, imo et Noachi, iam per totum terrarum orbem sparsi fuisset. Alij malunt a Triptolemo Rege Atheniensium terra colede praecepta primum tradita, sed Graecis, quemadmodum dixi. Sic Palaphatus, et Pausanias lib. 1. Alij a Brige quodam Atheniensi malunt, velut Plin. lib. 7. cap. 56. Alij ab Osiride Aegyptio, sicut Plutarchus in Osiride. Alij denique (et hi omnino verius) ab antiquissimo illo Saturno, qui idem est atq; Adamus. Itaque cum falce, qua fruges matura metuntur, solet a veteribus Saturnus ille vetus pingi. Certe vetustissimum inter mortales fuisse hoc vitae genus omnes fatetur, mariximeq; naturale et necessarium, quo vita humana post peccatum omnino carere non potuit. Inde illius laudes passim et ab Oratoribus, uti M. Tul. Cicerone lib. De Senectute; et a Poetis, velut a Virgilio lib. 2 Georgic. et ab aliis scriptoribus, quemadmodum a Varrone lib.
units.tr: Moses makes agriculture the first of all arts to be invented and practised, and from Adam, the first man. What do the Ethnics say? Varro in book 1, chapter 4, of On Farming writes that agriculture had the same beginnings as the world itself; therefore it must be most ancient. And what he writes in chapter 2, that herding is the life that stirs up, but agriculture the life that calms down, because in the earliest times men lived by herding, since they knew neither how to plough the earth, nor to plant trees, nor to prune them. Then, that agriculture was afterwards taken up by these, because men, as the same Varro says in book 2, chapter 1, first lived on those things which the earth brought forth of its own accord, untouched by iron; that men came down from this life into a second, namely agriculture: when Varro, I say, writes this, he speaks not from his own opinion but from that of Dicaearchus and Aristotle the Stagirite. Yet Aristotle himself, in the book I cited, Politics book 1, chapter 5, lists agriculture first, although, being inconsistent, he afterwards varies. Moreover, this opinion of Aristotle that agriculture came later, by its nature, plainly refutes itself. For it is and always has been prior to eat bread (which agriculture supplies) than the flesh of animals (which herding provides). Therefore agriculture is prior to herding by nature. Concerning the first inventor of agriculture, there is a bitter and troubled contest among the Ethnics themselves, since they have departed from Moses; and they take as first those who were merely the teachers of some parts of this art among certain nations only (who lived many centuries after Adam, the first parent of it). Some of them say that Ceres was the discoverer of the fruits of the earth, but for the Greeks. Hence, as Cicero says in book 3 of On the Nature of the Gods, following Plato in the Cratylus, Ceres is called Ἀνυντῆς (Anyntes), as if θηρ μυντῆς, because she taught them to gather food from the earth. But that at what first time this benefit was communicated to the world by Adam himself and Adam's descendants long before, and then passed on to the Greeks, Augustine records in book 18 of The City of God, chapter 6: namely in the reign of Argos in the Peloponnese (who had come from Egypt, as Ceres did), after the first descendants of Adam, and indeed of Noah, had already been scattered over the whole orb of the earth. Others prefer that the precepts of tilling the land were first handed down by Triptolemus, king of the Athenians, but to the Greeks, as I have said. So Palaephatus and Pausanias, book 1. Others prefer some Athenian named Brilus, as Pliny does in book 7, chapter 56. Others name Osiris the Egyptian, as Plutarch does in his work on Osiris. Finally others (and these much the truer) name that most ancient Saturn, who is the same as Adam. Accordingly that old Saturn is commonly painted by the ancients with the sickle with which ripe grain is cut. Certainly everyone admits that this way of life was the most ancient among mortals and most especially natural and necessary, without which human life could not at all do after sin. Hence its praises are sung everywhere, both by orators, such as Marcus Tullius Cicero in his book On Old Age, and by poets, such as Virgil in book 2 of the Georgics, and by other writers, as by Varro in book 1 of On Farming; Columella in book 1; and Pliny in book 18 of the Natural History, chapters 5 and 6. And, as Pollux says in book 9, in honour of agriculture King Ninus of the Assyrians himself named the son born to him in the fields Agrenus. Moreover, under the name of agriculture many arts are included, such as gardening, and planting and pruning trees, and
