units.tr: 1. On rural affairs: Columella, book 1; Pliny, Natural History, book 18, chapters 5 and 6, celebrated. And, as Pollux says in book 9, in honour of Agriculture, King Ninus of the Assyrians himself named his son, born to him in the fields, Agrenes. Moreover, the name Agriculture comprises several arts, such as gardening, and the planting, pruning and grafting of trees, and all others like them. Beekeeping also belongs here, that is, the gathering of honey from bees, as Plato wishes in book 8 of the Laws and in the Euthyphro, and Pliny in book 18, chapter 26.

units.la: PASTORITIA
units.tr: Pastoralism

units.la: ars sequitur,ordine secunda,quicquid & Aristoteles & Dicaarchus contrà senserint. Perperam enim & contra ipsam rerum naturā putant prius homines carnem, quàm panem,ad viuendum quasiuisse, quum vita humana post peccatum illā carere possit,hoc non possit. Imo verò vsque adeo necessarium est panis,vt eius nomine reliqua huius vita alimenta comprehendātur, quæ sunt solum velut quadam panis condimenta,& accessiones. Præterea primus homo
units.tr: The art follows in second order, whatever Aristotle and Dicaearchus may have thought to the contrary. For they wrongly think, and contrary to the nature of things itself, that men sought flesh before bread for living, since human life after sin can lack the former but not the latter. Indeed bread is so necessary that the other foods of this life are comprised under its name, which are only, as it were, certain seasonings and additions to bread. Moreover, the first man, Adam, was assigned by God after the rebellion, especially to cultivate the earth from which he had been taken, not to pasture flocks of animals. Yet this too flowed from sin. But that saying of the same Aristotle, Politics book 1, chapter 5, is most absurd: [They were the laziest of men, he says, who first followed the pastoral life, since their food came to them from tame animals without toil.] Indeed this way of life appears to be most laborious and always to have been so, from the very words that he goes on with there: [And since, he says, it is necessary for the animals to change place, the shepherds themselves are forced to follow together, as if following a certain living agriculture.] For what is more laborious and less leisurely than to be always wandering, to follow the flocks, to pasture them, tend them, heal them, handle them, separate them, and wean them? So much so that M. Varro, in book 2

units.la: De re rustica Pastionem infinitis pene partibus cõstare & dicat, & sentiat: quum tamen Agricultura paucis omnino contineatur, vt idem lib. 1. eiusdem operis docet. Ergo quemadmodũ Agricultura, sic & Pastura fuit ars victus naturaliter quaerendi: sed haec posterius & vsurpata & nota, quàm Agricultura. Itaque secunda fuit. Cui veritati assentiens Plato lib. 8. de Leg. prius de Agricolis, quàm de Pastoribus leges ferens, nimirū ordinem naturae, & inventionis harum artium secutus. Nomine vero Pastoralis vitae sen pastura, precipuè pastionem animalium cicurum & mansuetorum hic intelligimus, quanquã aliy postea Venatoriam artem huic subiecerunt, quae tamen demum post diluuium videtur & vsitata & exercita, & primùm quidè à Nembroto, Gen. 14.9. Etsi verò Pastoritia ars posterius, quàm Agricultura, inuenta est, vberius tamen, & diligentius postea fuit exculta, quàm agricultura, maiorâque ab hominum industria incrementa accepit. Nam Iabel Lamechi filius (qui fuit ex posteris Caini) Pastionem hanc mirificè auxit. Cuius rei & facti exemplum secuti sunt homines aliy postea, retinuerúntque. Ille enim Iabel primus pecoris multiplicis, & copiosi, quod habebat, pascendi gratiâ vitae genus à maioribus suis diuersum instituit. Quũ enim illi, exemplo patris Caini, in vrbibus & oppidis habitarent, feque continerent: iste primus, sequedi pascendiq; pecoris gratiâ, tabernacula in agris & syluis habuit, & tentoria, quae prout pecora ipsa progrederentur, aliò trasferret, eóque ipse migraret. Quod vita ac hominum genus à Græcis Νομάδες appellatur. Hinc igitur Nomadum genus exortum, quod per totum Orbem postea innotuit, sparsum q; esse tamen à primo illo labele cœpit. Nulla est enim Orbis terrarum pars, in qua aliqui Νομάδες & pecuarij eiusmodi ia non sint. Ratio autem est duplex, Huius vitæ nempe necessitas, & vtilitas, quæ ex eo vitæ genere promanat. Ac necessitas quidem, vt pecora, quorum carnibus, lacte fero, caseo, pinguedine vescimur, conferuentur. Vtilitas autem, quod magnus, imo verrimus quæstus ex hac pastione prouenit. Nam, vt vult 1 Linius lib. 7. cap. 56. ex ea lanificia etiam Aegyptij inuenere postea, & vestimentorum parandorum rationem. Ergo recte Aristoteles loco iam citato, [ Animalia hominū causa facta sunt (ait) mansueta quidem propter vtilitatem, & cibum: fera vero (etsi non omnia, sed plerăq;) propter cibum, & alia adiumenta, vt est vestis, & cetera instrumenta.)] Et Plinius lib. 18. cap 3: [Pascua, inquit, diu sola inter homines vetligalia fuerunt.] Varro in lib. de ling. Latin. Pecuniam (in qua posita sunt diuitiæ) à pecude dictam scribit quod olim soli diuites ÿ essent, qui pecudes pascerent. Vnde præclarißimarum inter Romanos & vetustißimarum familiarum cognomina, ait idem lib. 2. De re rust. cap. 1. derinantur, velut à minore pecore Porcius, Ouintus, Caprilius, à maiore, Equitius, Taurus, Vitulus. Cæterum, per totum terrarum orbem dispersos fuisse Pecuarios huiusmodi & Nomadas apparet. Erant enim Nomades inter Iudæos & Israelitas Rechabita, Hierem. 35. 2,2. Reg. 10.18: Inter Scythas ÿ,qui Hamaxobÿ diceban-
units.tr: both says and holds that pasturage consists of almost infinite parts, whereas agriculture is contained in very few, as the same author teaches in book 1 of the same work. Therefore, just as agriculture, so pasturage was an art of naturally seeking sustenance; but this came later, and was taken up and known later than agriculture. So it was second. Agreeing with this truth, Plato in Laws book 8, drafting laws about farmers before shepherds, followed, no doubt, the order of nature and of the discovery of these arts. By the name of pastoral life, or pasturage, we here understand chiefly the feeding of domestic and tame animals, although others afterwards added the art of hunting to it; yet hunting seems to have come into use and practice only after the Flood, and first by Nimrod, Gen. 14.9. But although the pastoral art was discovered later than agriculture, it was afterwards cultivated more richly and more diligently than agriculture, and it received greater increase from human industry. For Jabal, son of Lamech (who was of the posterity of Cain), greatly enlarged this pasturage. Other men afterwards followed his example in this matter and kept it. For Jabal was the first to establish a way of life different from that of his ancestors, for the sake of feeding his large and abundant herd. For while the others, following the example of their father Cain, lived and kept themselves in cities and towns, he, for the sake of following and feeding the flock, had tents and tabernacles in the fields and woods, which he moved elsewhere as the flocks themselves advanced, and he himself migrated with them. This way of life and kind of men is called by the Greeks nomads [Νομάδες]. Hence the race of nomads arose, which afterwards became known throughout the whole world, and yet it began to be scattered from that first Jabal. For there is no part of the earth in which some such nomads and herdsmen are not already present. The reason is twofold: the necessity of this way of life, and the usefulness that flows from that kind of life. The necessity, namely, that the animals, whose flesh, milk, cheese and fat we eat, be preserved. The usefulness, because a great, indeed the greatest, gain comes from this pasturage. For, as Livy wants in book 7 chapter 56, the Egyptians afterwards discovered from it the making of wool and the method of preparing clothing. Therefore Aristotle rightly, in the passage already cited: [Animals, he says, have been made tame for the sake of men, for their usefulness and food; wild ones (though not all, but most) for food and other aids, such as clothing and the other implements.] And Pliny, book 18 chapter 3: [Pasturages, he says, were for a long time the only revenues among men.] Varro, in the book on the Latin language, writes that money (in which riches are placed) was so named from cattle (pecude), because formerly only the rich were those who pastured cattle. Hence, says the same Varro in Rust. book 2 chapter 1, the surnames of the most famous and most ancient families among the Romans are derived, as from smaller livestock, Porcius, Quintus, Caprilius; from larger, Equitius, Taurus, Vitulus. Moreover, it appears that herdsmen and nomads of this kind were dispersed over the whole earth. For among the Jews and Israelites there were the Rechabites as nomads, Jer. 35; 2 Kings 10.18. Among the Scythians, who were called Hamaxobii,

units.la: [Quid tibi pastores Libya,quid pascua versu Prosequar,& raris habitata mapalia tectis? Sepè diem,noctemque& totum ex ordine mensem Pascitur,itaq; pecus longa in deserta sine villis Hospitijs,tantum campi iacet.Omnia secum Armentarium Afer agit,tectumque, Larémque, Armaq;, Amyclaumq; canem,Cressamq; phraatra.]
units.tr: [What shall I tell you of the Libyan shepherds, of their pastures and of the huts scattered with sparse roofs? Often for a day and a night, and for a whole month in order, the flock is pastured, and so the herd lies in long deserts without homes, so far does the plain extend. The African drives all his herd with him, his roof and his household gods, his arms, his Cretan dog and his Cretan bow.]

units.la: Athenaeus lib.11.Dipnosoph.ait, [Libycis Nomadibus(sed & aliys quoq;) nihil aliud in bonis est, quàm poculum,gladium, Aqualis: Mapalia verò ex Asphodelo ijs construuntur angusta, umbra tantum capienda gratia,quae,quocunq; ierint,circumferunt secum.] Viunt autem tum ferina,tum carne masuetorum animalium,ut Boum & ovium & caprarum, eorumq; lacte, caseo,sero lactis ouis,& aliys similibus. Et hac quidem de Pastoritia arte,& eius incrementis.
units.tr: Athenaeus, Deipnosophists book 11, says, [The Libyan nomads (and others also) have nothing else among their goods but a cup, a sword and a pail; their huts are made of asphodel, narrow, meant only to take shelter in the shade, and these they carry about with them wherever they go.] They live both on the flesh of wild animals and on the flesh of tame animals, such as oxen, sheep and goats, and on their milk, cheese, whey, eggs, and other similar things. And this is what I have to say about the pastoral art and its growth.

units.la: TERTIA Ars in Mundo reperta fuit Musica,eaq; organica,quam Iubal filius Lemechi ante diluvium invenit. Hac autem veritas etiam apud homines Ethnicos ex parte mansit,eiusque vestigia non pauca in eorundem libris extant. Ac primùm Plato in Politico Musicam quinto loco constituit inter eas artes,quae primae sunt ma sunt ab hominibus excogitata: quod non abest longè à nostra veritate. Itaque falsa est, & merito irrisa illa Iuliani Apostatæ sententia à Cyrillo lib. 5 contra eum, qui scripsit Musicam primum à Græcis repertam, & demum post ⋏Astrologiam & Geometriam iam notas, quasi Musica postrema ab hominibus reperta esset. Est quidem illud verù quod diuinus Plato in Phædro tradit, Hominum genus extitisse ante Musas natum: sed tamen artis Musicæ inventum ex omnium consensu est antiquissimum. Nam Musas (quod perinde erat, atque si Musicam dicerent) cœli filias esse dixerunt, ut commemorat Pausanias lib 9. Cœli autem filij dicebantur vetustissima quæque inter Ethnicos. Ergo, inquit Plato eodem illo Dial. (qui Phædrus appellatur) prisci mortales sic Musica delectati sunt, ut cibum, dum eâ audirēt, capere negligerent. Unde Horat. lib. de re poetica:
units.tr: The third art discovered in the world was music, and that organic (instrumental) music, which Jubal, son of Lamech, invented before the Flood. This truth has also remained in part among the heathen, and not a few traces of it are found in their books. And first Plato in the Statesman places music fifth among those arts which were devised by men; which is not far from our truth. Therefore that saying of Julian the Apostate is false, and rightly mocked, as Cyril refutes it in book 5 against him, who wrote that music was first discovered by the Greeks and only afterwards, once astrology and geometry were already known, as if music were the last thing invented by men. It is indeed true what divine Plato teaches in the Phaedrus, that the human race existed before the Muses were born; yet the invention of the art of music is, by the consent of all, most ancient. For they said that the Muses (which was the same as saying music) were daughters of heaven, as Pausanias records in book 9. Now the sons of heaven were called the most ancient of all things among the heathen. Therefore, says Plato in that same dialogue (which is called the Phaedrus), the early mortals were so delighted with music that they neglected to take food while they listened to it. Hence Horace, in the book on the art of poetry:

units.la: [Dictum & Amphion Thebana conditor arcis Saxa mouere sono testudinis, & prece blanda.
units.tr: [It is also said that Amphion, founder of the Theban citadel, moved stones with the sound of the lyre and with his persuasive prayer.

units.la: Ducere quò vellet, fuit hæc sapientia primum.]
units.tr: To lead wherever it wished: this was its first wisdom.]

units.la: Et M. T. Cicero Tusc. 1 idem sentit. Per Musicam igitur artis studiu primos homines excultos fuisse omnes Historici fatentur. Duplici enim disciplina, ut idem Plato lib. 7. de Leg. & ex eo Aristoteles lib. 8. Politic. scribit, vetustissima hominū ætas vtebatur. Ad corpus quidem exercendum, arte Gymnastica: ad animum autem expoliendū, arte Musica. Ex quo fit ut Plato lib. 3. de Rep. præcipiat, ut ipsi adeo ciuitatis Principes, eorumque filij diligenter in Musica instituantur, ex cuius immutatione innumerabilia mala & pericula ciuitati idem censet accidere, lib. 4. eiusdem operis De republ. tanti nimirum momenti,támque vetusta ea ars ab Ethnicis iudicata est. Quod cum S. Historia concordat. Caterum & a quo Musicam ydem illi Ethnici repertam fuisse velint, & ecquâ primum eius speciem, videndu est. Ac quidem de prima illius inuentione nequaquam inter eos constat. Quum enim vnaquæ gens ambitiosè tam excellétis artis inuentum sibi vendicare vellet,plures illius autores esse dixerunt: De primo auté illo excellentiq viro,qui eam mortales docuerat, non quæsierunt. Ergo Graci contendunt Amphionafuum primum illius repertorem fuisse,vt & Plinius lib.9,& Plutarchus in libro de Musica commemorant. Thraces autem id potius tribuunt Orpheo suo: Aegyptij Mercurio,qui apud se natus fit, quem eundé Toth seu Trismegistum vocant, vt ait Eusebius lib.1.Prapar.Euang. Plato lib.3.de Repubi.distinguit. Nam quâ Lyram pulsat & alia instrumeta, Musica,ea,ait,ab Amphione reperta est: sed qua voce,&oris sono velut tibiys fit & modulatur à Marsya(qui Lydus fuit)& Olympo, Plinius lib.7.cap.56.varios variarum Musices partium, variorumq instrumentorum repertores recitat. Verum nulli istorum primi Musicam pepererunt: sed quum inuenta iā esset,eam duntaxat primi ad suos homines deportarunt,& transtulerunt.Itaq Augustinus lib.18.cap.13. irridet fabulam de Amphione Graeco: Nimirum eum mouisse saxa sono cithare, quemadmodum etiā eandem explodút & Palæphatu& Phornutus homines Graeci natione,& religione Ethnici. Quin imo Plutarchus in lib.de Procreat.anima in Timeum, ait omnes penè veteres Deos cum Musico instrumento in in manu pingi solitos fuisse, quasi omnes eius artis autores esset, ac proinde illius primus autor apud eos incertus effet (quemadmodu etiam scripsit Heraclides, teste Plutarcho) vel quod in omnium Deorum sacris Musica adhiberetur, sicut Arnobius lib. 6. contra Gentes docet. Sed tandem eò res redit, vt velint Apollinem primum omnium huius artis Parentem habedum esse, vt tradit lib. 6. Pausanias. Hic autem antiquissimus fuit, & loge atate superior his omnibus, quos nominauit, nimirum Orpheo, Marsya, Amphione. Nam eum alij cæli, alij Iouis filium (ac proinde vetustissimum) fuisse fatentur, quemadmodum apparet ex Cicer. lib. 3. de Nat. deor. & Arnobij lib. 4. contra Gentes. Quamobrem eum inter Deos maiorum Gentium recensebant, vt demonstrat Lactantius lib. 1. Institut. Christ. cap. 15. Ergo quemadmodum Mercurium ille Iouis filius & antiquissimus .i. Iabal rei pecuariæ prima præcepta Mundo dedit: sic Apollo Iouis filius & primus (multi enim fuerunt post primum) id est, Iubal Musices primus Repertor fuit. Sed & [Iubal] nomen cantum significat. Athenæus autem lib. 9. Musicam inuentam fuisse ex vetustissimis scriptoribus tradit, ad imitationem auium, qui in folitudine degunt & cantillant. Macrobius vero manult ad imitationem fabrorum ad numerum certum, ordinem es & ferrū sub incude contundentium. Verum hæ sunt sola coniectura. Veritas autem est ea, quam nos ex obscuris de Apolline eius inuentore reliquijs collegimus, quæ sunt nobis ab ipsis met Ethnicis tradita. Sed ecquod genus Musica primum ex Ethnicorum sententia repertum est? Est enim Musica, vt definit Augustinus lib. 1.
units.tr: Marcus Tullius Cicero holds the same view in his Tusculan Disputations, book 1. All the historians agree that the first men were trained in the art of music. According to Plato, in book 7 of the Laws, and Aristotle after him, in book 8 of the Politics, the most ancient age of mankind used a twofold discipline: the art of gymnastics to exercise the body, and the art of music to refine the mind. Hence Plato, in book 3 of the Republic, directs that the rulers of the state themselves and their sons be carefully instructed in music, and in book 4 of the same work he holds that any change in music brings countless evils and dangers upon the state. So great, surely, was its importance, and so ancient was this art judged by the Gentiles. And this agrees with Sacred History. But we must examine who, according to these same Gentiles, is said to have discovered music, and what was its first form. On the first invention of music, the Gentiles by no means agree. For when each nation wished to claim for itself the invention of so excellent an art, they named several authors of it, but did not inquire about that first and outstanding man who had taught it to mortals. The Greeks therefore maintain that Amphion was its first discoverer, as Pliny (book 9) and Plutarch in his book on music also record. The Thracians, however, attribute it rather to their Orpheus; the Egyptians to Mercury, who was born among them and whom they call Thoth or Trismegistus, as Eusebius says in book 1 of the Preparation for the Gospel. Plato, in book 3 of the Republic, distinguishes these claims: the music of the lyre and of the other instruments, he says, was discovered by Amphion; but the music of the voice, and its sound and modulation like the pipe, by Marsyas, who was a Lydian, and by Olympus. Pliny, in book 7, chapter 56, lists various discoverers of various parts of music and of various instruments. Yet none of these first men truly brought music into being; rather, since it had already been invented, they only carried it across and transmitted it to their own peoples. Accordingly Augustine, in book 18, chapter 13, mocks the fable of the Greek Amphion, that he moved stones by the sound of the lyre; and the Greek Palaephatus and Phornutus, men of Gentile nation and religion, likewise reject it. Indeed, Plutarch, in his book on the Generation of the Soul in the Timaeus, says that almost all the ancient gods were customarily painted with a musical instrument in their hand, as if they were all authors of that art; and therefore its first author was uncertain among them (as Heraclides also wrote, according to Plutarch), or because music was used in the rites of all the gods, as Arnobius teaches in book 6 against the Gentiles. But in the end the matter comes to this: they wish Apollo to be regarded as the first parent of this art of all, as Pausanias relates in book 6. He was very ancient, and older by far than all those whom we have named, that is, Orpheus, Marsyas and Amphion. For some affirm that he was the son of heaven, others the son of Jupiter (and therefore the most ancient), as is evident from Cicero, book 3 of On the Nature of the Gods, and from Arnobius, book 4 against the Gentiles. Wherefore they counted him among the greater gods, as Lactantius shows in book 1 of the Christian Institutes, chapter 15. Therefore, just as that son of Jupiter, the most ancient Mercury, that is Jabal, gave the first precepts of herding to the world, so Apollo, son of Jupiter and the first (for there were many after the first), that is Jubal, was the first discoverer of music. Moreover, Jubal also means a song. Athenaeus, in book 9, records that music was invented, according to the most ancient writers, in imitation of birds, which live in solitude and sing their little songs. Macrobius, however, prefers that it was in imitation of smiths who strike iron on an anvil in a fixed rhythm and order. But these are mere conjectures. The truth is what we have gathered from the obscure remnants concerning Apollo, its inventor, which have been handed down to us by the Gentiles themselves. But what kind of music was first discovered, according to the opinion of the Gentiles? For music is, as Augustine defines it in book 1,

units.la: de Musica, generalis bene modulandi scientia. Itaque Plato lib. 3 de repub. primarium Musicae opus constituit in modulorum rationibus & symphonijs miscendis, ac temperandis: atque etiam varias etiam species facit. Sed quum idem Plato de Phrygio, & Dorico sono scribat, eos ad Musicam pertinere: & quiî autores reliqui de Musicae inuentione agentes de Lyra, Cithara, Monaulo, Tibijs, Chordis, & caeteris similibus tunc disputant, perspicue apparet omnes de Musica Organica loqui, & sentire, vbi de prima Musica inuenta loquuntur & scribunt: nō autem de Vocali, quae vel postea reperta est, vel quia naturalis est, (nam voce canere docet ipsa met natura) non dicitur à quoquam inuenta, sicut illa, quae est Organica. Quod ipsum planè cum Mose, id est cum Dei verbo conuenit. Denique de Musices vsu, & caussa (quamobrem reperta sit) ex ipsorum zorundem Ethnicorum sententia dicamus. In quo male, meo quidem indicio, Xenophon sensit Musicam nequaquam ad pietatem vtilem vel nunc esse, vel vnquam fuisse, licèt Xenophōtis iudicium ampleƈti videatur Eusebius lib. 14.de Praeparat. Euangel.cap.4. Melius verò & sanƈtius, vt alia pleráque, 'Plato lib.3.de Leg.his verbis, [Non enim, mihi credite, antiquarum legum olim erat dominus populus, sed ipse quodāmodo sponte, ac volens legibus parebat. M. Ecquibusnam verò? A. Iis videlicet primùm, quae illius Musicae (quae tunc temporis vigebat) rationibus continebantur, vt ab initio arcessamus libertoris vitae incrementum. Musica enim tunc in certas quasdā formas suas distribuebatur: & vna erat illius, Precatio ad Deos, quae Hymnorum nomine notabatur : & illi speciei alia erat contraria, quæ Threnos: alia,quos Paanas nuncupabant: & alia Liberi Patris inuentum, Dithyrambi nomine:alia Citharœdica leges nuncupabat.] Idem verò eiusdem operis lib. 7. Secunda erat lex Musica, ait, vt preces fiant illis Diis, quibus quotidie sacrificamus. Tertia lex erit,vt Poëta intelligant Preces ipsas esse hominū petitiones, quibus à diis aliquid postulant : Quare videant diligenter ne mala pro bonis à diis imprudenter precentur. Plutarchus in lib.de Musica, [Perspicuum est,inquit,veterem illam Græciam studiū operámque rerum omnium merito impendisse maximam,vt imprimis Adolescentes Musica erudirentur. Eorum enim animos molles ac teneros ad modestiam atque moderationem componi & temperari Musica oportere existimabant,quippe quam ad omnes occasiones, actionésque omnes, quas intenderes, vtilem, & commodam esse putarent:atque imprimis ad bellicos terrores, ad quos alacriter & fortiter capessendos & sustinendos aly,vt Lacedæmones, tibiis canentibus Castorium appellatum modum instructa acie cum hoste conferturi manu promouebantur: aly ad cantum Lyra in certamen aduersus hostes procurrebat.] Cui consentit Horatius. Nam à Poëtis & Musicis pueros ad virtutem edoctos fuisse scribit lib.2.epist.1: [Os tenerum pueri, balbúmque Poëta figurat, Arcet ab obscænis.] Ad prælia quoque adhibitam antiquitus Musicam idem lib. de Arte Poëtica docet: --[Post hos insignis Homerus Tirtaúsque mares animos in Martia bella Versibus exacuit.] Denique in deorū cultu & oraculis Musices visus fuit. --[ Dicta per carmina sortes Et vita monstrata via est.] Et lib. 2 Epist. [Discerret unde preces, Vatem ni Musa dedisset? Poscit opem chorus, & praesentia numina sentit: Coelestes implorat aquas docta prece blandus: Auertit morbos: metuenda pericula pellit: Carmine Dij superi placantur, carmine Manes.]
units.tr: On Music, the general science of making good melody. Hence Plato, in book 3 of the Republic, places the chief work of music in the principles of melodies and in the mixing and tempering of harmonies, and he also makes various kinds of it. But since the same Plato writes of the Phrygian and Dorian modes, and assigns them to music, and since the other authors who treat of the invention of music then discuss the lyre, the cithara, the single pipe, the flutes, strings and other such things, it is plainly evident that all of them speak and think of instrumental music whenever they write and speak of the first invention of music; not of vocal music, which was either discovered later, or, because it is natural (for nature herself teaches us to sing with the voice), is not said by anyone to have been invented, as instrumental music is. This very thing agrees plainly with Moses, that is, with the Word of God. Finally, let us speak of the use of music and its cause (why it was invented), according to the opinion of these same Gentiles. In this, in my judgement, Xenophon was wrong to think that music was by no means useful for piety, either now or ever; although Eusebius, in book 14 of the Preparation for the Gospel, chapter 4, seems to extol Xenophon's judgement. But Plato, in book 3 of the Laws, speaks better and more soundly, as in many other places, in these words: [Believe me, the people were not once the master of the ancient laws, but of their own accord and willingly they obeyed the laws themselves.] M. To which laws? A. Chiefly those contained in the principles of that music which then flourished, so that we may trace the growth of a free life from its beginning. For music was then distributed into certain forms of its own: one of these was prayer to the gods, which was known by the name of hymns; and opposed to this kind was another, the dirge; another was what they called paeans; another, the invention of Father Liber, was named dithyramb; another was called the citharoedic law. Again, in book 7 of the same work, he says: The second law of music is that prayers be offered to those gods to whom we sacrifice every day. The third law shall be that poets understand that the prayers themselves are petitions of men by which they ask something from the gods; wherefore let them take diligent care not to pray imprudently for evils instead of goods. Plutarch, in his book on music: [It is clear, he says, that that ancient Greece rightly devoted the greatest zeal and effort to all things, above all that young people be trained in music. For they believed that the soft and tender minds of the young ought to be formed and tempered to modesty and moderation by music, since they thought it useful and suitable for all occasions and all actions one might undertake; and above all for the terrors of war, for which some, such as the Lacedaemonians, were led forward to meet the enemy in battle array, with flutes playing the mode called Castorian, to take up and sustain the struggle eagerly and bravely; others rushed into battle against the enemy to the sound of the lyre.] Horace agrees with this. For he writes, in book 2 of the Epistles, that boys were trained to virtue by poets and musicians: [The poet shapes the tender mouth of boys and the stammering mouth, and keeps it from obscene things.] That music was also used in war in ancient times Horace teaches in his book on the Art of Poetry: [After these, the famous Homer and Tyrtaeus sharpened manly spirits for warlike battles with their verses.] Finally, music was seen also in the worship of the gods and in oracles. [Fates were declared through songs, and the path of life was shown.] And in book 2 of the Epistles: [How could the people learn whence to pray, unless the Muse had given the bard? The chorus asks for help, and feels the gods present: the gods of heaven are implored with a learned and winning prayer; it turns away diseases and drives off dangers; the gods above are appeased by song, the spirits of the dead by song.]

units.la: His consentit Athenaeus lib. 14 Dipnosoph. vbi varias Musicae laudes describuntur: & imprimis hoc, quod Musica & mores formant, & iracundos placat, & mente discordes lenit atque inter se conciliat. Ad eam fortium virorum facta canebantur: vrbes codebantur, Pausan. lib. 4. Imo vero etiam qui Atheniensium longos muros (qui ab vrbe ad Piraeum portu pertinebant) disiyceret Lysander ad fistulae & Tibiarum cantum, eos diruit, quemadmodum in Hellenicis scribit Xenophon. Ex quo factum est, vt multis in locis Musica certamina instituerentur, vt & Augustin lib. 6 de Musica, & Pausanias docet quod & in sacris, & profanis: in publicis, & privatis rebus: domi, foris, in comiuijs, & aliis hominum coetibus huius artis visus esset maximus. Huius enim esse triplicem visum ex veteribus scribit in lib. de Musica Plutarchus, nempe Voluptatem. Dolorem & Entho usiasmon. Quae sunt vestigia veritatis de inuenta primum Musica. Homines enim eam tum voluptatis sue gratia reperunt: tum vt in Dei cultu eam adhiberent. Et haec quidem de Musica.
units.tr: Athenaeus agrees with this in book 14 of the Deipnosophists, where he describes the various praises of music, and above all that music shapes character, calms the angry, soothes minds at odds and reconciles them with one another. To its accompaniment the deeds of brave men were sung, and cities were founded. Pausanias, book 4. Indeed, Lysander pulled down the long walls of the Athenians (which ran from the city to the port of Piraeus) to the sound of pipes and flutes, as Xenophon writes in the Hellenica. As a result, musical contests were instituted in many places, as Augustine (book 6, On Music) and Pausanias teach. The art was seen to be of the greatest importance in sacred and profane matters, in public and private affairs, at home and abroad, at banquets and in other gatherings of men. Plutarch, in his book On Music, writes from the ancients that music has a threefold effect: pleasure, pain and enthusiasm. These are traces of the truth about music's first invention. Men invented it then partly for the sake of their pleasure, and partly to use it in the worship of God. So much for music.

units.tr: The fourth art was bronze-working, and the fifth iron-working. Tubalcain invented both, and his sister Naamah is joined with him as a companion in the work. Of this truth

[Ignis quidem à Promethe o: artes autem à Vulcano, spjusq; cóiunge, eiusdem artis socia.] Quid magis cósentiens dici potest? Nam quis dubitat, quin ἡμέτερος Græcorum id est, Vulcanus ille vetustissimus (plures enim fuerunt, vt doc t Tullius lib. 3. de Nat. Deor. & Arnobius lib. 4 contra Gentes) Latinorum sit Tubalcainus Mosis, quum si mutetur T, in V, (quarum literarum facilis est in sese migratio) nomen ipsum & vox [Tubalcainus | sit [Vulcanus?] Præterea quis nescit [Ṽabhama] significare pulcram, seu Venerem, quæ quum ab ipsis Ethnicis dicatur, vti & Vulcanus, filia Iouis, certe soror est Vulcani: eadè vero ab ijs ipsis Ethnicis dicitur vxor quoq;, Vulcani, vt plane illi cū Mose in eo concordent. Verum vt hæc ipsa maiorem apud omnes fidem habeant, sunt paulo latius explicanda. Ac primùm quidè fuisse Æs prius quàm Ferrum inuentū apparet ex ipsismet profanis. Nam Plinius lib. 7. cap. 56. Nat. Hist. vtriusque artis inuentionem recitans, prius æs & ærariam artem, quàm ferrum & ferrariā commemorat, & repertam fuisse docet. Hanc eandem sententiam confirmat Pausanias lib 3. Nam inter mortales vsum æris, quàm ferri prius fuisse scribit. Confirmat etiam Homerus, qui heroum antiquissimorū hominum arma ex ære, nō ex ferro facta scribit. Cæterum & æris, & ferri inuentionem & vsum non modò post peccatum intemperiemq;, hominis omnes Ethnici collocat: sed etiam post longum tempus, & tunc primum, quum homines iam inter se contendere, rixari, & pugnare cœcœpisset. Plato in Politico id diserte docet, & testatur: atque idem lib. 12. de Leg. vetat ne Deorum imagines fiant ex ære, & ferro, quia ea sunt belli instrumenta.
units.tr: the clearest traces are found among the heathen themselves. These are Plato's words in the Politicus: "Fire indeed from Prometheus, and the arts from Hephaestus, and the sharing of them..." [Πῦρ ... ἀπ' Ἡφαίστου] . What could agree more closely? For who doubts that the Greek Hephaestus, that most ancient Vulcan (for there were several, as Cicero teaches in book 3 of On the Nature of the Gods and Arnobius in book 4 Against the Gentiles), is the Latin Vulcan, that is, Tubalcain of Moses? If T is changed to V (letters which easily pass into one another), the name and the sound become Vulcan. Moreover, who does not know that Naamah means beautiful, or Venus? Since the heathen themselves call her, like Vulcan, the daughter of Jupiter, she is certainly the sister of Vulcan; and the same heathen also call her the wife of Vulcan, so that they agree with Moses entirely on this point. But so that these things may win greater credence with everyone, they must be explained a little more fully. First, that bronze was discovered before iron is plain from the profane writers themselves. Pliny, in book 7, chapter 56 of the Natural History, recounting the invention of both arts, mentions and teaches that bronze and the art of working it were found before iron and ironworking. Pausanias, book 3, confirms the same view: he writes that among mortals the use of bronze came before that of iron. Homer also confirms it, writing that the arms of the most ancient heroes were made of bronze, not iron. Besides, all the heathen place the invention and use of both bronze and iron not only after the sin and intemperance of man, but also after a long time, and then first, when men had begun to contend, quarrel and fight with one another. Plato teaches and states this plainly in the Politicus; and the same Plato, in book 12 of the Laws, forbids images of the gods to be made of bronze or iron, because these are instruments of war.

units.la: Virgilius lib. 2. Georgic. idem demonstrat:
units.tr: Virgil, in book 2 of the Georgics, shows the same:

units.la: [Ante etiam sceptrum Dictæi regis, & ante Impia quàm cæsis gens est epulata iuvencis: Aureus hanc vitam in terris Saturnus agebat. Nec dum etiam audierant inflari classica, necdum Impositos duris crepitare incudibus ignes.]
units.tr: [Before the sceptre of the Dictaean king, and before the impious race fed on slaughtered oxen, golden Saturn lived this life on earth. Nor had they yet heard the trumpets sound, nor the fires crackling on the hard anvils.]

units.la: Horatius lib. 1. Satyra 3.
units.tr: Horace, book 1, Satire 3:

units.la: [Quum prorepserunt primis animalia terris, (Mutû, & turpe genus) gladem atq; cubilia propter Unguibus, & pugnis: dein fustibus, atque ita porro Pugnabant armis, quæ post fabricauerat vsus.]
units.tr: [When the animals first crept forth upon the earth, a dumb and base race, they fought for acorns and lairs with nails and fists, then with clubs, and so on, until they fought with weapons which later use had devised.]

units.la: Denique Tibullus libro primo, Elegia decima:
units.tr: Lastly, Tibullus, book 1, elegy 10:

units.la: [Quis fuit horrendos primus, qui protulit enses? Quàm ferus, & verè ferreus ille fuit?]
units.tr: [Who was the first who brought forth the dreadful swords? How fierce, and truly iron-hearted, was he!]

units.la: Cui consentit id, quod scribit Pausanias libr. 8, & 10. vtriusq; huius artis nimirum ararias, & ferrarias vsum esse multis seculis post homines natos: quodq; Diodorus Sicul. lib. 1. cap. 1, & 2. tradit: Aeraria tamen, quàm Ferraria, vetustior est. Illius autem meminit Aristoteles tum lib. 1. Politic. cap. 5. quam χαλκοργικὴν appellat: tum etiā in lib. de Admiral. Audition. his verbis, [Ferunt, ait, Moschinæcum æs nitidissimū & candidissimum esse, cui non admisceatur stannum: sed terra quodam genus, quæ ibi gignitur, & vnà cum ære coquitur.] Narrant autem eum, qui temperamentum illud invenerit, neminem hoc docuisse, & ideo opera illo loco vetera tera eximia esse, recentiora vero non item.] Hæc ille. Caterum Ioachimus Camerarius in suis annotationibus in Politica Aristotel. adhuc Germanico nomine hoc ex Moßinæcum appellari, & fortassis est χαλκολίβανον S. Scriptura, Apocal. 4. 1. 15. Caterum quis ex primus, aut ærariam artem .i. fundendi æris rationem repererit, dubitant Ethnici, & in eo sunt inter se vari, quum de primo illius autore non quærunt: sed illius inuenti gloria posteris, & alijs, quam primo, tribuunt. Aristotelus æris conflandi, & temperandi artem Lydo Scytha vindicat: Theophrastus autem Dela Phrygi, vt autor est Plinius lib. 7. cap. 56. Ipse vero Chalybus, & Cyclopibus eam tribuit. Pausanias lib. 8. Ɍæcum Phæi filium, & Theodorum Teleclis viros Samios primos ex fudisse, & ex eo simulacra conflasse manult. Plinius ip-se plane nutat, quia lib. 4. cap. 12. vult ex primum in Chalcide oppido Eubœa insula repertum: Lib. vero 7. cap. 56. in insula Cypro: at lib. 33. cap. 3. in Hispania. Ferri quoque inuentorem, quis fuerit, vbi a primo discessere, non reperiunt. Alij enim Dactylos Idæos in Creta primos ferrum inuenisse volunt: alij Polydorum Samium, vt scribit Pausanias lib. 3. Alij Glauconem, vt idem vult lib. 10. Plinius lib. 34. cap. 14 ferrum vbi¿ reperiri ait, in Catabria tamen esse montem totum ferreum. In Serica regione, quæ est Orientalis, esse optimū. Tubalcainus autem in Oriente vixit, quod cum nostra veritate consentit. Denique vt obiter dicam, ferrum humano sanguine contactum, statim rubiginem contrahit, vt idem Plinius scribit. Verum nos, his omissis, quod cateri vere dixerint, perpendamus. Constat porro inter
units.tr: This agrees with what Pausanias writes in books 8 and 10: that the use of both these arts, bronze-working and iron-working, came many centuries after men were born; and with what Diodorus Siculus teaches in book 1, chapters 1 and 2: that bronze-working is older than iron-working. Aristotle mentions the bronze art in book 1 of the Politics, chapter 5, which he calls chalkorgikē, and also in his book On Marvellous Things Heard, in these words: [They say, he says, that the most brilliant and whitest bronze is that of Moschinaecum, to which no tin is added, but a certain kind of earth which is found there and is fired together with the bronze.] They relate that the man who discovered that mixture taught it to no one, and therefore the ancient works in that place are outstanding, but the more recent ones are not. So he. Joachim Camerarius, in his notes on Aristotle's Politics, adds that in German this is called Moßinæcum, and perhaps it is the chalkolibanon of Holy Scripture (Apocalypse 1.15). The heathen are unsure who first discovered the art of bronze-working, that is, the method of casting bronze, and they differ among themselves; they do not ask about the first author, but ascribe the glory of the invention to later men and others rather than to the first. Aristotle claims the art of casting and tempering bronze for the Lydian Scythian; Theophrastus gives it to Delas the Phrygian, as Pliny reports in book 7, chapter 56. Aristotle himself attributes it to the Chalybes and the Cyclopes. Pausanias, book 8, prefers to say that Rhoecus, son of Phileus, and Theodorus, son of Telecles, Samians, were the first to cast bronze and make statues from it. Pliny himself plainly wavers: in book 4, chapter 12 he says it was first found in the town of Chalcis on the island of Euboea; in book 7, chapter 56, on the island of Cyprus; and in book 33, chapter 3, in Spain. Nor can they find who the inventor of iron was, or where he came from. Some want the Idaean Dactyls of Crete to have been the first to discover iron; others Polydorus of Samos, as Pausanias writes in book 3; others Glaucus, as he says in book 10. Pliny, in book 34, chapter 14, says iron is found everywhere, yet in Cantabria there is a mountain wholly of iron, and in the region of the Seres, which is in the East, the best iron is found. Tubalcain, however, lived in the East, which agrees with our truth. Lastly, to mention in passing, iron touched with human blood at once contracts rust, as Pliny also writes. But let us set these things aside and weigh what the others have said truly. It is agreed among

units.la: Ethnicos omnes eum Vulcanum quendam fuisse vetustissimum, quem Iouis filium propterea vocant. Quo- cunque enim antiquissimos esse volunt, eosdem faci nt filios Iouis, vel cœli. Ab huius Vulcani nomine primi, postea alii sunt Vulcani dicti ipso multis seculis iuniores. Hic vero Vulcanus antiquissimus est, ut nomen ipsum ostendit, Tubalcainus Mosis. Ab hoc igitur Vulcano Aerariam, & Ferrariam artem, adeoq; instrumentorum eiusmodi conficiendorum rationem primum repertam esse ipsimet Ethnici scribunt. Itaq; omnes opifices eiusmodi illi consecratos esse docet Plato, lib.11.de Legibus. Quare sic pingebatur, ut Albericus in lib.de imaginibus Deorum ait, videlicet Deus Ignium, fabri similitudine, malleum in manu tenens, & iuxta eum officina pingebatur: etsi Herodotus lib.3. ridiculè eum postea ab Aegyptijs depictum fuisse narrat. Ergo de Vulcano sic scribit Homerus, ὃν ἥφαιστος & ἈΣΙ ... ἀδάμαν, & apud eundem Iliad.lib.18. facta est mentio Tripodum admirandorum à Vulcano fabrefactorum. Sed & arma ab eodem Diis facta scribit ex Ethnicis Lactantius lib.1.cap.17: quanquam Pausanias lib.9. ait nullum in tota Gracia egregiû Vulcani opus extare praeter sceptrum Agamemnonis: sed nos non de Graco Vulcano, qui recens est: sed de primo, de quo Homerus & Lactantius loquimur. Ergo hic est Vulcanus, qui etiam ab Augustino Deus Artium ex Ethnicorum mente nominatur; lib.4.Ciuit.Dei, cap.10. Quod & ante eum Plutarchus in lib. Aquæ & Ignis Comparat. dixit. Nam vsum ignis ad fundendum, & conflandum metalla primus invenit Vulcanus ille, ut ait Lactant. lib.2.cap.6,& lib.de Ira Dei,cap.13. Ignis autè vsu istiusmodi reperto, facilè fuit artes ferrarias & ærarias inuenire, vti docent Diodorus Sicul.lib.1.cap.1, & Plato. Porrò quum vox [Vulcanus] ex voce [Tubalcainus] manifestè formata sit, (Nā & Ofirim Ae-gyptij vocant Thamec,vt ait Euseb. quem dicunt Vulcanum) inepta est Fulgentij Placiadis etymologia, qui Vulcanum quasi βυλκανον dici putat,id est,cupidum fumi & fuliginis hominem. Phornutus ηφαιςον ab incendendo deriuari putat. (Est autem ηφαιςος Gracis, Vulcanus Latinis) nempe ἀπὸ τ αὐσὲιν,quod & spirare, & inflamare significat. Melius Plato in Cratylo ηφαι-ςον deducit à verbo φαίνειν,& φῶς, quòd quis igni praesit Vulcanus,& luci quoq; praefectus est:Est enim ignis naturâ lucidus,& calidus. Ναhhama verò est proculdubio Venus,qua Vulcani illius primi & soror fuit,& vxor. Ναm Ναhhama significat Pulcra,formosam, venustâ,& eam cuius coitu deleƈtantur homines. Vnde pro Voluptate, Venus (quæ fuit mulier pulcherrima) sumitur,vt docent Athenæus & Augustinus lib.4.cap. II.& 15.cap.20.Ciuit.Dei. A qua dicta sunt omnes mulieres,quarū coitum expetunt,Veneres, qualia sunt ferè scorta. [Venus] autem Latinè à veniendo dicta est,sicut Josephus Scaliger annotauit, quoniam nulla inter populares mulier scortari sinebatur,id est,quæ esses eius loci ciuis:sed duntaxat si quæ erat peregrina & aduena,vt apparet ex veteribus Comœdijs:imò ex ipso Dei verbo velut ex libro Prouerbiorum,vbi Meretrices aduena & extranea vocantur. Sed ad reliqua pergamus.
units.tr: all the heathen that there was a certain most ancient Vulcan, whom for that reason they call the son of Jupiter. For whatever period they want to make the most ancient, they make the same men sons of Jupiter or of heaven. The first Vulcans were named after this Vulcan, and later Vulcans, many centuries younger, were named after him. This Vulcan is the most ancient, as the name itself shows: he is Tubalcain of Moses. From this Vulcan, then, the heathen themselves write that the art of bronze- and ironworking, and so the method of making instruments of that kind, was first discovered. So Plato teaches that all craftsmen of this kind were consecrated to him, in book 11 of the Laws. Hence he was painted in the way Albericus says in his book on the images of the gods: the god of fires, in the likeness of a smith, holding a hammer in his hand, with a workshop painted beside him; although Herodotus, book 3, mockingly relates that he was later depicted by the Egyptians. Homer writes of Vulcan in this way: "whom Hephaestus..." [ὃν Ἥφαιστος ... ἀδάμαν], and in the same Homer, Iliad book 18, mention is made of the wonderful tripods made by Vulcan. Lactantius, book 1, chapter 17, also reports from the heathen that Vulcan made arms for the gods; although Pausanias, book 9, says there is no outstanding work of Vulcan in all Greece except the sceptre of Agamemnon. But we are speaking not of the Greek Vulcan, who is recent, but of the first, of whom Homer and Lactantius speak. So this is the Vulcan whom Augustine, following the mind of the heathen, names the god of the arts (City of God, book 4, chapter 10). Plutarch, in his Comparison of Water and Fire, said this even before him. For that first Vulcan invented the use of fire for melting and casting metals, as Lactantius says (book 2, chapter 6, and On the Anger of God, chapter 13). With the use of fire discovered in this way, it was easy to invent the ironworking and bronzeworking arts, as Diodorus Siculus (book 1, chapter 1) and Plato teach. Further, since the word Vulcan is plainly formed from the word Tubalcain (for the Egyptians also call Osiris Thamec, as Eusebius says, whom they call Vulcan), the etymology of Fulgentius Planciades is absurd, who thinks Vulcan is called, as it were, bylkanon, that is, a man who loves smoke and soot. Phornutus thinks hephaiston is derived from burning. (Hephaistos is the Greek name, Vulcan the Latin.) It comes from apo tou haiein, which means both to blow and to set on fire. Plato in the Cratylus derives hephaiston more aptly from the verb phainein and phōs, because Vulcan presides over fire and is also set over light, for fire is by nature bright and hot. Naamah, however, is without doubt Venus, who was the sister and also the wife of that first Vulcan. For Naamah means beautiful, comely, lovely, and one by whose union men take delight. Hence Venus (who was a most beautiful woman) is taken for pleasure, as Athenaeus and Augustine teach (City of God, book 4, chapters 11 and 15; book 15, chapter 20). From her all women whose intercourse men desire are called Venuses, such as are mostly prostitutes. Venus, however, is derived in Latin from veniendo (coming), as Joseph Scaliger noted, because no woman of the locals was allowed to play the harlot, that is, one who was a citizen of that place, but only if she was a foreigner and a stranger, as appears from the old comedies; indeed from the very word of God, as in the book of Proverbs, where harlots are called strangers and aliens. But let us go on to the rest.

units.la: Ad IX. De Prim- o Hominum Memo- rabili Sacrificio.
units.tr: Chapter IX. On the First Memorable Sacrifice of Men

units.la: ORDO vero historia requirit, vt de Primo hominum Sacrificio, quod quidem fuit memorabile, dissetamus: & quae illius in Ethnicorum scriptis vestigia superstint, exponamus: praesertim quum totam hanc historiam suggillarit Iulianus Apostata, vt est apud Cyrillum Alexandrinum lib. 10. sect. 6. contra hunc eundem Iulianum. Ergo docet S. Scriptura Cainum primu obtulisse sacrificium Deo e frugibus terrae: Abelem vero eidem sacrificasse postea ex primogenitis sui gregis, cuius sacrificium fuerit Deo gratum, non item Caini. Vnde invidia commotus in Abelem fratrem Cainus eum occidit insidiose, & perfidiose. Huius autem veritatis quae in Ethnicis vestigia superstint, explicandum. Et certe quidem multa extant, licet fabulis, velut tenebris, ea veritas fuerit a Satana inuoluta, ne perspicue cerneretur, aut intelligeretur. At vero dico ego, sentio, Sacrificium hoc per illud repraesentari, quod Ethnici scribunt a Ioue & Prometheo fuisse oblatum Caelo auo, & in quo Promethei potiores partes fuisse aiunt: Iouis autem peiores. Nam addunt propterea Iouem in Prometheum iratu fuisse, eumque postea afflixisse, & miserè ad tormenta saeuissima monti Caucaso affixisse, & alligasse. (Sic Homerus, Hesiodus, Aeschylus, Plato, Higinus, Phornutus, Lucianus, & ante hos tres posteriores M.T. Cicero Tusc. 2.) Dico, inquam, ista esse huius historiae sacra & nostra obscuras quidem sed tamen verissimas, & tanquam ex tabula vetustissima reliquas lineas,
units.tr: The order of the history requires that I discuss the first sacrifice of men, which was indeed memorable, and set out the traces of it that survive in the writings of the heathen, especially since Julian the Apostate scoffed at the whole story, as Cyril of Alexandria reports in book 10, section 6, against this same Julian. Holy Scripture teaches that Cain first offered a sacrifice to God from the fruits of the earth, and that Abel afterwards offered to him the firstborn of his flock; God was pleased with Abel's sacrifice, but not with Cain's. Moved by envy, Cain treacherously and secretly killed his brother Abel. Now the traces of this truth that survive among the heathen must be explained. There are indeed many, though they are wrapped in fables as in darkness, so that Satan hid the truth so that it could not be seen or understood clearly. I say, and I hold, that this sacrifice is represented by that story which the heathen write, namely that Jupiter and Prometheus offered a sacrifice to their grandfather Heaven, and that Prometheus took the better part and Jupiter the worse. They add that Jupiter was therefore angry with Prometheus, afflicted him afterwards, and wretchedly fastened and bound him with the cruellest torments to Mount Caucasus. (So Homer, Hesiod, Aeschylus, Plato, Hyginus, Phornutus, Lucian, and, before these three latter, Cicero in the Tusculan Disputations, book 2.) I say, I repeat, that these are the obscure yet most true elements of this history, both sacred and ours, and, as if from a very ancient painting, the remaining lines,

units.la: * lineas, colores, piēturas, & reliquias. Hoc autem his rationibus confirmo. Ac primum quidem iam docui Io-uem illum Ethnicorum, qui fuit vetustissimus, esse Cainum Mosis. Nunc igitur mihi probandum est antiquissimum eorundem Ethnicorum Prometheum esse, imo fuisse Abelem Mosis: dico autem antiquissimum, quoniam uti Ioues multi ad primi imitationem dicti sunt: sic & Prometheî, praesertim a Graecis (ut ex Pausania lib. 2. & 7 facile colligi potest) qui vanitatis ambitionisque studio res notas & veteres interpolarunt, & veram obscurarunt, ut sua genti vetustatem Mundi omnem asscriberent, & falsò. Quorum errorem secutus Eusebius in Chronicis Prometheum in annum Mundi 3520 demum reiecit, quum omnium consensu ille Iovi aequalis atate, ac tempore fuerit. Ergo igitur haec inter Prometheum, & Abelem comparatio: Abel cum Caino fratre simul vixit longo tempore, & vsquequo ab eo occideretur: Sic Iuppiter & Prometheus unâ simul floruerunt, vixerunt, & coeuerfabantur, uti Phornutus scripsit lib. de natura Deorum. Abel & Cain erant fratres: sic Iuppiter & Prometheus consanguinei. Abel & Cain primi homines fuere, viri heroes, & praestantissimi: sic Iuppiter & Prometheus primi mortalium, adeo ut ceteri homines à Prometheo ficti & ex luto formati dicantur, fuerunt; hi duo viri illustres, & heroes primi & summi. Itaque inter se ab Ethnicis comparantur Iuppiter & Prometheus tanquam coaeui, & virtutibus pares, quemadmodum ait Plato in epist. 2. ad Dionysium. Et ut Iuppiter Deus à posteris habitus est, sic & Prometheus, uti docet Hesiodus in Theogonia, cuius etiam ara augusta
units.tr: lines, colours, pictures, and remnants. I confirm this by the following arguments. First, I have already shown that the Jupiter of the heathen, who was the most ancient, is Cain of Moses. It now remains for me to prove that the most ancient Prometheus of the same heathen is, indeed, Abel of Moses. I say "most ancient," since, just as many were called Jupiters after the pattern of the first, so too were there many Prometheuses, especially among the Greeks (as can easily be gathered from Pausanias, books 2 and 7), who, from a desire for vanity and ambition, altered well-known and ancient matters and obscured the truth, so that they might falsely ascribe to their own people the antiquity of the whole world. Following their error, Eusebius in his Chronicle placed Prometheus only in the year of the world 3520, although by the agreement of all he was of the same age and time as Jupiter. So the comparison between Prometheus and Abel runs as follows: Abel lived together with his brother Cain for a long time, until he was killed by him. So Jupiter and Prometheus flourished, lived and associated together at the same time, as Phornutus wrote in his book on the nature of the gods. Abel and Cain were brothers; so Jupiter and Prometheus were kinsmen. Abel and Cain were the first men, heroes and most outstanding; so Jupiter and Prometheus were the first and foremost of mortals, to such an extent that the other men are said to have been fashioned by Prometheus and formed from clay; these two illustrious men were the first and highest heroes. Thus the heathen compare Jupiter and Prometheus with each other as contemporaries and equal in virtues, as Plato says in his second letter to Dionysius. And just as Jupiter was regarded as a god by posterity, so too was Prometheus, as Hesiod teaches in the Theogony; his venerable altar

units.la: · ˙ " habita fuit in Attica, remansitque diutissime, quemadmodum Paufan. lib. 1. stradit. Abel primus cum Caino sacrificanit Deo, suitque piorum iudicio hoc Primum hominũ sacrificium: sic Iupiter & Prometheus omniũ primi Cœlo sacrificarunt. Abel primus animal obtulit & mastauit Deo: Sic Prometheus ille antiquissimus primus bouem mastasse Deo scribitur à Plinio lib. 7. cap. 56. Cainus propter sacrificium (quod uterq; fecerat, nimirum ipse & Abel) inuidit Abeli fratri suo, quòd potior, gratiorque Deo fuerat Abelis oblatio, quàm sua, propterea que Abelem, semotis arbitris, in Oriente occidit: Sic Iuppiter in communi sacrificio (quod primum omnium fuit) inuidit Prometheo consanguineo suo, quoniam in eo potiores Prometheii partes fuerant: eumq; vti dixi, crudelissimè ob eam causam ad Orientem in monte Caucaso, id est, in solitudine Iuppiter affixit. Abelis sacrificiũ idcirco Deo gratum apparuit, quòd cœlitus ignis delapsus illud assumpsit, saltem de cœlo eiusmodi aliquod fauoris Dei signũ extitit: Prometheus post sacrificium suum de cœlo ignem rapuisse, & eum hominibus dedisse ex veterum Ethnicorum traditione fertur. Sic Hesiodus, & Higinus in fabul. cap. 66, & 144. quod Plato in Philebo interpretatur fuisse Dei in Prometheum ipsum munus, non autem Promethei furtu. Ignis autem vsum & inuentionem in Græcia Paufanias lib. 2. tribuit ex recentiorum fabulis, Phoroneo. Augustinus tamen lib. 18. Ciuit. Dei, cap 8. hac de Prometheo vetustissimo narrationem aliter, sed fistra, explicat. Praterea idem Higinus tradit Promethei instituisse, vt in sacrificijs pars vistima adoleretur Deo, pars cõuinio reseruaretur: id quod in veris sacrificijs, & tunc etiā in Abelis sacrificio obtinuit. In summa, sacrificia esse rem antiquissimam apparet, adeoq; ab ipsis Arcadibus (qui primi mortalium censentur, & Lunæ ipsa priores) vsurpatam. Sic Higinus in fabulis cap 66, & 274. Denique Πεγμηθεὺς dictus est nō proprio nomine: sed à cognomine quodam à fide & prudentia, quod res futuras præuideret: vti & Abel ex fide & prospicientia futuri & venturi in mundum Messiæ sacrificauit, proptereáque illius sacrificium Deo gratum fuit. Vnum autem obijci potest in ista Promethei & Abelis comparatione, quod est refellendum, Nimirum Abelem nullos liberos reliquisse: Prometheum autem plures, velut Aethnæum, vt ait Pausanias libro 9: & Deucalionem, vt scribit Ouidius lib. 1. Metamorphos. Respondeo enim Græcos in ea re fuisse deceptos æquiuocatione nominis Promethei, dum filios recentissimi cuiusdam Promethei vetustissimo illi temerè & falsò attribuunt, & tempora confundunt. Falsum enim est Deucalionem Promethei primi filium fuisse. Et hæc quidem ostendunt eorum sacrificiorum (quæ separatim à Caino, & Abele facta sunt Deo) vestigia, quum Iupiter, Cainus sit: Prometheus autem Abel. Porrò Cainum prius ex terra frugibus obtulisse sacrificium, seu donum Deo, verum est: Abelem verò postea ex primogenitis gregis & animalium fuorū. Atque huius ipsius veritatis inter Ethnicos reliquiæ hæ sunt, Nēpe, Quòd ipsimet scribunt primum oblationes Dijs ex frugibus terræ factas, & datas: postea autem victimas seu animalia eisdem oblata. Quod utrumque ex eorum scri-
units.tr: was also held in Attica and remained there for a very long time, as Pausanias reports in book 1. Abel with Cain first sacrificed to God, and by the judgement of the pious this was the first sacrifice of men; so Jupiter and Prometheus first of all sacrificed to Heaven. Abel first offered and slaughtered an animal to God; so too it is written by Pliny in book 7, chapter 56, that that most ancient Prometheus first slaughtered an ox to God. Cain, because of the sacrifice (which both he and Abel had made), envied his brother Abel, because Abel's offering was more favoured and more pleasing to God than his own. Therefore he killed Abel, when no witnesses were near, in the east. So Jupiter, in the common sacrifice (which was the first of all), envied his kinsman Prometheus, because in it Prometheus's part was the better; and, as I have said, he most cruelly fastened him for this reason to the east, that is, to a solitary place, on Mount Caucasus. Abel's sacrifice appeared pleasing to God because fire fell from heaven and consumed it; at least some sign of God's favour came from heaven. After his sacrifice, Prometheus is said, according to the tradition of the ancient heathen, to have snatched fire from heaven and given it to men. So Hesiod and Hyginus (Fables, chapters 66 and 144) tell it, and Plato in the Philebus interprets it as a gift of God to Prometheus himself, not a theft by Prometheus. Pausanias, book 2, ascribes the use and discovery of fire in Greece to Phoroneus, from more recent fables. Augustine, however, in The City of God, book 18, chapter 8, explains this narrative about the most ancient Prometheus differently, but in vain. Moreover, the same Hyginus relates that Prometheus instituted that in sacrifices one part of the victim should be burnt to God and another part reserved for the feast, which was indeed kept in true sacrifices, and even then in Abel's sacrifice. In sum, it is clear that sacrifices are a most ancient custom, and that they were used even by the Arcadians (who are counted the first of mortals and were older than the Moon). So Hyginus, Fables, chapters 66 and 274. Finally, Prometheus (Promētheus) was so called not by a proper name but by a surname derived from faith and prudence, because he foresaw future things; just as Abel also offered sacrifice from faith and foresight of the future Messiah who was to come into the world, and therefore his sacrifice was pleasing to God. One objection may be raised against this comparison of Prometheus and Abel, which must be refuted: namely, that Abel left no children, whereas Prometheus left several, such as Aetnaeus, as Pausanias says in book 9, and Deucalion, as Ovid writes in the first book of the Metamorphoses. I reply that the Greeks were deceived in this matter by the ambiguity of the name Prometheus, when they rashly and falsely attribute the sons of a much more recent Prometheus to that most ancient one, and confuse the times. For it is false that Deucalion was the son of the first Prometheus. These things show the traces of those sacrifices which were made to God separately from those of Cain and Abel, since Jupiter is Cain and Prometheus is Abel. Further, it is true that Cain first offered a sacrifice or gift to God from the fruits of the earth, and Abel afterwards from the firstborn of his flock and animals. And among the heathen there remain these relics of this very truth: namely, that they themselves write that first offerings were made and given to the gods from the fruits of the earth, and afterwards victims or animals were offered to them. Both of these must be proved from their writings and monuments.

units.la: Q ptis & monumentis probandum est. Ac primùm quidem terræ fruges, & quæ ex ea nascuntur oblata Deo fuisse docet Theophrastus, vt refert Theodoritus in libro Ελληνικῶν πα𝛝ημάτων. Unde vult eas frugũ, veluti spicarum tritici, florum, fructuum arborum oblationes 𝛝υμιάματα, id est, suffitus, & odores appellatas: non autem 𝛝υσίας, id est, sacrificia & mactationes. 𝛝υμίαμα enim ἐπὶ τῆ 𝛝υμιᾶν, id est, vaporem vel suffitum emittere, deducitur. Unde & Thus Latinum vocabulum, quòd sit suffimentum odore, dum adoletur, gratissimum. Sacrificium autem, vt ait Isidorus, dicitur quasi sacrum factum, quod precè mystica Deo consecratur. At verò vt alij malunt, à [Sacrum & facere,] id est, mactare. Nec enim quanuis aliò sacra, sacrificium est: sed eadem demum, in qua victima Deo fit, id est, iugulatur, & mactatur. Virgilius in Eclogis:
units.tr: First, indeed, that the fruits of the earth and what grows from it were offered to God, Theophrastus teaches, as Theodoret reports in his book Graecarum affectionum curatio [Ἑλληνικῶν παθημάτων]. Hence he holds that such offerings of fruits, as of ears of wheat, flowers and fruits of trees, were called thymiamata [θυμιάματα], that is, fumigations and odours, and not thysiai [θυσίαι], that is, sacrifices and slaughterings. For thymiama is derived from thymiān [θυμιᾶν], that is, to send forth vapour or smoke. Hence also the Latin word thus, because it is a fumigation most pleasing in odour when it is burnt. But sacrifice, as Isidore says, is called as it were sacred made, because it is consecrated to God by a mystical prayer. Others prefer to derive it from sacrum and facere, that is, to slaughter. For not everything that is sacred is a sacrifice, but only that in which a victim is offered to God, that is, slain and killed. Virgil, in the Eclogues:

units.la: [Quum faciam vitula pro frugibus, ipse venito.]
units.tr: "When I offer a calf for the fruits of the field, come yourself."

units.la: Sed vt ad rem redeam, qua primùm dys, ex Ethnicorũ sententia, offerebantur, erant duntaxat suffimenta, fruges, flores, odores: non autem victima, aut animalia mactata. Quamobrem Plinius lib. 18. cap. 7. ex Maiorũ Libris ritualibus scribit frugum sacrificium fuisse primum omnium, ac antiquissimum. Verum ante Plinium Plato rerum inter Ethnicos diuinarũ scientissimus, lib. 6. de Leg. sic ait, Τὸ δὲ μὴν 𝛝υσιῶν ... καὶ τυναρτίον ἀχέομεν ἐν ἀλλοις, ὅτι ὑδὲ βοὸς ἐτολμῶμεν ... ἀλλὰ ταῦτα ἀγνὰ 𝛝υσέτα, id est, ex Ioannis Serrani doctissimi viri interpretatione, [Atqui vt alij homines alios homines sacrificent, apud multos etiamnum id perdurare videmus: contrariu etiam de aliis audiuimus, sicut quū nec bouillas quidem carnes gustare audebamus, neque animalia Diis immolabamus: sed liba, & fructus melle imbutos, & alia huiusmodi pura sacrificia.] Idē docet Cyrillus lib 9. contra Iulian. seɛt. 5. vbi tū ex veteris cuiusdam Poetæ profani versibus, tum ex Porphyrij libris, tum etiam ex antiquis monumentis testimonia eius rei, nempe Sacrificia prima fuisse ex frugibus, profert: Fuisse apud Delum insulam etiam vetustissimum altare vbi nullum animal offerretur diis, vel sacrificaretur: sed soli odores, & suffitus: quod, Piorum altare vocabatur. Idem Cyrillus ex Ethnicis scriptis tradit. Itaque huiusmodi sacrificia vocarunt Ethnici ipsi, propter eorum vetustatem (quæ purior semper, quam posterior atas apparet) & quoniam erant ἀναίιαχτα, id est, incruenta, appellarunt inquam, θυσίαν viφάλιον, & ἀκαπνον, & ἀχνὴν, quemadmodum docent Athenæus lib. 14. Dipnos. & G. Stuckius amicus meus, vir diligentissimus in vario & erudito opere Conuiual. Quæst. lib 1 cap. 5, quod carerēt huiusmodi sacrificia vino & obsonio .i. carne coëtâ & sacrificatâ, quæ tamen homines animalia sacrificates vesci solebat: Lac enim, & thuris aliquid, mel, fruges, & corolla Dijs tunc offerebatur, quæ postea exigua sacrificia visa sunt, præsertim Romanis hominibus, crescente hominum luxuria, & velut duntaxat rustica. Verum, ut scribit Plinius in proœmio lib. 1. Hist. Nat. non tantum Rustici: sed etiam gentes pleraque eum sacrificandi morem. atque illud sacrificij genus potius retinuerunt, ut lactè solùm, & mola falsa diis suis litarent. Fiebant autem potissimum post fruges collectas, ut idem Stuckius eodem lib. cap. 23. vult. Imo vero ab illo sacrificiorum genere Latina voces [Immolare, & Adorare] sunt professa, quae pro quamvis Dei colendi specie iam vsurpantur, nempe quod is primus Dei cultus publicus, notisque hominibus fuit. Nam Immolare dicitur a Mola. Est autem Mola placenta genus, quae primum ex hordeo tosto fiebat, quoniam hoc frugis & messis genus primum in vsu fuit inter mortales, ut ait Athenaeus lib. 1. Plinius lib. 18. cap. 7. [Antiquissimum in cibis hordeum.] Deinde autem ex tritico tosto fieri cepta est, quod sale conspergebatur. Sic enim Veteres molam vocabant Far tostum sale cosperfum, quod eo molito hostia, (id est, caput vitulinae) & ignis ipse, quo adurebatur, & cultri, quibus illa iugulabatur, aspergebantur. Festus Popeius, [Immolare est mola, id est, farre molito, & sale hostiam aspergere, ait. Maxima enim (ut scribit Plinius lib. 31 cap. 7) etiam in sacris fuit salis autoritas, quando nulla conficiuntur sine mola salsa.] Quod ipsum docte observavit idem Stuckius lib. 1. Convivial. Quaest. cap. 30. Hoc aut e farris genus, unde mola ista fiebat, erat optimum, & Ador ab Edendo dicebatur. Ex quo Adorea, & Adorare verbum deriuatum. Idem Festus, [Ador farris genus, ait, Edor quondam appellatum ab edendo: vel quod aduratur, ut fiat tostum: unde in sacrificio Mola salsa efficitur.] Nonius Marcellus, [Ador, inquit, farris genus, quod epulis & immolationibus pium putatur. Unde Adorare Propitiare religiones poterit dictum videri, & agere aliquid in alterius honorem,] ut vult Festus Pompeius. Ex quo fit, vt inepta proculdubio appareat Isidori sententia, qui lib.6. Etymolog. sic scribit, [Immolatio ab antiquis dicta, quod in mole altaris posita victima caderetur.] Nec enim Immolatio a Mole, sed a mola dicta est: nec victima in mole. i. supra altare cadebatur, sed ante altare, quemadmodum intelligitur ex lib.4 Aeneid. Virgilij. Maza vero Gracorum (quae erat placenta ex tritico & latte, nonnunquam etiam ex aqua & oleo conflans, vt ait Athenaeus lib.14 plebeius, communis, & promiscuus cibus) non est Mola Romanorum, etsi tamen idem Athenaeus lib.3. scribit Maza, quam dicebatur Hygeia, in sacris adhiberi, dijs offerri, & a sacrificatibus degustari solitam fuisse. De quo vide Stuckium meum libro iam citato cap.27. In summa, etiam ex Leuit.cap.23, & Deut.26 apparet sacrificia ex frugibus grata fuisse Deo, & imperata: adeo vt etiam victima ipsa, quae Deo vero mactabantur, oleo, smilagine, vino, & sale aspergerentur sub Lege veteri, vt est Leuit.cap.6. vbi Cyrillus tomo 1. Nimirum vt ex eo Deus autor omnium bonorum, ex sola sua misericordia, esse intelligatur, ac propterea haec omnia bonorum ad vitam hominum necessariorum genera in eius sacrificiis adhibentur. Porro post oblationem ex frugibus Dijs factam victimas quoque ijsdem oblatas, & mactatas fuisse scribunt ydem illi Ethnici autores, vti Plato, Theophrastus, & alij: adeo vt quemadmodum tradit Athenaeus lib.14. Dipnosoph.propterea sacrificijs Ethnicorum praefecti fuerint Coqui, quod scirent illi animalia & mactare seu iugulare, & in frusta dissecare. Nec autem Pythagorae ratio audienda, qui (vt est apud Ouid.lib 15. Metamorph. & Cyrillum lib. 10. contra Iulian.fect.6, & lib.9.fect. 5.) existimauit impium esse Deo victimas seu animalia sacrificare, quod cæde & sanguine nequaquam gauderet Deus. Nam verum quidem est, Deum per se cæde animalium minimè delectari: nec eorum nidore,ossibus, vel carne pasci, vt rectè sensit Poëta vetus & Ethnicus apud Porphyrium, lib.2.de Abstinentia carnium, his verbis:
units.tr: But to return to the point: at first, according to the opinion of the Gentiles, the offerings were only incense, grains, flowers and fragrances, not victims or slaughtered animals. Hence Pliny, book 18, chapter 7, writes from the ritual books of the ancients that the sacrifice of fruits was the first of all and the most ancient. Yet before Pliny, Plato, the most learned of the Gentiles in divine matters, says in book 6 of the Laws: "Τὸ δὲ μὴν θυσιῶν ... καὶ τυναρτίον ἀχέομεν ἐν ἀλλοις, ὅτι ὑδὲ βοὸς ἐτολμῶμεν ... ἀλλὰ ταῦτα ἀγνὰ θυσέτα." In the translation of John Serranus, a most learned man, it reads: "But just as other men sacrifice men, and we still see this custom persisting among many; we have also heard of the contrary practice among others, when we did not dare even to taste ox flesh, nor to offer living animals to the gods, but only cakes and fruits steeped in honey and other such pure sacrifices." Cyril teaches the same in book 9 against Julian, section 5, where he brings forward evidence of this, namely that the first sacrifices were of fruits, from the verses of an ancient profane poet, from the books of Porphyry, and also from ancient monuments. He reports that on the island of Delos there was a very ancient altar where no animal was offered or slain for the gods, but only perfumes and incense; this was called the altar of the Pious. Cyril also hands down the same from pagan writings. Therefore the Gentiles themselves called such sacrifices, on account of their antiquity (which always appears purer than later ages), and because they were bloodless [ἀναίμακτα], by the names "psiphalion" [θυσίαν ψιφάλιον], "akapnon" [ἀκαπνον] and "achne" [ἀχνὴν], as Athenaeus teaches in book 14 of the Deipnosophists, and my friend G. Stuckius, a most diligent man, in his varied and learned work, the Convivial Questions, book 1, chapter 5. Such sacrifices lacked wine and provisions, that is, cooked and offered meat, which people who sacrificed animals were accustomed to eat. For milk, some incense, honey, fruits and garlands were then offered to the gods; these later came to seem meagre offerings, especially to the Romans, as luxury grew and they seemed merely rustic. Yet, as Pliny writes in the preface to book 1 of the Natural History, it was not only rustic people but also most nations who kept this manner of sacrificing and retained this kind of sacrifice, so that they offered to their gods only milk and salted meal. Moreover, they were made chiefly after the harvest of the grains, as Stuckius himself wants in the same book, chapter 23. Indeed, from this kind of sacrifice the Latin words [Immolare and Adorare] took their origin, and are now used for any form of worshipping God, because this was the first public worship of God and was known to men. For Immolare is derived from Mola. Now Mola is a kind of cake, which was first made from roasted barley, since this kind of grain and harvest was the first in use among mortals, as Athenaeus says in book 1; Pliny, book 18, chapter 7: "Barley was the most ancient food." Afterwards it began to be made from roasted wheat, which was sprinkled with salt. For the ancients called this roasted spelt sprinkled with salt mola, and with this ground meal the victim (that is, the head of a calf), the fire itself in which it was burned, and the knives with which it was slaughtered were sprinkled. Festus Pompeius says: "To immolate is to sprinkle the victim with ground spelt and salt." For (as Pliny writes, book 31, chapter 7) the authority of salt was very great even in sacred rites, since nothing is performed in sacred matters without salted meal. Stuckius, in book 1 of the Convivial Questions, chapter 30, has rightly observed this very point. Now this kind of spelt from which that meal was made was the best, and it was called ador from edere (to eat). From it the word adorea and the verb adorare are derived. Festus again: "Ador is a kind of spelt, he says, formerly called edor from eating, or because it is roasted [adurere] so that it becomes toasted; whence salted meal is made for sacrifice." Nonius Marcellus: "Ador, he says, is a kind of spelt, which is thought pious for feasts and sacrifices." Hence adorare, to propitiate the gods, may seem to have been so named, and to do something in another's honour, as Festus Pompeius holds. From this it clearly appears that the opinion of Isidore is absurd, who in book 6 of the Etymologies writes thus: "Immolation was so called by the ancients because the victim was felled on the altar's mola, placed there." For immolatio is not derived from mole but from mola, and the victim was not felled on the mola, that is, upon the altar, but before the altar, as is clear from book 4 of Virgil's Aeneid. The Greek maza (which was a cake of wheat and milk, sometimes also of water and oil, as Athenaeus says in book 14, a plebeian, common and ordinary food) is not the Roman mola, although Athenaeus in book 3 writes that maza, which was called Hygieia, was used in sacred rites, offered to the gods, and was customarily tasted by the sacrificers. On this see my Stuckius in the book already cited, chapter 27. In sum, it also appears from Leviticus 23 and Deuteronomy 26 that sacrifices of fruits were pleasing to God and commanded, so that even the victims themselves, which were slaughtered to the true God under the old Law, were sprinkled with oil, fine flour, wine and salt, as in Leviticus 6; Cyril, in volume 1, notes this. Clearly from this it is understood that God is the author of all good things, from his mercy alone, and therefore all these kinds of good things necessary for human life are used in his sacrifices. Moreover, the same pagan authors write that after the offering of fruits to the gods, victims were also offered and slain in the same way, as Plato, Theophrastus and others relate; so much so that, as Athenaeus tells in book 14 of the Deipnosophists, cooks were therefore placed in charge of the Gentiles' sacrifices, because they knew how to slaughter or cut the throat of animals and cut them into pieces. Nor is the opinion of Pythagoras to be heeded, who (as Ovid has it in book 15 of the Metamorphoses, and Cyril in book 10 against Julian, section 6, and book 9, section 5) thought it impious to offer victims or animals in sacrifice, because God does not at all delight in slaughter and blood. For it is indeed true that God is in himself not at all delighted by the slaughter of animals, nor fed on their savour, bones or flesh, as an ancient pagan poet rightly perceived, quoted by Porphyry in book 2 of On Abstinence from Animal Food, in these words:

units.la: [Quis sic stultus, aut tam dissolutusPersuasibilis vir, qui speret DeosOssibus sine carne, & felle accensoGaudere, & honorem illum sortiri?] Sed quoniam illa victimarum, & caesorum animalium sacrificia erat futura Christi Passionis (in qua peccatorum Mundi expiatio continetur) vmbra, & repræsentatio, illa Deo grata fuerunt, vt ostendit Augustin. lib. 20. Ciuit. Dei cap. 26. Non autem quod eisdem elementis Animalia illa constent, atque nos vt scribit Arnobius lib.7. Ergo Athenienses, vt scribit Plato lib.7.de Leg. solebat excitare homines in hu-iusmodi animalium sacrificijs ad planctum, & lacrymas etiam adhibitis tibijs, quod illae mastationes animalium tristis pœnæ hominibus propter peccata debitæ symbolum ac signum erant. Fuit igitur tristis significatio istorum sacrificiorum, nempe mortis Christi, ad quam respiciebat Deus in ijs sacrificijs, quæ ipse præceperat: non etiam in ijs, quæ Ethnici ex voluntario ipsorum cultu absque fide offerebant, sicut docet Augustin. lib.10 cap. 5. Ciuit. Dei. Alioquin, & absq; ea significatione, & mortis Christi adhuc futuræ fide, & repræsentatione, vera est illa Platonis in Alcibiade secundo sententia, Sacrificia Animalium non tam placat Deum, quàm pius animus, piaq; precatio. Imo verò Apollonius aras ipsas hoc animalium in ijs sacrificatorum sanguine pollui potius, quàm sanctificari, Ethnicis (quanuis ipse Ethnicus) vere tamen exprobrauit. Erat enim ijs inutiles rerum sibi ad victum necessariarum cades, & damna, quia carebant fide in Christum venturu. Nec obstat etiam quod lib. 10. cap. 19. Ciuit. Dei, querit Augustinus, Cur Deus, qui est inuisibilis, visibilia sacrificia & oblationes sibi dari praeceperit. In eo enim Deus se fe nobis, nostroque captui at temperauit, ut ea à nobis exigeret, qua & tractare, & offerre possemus: non ante inuisibilia, qua contrectare nequimus. Ex quibus omnibus apparet huius nostra veritatis vestigia extare etiam apud Ethnicos, primum Deo oblata fruges terra: postea verò, animalia. Et ut totum hunc locum breuiter concludam, qua sacrificia à bonis & pijs Patribus acceperant primum homines Ethnici, ea non retinuerunt: sed sacrificia illa prorsus depravaruntt. Nam magnificentissimis quibusdam hostijs, & argenteis muneribus, tanquam pretio Deos emere sibi, eorumque fauorem studuerunt illi, ut ex Euhemero scriptore antiquissimo tradit Eusebius lib. 2. cap. 4. de Praeparat. Euangel. Vnde Alexander Magnus Leonidæ praeceptori suo profusionem sacrificiorum reprehendenti respondit, Diys sine parsimonia sacrificandum. At Spartani contrà, vtpote longè ab hac superstitione remoti, ut ait Plutarchus, Diys tenuia & facile parabilia sacrificia instituerunt, velut capras, & gallos gallinaceos. Ex quo factum est, ut ea potissimum reliqua gentes diys suis animalia in sacrificijs offerrent, quæ erant tabida, scabiosa,clauda, enesta: atque ex ijs ipsis solùm capita, & vngulas pedum detruncatas daret diis suis, vt docet Tertullianus in Apologet.cap.14: quod nimij sumptus in ijs fierent. Etsi autem de die solùm, & in aperto Diis suis illi Ethnici sacrificabant, vt ait Lactantius lib.2. cap.2.præterquàm Cereri seu Bonæ Deæ (cuius sacra Romæ fiebant in operto) tamen obscœna omnino & turpia erant, quæ illi in suis sacrificijs agebant, & committebant, qualia adulteria (Nam & sacra quædam nudæ mulieres celebrabant, Plin.lib.22.cap.1) furta cædes, vt scribit Arnobius lib.8.contra Gentes. Ergo, vt ait Athenæus, In sacris præco pronuntiabat, vt sacrificátes ante Solis occasum & noctem discederet, ne quid turpe in ijs perpetraretur. Denique in suis sacrificijs Ethnici ex sanctorum, & à Deo institutorum sacrificiorum κατοζηλία adhibebant far, merum, odorem seu suffitû thuris salem & sanguinem victima, Lactant.lib.6.cap.6 Institut.Christian. Demum & preces, vt docent Horatius, & Persius, & ante vtrumq; Plato, & Cicero in libris de Legibus in iisdem sacrificijs fiebant. In quibus erant tam miseri, ac superstitiosi, vt ne quid in ijs concipiendis vel recitandis ab ijs præposterum diceretur, soleret aliquis præponi, qui sacrificantibus præiret verbis: deinde custos dari, qui observaret, Vtrum sacrificans dictata sibi rectè & ordine pronuntiaret, ac redderet, vt ait Plinius lib.28.cap.2.Hist.Natur. Atque ista quidem de hoc veritatis capite, eiusq; reliquis dicta sunto.
