Nam qui Diis Templa primi instituerint, qui eis dem simulacra, omitto dicere, quoniam illa ad nostrum hoc argumētum, istamq; comparationem à nobis institutam minimè pertinent. Accedamus ad reliqua, velut ad caput vndecimum Historiæ, vbi de Excōmunicatione agitur, quæ prima in homines à Deo ipso propter crimen fulminata est, nimirum in Cainum homicidam seu potius fratricidam, vt quemadmodū ea pœna ex Dei verbo intelligitur horribilis, piacularis, tremēda, ipsaque morte grauior, & in conscientiam hominum ferri: Sic apud Ethnicos ipsos huius doctrinæ ac pœnæ vestigia quædā semper extitisse doceamus. Nam quod ad caput X. Historiæ nostræ pertinet, illud coniunctim cum capite IX. complexi sumus, vbi Prometheum à Ioue per inuidiam afflictum in solitudine montis Caucasi ad Orientem docuimus, quòd Promethei sacrificiū Deo Cœlo suo auo gratius fuisset, quàm suum .i. Ionis.
units.tr: [Who would be so foolish, or so loose-living and easily persuaded a man, as to hope that the gods rejoice in bones without flesh and in burnt gall, and obtain that honour?] But since those sacrifices of victims and slaughtered animals were to be a shadow and representation of Christ's Passion (in which the expiation of the world's sins is contained), they were pleasing to God, as Augustine shows in City of God 20.26. Yet this is not because those animals consist of the same elements as we do, as Arnobius writes in book 7. Therefore the Athenians, as Plato writes in the seventh book of the Laws, used to rouse people to lamentation and tears at such animal sacrifices, even with flutes employed, because those slaughterings of animals were a token and sign of the sad punishment that men owed for their sins. The sad meaning of these sacrifices was therefore the death of Christ, and it was to this that God looked in the sacrifices he himself had commanded; not in those which the heathen offered from their own voluntary worship without faith, as Augustine teaches in City of God 10.5. Otherwise, even apart from that signification and from faith in and representation of Christ's death still to come, that saying of Plato in the second Alcibiades is true: the sacrifices of animals do not so much placate God as a pious mind and devout prayer. Indeed Apollonius, though himself a heathen, truly reproached the heathen that the altars themselves are defiled by the blood of the animals sacrificed on them rather than sanctified; for the slaughter and loss of things needed for their sustenance was useless to them, because they lacked faith in the Christ who was to come. Nor does it stand in the way that Augustine, in City of God 10.19, asks why God, who is invisible, commanded visible sacrifices and offerings to be made to him. For in this God accommodated himself to us and to our capacity, so that he required of us things we could handle and offer, not invisible things that we cannot touch. From all these things it appears that traces of this truth of ours survive even among the heathen: first the fruits of the earth were offered to God, and afterwards animals. To conclude this whole point briefly: the first heathen did not keep the sacrifices they had received from the good and pious fathers; rather they utterly corrupted them. For they tried to buy the gods' favour for themselves with very splendid victims and silver gifts, as if with a price, as Eusebius reports from the most ancient writer Euhemerus, in Preparation for the Gospel, book 2, chapter 4. Hence Alexander the Great, when his tutor Leonidas rebuked his lavish sacrifices, replied that sacrifices must be made to the gods without stinting. But the Spartans, on the contrary, being far removed from this superstition, as Plutarch says, instituted for the gods slight and easily procured sacrifices, such as goats and cocks. As a result, the other nations chiefly offered to their gods those animals that were wasted, mangy, lame, and worn out; and from these they gave their gods only the heads and the severed hooves, as Tertullian teaches in the Apology, chapter 14, because otherwise excessive expense would be incurred. Although, as Lactantius says, those heathen sacrificed to their gods only by day and in the open, except to Ceres or the Good Goddess (whose rites at Rome were performed in secret), nevertheless the things they did and committed in their sacrifices were utterly obscene and foul: adulteries (for certain rites were celebrated by naked women, Pliny, book 22, chapter 1), thefts, and murders, as Arnobius writes in book 8 Against the Gentiles. Therefore, as Athenaeus says, at the sacred rites a herald proclaimed that those sacrificing should depart before sunset and nightfall, so that nothing shameful might be committed there. Finally, in their sacrifices the heathen used, in emulation [κατοζηλία] of the holy sacrifices instituted by God, spelt, unmixed wine, the smoke of incense, salt, and the blood of the victim, as Lactantius says in the Divine Institutes, book 6, chapter 6. Lastly, prayers were also offered in these same sacrifices, as Horace and Persius teach, and before them both Plato and Cicero in the books On the Laws. They were so wretched and superstitious in these matters that, lest anything absurd be said in framing or reciting them, someone was usually placed in front to dictate the words to the sacrificers, and then a guard was appointed to watch whether the sacrificer pronounced and rendered what had been dictated to him correctly and in order, as Pliny says in Natural History, book 28, chapter 2. Let these things be said about this head of the truth and the rest of it. For I pass over who first built temples to the gods and who first made their images, since those things have nothing to do with this argument of ours and the comparison we have undertaken. Let us turn to what remains, such as the eleventh chapter of our History, where excommunication is treated, which was the first penalty ever hurled by God himself upon men for a crime, namely against Cain the murderer, or rather fratricide. Just as this penalty is understood from the word of God to be dreadful, expiatory, and awful, heavier than death itself, and to strike into men's consciences, so let us show that traces of this doctrine and penalty have always existed even among the heathen themselves. As for the tenth chapter of our History, we have taken it together with the ninth, where we showed that Prometheus, afflicted by Jupiter out of envy on the lonely mountain of the Caucasus, had a sacrifice more pleasing to God, to Caelus his grandfather, than his own, that is, Jupiter's.

units.la: Ad XI. De Excommunicatione, quæ fuit Prima scelerum, præsertim ho- micidij, Pœna.
units.tr: On Excommunication, the First Punishment of Crimes, Especially Murder.

units.la: Ergo expendamus, Vtrum Ethnici quoque ipsi Excommunicationem voluerint pœnam esse scelerum perpetratorum, eámque teterrimā existimauerint: ac præsertim homicidijs imposuerint, homicidásque ipsos vagos & errones esse decreuerint, vti ex Dei præcepto & pœna illi data fuit Cainus. Est autem, fuitq; illis Excommunicatio, quemadmodum & nobis, Interdictio à Sacris, & cultu Dei externo, cœtúque aliorum hominū Deum colentium: in quā qui incurrebant, diris, execrationibúsque publicis feriebantur, subijciebantur, & dijs Manibus ac inferis sacri, .i. post hanc vitā torquendi vouebantur. Ergo ᴡιαεῖ dicebantur,id est, nefarij, & ἐναγεῖς detestādi, ἀπὸ τ̄ ἐναγίζειν. Ἐναγίζω vero Expio significat. Unde ἐναγεῖς homines expiandi dicti sunt, & quales qui à Latinis [Sacri] .i. Deo planè maledandi, & ex hominum consortio eiciendi nominantur, ac proinde abominabiles. Hinc quoque est illud Virgilij [Auri sacra fames] id est, detestabilis: & apud Liuiū Pecunia Cereri sacra .i. denota: & Sacrata Leges appellata, vt ait Pompeius [quibus sancitū est, si qui quid aduersus eas fecerit, sacer alicui deorum sit cum familia, pecuniaue.] Ἐναγίζω autem verbum ἀπὸ τ̄ ἁγιάζω deducitur, cui tamen contrariam, vt inquit Iulius Pollux lib. 1. Onomastici, significationem habet. Ἁγιάζω enim Sanctifico: Ἐναγίζω per antiphrasin Expio, voueo, & occido significat. Ἅγιοι, & Ἐναγεῖς, contraria prorsus notione intelliguntur. Ἅγιοι enim dicuntur, qui puri sunt, & mundi. Ἐναγεῖς autē, qui prorsus impuri, polluti, immundi, & execrabiles. Unde ὑλεμ à Platone lib. 7. de Leg. ἀναδάτοι vocantur. Pollux igitur eo libro, quem iam citauit, τοῖς ἀεὶ ἡμῖν ἁγνοῖς χρησάμενος, ἀδαεγί οἱ δ' ἐναντίοι ἀναδάπτοι ὡσαύτως τὰ ἐναντία τῆς ἀναδάπτων, ὅσιος, ἀνομιστος, ἀγνὰς, ἁγίως. τὰ ἀεγύματα, ἅγιον, ἀδάεγον, ὅσιον, ἁγνὸν, ἀναγὲς, ἀχρεῖον. τὸ δ' ἐναντίον, Ἐναγές, ἐξάγισμον, δυσαγές, ἀμιάγιον, πεπυλιάσμον, ὀιασμα, ἀυσρος, id est, Qui sacris ablutionibus & purgationibus vsi sunt, ac vtuntur, ὑ Puri dicuntur: contra verò ὑσδεμ interdicti qui sunt, vocantur Impuri: quemadmodum hac sunt, quae Impuris istis non conueniunt, Sancte, sanctificatē, pure, impollute. Res autem ipsa est Sanctitas, puritas, sacrum, impollutum, inabominabile, inconlaminatum. Quibus rebus hæc sunt contraria, Abominabile, exsanctificatum, detestabile, sceleratum, nefarium, pollutio, abominatio. ] At Latinè quoque ydem homines appellatur Profani. Vnde illud Virgil.lib.6 Aeneid. -[Procul ô procul este Profani, Conclamat vates, totoque absistite luco.] Et Claudianus lib. 1. de Raptu Proserpinæ [Gressus remouete Profani,] tanquam qui procul à deorum phanis & templis arcentur vel abiguntur. Ex quibus apparet, quàm execrabiles & odiosi inter Ethnicos ipsos olim censiti fuerint, quibusque vocabulis & probris ornati ἐξαρχῶμενοι, vt loquitur Plato, id est, homines inter eos sacris & templis Deorum suorum interdicti, ac excommunicati: Ἐσι γὰρ, ait Plutarchus lib. Quæst Rom. quæst 44 τὰ πάςα δυσσεβῆ ὁμοιωτὸν ἐπὶ ἑρπνώ. Ἐ᾿ταῦτα ἦν γὰρ ὡς Ἀθηναῖοι ἡ ἱερᾶτα μὴ δεῖ ἀπαλλάττειν ἀπὸ Ἀλκιβιάδης τῷ ἔγνωκε ἐξ ἀλκιβιάδης δυο·τὰ αὐτοῦ ᾿Αλκιβιάδης, [Est enim huiusmodi execratio res tristis, & infamis. Vnde Athenis laudata est sacerdos, quæ populo quanuis iubente, tamen Alcibiadem detonuere, & eo modo execrari noluit.] Ea autem fuit Theano Menonis filia, quemadmodum tradit idem Plutarchus in vita Alcibiadis. Plato lib. 7. de Leg. hanc pœnam & infamiam grauem fuisse ait, & qui tales erant, à sacrorum participatione remouebantur, etiam iussu Magistratus, & vi militari, si se ingerebant. Itaq; eiusmodi pœnam vetat Plato cuiquam temerè insligi. Ait enim, τὰς ἱερὰς τὰς ἱερᾶτας ἐπὶ τὸ Νομοφυλακῶν ἐξειργόντας, ὅπως ἐξειργεῖν, καὶ τὸ νόμον. Τὸν δ᾽ ἐξειργόμενον ἂν μὴ ἐξ ἀν ἐξειργνταμ, δίκας ἀσεβείας δι᾽ βίᾳ πάντος τῇ ἐλευθερίᾳ
units.tr: Let us therefore consider whether the Gentiles themselves meant excommunication to be a punishment for the crimes committed, and judged it the most dreadful of penalties; and especially whether they laid it upon murders and decreed that murderers should be wanderers and fugitives, as Cain was made by God's command and punishment. Excommunication was for them, as for us, an interdiction from the sacred rites, from the outward worship of God, and from the company of other men who worshipped God. Those who incurred it were struck with public curses and execrations, were made subject to them, and were devoted to the spirits of the dead and to the underworld, that is, to be tormented after this life. Therefore they were called [ἐναγεῖς], that is, wicked, and [ἐναγεῖς] accursed, to be detested, from [ἐναγίζειν]. Now [ἐναγίζω] means to expiate. Hence [ἐναγεῖς] were called men to be expiated, and such as are called sacri by the Latins, that is, to be cursed outright by God and cast out from human society, and therefore abominable. Hence too Virgil's phrase auri sacra fames, that is, detestable hunger for gold; and in Livy, pecunia Cereri sacra, money devoted to Ceres; and the laws are called sacratae, as Pompeius says: laws by which it was sanctioned that if anyone did anything against them, he should be sacred to some god, together with his family or property. Moreover [ἐναγίζω] is derived from [ἁγιάζω], though it has the opposite meaning, as Julius Pollux says in book 1 of his Onomasticon. For [ἁγιάζω] means to sanctify, while [ἐναγίζω], by antiphrasis, means to expiate, to vow, and to kill. [Ἅγιοι] and [ἐναγεῖς] are understood in utterly contrary senses. For [ἅγιοι] are called those who are pure and clean; [ἐναγεῖς], however, are utterly impure, polluted, unclean, and accursed. Hence Plato in book 7 of the Laws calls such people by another term. Pollux, in the book already cited, sets out the opposites: those who have used sacred ablutions and purifications are called pure; on the contrary, those who are interdicted are called impure, just as holy, sanctified, chaste, and undefiled are the words that do not suit those impure ones. The thing itself is sanctity, purity, the sacred, the unpolluted, the unabominable, the undefiled; the contraries of these are abominable, desanctified, detestable, wicked, impious, pollution, abomination. In Latin too the same men are called profani. Hence Virgil in book 6 of the Aeneid: "Far off, far off, you profane ones, the seer cries; keep away from the whole grove." And Claudian in book 1 of On the Rape of Proserpina: "Withdraw your steps, you profane ones," as those who are kept and driven far from the temples of the gods. From these things it appears how execrable and odious they were once thought to be, even among the Gentiles themselves, and with what names and reproaches they were marked; [ἐξαρχόμενοι], as Plato calls them, that is, men excluded and excommunicated from the sacred rites and temples of their gods. For Plutarch, in the Roman Questions 44, says that such an execration is a grave and infamous matter. Hence at Athens a priestess was praised who, though the people ordered it, refused to pronounce the curse on Alcibiades and would not execrate him in that way. This was Theano, the daughter of Menon, as Plutarch also relates in the life of Alcibiades. Plato in book 7 of the Laws says this penalty and grave infamy was imposed, and that such people were removed from participation in the sacred rites, even by order of the magistrate, and by military force if they pushed themselves in.

units.la: πυρέχειν, id est, [Sacerdotes tam mares, quàm fœminæ, vnà cum Legum custodibus, quum aliquem à sacris arcent, id piè & sanctè ex Legis formula agant: Is verò, cui sacris interdictum est, nisi lubes morem gesserit, impietatis pœnas per totâ vitam cuilibet persoluat.] Hac Plato, & cum eò alij scriptores Ethnici, quæ cum gravissima illa Caini per excommunicationem pœna à Deo indicta plane conueniunt. Statuebát enim, qui modò ex iis non erant prorsus ἀσεβεῖς, post hanc vitam sceleratis & excommunicatis hominibus in inferis pœnas repetere, quas sentirent, & quibus eos, dum sacris suis interdicebant, subiiciebant. Dijsque propterea Manibus eósdem devouebant, vt colligi facilè potest ex eodem Platone, lib.2. de Rep. Virgilio, lib.6. Aeneid. atque adeò ex ipsâ Homeri Odyss. qui vtrumq; ætate præcesssit. Extat etiam & aliud istarum execrationum, & dirarum exemplum in scleratos pronuntiatarum apud Plutarchum in vita M. Crassi. Ille enim ab Atteio Tribunopl. hoc modo iis obnoxius factus est. Atteius præcurrit ad portam, quâ M. Crassus paludatus Roma exiturus erat: ibi locum accendit, quo quum peruenisset Crassus, suffitibus iniectis, falsisque libaminibus, diras capiti Crassi atroces, & horrendas imprecatus est, & immanes Deos, ac tetros ibi in Crassum appellauit. Porro addit ex veteri traditione Plutarchus, [Has arcanas & vetustas devotiones Romani ea vi præditas ferunt, vt nemo, adversus quem concepta sint, euitare illas queat. Vnde neq; qualibet de causa has imprecari fas est.] Loquitur autem de publicis, non de priuatis imprecationibus. Eiusmodi enim imprecationes Interdictioni Sacrorum ad-
units.tr: Plato therefore forbids that such a penalty be inflicted on anyone rashly. Priests, both male and female, together with the guardians of the laws, when they keep someone from the sacred rites, should do so piously and holily according to the form of the law. But the one from whom the sacred rites are forbidden, unless he submits, should pay the penalties of impiety to anyone for his whole life. Thus Plato, and with him other Gentile writers, who plainly agree with that most grievous punishment of Cain, inflicted by God through excommunication. For they held that those who were not altogether impious would, after this life, suffer in the underworld the punishments of wicked and excommunicated men, which they would feel, and to which they had subjected them while forbidding them their rites. For this reason they also devoted them to the spirits of the dead, as can easily be gathered from Plato in book 2 of the Republic, from Virgil in book 6 of the Aeneid, and indeed from Homer's Odyssey, who preceded both in age. There is also another example of these dire curses pronounced against the wicked, in Plutarch's life of M. Crassus. For Atteius the tribune made him subject to them in this way. Atteius ran ahead to the gate through which Crassus, in military dress, was about to leave Rome; there he set up a fire, and when Crassus arrived, he threw incense and salted libations upon it, and called down dreadful and horrible curses upon Crassus's head, invoking there savage and foul gods against him. Plutarch adds from ancient tradition: "The Romans say these secret and ancient devotions have such power that no one against whom they are uttered can escape them. Hence it is not lawful to utter such imprecations for any cause." He speaks, however, of public, not private, imprecations. For such imprecations were attached to the interdiction from the sacred rites, as appears in the interdiction of Alcibiades by the Athenians.

units.la: debantur,vt apparet in interdictione Alcibiadis ab Athenienſibus facta. Qua tam erant horribiles, & con-
units.tr: Such curses were so horrible, and

units.la: ſcientia homines ad Dei tribunal citante timebantur etiam ab Ethnicis,vt pro ijs expiandis & aqua luſtrali uterentur, & ablutionibus, & ſacrificijs, quas, vt ait Plato,πλέτεις vocabant,lib.2.de Repub.nimirum quod εὺτέλεσιν est in morte ea ſacrificia fierent Dijs Manibus, ne iſti defuncti vllos paterentur manes & poenas. Expiationes igitur pro interdictis fiebant,& Deos in morte eorum exorabiles per teletas fieri ijsdem credebant: Imo vero etiam Agyrtae quidam & impoſtores homines eas ipsas pecunia,pretioq; appretiato vendebant, quas per carmina & quasdam incantamenta ſe facere poſſe iactabant. Vnde Virgil. lib.4.Aeneid.
units.tr: conscience, summoning men before God's tribunal, was feared even by the Gentiles; so that to expiate them they used lustral water, ablutions, and sacrifices, which, as Plato says in book 2 of the Republic, they called [τελεταί], namely because these sacrifices were performed at death for the spirits of the dead, so that the departed would suffer no spirits and no punishments. Expiations, therefore, were made for the interdicted, and they believed that the gods could be won over at their death through such rites. Indeed, certain charlatans and impostors even sold these very expiations for money at a fixed price, boasting that they could perform them by songs and certain incantations. Hence Virgil in book 4 of the Aeneid:

units.la: [Hæc ſe carminibus promittit ſoluere mentes, Quas velit: aſt aliys duras imponere curas.]
units.tr: "She promises to release minds by songs, whichever she wishes, but to lay hard cares upon others."

units.la: Propertius lib.1.Elegiarum, Eleg.1.
units.tr: Propertius, book 1 of the Elegies, elegy 1:

units.la: [At vos deducta quibus eſt fallacia Lunae, Et labor in Magicis ſacra piare focis.]
units.tr: "But you, to whom the deceit of the Moon is revealed, and the labour of performing sacred rites to expiate at magic hearths."

units.la: Quod ſcelerata dinundinationis, & falſæ expiationis genus notum ibidem irridet idem Plato. Soluti autem & expiati,qui prius fuerant excommunicati, ιάσαεσι dicebantur. Vnde verbum καθαίρεσθαι quo in Phædro vtitur Plato,id est, [Expiare.] Aemilius Probus in vita Alcibiadis [Recsacrare] dixit, cuius haec verba sunt,quæ describam,vt ratio & forma istius Excommunicationis inter Ethnicos vsurpata,& si qua postea fiebat, Absolutionis,intelligatur. [Postquam autem,ait, Alcibiades se capitis damnatum, bonis publicatis, audinit,& (id quod vsu venerat) Eumolpidas sacerdotes à populo coactos vt se devouerent : eiusque devotionis, quo testatior esset memoria, exemplum in pila lapidea incisum esse positum in publico, Lacedaemonem demigrauit.] Causa vero, cur sacris prohibitum publice fuerit Alcibiades à populo Atheniensi hęc erat, vt scribit Plutarchus in eius vita, & post eum Iustin. Histor. lib. 3. quòd mysteria Cereris, caeremonias Eumolpidarum, arcana sacerdotum Eleusinensium, initia sacrorum (nullo magis quam silentio) solennia euulgasset, domi, & enunciauisset. Et tamen illa erat per se absurda & obscoena, vt ostendit Eusebius in lib. de Praeparat. Euang. viaq; adeo ipsa, qua Athenis Eleusin, & ad ea sacra ibatur, erat scortis, & scortorum statuis plena quemadmodum tradit Pausanias lib. 2. Verum, vt ad rem redeā, haec fuit Interdictionis formula. At vero Absolutionis ista, vt describit idem Aemilius Probus, [Restituta ergo, ait, sunt Alcibiadi publice bona ab Atheniensibus. Idemq; illi Eumolpidae sacerdotes rursus resacrare sunt coacti, qui eum devouerat. pilaq; illa (in quibus devotio erat scripta) in mare praecipitata.) Et haec quidem de Excommunicatione & Interdictione a Sacris vestigia extant apud Ethnicos Scriptores: ex quibus probatur illius vsum inter eos fuisse propter grauissima peccata, habitamq; eam pro poena durissima, vt etiā apud Mosem Caterum pro homicidio praesertim impositam eam ipsam poenam, fuisseq; eos inter mortales vagos & errones, qui ea censura feriuntur, ex eorundem Ethnicorum scriptis apparet. Herodotus lib. 1 Histor. narrat Adrastum Phrygem, quum fratrem suum occidisset, sic patria sacrisque profugum ad Croesum Lydiae Regem peruenisse,& ab eo expiatum fuisse. Quem morem & inter Lydios, & inter Graecos suo seculo vsitatū fuisse scribit idem Herodotus. Huic consentit Thucydides. Nam lib.1.Belli Peloponnes. referi Eurystheum propter cædem Chrysippi patriā & sacris interdictū, prohibitumque fuisse, donec absoluereretur. Ouidy testimonio nihil clarius, qui id etiam inter Romanos obtinuisse docet: Sed & idem istius pœnæ in homicidas varia exempla recitat, vt Patrocli, qui Astydamantis filium occiderat: Pelei, qui Phocum: Medea, qui Absyrtum fratrem: Alcmæonis, qui matrem: quibus addi quoque potest Orestes, qui, vt superiores illi, & sacris interdictus & erro vagúsque fuit: quemadmodum etiam Oedippus, & quidē omnes propter homicidia perpetrata fugitiui, & sacris patriaq;, interdicti. Ouidy verò versus lib.2.Fastorum, hi sunt:
units.tr: Plato himself mocks this wicked kind of trafficking and false expiation. Those who had been excommunicated and were released and expiated were called [λελυμένοι], and hence Plato uses the verb [καθαίρεσθαι] in the Phaedrus, that is, to expiate. Aemilius Probus, in the life of Alcibiades, used the word resacrare, to re-consecrate, and his words, which I shall set down, will make clear the form of this excommunication used among the Gentiles, and of the absolution if it was afterward granted: "After Alcibiades heard that he had been condemned to death and his goods confiscated, and that (as usually happened) the Eumolpidae priests had been compelled by the people to curse him, and that a record of that curse, so that its memory might be the more lasting, had been carved on a stone pillar and set up in public, he withdrew to Lacedaemon." The cause for which Alcibiades was publicly forbidden the sacred rites by the Athenian people was, as Plutarch writes in his life, and after him Justin in book 3 of his Histories, that he had publicly divulged and disclosed at home the mysteries of Ceres, the ceremonies of the Eumolpidae, the secrets of the Eleusinian priests, and the initiatory rites of the sacred things, which ought to be kept above all in silence. Yet those rites were in themselves absurd and obscene, as Eusebius shows in his book On the Preparation for the Gospel; and the very place to which people went at Athens for Eleusis and those rites was full of prostitutes and statues of prostitutes, as Pausanias relates in book 2. But to return to the matter: this was the form of the interdiction. The absolution, however, as the same Aemilius Probus describes it: "Therefore, he says, the Athenians publicly restored Alcibiades's goods. And the same Eumolpidae priests were again compelled to re-consecrate him whom they had cursed, and those pillars (on which the curse had been written) were hurled into the sea." These are the traces of excommunication and interdiction from the sacred rites that survive among the Gentile writers, from which it is proved that it was in use among them on account of the gravest sins, and that they regarded it as the harshest of penalties. That it was imposed especially for homicide, as also among Moses's people, and that those struck with this censure were wanderers and fugitives among mortals, appears from the same Gentile writings. Herodotus, in book 1 of his Histories, relates that Adrastus the Phrygian, after killing his brother, came in this way, exiled from his country and his sacred rites, to Croesus king of Lydia, and was expiated by him. Herodotus writes that this custom was in use among the Lydians and the Greeks in his own age. Thucydides agrees: in book 1 of the Peloponnesian War he says that Eurystheus, on account of the killing of Chrysippus, was barred from his country and his sacred rites, and forbidden them until he was absolved. Nothing is clearer than Ovid's testimony, who shows that this also prevailed among the Romans. He likewise recites various examples of this penalty for murderers: Patroclus, who killed the son of Astydamas; Peleus, who killed Phocus; Medea, who killed her brother Absyrtus; Alcmaeon, who killed his mother. To these may be added Orestes, who, like those men, was barred from the sacred rites and was a wanderer; and likewise Oedipus, and indeed all of them, as fugitives on account of the murders they had committed, were barred from sacred rites and from their fatherland. Ovid's verses in book 2 of the Fasti are these:

units.la: [Omne nefas, omnémque mali purgamine caussam Credebant nostri tollere posse senes. Gracia principium moris dedit, illa nocentes Impia lustratos ponere facta putat. Ἀλκηστιδη Pelεus, ipsum quoque Pelea Pheci Cade per Aemonias soluit Acastus aquas. Vestam frenatis per inane dracombus Aegeus Credulus immerita Phasida souit ope. Ἀmphiaraides Ναupacteo Acheloo Solue nefas dixit: soluit & ille nefas. Ah nimium faciles qui tristia crimina cedis Fluminea tolli posse putatis aqua.]
units.tr: Our elders believed they could remove every wrong and every cause of guilt by a purifying rite. Greece gave the custom its beginning; she thinks that guilty deeds are set aside once the doer has been purified. Peleus, and Acastus too, freed Peleus himself from the killing of Phocus in the waters of Aemonia. Aegeus, too readily trusting, cleansed Medea of a crime she had not committed, with the help of the winged dragons drawn through the empty air. Amphiaraus said, "Wash away the wrong in the Naupactian Achelous," and he too washed it away. Ah, you who think you can wash away grievous crimes with river water, you are too easily satisfied!

units.la: De Oreste, Virgil. lib.4. Aeneid. De Oedippo, Euripides in Tragœdiys. Vnde Aqua lustrales & expiatoria apud eosdem, de quibus etiam Paufanias lib 2. Porro Iouem sumilli Ethnici profugum & sacris interdictum fuisse propter eadem Promethei manifeste non referunt (quanquam tamen Iouis exules meminit Paufanias lib. 3.) quoniam talem Dei sui summi ignominiam tegunt, quem tamen gaudere sanguine humano scribunt idem, & humanis victimis, quae ne et offerrentur, Darius rex Persarum vetuit, vt aut Iustinus lib. 10. Sed non semper omnia nostra veritatis vestigia reti-nerunt, aut in ijs sunt quaerenda.
units.tr: Virgil, Aeneid book 4, speaks of Orestes; Euripides, in his tragedies, of Oedipus. From these come the lustral and expiatory waters among the same peoples, of which Pausanias also writes, book 2. Moreover, the heathen clearly do not report that Jupiter was likewise an exile and barred from the sacred rites on account of the same things as Prometheus (although Pausanias, book 3, does mention the exiles of Jupiter), since they conceal such disgrace to their supreme god. Yet the same writers say that he delighted in human blood and in human victims, which King Darius of the Persians forbade them to offer, as Justin says in book 10. But they have not always kept all the traces of our truth, or they are to be sought in those things.

units.la: Ad XII. Vrbs prima in mundo condita.
units.tr: Chapter 12. The first city founded in the world.

units.la: - DE Vrbe vero, quae prima condita fuerit in mundo, videamus. De qua Moses ait & a Caino aedificata, & Enochiam vocatam, & quidem post primi hominis peccatum aliquot seculis, propter metum a reliquis hominibus. Huius autem historiae quae restant apud Ethnicos vestigia, perpendamus: quod fortassis eo difficilius erit, quod Graeci tota huius inventionis laudem sibi tribuere, & in ea tempora, quae sunt posteriora, collocare conantur. Enitar tamen reliquias istius naufragij, et si vetustissimas, colligere. Ac primum illud cosentii cum Mosis dicto, nempe Vrbem primum a Caino conditam fuisse, quod illi scribunt ab antiquissimo illo (quae appellant) Ioue rationem & primum condendarum, & postea conferuandarum Vrbium traditam, ac inventa esse. Id quod docet ex veteri Maiorumque memoria Plato in Protagora. Iouem autem illum fuisse Cainum Mosis antea perspicue demonstrauimus. Verba vero Platonis haec sunt, Ζεὺς ἐν δείους &c. ὑμῶν, ὡς xnó- ἀπώλοιτο πᾶν, Εʼ ῥμὴν πέμπει ἀγοντα εἰς ἀνδρώπους Αἰδῶτ· ἡ Δίκλω, ἵνα εἰεν πόλεων κοσμοί τε ἡ διομοι φιλίας σωα-γωγοί. ἡ γὰρ ἐγένοντο πόλεις, εἰ ὀλίγοι αὐτῆς μετέχοιεν.
units.tr: Concerning the city that was first founded in the world, let us see. Moses says of it that it was built by Cain and called Enoch, and indeed some centuries after the first man's sin, for fear of the rest of mankind. Let us weigh the traces of this history that remain among the heathen, though this will perhaps be harder, because the Greeks try to claim the whole credit for this invention and to place it in later times. Still, I will try to gather the relics of this shipwreck, though they are very ancient. First, there is agreement with the words of Moses, namely that the city was first built by Cain, since the Greeks write that from that most ancient Jupiter (as they call him) the method of founding cities and then of preserving them was handed down and discovered. Plato in the Protagoras teaches this from the old memory of our ancestors. I have already clearly shown that this Jupiter was Cain. Plato's words are these: Ζεὺς οὖν δείσας μὴ πᾶν ἀπόλοιτο τὸ γένος ἡμῶν, Ἑρμῆν πέμπει ἄγοντα εἰς ἀνθρώπους αἰδῶ τε καὶ δίκην, ἵνα εἶεν πόλεων κόσμοι τε καὶ δεσμοὶ φιλίας συναγωγοί. οὐ γὰρ ἂν γένοιντο πόλεις, εἰ ὀλίγοι αὐτῆς μετέχοιεν.

units.la: Ioanne Serrano interprete, [Iuppiter ergo, dum generi nostro metueret (ne prorsus periret) Mercurium misit, qui Pudorem & Iustitiam ad homines deduceret, quae nimirum essent Ciuitatum ornamenta & vincula, sanctaeque inter cives amicitiae auspices & conciliatrices, aliique ciuitates minime existerent, si pauci essent ipsarum participes.] Confirmat hanc Platonis sententiam Higinus, qui in libro de fabulis, cap. 275 (quanquam varias à variis urbes conditas recenset) primam tamen ab antiquissimo Ioue aedificatam fuisse tradit, & quidem in India ac Oriente (quod plane convenit cum Mosis historia) latissimam, quae Thebae Thebaidae, & Hecatompyle (quod centum portas haberent) dictae fuerint. Eodem vero pertinet, quod idem Iupiter ab Ethnicis πολιεύς, Vrbium autor est nuncupatus est: & Εʼ ϝκμος seu Εʼ ϝκεως ἀπὸ ϝ ἑϝκίᾳ (quod septum & vallum significat) quae sunt urbium condendarum partes, & conditarum munimenta, quoniam illa excogitavit Iupiter ille, quemadmodum & Phornutus in lib. de Nat. Deor. & Pausanias lib. 4. 5. & 10. memoriae prodiderunt, & Iouis Hercaei statuae passim positae, cultaeque. Eusebius ex Ethnicorum monumentis lib. 1. cap. 7. Praeparat. Euangel. scribit primam urbem à Saturno conditam: sed pro Ioue Saturnus substitutus est. In summa, Vrbium exstructionem fuisse Deorum inventum perspicue censuerunt veteres Ethnici: ac proinde unamquamque urbem alicui Deo suo consecrarunt, ut scribit Plinius lib. 28. cap.
units.tr: Translated by John Serranus, [Therefore Jupiter, fearing for our race lest it perish utterly, sent Mercury to lead to men Reverence and Justice, that they might be the ornaments and bonds of cities, and the guides of friendship among citizens; for cities could not exist if only a few shared in these.] Higinus confirms this opinion of Plato. In his book On Fables, chapter 275 (although he lists different cities founded by different people), he nevertheless hands down that the first city was built by the most ancient Jupiter, and indeed in India and the East (which agrees plainly with the history of Moses), and that it was very large and was called Thebes of Thebais and Hecatompylos (because it had a hundred gates). To the same point belongs the fact that this same Jupiter was called by the heathen polieus, author of cities, and herkeios or herkeos, from herkos (which means fence and rampart), which are parts of cities being founded and the defences of those founded. For that Jupiter devised these things, as Phornutus in his book On the Nature of the Gods and Pausanias in books 4, 5 and 10 have recorded, and statues of Jupiter Herkeios were set up and worshipped everywhere. Eusebius, from the monuments of the heathen, in book 1, chapter 7, of the Preparation for the Gospel, writes that the first city was founded by Saturn, but Saturn was put in place of Jupiter. In sum, the ancient heathen clearly held that the building of cities was an invention of the gods, and therefore they consecrated each city to some god of theirs, as Pliny writes in book 28, chapter 2.

Vnde talis vitlus,vitaque ratio,Comessatio fuit appellata,quemadmodum vult Festus Pompeius. Caeterum etiam ante Diluuium Vrbes fuisse inter mortales ex nostra veritatis superstitibus reliquis tradiderunt idem Ethnici.Plato in Protagora. Docet enim postquam aliquandiu extitissent homines,statim vrbes ab ys conditas fuisse. Quin & ante diluuium hoc fastu fuisse tradit idem diserte lib.3.de Leg. [Ait enim infinitum esse temporis spatium,quo Vrbes inter homines esse coeperunt:vsumque habuisse etiam ante ϕ&oegrave;oegrave;ν πλὼ τῆ̀ χαταχλυσμῶ ποτὲ γενομέν́ω, id est,ante eam hu- mani generis cladem, quae per celebre illud Diluuium quondam contigit.] Nec aliud sentit Diodor.Siculus lib.1.Bibliothec. cap.1. dum ait homines paulò postquam feras sibi infestas sensissent, habitacula tuta, & vrbes sibi comparasse. Quod quum post hominis peccatum acciderit,certè demum post hominis lapsum huiusmodi externa munimenta quaesita sunt, ipsis quoque iam testibus Ethnicis.Hoc ipsum est,quod ait in Polit. Plato:Nullas quidem in Mundo fuisse Vrbes prima illius aetate, & ante hominū intemperiem: verum postquam Deo immorigeri & inobsequentes esse coepissent, tunc vrbes,& praesidia sibi excogitasse. Quo quid magis cum nostra veritate concordare potest? Certè qui diligèter Ethnica scripta legerit fatebitur,eos hac vestigia veritatis retinuisse, vt & statim primis Mundi temporibus,& à prudentissimis ac perspicacissimis hominibus vrbium condendarū rationem extitisse docueint. Sic Cicero lib. 1. de Inuent. & Tusc. quaest.1. Sic
units.tr: Moreover, before cities were founded, men lived in villages and hamlets, which were called vici and pagi, because they dined together. Hence this manner of feasting and living was called comessatio (revelry), as Festus Pompeius wishes. Besides, the same heathen writers have also handed down, from the survivors of our truth, that cities existed among mortals even before the Flood: Plato in the Protagoras teaches that after men had existed for some time, cities were at once founded by them. Indeed the same author plainly says in book 3 of the Laws that cities existed before this flood. [For he says that the span of time in which cities began to exist among men is infinite, and that they had the custom even before the flood which once happened (before the destruction of the human race, the famous flood) πρὸ τοῦ καταχλυσμοῦ]. Diodorus Siculus, book 1 of the Library, chapter 1, thinks no differently, when he says that men, a little after they perceived wild beasts to be hostile to them, provided themselves with safe dwellings and cities. Since this happened after the sin of man, certainly it was only after the fall of man that such external defences were sought, the heathen witnesses themselves already testifying to it. This is exactly what Plato says in the Statesman: that in the first age of the world, and before the lawlessness of men, there were indeed no cities; but after they began to be disobedient and not compliant with God, then they devised cities and defences for themselves. What could agree more with our truth? Certainly whoever reads the heathen writings diligently will admit that they kept these traces of the truth, so that both in the earliest times of the world and by the wisest and most perceptive men they taught that the method of founding cities came into being. So Cicero in book 1 of On Invention and in the Tusculan Disputations, book 1. Thus

units.la: Poëtis Græcis sumpsit. Sed & propter metum Vrbes primas ab hominibus conditas fuisse sentiunt idem Ethnici, velut Plato in Protagora, his verbis, [Hunc in modum, ait, homines instructi atque comparati principio, dissipati variis in locis sparsim habitabant, necdum Vrbes exstiterant. Fera igitur illis, quod imbecilliores essent, passim perniciem importabant. Vt igitur aduersus hæc incommoda parārent remedia, quæq; saluti prospicerent, quærebant, & in vnum congregari, & Vrbes cœtibus excipiendis condere.] Eodem plane modo & Diodorus Sicul. scribit lib. 1. cap. 1: [Beluas in super hominibus infestas fuisse, quibus vt obsisterent, cœtus hominum ob timorem factos aiunt communis vtilitatis gratia: auxiliaq; inuicem præbita, & loca habitaculis quæsita.] Ex quo factum est, vt oppida & mœnibus, & vallo, & fossa ad firmiorem tutelam cingerentur, vt docet Plutarchus in vita Romuli primi Romanorum Regis. Nec obstat quod idem Plato lib. 2. de Repub. contendit, Propter vsum nempe, & mutuam hominum aliorum ab aliis commoditatem ac necessitatem Vrbes & oppida primum fuisse fundata: Hoc enim ipsum nostram sententiam confirmat. Egent enim homines mutuo auxilio ad se tuendos, quoniam & à feris bestiis, & ab aliis etiam hominibus metuunt sibi homines. Deniq; primam, quæ in Mundo extitit, Vrbem Enochiam inOriente vocatam, fuisse vult, & quidem vere Moses: cuius veritatis haec sunt ex Ethnicorum scriptis vestigia. Primum, quod Plinius lib.6. cap.16. prope Bactros in Oriente constituit Henochios. Sic enim apud Plinium pro Heniochys legendum puto. Atque idem eodem lib.cap.20. collocat in India Orientali Nodumbas populos. Haec autem plane cum Mosaicis [Enoch, & Nod] conveniunt. Nam abunde, ut ait Plato, gratulandum nobis est, ac satis esse debet, si tanta, tamque pene abolita & obsoleta vetustatis vestigia quaedam saltem ex veteribus regionum, locorum, & populorum appellationibus restent, uti hic fit. Deinde quod & Plinius, & Pomponius Mela distinguunt Heniochios populos ab Henochis seu Henochys. Nam Heniochy a Mela lib.1. Situ Orbis, cap.22. collocantur cis mare Caspium, vicini Colchis & Alanis populis, quemadmodum & a Valerio Flacco lib.6. Argonaut. eosque nonnulli scribunt Heniochios, uti Valerius ipse aliy per œ, Oenochios sicut apud Lucan. lib.3. Pharsal. Plinius eos Heniochios constanter nominat, lib.6.cap.4 & 11, quos, uti dixi, circa Caucasum montem cis Caspiu mare sitos ait, & late per multas gentes extendi. Idem asserit Strabo lib.2, & 11 Geographiae. Idem ante hos omnes Xenophon in lib.de Expedit.Cyri. Denique hos ipsos Heniochios a Graecis, & praesertim Lacedaemonys (nimirum a Castoris & Pollucis aurigis) oriundos fuisse, & propterea sic vocatos scribit Dionysius Alexandrinus in descriptione Orbis. Verum eos ex posteris & filiis Abrahami ex Cethura natos ac profectos esse potius ipse crediderim, uti & Medos illis vicinos populos argumento eorum quæ extant Genef. 25.3,& 4. Et hi quidem sunt Heniochi, nempe prope Pontum Euxinū, & cis Caspiū mare. At Henochi seu Henoche(ut vocat Pompon. Mela lib.1.cap.2)sunt in vlteriore Oriente trans mare Caspium,ut ex eodem illo Melæ loco apparet,& Plin.lib.6.cap.16,vti iam docui. Hos verò Henochos quis dubitet esse illius Enoche vel Enochia vrbis prime & vetustissime(vt etiam & Ioseph.lib.1 cap.4. Antiquit.Iudaic. & Augustinus lib.15.Ciuit. Dei,cap.8.scribit)verissimas reliquias,& tanquam ex notissimo memoria ac Orbis terrarū naufragio tabulas, quæ (summo Dei beneficio) nobis ad fidem tanta antiquitatis faciendam supersunt,etiam in ipsis Ethnicorū scriptis?Itaque quod Stephanus in lib.de Vrbibus Heniochiam vult esse eam,de qua Strabo agit lib.11,quæq; est Heniochiorum metropolis,rectè ille quidem:sed illa Stephani & Strabonis Heniochia cum hac nostra Enochia vel Enocha (à qua dicti sunt Enochi vel Enoche populi planè Orientales & Indici) non est cofundenda. Nostram autem hanc nonnulli in ea regione Orientis sitam fuisse putant,in qua est vrbs Cambalu que nūc vocatur,& Orientalis Scythia seu Tartaria. Et hac quidem nostra veritati vestigia durant etiam inter Ethnicos. Porrò ineptiūt,qui aliam vrbem primam omniū statuunt,velut Phenices suam Biblida,vt ait Eusebius lib.1.cap.7.Præparat.Euang. Athenienses & Graci, Cecropiam, Plin.lib.7.cap.56: Latini,Saturniam & Ianiculum,Virgil.lib.8.Aeneidos: Peloponnesij,Argos: Assyrij,Niniuem:Chaldei,Babylonem: Aegyptij, Thebas suas. Hæ enim sunt nostra illa Enochia longè recentiores, & demum post diluuium aedificata: deinde non prima omnium, sed in his demum populis, quarum sunt metropoles condita prima: nos autem de ea, quae omnium prima fuit disputamus. Et haec quidem hactenus. Reliqua vero historiae capita partim supra fuerunt explicata, quum de primarum artium Inuentione ageremus: partim ex iis, quae tam demonstrauimus, colligi, & quidem facile possunt, quale illud, Qui fuerint Caini posteri, & quae illius familiae propagatio, atq; totius huius historiae ecquae reliquiae apud Ethnicos. Docuimus enim, vt breuiter id repetam, Adamum esse antiquissimum illum Ethnicorum Saturnum: Cainum Moysis esse Iouem eorundem: Tubalcainum araria, & ferraria artis repertorem, esse Vulcanum: Noemam eius sororem esse Venerem illam Ethnicorum veterem: & vtrumq; ex Iouis illius, id est, Caini stirpe, & prosapia natum. Reliquat igitur, vt quemadmodum Iabal, & Iubal dicuntur ex Caini genere, & nepotes (quorum ille pastoritiam artem & commercia auxit: hic vero Musicam inuenit) sic idem isti censeantur esse Iabal quidem antiquissimus Ethnicorum Mercurius. Iubal autem Apollo, qui omnes itidem Iouis illius primi feruntur esse filij & geniti. De quibus Lactantius lib. 4: cap. 27. Hos enim omnes nefarios fuisse docet idem scriptor, & inferis. Quos vero Iouis filios Higinus in fabul. cap. 155 recenset: y sunt Iouis Graeci & iunioris liberi, non antiqui. Denique conferantur cum his omnibus Caini posteris Aegyptiorum Thanut, Osiris, Isis, Mercurius, de quibus & Diodorus Siculus lib. 1. & Eusebius lib. 1. cap. vltimo, & lib. 2. Praeparat. Euangelica, multa nostra veritatis testimonia, vestigiaq; certissima adhuc supererunt, atque apparebunt.
units.tr: The Greek poets were the source of this idea. But the same Gentile writers also hold that the first cities were founded by men out of fear. Plato, in the Protagoras, says: "In this way, as I say, men, once created and equipped, lived dispersed and scattered in various places, and cities did not yet exist. So wild beasts, which were stronger than they were, attacked them everywhere and destroyed them. To guard against these dangers they sought remedies and means of safety: they gathered together into one place and founded cities to receive their assemblies." Diodorus Siculus writes in the same way in book 1, chapter 1: "Wild beasts, dangerous to men, were a threat, and to resist them, the aim of common advantage led men to form assemblies out of fear; they gave each other mutual help and sought out places to live." From this it came about that towns were surrounded for firmer protection with walls, a rampart and a ditch, as Plutarch teaches in the life of Romulus, the first king of the Romans. Nor does it count against this that Plato, in book 2 of the Republic, maintains that cities and towns were first founded for use, and for the mutual advantage and need that men have of one another. For this very point confirms our view. Men need mutual aid to defend themselves, since they fear both wild beasts and other men. Finally, Moses indeed holds that the first city that existed in the world was Enochia, called in the East; and there are traces of this truth in the writings of the Gentiles. First, Pliny in book 6, chapter 16, places the Henochians near Bactra in the East. For I think that in Pliny we should read "Henochii" for "Heniochys." And in the same book, chapter 20, he places the Nodumbae peoples in East India. These names agree exactly with the Mosaic ones, Enoch and Nod. For, as Plato says, we ought to be well pleased, and it should be enough, if some remnants of such ancient and almost wholly obliterated antiquity survive in the names of old regions, places and peoples, as happens here. Next, Pliny and Pomponius Mela distinguish the Heniochian peoples from the Henochians or Henochys. For Mela, in book 1, chapter 22 of the Description of the World, places the Heniochys on this side of the Caspian Sea, neighbours of the Colchians and Alani, just as Valerius Flaccus does in book 6 of the Argonautica; some write them as Heniochians, while Valerius himself, and others with an oe, write Oenochians, as in Lucan, book 3 of the Pharsalia. Pliny consistently calls them Heniochians, in book 6, chapters 4 and 11, and, as I said, places them around Mount Caucasus on this side of the Caspian Sea, and says they extended widely through many nations. Strabo says the same in book 2 and book 11 of his Geography, and Xenophon before all of them in his book on the Expedition of Cyrus. Finally, Dionysius of Alexandria, in his description of the world, writes that these very Heniochians were descended from the Greeks, and especially the Lacedaemonians (namely from the charioteers of Castor and Pollux), and that this is why they were so called. But I am rather inclined to believe that they were descended from the posterity of Abraham and from Keturah's sons, as are the Medes, neighbouring peoples to them, as the passage in Genesis 25:3 and 4 proves. These, then, are the Heniochians, namely near the Euxine Sea and on this side of the Caspian. But the Henochians, or Henoche (as Pomponius Mela calls them, book 1, chapter 2), are in the farther East beyond the Caspian Sea, as appears from that same passage of Mela and from Pliny, book 6, chapter 16, as I have already shown. Who could doubt that these Henochians are the most true and most ancient remnants of that first and most ancient city, Enoch or Enochia (as Josephus also writes in book 1, chapter 4 of the Jewish Antiquities, and Augustine in book 15, chapter 8 of the City of God), and, as it were, tablets salvaged from the most famous wreck of memory and of the world's lands, which by God's supreme kindness survive to us, even in the writings of the Gentiles, to establish our faith in so great an antiquity? So Stephanus, in his book on cities, is right in holding that Heniochia is the city that Strabo discusses in book 11, the metropolis of the Heniochians. But that Heniochia of Stephanus and Strabo must not be confused with this Enochia or Enocha of ours (from which the Enochians or Enoch peoples, clearly Eastern and Indian, were named). Some think that this city of ours lay in that region of the East where the city now called Cambalu is, and in Eastern Scythia or Tartary. And indeed traces of this our truth persist even among the Gentiles. Moreover, they are foolish who set up some other city as the first of all: the Phoenicians their Byblos, as Eusebius says in book 1, chapter 7 of the Preparation for the Gospel; the Athenians and Greeks Cecropia (Pliny, book 7, chapter 56); the Latins Saturnia and the Janiculum (Virgil, book 8 of the Aeneid); the Peloponnesians Argos; the Assyrians Nineveh; the Chaldeans Babylon; the Egyptians their Thebes. For these are far more recent than our Enochia, and were built only after the flood; moreover, they were not the first of all, but were founded first among those peoples whose metropolises they are, whereas we are discussing the one that was first of all. And so far on this matter. The remaining chapters of this history were partly explained above, when we dealt with the invention of the first arts, and partly can easily be inferred from what we have demonstrated, such as who the posterity of Cain were, what that family's line of descent was, and what traces of the whole of this history survive among the Gentiles. For we have shown, to repeat it briefly, that Adam is that most ancient Saturn of the Gentiles; that Cain is Moses' Jupiter, the same god; that Tubalcain, the inventor of the art of bronze and iron working, is Vulcan; that Naamah, his sister, is that old Venus of the Gentiles; and that both were born of the stock and lineage of that Jupiter, that is, of Cain. It remains, then, that just as Jabal and Jubal are said to be of Cain's kin, grandsons (of whom the one increased the art of herding and trade, and the other invented music), so these same men should be counted as follows: Jabal is indeed the most ancient Mercury of the Gentiles, and Jubal Apollo, both of whom are likewise said to be sons and offspring of that first Jupiter. Lactantius teaches of them in book 4, chapter 27, that all of them were wicked, as the same writer shows, and below. But the sons of Jupiter whom Hyginus lists in his Fables, chapter 155, are the sons of the Greek and younger Jupiter, not the ancient ones. Finally, let the Egyptian Thoth, Osiris, Isis and Mercury be compared with all these posterity of Cain; of these Diodorus Siculus speaks in book 1, and Eusebius in book 1, last chapter, and in book 2 of the Preparation for the Gospel. Many testimonies to our truth, and most certain traces, will still survive and will appear.

units.la: CAPVT IIII.
units.tr: CAPUT IIII.

units.la: Quæ Politia tum Ciuilis, tum Ecclesia- stica toto illo seculo & tempore (quod 235. annos à Mundo condito complectitur) extiterit inter homines.
units.tr: What polity, both civil and ecclesiastical, existed among men throughout that whole age (which spans 235 years from the creation of the world).

units.la: EQVITVR autem dicere quæ fuerit toto illo seculo Politia tum Ciuilis, tum etiam Ecclesiastica. Seculum autem hoc Tempus à primo lapsu Adami ad publicā Nominis Dei profanationem complectitur, quod pene habet annos ducentos triginta quinque, dempto nimirū ex eo numero dierum tanto spatio, quanto purus idem Adamus permásit. Hi vero siue vnus dies fuerit post illius creationem, siue plures (est enim incertū, & verbo Dei indefinitum) hi tollendi sunt. Sed tam parua portio numerorum illū annorum rotundum imminuere neq; debet, neque potest. Porrò Ciuilis Politia illius ætatis in his quatuor potissimū posita est, ac quarenda, Quis fuerit illo tempore Magistratus: Quæ forma Reipub. Quæ leges: Quæ hominū instituta, & mores. Ac quidem communis Magistratus & rex (qui omnibus imperaret) nullus ea aetate creabatur: sed (quemadmodum & ipse pudor naturalis a Deo insitus monebat, & Dei verbum declarat Gen.4. 7) maiores natu minoribus in eadem familia imperabant, eosque sibi subiectos habebant, ac retinebat, velut Adamus Cainum & Abelem, quamdiu Cainus cum patre Adamo vixit: imo vero etiam Abel Caino fratri maiori natu subiectus erat, in eadem familia manens. Postquam autem discessit Cainus a familia Adami, ipse posteris suis magistratum erat: & inter ipsos Caini posteros maior natu minori, quandiu in eadem familia, atque sub eodem tecto, & autore generis sui manebant. Ubi vero ab eo separabatur, & familiam seorsum sibi constituebant eiusdem patris liberi, tunc ipsi in suos Magistratus erant, quisque nimirum in illa familia, cuius ipse erat autor & caput. Nemo autem unus Rex, aut Dominus censebatur, uti dixi, omnium (quae tunc in Mundo, aut in eadem Orbis Regione erant) familiarum. Itaque nulla tunc erant inter mortales regna, id est, nulla imperia in plures, distinctas, diversasque familias: nulla totius Orbis Monarchia, quemadmodum postea tamen, id est, post diluvium, extiterunt. Id quod ex Dei verbo facile colligi poterit, ubi nulla fit omnino Regum, aut Principum, aut Imperatorum similiumque inter homines potestatum mentio, licet post diluvium earum Mises meminerit, velut Nebroti, Melchisedechi, Pharaonis. Idem confirmatur autoritate Platonis in Politico, Aristotelis lib. 1. Politicorum, Iustini lib. 1. Historia, Diodori Siculi lib. 1 cap. 1. Itaque, ait idem, qui primi in Orbe terrarum reges fuerint, incertum est. Ex quo apparet in primo-
units.tr: IT remains to say what the polity, both civil and ecclesiastical, was throughout that whole age. This age covers the time from Adam's first fall to the public profanation of the name of God, and it is about two hundred and thirty-five years long, minus, of course, the number of days that Adam himself survived. Whether that was one day after his creation or more (it is uncertain, and left undefined in God's Word), those days must be set aside. Yet so small a fraction of the years cannot and should not be counted to alter the round total. In that age, civil polity rested mainly on four points, which we must investigate: who the magistrate was at that time; what the form of the commonwealth was; what the laws were; and what the human customs and morals were. Now, a common magistrate or king, ruling over everyone, was not appointed in that age. Rather (as natural shame implanted by God itself advised, and as the Word of God declares, Gen. 4. 7), elders ruled over younger men within the same family, and held them under their authority, as Adam did with Cain and Abel while Cain lived with his father Adam. Indeed, Abel too was subject to his elder brother Cain while he remained in the same family. But after Cain departed from the family of Adam, he became magistrate over his own descendants; and among Cain's descendants the elder ruled the younger as long as they remained in the same family, under the same roof, and under the author of their stock. When, however, the children of one father separated from him and set up their own households apart, then each of them became a magistrate over his own family, of which he was the author and head. No one, as I have said, was regarded as a single king or lord over all the families (whatever there was in the world, or in the same region of the earth). Therefore there were then no kingdoms among mortals, that is, no empires spread over several distinct and different families; there was no monarchy of the whole world, such as came into being afterwards, that is, after the flood. This can easily be gathered from God's Word, where there is no mention at all of kings, princes, emperors, or similar powers among men, although after the flood Moses does mention such powers, as those of Nimrod, Melchizedek, and Pharaoh. The same is confirmed by the authority of Plato in the Politicus, of Aristotle in the first book of the Politics, of Justin in the first book of his History, and of Diodorus Siculus in the first book, chapter 1. Thus, as the same writer says, it is uncertain who were the first kings on the earth. From this it appears that among the first-born...

units.la: genitis... genitura iam inde à Mundi exordio, & maximè post lapsum Hominis à Deo ipso saltem in eo constitutum, fuisse, ut minores natu maioribus in eadem familia parerēt: omnes autem ipsius familiæ autori & capiti. Vrbes habebāt, quas incolebant, & in quibus hoc modo regebantur per familias singulas. Nec enim unus in omnes inspectionem habebat: sed unusquisque, in suam dūtaxat, non in alienam familiam. Ex quo apparet ecquā tunc fuerit Rẹipub. forma, non Regia, si proprie spectetur: non Aristocratica, neque enim plures, sed unus maior natu alijs imperabat: nō Democratica, neque enim tota familia velut populus tenebat ius. Quid igitur? Erat duntaxat Paternum in liberos imperium, quod (vt ait Aristoteles lib. 1. Politic. & lib. 8. Ethic. ad Nicomachum) est regio minus: Proximè tamen accedit ad regium, id est, in liberos homines est imperium, non est tamen verè Regium. Pudore enim potius, quàm metu: voluntate, quam vi: spontanea obedientia, quàm poenis, carcere, & coactione in inuitum illud paternum imperium continetur. Ergo pene parebat unusquisque tantùm, quantum volebat, & cui volebat. Nulla vis, nulla coactio, nulla manus militaris, nulla poena adhibebatur, quà parere alijs alij cogerentur, aut etiam recte viuere: nulli carceres erant: nulla vincula legum incisarum, & promulgatarum, quibus homines in officio, & rationis gyro inuiti continerentur: sed tunc libera erat (exceptâ naturali verecundiâ) parendi, aut non parēdi voluntas. Primum autem imperium minis plenum, sœuum, & tyrannicum natum est in familia Lemechi ab ipso Lemecho in mulieres, id est, in suas coniuges, à quibus sibi timebat ille propter Polygamiâ, vt apparet, Gen. 4. 23: antea verò nullum etiam in fœminas eiusmodi erat, nec etiam erat in mares. Denique, ecquæ leges tunc fuerint, ex superioribus quoque apparet. Nulla enim erat tunc Leges scripta, & edictis pœnisque sancita. Reliquæ tamen erant boni, malique notitia, ex prima natiua luce (quam Deus hominis mëti inseruerat) superstites. Hæ erant voces, & testimonia conscientiæ nondum omnino depravatæ, vel diuturna consuetudine peccandi, vel opinione hominum, quemadmodum postea fuit, & nunc est. Has lucis primeuæ scintillas nondum obsoletas, & communes boni, malique irvoiaς homines illo seculo sequebantur, his regebantur velut publicis legibus: quibus tamen neque semper parebant, neque eas etiâ tunc retinuerunt illibatas. Verum quantu, & quandiu volebant, iis velut legibus mutis obsequebantur. Ergo paulatim posteri Caini primùm, post etiam reliqui mortales eas ipsas leges ac scintillas, conscientiæque notitias licentia effreni peccandi, perque magnam iniustitiam suppresserunt, ac tandem penitus deleuerunt, vt nullo prorsus modo sonarent in mente hominum, sed plane coticescerent. Itaque illud euenit, quod ait D. Paulus Rom. 1. 18, & 32. nimirum vt homines veritatem Dei iniustè detinerent, occultarent, ac tandem in se extinguerent. Denique hæc ipsa docent, Quales tunc fuerint mores hominum, imprimisque posterorum Caini, qui soli (Abele sublato) in Mundo reliquerant, qualiaque eorum instituta, & facta. Primùm, quòd Nemo vnus pro summo imperio in omnes iniectionem & coercitionem haberet, sed singuli auctorum solum in singulas suas, vti diximus, familias, fiebat, vt quamuis in urbibus habitarent, nemo tamen in illis urbibus unum esset eorum omnium Magistratum communis, ad quem recurrerêt, qui cæteros ad officium faciendum cogeret, maleficia publicè punirêt: sed quisque sua tantum familia autorem spectabat, & sequebatur, ad eū offensus confugiebat, vti nunc etiam liberi lasi ad parentes, servi ad dominos suos solum refugiunt, vt est Psal. 123: & res ipsa id verum esse declarat. Deinde accidebat, vt mleficiorū nulla esset publica animaduersio, & pœna, quæ ab hominibus velut Magistratibus infligeretur, tam dissoluta fuit illius sæculi disciplina, & forma vivendi. Propter enim lenes in suam familiam affectus facilè suis peccantibus parentes parcebant. Sic manebant inulta scelera. Sic neque Adamus ex nimia lenitate Cainum filium propter fratricidium puniuit vlla publica pœna: sed Deus solus eum castigauit: neque Cainus ipse in Lemechu, qui erat ex sua familia propter violatum coniugium & veram fornicationem pœnā vllam statuit. Denique factum est, vt esset effrenis hominum vita, sæua, voluptaria, lasciua, licentiàque in peccando immanis tum in Deum, cuius reuerentiam & numen paulatim continere homines cœperunt: tum etiā in homines seu proximos suos, in quos iniurij esse ausi sunt, & ad omne genus flagitij licentiosè dediti, & proclines extiterunt. Interea tamen fuit valde ingeniosa, & industria Caini posteritas, quamquam improba. Nam & Pastoritiam, & Agriculturam artem, & Musicā, & Aerariam, & Ferrariam, & Urbiū exstructionem reperit. Imo verò propter tanta Dei in se dona insolēs, & Dei contemptrix euasit. Cæterum antequam urbes conderentur, homines in pagis & vicis simul habitabat. Quod autem quarunt nonnulli, utrum Cainus expulerit Adamum patrem, ut Iupiter Saturnu iam senem, ex Dei verbo definiri non potest. Et hac quidem de Ci-
units.tr: ...firstborn, from the very beginning of the world, and especially after man's fall, it was established by God himself, at least in this, that the younger sons obeyed the elder within the same family, while all of them were subject to the author and head of that family. They had cities, which they inhabited, and in these they were governed in this way, family by family. For no single person had oversight over all, but each only over his own family, not over another's. From this it appears what the form of the commonwealth was then, if it is properly considered: it was not royal, for there was no single king; nor aristocratic, for not several but one elder ruled over the others; nor democratic, for the whole family did not hold the right as a people would. What then? There was only paternal rule over the children, which (as Aristotle says in the first book of the Politics and the eighth book of the Ethics to Nicomachus) is a kind of kingship, though a lesser one. It comes closest to royal rule, that is, it is rule over free men, yet it is not truly royal. For that paternal rule is held together by shame rather than fear, by will rather than force, by voluntary obedience rather than by punishments, prisons, and compulsion against an unwilling party. Therefore each person obeyed almost only as much as he wished, and whomever he wished. No force, no compulsion, no armed hand, and no punishment was employed by which some were compelled to obey others or even to live rightly. There were no prisons; there were no chains of laws carved and published, by which men were held in duty and in the course of reason against their will. Rather, the will to obey or not to obey was free then (apart from natural modesty). But the first rule full of threats, savage and tyrannical, arose in the family of Lamech, from Lamech himself against women, that is, against his own wives, of whom he was afraid because of his polygamy, as appears from Gen. 4. 23; before that there was no such rule over women, nor indeed over men. Finally, what laws there were then also appears from what has been said above. For there was then no written law, sanctioned by edicts and penalties. Nevertheless, there remained the knowledge of good and evil, surviving from the original natural light (which God had implanted in the mind of man). These were the voices and witnesses of a conscience not yet wholly corrupted, either by long habit of sinning or by the opinion of men, as it later became and as it is now. These first sparks of light, not yet worn away, and these common notions [ἐννοίας] of good and evil, men of that age followed; they were governed by them as by public laws, though they did not always obey them, nor did they keep them unimpaired even then. Yet as far and as long as they wished, they obeyed them as if they were unwritten laws. Therefore, gradually, first the descendants of Cain, and afterwards the rest of mortals, through unbridled licence in sinning and through great injustice, suppressed those very laws and sparks, and the knowledge of conscience, and at last utterly destroyed them, so that they no longer sounded at all in the minds of men, but became completely silent. And so there happened what St. Paul says in Rom. 1. 18 and 32, namely, that men unjustly held down, hid, and at last extinguished in themselves the truth of God. Finally, these very things show what the customs of men were then, especially those of the descendants of Cain, who alone remained in the world (Abel having been slain), and what their institutions and deeds were. First, no one held supreme power over everyone for the purpose of imposing restraint and coercion; rather, each man was an author only over his own family, as we have said. So although they lived in cities, no one in those cities was a common magistrate of them all to whom they could appeal, who could compel the rest to do their duty and publicly punish wrongdoing. Each person looked only to the author of his own family and followed him; when wronged, he fled to him alone, just as now children flee only to their parents when harmed, and servants only to their masters, as in Ps. 123, and the matter itself declares this to be true. Next, it followed that there was no public punishment of wrongdoers, inflicted by men as magistrates; so lax was the discipline and form of living of that age. For, because of their affections being too indulgent toward their own families, parents easily spared their sinning children. Thus crimes went unpunished. Thus Adam, from excessive leniency, did not punish his son Cain for fratricide with any public penalty; God alone chastised him. Nor did Cain himself impose any penalty on Lamech, who was of his own family, for violating marriage and for his true fornication. Finally, it came about that human life was unbridled, cruel, voluptuous, wanton, and that licence in sinning was monstrous, both against God, whose reverence and divine power men gradually began to restrain, and also against men or their neighbours, against whom they dared to act unjustly; and they were given over to every kind of shameful deed without restraint and were inclined to it. Meanwhile, the posterity of Cain was very clever and industrious, though wicked. For they discovered the arts of herding and of agriculture, of music, of working bronze and iron, and of building cities. Indeed, they grew haughty and despisers of God because of such great gifts of God bestowed upon them. Moreover, before cities were founded, men lived together in villages and hamlets. As for the question some ask, whether Cain drove out his father Adam, as Jupiter drove out Saturn when already old, that cannot be determined from God's Word. And these things, concerning the civil polity of that age, are enough; now let us look at the ecclesiastical.

units.la: vili Politia illius seculi: iam de Ecclesiastica videamus. Illa autem ex his quinque spectanda est, nempe Quod Dei verbum in Dei Ecclesia tunc sonabat, & prædicabatur: Quis cultus Dei externus: Quis Minister: Vbi erat & colligebatur Ecclesia, siue Quis locus externo Dei cultui assignatus, ac consecratus erat: Denique ecquod tempus à Deo definitum erat externo ipsius cultui peragendo, ac celebrando. Ac quidem verbum Dei, quod tunc sonabat in Ecclesia Dei, nō fuit quidem scriptum, erat tamen ore Dei emissum, ab eo ipso traditum Adamo, & pronuntiatum, uti postea idem Deus eodem ore suo Legem in monte Horebo pronuntiauit, Exo. 20
units.tr: On the civil polity of that age, let us now see the ecclesiastical. That is to be viewed under five heads: what the Word of God was then sounding and being preached in the Church of God; what external worship of God there was; who the minister was; where the Church was assembled and gathered, or what place was assigned and consecrated to God's external worship; and finally what time God had appointed for performing and celebrating his external worship. The Word of God that then sounded in the Church of God was indeed not written down, yet it was uttered from God's own mouth, delivered by him to Adam and proclaimed, just as afterwards the same God with the same mouth proclaimed the Law on Mount Horeb, Exod. 20.

units.la: Continebat autem illud Verbum Minas Dei in peccatum, & Promissionem de futuro Messia & Redemptore mundi, qui nasciturus erat ex femine solius Mulieris, non autem Viri, & qui caput Serpentis seu Diaboli erat contriturus, einsq; vires fracturus, Gen. 3. 15
units.tr: That Word contained God's threats against sin and the promise of the future Messiah and Redeemer of the world, who was to be born of the seed of the woman alone, not of a man, and who was to crush the head of the Serpent or Devil and break his power, Gen. 3:15.

units.la: Hoc verbū atque hanc promissionem fide amplexus est Abel, ut est Hebr. 11. 3: atque postea Enoch, vers. 4. Vnde vterq; propterea Deo placuit, & Abelis sanguis Deo pretiosus fuit, & præstantia coram eo loquebatur Hebr. 12. 24. Hoc idem Verbum Dei & firmissime memoria ad suam cosolationem retinebat Adamus, & toti familiæ suæ sæpè inculcabat, uti & Minas Dei in peccatum, ut eam doceret viam salutis aeterne, utque in eam doctrinā posteri futuriq; h m nes crederent certissime. tissimè. Et hac de Verbo Dei, & fide, qua tunc erat. Nondum enim sciebat Adamus ex qua distinctè familia nasciturus erat ille Messias, quem tamen sperabat, quemadmodum postea distinctius id ipsum cognovit Abrahamus, postquam illi à Deo dictum est, [In semine tuo benedicentur omnes Gentes, Gen. 17.] Et magis adhuc perspicuè cognovit David, nempe ex qua domo, & ex sua oriturum esse Messiam, postquam illi patefecit Deus, Psal. 132.11 [De fructu ventris tui ponam super sedem tuam.] Ergo per tempora magis inclaruit hac Dei promissio & fides. Externum verò Dei cultus tunc positus erat in precibus ad Deum, & Sacrificiis, quæ eadem erant Sacramenta quoque. Ac homines direxisse preces suas ad Deum natura ipsa conscientiaque probat, quod omnes homines id facere docet: & quòd Sacrificia absque precibus ad Deum sint res muta, & inanes, vt etiam inquit Plato. Sacrificia verò, quæ Deo tunc offerebantur, erant partim incruenta, velut ex frugibus terræ: partim cruenta, sicut victima, quæ in repræsentationem passuri pro genere humano Messiæ seu Christi macta-bantur, & Deo ex fide à pijs offerebatur. Quare oportuit tunc quoque esse Aram seu Altare, in quo cremaretur victima: & sacerdotem, qui eam offerret Deo: & Preces pro peccatis eius, qui offerret, delendis ad Deum concipi, ne hæc sacrificia essent inanè spectaculū, & mutum theatrum. Porrò eadem hæc sacrificia erat quoque Sacramenta: nam & ijs (quum erant Eucharistica) epulabantur homines, quemadmodum postea sub Lege, Leuit. 3. factum est (nec enim omnia sacrificia erant expiatoria, & ἱλασμα.) Epulum autem illud sacrum erat sacramentum & signum donorum & gratiarum spiritualium,& salutarium(velut alimonia cœlestis animarum) quas sese à Deo propter Messiam habere homines pij fatebantur. Et quæ ante Legem fuerunt Patribus sacrificia, illa quoq; fuerunt eisdem sacramenta, & salutis æterna, & remissionis peccatorum pignora,& significationes. Caterùm, Minister huius externi ritus & cultus diuini,id est,à Deo ipso sibi instituti,quis fuerit,queritur. Respondeti vero breuiter potest, In singulis familijs quemq; maximum natu fuisse cultus istius externi ac diuini Ministrum,& sacerdotem. Itaque Adamus fuit sacerdos & Minister primus in mundo: post eum maiores natu in ijs familijs, in quibus Dei metus,cultúsque retetum fuit,vt Sethus in sua familia.In summa ex pluribus fratribus semper Primogeniti erant sacerdotes, mortuis patribus,quandiu illi in eadem familia manebant. Fuit enim & hoc ipsum Ius primogenitura nempe Sacrificare Deo,quèadmodum & regere familiam,illiq; imperare, vti ex cap.19.22.& 24 Exod.& Num.8.16,& 17 facile colligitur. Nam in singulis familijs fuerunt sacrificatores,antequam Leuita,& Aaronita ad id munus à Deo deligerentur. Quod ipsum doctè Cornelius Bertramus obseruauit in libro de Politia Iud. cap. 2, & ante eum Hieronymus Epistola ad Euagrium,Tomo 3.Epistol. Non erat igitur tunc vnus duntaxat summus Sacerdos in Ecclesia,vt postea fuit post constitutam nimirum in Horebo monte Ecclesiam:sed plures erat,nempe singuli in singulis,ijsque diuersis familijs,vbi verus Deus colebatur. Quod verò Cainus,& Abel in Adami familia manentes adhuc, dicuntur tamen sacrificasse. sic intelligendum est, quod ad Patrem Adamum sua sacrificia Deo offerenda adduxerint ipsi. Adamus autem eas obtulit Deo, vtpote illius familiae sacerdos: id quod verbi Hebraici proprietas, quo vtitur Moses, [Adduxit] declarat. Porro post quam a facie Dei, & consortio Adami patris, coëunque Ecclesia fuit a Deo ipso eiectus Cain, ut propter suum fratricidium, neque ipse legitur Deo sacrificasse: neque ex eius posteris vlli. Fuerunt enim illi impii, & contemptores nominis diuini. In sola igitur Adams familia, vbi Sethus vixit, mansit & Sacerdotium, & Dei cultus, ac invocatio, quam retinuit postea Sethus. Locus autem, in quem Ecclesia publice ad preces & sacrificia conueniebat, fuit is, in quo Altare sacrificijs destinatum exstructum erat. Qui locus [Facies Iehova] dictus est, Gen. 4. 16. Sic Iosua 24. 1 Facies Dei vocatur, vbi erat Arca foederis, & Deo sacrificabatur. Sic Iona 2. 5. Sic Psal. 84. Sic passim alibi in S. Scriptura. Fuit autem is locus & Altare vel in tentorio & adibus Adami, & Primogenitorum: vel in loco aliquo illis vicino, ad quem vicini omnes, totaque familia congregabantur. Et tot Altaria fuerunt, quot diuersa familiae, in quibus verus Deus colebatur, quae ob locorum distantiam simul conuenire non poterant. Non fuit autem vnicum duntaxat Altare in orbe terrarum, velut sub Lege: nec vnicus locus vel Templum in toto terrarum Orbe, in quod omnes pij simul conuenirent, sed loca plurima. Tempus denique, quo ad preces & sacrificia in ea loca publice conueniebant, singula Ecclesiae Dei per suas familias, fuit Septimus cuiusque Septimana dies.
units.tr: Abel embraced this word and this promise by faith, as Heb. 11:3 says, and afterwards Enoch, ver. 4. Hence both of them pleased God, and Abel's blood was precious to him, and the sprinkled blood spoke better things before him, Heb. 12:24. Adam too kept this same Word of God most firmly in memory for his own consolation, and often impressed it on his whole family, as also the threat of God against sin, so that he might teach them the way of eternal salvation, and that posterity and future generations might most certainly believe in that teaching. This is what may be said of the Word of God and of the faith that existed then. For Adam did not yet know clearly from which family that Messiah, whom he nevertheless hoped for, was to be born; this he later came to know more distinctly, as Abraham did after God had said to him, [In your seed all the nations shall be blessed, Gen. 17]. David knew even more clearly that the Messiah would come from his own house and line, after God had revealed it to him, Psal. 132:11 [I will set upon your throne the fruit of your body]. So this promise and faith of God grew more famous with the passing of the ages. The external worship of God at that time consisted of prayers to God and of sacrifices, which were also the sacraments. That men directed their prayers to God is proved by nature itself and by conscience, which teaches that all men do this; and sacrifices without prayers to God are dumb and empty things, as Plato also says. The sacrifices then offered to God were partly bloodless, such as those of the fruits of the earth, and partly bloody, such as the victims slaughtered to represent the Messiah, or Christ, who was to suffer for the human race, and were offered to God by the godly in faith. Therefore there had to be then also an altar or hearth on which the victim was burned, and a priest who would offer it to God, and prayers to God for the expiation of the sins of him who offered, lest these sacrifices be an empty spectacle and a dumb show. Moreover these same sacrifices were also sacraments; for men feasted on them (since they were eucharistic), as was later done under the Law, Lev. 3 (for not all sacrifices were expiatory, [hilasmos]). That sacred feast was a sacrament and sign of the spiritual and saving gifts and graces (like heavenly nourishment of souls) which godly men confessed they had from God on account of the Messiah. And the sacrifices which the Fathers had before the Law were also sacraments for them, and pledges and signs of eternal salvation and remission of sins. Next, it is asked who was the minister of this external rite and divine worship, that is, one instituted by God himself. A brief answer can be given: in each family the eldest was the minister and priest of this external and divine worship. Thus Adam was the first priest and minister in the world; after him the eldest in those families in which the fear and worship of God was preserved, as Seth in his family. In sum, from several brothers the firstborn were always the priests, once the fathers had died, for as long as they remained in the same family. For this very right of primogeniture included offering sacrifice to God, just as it included ruling the family and commanding it, as is readily gathered from Exod. 19:22, 24, and Num. 8:16, 17. For in each family there were sacrificers before the Levites and Aaronites were chosen by God for that office. Cornelius Bertram observed this learnedly in his book on the Jewish polity, ch. 2, and before him Jerome in his letter to Evagrius, Tome 3 of the Epistles. There was therefore not then one single high priest in the Church, as there was afterwards when the Church was established on Mount Horeb, but many: each man in his own household, in those different families where the true God was worshipped. As for Cain and Abel, although they are said to have sacrificed while still remaining in Adam's family, this must be understood as meaning that they brought their sacrifices to be offered to God to their father Adam. Adam then offered them to God as priest of that family; the peculiar force of the Hebrew word that Moses uses, [Adduxit, he brought], makes this clear. Furthermore, after Cain had been cast out by God himself from the face of God and from the fellowship of his father Adam and the assembled Church, because of his fratricide, he is not read of as having sacrificed to God, nor does any of his posterity. For they were ungodly and despisers of the divine name. Thus the priesthood, the worship and invocation of God, which Seth afterwards retained, remained in the family of Adam alone, where Seth lived. The place to which the Church came together publicly for prayers and sacrifices was that in which an altar set apart for sacrifices had been built. That place was called [the face of Jehovah], Gen. 4:16. So in Josh. 24:1 it is called the face of God, where the Ark of the covenant was and sacrifice was offered to God. So in Jonah 2:5, so in Psal. 84, and so elsewhere throughout Holy Scripture. This place and altar was either in the tent and dwelling of Adam and of the firstborn, or in some place near them, to which all the neighbours and the whole family gathered. And there were as many altars as there were distinct families in which the true God was worshipped, which could not come together at the same place because of the distance between them. There was not, as under the Law, a single altar in the whole world, nor a single place or temple in the whole world to which all the godly would assemble at once, but many places. Lastly, the time at which the Church of God in its families came together publicly in those places for prayers and sacrifices was the seventh day of each week.
