Enos, however, is interpreted as 'man' in such a way that those skilled in that language affirm a woman cannot be called by this name, as 'a son of resurrection' (for Seth means resurrection), where people neither marry nor take wives. So I think it is not idle to note also that in those generations which descend from him who is called Seth, though it is said that he begot sons and daughters, no daughter born there is named by name. But in those descended from Cain, at the very end, where the line is extended, the last-born woman is named, so that it may be understood that the earthly city, whose founder was Cain, has an earthly beginning and end. For its root, of course, is named Eve. The earthly city, however, which is represented in Seth, neither begets nor is begotten in the flesh; for there will be no carnal generation there, since regeneration will have led us there." Thus far Augustine. These things are certainly rather subtle, but altogether untrue. For women, or wives, are also called by the Hebrews [Nasschim], as if [Enasschim], from the same theme, from which also comes the word [Enosch]. So Augustine's observation is weak and unsound. The learned man, very skilled in Hebrew letters, John Mercer, once royal professor at Paris, taught this more accurately: the name [Adam] refers to his formation from the earth, but [Enosch] refers to a weak, feeble, troubled condition, full of toil and danger, into which man afterwards fell and lapsed through sin. Hence the word carries the sense of great weakness, which pertains to men and women alike, indeed to all nations and to the human condition, as in Psalm 9:12: ["Let the nations know," says David, "that Enosch, that is, they are men."] These are most true. Some think the word Enosch is so called because men are quickly brought to oblivion. So Eusebius, in book 2 of the Preparation for the Gospel, chapter 4, although in book 7, chapter 3, of the same work he holds that [Enos], which is the same as Enosch, signifies what the word [Homo] signifies, namely a mortal and weak condition. Others think Enosch is derived from the Hebrew root that means "to despair," so that Enosch for them is desperate and violent. So Philo in his book on Hebrew names in Genesis. But these views are unsteady. From this it appears how great was the difference between Cain and Seth in naming their firstborn. For Cain, a hypocrite and wicked man, even after he had been driven from the face of God and cast out of the Church of God, named his firstborn [Hanoch], that is, learned, well instructed and well mannered. But Seth, a pious and good man, called his firstborn [Enosch], that is, mortal and wretched. Thus hypocrites almost always aim at and pursue showy things, so that they may seem true believers to men, while true believers judge things by truth so that they may serve God. Q. Whether Enosch was the firstborn of Seth, since he is said to have been born only in the 105th year of Seth's life; others, however, say that Seth's descendants had their children earlier, as Enosch himself had a son at the age of 90, Kenan; and Kenan had Mahalalel at 70, and Mahalalel had Jared at 65.

units.la: R. Qua ratione Cainum colligimus ex Mose fuisse primogenitum Adami, quia primus refertur ex eo natus, Gen.4 1.7 eādem & Enoschum hunc esse primogenitum Sethi dixerimus, Gen.4.26. Sicq; omnes sentiunt, maximeq; Iosephus lib.1. Antiquit. Iudaic.cap. 5. & Philo in Antiquit Biblicis. Quanquam tamen alibi Moses primo loco recenset postea natos, non primogenitos, velut Schemu inter liberos Noachi, Gen.5. 32, & 6.10, qui post Iephethum tamen natus est ex Noacho. Porro tradit Moses Sethum post Enosch genuisse filios, & filias Gen.5.7. & ex eo Iosephus lib.1. Antiquit.cap.5. Verum Philo in Antiquit.Biblic. & numerum, & nomina & filiorum, & filiarum Sethi addit (si quis fortassis exististmet id eum scire, etiam tacente Mose, potuisse, uti Paulus expressit nomina Magorum Pharaonis, qui Mosi ipsi restiterunt, nempe 2. Tim 3.8.) Ait enim eum Enosch postea suscepisse filios tres, & tres filias. Filiorum autem nomina hæc fuisse, Elidia, Phonna, & Matha: Filiarū verò hæc, Malida, & Thita, vbi proculdubio nomen vnius deest, estque locus ille mancus, vel non omnium nomina filiarum sciuit Philo. Q. Virum Sethus ipse pater Enoschi sit susceptus ex Eua primus ab Adamo post eius e Paradiso eiectionem, quia quum de Sethi procreatione ageret Moses, addidit, [Genuit filium Adam in imagine sua Gen. 5. 3] Alij autem priores Adami filij, velut Cainus, & Abel fuerint ex eo nati in Paradiso ipso, quia de iis nihil simile scripsit Moses, vt de Setho, tanquam illi ad veram ipsius Dei, non tantùm Adami patris imaginem nati sint, videlicet nondum per peccatum corrupta in Adamo imagine Dei. R. Quum post eiectionem Adami è Paradiso terrestri commemoret Moses Cainum, & Abelem ex eo natos, Gen. 4:dubium non est, quin ille vterq; neque in Paradiso conceptus sit, vt nonnulli tamen putant, neque etiam natus: sed extra Paradisum. Secutus enim est Moses in hac Historia sacra cōtexenda rationem, atq; seriem temporis. Q nid autem hac verba [Genuit Adam ad imaginem sui Sethum] notent, & cur addita fuerint, est à nobis antea explicatum.
units.tr: A. By the same reasoning by which we conclude from Moses that Cain was the firstborn of Adam, because he is first mentioned as born of him (Gen. 4:1, 7), we may say that this Enosch was the firstborn of Seth (Gen. 4:26). And so all agree, especially Josephus in book 1, chapter 5, of the Jewish Antiquities, and Philo in the Biblical Antiquities. Yet elsewhere Moses lists in the first place those born afterwards, not the firstborn, as Shem among the sons of Noah (Gen. 5:32; 6:10), who was nevertheless born after Japheth. Moreover, Moses reports that Seth begot sons and daughters after Enosch (Gen. 5:7), and Josephus follows him in book 1, chapter 5, of the Antiquities. But Philo, in the Biblical Antiquities, adds both the number and the names of Seth's sons and daughters (if perhaps someone thinks he knew this even though Moses was silent, just as Paul gave the names of Pharaoh's magicians who resisted Moses himself, namely in 2 Tim. 3:8). For he says that Enosch afterwards had three sons and three daughters. The names of the sons were, he says, Elidia, Phonna, and Matha; of the daughters, Malida and Thita, where without doubt the name of one is missing, and that place is defective, or Philo did not know the names of all the daughters. Q. Whether Seth himself, the father of Enosch, was the first begotten by Adam from Eve after her expulsion from Paradise, since when Moses was speaking of Seth's begetting he added: ["Adam begat a son in his own image"] (Gen. 5:3). But others think that the earlier sons of Adam, such as Cain and Abel, were born to him in Paradise itself, because Moses did not write anything similar about them as he did about Seth, as though those others were born in the true image of God itself, not merely of their father Adam, namely while the image of God in Adam was not yet corrupted by sin. A. Since, after the expulsion of Adam from the earthly Paradise, Moses mentions that Cain and Abel were born of him (Gen. 4), there is no doubt that neither of them was conceived in Paradise, as some nevertheless think, nor indeed born there, but outside Paradise. For in weaving together this sacred history Moses followed the order and sequence of time. What the words [Adam begot Seth in his own image] mean, and why they were added, we have explained earlier.

units.la: Ad II. Publica nominis Dei profanatio.
units.tr: On the second point: the public profanation of the Name of God.

units.la: Iam verò ad publicā Nominis Dei Profanationem accedamus, In qua quaeritur, Quid verba hac Mosis significent, [Az Huchal Liqra beschem Iehova, Gen. 26] R. Multe sunt hic & varie multorum sententiae. Dauid Kimhi eruditissimus Hebraeorum sic interpretatur, [Tunc profanatum est, in invocando, nomen Dei.] Alij sic, [Tunc profanata est invocatio nominis Dei.]
units.tr: Now let us come to the public profanation of the Name of God, where the question is what these words of Moses mean, [Az Huchal Liqra beschem Iehova, Gen. 4:26]. R. There are many and varied opinions of many people here. David Kimhi, the most learned of the Hebrews, interprets it thus: [Then the name of God was profaned in invoking]. Others render it thus: [Then the invocation of the name of God was profaned].

units.la: Nonnulli vero, [Tunc cœpit esse profanari nomen Dei] Et hi quidem doctis, peritique, siqui alij, lingua Hebrea, quorum sententia eo redit, vt doceat Moses tunc ( .i. sub tempus nativitatis Enoschi) publicè & popula riter ab hominibus, qui tunc erat, profanatum fuisse Dei nomen, & cultum. Verùm hæc interpretatio dissplicuit aliis, contrariumq; huic superiori sententiæ scripturæ propterea affinxere his verbis: Sic igitur illi hæc verba Moysis explicant, [Tunc cœptum est invocari Nomen Dei.] Alij sic, [Tunc cœptum est ad invocandum nomen Dei.] Denique quidam ex illis sic, [Tunc cœpit vocari de nomine Dei,] quod videlicet tunc cœperint homines de Dei nomine appellari, quoniam quidam Filij Dei ditti fuerint, vt Gen. 6. 2, quosdam vocat Moses ipse filios Dei: quasi nimirum Moses de stabilitate inter homines Dei invocatione, non autem de Dominis illius profanatione agat. Cyrillus lib. 9. contra Iulian. sol. 1. longè abest à sententia Moysis: Vult enim hic ostendi à Moyse Enoschum ab hominibus sui sæculi vocatu fuisse Deum, honoris & pietatis, quam præ se ferebat, ergo. Omnium verò logissime Augustinus lib. 15. Civit. Dei, cap. 18. à vera huius loci mente discedit, quòd hic prophetiam de exorituro populo pio contineri scribit, his verbis, [Hic Enosch us sperauit invocare nomen Domini Dei. Quid sibi vult, sperauit invocare, nisi quia prophetia est exoriturus populum, qui secundum electionem gratia invocaret nomen Domini Dei?] Hac Augustinus. Caterum ipse Dauidis Kimchi sententia atque interpretationi subscribo, eámque sequor. Hic enim de publica nominis, cultúsque Diuini profanatione & contemptu (qui tunc popularis inter homines esse coepit) agit Moses: & gradus describit, tu quibus ad tam horribile sceleus peruentum est: tum etiam quibus tadem omnis caro corrupit viam sua, ac propterea diluuium illud, atque tremendum Dei iudicium in Mundum vniuerfum est effusum, Gen. 6. Sunt autem hi: Primum quidem, Peccatum ipsum primum primi hominis: Secundum, Fœtura, quam in singulorum hominum animis & cordibus clam & priuatim semel coccepta corruptio & infusa vitiositas ex primo illo Adami peccato pariebat & proferebat: Tertium, Publicum Caini fratricidium: Quartum Stuprum, violatioque coniugy publice a Lamecho (qui fuit vnus ex Caini posteris) indudta: Quintus, Ipsa publica iam neglectio omnis veri cultus Dei, & pro eo profanatio contemptioque nominis ipsius publica, ergo & alterum, quam veri Dei invocatio. Diuini cultus noua institutio ab hominibus facta est. De quibus vide Epiphanium initio lib. 1. contra 80. Haereses. His enim tot gradibus ad immane istud flagitium deuentum est, vt Dei nomen ab hominibus populariter, ac publice contemneretur, qui tot improbitatis, & quidem inulta, publica exempla viderent homines in mundo, quum in tota Caini familia (postquam ipse a Dei facie fugisset Gen. 4. 16.) ac proinde in eius posteris iam eeffasset, ac intermisus esset verus Dei cultus. Ergo qui inter illos homines, nimirum Caini posteros, superabat ex veteribus humanæ mentis & lucis reliquijs metus Dei, & illius Maiestatis sensus, honor, & tremor, ex hominum istorum animis deletus & extinctus est. Qui fuerunt triflissima peccati primi hominis effecta: & ad sequen-
units.tr: Some, however, render it: [Then the name of God began to be profaned]. These men, learned and skilled in the Hebrew language, as well as others, hold that the sense comes to this: Moses teaches that at that time (that is, around the time of Enosh's birth) the name and worship of God were profaned publicly and openly by the men who then lived. But this interpretation displeased others, who, to oppose the former view, twisted the words of Moses in the following ways. Thus they explain these words of Moses: [Then it began to be called upon the name of God]. Others thus: [Then men began to call upon the name of God]. Finally, some of them read it thus: [Then it began to be called of the name of God], that is, that men then began to be called by the name of God, since some were called sons of God, as in Gen. 6:2, which Moses himself calls the sons of God. As if Moses were speaking of the public calling upon God among men, and not of the profanation of his name! Cyril, in book 9 against Julian, is far from the meaning of Moses. For he wants it shown here that Enosh was called God by the men of his age, on account of the honour and piety which he displayed. But Augustine, in book 15 of The City of God, chapter 18, departs most widely from the true sense of this passage, since he writes that a prophecy of a pious people who would arise is contained here, in these words: [Here Enosh hoped to call upon the name of the Lord God. What does "hoped to call upon" mean, unless it is a prophecy that there would arise a people who, by the grace of election, would call upon the name of the Lord God?]. So far Augustine. For my part, I subscribe to the interpretation of David Kimchi and follow it. For here Moses deals with the public profanation and contempt of the name and worship of God, which then began to be common among men, and he describes the steps by which men came to such a horrible crime, and by which at last all flesh corrupted its way, and for this reason that flood and terrible judgment of God was poured out upon the whole world (Gen. 6). These steps are as follows. First, the sin itself, the first sin of the first man. Second, the offspring which the corruption, secretly and privately conceived once in the minds and hearts of individual men, and the vice infused from that first sin of Adam, bore and brought forth. Third, the public murder of his brother by Cain. Fourth, the public defilement and violation of marriage introduced by Lamech (who was one of Cain's descendants). Fifth, the now public neglect of all true worship of God, and in its place the public profanation and contempt of his very name, and the new institution of a worship of God different from the true invocation of God, devised by men. On these matters see Epiphanius at the beginning of book 1 against the eighty heresies. For men had come by these many steps to that monstrous wickedness, so that the name of God was openly and publicly despised by the people. They saw so many public examples of wickedness in the world, and unpunished ones at that, since in the whole family of Cain (after he himself had fled from the face of God, Gen. 4:16), and therefore among his descendants, the true worship of God had already died out and ceased. Therefore among those men, that is, the descendants of Cain, whatever remnants of the human mind and light had survived, the fear of God and the sense, honour and trembling before that Majesty were blotted out and extinguished from the hearts of those men. These were the most sorrowful effects of the first sin of man, and they led on to the foul corruption, depravity and most unjust condition of nearly all men (very few excepted), which was a most certain step and a very ready and easy slide, and finally the cause of God's wrath upon the whole world. For impiety towards the true God is the source of all crimes, while true faith and religion, as Augustine says, is the mother of all virtues.

units.la: quenquætem hominū omnium (paucissimis omnino exceptis) corruptelam teterrimam, depravationem, sa dissimā certissimus gradus, & proclinissimus facilimusque lapsus, denique tusla Dei in vniuersum Mundum ira caussa. nam in vero Deum impietas est scelerum omnium fons: contráque vera fides & religio mater, vt ait Augustinus, omnium virtutum. Q̄ num igitur Cainini posteri (necdum enim alÿ in Mundo erant, nec vlla alia adhuc familia creuerat) & homicidia in domo sua, & adulteria publica, atque ab hominibus impunita cernerent: quum nulli communi ac potentiori, quàm ipsi singulí essent, Magistratui parerent: quum voluptatibus omnis generis lasciuisque cantionibus dediti essent : quæ arma, prout cuiusq; ferebat audacia, tractarent: quum denique inter eos, maximèque in anita illa Caini domo (in quam omnes illius posteri oculos coniciebant) verus Dei cultus iam cessasset, quomodo in publicam nominis Dei profanationem illi ýdē homines non facilè ruerent, aut laberentur ? Improbitatis enim & nequitiæ seu licentia hominum coërcenda frænum ac vinculum proculdubio summum, est veri Dei metus, & cultus: qui vbi cessat, omnia in peius ruunt: vbi retinetur, virtus viget, vitiū decrescit. Præclarè enim in Agesilao Xenophon, Ὅπυ γὰρ ἀιδῆς θεὸν μὲν σέβοιεν, πολιτικὰ δὲ ἀσοσίεν, πίδαρχίαν δὲ μελέλωσιν, πῶς ἐκ ἐιχός ἐιταῖς θα πάντα υεσᾶ ἐλ- πίδων ἀγαθὸν εἶναι, id est, [Vbi enim Deum colunt homines, arma tractant, Magistratibus parent, quomodo non credibile est illic omnia bona spe plena esse?] Q̄uod vero stabilitam tùc demum nominis Dei invocationem nonnulli ex eo loco existimant, idque à Mose dici, fruStra est. Nam & Deus antea innocabatur, & ipse cultum sui hominibus præscripserat, & declararat, eum ꝗ retinebat Adami familia. Sed ordo historiæ ipsius postulabat, vt quibus de caussis Deus diluuium in terram immissiet, hominésque (quos ad sui imaginem condiderat) prorsus deleuisset, explicaretur à Mose. Id quod illè fecit: Itaque gradus, quibus sensim omnes homines ad summam primum impietatem in Deum: deinde Iniustitiam in proximos peruenerunt⸗ ordine recitat, & proponit. Atq; hæc quidè est mea de hoc loco sententia.
units.tr: What, then, would the descendants of Cain (for there were as yet no others in the world, nor had any other family yet grown up) do, when they saw murders in their own house, and public adulteries, and these unpunished by men? Since each of them was equal to the others, and none was greater or more powerful than the rest, and they were subject to no common and stronger magistracy; since they were given over to pleasures of every kind and to lascivious songs; since each handled weapons as his boldness prompted; since finally among them, and especially in that house of Cain (on which all his descendants fixed their eyes), the true worship of God had now ceased: how would those same men not easily rush into, or slip into, the public profanation of the name of God? For the restraint and bridle on the wickedness and licence of men is undoubtedly the highest fear and worship of the true God. Where this is lost, all things rush to ruin; where it is kept, virtue flourishes and vice declines. Xenophon put this admirably in his Agesilaus: (Greek: Ὅπου γὰρ ἀνθρῶποι θεὸν μὲν σέβοιεν, πολεμικὰ δὲ ἀσκοῖεν, ἀρχομένοις δὲ πείθοιντο, πῶς οὐκ εἰκὸς ἐκεῖ πάντα ἀγαθῶν ἐλπίδων μεστὰ εἶναι) that is, [For where men worship God, practise the arts of war and obey their magistrates, how is it not reasonable to believe that everything there is full of good hope?] As for the view that some take from this passage, that the stable invocation of the name of God began only then, and that Moses says so, it is groundless. For God was already invoked before, and he himself had prescribed and declared his worship to men, and the family of Adam kept it. But the order of the history required that Moses should explain for what reasons God sent the flood upon the earth and utterly destroyed the men whom he had created in his own image. This Moses did. Therefore he recounts and sets out in order the steps by which all men gradually came first to the greatest impiety towards God, and then to injustice towards their neighbours. And this is my opinion on this passage.

units.la: Q. Inter quos tunc cœpit hæc publica Nominis Dei profanatio? R. Q uidam existimat etiam inter Sethi posteros cœpiu esse profanari nomen Dei, propterea quod tota Caini familia iam⸗ vero Deo seruire desierat, eiusque cultum (quum Cainus pater à facie Dei eieɛtus esset, & extra Ecclesiā) sequi, & retinere. Q uā-ob-em hoc de Sethi posteris, qui nondum Dei cultum violarant, dislum malunt. Ego vero de solis Caini posteris ista sumenda iudico. Q uum enim cœpit nomenDei profanari, nulli dum erant⸗ posteri Sethi, vtpote quum illa profanatio cœperit sub tempus natiuitatis Enoschi, quemadmodum ait & quidem disserte Moses, Gen. 4. 26. Fuit autem hic Enoschus, vt antea demostrauimus, primogenitus Sethi. Q uanquàm autemCaini posteri verum Dei cultum non retinebant, publicam tamen illam nominis, culusq; Dei profanationem adhuc nec excogitarant, nec admiserant, quam sequenti tempore tamen, vt hic docet Moses, sequi, & ampleƈti cœperunt. Itaque tũc demum manifestè publice & populariter profanari inter eos sœpit nomen, veneratioq; veri
units.tr: Q. Among whom did this public profanation of the name of God begin then? R. Some think that the profanation of the name of God began even among the descendants of Seth, because the whole family of Cain had by then ceased to serve the true God, and (since Cain their father had been cast out from the face of God and from the Church) had followed and kept a worship of their own. For this reason they prefer to say this of the descendants of Seth, who had not yet violated the worship of God. I, however, judge that these things must be taken only of the descendants of Cain. For when the name of God began to be profaned, there were as yet no descendants of Seth, since that profanation began around the time of Enosh's birth, as Moses clearly says (Gen. 4:26). Now this Enosh, as I have shown above, was the firstborn of Seth. Although the descendants of Cain did not keep the true worship of God, they had not yet devised or admitted that public profanation of the name and worship of God, which nevertheless they afterwards began to continue and extend in the following time, as Moses teaches here. Therefore it was only then that the name and the veneration of the true God began to be openly and publicly profaned among them, which had not happened before.

units.la: ꝗ veri Dei,quod antea nõ fiebat. Hoc autem publica impietatis a Caini familia primùm introductâ, & postea in ea sola diu retenta exercitatâ, exemplum secuti sunt postea & suo tempore posteri Sethi,nempe postquam ipsi multiplicati essent in terra,& filiæ hominum in vxores accepissent non autem prius,meo iudicio,Gen.6. 2.4. Tunc enim(exceptis omnino paucis)& illi quoque posteri Sethi plerique fere omnes defectores a Deo fuerunt,quæ antea tales non essent,sed pij essent. Ergo multis antea seculis in Caini familia ea profanatio nominis Dei contigit,ut ordo feriesq; conscripta a Mose historiæ docet. Fere enim inter hanc profanationem publicam, illiusque inter Caini posteros initium,& eandem ad posteros Sethi deriuatam intercedunt anni 287, ut colligi potest ex Gen.cap.5. Eam enim deriuationem colloco in tempus Iaredi,id est,nati quidem,sed non transflati adhuc Chanochi. Translatus enim est a Deo,ut defectores ex Dei familia potissimum percellerentur metu, & ut boni,qui in Dei cultu perstabant in eadem familia,confirmarentur,ac recreatentur. Atque hanc meã sententiam confirmat Epiphanius lib.1.contra hæreses his verbis, Ἀ'ἀ ἀ ... Κaiva, Μαλαλεὴλ, Ἰαρὲδ ... Ἰαρὲδ ἡμᾶς ἐλθῶν ... ἰ ... ἐ ἐ. id est,Adami filius Seth, filius autem huius Enos,& per successionem Kainan, Malaleel,Iared. Vt verò maiorum traditio,quæ ad nos peruenit,habet,tunc capit illa famosa nequitia in mundo esse. Hæc Epiphanius. Verum Iosephus lib.1.Antiquit. cap.4.videtur demum septima generationis Sethi tempori hoc attribuere, quasi sub Mathusale patre pÿ Lemechi: non sub Jaredo patre pÿ Chanochi hæc euenerint. Ego vero potius Epiphanio assentior, eumque sequor. Q. Qualis fuerit ista nominis Dei Profanatio, & quid significet. R. Synecdochica est locutio in voce [Nominis] & verbo [Invocare.] Nec enim Nomen ipsum Dei duntaxat, i. ipsius appellatio fuit profanata, velut, Quòd Dei nomen in vanum sumeretur, per Deum temerè & iuraretur ab istis hominibus, & peieraretur, & denique sanctum illud Dei benedictum Nomen (quod prius sacrosanctum inter homines fuerat) blasphemaretur: verum etiam quòd Dei Potentia, maiestas, iustitia, sapientia, misericordia contemneretur, sperneretur, irrideretur, negaretur. Nec id quidem solum, dum in publicis cœtibus aderant homines ad Deum colendum, & invocandum (nec enim gens vlla religione aliqua caruit) verùm vbique, & quoties vel conscientia contemptores istos arguebat: vel ipsius Nominis Dei appellationi, interpositi, invocative ab aliis hominibus reverentia, & obtestatio istis profanis proponebantur, Dei Nomen isti impudenter, & impiè profanabat. Ergo in vniuersum Dei contemptum, præsertim in ipso Deo colendo & venerando inualuit inter illius sæculi homines .i. Caini posteros, quæ postea tamen etiam ad posteros Sethi quoque dimanauit. Ergo idola tunc pro vero Deo culta sunt, vt scribit Philo in Antiquit. & verum legitimusque cultus Deo præstari inter eos desiit, quemadmodum ait Iosephus lib. 1. cap. 5. Antiquit. Denique Epiphanius hæ verbis illam Profanationem describit quibus intelligatur ipsa fuisse trisissimum peccati effectum, quòd Dei metum omnem & verum cultum inter homines extingueret, & quæ Profanatio impietatem pro pietate, infidelitatem pro fide in Deum doceret, ac promoveret: quanquam idem Epiphanius censet post Diluuiū demum idola & Thare temporibus introducta in mundum: hoc vero tempore nondum fuisse recepta. Contrà, Tertullianus in lib.de Idololat. ea tunc in Mundum putat inducta. Nec enim, ait idem Epiphanius, Adamum fuisse idololatram, nec simulacra, vel aliud quicquam, præter verum Deum, adorasse. Imò etiam Prophetam fuisse Adamum, sciebátque Patrem dixisse Filio, [Faciamus hominem ad imaginem nostram, Gen.1] Ego Tertulliano non assentior. Atqui hæc est prima malitia, quod mundi post hæc innatum, labes, nimirum impietas in Deum, quæ totius probitatis & iustitiæ postea labefactationem secum intulit mundo. Hic maximus eius rerum omnium confusionis (quæ inter homines postea fuit) impulsus, & gradus ad eum Mundi teterrimum statum, quem idem Epiphanius vocat Barbarismum lib.1.Tom.1. contra Hæreses.
units.tr: of the true God, which had not happened before. But this public impiety, first introduced by the family of Cain and for a long time practised in that family alone, was afterwards followed as an example by the descendants of Seth in their own time, namely after they had multiplied on the earth and the daughters of men had been taken as their wives, and not before, in my judgment (Gen. 6. 2, 4). For then (with very few exceptions) nearly all the descendants of Seth also became apostates from God, though previously they had not been such but had been godly. Therefore that profanation of God's name occurred many centuries earlier in the family of Cain, as the order and sequence of the history written by Moses teaches. For between this public profanation and its beginning among the descendants of Cain, and its spread to the descendants of Seth, there lie about 287 years, as can be gathered from Gen. chapter 5. I place that spread in the time of Jared, that is, when Enoch had been born but not yet translated. For he was translated by God so that the apostates from God's family would be struck chiefly with fear, and so that the good who persevered in the worship of God in the same family would be confirmed and refreshed. Epiphanius, in book 1 against the heresies, confirms my opinion with these words: Adam's son Seth, the son of this Enos, and by succession Kainan [Καϊνάν], Malaleel [Μαλελεήλ], Iared [Ἰαρέδ] ... Iared ... Enoch ... As the tradition of our ancestors, which has come down to us, has it, then that notorious wickedness began to exist in the world. Thus Epiphanius. But Josephus, Antiquities book 1 chapter 4, seems to attribute these events only to the seventh generation of Seth, as if they happened under Methuselah, the father of Lamech, and not under Jared, the father of Enoch. I, however, agree rather with Epiphanius and follow him. Q. What was this profanation of the name of God, and what does it mean? A. The words "name" and "invoke" are used synecdochically. For it was not only the name of God itself, that is, his designation, that was profaned, as when the name of God was taken in vain, and God was rashly sworn by and perjured by those men, and finally that holy and blessed name of God, which had previously been most sacred among men, was blasphemed; but also God's power, majesty, justice, wisdom and mercy were despised, scorned, mocked and denied. Nor did this happen only while men were gathered in public assemblies to worship and invoke God (for no nation has been without some religion), but everywhere and whenever either conscience accused those despisers, or reverence and entreaty offered by other men in the invocation of God's name were set before them; those men shamelessly and impiously profaned God's name. Therefore contempt for God in general, especially in the very worship and veneration of God, grew strong among the men of that age, that is, the descendants of Cain, and this afterwards also spread down to the descendants of Seth. Therefore idols were then worshipped in place of the true God, as Philo writes in the Antiquities, and the true and lawful worship of God ceased among them, as Josephus says in book 1 chapter 5 of the Antiquities. Finally, Epiphanius describes that profanation in words by which it may be understood that it was the most sorrowful effect of sin, since it extinguished among men all fear of God and all true worship, and since this profanation taught and promoted impiety in place of piety and unbelief in place of faith in God. Yet the same Epiphanius holds that idols were introduced into the world only after the Flood, in the times of Terah, and that at this time they had not yet been received. On the contrary, Tertullian, in his book On Idolatry, thinks they were then introduced into the world. For, says the same Epiphanius, Adam was not an idolater, nor did he worship images or anything else besides the true God. Indeed Adam was also a prophet, and he knew that the Father had said to the Son, "Let us make man in our image" (Gen. 1). I do not assent to Tertullian. Yet this is the first wickedness, the stain that was then born in the world, namely impiety against God, which afterwards brought with it the weakening of all integrity and justice in the world. This was the greatest impulse to all the confusion of things that afterwards existed among men, and a step towards that most foul state of the world, which the same Epiphanius calls barbarism (book 1, vol. 1, against the heresies).

units.la: Ad III. Propagatio familiæ Sethi.
units.tr: III. The propagation of the family of Seth

units.la: Iam vero ad tertium Historiæ caput accedamus, in quo agitur de Propagatione piæ familiæ Sethi viri pij: In qua primum quæritur, Cur plures gradus in recensenda Sethi progenie numerentur à Mose, quàm in posteris Cain, quum tamen hi, sicut & illi ad tempus Diluuij & generarint, & superfuerint. nam in Caini stirpe & prosapia recitanda Moses subsitit in Iubal imo Lemechi filio, qui fuit ab Adamo (eodem non comprehenfo) septimus, ficnepe Cainus, Chanochus, Hiradus, Mechuiael, Methufael, Lemechus, Iubal. Ergo substitit in septimo eius gradu. In progenie vero Sethi describenda peruenit vsque ad Noachum Lemechi py-filium, qui fuit decimus ab Adamo, fi ipsum Adamum in eo numero complectaris, sic nempe, Adamus, Sethus, Enoschus, Kainan, Malaleelus, Iaredus, Chanochus, Mathusael, Lemechus, Noachus, quemadmodum & Iosephus lib. 1. Antiquitat. cap. 5. & Epiphanius lib. 1 contra Haereses: & Augustinus lib. 15. Ciuit. Dei, cap. 20 etiam scribunt: sed imprimis Moses. Dempto vero Adamo, nouem tantum generationes Sethi recenseatur. Addito vero Adamo in Caini prosapia, gradus sunt octo. Nam Patres, qui eos solum septem faciunt, etiam coniuncto Adamo, subsistunt in Lemecho impio, ad Iubalem vsque lineam non perducunt, quod tamen fieri oportuit. R. Varia sunt variorum de hac gradnum in his duabus familys Caini, & Sethi diuersitate philosophamenta, sed imprimis Augustini. Is enim loco iam citato precise septenario graduū posteritatis Caini numero inhaerens, ait tres postea illi numero adjici a Mose, vnde fiat vndecim personae in posteris Caini, quae numero in S. Scriptura, vt idem ille vult, peccatum significatur: vti per denarium numerum vitium & obedientia Dei, quoniam Lex ipsa Dei decem praeceptis continetur. [Progenies ergo Adam (inquit Augustin.) per Cain scelerati vndenario numero finitur, quo peccatum significatur: & ipse numerus a foemina clauditur, a quo sexu initium factum est peccandi. Nam & ipsa filia Lemech Noema voluptas interpretatur. Per Seth
units.tr: Now let us come to the third part of the history, in which the propagation of the pious family of the godly man Seth is treated. In this, the first question is: why does Moses count more generations in recounting the progeny of Seth than among the descendants of Cain, although both lines both produced offspring and survived until the time of the Flood? For in reciting the stock and lineage of Cain, Moses stops at Jubal, or rather at the son of Lamech, who was the seventh from Adam (Adam himself not being counted): Cain, Enoch, Irad, Mehujael, Methusael, Lamech, Jubal. So he stopped at the seventh generation. But in describing the progeny of Seth he comes down to Noah, the son of Lamech, who was the tenth from Adam if you include Adam himself in the number, thus: Adam, Seth, Enos, Kenan, Mahalalel, Jared, Enoch, Methuselah, Lamech, Noah. Josephus (Antiquities book 1 chapter 5), Epiphanius (book 1 against the heresies), and Augustine (City of God book 15 chapter 20) also write this, but above all Moses. If Adam is removed, only nine generations of Seth are counted. If Adam is added in Cain's line, there are eight generations. For the Fathers, who make them only seven even with Adam included, stop at the impious Lamech and do not bring the line down to Jubal, which nevertheless ought to have been done. A. Various writers have various speculations on this difference between the two families, Cain's and Seth's, but above all that of Augustine. For he, in the place already cited, clinging precisely to the septenary number of Cain's posterity, says that three more persons were afterwards added to that number by Moses, so that there are eleven persons in the posterity of Cain. In Holy Scripture, as the same writer maintains, the number eleven signifies sin, just as the number ten signifies vice and obedience to God, since God's own law is contained in ten precepts. [The progeny of Adam through the wicked Cain (says Augustine) is ended with the number eleven, by which sin is signified; and that number is closed by a woman, from whose sex the beginning of sinning was made. For the daughter of Lamech, Noema, is also interpreted as pleasure. Through Seth

units.la: ς Seth autem ab Adam vsque ad Noé denarium insinuatur legitimum numerum. | Hæc ille subtilius meo qui-dem iudicio. Itaque idem eodem loco rationem aliam, & quidem probabiliorem affert, Cur Moses in recitandis Caini generationibus subsitterit in Lemecho, non à numero isto septenario, vel vndenario petitam, his verbis, [ Potuit autem viuente adhuc Lemech, atque regnante fieri Diluuium, vt ipsum cum alijs omnibus hominibus, exceptis qui in Arca fuerunt, quem perderet, inueniret. Et idcirco non vnus filius Lemech, sicut inceteris superius, sed plures commemorati sunt, quia incertū erat quis ei fuisset mortuo successurus si regnandi tempus inter ipsum Lemech, & diluuium remansisset.]
units.tr: Seth, however, from Adam down to Noah is pointed out as the legitimate number ten. These things he states more subtly, in my judgment. Therefore the same writer, in the same place, gives another reason, and a more probable one, why Moses, in reciting the generations of Cain, stopped at Lamech, a reason not drawn from that septenary or undenary number, in these words, [Lamech could still have been alive and reigning when the Flood came, so that it would destroy him together with all the other men, except those who were in the Ark. And for this reason not one son of Lamech is mentioned, as in the others above, but several, because it was uncertain who would succeed him when he died, if the time of his reign had remained between Lamech himself and the Flood.]

units.la: Sic igitur piū illud Augustini pectus, ne cuiquam, quātumvis malitioso, relinqueret calumniandi verbū Dei, & hanc diuersitatem, occasionem, seipsum retractauit, & veriorem illam rationem conquisiuit. Ego autem sic sentio, Plures gradus ex posteris Sethi fuisse descrip-tos, quod continua successio Ecclesiæ à Mundo condito ad Diluuium vsque pijs proponenda erat, quorū caussa hæc scribuntur: vti eiusdem successio continuatioque Ecclesiæ Dei post diluuium ab eodem Mose feriatim narratur. Caini vero Genus vsque ad Diluuium continuū non fuit enumeratum, quoniam illud à pijs sciri eatenus intererat, quatenus aliqua Dei dona, eáque egregia in eo extiterant. Quæ vsque ad Noemam filiam Lemechi durarunt. Quū autem ea esse desyssent: neque post diluuium hoc genus hominū superfuisset, sed in diluuio totum periisset, desyt quoque eius meminisse Moses, & seriem illius describere, vtpote quod neq; propter dona Dei,neque ad cosernationem, neque ad propagationem futuram generis humani cognitu necessarium: amplius erat: sed potius ob scelera sua execrandum. Q. Cur nullius mulieris in huius posteritatis, i. Sethi descriptione nomen additum est, quum & ibi quoq; filia sicut filij,id est, fœmina sicut mares, fuerint: & in Caini generationibus Noema filia Lemechi nominatim & diserte cōmemorata fuerit. R. Nequaquam id factū esse, quia inter filias & fœminas, quæ ex Sethi posteris natæ sunt, nulla vel verè pia fuerit (nec enim vlla ex diluuio seruata à Deo fuissent) vel industria mulier, qualis illa Noema, quæ propterea de nomine appellatur: sed quia ad historiæ seriem ea res minimè pertineret. Breuitatis verò studuit Moses. Noema verò illa, quam refert Moses Gen.4 22.præter sexum fabrica & officina arariя intenta fuisse videtur, atque vel propterea, vel ob formā, cuius abusu postea nocuit Mundo, innotuisse. Quare non in laudem, sed potius in probrum eius memintsse Moses videtur, vt Dina filia Iacobi. Porro istius rei rationem aliam profert Augustinus, libr. 15. Ciuit. Dei, cap. 17: quam apud eum legat, qui volet: suprà nos eam exposuimus. Q. Cur posteri Sethi homines pij acceperunt quædam nomina impiorum hominum, nempe posterorum Caini, vel saltem illis cum improbis istis communia quum Psal.16.4 ista nominū communio damnari videatur. Habuerunt autem hæc nomina communia, vt apparet toto capite 5. Geneseos, nempe [Kaina,Chnoch, Mathusael,Lemech.] Porro [Tubal, Iubal, Iabal] nomina sibi accommodasse nō leguntur filij Sethi. R. Non ad morum imitationem sumsumpserunt pij nomen impiorum: sed ob egregiam eiusmodi appellationum significationem, ut hac ratione vel de sorte sua miseriaque humana: vel de suo officio commonefierent pij. [Kainan] enim lamentatione designat, in quo vocabulo humana miseria notatur. Philo tamen [Possessionem] ut in Caino, notari putat. Ego vero potius ut in Abele, luctu, questu, & lamentationem. [Chanoch] est eruditus, ac bona disciplina imbutus, aut etiam, ut vult Philo, & alij, dedicatus Deo. Eusebius tamen lib.7. Præparat. Evangel. cap.3 Gratia interpretatur. [Mathusael] mortis cupidus & sepulcri, quod conditionem hominis per peccatum impositam refricat. [Lemech] est attenuatus, pauper, & deiectus, quæ significatio notatioque hominis nos ad modestiam animi, sensumque nostra vanitas reuocat. At vero [Tubal, Iubal, & Iabal] visa sunt pijs nomina nimium vel superba, vel infausta. Quamobrem eadem sibi sumere noluerunt. [Tubal] enim est Orbis totius appetens, vel permiscens ac confundens multa: quod utrunque est reiiciendum. [Iubal, & Iabal] est Perdens, sive desolans: quæ sunt infausta nomina, quanquam Philo, & alij aliter ea interpretantur. Porro [Iared] est Subiectus, & inferior: [Malaleel] Laudans Deum: [Noachus] Quietus, sen pacem afferens, quæ sunt reliqua piorum appellationes, quorum meminit Moses ex Setho descendentium, Gen.5.
units.tr: Thus that pious mind of Augustine, lest he leave anyone, however malicious, a pretext for slandering the Word of God over this discrepancy, retracted his own view and sought out the truer explanation. I, however, think as follows. Several generations of the posterity of Seth were listed because the continuous succession of the Church from the creation of the world to the Flood had to be set before the godly, and for this reason these things are written, just as the succession and continuity of God's Church after the Flood is narrated in order by the same Moses. The line of Cain, however, was not listed continuously down to the Flood, because it concerned the godly to know of it only so far as certain gifts of God, and outstanding ones, had appeared in it. These lasted until Noema, the daughter of Lamech. When they had ceased, and this kind of men had not survived the Flood but had perished entirely in it, Moses also ceased to mention them and to describe their series, since it was no longer necessary to know them for the gifts of God, for the preservation, or for the future propagation of the human race; rather, the line was to be execrated for its crimes. Q. Why was no woman's name added in the description of the posterity of Seth, since there too there were daughters as well as sons, that is, females as well as males, whereas in the generations of Cain Noema, the daughter of Lamech, is mentioned by name and expressly? A. That was not done for this reason: among the daughters and women born of the posterity of Seth, none was either truly pious (for none of them would have been preserved by God from the Flood) or an industrious woman like that Noema, who is therefore named. The reason is rather that this matter did not belong to the course of the history, and Moses aimed at brevity. That Noema whom Moses mentions in Gen. 4.22 seems to have been, apart from her sex, devoted to the forge and workshop of bronze, and to have become known either for this or for her beauty, the misuse of which later harmed the world. Therefore Moses seems to mention her not in praise but in reproach, as he does with Dinah the daughter of Jacob. Augustine offers another explanation of this matter, in book 15 of The City of God, chapter 17, which whoever wishes may read there; we have set it out above. Q. Why did the pious posterity of Seth take some names of the impious, namely of the posterity of Cain, or at least names held in common with those wicked men, since the sharing of such names seems to be condemned in Ps. 16.4? These names were held in common, as appears throughout chapter 5 of Genesis: [Kaina, Chnoch, Mathusael, Lemech]. Moreover, the sons of Seth are not read to have adopted the names [Tubal, Iubal, Iabal]. R. The pious did not take the names of the impious in order to imitate their morals, but on account of the excellent meaning of such names, so that the godly might be reminded either of their own lot and human misery, or of their duty. [Kainan] indicates lamentation, and in this word human misery is noted. Philo, however, thinks that [possession], as in Cain, is noted. I, however, think it rather denotes, as in Abel, mourning, complaint and lamentation. [Chanoch] means learned and imbued with good discipline, or, as Philo and others hold, dedicated to God. Eusebius, however, in book 7 of the Preparation for the Gospel, chapter 3, interprets it as grace. [Mathusael] means one who desires death and the grave, which recalls the condition of man imposed through sin. [Lemech] means weakened, poor and cast down, and this meaning and etymology call us back to humility of mind and to a sense of our vanity. But [Tubal, Iubal and Iabal] seemed to the pious names too proud or too ill-omened, and so they were unwilling to take them. [Tubal] means one who seeks after the whole world, or one who mixes and confuses many things, both of which are to be rejected. [Iubal and Iabal] mean one who destroys or lays waste, which are ill-omened names, although Philo and others interpret them differently. Further, [Iared] means subject and inferior; [Malaleel] praising God; [Noachus] quiet, or bringing peace. These are the remaining names of the pious descended from Seth, which Moses mentions in Gen. 5.

units.la: Q. Quid posteri Sethi (in quibus solis ante diluuiu durauit Ecclesia Dei) habuerint melius, præstantiusve, quam posteri Caini, quu & ipsi, sicut Cainini, sese postea corruperint, & diluuio, ut hi, quoque perierint, paucis exceptis nimirum octo duntaxat personis, 1.Pet 3.20 Gen.6.17, & 7.21.22.23. Denique quum nullius artis laus huic Sethi progeniei tribuatur: multas autem artes inuenerint posteri Caini, uti diximus, & docuit Moses. Gen 4 20.21. Iosephus lib.1. Antiquit. Iudaic.cap.4, & ex eo postea Zonaras lib.1. Annalium scribunt in duobus hisce posteritatem Sethi felicciorem fuisse posteris Caini: Primum,quod quum Sethi liberi boni fuissent, felicissimè in sua terra cum patre suo Setho vixerunt, ac cōmorati sunt absque ulla vexatione. Nihil enim,ait, crudele iis prouenit usque ad terminū vitæ. Deinde, quod idem hi disciplinam rerum cœlestium,motuúnque cœli & Astrorum repererunt,quum posteri Caini in rerum tantum terrenarum cognitione versarentur,seque occuparent. Verum posteri Caini, qui fuerunt improbi, hos quoque mites homines vexarunt,& Gigates omnia cædibus,rapinis etiam in familiis Sethi implerunt ut non videantur magis tuti fuisse, quam reliqui mortales: & quum essent posteri Caini Agricolæ,& Pastores, disciplinámque à Patre Caino (quum ille ab Adamo,uti & Sethus,acceperat)retinerent, nequaquā verisimile est eos ignorasse res cœlestes, velut motum Solis & Lunæ,conuersionémque Astrorū, quæ ad huius vitæ corporea cōmoditatem maximè pertinent. Sunt enim in hisce rebus fily huius seculi prudentiores filijs lucis,Luc.16.8. Ergo,meo quidem iudicio,nutat Iosephi sententia. In quo igitur fuit ꞓ vt loquitur Paulus Rom.3.1,id est,præstantia filiorū Sethi?nimirum in donis Dei spiritualibus,& salutaribus. Nam quemadmodū Deus dederat posteris Caini dona terrena & caduca (qui posteri sunt fuerúntque ci-
units.tr: Q. What did the posterity of Seth (in whom alone before the Flood the Church of God endured) have that was better or more excellent than the posterity of Cain, since they too, just like the Cainites, afterwards corrupted themselves and perished in the Flood as the others did, except for eight persons only, 1 Pet. 3.20; Gen. 6.17, and 7.21, 22, 23. Finally, since no praise of any art is attributed to this line of Seth, whereas the posterity of Cain invented many arts, as we have said and as Moses taught (Gen. 4.20, 21; Josephus, Jewish Antiquities, book 1, chapter 4; and after him Zonaras, Annals, book 1), they write that the posterity of Seth was happier than that of Cain in two respects. First, because the sons of Seth were good, they lived most happily in their own land with their father Seth and dwelt there without any vexation; for nothing cruel, he says, befell them until the end of their lives. Second, because these same men discovered the science of heavenly things and the motions of the heavens and the stars, whereas the posterity of Cain occupied themselves only with knowledge of earthly things. But the posterity of Cain, who were wicked, also harassed these gentle men, and the giants filled everything with slaughter and rapine, even among the families of Seth, so that they did not seem any safer than other mortals. And since the posterity of Cain were farmers and herdsmen, and kept the discipline they had received from their father Cain (who had received it from Adam, as Seth had), it is by no means likely that they were ignorant of heavenly things, such as the motion of the Sun and Moon and the revolution of the stars, which pertain most to the bodily convenience of this life. For in these matters the sons of this age are wiser than the sons of light, Luke 16.8. Therefore, in my judgment, Josephus's opinion wavers. In what then lay the advantage (as Paul speaks, Rom. 3.1), that is, the excellence of the sons of Seth? Namely in the spiritual and saving gifts of God. For just as God gave to the posterity of Cain earthly and perishable gifts (they who were and are citizens of that earthly and mortal state, which Augustine compares with the heavenly and explains), so he gave spiritual and saving goods to the sons of Seth, in whom the true Church was. Therefore the true worship of God among them was drawn from the very word and mouth of God

units.la: uitas nitas illa terrena & mortalis, quam confert cum cœlesti & explicat Augustinus) sic bona spiritualia & salutaria dedit filijs Sethi, in quibus erat Ecclesia vera. Ergo verum Dei cultus inter eos erat ex ipsius Dei verbo & ore descriptum, nempe Sacrificia, & Sacramenta. Inter eos erant, repetebantúrque articuli fidei, etsi non pleni, Heb. 6. Nam durabat memoria, repetitiõ salutaris illius promissionis Dei de futuro Messia Redemptore generis humani ex femine solius Mulieris, ac proinde fides iustificans in ea sola familia erat, Gen 6.8: Inter eos erat donum Prophetia de vita aeterna piis reservata, de futuro Dei in impios cum vniuersali iudicio, tum etiam de diluuio certissime in eos ventūro, quod vtrumque predixit pius Chanochus vnus ex posteris Sethi, vt testatur etiam Tertullianus in lib. de Idololatria: item & Lemechus nascente Noacho. Inter eosdem denique posteros Sethi diu disciplina morum retenta est, & detestatio impietatis in Deum, & iniustitia in homines, vt apparet ex vita Chanochi, Lemechi py. & Noachi, qui mores hominum sui temporis dissolutos aperte damnarunt, Gen.6.8.9. & 7 13 &8.1, Heb.11.7, 1.Pet. 3.20, Iud epist. vers. 14. Eusebius lib 7. cap. 3 Præpar. Euangel. Perierunt tamen postea diluuio, vti & caeteri, id est, posteri Caini, quia sese, quemadmodum & illi, postea corruperant, paucis tamen demptis, in quibus Deus suam Ecclesiam, atque illa dona sua conseruauit. Ergo omnibus modis Sethi posteritas felicior fuit, quàm Caini. Q. Vtrum tunc verbum aliquod Dei fuerit, extiterit, scriptum. R. Ante Chanochi pij aetatem nullum videtur fuisse verbum Dei scriptis literisque mandatum: Chanochus autem ipse librum edidit, Iud. epist.verf.14, in quo ira Dei grauissime in impios, & illius seculi homines continebantur: & in quo Excommunicatio acerbissima nimirum Anathema, Maranatha, vt vocat Paulus 1.Cor.16.22. aduersus eos fulminabatur, atque pronunciabatur: in quo denique homines de extremo Dei Iudicio, Vita fidelium Deo credentium aeterna, & Ira Dei in iniustos admonebantur. Sic enim nonnulli locum illum Pauli explicant, & cum verf.illo 14. Iudae comparant. Videtur autem primum Dei verbum scriptum extitisse circa annum a Mundo condito fexcentefimum octogesimum septimum, nimirum post natum ex Chanocho Methufchelechem, & post annum ipsius Chanochi 65: A publica vero Profanatione nominis Dei, 452. Huius autem Chanochi libri meminit Tertullianus in lib.de Idololatria, & lib.Duodecim Patriarchar.Testamentum qui vocatur, citatúrque ab Origene, & Procopio, Graecis scriptoribus. Sed idem Tertullianus quoque libri Chanochi facit mentionem in lib de Habitu Muliebri. Caeterum, quod scribunt Iosephus lib.1.Antiquit.cap.4, & Zonaras lib.1.Animilium,duas columnas(vnam lapideam,alteram lateritiam) iam inde ab ipsius Adami temporibus collocatas, in quibus & futurum Diluvium, & quas artes quisque reperiffet, erat descriptum, ac proinde scripturam ante Chanochi aetatem fuisse, hoc ex Mose probari non potest, neque ex vllo alio S.Scriptura loco. Credat tamen qui volet. Illarum enim columnarum (sed quas a Chaldaeis positas dicit) meminit etiam M.T.Cicero lib. 1. de Diuinat. Ioann.s Annius Viterb.in Berosum. He vero differunt, & à Saturni, & à Dionysij Bacchi Columnis, quas vocat Dionysius Alexandr. de Situ orbis: quarum illa in fneto Gaditano ad Occidentem: hæc in India ad Orientem sitæ sunt. Alia quoque fuit columna illa bina, quæ in Ægypto fuerunt, vt scribit Diodorus Siculus lib. 1 cap. 2, quarum vna Isidi, altera Osiridi dedicata fuit. Q. Quomodo anni vitæ Patrum illorum sunt supputandi, vtrum Solares, an Lunares: menstrui, an plurium mensium, quum dicantur vixisse nongentos, octingentos, septingentos, sexcentos annos, Gen. 5. R. Eusebius lib. 8. Demonstr. Euangel. cap. 2. scribit Hebræos exegisse annum suum ad cursum Lunæ, qui totis undecim diebus est minor, quàm annus Solaris. Ergo supputationem illam annorum de Lunaribus, non autem de Solaribus annis vult esse intelligendam. Augustinus lib. 15. Ciuit. Dei, cap. 12. ex aliorum sententia refert annos illos fuisse decimam tantum partem nostri anni, adeo vt nongenti illius seculi anni sint ex hac interpretatione nonaginta dunta vat anni nostri. Et certè diuersam fuisse annorum definiendorum apud diuersos populos rationem tradit Plinius lib. 7. Natur. Hist. Cefforinus, & Solinus Polyhistor, cap 3. Alij enim Annum solum mensium trium, alij quatuor, alij sex constituunt. Diodorus Siculus lib. 1. cap. 2. scribit apud Ægyptios annum triginta tantum diebus constitisse: atque eos annos intelligendos, quum homines nonnulli dicuntur mille, vel nongentos, vel octingentos annos vixisse. Verum vt tota hæc controversia placetur, & quomodo anni illi sint supputandi intelligatur, Augustini, eodem illo lib. 15. cap. 14. Audiamus hæc vere, & Dei verbo, & sententia Mosis consentienter scribentem, [ Prorsus, ait, tunc dies fuit, quantus & nunc est, quem viginti & quatuor horas diurno curriculo, noctúrnoq; determinant. Tantus mensis, quantus & nunc est, quem Luna cœpta & finita concludit. Tantus annus, quantus & nunc est, quem duodecim menses Lunares, additis propter cursum Solaré quinque diebus, & quadrante, consumant. ] Hæc ille, quæ sunt verissima. Ergo anni illi sunt Solares intelligendi: nullo vero modo Lunares, quemadmodum etiam elegantissimè aliì probarunt. Josephus autem Scaliger lib. 3. de Emendat. Temp. veterem Hebræorum annum fuisse Solarem, non Lunarem contendit: sed alio speciès. Utrum vero ydem hi anni sint Politici, an Sacri, id est, à mense Tisri, vel Nisan inchoandi, in Diluuij explicatione dicemus. Sed pergamus ad alia, & de Chanochi translatione videamus.
units.tr: vanity of that earthly and mortal life, which he compares with the heavenly one and explains, as Augustine does). So He gave the spiritual and saving blessings to the sons of Seth, among whom the true Church was. Therefore the true worship of God among them was laid down from God's own word and mouth, namely the sacrifices and the sacraments. Among them the articles of faith were also handed down and repeated, though not in full (Heb. 6). For the memory endured, and the repeated promise of God concerning the future Messiah, the Redeemer of the human race from the seed of the Woman alone, was kept alive; and so justifying faith existed in that family alone (Gen. 6.8). Among them was the gift of prophecy, concerning eternal life reserved for the godly, and concerning God's future coming against the wicked with a universal judgment, and also concerning the flood that was most certainly coming upon them. Both of these the godly Enoch, one of the posterity of Seth, foretold, as Tertullian also attests in his book On Idolatry; likewise Lamech did so when Noah was born. Finally, among the same posterity of Seth, a discipline of morals was long maintained, and a hatred of impiety against God and of injustice towards men, as is evident from the lives of Enoch, Lamech and Noah, who openly condemned the dissolute morals of the men of their time (Gen. 6.8, 9; 7.13; 8.1; Heb. 11.7; 1 Pet. 3.20; Jude, verse 14; Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel, book 7, chapter 3). Yet they perished afterwards in the flood, as did the rest, that is, the posterity of Cain, because they, like those others, had since become corrupt; a few were excepted, however, in whom God preserved His Church and those gifts of His. Therefore in every way the posterity of Seth was happier than that of Cain. Q. Whether any word of God existed or was written at that time. R. Before the time of the godly Enoch there seems to have been no word of God committed to writing and letters. But Enoch himself published a book (Jude, verse 14), in which the wrath of God against the impious and the men of that age was contained, and in which the most bitter excommunication, namely the anathema and the maranatha, as Paul calls it (1 Cor. 16.22), was hurled and proclaimed against them; in which finally men were warned about the last judgment of God, the eternal life of the faithful who believe in God, and the wrath of God against the unrighteous. For some explain that passage of Paul in this way, and compare it with verse 14 of Jude. It seems, however, that the first written word of God came into existence around the year 687 from the creation of the world, that is, after Methuselah was born to Enoch, and 65 years after Enoch's own birth; but from the public profanation of the name of God, 452 years. Tertullian mentions this book of Enoch in his On Idolatry, and the so-called Testament of the Twelve Patriarchs, and it is cited by Origen and Procopius, Greek writers. But Tertullian also makes mention of the book of Enoch in his On the Dress of Women. Otherwise, as to what Josephus (Antiquities, book 1, chapter 4) and Zonaras (Annals, book 1) write, that two columns, one of stone and the other of brick, were set up from the very times of Adam, on which both the coming flood and what arts each man had discovered were inscribed, and that therefore writing existed before the age of Enoch, this cannot be proved from Moses, nor from any other passage of Holy Scripture. Let whoever wishes believe it. For M. T. Cicero also mentions those columns (though he says they were set up by the Chaldeans) in book 1 of On Divination; so does Annius of Viterbo, in his commentary on Berosus. But these columns differ both from the Columns of Saturn and from the Columns of Dionysus-Bacchus, which Dionysius of Alexandria mentions in his On the Situation of the World: the former stand in the sea at Gades, in the west; the latter in India, in the east. There was also another pair of columns in Egypt, as Diodorus Siculus writes (book 1, chapter 2), one of which was dedicated to Isis and the other to Osiris. Q. How are the years of life of those patriarchs to be reckoned: whether as solar or as lunar years, as months or as periods of several months, since they are said to have lived nine hundred, eight hundred, seven hundred, six hundred years (Gen. 5)? R. Eusebius (Demonstration of the Gospel, book 8, chapter 2) writes that the Hebrews measured their year by the course of the moon, which is shorter than the solar year by a full eleven days. Therefore he wishes that reckoning of years to be understood as lunar, not solar. Augustine (City of God, book 15, chapter 12), reporting the opinion of others, says that those years were only a tenth part of our year, so that on this interpretation the nine hundred years of that age would be ninety of our years. And Pliny (Natural History, book 7), Censorinus and Solinus the polyhistor (chapter 3) hand down that peoples differed in their method of defining the year: for some fix the year at only three months, others at four, others at six. Diodorus Siculus (book 1, chapter 2) writes that among the Egyptians the year consisted of only thirty days, and that those are the years to be understood when some men are said to have lived a thousand, or nine hundred, or eight hundred years. But to settle this whole controversy, and to understand how those years are to be reckoned, let us hear Augustine in the same book 15, chapter 14, writing truly and in agreement with the word of God and the opinion of Moses: [Indeed, he says, the day was then just what it is now, which they fix by a course of twenty-four hours, by day and by night. The month was just what it is now, which the moon concludes when it begins and finishes. The year was just what it is now, which twelve lunar months, with five days and a quarter added for the course of the sun, complete.] So he writes, and these things are most true. Therefore those years are to be understood as solar years, and in no way as lunar, as other writers have also very elegantly proved. Joseph Scaliger, however (On the Emendation of Times, book 3), contends that the ancient Hebrew year was solar, not lunar, though on a different basis. Whether these years were civil or sacred, that is, to be begun from the month Tishri or Nisan, we shall discuss in the explanation of the Flood. But let us go on to other matters, and look at the translation of Enoch.

units.la: Ad IIII. Translatio Chanochi in cœlum.
units.tr: To the Fourth: The Translation of Enoch into Heaven.

units.la: Q. Quomodo hic pius Chanochus sit septimus ab Adamo, quum ab eo tantum sextus esse videatur, Iud. vers. 14. Inter eum enim & Adamum hi quinque duntaxat intercedunt, nempe Seth, Enosch, Kainan, Malalaeel, Iared: tamen eum à Setho sextum facit August. lib. 15. Ciuit. Dei, cap. 19: & Iud. vti dixi, septimū ab Adamo. R. Comprehendunt Iudæi, & Augustinus omnes personas, ipsumq; m̄t Adamum, quì hunc Chanochum ab Adamo septimum faciunt: & ipsum Sethū, ab hoc illum sextum: sic 1. Adamus: 2. Sethus: 3. Enoschus: 4. Kainan: 5. Malaleel: 6. Iared: 7. Chanochus: alioqui si hæ personæ (de quibus, quantum ille 'absit, quæritur) de mãtur, erit solum sextus ab Adamo: quintus autem à Setho atauo suo Chanochum hic pius. Hic autem, qui ex Hebraica scriptura ratione [Chanochus] scribitur ab Apostolo ad Hebr. 11. 5: Iuda in epist. vers. 14: Epiphanio tu lib. 1. Panarÿ seu Capsula, tum etiam in Ancorato Εὐνὸχ euphonie gratiâ Græce nominatur, ne quem nominis varietas fortasse turbet. Q. Quid in libro Chanochi istius pÿ continebatur? R. Et increpationes improborum, & confolationes piorũ. Nam & promissionem de vita æterna pÿs à Deo, per & propter Messiam futurum, fastam proponebat, ac refricabat, & acerbissima Dei in impios futura iudicia commemorabat, præsertim internecionem eorum proximâ, quum essent iam hominum mores intolerabiles. Itaque & Idololatriam, blasphemiamq; Nominis Dei iam publicè receptam condemnabat, & scelerum morum corruptores, lasciuamque hominum tum marium, tum fœminarum vitam grauiter reprehendebat, vt docet Tertullianus in lib. de Idololat. & in eo, quem de Habitu Mulieb ri scripsit. Imò verò in eos Anathema illud grauissimum, quod Maranatha vocat Paulus 1. Cor. 16. 22. iaculatum est, vt versiculum illi 14 apud Iudam explicant nonnulli. Huius autem libri aliquot testimonia & particulas quasdam in libro, qui dicitur Duodecim Patriarcharũ Testamentum (quem probant Origenes & Procopius) volunt extare: & exti tisse. Ceterum frustrà iam quæritur, vtrum inter Apocryphos, vel Canonicos liber ille sit recẽsendus, de quo se frustra fatigat in Tertullianum Laurent. Barreum homo (de quo affirmare non possis curiosiorne sit, an inaprior: utrumque enim hoc vitium summum habet, quod sit nefandi monstri G. Postelli compatriota, ut ipse loquitur, & de quo ipse gloriatur) Nam liber iste iam non extat: et si γνώσι ǀ non autem interpolatum extaret, quum eius testimonio diiserre velut veri Dei Prophetae utatur Iudas, dubitandum minime esset, quin liber ille esset inter Canonicos reponendus. Q. Cur a Deo translatus est Chanochus in tanta Mundi totius corruptela. R. Translatum quidem eum a Deo fuisse omnes affirmant: Cur autem, pauci explicant. Nam & Iosephus lib.1 cap.5. Antiquit. & Philo in Antiquit. Biblicis: & Zonaras lib.1. Animal. & Hieronymus contra Iovinianum, & alii pene infiniti rem gestam agnoscunt, & id verissime, Gen.5. Cur vero a Deo id factum sit, non docent. Certe ridicula prorsus est Hieronymi ratio, qui negat eum translatum, quia uxorem habuisset. Tam enim, ut docet Epiphanius in Ancorato, coniugatus translatus est Chanochus, quam caelebs Helias. Imo prior Chanochus coniux: posterior autem Helias caelebs: Sed & quis ipsos docuit Heliam fuisse caelibem potius, quam & Chanochu, & Mosem? Irenaeus igitur causam istius translationis unam hanc affert lib.5. contra Valentin. ut Deus in eo iustorum & piorum hominum in caelum translationem corpore & animo futuram praemonstraret etiam praeputiatorum. Id quod contra Iudaeos Tertullianus & Epiphanius scribunt, uti postea in Helia eorundem piorum circumcisorum eandem fore conditionem ostendit. Hos enim duos inter se coparat Irenaeus, lib.4.cap.30. Tertullianus variis in locis huius Chanochi translationis meminit, eumque candidatum aeternitatis latus vocat, velut lib. contra Judaeos, & de Resurrectione carnis. Transflatum autem eum a Deo in caelum idem Tertullianus putat etiam ob aliam causam, nempe lib. de Anima, cap. 28 ut peste a in hunc Mundi cum Helia redeat, & suo sanguine Antichristum extinguat. Ad quod Augustinus quoque lib. 20. Civit. Dei, cap. 29. capit 11.3. Apoc. accommodat: sed omnino frustra. Epiphanius melius. Nam in Ancorato translatum Chanochum scribit, ut effet pijs etiam ante dilnsum viventibus typum & exemplum aliquod futurae resurrectionis, & salsissimi carnis nostrae flatus. Cui sententiae suffragatur Augustinus lib. 15. Civit. Dei, cap. 19. his verbis, [Huius Enoch translatio nostrae dedicationis est prefigurata dilatio, quae quidem iam facta est in Christo capite nostro, qui sic resurrexit, ut non moriatur ulterius, sed etiam ipse translatus est.] Cyrillus tertiam quoque huius facti causam affert lib. 3. contra Julianum, sect. 6 nempe vult eum translatum esse a Deo in caelum, ut Deus hoc facto perpetuum suum in pios & sui timentes homines amorem quocunque tempore illi fuerint, demonstraret, sicque eos ad bene viuendum cohortaretur, & a mundi corruptione retraheret. Et haec quidem tertia est verissima huius translationis causa, nimirum, ut pios illius saeculi primum, post autem etiam nascituros homines omnes confirmaret Deus in spem reseruata illis propter Messiam vitam aeternam, quam & animo & corpore possessuri tandem sunt in caelo. Consentit cum eo quod scriptum est Sapient. 4. 11. translatum Chanochum, ne malitia, quae tunc in Mundo inualuerat, immutaret eius pietatem & animum: & ut, quemadmodum traditur Eccles.44.16. esset infidelibus exemplum pœnitentiæ. Q. Quomodo translatus est à Deo Chanochus, utrum per mortem, an cum corpore: item, utrum visibiliter & in conspectu omnium, an secreto & clanculum. R. Epiphanius lib.2. Tomo 1. contra Hæreses, hæresi 64 ait Chanochum cum suo corpore translatum fuisse: [Non enim translatus est Enochus, ait, & reliquit corpus inhis terris, aut corporis partem. Si enim reliquit corpus, ergo vidit mortem. Ipse vero cum corpore translatus non vidit mortem, ut est Heb.11.5, Eccles.44.16. Sic igitur Gen.5.24. verba hæc sunt intelligenda, [Et assumpsit eum Deus.] Hoc idem ante Epiphanium sensit, scripserat, Irenæus lib.5: [In quo corpore, ait, placuit Deo Enoch, in eo translatus esse. Quare nequaquam ille mortuus est, separatà ab eius corpore anima, sed mutatus est momento temporis, & illu oculi: sicut plerique pij in ipso die Resurrectionis mutabuntur, ait Paulus 1.Cor.15.51: & Helias postea raptus est à Deo, & mutatus, 2.Reg.2. Ergo quod scribit Tertullianus in lib. de Resurrect. Carnis, eum cum aliis in resurrectione coram Christo apparituram, & resurrecturum, verum est: quemadmodum illi quoque, qui sunt in Mundi consummatione mutandi, resurgent. Quod autem idem Tertullianus addit, eum moriturum postea, & ante extremam resurrectionem esse, id est, morti debitum persoluturum, ut loquitur ipse, & ex Tertulliano sentit Augustinus, lib.9.Genes. ad liter. cap.6. id vero falsum est. Neque enim postea morietur Chanochus, quemadmodum neque Helias. Ceterum quid agat, ubi sit, & alia eiusdem generis quaerere curiosum est, idque salua
units.tr: Q. How is this pious Enoch the seventh from Adam, when he seems to be the sixth from him only? Jude, verse 14. For between him and Adam there lie only these five: Seth, Enos, Kenan, Mahalalel, Jared. Yet Augustine, in De civitate Dei 15, chapter 19, makes him the sixth from Seth, and Jude makes him, as I have said, the seventh from Adam. A. The Jews and Augustine count all the persons, Adam included, and so make this Enoch the seventh from Adam and the sixth from Seth: thus (1) Adam; (2) Seth; (3) Enos; (4) Kenan; (5) Mahalalel; (6) Jared; (7) Enoch. Otherwise, if these persons (whose number is in dispute, though I do not say wrongly) are not counted, he will be only the sixth from Adam, and the fifth from his great-grandfather Seth, as this pious man is. He is written [Chanochus] in the Hebrew Scripture. The Apostle to the Hebrews, chapter 11, verse 5, and Jude in his epistle, verse 14, and Epiphanius in the first book of the Panarion, or Capsula, and also in the Ancoratus, name him in Greek [Enoch, Εὐνὸχ], for the sake of a smoother sound, lest variation in the name perhaps confuse someone. Q. What was contained in the book of this pious Enoch? A. Both rebukes of the wicked and consolations of the godly. For he also set forth and renewed the promise of eternal life made by God to the godly, to be fulfilled through and for the sake of the coming Messiah, and he recalled the most severe judgments of God to be coming upon the impious, especially their destruction, which was near, since the morals of men were by then intolerable. Accordingly he condemned idolatry and blasphemy of the Name of God, now publicly accepted, and he sharply rebuked the corrupters of morals and the licentious lives of men and women alike, as Tertullian teaches in his book On Idolatry and in the one he wrote On the Dress of Women. Indeed that most grievous anathema which Paul calls Maranatha, 1 Corinthians 16, verse 22, was hurled against them, as some explain the verse 14 in Jude. Some hold that some testimonies and certain fragments of this book are, and were, found in the book called the Testament of the Twelve Patriarchs, which Origen and Procopius approve. But it is now pointless to ask whether that book should be reckoned among the Apocrypha or the Canonical books. Laurentius Bareus, a man who wears himself out in vain against Tertullian (and one about whom you cannot say whether he is more meddlesome or more foolish, for he has both of these great faults, being, as he himself says, a fellow-countryman of the unspeakable monster G. Postel, and he glories in the fact), has tried to argue this. For the book no longer exists. And if it survived complete and uninterpolated, since Jude uses its testimony as that of a true prophet of the true God, there would be no doubt that it ought to be placed among the Canonical books. Q. Why was Enoch taken up by God in such a corruption of the whole world? A. All affirm that God indeed translated him, but few explain why. Josephus, in Antiquities book 1, chapter 5, and Philo in Biblical Antiquities, and Zonaras in book 1 of his Annals, and Jerome against Jovinian, and almost countless others acknowledge the event, and most truly, from Genesis 5. But they do not teach why God did it. Certainly the reasoning of Jerome, who denies that he was translated because he had a wife, is utterly ridiculous. For, as Epiphanius teaches in the Ancoratus, Enoch was translated while married, just as Elijah, who was unmarried, was taken up. Indeed Enoch was the earlier and married, Elijah the later and unmarried. But who taught them that Elijah was rather unmarried, and not Enoch too, and Moses? Irenaeus therefore gives one cause of this translation in book 5 against Valentinus: that God might show beforehand, in him, the translation into heaven, in body and soul, that would be the lot of righteous and godly men, even of the uncircumcised. Tertullian and Epiphanius write this against the Jews, as they show that the same condition will apply to the circumcised godly in Elijah. For Irenaeus compares these two with each other in book 4, chapter 30. Tertullian mentions this translation of Enoch in various places, and calls him a candidate of eternity, as in his book against the Jews and in On the Resurrection of the Flesh. The same Tertullian thinks that God translated him into heaven for another reason also, namely in On the Soul, chapter 28, so that he might return with Elijah to this world and destroy Antichrist with his blood. Augustine too applies this to Revelation 11, verse 3, in De civitate Dei 20, chapter 29, but quite in vain. Epiphanius is better. For in the Ancoratus he writes that Enoch was translated so that he would be, even for the godly living before the flood, a type and some example of the future resurrection and of the healing of our flesh. Augustine supports this opinion in De civitate Dei 15, chapter 19, in these words: [The translation of this Enoch was a foreshadowing of our dedication, which has indeed already taken place in Christ our head, who so rose that he does not die any more, but was also himself translated.] Cyril gives a third cause of this event as well, in book 3 against Julian, section 6: he wants Enoch to have been translated by God into heaven so that God might show by this deed his perpetual love towards the godly and God-fearing men, at whatever time they lived, and so might encourage them to live well and withdraw them from the corruption of the world. And this third is indeed the truest cause of this translation: namely, that God might confirm the godly of that age first, and afterwards all men yet to be born, in the hope of eternal life reserved for them through the Messiah, which they will at last possess in heaven both in soul and in body. It agrees with what is written in Wisdom 4, verse 11: Enoch was translated lest wickedness, which had then prevailed in the world, should change his piety and his mind; and, as is handed down in Ecclesiasticus 44, verse 16, that he should be an example of repentance to the unbelievers. Q. How was Enoch translated by God: whether through death, or with his body; and likewise, whether visibly and in the sight of all, or secretly and privately? A. Epiphanius, in book 2, volume 1, of his Against Heresies, heresy 64, says that Enoch was translated with his body: [For Enoch, he says, was not translated and left his body in these lands, or a part of the body. For if he left his body, then he saw death. But he was translated with his body and did not see death, as in Hebrews 11, verse 5 and Ecclesiasticus 44, verse 16. So then Genesis 5, verse 24, must be understood in these words: And God took him.] Irenaeus, who wrote before Epiphanius, thought the same, in book 5: [In the body in which Enoch pleased God, he, says Irenaeus, was translated in that same body. Therefore he by no means died, with his soul separated from his body, but he was changed in a moment of time, in the twinkling of an eye, just as many of the godly will be changed on the very day of the resurrection, as Paul says, 1 Corinthians 15, verse 51. And Elijah was afterwards caught up by God and changed, 2 Kings 2.] Therefore what Tertullian writes in On the Resurrection of the Flesh, that he will appear before Christ in the resurrection with the others and will rise again, is true; just as those also who are to be changed at the consummation of the world will rise. But what the same Tertullian adds, that he will die afterwards, before the final resurrection, that is, will pay the debt of death, as Tertullian himself puts it, and Augustine follows Tertullian in this, in De Genesi ad litteram 9, chapter 6, that is false. For Enoch will not die afterwards, any more than Elijah. As for what he is doing, where he is, and other questions of this kind, it is a curious matter to inquire; and these may easily be left unknown while the Christian faith is kept safe, as Augustine says in his book On the Original Sin, against the Caelestians.

units.la: (margin-less page; no further notes) salua fide Christiana ignorari facilè potest, ait idè Augustinus lib. de Peccato Originali contra Cœlestiū. Eius tamen, vt Heliæ, status est selicissimus, quem sic describit Tertullianus: [Duo illi, ait, tam æternitatis candidati, ab omni vitio, & ab omni damno, & ab omni injuria & contumelia immunitatem carnis edissunt.] Et hæc quidè de prima parte quæstionis. De secunda verò sic est sentiendum, Eum notoriè & visibiliter, id est, in conspectu hominum, non clàculum à Deo e terris suisse subductum, vt res testatior etiam improbis ipsis esset, qui Deum contemnebant, idque ad eorum iudicium: pijs verò ad suam consolationem. Itaque postea sedulo quæsitus est ab hominibus quemadmodum & Heliæ: nec tamen ab iis vsquam repertus, aut inuentus in terris.
units.tr: It may easily be ignored without harm to the Christian faith, as Augustine says in his book On Original Sin against the Celestians. Yet his state, like Elijah's, is most happy, which Tertullian describes thus: [Those two, he says, candidates for eternity, have been freed by the immunity of the flesh from every vice, every loss, every injury and insult.] And these things are said about the first part of the question. About the second, however, it must be judged thus: that he was taken from the earth by God not secretly but openly and visibly, that is, in the sight of men, so that the fact would be more evident even to the wicked who despised God, for their judgement; but to the pious, for their consolation. Therefore afterwards he was diligently sought by men, as Elijah was; yet he was nowhere found or discovered on earth.

units.la: Q. Quò raptus est Chanochus, in cœlumne, an in his terris substitit, ac repositus est nos latens. sicut corpus Mosis, Deut. 3. 4. R. Nonnulli existimant Chanochum hunc raptum & sepositum à Deo fuisse in Paradiso terrestri: sic Thomas Aquinas in 3. p. 49. 5. 2: Heliam verò in cœlum aëreum, id est, in hunc aërem nobis superiorem. Verùm Apostolus ad Hebræos, id est ipsa veritas cap. 11. 5, ait μετετεθη Ενωχ. Quod si quis recte intellexerit, fatebitur hunc ex his terris in cœlu .i. aliquem nobis superiorem locum à Deo raptu & translatum fuisse, vt etiam dicitur Eccles 49. 16. Ergo ex oculis hominum ablatus est, & iis inspicientibus in cœlu eleuatus, vti Helias, 2. Reg. 2. 11. Itaque ait Moses Gen. 5. 24, [Deus eu assumpsit] vt de Helia 2. Reg. 2. 9. Nec eum, quem Deus relinquit in his terris dicitur assumere: sed quem ex hu inferioribus locu in superiora transfert. Etsi vero Christus in cœlum post resurrectionem ascendens, in cœlum supremum & beatorum ab his terris sublevatus est, Act. 1. 9: nō censuerim tamen Heliam vel Chanochum in cœlum illud supremum ac beatorum sive hominum, sive Angelorum domicilium adhuc cum corpore esse receptum, in quem locū primus cum corpore ingressus est D. N. Iesus Christus, qui propterea dicitur à Paulo Primogenitus mortuorum, Colof. 1. 18. Q. Quando translatus est Chanochus ex his terris? R. A Mundo condito anno 987. A Profanatione nominis Dei anno 762. Ante Diluuium vniuersale anno 669. Nam ab Orbe condito ad Profanationem nominis Dei intercedunt anni 235: ab hac ad natum pium Chanochum sunt anni 387: ab eo nato ad eundem translatum 365. Hi omnes collecti faciunt summam 987, qui ab annis, quibus contigit Diluuium nempe annis 1656 subductis, relinquunt 669: quo toto temporis spatio precessit haec translatio Diluuium. Erratigitur Laurentius iste Barrau, qui in Tertullianū scribit hanc translationem accidisse anno 1015 ab orbe condito. Verum ille pluribus aliis in locis dormitat, aut potius cacutit. Accedamus ad quintum nostra historia caput.
units.tr: Q. Where was Enoch taken, into heaven, or did he remain in these lands and was he hidden, concealed from us, like the body of Moses, Deut. 3. 4.? A. Some think that this Enoch was taken up and laid aside by God in the earthly Paradise, as Thomas Aquinas holds in 3 p. 49. 5. 2. Elijah, however, was taken into the aerial heaven, that is, into this air above us.
