But the Apostle in the Epistle to the Hebrews, that is, the truth itself, chapter 11, verse 5, says that Enoch was translated [μετετέθη Ενωχ]. If anyone understands this rightly, he will confess that this man was taken and transferred from these lands into heaven, that is, into some place above us, by God, as is also said in Ecclesiasticus 49. 16. Therefore he was removed from the eyes of men and, while they looked on, was lifted up into heaven, as Elijah was, 2 Kings 2. 11. Thus Moses says in Genesis 5. 24, [God took him], as of Elijah in 2 Kings 2. 9. For the one whom God leaves on this earth is not said to be taken up; rather, he is one whom God transfers from these lower places to higher ones. Although Christ, ascending into heaven after the resurrection, was lifted from this earth into the highest heaven, the dwelling of the blessed, Acts 1. 9, I would not, however, think that Elijah or Enoch has yet been received bodily into that highest heaven, the dwelling of the blessed, whether of men or of angels, into which our Lord Jesus Christ first entered bodily; for which reason he is called by Paul the firstborn from the dead, Colossians 1. 18. Q. When was Enoch taken from these lands? A. In the year 987 from the creation of the world, in the year 762 from the profanation of the name of God, and in the year 669 before the universal Flood. For from the creation of the world to the profanation of the name of God there are 235 years; from that to the birth of pious Enoch there are 387 years; from his birth to the same Enoch's translation, 365. All these added together make the sum of 987, which, when the years in which the Flood happened, namely 1656, are subtracted, leave 669: in all this span of time this translation preceded the Flood. Therefore Laurentius Barrau, who writes against Tertullian that this translation happened in the year 1015 from the creation of the world, is mistaken. But he nods off, or rather is blind, in many other places. Let us come to the fifth chapter of our history.

units.la: Ad V. Deprauatio reliquorum Piorum per connubia cum impijs mulieribus.
units.tr: Chapter V. The corruption of the other godly by marriages with ungodly women.

units.la: Quaeritur, Quid voces hæ, [Filij Dei, Filiae hominum] significent ac notent. R. Filij, Filiæq, nomen vel proprie sumitur, vel metaphorice. Proprie sumsumptum significat eũ qui ex altero vel tota essentia, vel jemine natus est. Sic Christus est filius, & quidem solus Dei Patris, quoniam ex eius tota essentia est, Ioan. 1.1.2.3. Simo Petrus fuit Bar .i. filius Iona, Math. 16.17: quoniam ex eius femine procreatus erat. Metaphoricè quis Filius appellatur variis modis, propterea quod & qui a nobis affectu paterno alitur, ac diligitur, etiam non adoptatus: & qui ab alio adoptatus est in locum filij: & qui sese ad nostros mores immitandos totum comparat, [Filius nostER] tropicè appellatur. Sic Epiphanius lib.3.Tom.3.Haref.73.distinguit. Sic Basilius contra Eunomium. Sic vsus linguarum omnium. Ergo dum Deo paremus, nosque ad illius voluntatem coformamus, [Filij Dei] metaphoricè vocamur, Ioan. 1.12,1.Ioan.3.1.10. Qui vero ad Diaboli voluntatē sese componunt exprimendam ij quoque dicuntur Filij Diaboli, Ioan.8.44. Sic qui hominum (quatenus eorum voluntas Dei voluntati repugnat) nutum, affectus, mores, vitam improbam probat, sequuntur, & imitantur, ij dicuntur hoc loco filij hominum. Quemadmodū contrà Filij Dei nominantur hic à Mose, qui Deum tunc pie colebant, eius praeceptū obtemperabāt, & a vitiosa hominū vita sese segregabant. Ergo homines verè pij sunt ij, quos Dei Filios vocat Gen.6.2. Impiorum autem hominū filia & ipse quoque impie sunt ea, quas idem ibidem appellat Filias hominū. Nec verò me latet, Iob.1.6, Angelos vocari Filios Dei: & alio quoq; sensu homines etiam improbos dici à Deo genitos, & alitos, Isa.1.2. Verum hoc loco sumuntur Filij Dei, & Filia hominum eo sensu, quo dixi. Nostram sententiam confirmat Augustinus lib. 15. Ciuit. Dei cap. 22: Cyrillus lib. 9. contra Iulian. sect. 1: Zonaras lib. 1. Annal. his verbis, [Vocat autem Dei Filios Scriptura Sethi posteros ob studium, & cultum virtutis, quo patre etiam filios Altissimi vocat eos, qui sunt virtute praediti. Hominum vero filias nominat oriundas ex Caini posteris.] Q. Virum Angeli quoque cum filiabus hominum tunc concubuerint. R. Augustinus lib. 15. Ciuit. Dei, cap. 23. ait esse impudentis hominis negare malignos spiritus, quales sunt Daemones mali, (qui procul dubio sunt Angeli) posse, & solere mulieribus misceri, earumq; immunditiam attentare, & libidinem peragere. Nam & Fauni, & Syluani, & Incubi Daemones, & Dusii, quos Galli vocant, id efficiunt. Ex quo factum est, ut Patrum plerique exististimauerint, dixerintque hic quoque intelligendum malignos illos, & immundos Spiritus cum foeminis coitu habuisse, ex quo coitu nati sint Gigantes, Gen. 6. 4. Sic Iosephus lib. 1. Antiquit. Iudaic. cap. 5, licet eum excusat Zonaras. Philo Iudaeus in Antiquit. Bibl. Tertullianus lib. 5. contra Marcion. & de Habitu Muliebri: Imo etiam idem vult eas foeminas (quas isti Angeli iniuerint) fuisse virgines, non viduas: atque etiam Angelos illos fuisse non adulteros, sed maritos huiusmodi filiarum & mulierum, in lib. de Velandis Virginibus. Quae opinio ex eo etiam confirmata est, quod Ethnici (ut scribit Varro apud Augustin. lib. 3. Ciuit. Dei, cap. 4) censuerunt omnes egregios viros ex Dijs natos: quae res eos commendabat. Denique hoc quoq; ipsum Lactantius lib. 2. cap. 14 sentit, secutus Tertullianum. Verum refellitur haec sententia & ratione, ex fine Mosis. Itaque sine circuitione vocatur falsa ab Isidoro lib.1. Etymologic. & à Cyrillo,loco,quem tam demonstrauimus. Consentit cum his Augustinus libro Quæst.in Genef.cap.3. Ac quidè ratione confutatur, quod ex Animalium diuersa speciei cömixtione & coitu nihil gigni potest. Dixit enim Dominus,iussitque vt res vnaquæque produceret sibi simile,& secundum speciem suam Gen.1.21.24. Iac.3.12. Itaque in vnoquoq; Animantium genere Masculum & fœminam creauit Deus. At vero ex isto filiorū Dei & filiarum hominū concubitu nati sunt Gigantes, id est,homines Gen.6.4. Ergo ex hominis Maris & fœmina coitu concubitúque isti nati iunt:non autem Angeli cum homine fœmina coierunt,quæ sunt duo,diuersaq; rerum genera, ex quibus nihil procrearetur. Nam quod videtur obyci posse de Minotauro (qui, vt est in fabulis, ex Pasiphaë fœmina homine,& Tauro animali bruto,natus est) facilè conuellitur. Istud enim est cömentum poëticum falsum & fabulosum. Deinde hoc ipsum aliter interpretatur Palæphatus in lib.de Fabul.Narration. Aiit enim illum,cum quo Pasiphaë scortata est,fuisse Minois regis secretarium,qui Taurus nominabatur:non autem Taurum animal brutū. Et hæc quidem est prima superioris sententiæ cöfutanda ratio. Altera vero hæc,Quod plane pugnat cum scopo Mosis, Agere de Angelis hoc loco , quum totius huius historiæ finis sit demonstrare, non quid Angeli:sed quid homines in his terris versantes inter se perpetrarint,ac egerint,per quod Dei iudicium in sese pronocarunt. Q. Cur damnentur Filij Dei seu impij homines,quod filias hominum,id est,impias in vxores propter formam sibi duxerint, Gen 6.2: quum forma pulchritudoque sit Dei donum, vt scribit Augustinus lib. 15. Ciuit. Dei, cap. 22. R. Forma quidem pulchritudoque corporis est Dei donum, quae etiam in Rachele laudatur, Gen. 29.17. & laudandum, & optandū: vt & Homerus lib. 3. Iliad. & Plato in dial. de Pulcro fatentur: tamen huiusmodi donum est, vt illis pietas, mstus, cultusque Dei sit praeferendus. Recte enim Augustinus ait, [ Sic corporis pulcritudo a Deo quidem factum, sed temporale, carnale, infimum bonū male amatur, postposito Deo aeterno, interno, sempiterno bono. Ergo filij Dei filiarum hominum amore sunt capti: atque vt eis fruerentur, in amorem societatis terrigenae defluxerunt, deserta pietate, quam in sancta societate seruabāt.] Ergo nihil in istis mulieribus spectabant viri isti praeter solam corporis formam, ac venustatem: non autem earum bonos mores & pietatem. Quā-obrem, hac duo mala inde promanarunt: Vnum, quod ipsimet pij qui prius erant, per eiusmodi connubia tanquam mali contagia euaserunt malt: (Corrumpunt enim bonos mores colloquia conuersationesque prauae) & idololatrae, & impij & improbi. Id quod & Esauo postea propter suum cum improbis foeminis coniugium euenit, vt esset profanus, Gen. 26.34. Heb.12.16: & Salomoni sapientissimo Regi, 1.Reg.11. Itaque merito semper damnatū est velut Exo.34 16, Deut.7.3. Nehe. 13.2 Cor.16.14, Iudic.3.5.6, tale coniugium. Alterum malum fuit, quod qui liberi ex eo coniugio nascebantur, impie à matribus educabantur, quarum mores potius imitatur filij, fiebantque & ipsi postea impij. Cuius rei exemplum est Nehem. 13.24. Q. Vnde ista filiorum Dei cum filiabus hominum, imò cum ipsis hominibus, id est, impijs coniunctio, copulatio, affinitas quæ primùm nata est. R. Philo scribit in Antiquit. Biblic. hæc affinitatem à filijs Caini primum ambitam, ac quæsitam fuisse. Chanochum enim Caini filium coniugium sibi in domo Sethi quæsiisse, & ex eius filiabus vxorem sibi sumpsisse. Itaque misceri per coniugia alios cum alijs ex eo tempore cœpisse, nempe pios cum impijs. Verum non potuit, nisi admodum iam senex & pene decrepitus, Chanochus impius, id est Caini filius ducere in vxorem filiam vllam Sethi, qui eodem illo iam grādæuo natus est. Ego verò sentio, Primùm pios ab impijs, id est, filios Sethi à filijs Caini familia, conuersatione familiari, & conuictu, imo etiā sedibus distinctos separatosque fuisse: idq; diu durasse, donec multū multiplicaretur genus humanum ipsaque adeo familia ex Setho nata in varios ramos & loca diffusa dispersaq; essent. Ex quo factū est, vt tum propter paulatim in posteris etiam Sethi labascentem pietatem (facilè enim tepescere pietatis æstus inter homines solet) iū propter vitæ huius necessitatem, Sethi posteri cōmercium cum posteris Caini hominibus industrijs frequentius, quam antea haberent. Erat enim, vti supra demonstratū est, filij Caini homines industrij, quorum ingenium admirarentur, quorumque opera & artificijs egerent Sethiani. Sic consilio Iethronis fecerit fui, licet hominis infidelis, eguit, ac vsus est Moses socer Dei, eumque secum in castris Israelitarum habuit Exod. 18.17. Praterea, vt ait Paulus 1.Cor. 5.10. omnino nobis ex hoc Mundo esset exeundum, si cum nullo huius mundi homine improbo cogredi vellemus. Quandam enim cum ys communicationem exigit ipsa humanae vitae necessitas. Denique Homo est natura animal gregarium, ut ait Tullius libr. 1 .Offic. Quare primum pij cum impijs commercia propter eam causam exercuerunt, illisque familiares sunt, effectis: tum denique instigante libidine, & forma illa filiarum impiarum egregia & venusta eosdem vrente & rapiente, conjugia cum illis contraxerunt, seq; it a paulatim omnino corruperunt. Ergo nobis sedulo cauendum hodie quoque est, ne huiusmodi conuersatione & consuetudine depravemur primum: post autem penitus corrumpamur. Q. Vtrum illae hominum filiae, id est mulieres impiae, sed formosae ex solis Caini posteris fuerint, an iam etiam quaedam tales extiterint ex filijs ipsius Sethi. R. Philo in Antiquit. putat promiscue tales ex utroque genere, nempe Caini, & Sethi, exitisse. Cyrillus lib. 9. contra Iulian. tales ex solis Caini posteris fuisse. Moses autem, Gen 6.2. sic scribit, & quidem generaliter, [Videntes filij Dei filias hominum bona forma esse, acceperunt sibi mulieres (id est vxores) ex omnibus, quas eligebant.] Ex quibus verbis videtur colligi tam tum quoque ex Sethanis nonnullas mulieres formosas quidem fuisse, sed impias, quas tamen viri Dei & pij potius sibi coniuges esse malebat, quam pias & deformes feminas. Sic pulcritudo pietati, venustas sanctitati, color cordi vbiq; ab istis in coniugijs quarendis praeferebatur. At nos in Domino coniugia quaerere oportet, quemadmodum docuit 1.Cor. 7.39. Q. Quando ista piorum depravatio per connubia cum impijs contigerit. R. Quoniam hoc pro certo statuimus, Mosen in texenda scribendaq̃, hac historia rationem temporis secutum, & qua prius euenerunt, priore quoque loco recitasse sentimus hanc deprauationem contigisse post translatum Chanochum illumpium interiecto temporis spatio, antequã tota humani generis corruptio euenisset. Ergo hæc facta sunt sub Mathuselacho & Lamecho, quū iam illud exemplum munerata & beanda in Chanocho translato hominum pietatis obsoleuisset, & ex hominũ memoria pene perisset. Contigerit igitur hæc depravatio piorum circiter annũ à Mundo condito 1100: post translatum Chanochum, annis 120: ante Diluuium, annis 550. Verum ad Gigantum procreationem, qui ex isto cõiugio nati sunt, veniamus.
units.tr: The question is: what do these words, [sons of God, daughters of men], signify and mean? Answer: The words son and daughter are used either properly or metaphorically. Used properly, a son is one born of another, either from his whole substance or from his seed. Thus Christ is the Son, and indeed the only Son, of God the Father, since he is from the Father's whole substance (John 1.1, 2, 3). Simon Peter was Bar-Jona, that is, the son of Jona (Matt. 16.17), since he was begotten of Jona's seed. Metaphorically, a son is called such in various ways: whoever is nourished and loved by us with fatherly affection, even if not adopted; whoever has been adopted by another in place of a son; and whoever wholly sets himself to imitate our manners is called a son figuratively. So Epiphanius distinguishes in book 3, volume 3, heresy 73; so Basil against Eunomius; so the usage of all languages. Therefore, when we obey God and conform ourselves to his will, we are called sons of God metaphorically (John 1.12; 1 John 3.1, 10). Those who set themselves to express the will of the devil are also called sons of the devil (John 8.44). In the same way, those men who approve, follow and imitate the nod, passions, manners and wicked life of men (insofar as their will is opposed to the will of God) are called here sons of men. Conversely, those who worshipped God devoutly at that time, obeyed his commandment, and kept themselves apart from the sinful life of men are called by Moses sons of God. Therefore the men who are truly godly are those whom Genesis 6.2 calls sons of God. The daughters of ungodly men, however, are themselves also ungodly, and the same passage calls them daughters of men. I am not unaware that in Job 1.6 angels are called sons of God, and in another sense men, even wicked ones, are said to be begotten and reared by God (Isa. 1.2). But here the sons of God and the daughters of men are taken in the sense I have stated. Our view is confirmed by Augustine, City of God, book 15, chapter 22; Cyril, against Julian, book 9, section 1; Zonaras, Annals, book 1, in these words: [Scripture calls the posterity of Seth the sons of God because of their zeal and cultivation of virtue, as it also calls those endowed with virtue sons of the Most High. But it names as daughters of men those descended from the posterity of Cain.] Question: Did the angels also then lie with the daughters of men? Answer: Augustine, City of God, book 15, chapter 23, says it is the mark of a shameless man to deny that evil spirits, such as the wicked demons (who are without doubt angels), can and do mix with women, attempt their impurity and carry out their lust. For Fauns, Satyrs, incubi demons and the Dusii, whom the Gauls call such, do this. Hence it came about that many of the Fathers thought, and said, that here too we must understand those wicked and unclean spirits to have had intercourse with women, and from this union the Giants were born (Gen. 6.4). So Josephus, Jewish Antiquities, book 1, chapter 5, though Zonaras excuses him. Philo the Jew, in Biblical Antiquities; Tertullian, against Marcion, book 5, and On the Dress of Women. Indeed, Tertullian holds that the women these angels lay with were virgins, not widows, and that the angels were not adulterers but husbands of such daughters and women, in his book On the Veiling of Virgins. This opinion was also confirmed by the fact that the heathen (as Varro writes, quoted in Augustine, City of God, book 3, chapter 4) believed that all outstanding men were born of the gods, and this made them celebrated. Finally, Lactantius, book 2, chapter 14, also holds this view, following Tertullian. But this opinion is refuted by reason, from the purpose of Moses. Hence Isidore, Etymologies, book 1, and Cyril in the passage we have cited, rightly call it false without qualification. Augustine agrees with them in Questions on Genesis, chapter 3. It is also refuted by reason, since nothing can be generated from the mixing and union of animals of different species. For the Lord said, and commanded that each thing should produce what is like itself, and according to its kind (Gen. 1.21, 24; James 3.12). So God created male and female in each kind of living creature. But from that union of the sons of God and the daughters of men the Giants were born, that is, men (Gen. 6.4). Therefore they were born from the union and intercourse of a male man and a female man, and not of angels with a human woman; these are two different kinds of beings, from which nothing could be produced. As for the objection that might seem to be raised about the Minotaur (who, as the fables tell, was born of Pasiphae, a woman, and a bull, a brute animal), this is easily overturned. For that is a false and fabulous poetic invention. Moreover, Palaephatus, in his book On Fabulous Narrations, interprets this very story differently: he says that the man with whom Pasiphae committed adultery was a secretary of King Minos, who was called the Bull, and not a brute animal bull. And this is the first reason for refuting the view above. The second is this, which plainly conflicts with the purpose of Moses: to treat of angels in this place, when the whole aim of this history is to show not what the angels did, but what men living on this earth committed and did among themselves, by which they provoked God's judgment upon themselves. Question: Why are the sons of God, that is, ungodly men, condemned for taking as their wives the daughters of men, that is, ungodly women, for their beauty (Gen. 6.2), when beauty of form and body is a gift of God, as Augustine writes in City of God, book 15, chapter 22? Answer: The beauty and comeliness of the body is indeed a gift of God, and it is praised even in Rachel (Gen. 29.17), and it is to be praised and desired; Homer, Iliad, book 3, and Plato in his dialogue on the beautiful also confess this. Yet such a gift must be ranked below piety, chastity and the worship of God. For Augustine rightly says: So the beauty of the body, made indeed by God but temporal, fleshly and the lowest good, is loved wrongly, when the eternal, inward and everlasting good, God, is set aside. Therefore the sons of God were captivated by love of the daughters of men, and in order to enjoy them they slid into love of earthly society, abandoning the piety they had kept in the holy society. Therefore these men regarded nothing in those women except the bare form and charm of the body, and not their good manners and piety. For this reason two evils came forth from it. The first is that those who had been godly before, through such marriages, like contagions of evil, became wicked (for evil conversations and associations corrupt good manners), idolaters, ungodly and wicked. The same thing later happened to Esau, who, because of his marriage with wicked women, became profane (Gen. 26.34; Heb. 12.16), and to Solomon, the wisest king (1 Kings 11). So such a marriage has always been rightly condemned (Exod. 34.16; Deut. 7.3; Neh. 13.25; 2 Cor. 6.14; Judg. 3.5, 6). The second evil was that the children born of such a marriage were brought up impiously by their mothers, and the sons imitated their mothers' manners more than their fathers', and so they themselves too became ungodly. An example of this is in Nehemiah 13.24. Question: Where did this union, joining and kinship of the sons of God with the daughters of men, or rather with men themselves, that is, the ungodly, first arise? Answer: Philo writes in Biblical Antiquities that this kinship was first sought and courted by the sons of Cain. For Enoch, son of Cain, sought a wife for himself in the house of Seth and took one of Seth's daughters as his wife. So from that time people began to mix with one another through marriages, namely the godly with the ungodly. But Enoch the ungodly, that is the son of Cain, could not have taken any daughter of Seth as his wife unless he had been already very old and nearly decrepit, since Seth was born in that same age. For my part, I think that, first, the godly were separated from the ungodly, that is, the sons of Seth from the family of the sons of Cain, by distinct family life, association and living together, and even by separate dwellings; and that this lasted for a long time, until the human race had multiplied greatly and the family descended from Seth had spread and been scattered into various branches and places. From this it came about that the descendants of Seth, partly because of the gradual cooling of piety in their posterity (for the fervour of piety is apt to grow lukewarm among men), and partly because of the necessities of this life, had dealings with the posterity of Cain, the industrious men, more often than before. For, as has been shown above, the sons of Cain were industrious men, whose talent they admired and by whose works and skills the sons of Seth were served. Thus Moses, the son-in-law of God, made use of the counsel of his father-in-law Jethro, though he was an unbeliever, and kept him with him in the camp of the Israelites (Exod. 18.17). Moreover, as Paul says (1 Cor. 5.10), we would have to go out of this world altogether if we wished to have no dealings with any wicked man of this world. For the very necessity of human life requires some fellowship with them. Finally, man is by nature a gregarious animal, as Cicero says in On Duties, book 1. Therefore the godly first had dealings with the ungodly for that reason, and became familiar with them; then at last, driven by lust, and seized and inflamed by the outstanding and charming beauty of those ungodly daughters, they contracted marriages with them, and so gradually corrupted themselves altogether. Therefore we too today must take careful heed lest we first be depraved by such association and intimacy, and afterwards be utterly corrupted. Question: Were those daughters of men, that is, ungodly but beautiful women, drawn only from the posterity of Cain, or were some such women already found among the sons of Seth himself? Answer: Philo, in Antiquities, thinks that such women were found indiscriminately from both lines, that is, from Cain and from Seth. Cyril, against Julian, book 9, holds that such women were only from the posterity of Cain. Moses, however, writes in Genesis 6.2 in a general way: [The sons of God, seeing that the daughters of men were fair, took for themselves wives (that is, wives) from all whom they chose.] From these words it seems to be inferred that even then there were some women of the line of Seth who were indeed beautiful but ungodly, yet the sons of God and the godly preferred to have them as their wives rather than pious and plain women. Thus beauty was preferred to piety, charm to holiness, and colour to the heart in the seeking of marriages by those men everywhere. But we ought to seek marriage in the Lord, as 1 Corinthians 7.39 teaches. Question: When did this corruption of the godly through marriages with the ungodly take place? Answer: Since we hold this as certain, we think that Moses, in weaving and writing this history, followed the order of time, and recounted first what happened earlier. So this corruption happened after the translation of Enoch the godly, with an interval of time before the whole corruption of the human race had come about. Therefore these things were done under Methuselah and Lamech, when that example of the piety of men, honoured and celebrated in the translated Enoch, had grown obsolete and had nearly perished from men's memory. This corruption of the godly therefore happened about the year 1100 from the creation of the world, 120 years after the translation of Enoch, and 550 years before the Flood. But let us now come to the birth of the Giants, who were born of this union.

units.la: Ad VI. Gigantum Procreatio.
units.tr: Chapter VI. The Procreation of the Giants.

units.la: Quæritur, Quid vox Nephilim apud Mosen Gen. 6.4. significet. R. Nonnulli hac vocem conuertunt [Defectores, seu Apostatæ] nempe qui à Dei cultu publicè ac palàm deficiunt, vel defecerãt, vti Iere. 37.13. Alij vertunt, [Angeli] vt veterum Patrum tam Grecorum, quàm Latinorum multi, qui hic de Angelis, non de hominibus agi putant. Tertij denique accipiunt hac vocem aliter, conuertúntque [Gigantes:] quorum sententiâ & nos quoque hoc loco sequimur. Nam sic quoq; Numer. 13 . 34 sumitur: & in nostrã sententiam transeunt Josephus lib. 1.cap. 5. Antiquit. Augustinus lib. 3 Ciuit. Dei, cap. 4. Cyrillus lib. 9. contra Julian. sect. 1. Isidorus lib. 11. Etymolog. Zonaras lib. 1. Annal. hūc Mosis locum interpretátes. Philo verò Iudæus in Antiquit. Biblic. hanc vocem non explicat. Sed imprimis nostram interpretationem confirmat Moyses ipse, qui hos Nephilim ait fuisse homines mortalium omnium, qui vnquam vixerunt, robustissimos, maximeque propterea apud posteros omnes celebres, & formidolosos. Et certè conuenit huic rei vocis huius etymon & ratio. Gigantes enim ab Hebraeis multis nominibus appellantur, velut [Nephilim,] quòd ad illorum aspectum categori homines tremore cadant, tanta nimirum, tam magnae sunt statura, atque formidabilis aspectus. Vnde idem illi etiam [Aemim] ab ijsdem Hebraeis dicuntur, id est, caeterorum hominum terror. Cyrillus loco iam citato [Fuerunt (inquit) Gigantes potentes quidem & fortissimi, sed aspectu valde deformi. Mos autem S. Scriptura est Gigantes vocare agrestes, & feroces, & robustos. Vnde viuerfarum Deus de Persis & Medis Iudaam deuastaturis dicit, Gigantes venient, vt impleant furorem meum, Isa. 13. Non tamen secundum Graecos nos tatos illos fuisse dicimus, vt insulas ex medio mari raperent, & in coelum proiicerent: sed fœdos aspectu, & monstrosos, & temerarios homines.] Haec Cyrillus, quae maxime locum hunc Moysis illustrant. Vocatur autem idem Gigantes ab Hebraeis [Hanaquim] vel a Torque, quem pro insigni gestabant, vel a nomine celeberrimi cuiusdam Gigantis, qui [Hanaq] vocabatur. Dicuntur etiam [Rephaim] quòd ad eorum conspectum languescerent, & velut deficerent, & obstupescerent pra metu. Denique nominatur quoque [Zan{ummim,] vel quòd ingenio solertes essent, vel astuti, vel fraudulenti, sceleratissimi, atque abominabiles, Deut. 2. 19. Gigantes autem Γηγενεῖς, Græcè, id est, è terra ipsa velut adhuc fœcunda & principio Mundi geniti. [Terrigenæ] Latinè, quod eos, vt ait Isidorus lib. 11. Etymolog. terra ipsa parens immensa mole corporis genuerit & profuderit. Et hac de voce Nephilim, & Gigantibus. An isti Gigantes ante Mundi diluuiû vniuersale nati, ý fuerint, quos postea sequens ætas, profanaq; vetustas, i. idololatræ homines Saturnos, Iones, Mercurios, aliosq; nominibus, vt ait Moses Gen. 6.4. vocarunt, & velut Deos postea coluerunt, Auerruncatores, & Ἀπότροπαιους. Etsi multa, quæ de istis Diis suis Idololatræ narrant, ante natos homines istos Gigantes facta sunt, vti antea docuimus: tamen illa ipsa postea fuerunt & his quoque ipsis attributa ab idololatris, & superstitiosis hominibus posteris, tum quòd quo tempore illa (quæ facta ac inuenta fuisse audiebât) contigissent, ignorabant: itaque ad homines sua ætati viciniores, & sibi notiores ea retulerunt: tum vt maiorem eorum colendorum rationem, iustiorémque habere viderentur, quum propter vel tot inuenta ab iis, vel gesta, vt putabant, eos credérent habere numen ferè diuinum. Fuit igitur hæc astutissima & robustissima Diaboli seu dæmonum fraus, vt tradit Lactant. lib. 2. cap. 14 15, & 16, nempe vt sub istorum hominum (qui tot benefici a generi humano tribuisse videbatur, quod fecerunt Caini posteri filij impij Lemechi, vel qui tam formidabiles aliis hominibus visi fuisse noscebantur, quales Gigantes isti fuerant) sub istorum. inquam, hominū nominibus & numinibus ipsimet Dæmones colerentur. In summa, & textus Mosis, hoc loco, Gen. 6.4: & Iosephi verba, lib. 1. cap. 5. docent,
units.tr: The question is what the word Nephilim in Moses, Gen. 6.4, means. Answer: some render this word "Defectors, or Apostates," that is, those who openly and publicly fall away, or have fallen away, from the worship of God, as in Jer. 37.13. Others render it "Angels," as many of the ancient Fathers, both Greek and Latin, did, who think that this passage speaks of angels and not of men. Finally, others take the word in a different sense and render it "Giants," and this is the view we also follow here. For it is used in this sense at Num. 13.34, and Josephus (Antiquities, book 1, chapter 5), Augustine (City of God, book 3, chapter 4), Cyril (against Julian, book 9, section 1), Isidore (Etymologies, book 11) and Zonaras (Annals, book 1), in interpreting this passage of Moses, agree with our view. Philo the Jew, however, does not explain this word in his Biblical Antiquities. But Moses himself above all confirms our interpretation, for he says that these Nephilim were the most robust of all mortals who have ever lived, and for that reason especially famous and dreaded among all later generations. The etymology and meaning of the word certainly agree with this. For the Hebrews call giants by many names. One is "Nephilim," because men fall down trembling at the sight of them, since they are so huge in stature and so formidable in appearance. For the same reason the Hebrews also call them "Aemim," that is, the terror of other men. Cyril, in the passage already cited: "The giants (he says) were indeed powerful and exceedingly strong, but of very ugly appearance. The manner of Holy Scripture is to call fierce, wild and robust men giants. Hence the God of hosts, speaking of the Persians and Medes who were to lay waste Judea, says: 'The giants shall come, to fulfil my wrath' (Isa. 13). Yet we do not say that those giants were so huge that they could snatch islands out of the middle of the sea and hurl them into heaven, as the Greeks tell; but that they were foul and monstrous in appearance and reckless men." These are Cyril's words, which most of all illustrate this passage of Moses. The giants are also called by the Hebrews "Hanaquim," either from the torque which they wore as a badge, or from the name of a very famous giant who was called "Hanaq." They are also called "Rephaim," because at their sight men grew faint, as if they failed and were stunned with fear. Finally they are also named "Zamzummim," either because they were skilful in mind, or clever and crafty, or most wicked and abominable deceivers (Deut. 2.19). The giants are called in Greek "Gēgeneis" [Γηγενεῖς], that is, born from the earth itself, as if it were still fruitful and had given birth at the beginning of the world. In Latin they are called "Terrigenae," because, as Isidore says (Etymologies, book 11), the earth itself, a huge parent, brought them forth and gave them birth with the immense mass of their bodies. So much for the words "Nephilim" and "giants." Whether these giants, born before the universal Flood, were those whom a later age, a profane antiquity, that is, idolatrous men, afterwards called, as Moses says (Gen. 6.4), Saturns, Iones, Mercuries and by other names, and afterwards worshipped as gods, as averters of evil and "Apotropaioi" [Ἀποτρόπαιοι], is a further question. Although many of the things which idolaters tell about their gods happened before these giants were born, as we showed earlier, nevertheless those very things were later also ascribed to these men by idolatrous and superstitious people of later times. This happened partly because they did not know when those events (which they heard had been done or discovered) had taken place, and so they referred them to men nearer their own age and better known to them; and partly so that they might seem to have a greater and more righteous reason for honouring them, since they believed that these men, because of the many inventions made by them or deeds done, as they thought, had almost a divine power. This was therefore the most cunning and most powerful fraud of the Devil or of demons, as Lactantius relates (Divine Institutes, book 2, chapters 14, 15 and 16): namely, that under the names and divinities of these men (who seemed to have conferred so many benefits on the human race, or who were known to have been so formidable to other men, as these giants were), the demons themselves should be worshipped. In sum, the text of Moses in this place (Gen. 6.4) and the words of Josephus (book 1, chapter 5) teach that these were the men whom idolatrous people later worshipped as Saturn, Jupiter, Mercury, Vulcan, and so on, and as Adam, Cain, Jabal and Tubal-cain under changed names, ascribing to these giants, that is, to their sons and descendants, the very things which Adam, Cain, Jabal and Tubal-cain had done or discovered.

units.la: Hos fuisse, quos Idololatrae homines postea Saturni, Iouis, Mercurij, Vulcani, &c. Ad ími, Caini, Iabalis, Tubalcaini, mutato nomine venerati sunt, his Gigantibus, eorum nempe filijs & posteris tribuêtes ea ipsa, quae Adamus, Cainus, Iabal, Tubalcainus fecerant, vel repererát. Ergo isliusmodi primorum parentum suorum, & primorum Mundi hominum vocabula, sed interpolatis, sanctiti, adorati, & celebres facti sunt hi Gigantes, videlicet eorum successores & posteri, quòd longa ætas nomen Adami, Caini, Iabalis ex hominum memoria iam deleuerat: vel quòd magno astu Satan (ne rerum veritas posthac agnosceretur) eam obscurauerat, immutaratq; illas veteres appellationes & voces in nouas. Cur homines isti & corpore tam robusti fuerint, quum ex prauis foeminis nascerentur, nec tam robustos homines natura, quāuis adhuc recès, protulisset: & moribus tam praui, quū ex filijs Dei essent procreati, quemadmodū scribit Moses, Gen.6.2. Robusti, magni, procerique corpore prā cateris etiā sui seculi hominibus fuerunt Gigantes, etsi ex foeminis nihilo, quàm catera, maioribus, grandioribus, & fortioribus nascerentur, quòd Deus illi feminì piorum maritorum insigniter, praeterquàm reliquorū hominum benedixerat. Deinde, quòd Deus ostendere ante diluuium vellet in quam maximâ corporis magnitudinem homines excrescere possunt, vt quum eos tam magnos validósque homines destrueret, maior ipsius gloria potentiaq; agnosceretur, atque etiânum à nobis hodiè agnoscatur, nimirū ne viribus corporis nostri cofisi putemus nos Deo resistere posse. Quale exemplum Deus in euertendis Chananaeis & filijs Enacim cim postea quoq; edere voluit, Deut. 1.28, & 9.2. Denique, quòd quum filÿ Dei seu pÿ homines illas fœminas propter egregiam earum formā duxissent, ac ducerent, maiore vi libidinis & astu cum ÿs rem habebant, & in eas irruebant. Itaque vis caloris naturalis (qui erat in virorum semine) maior erat, ac proinde magis materiā fœtus, id est, semen multebre extendebat. Id quod ex verbis Mosis colligi posse videtur, si conferatur series narrationis. Gen. 6.2 & 8.4. Nam antea etsi erat recens hominum natura, tātos tamen homines non producebat, nec pÿ tales antea suscipiebāt. Fuerunt nihilominus ÿdem isti Gigantes moribus corruptissimis, primùm propterea quod eò studiosiùs à matribus impÿs ad omnem nequitiam liberi isti ambitiosè informabantur, & fingebātur, quò ex pÿs nati erant patribus, ne quam nimirũ paterna pietatis scintillā retinerent, sed vt omnem probitatem exuerent. Ergo matrum ipsarũ, auorumq; maternorum similes potius fuerunt, quam Patrum suorum. Deinde hoc siebat, sic collubtante Satana cũ Deo, eiusque regnum in illis familÿs (vbi aliqua pietatis vestigia restabant) fortiùs expugnante, vt in his tandem penitus ipse Satan dominatum obtineret, regnum Dei extingueret, Matth. 12.25.43, Luc. 11.22.26: metuēs ne Deus ex ÿsdem familÿs sese eyceret, suimque in homines ius & regnū reciperet & recuperaret. Præterea quòd homines illi dono Dei tam egregio .i. robore corporũ ad quoduis scelus perpetrandū absq; vllius metu abuterentur. Quare nequiores & sceleratiores ceterÿs euaserunt. Denique quòd impietatis, quàm pietatis vis post peccatum fortior ac efficacior in animis hominum semper fuit, plusquam etiamnum hodie valet, ac perficit. Porro Gigatum (ne semel, aut uno duntaxat anno, id est post diluuium in Mundo extitisse credantur) facta est mentio etiam post diluuium, vixerúntque eiusmodi homines, etsi non ex istis (nam isti in diluuio extincti sunt omnes) nati, quemadmodum apparet Deut. 1.28, & 2 10.19, & 3.11, Iof. 14.15, 1.Sam. 17.4. Sed haec hactenus. Nunc ad Noachi viri pijssimi natiuitatem, quae est caput septimum huius historiae, accedamus.
units.tr: These were the men whom idolatrous people later worshipped as Saturn, Jupiter, Mercury, Vulcan, and so on, and as Adam, Cain, Jabal and Tubal-cain under changed names, ascribing to these giants, that is, to their sons and descendants, the very things which Adam, Cain, Jabal and Tubal-cain had done or discovered. Thus the names of our first parents and of the first men of the world, though corrupted, were made holy, adored and famous in these giants, that is, in their successors and descendants, because a long age had already erased the names of Adam, Cain and Jabal from the memory of men, or because Satan, by great cunning (so that the truth of things might not be recognised hereafter), had obscured it and changed those ancient appellations and words into new ones. Why these men were so robust in body, since they were born of wicked women, and nature had not yet brought forth such robust men, though still young; and why they were so wicked in morals, since they were begotten of the sons of God, as Moses writes (Gen. 6.2). The giants were robust, large and tall in body beyond the other men even of their own age, although they were not born from women who were in any way greater, larger or stronger than others; this was because God had singularly blessed that seed of pious husbands beyond the rest of men. Next, God wished to show before the Flood to what greatest bodily size men can grow, so that when he destroyed men so large and strong, his greater glory and power might be recognised, and may still be recognised by us today, lest we think that we can resist God by trusting in the strength of our bodies. God later wished to give a similar example in overthrowing the Canaanites and the sons of Anak (Deut. 1.28; 9.2). Finally, because the sons of God, that is, pious men, took those women for the sake of their outstanding beauty, and were taking them, they had to do with them and rushed upon them with greater force of lust and cunning. So the force of natural heat (which was in the men's seed) was greater, and therefore the seed, that is, the matter of the offspring, extended more abundantly. This seems to be what can be gathered from the words of Moses, if the sequence of the narrative is compared (Gen. 6.2 and 8.4). For before this, although human nature was still fresh, it did not produce men so large, nor did the sons of God before this take such women. Nevertheless these same giants were of most corrupt morals, first because their children were more eagerly and ambitiously trained to every wickedness by their impious mothers, and were so shaped, so that they might not retain any spark of their fathers' piety, but might cast off all uprightness; so they were more like their mothers and maternal grandfathers than their fathers. Next, this happened because Satan, colluding with God's enemy, attacked more strongly the kingdom of God in those families where some traces of piety still remained, so that at last Satan himself might gain dominion over them and extinguish the kingdom of God (Matt. 12.25, 43; Luke 11.22, 26), fearing lest God should cast himself out of those families and recover and reclaim his right and rule over men. Moreover, those men abused the excellent gift of God, namely the strength of their bodies, to commit any crime whatever without fear of anyone, and so they became more wicked and criminal than the others. Finally, because the force of impiety after sin has always been stronger and more effective in the minds of men than the force of piety, and it still prevails and accomplishes more even today. Further, mention of the giants is made even after the Flood, so that they should not be believed to have existed only once, or for a single year; and men of this kind lived afterwards, though not born of those (for all of those perished in the Flood), as appears in Deut. 1.28; 2.10, 19; 3.11; Josh. 14.15; 1 Sam. 17.4. But so much for these matters. Let us now come to the birth of Noah, a most pious man, which is the seventh chapter of this history.

units.la: Ad VII. Noachi natiuitas, & Lemechi de eo Prophetia.
units.tr: Chapter 7. The birth of Noah, and Lamech's prophecy about him.

units.la: Quaeritur, Quid [Noachus] vox [Noach] Hebraeis significet. Philo quietem interpretatur: aliy cessationem. Ratio nominis est Gen. 5.29: nempe quod ira Dei in mundum sub eo, i. illum tempore cessauit, ac quieuit post diluuiū: nam dicitur Deus odoratus gratum odorem vtpote sacrificium ab Noacho post diluuiū oblatum, atque ita Mundo placatus est Deus, Gen. 8. 21. Ergo Deus postquam hominum nequitiam aquis diluuij castigasset, & purgasset, Mundo placatus apparuit postea, subsidentibus ysdem aquis, Gen. 8.1.2, 2. Pet. 2.5. Graece autem Apostoli ipsi conuerterunt Nōε, Math. 24.37, 1.Pet. 3 20. Q. Quomodo Lemechus pius pater Noachi de eo statim nato dixit, [Hic recreabit nos ab omni opere nostro] Vtrum extraordinaria aliqua reuelatione a Deo accepta, an ex prudenti tantum coniectura, quod pius ille vir Deum tandiu minime passurum impunitam tam effrenem hominum im- probiprobitatem prudenter perspiceret : an ex libro potius Chanochi py.qui Dei inaucta, & Diluuium hoc ipsum hominibus sceleratis praedixisset, quasi Lemechus denuntiaret hoc ætate Noachi futurum. R. Concurrerunt haec omnia: Primum conciliura Lemechi pia & prudens, Deum nempe, qui iustus est, tam iniustam hominum vitam nequaquam semper toleraturum esse, sed eam vindicaturū & grauissime tandem ultu rum. Deinde legebatur liber Chanochi py, eiusque mina in mundū extabat scripta, vel potius priorū memoria inhaerebant.
units.tr: It is asked: what does the name Noah [Noach] mean in Hebrew? Philo interprets it as rest; others as cessation. The reason for the name is in Genesis 5:29: namely, that the anger of God against the world ceased and was quieted under him, that is, in his time, after the flood. For God is said to have smelled a pleasing odour, that is, the sacrifice offered by Noah after the flood, and so God was appeased towards the world, Genesis 8:21. Therefore, after God had punished and cleansed the wickedness of men by the waters of the flood, he afterwards appeared placated towards the world, when the same waters had subsided, Genesis 8:1-2; 2 Peter 2:5. The apostles themselves, moreover, in Greek rendered it Noe [Nōε], Matthew 24:37; 1 Peter 3:20. Q. How did Lamech, the pious father of Noah, say at once of the newly born child, "This one will give us rest from all our work"? Did he say this by some extraordinary revelation received from God, or only by prudent conjecture, because that pious man wisely perceived that God would not for long allow such unbridled and wicked lawlessness to go unpunished; or rather from the book of Enoch, who had prophesied both God's coming and this very flood to wicked men, as if Lamech were announcing that this would happen in the age of Noah? R. All of these things came together: first, Lamech's pious and prudent judgement, namely that God, who is just, would by no means always tolerate so unjust a life of men, but would at last avenge it and punish it most severely. Then the book of Enoch was being read, and its threats were still extant in the world, written down, or rather the memory of them remained with the earlier people.

units.la: Denique Spiritu vere Prophetico (quod donum Deus dederat Ecclesiae sua) praeuidit, sciuitque Lemechum hic pium Noachum filium esse eum, sub quo improba illa deploratáque hominum vita castigaretur a Deo, piorumque labores in collustando cum illa impietate subleuarentur. Itaque ipsi recreatentur ab illis suis laboribus, & inimicitys, quas pro retinendo Dei cultu cum impiis exercebant. Q. Quid verba haec significent, Gen. 5.29 [Recreabit nos ab omni opere nostro] utrū indicent cessaturos posthac homines ab omni opere, velut à colenda terra.
units.tr: Finally, by a truly prophetic Spirit (which gift God had given to his Church), he foresaw and knew that this Lamech would be the father of the pious Noah, under whom that wicked and desperate life of men would be punished by God, and the labours of the godly, in holding out against that impiety, would be lightened. Thus they would be refreshed from their labours and hostilities, which they endured with the wicked in order to keep the worship of God. Q. What do these words mean, Genesis 5:29, "He will give us rest from all our work": do they indicate that men would thereafter cease from all work, such as tilling the earth?

units.la: R. Verba haec [Opere nostro] moerorem animi significat, quem py ex Dei contemptu sentiebant. Nam vt de Lotho scriptum est 2 Pet 2.8. sic de iis piis verum est, Illos, quum essent iusti, & habitarent inter impios, ipsos in hoc mundo, in dies magis ac magis excruciasse animam suam videndo, & audiendo iniqua Gigantū, & aliorum hominum nefandaq; facta.
units.tr: R. These words, "our work", signify the grief of mind which the pious felt from the contempt of God. For as it is written of Lot, 2 Peter 2:8, so it is true of these pious men: that being righteous and dwelling among the impious, they tormented their soul day by day more and more in this world, seeing and hearing the iniquitous and nefarious deeds of the Giants and of other men.

units.la: Non pertinet autem ad laborem manuū haec sententia, quasi sub Noacho & posthac homines absque labore, & opere victuri essent. Illa enim Dei in peccatum hominis sententia, [Infudore vultus tui comedes panem tuū] manet quoniis tempore immota, Gen.3.19, 2.Thef.3. 10. Quamobrem Noachus ipse & ante, & post Diluuium dicitur arasse terrā atq; fuisse agricola, Gen.9. 20. Q. Quando natus est Noachus. R. In hiltoria iam dictum est. Natus enim est post mortuum Adamum primum hominem annis 120: post publicam profanationem, annis 821: ante Diluuium annis 600: à Mundo condito, annis 1056. Pergamus autem ad corruptissimum illud vita hominum genus, & modum, in quo omnis caro viam suam corruperat.
units.tr: This sentence, however, does not pertain to labour of the hands, as if under Noah and afterwards men were to live without labour and work. For that sentence of God upon the sin of man, "In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread" (Genesis 3:19; 2 Thessalonians 3:10), remains unchanged through all time. Wherefore Noah himself, both before and after the Flood, is said to have ploughed the land and to have been a farmer, Genesis 9:20. Q. When was Noah born? R. This has already been said in the history. For he was born 120 years after the death of Adam the first man; 821 years after the public profanation; 600 years before the Flood; and 1056 years from the creation of the world. Let us now proceed to that most corrupt kind and manner of human life, in which all flesh had corrupted its way.

units.la: Ad VIII. Omnis Caro viam suam corruperat.
units.tr: On verse 8: All flesh had corrupted its way.

units.la: Q. Quid vox Carnis significet hoc loco, Gen.6. 12. R. Carnis vox est σαρξ. Nam primum significat eam substantiam à Deo creatā, quae sanguine & ossibus constat, siue ea praedita sit anima λογικῇ, siue ἀλόγῳ: siue etiam anima ex eadem excesserit, Gen.6. 19, & 7.21. Sic volucres, sic animalia bruta sic pisces, vt ait Paulus, carnem habent, 1.Cor.15.39. Secundo loco Carnis significatio restringitur ad hominem Psal.78.39, vti etiam Creaturae nomen, Marc.16.15. idque κατ' ἐξοχὴν. Denique Caro μετωνυμικῶς pro corruptione, & vitio, quod carni inhaeret, sumitur. Sic Caro dicitur pugnare aduersus Spiritū Gal.5.17 opera carnis esse mortificāda: & similes phrases inde profectae Rom.8.12. Hoc vero loco [Caro] pro solis hominibus accipitur siue masculis, siue foeminis. De iis enim solis loquitur Moses, quum ait, [Et Omnis caro corruperat viam suam. Nec enim peccatum in pecudes (quum careant ratione) cadit, nec illæ Deum offendunt, nec ab instituto præceptoq; Dei recedunt: sed homines soli sunt coram Deo rei peccati, & propter eos solos Diluuium in mundum immissum est, Rom. 8. 20. quod tamen pecudes extinxit. Q. Quod quàm iustum fuerit fieri, postea suo loco demonstrabimus. Q. Quid hæc verba significent, [Corruperat viam suam, Gen 6.12.] R. Via hæc non est via pedum, quanquam additum est, [viam suam super terram:] sed via morû vti & alibi sæpè [Vta, iter, semita] sumitur pro moribus, ac vita ratione in S. Scriptura. Sic Isa. 40. 3, Math. 3. 3 Ioa. 1. 23. Q. Quum sit enim vita hæc nostra velut quadà peregrinatio, vti est 1 Pet. 2. 11, recte nostræ in ea actiones dicuntur [Via,] imo ipsamet tota vita nostra recte Via nominatur. Q. Quamobrem & nostrum erga Deum officium, & erga proximos, Via dicitur: quod vtrunq; homines illius seculi prorsus depravauerant, non modo illud negligentes, verumetiam omnia contra suum officiu impune & palam perpetrantes. Ergo hic [Via] vitam & officiu significat. Q. Q. Quid sibi vult Moses, qui ait, [Omnis caro corruperat viam suam coram IEHOVA] Vtrum Hypocritas tantum eos appellat? R. Illius tempestatis homines non tàtum hypocritas, & occulte malos, palam autem & in speciem viros bonos fuisse significat Moses: sed etiam manifeste, & absq; vllo pudore (quem proiecerant) & vllo vel Dei vel hominum metu impios, & improbos fuisse declarat. Addit enim ibide eosdem violentos, & iniuriosos inter se fuisse. Nam Dei quidem metus omnis post publicam nominis ipsius Profanationem ex hominum mentibus abscesserat: Hominum autem timorem, & talionis metum (si quis reliquum post illa profanationem inter homines fuerat) excusserat ex eorundem animis, Exemplum, & Audacia Gigatum, quos aliq quoque homines imitari, & probare iam pridem coeperant. Quamobrem etsi haec verba [Coram Iehoua] saepe hominum hypocrisi & occulta malitia opponuntur (qui externis operibus nihilominus apparent sanctis) veluti Luc. 1.6: hic tamen quoddam genus improbitatis tum occultae, tum manifestae (quam Deus condemnat) declarat. Tales enim & tam improbi fuerunt homines isti, de quibus agit Moses, ut neque in externis, neque in internis operibus iam a Deo tolerari possent. Sic passim haec phrasis sumitur pro Manifeste quidpiam agere, 1.Reg.8.62, & 9.3.4. Q. Ecquae fuerit ista hominum & morum corruptio tanta, propter quam Deus in universum mundum diluuium immiserit, Gen.6.3.13, & propter quam Deus tam graviter omnibus hominibus, imo rebus iratus fuit, qui tamen est patientissimus. R. Nonnulli hanc hominum corruptionem ad solam violentiam, i. vim & iniuriam, quam homines alij aliis armis inferebat, restringunt & referunt, propter versiculum undecimum cap.6 Genes. Philo in Biblic. Antiquit. ad scortationem publicam refert, qua exemplo impij Lamechi exercebant homines, ait. Alij ad foedissimum illum concubitum masculorum cum masculis, & foeminarum cum foeminis, qui contra naturam est, vocaturque Sodomia: Epiphanius videtur revocare ad Magiam, & veneficia, quae tunc exercebantur. Sic scribit in Panario: nec ab eo abludit Lactantius tius lib.2.cap.16. Verum alij,& quidem melius,aliiter,latiusq; hanc corruptionem interpretantur: Et primum quidem Philo Iudæus lib.1.Antiquit.cap.5.tum de publica & omnimoda hominum in Deum impietate: tum de publica & impunita aliorum in alios iniustitia summa corruptione istam accipit,his verbis, [ Deinde, ait, tempore procedente de paternis pietatis studijs ad mala progressi sunt filij,neq; legitimos honores vlteriùs prebentes Deo: neque circa homines iustitia verba facientes:sed ζelum virtutis,quem priùs habuerant, induplam malitiam conuertentes, eámque per ea,que agebant,demóstrantes.] Cyprianus in lib.de Spiritu S. de illius ætatis moribus sic scribit, [Bestiali petulantia effrenes erat homines:nec diuinos,nec humanos aspeētus in flagitijs verebantur.] Gregorius Turonensis lib.1. Histor. Addo Viennensis in prima Mundi ætate cum eo vtriq; consentiunt. Et generaliter Tertullianus lib. de Monogamia ait, [ Iniquitates diluuium prouocauerunt.] Et certè vera est hæc sententia confirmatúrq; verbo Dei. Primùm enim illius seculi homines manifesta impietatis damnantur,& impij appellátur,2.Pet. 2.5:imò Mundus ille totus,dicitur Mundus impiorum. Deinde vocátur ἀπῶς Immorigeri & rebelles Deo,1. Pet.3.20, id est,in omnibus illius præcepta spernentes: Præterea iniurij & violenti alij in alios Gen.6.11.Denique dissolutissimi omni modo & vita genere, & intēperantissimi fuerunt, vt à Christo ipso pronuntiatur, Math.24.37. In summa, fuerunt y istorum omnium (paucissimis exceptis) hominũ tunc mores,quos Paulus eleganter describit,Rom.1.his verbis ad eam maximè Υ 2 aetatem respiciens, [Vt qui veritatem, ait, mutarunt in mendacium, ac seruierint rebus creatis, praeterito creatore, qui est benedictus in secula. Itaque eos tradidit Deus foedis affectibus. Nam & foemina illorum mutarunt vsum naturalem in eum, qui est praeter naturam: similiterque etiam masculi, relicto naturali vsu foeminae, exarserunt sua libidine alius in alium, masculi in masculos foeda perpetrantes, oppleti omni iniustitia, fornicatione, improbitate, auaritia, malitia, pleni inuidia, caede, contentione, dolo, malignitate, susurrones, obtrectatores, Dei osores, contumeliosi, superbi, gloriosi, inuentores malorum, parentibus immorigeri, desipientes, foedifragi, charitatis expertes, implacabiles, immisericordes.] Quod vita sceleratissime genus postea Sodomita representarunt, & effinxerunt: & post eos Gabaonita, Gen. 19, 2. Pet. 2. 6, Iudae verf. 7, Iudic. 19: inter quos fuit effrenis peccandi licentia. In summa, omnis impietas, iniustitia, & intemperantia inter eos locum habuit: quae vitia inter pios exulat, Tit. 2 12, vt mirum non sit postea tantam fuisse iram Dei in genus humanum vniuersum.
units.tr: Q. What does the word "flesh" mean in this place, Gen. 6:12? R. The word "flesh" is σάρξ [sarx]. Firstly, it signifies the substance created by God that consists of blood and bones, whether it is endowed with a rational soul [λογικῇ] or an irrational one [ἀλόγῳ], or even when the soul has left it, Gen. 6:19 and 7:21. So birds, so brute animals, so fishes, as Paul says, have flesh, 1 Cor. 15:39. Secondly, the meaning of flesh is restricted to man, Ps. 78:39, just as the name "creature" is, Mark 16:15, and that κατ' ἐξοχήν [kat' exochēn], preeminently. Finally, flesh is taken metonymically [μετωνυμικῶς] for the corruption and vice that clings to flesh. So flesh is said to fight against the Spirit, Gal. 5:17; the works of the flesh are to be mortified, and similar phrases derived from this, Rom. 8:12. In this place, however, [flesh] is taken for men alone, whether males or females. For it is of these alone that Moses speaks when he says [And all flesh had corrupted its way]. Sin does not fall upon beasts (since they lack reason), nor do they offend God, nor do they depart from God's ordinance and command. But men alone are guilty of sin before God, and on account of them alone the Flood was sent into the world, Rom. 8:20; though it did destroy the beasts too. Q. How just this was to happen, we will demonstrate later in its place. Q. What do these words mean, [corrupted its way, Gen. 6:12]? R. "Way" here is not the way of feet, although it is added [its way upon the earth]; but "way" in the sense of conduct, as often elsewhere in Scripture "way" (derek, iter, semita) is taken for manners and way of life. So Isa. 40:3, Matt. 3:3, John 1:23. Q. Since this life of ours is like a kind of pilgrimage, as 1 Pet. 2:11 says, our actions in it are rightly called "ways"; indeed our whole life itself is rightly named "Way". Q. Wherefore both our duty towards God and towards our neighbours is called "way"; and both of these the men of that age had utterly depraved, not only neglecting them but committing everything contrary to their duty with impunity and openly. Therefore here "way" signifies life and duty. Q. Q. What does Moses mean when he says [All flesh had corrupted its way before the LORD]? Does he call only hypocrites that? R. Moses signifies that the men of that time were not merely hypocrites, secretly evil but openly and outwardly good men; he also declares that they were manifestly, and without any shame (which they had cast off) and without any fear either of God or of men, impious and wicked. For he adds there that they were violent and wronged one another. For all fear of God had departed from men's minds after the public profanation of his name; and the fear of men and dread of retaliation (if any remained among men after that profanation) had been shaken out of their minds by the example and audacity of the Giants, whom some men had already begun to imitate and approve. Therefore, although these words [before Jehovah] are often set against the hypocrisy and hidden malice of men (who nonetheless appear holy in outward works), as in Luke 1:6, here nevertheless they declare a kind of wickedness both hidden and manifest, which God condemns. For these men of whom Moses speaks were so wicked that they could no longer be tolerated by God, neither in their outward nor in their inward works. So this phrase is commonly taken for doing something openly, 1 Kings 8:62; 9:3-4. Q. What was the corruption of men and morals so great, on account of which God sent the Flood upon the whole world, Gen. 6:3, 13, and on account of which God was so gravely angry with all humankind, indeed with all things, though he is most patient? R. Some restrict this corruption solely to violence, that is, force and injury, which men inflicted on one another with various weapons, on account of the eleventh verse of Genesis 6, and refer it to that. Philo, in the Biblical Antiquities, refers it to public fornication, which men were led to practise by the example of the impious Lamech. Others refer it to that most foul intercourse of males with males and of females with females, which is against nature and is called sodomy. Epiphanius seems to refer it to magic and poisonings, which were then practised; so he writes in the Panarion, and Lactantius does not differ from him, book 2, chapter 16. But others, and indeed better, interpret this corruption otherwise and more broadly. First, Philo the Jew, in book 1 of the Antiquities, chapter 5, takes it as the highest corruption, both of the public and universal impiety of men against God and of the public and unpunished injustice of some against others, in these words: [Then, he says, as time went on, the sons fell away from their fathers' pious pursuits into evils, no longer paying due honour to God nor dealing justly with men; but turning the zeal for virtue which they had previously had into twofold malice, and displaying it in what they did.] Cyprian, in the book On the Holy Spirit, writes thus of the morals of that age: [Men were unbridled with bestial wantonness; they feared neither divine nor human eyes in their shameful deeds.] Gregory of Tours, book 1 of the Histories. I add the Viennese writer, who in the first age of the world agrees with both of them. And in general Tertullian, in the book On Monogamy, says: [Iniquities provoked the Flood.] And certainly this opinion is true and confirmed by the Word of God. For first, the men of that age are condemned for manifest impiety and are called impious, 2 Pet. 2:5; indeed that whole world is called the world of the impious. Then they are called [ἀπειθεῖς] disobedient and rebellious against God, 1 Pet. 3:20, that is, spurning his precepts in all things. Besides, others were unjust and violent towards others, Gen. 6:11. Finally, they were most dissolute in every way and kind of life, and most intemperate, as Christ himself pronounces, Matt. 24:37. In sum, the morals of all of them (with very few exceptions) were such as Paul elegantly describes in Rom. 1, looking especially to that age, in these words: [Because they changed the truth of God into a lie, and served created things rather than the Creator, who is blessed for ever. Therefore God gave them up to shameful passions. For their women exchanged natural use for that which is against nature; likewise also the men, leaving the natural use of women, burned in their lust for one another, men committing shameful acts with men, filled with all unrighteousness, fornication, wickedness, covetousness, malice; full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, malignity; whisperers, backbiters, haters of God, insolent, proud, boastful, inventors of evils, disobedient to parents, foolish, covenant-breakers, without natural affection, implacable, unmerciful.] This most wicked way of life the Sodomites afterwards represented and fashioned, and after them the Gibeonites, Gen. 19; 2 Pet. 2:6; Jude v. 7; Judg. 19, among whom there was unbridled licence to sin. In sum, every impiety, injustice and intemperance had its place among them, vices which are absent among the pious, Titus 2:12. So it is no wonder that God's wrath afterwards against the whole human race was so great.

units.la: Q. Quibus tandem gradibus tanta hominum nequitia irrepserit, & obtinuerit. R. Iam quidem ex parte fuit a nobis explicatu. Nec enim coepit illa tam nefaria hominum vita demum centum duntaxat viginti annis ante Diluuium, vt nonnulli tamen existimant ex Gen. 6. 3. sed perperam. Quid ergo? Longe antea, & statim post peccatum primum primi hominis illa mali labes coepit, & serpsit. Ergo malum hoc tam foedum concipitur in corde hominum, velut in aluo, ab illo, vt dixi, primo primi hominis pescato vsque ad publica nominis Dei profanafanationem, Primùm per fratricidium Caini : Deinde per Iluprum Lemechi:praterea per posterorum Caini andaciam & superbiam,vsque ad publica nominis Dei profanationem per annos 135.conceptum iam hoc malum omnibus suis membris corruptissimis & fœdissimis postea formatur,& augetur in hominum corde,& voluntate,tanquam in aluo pragnante,nimirum à Prosanatione illa nominis Dei vsque ad tempora nativitatis Gigantum, & ad piorum ipsorum depravationem per conubia cum impijs mulieribus per annos 872. Aeditur in lucem,& per opera, omnis generis hominum externa apparente & erumpente,cœpit postea Gigantes natos annis circiter 120: Et ante natu Noachum ex pio Lemecho, annis quoque 127. Videtur enim Deus tot annos nempe 120 dedisse hominibus ad respiscentiam, quotannis corruptissimum illud vitæ genus cœpit manifeste in mundum introduci,& edi ab hominibus, atque inualescere,maximè vero in omnes mundi partes exundauit,sparsus, confirmatus,immedicabiliterque corroboratus est hic publicus morbus post nativitatem Noachi, & ante susceptos ab eo liberos. Regnat igitur & grassatur in mundo ab ista editione sua hoc malu vsque ad Diluuiu à Deo immissum pene per totos annos 727 ab ista cōfirmatione 500 annos,per quos Deus illos homines manifeste sceleratissimos patientissime tolerauit. Et hac quidem mea est sententia de gradibus, quibus hoc malu obtinuit. Tertullianus autem lib. Monogam. sic eos explicat, vt fratricidium Caini esse velit primum gradum ad Diluuium,& iram Dei in mundum prouocandā. Deinde fornicationem,siue violationem coniugij,
units.tr: Q. By what steps did such great wickedness of men creep in and prevail? R. This has already been explained by us in part. For that most wicked life of men did not begin only one hundred and twenty years before the Flood, as some think from Gen. 6:3, but wrongly. What then? Long before, and immediately after the first sin of the first man, that evil stain began and crept in. So this most foul evil is conceived in men's hearts, as in a womb, from that first sin of the first man, as I said, down to the public profanation of God's name: first through the fratricide of Cain; then through the lust of Lamech; besides through the audacity and pride of Cain's posterity, over 135 years, until the public profanation of God's name. Once conceived, this evil is afterwards formed and increased, with all its members most corrupt and foul, in men's hearts and wills, as in a pregnant womb: namely from that profanation of God's name until the time of the birth of the Giants, and to the depravation of the pious themselves through marriages with impious women, over 872 years. It is brought into the light, and appearing and breaking out through the works of men of every kind, it began afterwards: the Giants were born about 120 years later, and Noah was born from the pious Lamech before that, also 127 years. For God seems to have given men those 120 years, that is, so many years, for repentance, during which that most corrupt way of life began to be clearly introduced into the world and brought forth by men, and to grow strong; and especially it overflowed into all parts of the world. This public disease was spread, confirmed, and incurably strengthened after the birth of Noah and before he had children. So from its emergence this evil reigns and rages in the world until the Flood sent by God, nearly 727 years in all, counting 500 years from its confirmation, during which God patiently tolerated those men who were manifestly most wicked. This is my opinion on the steps by which this evil gained ground. Tertullian, however, in his book On Monogamy, explains them thus: he wishes the fratricide of Cain to be the first step towards the Flood and towards provoking God's wrath upon the world. Then fornication, or the violation of marriage,

units.la: {y} Ioan. 3. quæ à Lamecho impio facta est. Demum vltimũ gradum fuisse reliquas mundi iniquitates. Epiphanius lib. 1 .contra hæres. hos gradus recitat,& enumerat, Τὰτε Α᾿δὰμ πρὸς Σὴθ, ὑὸς δὲ τύτε Ἑνὼς·ἢ κατὰ διαδοχὴν Καϊνὰν, Μαλαλεὴλ, Ιαρὲδ·ὡς δὲ ἡ σφόδρα ἡ εἰσφήμως ἐλθόσα ἐντευθεν ἤρξατο ἡ χαουνχανία ἐν κόσμῳ γίνεσθαι, ἡ ἀπ᾽ ἀρχῆς μὲν δὲ τῆς Ἀδὰμ σφαγὴς ἔπεσεν δὲ δὲ τῆς Καῖν ἀδελφοκτονίας· νῦν δὲ ἐν χεύρνοις Ιαρὲδ, ἡ ἐπέκεινα φαμ-μαχεία, ἡ Μαγεία, Ἀσέλγεια, Μοιχεία τε, ἡ ἀδικία. Οὐ γνώωη τις ἑτέςῳ· ὑ δόξα ὑσηλλαγμένη, ἀλλὰ μία γλῶσα ἡ γένθ' ἐν δὴ γῆς καὶ' ἐκεῖνο χαρᾶς ἐπαμένον, id est [Adami filius Seth, filius autem huius Enos, & per succes-sionem Kainan, Malaleel, Iared. Quemadmodum autem veterum traditio habet, quæ ad nos usque peruenit, ex eo tempore cœpit in mundo esse malorum omnium inuentio, quæ quidem ab Adamí peccato primum orta fuerat, postea verò per fratricidium Cainí: nunc autem tempore nempe Iared & postea viguit Veneficiū, Magia, lasciuia, scortatio, & iniustitia. Nec enim tunc sententia hominum diuersa erant, non erant variæ opiniones: sed vna omnium lingua erat, vnum genus hominum in terris tunc erat sparsum.] Ex quo apparet eo ipso homines sese facilius corrupisse exemplis, & conuersatione cum aliis, quòd omnes tunc essent vnius labij (vt loquitur Scriptura) & lingua, & alij alios scelera docerent: & oratione, vt & vita sua, ad malum alij alios inducerent. Ado Viennensis denique in prima ætate sic scribit, [In Cain, & Abel duorum populorum esse figuram Iudæorum, & Christianorum, vbi sacrificiũ maioris respuitur, & minoris placitum consumitur: electorum rum rum multitudinem ad veram & æternā dedicationem transferendam, & homicidaʃ filios vitæ suæ ordinem corrumpentes, & iusto & manifesto iudicio omnipotentis Dei intercipiendos.] Q. Vtrum hoc vita tam corrupta ac dissoluta genus ab Epiphan.lib.1.haref.rest Barbarismus appelletur potius, quam Scythismus.
units.tr: {y} Ioan. 3. Under Lamech, the impious man, these things were done. Lastly, the final stage was the remaining iniquities of the world. Epiphanius, in book 1 of his work Against the Heresies, recites and enumerates these stages: Adam begat Seth, and Seth begat Enos, and in succession Cainan, Malaleel, and Jared. From there, as the tradition of the ancients, which has reached us, has it, the invention of every evil began in the world. It had first arisen from Adam's sin, then from Cain's fratricide. But now, in the time of Jared, and afterwards, witchcraft, magic, lasciviousness, fornication and injustice flourished. For at that time men's opinions were not divided and there were no differing views. Rather, all had one language, and the human race was then scattered over the earth as one. [Ἀδὰμ πρὸς Σὴθ, υἱὸς δὲ τούτου Ἐνώς· ἢ κατὰ διαδοχὴν Καϊνάν, Μαλελεήλ, Ἰαρέδ· ὡς δὲ ἡ σφόδρα ἡ εἰς φήμως ἐλθοῦσα ἐντεῦθεν ἤρξατο ἡ κακουργία ἐν κόσμῳ γίνεσθαι, ἡ ἀπ᾽ ἀρχῆς μὲν ἀπὸ τῆς Ἀδὰμ παραβάσεως ἔπεσεν, ἀπὸ δὲ τῆς Καΐν ἀδελφοκτονίας· νῦν δὲ ἐν χρόνοις Ἰαρέδ, ἡ ἐπέκεινα φαρμακεία, ἡ μαγεία, ἀσέλγεια, μοιχεία τε, ἡ ἀδικία.] From this it appears that men corrupted one another all the more easily by examples and by living together, since they were all then of one speech (as Scripture puts it) and one tongue, and since they taught one another wickedness; and by their words, as by their lives, they led one another into evil. Lastly, Ado of Vienne writes thus of the first age: [In Cain and Abel is a figure of the two peoples, the Jews and the Christians: where the sacrifice of the elder is rejected and that of the younger is accepted; the multitude of the elect is to be carried over to the true and eternal dedication, while the murderous sons, who corrupt the order of their life, are to be cut off by the just and manifest judgment of almighty God.] Q. Whether this kind of life, so corrupt and dissolute, should be called barbarism rather than Scythism, as Epiphanius, in book 1 of the Heresies, puts it.

units.la: Quum pius ille pater ex loco Pauli, Colos. 3. 11. totam atatem Mundi, quæ à prima eius creatione ad Christi Domini nostri resurrectionem præcesserit in quatuor χρόνοις, & partes dividere instituisset, vocavit Barbarismum totum illud seculum, quod à mundo condito fluxit ad Diluvium. Scythismum, à Diluvio ad Phalecum usque, & Tharam patrem Abrahami. Hellenismu seu Græcismu, à Thara ætate usque ad Legem à Deo Mosi datam in monte Horeb. Deinde Iudaismum, à Lege data ad Christum. Ergo Barbarismu ea de causa totū hoc tempus nominat, [quod (ut ait idem) homines toto illo seculo neque unum quendam Principem & caput haberent, neq; consensum Lege ulla firmatū: sed quivis sibi præscribebat, & lex erat pro animi sui arbitratu.]
units.tr: When that pious father set out to divide the whole age of the world, from its first creation to the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, into four periods, based on the passage of Paul in Colossians 3:11, he named the whole age that flowed from the created world to the Flood "Barbarism." He named the period from the Flood to Phalek and Terah, the father of Abraham, "Scythism." From the age of Terah to the Law given by God to Moses on Mount Horeb, he named it "Hellenism" or "Grecism." Then came "Judaism," from the giving of the Law to Christ. He called this whole time "Barbarism" for this reason: [because (as the same author says) during that whole age men had neither one prince and head, nor agreement fixed by any law; but each prescribed for himself, and the law was according to the judgment of his own mind.]

units.la: Quod barbarorū hominum proprium est. Q. Vtrū Deus in hoc tam corrupto vitæ genere inter homines & liberē, atq; impune grassante, mundum diuinā sua providentia & sapientia rexerit. R. Regebat etiam tunc Mundum Deus & sapientia, & providentia sua: sed homines illos incredibili quadam patientia tolerabat, & expectabat, si forte resipiscerent, ut est 1.Pet.3. 20 2.Pet.2.5, Rom.2.4: nimirū ut hac ratione redderet eos inexcusabiles. Fuit igitur summa Dei potentia potuisse Mundi huius statum aduersus tantum scelerum in dies crescentium impetum conseruare tamen firmum, & in tanta hominū aliorum in alios violentia efficere, vt & multiplicarentur, & superessent homines. Fuit summa eiusdem Dei Sapientia iot hominū conatibus impijs & iniustis obuiam ire, eorūmque effecta sistere, ne omnia subuerterent. Fuit summa misericordia Dei tam pravos & immorigeros homines tamen in his terris alere, & Solis, Lunæ, ac Terrae vsum illis relinquere, ac largiri. Fuit denique summa eiusdem iustitia ad eos per sua ipsorum peccata coercendos tradere eos ipsos suis cupiditatibus, & diu toleratos semel postea funditus delere. Ergo Mundus tunc quoque Dei prouidentia regebatur, vti & nunc. Sed veniamus ad denuntiationem primam futuri Diluuij Noacho a Deo factam. Historia temporis ordine sequitur.
units.tr: This is the mark of barbarous men. Q. Whether God, in this kind of life so corrupt, with men raging freely and with impunity, governed the world by his divine providence and wisdom. A. God then also governed the world by his wisdom and providence, but he bore with those men with an incredible patience and waited, if perhaps they would repent, as in 1 Peter 3:20, 2 Peter 2:5, Romans 2:4; namely, so that in this way he might render them inexcusable. It was therefore the sovereign power of God to be able to keep the state of this world firm against the assault of crimes that grew day by day, and to bring it about, amid such great violence of men against one another, that they both multiplied and survived. It was the supreme wisdom of the same God to meet the impious and unjust endeavours of so many men and to check their effects, lest they overturn everything. It was the supreme mercy of God to nourish such depraved and unruly men on this earth, and to leave and grant them the use of the sun, moon and earth. It was finally the supreme justice of the same God to hand them over to their own lusts, so that they might be restrained by their own sins, and, once they had been long endured, to destroy them utterly. Therefore the world was then also governed by the providence of God, as it is now. But let us come to the first announcement of the coming Flood made by God to Noah. The history follows in chronological order.

units.la: Ad IX. Denuntiatio prima futuri Di- luuij à Deo facta Noacho.
units.tr: Chapter IX. The first announcement of the coming Flood, made by God to Noah.

units.la: Quaeritur, Vtrum Noacho nati sint filij, quos commemorat Moses ante primam hanc Denunciationem futuri Diluuij diserte à Deo illi factā, Gen 6.3. R. Nequaquam. Nam praecessit haec Denuntiatio prima futuri Diluuij, quae à Deo facta est Noacho, natiuitatem triū Noachi liberorū, quos recensēt Moses Gen.5. 32, & 6.10. Facta est enim hac praedictio Noacho anno aetatis 480, annis nimirū 120 ante diluuium Gen.6 3. Nati vero sunt Noacho primū liberi anno eius 500 vt apparet Gen. 5.32. Ergo intercedunt anni 20. toti inter virumq; tempus. Q. Quomodo sunt intelligendi gendi illi 120 anni, quos fore dies hominis pronuntiat Deus in illa Denunciatione futuri Diluvij, Gen.6. 3.
units.tr: Question: Were the sons whom Moses mentions before this first announcement of the coming Flood, which God explicitly made to Noah, already born to him (Gen. 6.3)? Answer: Not at all. For this first announcement of the Flood, made by God to Noah, came before the birth of the three sons of Noah whom Moses records (Gen. 5.32 and 6.10). The prediction was made to Noah in the 480th year of his life, that is, 120 years before the Flood (Gen. 6.3). His first sons were born in his 500th year, as appears from Gen. 5.32. So there are twenty full years between the two events. Question: How are we to understand those 120 years, which God declares will be the days of man in that announcement of the Flood (Gen. 6.3)?

units.la: Pleriq; sic eos annos acceperūt, quasi hominū vita esset in posterum atque in aetates sequentes tantùm 120 annorum futura, eamque metam Deus futurorum hominum vitæ prescripsisset, & prasixisset, quoniā illi ob superiorem longanimitatem peiores deterioresque effecti fuissent. Nam illi sese antea putabant ob diuturnū vitæ tempus futuros hic immortales. Sic Iosephus lib.1. Antiquit.cap.5. Philo lib.1.Antiq.Biblic. Lactantius lib.2.cap.13.Institit.Christ. Zonaras lib.1.Annal.& plerique alij. Verùm Augustinus, & ante eum Hieronymus aliter. Sic enim ille lib.15.Ciuitat.Dei,cap.24, [Erunt dies eorum centum & viginti anni, nō sic accipiendum est, quasi pronuntiatum sit posthac homines 120 annos viuendo non transgredi,quum & post Diluuium 500 excessisse annos inueniamus.] Quid igitur? Hos annos 120 dedit illi seculo, quantumvis corrupto, Deus concessit, ad resipiscendum, si forte homines illi cor haberent. In quo apparet incredibilis Dei in malis tolerandis patientia: ob quam magis illi reddebātur inexcusabiles, nempe tot annis à Deo expectati & sollicitati, 1.Pet.3.20. Hæc autem est Prima Denuntiatio Diluuij, quæ Noacho à Deo facta fuit, nimirum anno 480, mature, vt suum exitium impij & prasciret, nisi resipiscerent: & canerent tam serio à Deo moniti. Sed Moses ἀντιφροντιστής narrat Deum apud se de Hominū improbitate stomachatū: deinde quid propterea facturus esset, Noacho denuntiasse, Gen.6.3. Q. Verum eam poenam futuram annuntiarit improbis hominibus Noachus, an silverit. R. Eam poenam, iustitiamque Dei futuram Noachus publice palamque hominibus illis impijs & iniustis intrepidè, liberè, & constanter denuntiauit, & quidem sæpè sapius, & per totos illos 120 annos. Itaque dicitur Præco iustitiæ Dei, 2. Pet. 2 8. Deus immorigeris illis per Noachum seruum suum fidelissimum iam tunc dicitur prædicasse, 1. Pet. 3.19.20. Dicitur denique Noachus mundum & concionando de futura Dei ira, & Arcam ædificando condemnasse, Heb. 11.7. Ergo in sinu tacitus illam denuntiationem sibi à Deo factam non tenuit, non occultauit metu mortis: sed vt Propheta summi Dei constantissimus, vt Athleta Dei inuictus eâ eunlgauit, & homines per tantum tempus ad pœnitentiam inuitauit, ipse fidem habens Deo de iis rebus, quæ nondum, vel ipse quidem tenuissima, apparebat, Heb. 11.7. Quare Noachus inter præstantissimos Dei seruos & Prophetas ab Ezechiele recensetur, cap. 14.14 20, Eccles 44.17.18.
units.tr: Many have taken these years to mean that human life in the future, and in the ages that followed, would last only 120 years, and that God had fixed and set this limit on the lives of men to come, because they had become worse and more corrupt through the earlier long-suffering of God. For they had previously supposed that, because of the long span of life, they would be immortal here. So Josephus (Antiquities, book 1, ch. 5), Philo (Biblical Antiquities, book 1), Lactantius (Divine Institutes, book 2, ch. 13), Zonaras (Annals, book 1) and many others. But Augustine, and before him Jerome, take it differently. Augustine says in The City of God, book 15, ch. 24: "These words, 'their days shall be a hundred and twenty years', should not be understood as if it were declared that from then on men would not live beyond 120 years, since we find that after the Flood men lived more than 500 years." What then? God granted that age, however corrupt, these 120 years in order that they might repent, if perhaps those people had hearts for it. In this appears the incredible patience of God in bearing with evils, and for this reason those people were made all the more inexcusable, since God had waited for them and urged them for so many years (1 Pet. 3.20). This, then, is the first announcement of the Flood, which was made to Noah by God, namely in the year 480, early, so that the wicked might foresee their own destruction unless they repented, and might take seriously the warning they had received from God. But Moses, in his turn [ἀντιφροντιστής], relates that God was vexed in himself at the wickedness of men, and then tells us that he declared to Noah what he would therefore do (Gen. 6.3).
