Question: Did Noah announce that punishment and the coming judgment of God to the wicked men, or did he keep silent? Answer: Noah openly and publicly announced that punishment and justice of God to those impious and unjust men, boldly, freely and steadfastly, and indeed often and repeatedly, throughout all those 120 years. So he is called a herald of God's righteousness (2 Pet. 2.5). It is said that God then preached through Noah, his most faithful servant, to those disobedient men (1 Pet. 3.19, 20). Finally, Noah is said to have condemned the world by preaching of the coming wrath of God and by building the ark (Heb. 11.7). Therefore he did not keep that announcement made to him by God hidden in his heart, nor conceal it out of fear of death; rather, as the most steadfast prophet of the Most High and the unconquered athlete of God, he proclaimed it and invited men to repentance for so long a time, trusting God in things not yet seen, and at that time only dimly apparent (Heb. 11.7). Hence Noah is listed by Ezekiel among the most excellent servants and prophets of God (Ezek. 14.14, 20; Ecclus. 44.17, 18).

units.la: Q. Virum illius sculi homines respuerint ad eam Noachi prædicationem. R. Minimè verò. Imo cõtum iciores etiam facti videntur, quū illa Dei iudicia sibi denuntiata statim euenire neque cernerent, neq; Dei duram illam manum experirentur homines illi superbi Math. 24 37.38, Luc. 17 17, 1. Pet. 3 20. Itaque liberè vitijs suis, vt antea, indulgebant. Q. Utrum, quū non emendarentur homines, Noachus ex ea terra, & ab iis hominibus cum liberis suis fugerit, cum quibus prius erat, quibusque prædicauerat, ob mortis metum, quemadmodum scribit Iosephus lib. 1. Antiquit. cap. 5. R. Nusquam hoc in Dei verbo extat, estq; Rabbinicum nicum commentum, vt pleráque alia apud eundem au-torem. Pratere a facit ea sententia summam vero Dei Prophetæ Noacho iniuriâ, quem fingit timidum. Denique quum omnis caro corrupisset vbique viam suam, & tota terra, vniuersaq; Orbis partes plena essent violentia, vt est Genes.6.11 & 12, quò fugisset, quòve se recepisset Noachus, vbi eadem nō timeret, nempe mortem ab improbis, qui supra totius terra faciem sparsi, & immanes erat, & violenti? Nusquam enim tutus ab ijs futurus erat. Q. Quomodo Deus pœnitere dicatur, Gen.6.7. R. Ἀνθρωπομόρφως, & phrasi ex hominum moribus sumpta, quomodo & Irasci, & Videre dicitur, Augustinus lib.15.Cinit.Dei,cap.25.
units.tr: Question: Did the men of that age receive Noah's preaching? Answer: Not at all. Indeed they seem to have become even more contemptuous, since those proud men did not see those judgments of God, announced to them, come to pass at once, nor did they experience God's heavy hand (Matt. 24.37, 38; Luke 17.27; 1 Pet. 3.20). So they freely indulged their vices as before. Question: Since the men did not mend their ways, did Noah flee from that land and from those men with his sons, with whom he had previously lived and to whom he had preached, out of fear of death, as Josephus writes (Antiquities, book 1, ch. 5)? Answer: This is nowhere found in the word of God, and it is a Rabbinic fabrication, as are most other things of that author. Moreover, that opinion does great wrong to Noah, the prophet of the Most High, by portraying him as timid. Finally, since all flesh had corrupted its way upon the earth, and the whole earth and all parts of the world were full of violence (Gen. 6.11, 12), where could Noah have fled or withdrawn to, where he would not fear the same thing, namely death at the hands of wicked men, who were scattered over the whole face of the earth and were fierce and violent? For nowhere would he have been safe from them. Question: How is God said to repent (Gen. 6.7)? Answer: Anthropomorphically [Ἀνθρωπομόρφως], by a figure of speech taken from human behaviour, just as he is said to be angry and to see. Augustine, The City of God, book 15, ch. 25.

units.la: Q. Cur Deus minatur se animalia bruta perditurum quoque in diluuio Gen.6.7, & 17, quod & postea euenit Gen.7.21,22, quum illa minimè peccassent, sed homines solt Gen 6.13. R. Augustinus lib.15.Cinit. Dei,cap.25 ait, [Quod autem etiâ interitum omnium animalium terrenorum, volatiliúmque denuntiat, magnitudinem futura cladis effatur. Nam animantibus rationis expertibus(tanquam & ipsa peccauerint)minatur exitium.] Iuste verò & Animantia terrena, & Volatilia propter hominum peccatum extinxit Deus, quòd ea res essent hominis, & hominum vel alendorum, vel deleCtandorum, vel adiuuandorum gratiâ condite à Deo. Ergo quemadmodum in crimine læse maiestatis humanæ non ipse duntaxat autor sceleris: sed etiam eius res omnes bonáque merito ad tanti criminis fœditatem demonstrandâ puniuntur, ac perduntur: sic, & quidem multò æquius, in crimine læse maiestatis diuinæ: in quod fugitium inciderant illius seculi homines omnes. Cur Terra ipsa, in qua homines illi habitabant, etiam & ipsa polluta quoque dicitur Gen.6.11:quum sit Terra bruti & sensu carens elementum. Quia hominibus destinata sit a Deo terra, velut eorum domicilium. Psal.115.16, certe prout homines ipsi terra cum suisque incolae sunt aut puri, aut impuri: aut sancti, aut polluti: sic terra quoque ipsa in qua sunt, pura vel impura, sancta vel polluta est, & a Deo benedicitur vel maledicitur, ut est Psal.107 34, Deut.28, Leuit.18 25.28. Sed iam ad X. historiam nostram caput, quod est de nativitate & serie filiorum Noachi, accedamus.
units.tr: Question: Why does God threaten that he will destroy the brute animals also in the Flood (Gen. 6.7, 17), which in fact later happened (Gen. 7.21, 22), when those animals had not sinned, but only men (Gen. 6.13)? Answer: Augustine, The City of God, book 15, ch. 25, says: "That he also threatens the destruction of all the earthly animals and birds declares the greatness of the coming disaster. For he threatens destruction to living creatures lacking reason, as though they too had sinned." God justly destroyed both the earthly animals and the birds on account of men's sin, because these creatures belonged to man and had been made by God for the sake of feeding, delighting or helping man. Therefore, just as in the crime of treason against human majesty, not only the author of the crime but also all his goods are rightly punished and destroyed, to show the foulness of so great a crime, so much more justly is this true in the crime of treason against divine majesty, into which all the men of that age had fallen. Why is the earth itself, on which those men lived, also said to be corrupted (Gen. 6.11), since the earth is a body without sense or feeling? Because the earth was destined by God for men as their dwelling (Ps. 115.16). Certainly, just as men themselves, with their inhabitants, are either pure or impure, holy or defiled, so the earth itself on which they live is pure or impure, holy or defiled, and is blessed or cursed by God (Ps. 107.34; Deut. 28; Lev. 18.25, 28). But now let us come to the tenth section of our history, which concerns the birth and succession of the sons of Noah.

units.la: Ad X. Nativitas filiorum Noachi.
units.tr: On X. The birth of Noah's sons.

units.la: Queritur, Quid vox [Genuit] significat, quā Gen. 5.32 dicitur, [Postquam autem natus fuit Noachus 500 annos, genuit Semum, Chamum, & Iaphetum.] Verum omnes isti uno & eodem anno suscepserit ex uxore sua Noachus. Nequaquam, uti ex Gen. 11.10, & 10.21 apparet. Ergo Genuit, id est, Gignere coepit, uti sumitur Gen. 11.26. Id quod Franciscus Lunius in annotat. suis in Genesi primus observavit. Ecquis inter tres istos Noachi filios fuerit primogenitus, & quo quisque eorum ordine natus sit Noacho, quemadmodum ex Mose colligi potest. Matthaeus Beroaldus in Chronicis vir diligentissimus primum id annotavit lib.3.cap.2, probatque Iaphetum fuisse liberorum Noachi natu maximum, uti dicitur Gen.10 21, qui natus sit anno aetatis Noachi 501:Semum vero secundum natu esse, utpote qui natus sit anno
units.tr: The question is: what does the word [begat] mean, where Gen. 5.32 says, ["Now after Noah was 500 years old, he begat Shem, Ham and Japheth."] But did Noah have all these sons by his wife in one and the same year? By no means, as appears from Gen. 11.10 and 10.21. Therefore "begat" means "began to beget", as it is used in Gen. 11.26. Franciscus Lunius was the first to observe this in his notes on Genesis. Which of Noah's three sons was the firstborn, and in what order each was born to Noah, can be gathered from Moses. Matthaeus Beroaldus, a most diligent man, was the first to note this in his Chronicles, book 3, chapter 2, and he proves that Japheth was the eldest of Noah's sons, as is said in Gen. 10.21, and was born in Noah's 501st year. Shem was second in birth, since he was born in the

units.la: Noachi 502,Gen 11.10: Chamum denique natu minimum ex istis tribus fuisse. Id quod diuerse scribi idem Moses Gen 9.24. Itaque filij Iaphethi velut primogeniti recensentur primo loco,Gen. 10.1.2.3, quos nepe suscepit post diluuium Iaphetus. Q. Cur igitur Semus semper prior nominatur Gen.5 32,6.10,10 I. R. Non propter prærogatiuam ætatis,qui eo maior annis esset Iapheth:sed propter prærogatiuā dignitatis & electionis Diuinæ. Ille enim nempe Semus fuit Electorum,& Ecclesiæ Dei post diluuium parens,Gen.10 10,& deinceps. Sic Abrahamus inter filios Thare primus non ratione ætatis, sed dignitatis in eum à Deo collata recensetur, Gen.11.26. Nachor enim primogenitus fuit inter filios Thare,Gen.12.1. Q. Cur nomen vxoris Noachi non additur,ex qua homines restituti sunt, vt Eua nomen supra commemoratum fuit .i. eius mulieris,ex qua primùm genus humanum satiū fuit:quum ex hac vxore Noachi, & ex Noacho ipso perinde omnes homines propagati fuerint ,vt ex Eua & Adamo primùm progeniti erant. R. Propterea quòd non ex sola fœmina & Noacho totū genus humanum propagatum fuit,vt ex solo Adamo & Eua: sed etiam ex nuribus & filijs ipsius. Idcirco idem prærogatiuam (vt vel hac nominaretur,vel etiam illæ filiorū Noachi vxores)non obtinuit, neque nurus ipsius quoque. Erga prætermissa sunt à Mose omnium earum nomina: neque etiā ea habet Philo Iudæus. Verū Epiphanius haref.26 putat nomen eius fuisse Bapthenes:At Gnostici Noriā vocant: alij verò Pyrrham. Apud Berofum tamen sic nominantur, Tythea magna Pandora, Noela, & Noegla, quatuor illæ. Caterum his expositis, ad caput vndecimum huius historiæ veniamus. Est autem Præceptum Dei de fabricanda Arca, propter iam iam instans diluuium.
units.tr: 502nd year of Noah, Gen. 11.10. Ham was the youngest of the three. The same Moses writes this in Gen. 9.24. Accordingly the sons of Japheth are listed first, as the firstborn, Gen. 10.1, 2, 3, since Japheth begat them after the flood. Q. Why, then, is Shem always named first, Gen. 5.32, 6.10, 10.1? R. Not because of seniority of age, since Japheth was older than him, but because of the priority of dignity and of divine election. For Shem was the parent of the elect and of the Church of God after the flood, Gen. 10.10 and following. So Abraham is listed first among the sons of Terah, not by reason of age, but of the dignity bestowed on him by God, Gen. 11.26. For Nahor was the firstborn among the sons of Terah, Gen. 12.1. Q. Why is the name of Noah's wife not added, through whom mankind was restored, as the name of Eve was mentioned above, that is, of the woman through whom the human race was first propagated, since from this wife of Noah and from Noah himself all men were propagated in the same way as the first men were from Eve and Adam? R. Because the whole human race was not propagated from the woman and Noah alone, as from Adam and Eve alone, but also from his daughters-in-law and sons. Therefore she did not obtain the same prerogative (so that she would be named, or those wives of Noah's sons as well), nor did his daughters-in-law. Moses has omitted the names of all of them, and Philo the Jew does not give them either. But Epiphanius, in heresy 26, thinks her name was Bapthenes; the Gnostics call her Noria; others, Pyrrha. Yet among Berosus they are named thus: Tythea the Great, Pandora, Noela and Noegla, those four. But, these things having been explained, let us come to the eleventh chapter of this history. It contains God's command concerning the building of the Ark, since the flood was now imminent.

units.la: Ad XI. Præceptum Dei de fabricanda Arca Noacho factum.
units.tr: On XI. God's command to Noah to build the Ark.

units.la: Quæritur, Quando Deus Noacho præcepit, vt Arcam fabricaretur, vtrum totis centum viginti annis ante diluuium, an sub finem duntaxat illorum 120 annorum? R. Videtur nonnullis ex Hebr. 11.7, Arca cœpta primum ædificari à Noacho anno 120 ante Diluuium, & per totum illud tempus continuata, tandemq; perfecta. Augustinus lib. 12. contra Faust. cap. 18. censet per cetum totos annos fuisse fabricatam à Noacho. At series historiæ à Mose conscriptæ videtur id refutare, quum aliud tempus diserte statuatur primæ Diluuij denunciationis à Deo factæ, & Præcepti de Arca constructa editi, Gen. 6.7.13. Illud enim longè prius, hoc posterius fuit. Imo vero ex Berosi cuiusdam fragmentis apparet Arcam hanc annis tantum 78 ante diluuium ædificari cœptam. Verum dixerim ego, quem admodum ex ipsis textus verbis colligitur verf. 13, tum demum Noachŭ iussum de Arca ædificanda accepisse, quum instaret finis omnis carnis .i. quum propinquum iam esset diluuium, paucis nimirum omnino annis antequam pluuia illa è cælo deciderent. Sic quoque Philo in Antiquit. Bibl. Nec enim Deus hoc opus tandiu languere & trahi voluit. Antea tamen Noachum & mundum dum dum condemnabat, & de futuro Diluuio concionabatur palàm, & publicè prout à Deo ipso iussum fuerat. Porrò, Vtrum tres tantùm filij cum patre Noacho banc Arcam ædificarint, incertum est. Verisimile est adhibitos quoque ab ys fuisse alios operarios, & coadiutores etsi dictùm est Noacho ipsi, [Fac tibi] Gen.6.14.quic. quid disputet Augustinus libr. Quæst.in Genes.cap.5. Sed operarij illi in Arcam tamen non intraverunt, quoniam minas istas Dei veras esse non crediderunt. Ergo fide caruerunt, quam Noachus & filij eius habuerunt.
units.tr: It is asked: when did God command Noah to build the Ark: was it throughout the whole 120 years before the flood, or only toward the end of those 120 years? R. Some hold, from Heb. 11.7, that the Ark was begun to be built by Noah 120 years before the flood, and continued through that whole time, and finally completed. Augustine, in book 12 against Faustus, chapter 18, holds that the Ark was built by Noah over all those years. But the sequence of the history written by Moses seems to refute this, since a different time is expressly given for the first announcement of the flood by God and for the command to build the Ark, Gen. 6.7, 13. For the former was much earlier, the latter later. Indeed, from the fragments of a certain Berosus it appears that this Ark was begun only 78 years before the flood. But I would say, as is gathered from the words of the text itself in verse 13, that Noah received the command to build the Ark only when the end of all flesh was at hand, that is, when the flood was already near, surely only a few years before that rain fell from heaven. So Philo also says in his Antiquities of the Bible. For God did not want this work to drag on and be delayed so long. Meanwhile, however, he was condemning Noah and the world at every moment, and openly and publicly preached about the coming flood, as God himself had commanded. Furthermore, it is uncertain whether only the three sons built this Ark with their father Noah. It is likely that other workmen and helpers were also employed by them, although it was said to Noah himself, "Make for yourself" (Gen. 6.14). What Augustine argues on this, in book Questions on Genesis, chapter 5. But those workmen did not enter the Ark, because they did not believe that these threats of God were true. Therefore they lacked the faith which Noah and his sons had.

units.la: Q. Cur eiusmodi vas & ædificiũ tantũ Arca, Thebat Hebraicè, Græcè κάρνακ vocatur: nõ autem Navis, vel navigium, quod in aquis versaretur, & navigàdi gratiâ constructum esset, paratúmque. R. Iosephus lib.1. Antiquit.cap.5.eam generaliter vocat μνχανὴν, & arte cõfectam structuram asserum & camerarum. Sacra verò Scriptura in nouo Testamento vbique κιβωτὸν, vt Arcam, vti Heb.11.7, 1.Pet.3.20. Epiphanius in Ancorato [Aron] Hebraicè dici putat, eamq; vocem ipse conuertit Græcè λάρναξ. Verum Hebræi vocant [Thebat] quam vocem à nomine [Aron] differre seribunt. Nam Aron significat generaliter Arcam, & tectam vndique structuram quamuis, qualis fuit Arca Sanctuarij. Thebat autem eam Arcam tâtùm seu structuram, cuius vsus est in aquis. Sic Exo.2.3. Aliy igitur hoc nomen vertunt Tectum navigium, à forma. Ex lignis autè Gopher exstructa est Arca, id est, cedrinis, vt interpretatur Philo, quæ putrescere non solent in aquis: sed in illis robur suum integrum seruat. Albinus Præceptor Caroli Magni in Quæst.in Genes.ait, [Ligna leuigata, de quibus Arca praecipitur fieri fuerunt fortia, & indissolubilia: denique quadrata, ne Arca vi ventorum, aut aquarum impetu soluereatur. Bitumine quoque illini iubetur, quod est feruentissimum & vio- lentissimum gluten, cuius hac est virtus, vt ligna eo oblita nec vermibus exedi, nec Solis ardore, nec fluctibus ventorum, nec aquarum possint inundatione dissolui. ] Cur autem hoc tectum aedificium non appellatur Navis ratio est, ne videretur Deus Noachum, eiusque familiam in ea Arca seruare velle ordinario modo, & quo solent homines in navibus velo, & remis instructus incolumes per medias aquas euadere. At hoc vas & aedificium nihil tale habuit, non vela, non remos, non remiges, non rudentes, aut vllos funes nauticos, non anchoram, qua regeretur: sed his omnibus destitutus Noachus in medijs tamen aquis & tempestatibus illis magnis per annum saluus & incolumis a Deo miraculose, & extraordinarie seruatus est. Ergo non iubet Deus nauem aedificari, qua media & instrumenta navigationi apta haberet: sed adificium quoddam, & illud quidem in imo seu fundo planum, quod omnium navium exstructioni repugnat. Habent enim naues fundum definens in angustum: in lateribus diffunduntur. Arcam vero ea appellauit Deus a forma & vsu, quod in ea, velut capsula & sepulcro, tutus tamen lateret, ac veraretur Noachus. Q. Cur has dimensiones, quas commemorat Moses, Arca habuit, videlicet 300 cubitos in longitudine: 50 in latitudine: 30 in altitudine? R. De harum dimensionum significatione Patres anxie quaesiuerunt, & cur eadem hac proportione habuerit: imprimis autem Origenes. Tandem vero Augustinus lib. 15. Ciuit. Dei, cap. 26. sic eas exposuit, [Arca (inquit) in quam Noachus ingressus est, proculdubio figura est perigrinatis in hoc feculo ciuitatis Dei, hoc est, Ecclesia, quae fit salua per lignum, in quo pependit Mediator Dei & hominum homo Christus Iesus. Nam & mensura ipse longitudinis, altitudinis, latitudinisque eius significant corpus humanum, in cuius veritate ad homines praenuntiatus est venturus, & venit. Humani quippe corporis longitudo a vertice vsque ad vestigia sexies tatum habet, quam latitudo, quae est ab vno latere ad alterum latus: & decies tantum, quam altitudo, cuius altitudinis mensura in latere a dorso ad ventrem: velut fi iacente hominem metiaris supinum, seu pronum, sexies tantum longus est a capite ad pedes, quam latus a dextra in sinistram: & decies quam altus a terra. Vnde fabla est Arca trecentorum in longitudine cubitorum, & quinquaginta in latitudine, & triginta in altitudine. Et quod oflium in latere accepit, profecto illud est vulnus, quando latus crucifixi lancea perforatum est. Hac quippe ad illum venientes ingrediuntur, quia inde Sacramenta manarunt, quibus credentes initiantur. Et quod de lignis quadratis fieri iubetur, vndique stabilem vitam Sanctorum fignificat. Quacunque enim verteris, quadratum stabit. Et cetera, quae in eiusdem Arcae constructione dicuntur, Ecclesiasticarum signa sunt rerum,] quemadmodum idem Augustinus explicat lib. 12. contra Manich. cap. 14. 15. 16. 17. 18. Caeterum vt, quod ipse sentio, pronuntiem, & aperiam, sic dico, Recte quidem Arcam cum Ecclesia Dei conferri, vt apparet ex 1. Pet. 3. 20
units.tr: Q. Why is such a vessel and building called an Ark (in Hebrew Thebat, in Greek kibōtos [κάρνακ]), and not a ship or vessel, which would float on the waters and be constructed and prepared for the purpose of sailing? R. Josephus, in book 1 of the Antiquities, chapter 5, calls it generally a machine (mēchanē), a structure of planks and chambers put together by art. But Holy Scripture in the New Testament everywhere calls it kibōtos, that is, Ark, as in Heb. 11.7 and 1 Pet. 3.20. Epiphanius, in the Ancoratus, thinks the word is Hebrew [Aron], and he himself renders this word in Greek as larnax. But the Hebrews call it [Thebat], and write that this word differs from the name [Aron]. For Aron signifies generally a chest, and any structure enclosed on all sides, such as was the Ark of the Sanctuary. But Thebat signifies only that chest or structure whose use is on the waters. So in Exod. 2.3. Others therefore translate this name as "a covered vessel", from its form. The Ark was built of gopher wood, that is, cedar, as Philo interprets, which is not wont to rot in the waters, but preserves its strength whole in them. Albinus, tutor of Charlemagne, in his Questions on Genesis, says: "The smoothed planks, of which the Ark is commanded to be made, were strong and indissoluble; finally, they were squared, so that the Ark would not be loosened by the force of the winds or the onslaught of the waters. It is also commanded to be smeared with bitumen, which is the most fervent and violent glue, whose power is such that wood coated with it cannot be eaten by worms, nor be dissolved by the heat of the sun, nor by the waves of the winds, nor by the flooding of the waters." Now the reason why this covered building is not called a ship is that it might not seem that God wished to preserve Noah and his household in that Ark in the ordinary way, in which men usually escape safely through the midst of the waters in ships equipped with sails and oars. But this vessel and building had nothing of the kind: no sails, no oars, no rowers, no ropes or any nautical cables, no anchor by which it could be steered. But Noah, deprived of all these, was nevertheless preserved safe and sound for a year in the midst of the waters and those great tempests, miraculously and extraordinarily by God. Therefore God did not command a ship to be built, which would have had the middle parts and instruments fit for navigation, but a certain building, flat indeed at the bottom or base, which is opposed to the construction of all ships. For ships have a bottom that narrows to a point, and they spread out at the sides. But God called it an Ark from its form and use, because in it, as in a casket and tomb, Noah would lie hidden yet safe and be preserved. Q. Why did the Ark have these dimensions which Moses records, namely 300 cubits in length, 50 in breadth, 30 in height? R. The Fathers eagerly inquired into the meaning of these dimensions, and why they had this proportion, above all Origen. Finally, however, Augustine, in book 15 of The City of God, chapter 26, explained them thus: "The Ark into which Noah entered is undoubtedly a figure of the city of God as it sojourns in this age, that is, of the Church, which is saved through the wood on which hung the Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus. For its measures of length, height and breadth signify the human body, in whose truth it was foretold to men that he would come, and he came. For the length of the human body from the crown to the soles of the feet is six times its breadth, which is from one side to the other, and ten times its height, whose measure is from back to belly; so that, if you measure a man lying on his back or face, he is six times longer from head to feet than he is broad from right to left, and ten times as high as he is from the earth. Hence the Ark is said to be three hundred cubits in length, and fifty in breadth, and thirty in height. And the door that it received in its side, surely that is the wound, when the side of the crucified one was pierced by the lance. For those who come to him enter by this, because from it the sacraments flowed, by which believers are initiated. And that it is commanded to be made of squared planks signifies the life of the saints being stable on every side. For wherever you turn it, the square will stand. And the rest which is said in the construction of the same Ark are signs of ecclesiastical realities," as Augustine himself explains in book 12 against the Manichaeans, chapters 14 to 18. But, that I may state and reveal what I myself think, I say thus: the Ark is rightly compared with the Church of God, as appears from 1 Pet. 3.20.

units.la: Tertulliano, Cypriano, Hieronymo, Augustino, Gregorio, & omnibus Patribus. Illa vero dimensiones argutè numium & subtiliter cum corpore humano (quasi illius essent figura) comparari. Sequatur tamen id, qui volet. Verum Gregorius Magnus Homil. 16 in Ezech. aliter easdem interpretatur. Ego vero illas à Deo additas & praescriptas puto, quod aedificium, & navigiū eiusmodi magnitudinis, id est, latitudinis, altitudinis, & longitudinis satis esse viderit, cognoueritque Deum fore capax ad numerum eum & animalium, & Hominum commodè capiendum, quantum Deus in Diluuio seruare decreuerat. Gregor. Magnus, [Ipsa ratio exigit, ait, ut credamus, quòd in illa latitudine omnes bestiae, cunctaq; quadrupedia, atque reptilia in inferioribus fuerunt: Homo vero, atque volatilia nimirū in superioribus.]
units.tr: Tertullian, Cyprian, Jerome, Augustine, Gregory, and all the Fathers. Those dimensions have been subtly and cleverly compared with the human body, as though they were its figure. Let whoever wishes follow that. But Gregory the Great, in Homily 16 on Ezekiel, interprets them differently. I, however, think that God added and prescribed them, because He saw that a building and a vessel of this size, that is, of this breadth, height and length, would be sufficient, and He knew that it would be large enough to hold conveniently the number of animals and men that God had decided to preserve in the Flood. Gregory the Great: Reason itself requires, he says, that we believe that in the lower part of that breadth were all the beasts, all the quadrupeds and reptiles; but man and the birds were in the upper part.

units.la: Nec enim in ea Arca Deus Noachum tanquam in palatio collocauit, vbi haberet diuersas cœnationes, alias æstiuas, alias hybernas, item deambulationes latas, & spatiosa quaedam cubicula spatiandi vel animi caussa, & aulas ad mutandū hospitium diuersas. Sed in ea Arca tanquam in sepulcro Noachum esse & iacere, id est, versari angusto in loco voluit Deus. Ergo eas tantum cameras, eosq; nidos seu cubicula habuit, quae & homines, & animalia à Deo seruanda commodè quidem, sed angustè & arctè continere possent. Porro nauium multarum longè maioris, quàm hæc Arca fuerit, magnitudinis exempla extant apud Athenæum lib. 5. Dipnosoph. & apud Plutarchū in vita Demetrij, qualis nauis Hieronis regis Syracusarum, & Ptolomei Philopatoris fuit. Ecquis ante Cubitum sit hic intelligendus, vtrum communis, & qualem homines illius seculi habuere: an vero alius quidam eo maior, qualis est Geometricus, qui tantum capit, quantum sex nostri, seu hominum illius aetatis cubiti continent. Anxiè quaesitum est. Origenes, vt tradit Augustinus lib. 15 Ciuit. Dei, cap. 27 de Geometrico cubito hunc interpretatur. Joannes Buteo de communi, qualem illius aui homines habuere, cui potius equidem assentior. Q. Quot contignationes seu concamerationes tota illa Arca habuit? R. Iosephus scribit eas in Arca fuisse quatuor lib. 1 cap. 5 Antiquitatum. Albinus in Quaest. in Genes. quinque: nempe infimam Stercorariam: secundam Apothecaria vbi cibi fuerunt repositi: Tertiam feris animatibus destinata: Quartam, mansuetis: Quintam & supremam, hominibus ipsis. Augustinus lib. quaest. in Genes. cap 6. tres solum contignationes in ea agnoscit. [In prima enim habitatione, ait, id est, in inferioribus semel camerata erat Arca: In secunda habitatione etiam supra inferiorem camerata erat, ergo iam bicamerata: ac per hoc in tertia supra secundam tricamerata erat.] Hac sententia vera est, & confirmatur Gen. 6. 16. Porro supra tres illas contignationes erat tectum Arca, quod totam eam cooperiebat, & contignationes a pluuia, & reliquis iniuriis coeli defendebat. In singulis quoque concamerationibus seu contignationibus erant plures camerae, stabula, seu nidi asseribus inter se distincti ac separati, intra quos vniuscuiusque generis animantia collectim, simul & vna (qua erat vnius generis) asseruabantur: In alio nido animalia alterius generis: sic vt genus quodque animalium ab alio diuersum peculiariter quoque & singillatim in vna aliqua cötignatione suâ nidum, & cau-lam ab alio distinctam haberet. Q. Cur fuerint in Arca tres tantum contignationes, praeter tectum, nō autem plures: quū eorum tamen (quae in Arca servari debebant) animaliū, praeter homines, videtur fuisse quatuor ad minus genera, nempe Bestiae seu fera animatia, Iumenta, Reptibilia, & Volatilia, & quidem hae ipsa secundū species suas, vti docet Moses Gen. 6. 20, & 7. 14. R. Homines eādem cum iumentis seu cicuribus animātibus terrenis habitationem habuisse, atque occupasse omnino verisimile est. Ergo virúmque hoc genus vnam tantum habitationem (siue ea media, siue suprēma fuit) id est, Iumenta, & Homines vnam duntaxat cōignationem in varias cameras diuisam possederunt. Reptilia verò velut serpentes beslys seu feris animantibus accensebantur. Ergo & hac duo quoque animaliū terrenorum minimè cicurum genera vnam solum contignationem in varios nidos separatam obtinebat quoq, quae videtur fuisse infima concameratio. Volatilia denique omnia vnam quoque habitationem (quae suprema videtur fuisse) in varios nidos partita habebant. Itaq, quanuis eorum, quae in arca fuerunt, animalium genera quinque distingui possint, videlicet Homines, Iumenta seu cicura animantia, Bestiae seu fera animalia, Reptilia, & Volatilia, tres tamen concamerationes seu contignationes ad haec omnia capiēda in illa Arca satis erāt. Q. Quomodo tantulum seu aedificium seu nauigiū tot animantium species (quot & Deus creauerat, & tunc viuebant) capere quiuerit, & illa in Arca tam parua continēri potuerint, Gen. 6. 19, & 7. 14. R. Augu-stinus
units.tr: For God did not place Noah in that Ark as in a palace, where he would have had various dining rooms, some for summer and some for winter, also wide walkways and spacious chambers for walking or for relaxation, and halls for changing his lodging. Rather, God willed that Noah should be, and lie, in the Ark as in a tomb, that is, that he should dwell in a cramped place. So God gave it only those chambers and nests or cells which could conveniently, but narrowly and tightly, hold the men and animals God meant to preserve. Moreover, examples of ships much larger than this Ark exist in Athenaeus, Deipnosophistae book 5, and in Plutarch's Life of Demetrius, such as the ship of King Hiero of Syracuse and that of Ptolemy Philopator. Whether this cubit is to be understood as the common cubit, of the kind men of that age had, or rather some other cubit larger than that, such as the geometrical cubit, which holds as much as six of ours, or of the cubits of men of that age, has been anxiously debated. Origen, as Augustine reports in book 15 of The City of God, chapter 27, interprets it as the geometrical cubit. John Buteo takes it as the common cubit, such as its ancestors had, and to that view I rather assent. Q. How many floors or stories did the whole Ark have? A. Josephus writes that there were four in the Ark, Antiquities book 1, chapter 5. Albinus, in Questions on Genesis, says five: namely, the lowest for dung; the second, the storeroom where food was put; the third, assigned to wild animals; the fourth, to tame animals; and the fifth and highest, to the men themselves. Augustine, in Questions on Genesis, chapter 6, recognises only three floors in it. [For in the first habitation, he says, that is, in the lower part, the Ark was vaulted once; in the second habitation it was vaulted also above the lower part, so already twice vaulted; and so in the third, above the second, it was thrice vaulted.] This opinion is true, and it is confirmed by Genesis 6:16. Moreover, above those three floors was the roof of the Ark, which covered it entirely and protected the floors from rain and the other injuries of the sky. In each of the floors or storeys there were several chambers, stalls or nests, separated and divided from one another by partitions, in which the animals of each kind were kept together, and in one nest the animals of one kind, and in another those of a different kind; so that each kind of animal, distinct from the others, had its own nest and stall, separate from the others, in one particular storey. Q. Why were there only three floors in the Ark, apart from the roof, and not more, since the animals that had to be kept in the Ark, apart from men, appear to have been at least four kinds: namely beasts or wild animals, cattle, reptiles, and birds, and these according to their species, as Moses teaches in Genesis 6:20 and 7:14? A. It is quite probable that men shared a dwelling with the cattle or tame land animals and occupied it. So these two kinds, men and cattle, possessed one dwelling only (whether it was the middle or the top floor), that is, cattle and men possessed one storey only, divided into various chambers. Reptiles, such as snakes, were counted among the wild animals. So these two kinds of land animals, which are not tame, also occupied one storey, divided into various nests, which seems to have been the lowest floor. Finally, all the birds shared one dwelling, which seems to have been the top floor, divided into various nests. So, although the kinds of animals that were in the Ark can be distinguished into five, namely men, cattle or tame animals, wild animals, reptiles, and birds, three floors were enough in that Ark to hold all of them. Q. How could such a small building or ship hold so many species of animals (as many as God had created and as were then living), and how could they be contained in so small an Ark, Genesis 6:19 and 7:14? A. Augustine

units.la: Ergo, consistentes; a 356. stinus de hoc ipso dubitat lib. 1. in Genes. cap. 6: sed tandem recurrit ad cubitum geometricum, quem intelligendum putat in Arca fabricanda. Is autem quum sit maximus (singuli enim cubiti Geometrici valent senos nostros) maxima quoque capacitatis, ait, Arca seu ædificium illud fuit. Verum idem hanc solutionem nequaquam satis firmā esse animadvertens, decurrit ad alia, nempe lib. 15. Ciuit. Dei, cap. 27. Negat enim omnia animalium genera in Arca ista fuisse. Nam in ea vel in aquis viuunt, inquit, vel non. Quæ viuunt in aquis, uti Pisces, & alia quædam animatia, non fuerunt in Arca. Eorū vero, quæ duntaxat extra aquas degunt, alia sine concubitu maris & fœminæ nascuntur, uti locustæ, apes, pulices, mures, & quædam alia minuta bestiolæ, quæ ex quibusdam rebus & sordibus nascūtur. Hæc quoque animantia non fuerunt in Arca. Sed & quæ ex coitu quidem maris & fœminæ generātur, sed nō eiusdem generis (quoniam etsi sexum habent, non habent tamen fœtum, velut Mulæ) nec ea quoq; in Arca collocat, quales sunt Muli, qui ex Asina & Equo gignuntur. Gen. 35. 24. Augustinus lib. 3. Genesi ad liter. cap. 12 & 14. Verū Ioannes Buteo melius, quo modo tot animantium terrenorum & volatilium genera secundum suas species in Arca distincte collocata & manere potuerint, docet: Primum feras bestias seu super ventrem repentes, seu gradientes pedibus suis in suas species distribuit, quas vix quindecim, vel ad summum sexdecim numero reperies. Ergo in prima seu infima contignatione collocentur hæ species omnes animaliū numero sexdecim. Iumenta seu mansueta animalia (quod est secundū genus terrenorū) in suas species quoque diuidito: Hai vix quindecim inueneru. Ha vero in sua .i. in secunda seu media contignatione vna cum Noacho & filijs eius ponantur. Quanquam Gregorius Magnus Homil. 16 in Ezechiel. Volatilia & Hominem in superioribus collocat. Volatilia denique in suas similiter species tribuito, quas vix efficerus viginti numero diuersas. His sua pariter contignatio nempe suprema destinata est, quae eadem contignatio, praeter omnes animum species, vna cibos ad animalium & hominum victum coacernatos inuectos in Arcam, certis cellulis distinctis, habebit. Iam vero facile in vnaquaq; contignatione cellula seu stabula aedificari potuerunt, alia quidem ampliora, alia vero minora pro ratione animalium quae ijs contineri, & concludi debebat. Maium enim stabulum Elephantis, quam Lupis in infima concameratione fuit aedificandum: item latius Leonibus & Leanis, quam Vulpibus & Stellionibus. Eodem modo de mansuetorum animalium cellulis, quae in medio tabulato fuerunt, sentiendum, Eas maiores vel minores a Noacho viro prudentissimo constitutas pro magnitudine vel numero bestiarum in ijs cellulis collocandarum, ac recipiendarum. Iam vero vnaquaq; contignatio habuit 300 cubitos, id est, ad minus 450 pedes in longitudine, qui si in quindecim species seu cellulas diuidatur, habebit vnaquaq; cellula pedes 30 in longitudine. Latitudo Arca continebat 50 cubitos, qui vel minimum efficiunt iustos pedes 75. Haec latitudo, si in quindecim partes & cellulas diuidatur, habebit vnaquaque cellula vel stabulum pedes 5. in latitudine: ex quibus iam apparet quam facile omnia animantia illa in Arca contineri potuerunt. Nam ex minoribus cellulis est detrahendu quod maioribus addas, ut omnia cômode animalia in illis collocentur. Q. Quomodo cum tot animalibus, eorumque fœtore & sordibus versans tanto tempore & in eodem ædificio Noachus & filii, tamen nec ipse, nec filii eius illic coputruerunt, neque mortui sunt? R. Certissimum quidem est neque ex animalibus, neque ex hominibus, qui in Arcam ingressi sunt, vllum in ea mortuum esse. Nam Moses diserte docet omnia viuentia, quæ in eam intrauerant ante Diluuium, etiā ex eadem post Diluuiu exijsse nihil quoque perijsse, Gen. 7. 15, & 8. 16. 17. 18. 19. Nam Deus ea singula conseruauit, vt fuerat pollicitus. Non computruit igitur in Arca vel Noachus, vel filij eius, vel vxor, vel nurus: neque tetro sordium ex tot animalibus collectarum odore extincti sunt homines illi: simò nec alia animalia vlla, quoniam ea Deus sustentauit, & superesse diluuio voluit.
units.tr: Augustine himself doubts this very point in book 1 on Genesis, chapter 6, but in the end he has recourse to the geometrical cubit, which he thinks should be understood in building the Ark. Since that cubit is very large (for each geometrical cubit is worth six of ours), he says that the Ark, or that building, had very great capacity. But the same Augustine, noticing that this solution is by no means firm enough, turns to other arguments, namely in book 15 of The City of God, chapter 27. For he denies that all kinds of animals were in that Ark. For, he says, they either live in water or they do not. Those that live in water, such as fish and certain other animals, were not in the Ark. Of those that live only outside water, some are born without the mating of male and female, like locusts, bees, fleas, mice, and certain other tiny creatures that arise from certain filth and refuse. These animals too were not in the Ark. And those that are indeed generated by the union of male and female, but not of the same kind (since, although they have a sex, they do not have offspring, like mules), he also does not place in the Ark, such as mules, which are born of a she-ass and a horse. Genesis 35:24. Augustine, On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, book 3, chapters 12 and 14. But John Buteo teaches better how so many kinds of land animals and birds, distinguished according to their species, could be placed and remain in the Ark. First he distributes the wild beasts, whether creeping on their belly or walking on their feet, into their species; you will find them barely fifteen, or at most sixteen, in number. So these species of animals, sixteen in number, should be placed in the first or lowest floor. Divide the cattle or tame animals (which is the second kind of land animals) into their species likewise; they have been found to be barely fifteen. These should be placed in the second or middle floor, together with Noah and his sons, in their own place. Although Gregory the Great, in Homily 16 on Ezekiel, places the birds and man in the upper part. Finally, distribute the birds likewise into their species; they can be made barely twenty in number. To these the top floor is similarly assigned, which, apart from all these kinds of animals, will have one store, with cells set apart, for the food gathered and brought into the Ark for the sustenance of the animals and men. Now, in each floor the cells or stalls could easily be built, some larger, some smaller, according to the size of the animals that had to be contained and shut in them. For a larger stall had to be built for elephants than for wolves in the lowest vault, and likewise wider ones for lions and lionesses than for foxes and lizards. In the same way it should be thought of the cells for tame animals, which were in the middle storey: Noah, a most prudent man, set them up larger or smaller according to the size and number of beasts to be placed and received in those cells. Now each floor had 300 cubits, that is, at least 450 feet in length; if this is divided into fifteen species or cells, each cell will have 30 feet in length. The breadth of the Ark was 50 cubits, which make at least 75 full feet. If this breadth is divided into fifteen parts and cells, each cell or stall will have 5 feet in breadth. From this it is already clear how easily all those animals could be contained in the Ark. For from the smaller cells what you add to the larger ones must be taken away, so that all the animals can be conveniently placed in them. Q. How, when Noah and his sons lived for so long in the same building with so many animals and their stench and filth, did neither he nor his sons rot there, nor die? A. It is quite certain that none of the animals or men who entered the Ark died in it. For Moses clearly teaches that all living things which had entered it before the Flood also came out of it after the Flood, and that nothing perished, Genesis 7:15 and 8:16-19. For God preserved each of them, as He had promised. So neither Noah, nor his sons, nor his wife, nor his daughters-in-law rotted in the Ark, nor were those men killed by the foul odour of so many animals gathered together in it; nor indeed any other animals, since God sustained them and willed them to survive the Flood.

units.la: Fuit quidem miserù, sanctos illos homines cum tot brutis animantibus esse: Nam in Arca velut in sepulcro inter medias feras, in mediis earum sordibus, in aquis & mortis horrore perpetuo oculis obuersate versati sunt: verum hoc sepulcrum Deus ipsè parauerat, in quo eos ex morte conseruaret, & ex mediis aquis eriperet. Fera vero bestia tunc ferociam suam ad tempus deposuerat, Deo sic eas subigente, & metu mortis earum sanitiam domante, denique incussò eisdem feræ quantumuis trucibus terrore à Deo. Q. Quantum vero ad sordes, etsi peculiariter qua ratione purgaretur ex arca, non describit Moses saltem aliquo tamen pacto, & ex aliqua Arca parte velut per fenestram eiectas nonnunquam fuisse indico, ne nsmius earum fœtor hominibus nocereț. Certè si in Arca per tantum tempus retenta fuerunt ea sordes, iacueruntve, quantum diluuium fuit, quantumque animalia fuerunt ac manserunt in Arca, Deus temperauit, cohibuitque istum putorem ac fœtorem, ne homines, ipsáue animalia laederet. Ergo fuit Noachi conseruatio extraordinarium Dei opus. Q. Cur Deus animalia quædam ex iis, quæ cum impiis illis hominibus fuerant, & in primo illo impuro Mundo vixerant, reseruauit: quia omnia immundorum hominum sint immunda, Tit. 1. 15: & Deus alia noua in nouo & repurgato post Diluuium mundo denuo, ut in prima Mundi origine, creare potuerit: denique quum infantes impiorum seruare noluerit, sed eos aquis perdiderit? R. Ne vilesceret miraculū illud prima rerum Creationis, Deus vel animalia, vel homines denuò creare noluit ex nihilo, vel etiam ex terra, quemadmodum primum fecerat. Verum ut verbi & præcepti sui semel rebus creatis dati vis & robur intelligeretur perpetuū, nempe [Crescite, & multiplicamini] voluit in futuro post diluuium seu repurgato mundo & animalia, & homines ex iis, quæ iam a sa creata erant, illudque præceptū acceperant, propagari & oriri. Sic enim maior verbi diuini efficacitas animadiuersa est, & Lex à Deo semel natura data firmior intellecta. Sic post diluuium idem Deus ordinem naturalem à se antea constitutum denuò sanxit, & durare voluit, Gen. 8.22. Porrò illa Animalia, quæ seruauit in Arca Deus, nequaquam fuerunt vel per se, vel ex eo polluta, quòd in eodem cū impiis illis hominibus mundo & eodem tempore vixissent. Nam quū ratione careat, peccatum in ea non cadit. Quod tamen quaedam animalia iam tum immunda dicebantur, alio pertinet, vt mox exponetur. Cur denique impiorum nullos infantes ex isto diluvio eripuerit Deus, quum tamen animalia quaedam ex eodem exemerit, in sequenti historia capite declarabitur. Q. Cur quaedam animalia bruta iam tum vocabantur immunda, Gen. 7. 2: quaedam vero munda, quum omnis caro corrupisset viam suam? Gen. 6. 12.
units.tr: It was indeed a wretched thing for those holy men to be with so many brute animals. In the ark, as if in a tomb, among the wild beasts, in the midst of their filth, amid the waters and the constant horror of death, they lived with death ever before their eyes. Yet God himself had prepared this tomb, in which he preserved them from death and snatched them from the midst of the waters. The fierce beast, moreover, had laid aside its ferocity for the time, God so subduing them, and the fear of death taming their savagery; finally, terror from God was struck into even the fiercest wild beast. Q. As for the filth, although Moses does not describe how it was specifically cleared out of the ark, I suspect that at least in some way, and from some part of the ark as through a window, it was sometimes thrown out, lest its stench harm the people. Certainly, if that filth was kept and lay in the ark for as long as the Flood lasted and the animals remained in the ark, God tempered and restrained that stench and reek so that it would not harm the people or the animals themselves. Therefore Noah's preservation was an extraordinary work of God. Q. Why did God keep certain animals from among those that had been with those impious men and had lived in that first impure world, since "all the things of impure men are impure" (Tit. 1.15), and since God could have created other new animals anew in the new and purified world after the Flood, as at the first origin of the world; and finally, why did he not wish to save the infants of the impious, but destroyed them by the waters? R. So that the miracle of the first creation of things would not become cheap, God did not wish to create animals or humans anew out of nothing, or even out of earth, as he had first done. But so that the force and strength of his word and precept, once given to created things, might be understood as perpetual, namely "Increase and multiply," he willed that in the future, after the Flood or in the purified world, both animals and humans should be propagated and arise from those things already created by him, which had received that command. For thus the greater efficacy of the divine word is observed, and the law once given by God to nature is understood as firmer. Thus after the Flood the same God again sanctioned the natural order he had previously established and willed it to endure (Gen. 8.22). Moreover, those animals that God preserved in the ark were in no way polluted, either in themselves or by this, that they had lived in the same world and at the same time as those impious men. For since it lacks reason, sin does not fall upon it. That some animals were even then called unclean belongs to another matter, as will soon be explained. Finally, why God rescued none of the infants of the impious from this flood, although he did bring certain animals out of it, will be declared in the following chapter of the history. Q. Why were certain brute animals already then called unclean (Gen. 7.2), but certain clean, when all flesh had corrupted its way (Gen. 6.12)?

units.la: R. Supra demonstratum est, quod dicitur, [Omnis caro corruperat viam suam supra terram] de solis hominibus intelligendum esse. Via enim illa est via mortis, non via pedis. Ergo quaedam animantia, imo vero omnia bruta ratione ea, qua peccatum cadit in hominem, fuerunt munda: nam omnia peccato carent, quum & voluntate & intelligentia sint spoliata, minimeque pradita. Q. Quamobrem ἄλογα nominantur. Q. Quaedam tamen ex brutis istis animantibus appellantur Immunda, duplici nomine nempe tum sacrificiorum, quae vero Deo fiebat: tum etiam ipsorum hominum vsus gratia, nempe quod eiusmodi animalium genera neque tunc ad diuina sacrificia adhiberentur, neque ad esum hominum. Haec autem genera postea Lege sua Ceremoniali declarauit Deus, etsi fortassis ea in Lege sua postea amplificauit, & plures eorum species per Mosem constituit, Leuit. 11, Deut. 14. 4. 5. & deinceps.
units.tr: R. It has been shown above that what is said, "all flesh had corrupted its way upon the earth," must be understood of humans alone. For that way is the way of death, not the way of the foot. Therefore certain animals, indeed all brute beasts, were clean in that respect in which sin falls upon man: for they are free of sin, since they are deprived of will and understanding and are not endowed with them at all. Q. Why are they called irrational [ἄλογα]? Q. Yet certain of those brute animals are called unclean, under a double title: namely, with respect to the sacrifices that were offered to God, and also for the sake of human use, because these kinds of animals were then neither employed for divine sacrifices nor for human food. These kinds God afterwards declared in his ceremonial law, although perhaps he later enlarged them in his law and, through Moses, established more of their species (Lev. 11; Deut. 14.4, 5 and following).

units.la: Q. Cur plura mundorum, quam immundorum animalium genera seruat Deus? R. Apparet ex Gen. 7. 2. septena marem & foeminam ex animalibus mundis iussu Dei sumpta fuisse, id est quatuordecim capita, septem nimirum ex eo genere Mares, & septem foeminas: At ex immundis bina tantum, Marem, & fœminam .i. quatuor duntaxat ex eo genere capita videlicet duos mares, & duas fœminas. Ergo mundorum fuerunt paria septem: Immundorû autem paria solùm duo. Falluntur enim qui ex Gen. 6.19 putat ex omnibus animalibus brutis bina tantùm, nempe marem & fœminam, ingressa fuisse Arcam: ex quouis nimirum eorû genere, non plura. Nam ut scribit Augustin lib.quaest. in Genesi cap. 8, locus ille non definit numerum recipiendorum animalium, sed ostendit paria & coniugia in omnibus recipiedis sive mundis, sive immundis esse oportere, nempe marem & fœminâ. Ergo longè maiorem mundorû, quàm immundorum animalium numerû Deus in Arca seruari voluit, ex quo singula eorum genera postea propagaret, quod & ad sacrificia diuina, & ad vitâ hominum vsus erat futurus mundorum animalium, Gen. 8.20, & 9.3. Nullus autem ad vtrumq; immundorû vsus. Caeterum ad terna mundorum paria septimû adiecit Deus, vt post diluuium ex eo septimo pari sibi sacrificium à Noacho posset offerri, quemadmodum obseruauit Ioan. Calvinus idque postea factû esse, Gen. 8.20.
units.tr: Q. Why does God preserve more kinds of clean animals than unclean? R. It appears from Gen. 7.2 that seven pairs of male and female of the clean animals were taken at God's command, that is, fourteen individuals: seven males and seven females. But of the unclean only two, a male and a female, that is, four individuals of that kind, namely two males and two females. So there were seven pairs of clean animals, but only two pairs of unclean. For those are mistaken who, from Gen. 6.19, think that only two of each of all brute animals, namely a male and a female, entered the ark: of each kind, that is, no more. For, as Augustine writes in his Questions on Genesis, ch. 8, that passage does not define the number of animals to be received, but shows that pairs and matings must be taken in all cases, whether clean or unclean, namely male and female. Therefore God willed that a far greater number of clean than unclean animals be preserved in the ark, so that from them he might afterwards propagate each kind, since clean animals were to be used both for divine sacrifices and for the life of humans (Gen. 8.20; 9.3). But no unclean animal was to serve either use. Moreover, God added a seventh pair to the three pairs of clean animals, so that after the Flood a sacrifice could be offered to himself by Noah from that seventh pair, as John Calvin observed, and that this was afterwards done (Gen. 8.20).

units.la: Q. Quomodo intelligenda sunt hæc verba Mosis [Bina, & septena, Marem, & fœminam] vti extat diserte Gen. 7.2.
units.tr: Q. How are these words of Moses to be understood, "two" and "seven," "male and female," as is expressly found in Gen. 7.2?

units.la: R. [Bina, Marem & fœminam] denotât bis marem, & bis fœminam ex eo animantiû genere sumenda: ergo quatuor capita, duos mares, & duas fœminas. Septena marem & fœmina significant septies marem, & septies fœminam ex ea specie animalium capi debere: ergo quatuordecim capita, septem mares & septem fœminas. Sic Philo, & Epiphanius.
units.tr: R. "Two, male and female" means that two males and two females are to be taken from that kind of animal: so four individuals, two males and two females. "Seven, male and female" signifies that seven males and seven females must be taken from that species: so fourteen individuals, seven males and seven females. So Philo and Epiphanius.

units.la: Q. Cur Deus animalia quædam immunda in futurum post diluuium luuium seculũ restare & reseruari voluit, qui Munaũ propter immunditiem delebat? R. Quum Deus animalia immunda seruari præcipit, vt post Diluuium genus quoque eorum propagaretur, non propterea vult aut probat Deus peccatum & nequitiam propagari, propter quam priorem illum Mundum perdebat: (nec enim Immunda dicuntur illa animalia, quod peccatum perpetrarent) sed species omnes rerũ à se in prima mundi origine creatarũ seruari voluit Deus. Nam inquit Epiphanius lib.1.contra hæres. ... ea custodiuit in arca Deus, ne mundus post diluuiũ esset imperfeCtior, aut in eo minus Dei sapientia, bonitas, potentia ad se agnoscendum eluceret, quã in primo illo & deleto, Rom.1.20. Quã vero ratione primùm Deus Immunda animalia creauit, eãdem illa retinere in mundo & conseruare voluit, iussitque etiam post diluuium esse. Q. Ecquis cibum ad vitẽtum animalium in Arcam coportatus fuit, quod scribitur Gen.6.21: quum non omnia animalia esca eadem vtãtur, & alantur, vt Leones, & Equi. R. De hoc ipso quærit Augustinus lib.quæst.in Gen. cap.71. Verum quũ sic disertè præscripserit Deus, [Accipe tibi de omni cibo, qui comeditur, & collige penes te, vt sit tibi & illis ad comedendum:] & quum Gen.7.7 dicatur Noachus fecisse secundũ omnia, quæ præceperat Deus, mihi dubium non est, quin ex omni cibo Noachus tanquam bonus Paterfamilias promus & condus collegerit, ex quo animaliũ tot species pasci solent, & possunt commodè, easque escas certis in cellulis & apothecis in Arca reposuerit, velut in suprema contignatione, quale est frumentum, fœnum, herbæ quos cibos in tanta tamen aeri pluuiy humiditate Deus conseruauit, ne putrescerent in eadem Arca. Q. Vtrum in Arca plures, quàm vnica fenestra fuerint, Gen 6.16. Q. Quid aliì sentiant, ego Francisci Iunij viri eruditissimi, atque optimi Theologi sententiæ subscribo, qui sic locum illum Genesis interpretatur, [Clarum lumen adhibeto Arcæ] additq; postea colum distinguens. tum sequitur, [ad cubiti altitudinem consummato ea arcam à superiore parte.] Itaq; plures vnà fenestras in Arca fuisse existimo, vt clarum lumen in eam reciperetur, quo opus erat. Illa verò cubiti altitudo, de qua illic agitur eodem illo vers. 16. non ad fenestram Arcæ pertinet, sed ad spatium definiendum, quo testum Arcæ à suprema eius contignatione seu tabulato attollebatur. Erat enim testum Arcæ in fastigium definens, non autem in planum, quales postea domus inter Iudæos, & in Iudæa ædificari à Deo ipso præcepta sunt, Deut. 22.8. Et hæc quidem hactenus. Iam ad Diluuium ipsum, à Deo in vniuersam terræ superficiem immissum, accedamus.
units.tr: Q. Why did God wish certain unclean animals to remain and be preserved into the age to come after the Flood, he who destroyed the world because of its uncleanness? R. When God commands unclean animals to be preserved so that their kind may also be propagated after the Flood, he does not thereby will or approve that sin and wickedness be propagated, on account of which he destroyed that former world (for those animals are not called unclean because they committed sin); but God willed that all the species of things created by him at the first origin of the world be preserved. For, says Epiphanius in book 1 against heresies, God guarded them in the ark so that the world after the Flood would not be more imperfect, or that in it the wisdom, goodness and power of God would not shine less for being acknowledged, than in that first world which was destroyed (Rom. 1.20). In the same manner in which God first created unclean animals, he willed to retain and preserve them in the world, and ordered that they should be after the Flood as well. Q. Who brought food for the sustenance of the animals into the ark, as is written in Gen. 6.21, since not all animals use and are fed by the same food, such as lions and horses? R. Augustine asks about this very point in his Questions on Genesis, ch. 71. But since God expressly prescribed, "Take for yourself of every food that is eaten, and gather it by you, so that it may be for you and for them to eat," and since Gen. 7.7 says that Noah did according to all that God had commanded, there is no doubt in my mind that Noah, like a good householder, gathered stores and provisions from every kind of food, from which so many species of animals are wont and able to be conveniently fed, and stored those foods in certain cells and storerooms in the ark, as in the highest storey. Such as grain, hay and herbs, which foods God preserved, despite the great humidity of air and rain, so that they would not rot in the same ark. Q. Whether there were more windows in the ark than one (Gen. 6.16)? Q. What others think: I subscribe to the opinion of Francis Junius, a most learned man and excellent theologian, who interprets that place of Genesis thus, "Make a bright light for the ark," and afterwards adds, distinguishing the roof, "then follows, to a cubit's height, finish the ark from the upper part." So I judge there were several windows in the ark, so that bright light, which was needed, could be let in. But that cubit's height, of which the same verse 16 speaks, does not pertain to a window of the ark, but to fixing the space by which the roof of the ark was raised above its uppermost storey or deck. For the roof of the ark ended in a pointed ridge, not flat, like the houses that were afterwards commanded by God himself to be built among the Jews and in Judea (Deut. 22.8). And so far, thus far. Now let us come to the Flood itself, poured by God over the whole surface of the earth.

units.la: Ad XII. Diluuium in terras immissum.
units.tr: On XII. The Flood let loose upon the earth.

units.la: Quæritur, Quum Moses scribit Gen. 7.11 [Anno sexcentesimo vitæ Noachi, mense secundo,] fontes abyssi sese rupisse, & cataractas cœli sese aperuisse, id est Diluuium à Deo in terras immissum, quomodo annus ille, & reliqui (quorū ab eodem Mose in annis vitæ Adami, Sethi, Enoschi, ac cæterorum recensendis fit mentio) sint numerandi, Vtrum à conditu & origine Mundi, ac proinde à mense Tisri: an à mense Nisan. In summa, ma, Vtrum annus ille similis fit, an sacer. quæstio intelligatur, sciendum est Iudæos post exitum suum ex Ægypto habuisse duo capita anni dinumerandi: Vnum, quo semper vsi antea fuerant, à mense Tisri, vel Ethanim, qui nostro Septembri respondet: Alterum à mense Nisan, qui in nostrum Martium mensem incurrit. Annus qui inchoabat à Tisri mense vocabatur Annus Civilis, quo in contractibus, iudiciis, negotiisque suis omnibus Politicis tum privatis, tum publicis vtebantur Iudæi, ac numerabatur. Itaque huius anni caput erat in Libra, quemadmodum eruditissime docet Iosephus Scaliger lib. 3. Emend. Temp. cap. De Anno prisco rum Hebr. Math. Beroaldus lib. 1. Chron. cap. 7. Ioan. Lalamatim, cap. de Anni Hebr. ratione. G. Stuckius lib. 1. Continual. Quæst. cap. 33: & ante hos Iosephus lib. 1. Antiquit. cap. 5. Annus vero, qui à mense Nisan incipiebat, dicebatur Sacer, quem in cæremoniis, rebusque sacris & Ecclesiasticis tradendis sequebantur ex Dei præscripto, quum ex Ægypto exirent, Exod. 12. 2. Huius autem anni & capitis epocha erat in Ariete signo Zodiaci. Iam vero quo Anno vsus fit Moses in annis vita Patriarchæ & Noachi, ac proinde Diluvij immissi supputandis, quæritur, Vtrum Civili, qui à Tisri: an Sacro, qui à Nisan incipit (inter hæc autem initia duo anni mensis sex totis intercedunt, quod est magnum ac notabile spatium). Cuius sententia videtur esse Iosephus lib. 1. Antiquit. cap. 5. Sed aliorum mihi videtur magis probanda sententia, qui hos Annos & vita Patrum a conditu Mundi inchoant & a mense Tisri, & Ciuiles esse contendunt. Ergo quod vulgo dicitur Diluuiū anno Noachi 600 contigisse, & anno mudi 1656 intelligendum est a mundo condito, etsi annum a Tisri vel Ethanim .i. Septembri incipias: non autem a mense Nisan. Sic Philo Iudæus in Antiquit. Biblic. Sic Scaliger lib. 5 .de Emend.Temp.cap. De Diluuio. Math.Beroaldus, & alij. Ecquod fuerit illud mensis secundi nomen, cuius die 17. fracta sunt catarac̃ta cœli, & fontes abyssi rupti, vt aqua vndique crescerent, & pluerent. Iosephus lib. 1. cap. 5. vocat [Marachat] quæ vox est nihili, & quæ nullum Hebraeorum mensis nominatus est. Ergo apud Iosephum verū illius mensis nomen est restituendū, nempe [Marefuan] vel, vt alij scribunt, [Marchefchuan.] Id quod Lalamantius primus obseruauit. Is respondet mensi Macedonum, qui Dius appellatur: & nostro Octobri, cuius die 17 Pluuia illa immensa, & imbres cœperunt. Nonnulli vero mensem hunc Marefuan coferunt cum dimidio Nouembri. Quomodo animalia venerunt ad Noachum in Arcam, præsertim quum ex ijs multa fuerint fera, & truculenta, Gen. 7. 15: & nondū pluuit. Pluit enim demum post dies septem, quàm Noachus fuit in Arca, & illa ad se recipere cœpit, vti colligitur ex Gen. 7.4, si coiungatur cū vers. 16. Nonnulli existimat pecudes naturali quodam instinctu magnos imbres præsentire, eosq; euitare, si qua possunt. Est enim earum rerum, id est, tempestatum præsaga quorundam brutorum animalium natura, quemadmodū tradunt & Aratus, & Plinius lib. 18. Hist. Natur. cap. 35.
units.tr: The question is: since Moses writes (Gen. 7.11) that in the six hundredth year of Noah's life, in the second month, the fountains of the deep burst open and the windows of heaven were opened, that is, the Flood was sent by God upon the earth, how that year and the others (the years of the lives of Adam, Seth, Enoch and the rest, which Moses also mentions) are to be counted: whether from the creation and origin of the world, and therefore from the month Tishri, or from the month Nisan. In sum, whether that year is to be understood as civil or as sacred. To understand this question, it must be known that the Jews, after their departure from Egypt, had two beginnings of the year for reckoning: one, which they had always used before, from the month Tishri, or Ethanim, which corresponds to our September; the other from the month Nisan, which falls in our March. The year that began with Tishri was called the Civil Year, and the Jews used it and reckoned by it in all their contracts, judgments and business, both political, private and public. Accordingly the head of this year was in Libra, as the learned Joseph Scaliger teaches very well in book 3 of his De emendatione temporum, chapter "On the ancient year of the Hebrews"; Matthaeus Beroaldus, book 1 of his Chronicon, chapter 7; John Lalamantius, chapter on the Hebrew reckoning of the year; G. Stuckius, book 1 of his Continuationes, question 33; and before these, Josephus, book 1 of the Antiquities, chapter 5. The year that began from the month Nisan, however, was called Sacred, and in ceremonies, sacred matters and ecclesiastical affairs they followed it by God's prescription when they came out of Egypt (Exod. 12.2). The epoch of this year and of this beginning was in the sign of Aries of the zodiac. Now the question is which year Moses used in reckoning the years of the lives of the patriarchs and of Noah, and therefore in reckoning the time when the Flood was sent: whether the Civil year, which begins with Tishri, or the Sacred year, which begins with Nisan (between these two starting points of the year there lies a space of six whole months, which is a great and notable interval). The opinion of Josephus, book 1 of the Antiquities, chapter 5, seems to be this one. But to me the opinion of others seems more worthy of approval, who begin these years and the lives of the Fathers from the creation of the world and from the month Tishri, and contend that they are civil years. Therefore what is commonly said, that the Flood happened in the year 600 of Noah, is to be understood as the year 1656 of the world counted from its creation, even if you begin the year from Tishri or Ethanim, that is, September, and not from the month Nisan. Thus Philo the Jew in the Antiquities of the Bible; thus Scaliger, book 5 of De emendatione temporum, chapter "On the Flood"; Matthaeus Beroaldus and others. What was the name of that second month, on whose seventeenth day the windows of heaven were broken open and the fountains of the deep burst, so that the waters grew and poured down from every side? Josephus, book 1, chapter 5, calls it [Marachat], a word of no meaning, and it is not the name of any Hebrew month. Therefore in Josephus the true name of that month must be restored, namely [Marefuan], or, as others write, [Marchefchuan]. Lalamantius was the first to observe this. It corresponds to the Macedonian month called Dius, and to our October, on whose seventeenth day that immense rain and the downpours began. Some, however, compare this month Marefuan with the middle of November. How did the animals come to Noah into the ark, especially since many of them were wild and fierce (Gen. 7.15), and it had not yet rained? For it only began to rain seven days after Noah had entered the ark and it began to receive them, as is gathered from Gen. 7.4, if it is joined with verse 16. Some think that cattle, by a certain natural instinct, sense great rains beforehand and avoid them, if they can. For there is in certain wild animals a natural power of foreseeing weather, as Aratus and Pliny, Natural History, book 18, chapter 35, also relate.

units.la: 35. Cuius rei rationem etiam affert Virgilius lib.1. Georgic hanc nempe,
units.tr: 35. Virgil also gives the reason for this, namely this:

units.la: [Haud equidem credo, quia sit diuinius illis Ingenium aut rerum fato prudentia maior. Verum vbi tempestas, & cœli mobilis humor Mutauere vias, & Iuppiter humidus Auster Denset, erat qua rara modo: & qua densa, relaxata Vertuntur species animorum, & peccora motus Nunc alios (alios dum nubila ventus agebat) Concipiunt. Hinc ille auium concentus in agris,
units.tr: [I do not indeed believe that they have a mind more divine than ours, or a greater wisdom of the fates. But when the storm and the changeable moisture of the sky have altered their courses, and the moist South Wind thickens what was thin, and thins what was thick, the appearances of their minds are changed, and the cattle conceive various impulses: now others, while the wind was driving the clouds. Hence comes that concert of birds in the fields,

units.la: Et lata pecudes, & ouantes gutture Corui.
units.tr: and the joyful cattle, and the crows croaking with their throats.

units.la: Namque Deum ire per omnes,] (ait idem)
units.tr: For God, as the same poet says, goes through all things]

units.la: [Terrasque tractusque maris, cœlumque profundum.]
units.tr: [the lands and tracts of the sea, and the deep sky.]

units.la: Deum igitur hunc sensum infusum esse quibusdam animalibus brutis aiunt, vt naturaliter temperstatesque mutationem aeris ante percipiant, atque propterea latebras quærant. Sed cur vna Noachi Arcam illa petiuissent, quum tunc haberent lustra sua & cauernas, & nondum vehementes maximique illis imbres e cœlo caderet ac ruerent. Ergo non naturali, sed supranaturali, imo diuina instinctu (id est, Deo Opt. Max. qui ea feruare volebat, sic impellente) quæ Bruta animantia venerunt in Arcam, eo decurrerunt. Et quæ fera ac truculenta erat, ferociam illam suam (Deo sic ea domate, ac subigente) posuerunt ad tempus adeo vt tunc & manu tractari à Noacho filiisque eius potuerint, & cum aliis animantibus versari. Siue autem ista animalia ipsa per se sine Angelis boni abigentibus venerint in Arcam perinde est. Sic enim Deus voluit ea se sistere coram Noacho, vt seruarentur: quemadmodum autem prius Adamo hominí primo illa sese sisterant, vt ab eo propriis nominibus appella‑ rentur. Porro quod nonnulli huius Diluuij caussam tri‑ buunt magna cuidam syderum coiunctioni, salsissimum esse docet Picus Mirandula. Probat enim tunc neq; vl‑lam esse potuisse eiusmodi syderum coniunctionem: neq;, si qua fuisset, eam aquas, sed ignem fuisse in Mundum inducturam. Vide Plesseium in lib.de Relig. Christ. cap.26. In summa, propter hominum peccata: non ex conuersione syderum contigit in terris hoc vniuersale di‑ luuium. Q. Cur homines ipsi primi velut Noachus, & filij eius in Arcam iussu Dei sunt ingressi, Gen.7.1. 7.8: quum in creatione prima rerum Homo postremus conditus a Deo fuerit, id est, post animalia e terra nata in hunc mundu introductus, vt homini omnia inseruire intelligeretur. Q. Quu conseruanda duntaxat animalia Deus in Arca introire vellet, eisq; secundu suas species, nidos, & stabula a Noacho confici iussisset, necesse fuit, vt Noachus eiusq; filij primi in illa Arcam ingredcrentur, animaliaq; accedētia exciperent, eaque in stabula ijs a se praeparata deducerent, ac distribuerent. Nec enim ipsa animalia per se qua sibi suaq; speciei destinata camera erat, quae vero aliys designata, dignoscere per sese, inquā, poterāt. Q. nare sic ea per singula stabula dividi a Noacho prius introgressio oportuit. Quod vero Adamus postremus omnium, velut Dominus, in mundum a Deo introductus fuit, honoris ipsius gratia factum est. Qua nunc geruntur salutis causa, & ordinis fiunt: cui solos homines praesse oportuit. Q. Utrum Pisces nulli in Diluuio perierint, an etiam aliqui. R. Hoc praclare docet Augustinus lib.15. Ciuitate Dei cap.27. Ea quæ possunt in aquis viuere, nõ solum mersa sicut Pisces: sed etiam supernatantia, sicut quedamaues vel Halcyones, non fuisse necesse seruari in Arca. Verum, Verū ex iis ipsis Animalibus aquatilibus quo-dam in Diluuio perierint, ac imprimis Pisces, non definit S. Scriptura. De iis tātum loqui videtur, quæ superterra faciem, non etiam in aquis degebant, Gen.7.22. [Quicquid, ait Moses, in cuius naribus est halitus spirationis vitæ, ex vniuersis quæ degunt in sicco, mortuumest.] Verba autem hæc, [In quibus est spiritus vitæ] non tantum ad homines pertinēt, sed etiam ad pecudes, vt docet Augustinus in Gen.quæst.9. Nonnulli tamenexistimant etiam multos Pisces tunc propter nimiam aquarum copiam periisse: quòd ab ea abriperentur natantes, & suffocarentur. Cur autem tunc pisces nõ perdiderit Deus, vt terrena animantia, ratio est, Non ea, quam nonnulli proferunt, Quòd pisces tunc homini incibum non erant, vti postea fuere .i. post Diluuium destinati, Gen.9.2.3. Præterea Deus animalia immunda & fera perdidit in Diluuio, quæ nec ipsa tamen hominibus in cibū erant. Verum ratio est, quia quū nondum mare tentassent homines, & pisces in diuerso prorsus ab hominibus illis improbis elemento habitarent, inquo Deus ab iis offensus fuerat. Idcirco ea duntaxat animalia perdidit, ac cōsumpsit Deus, quæ erat in terra. i. in elemento, vbi peccata ab hominibus fuerat perpetrata, Psal. 107.34: non autem deleuit animalia, quæin aquis adhuc ab ista nequitie hominum puris erant. Q. Cur pueri ipsi, quanuis improborū hominum, tamen adhuc infantes extincti sunt in diluuio omnes: quū tamen Deus quedam bruta animantia ex eo Diluuio conseruarit. R. Propterea quòd Infantes illi fuerũt & ipsi coram Deo rei propter peccatũ originale, cuius labe fuerunt infecti à momento conceptionis. Ergo & hi quoq; iustè perierunt. Animalia verò bruta caruerunt peccato. Q. Quando diluuiũ fuerit, id est, quo anno ab origine & condito Mundi. R. Epiphanius lib.1 contra haref. & Augustinus lib. 15. Ciuit. Dei, cap.20 ex Graecis codicibus volunt Diluuium contigisse anno à mundo condito 2262. Eusebius, & Beda, anno 2242. Philo, anno 1652. Verùm hi omnes errant. Euenit enim anno vitae Noachi 600 iam peracto, qui incidit in annum à condito Mundi 1656, Gen.7.6. Eo autem ipso anno Mathusael pius, contra quàm vult Augustinus Quaest.4. in Genesim, mortuus est ante Diluuium immissum. Neque enim piorum quisquam in Diluuio perijt, etsi dubitat Augustinus lib.15 de Ciuitate Dei, cap.11. Q. Utrum hic Mundus igne sit periturus, quandoquidem primus aqua interijt. R. Mundum hunc igne soluendum esse testatur aperte S. Scriptura. Ait enim Petrus 2.Epist.cap.3 ver.10, & 12 Στοιχεῖα καυσούμενα, λύεσθαι πυρούμενοι λυθήσονται. Cur verò non explicat. Certè quia consumendus est, igne peribit. Prior verò Mundus erat duntaxat purgandus: Ergo aquam, non ignem immisit Deus. Nondum enim eum euertere & soluere volebat. Et hæc quidem satis.
units.tr: They say, then, that this sense is poured into certain brute animals by God, so that they perceive beforehand by nature the temperature and change of the air, and therefore seek hiding places. But why would they have made for Noah's ark alone, since they then had their dens and caves, and the violent and very great rains had not yet fallen and rushed from heaven? Therefore it was not by natural but by supernatural, indeed by divine, instinct (that is, God the Best and Greatest, who wished to preserve them, thus impelling them) that these brute animals came into the ark and ran there. And those that were fierce and savage laid aside their ferocity for a time (God so taming and subduing them), so that they could be handled by hand by Noah and his sons, and could live among the other animals. But whether those animals themselves came into the ark of their own accord, without good angels driving them, makes no difference. For God so willed that they should present themselves before Noah to be preserved, just as they presented themselves before Adam, the first man, to be named by him with their proper names. Moreover, that some attribute the cause of this Flood to a great conjunction of the stars, Pico della Mirandola teaches is most foolish. For he proves that no such conjunction of stars could have happened then, and that if there had been one, it would have brought fire and not water upon the world. See Plessis, in his book On the Christian Religion, chapter 26. In sum, this universal flood happened on earth on account of men's sins, not from a conversion of the stars. Q. Why did the men themselves, Noah and his sons, enter the ark at God's command (Gen. 7.1, 7.8), since in the first creation of things man was made last by God, that is, was introduced into this world after the animals born from the earth, so that it might be understood that all things serve man? Q. Since God wished only the animals to be preserved to enter the ark, and had ordered Noah to make nests and stalls for them according to their kinds, it was necessary that Noah and his sons enter the ark first, receive the animals as they came, and lead them to the stalls prepared for them and distribute them. For the animals could not by themselves recognize which chamber was destined for them and their kind, and which was designated for others. Q. It was therefore fitting that Noah should first enter and divide them among the individual stalls. But that Adam, last of all, was introduced by God into the world like a lord, was done for the sake of his honour. The things now done for the sake of salvation and become orderly are such that only men ought to rule over them. Q. Whether none of the fish perished in the Flood, or some did. A. Augustine teaches this clearly, book 15 of The City of God, chapter 27: those creatures that can live in water, not only the submerged ones such as fish, but also those that float on the surface, such as certain ducks or kingfishers, did not need to be preserved in the ark. But Holy Scripture does not state that some of those aquatic animals, and especially the fish, perished in the Flood. It seems to speak only of those that lived on the face of the earth and not also in the waters: Gen. 7.22, Whatever, says Moses, has the breath of the spirit of life in its nostrils, of all that live on the dry land, has died. But these words, In whom is the spirit of life, pertain not only to men but also to cattle, as Augustine teaches in his Questions on Genesis, question 9. Some, however, think that many fish also perished then, because of the excessive abundance of waters, since they were swept away from it while swimming and were suffocated. Why God did not destroy the fish then, as the land animals, has a reason that is not the one some put forward, namely that fish were not then food for man, as they were afterwards, that is, appointed after the Flood (Gen. 9.2, 3). Moreover God destroyed in the Flood unclean and wild animals, which were not in any case food for men. The true reason is this: since men had not yet tried the sea, and the fish lived in an element entirely different from that in which those wicked men were, by which God had been offended, therefore God destroyed and consumed only those animals which were on the land, that is, in the element where the sins had been committed by men (Ps. 107.34), and did not destroy the animals which in the waters were still pure from that wickedness of men. Q. Why were all the children themselves, though of wicked men, still infants, destroyed in the Flood, when God preserved some brute animals from that Flood? A. Because those infants were themselves guilty before God on account of original sin, by whose stain they had been infected from the moment of conception. Therefore they also perished justly. But the brute animals were free from sin. Q. When was the Flood, that is, in what year from the origin and creation of the world? A. Epiphanius, book 1, Against the Heresies, and Augustine, book 15, The City of God, chapter 20, following the Greek manuscripts, hold that the Flood happened in the year 2262 from the creation of the world. Eusebius and Bede, in the year 2242. Philo, in the year 1652. But all these are wrong. For it happened in the year 600 of Noah's life, now complete, which falls in the year 1656 from the creation of the world (Gen. 7.6). In that very year Methuselah, a pious man, died before the Flood was sent, contrary to what Augustine wishes in his Questions on Genesis, question 4. Nor did any of the pious perish in the Flood, though Augustine doubts it in book 15 of The City of God, chapter 11. Q. Whether this world is to perish by fire, since the first one perished by water.
