A. Holy Scripture openly testifies that this world is to be dissolved by fire. For Peter says in 2 Peter, chapter 3, verses 10 and 12: [Στοιχεῖα καυσούμενα, λύεσθαι πυρούμενοι λυθήσονται] The elements, being burned up, shall be dissolved, being set on fire. But why he does not explain. Certainly because it is to be consumed, it will perish by fire. But the earlier world was only to be cleansed; therefore God sent water, not fire. For he did not yet wish to overthrow and dissolve it. And these things are indeed enough.

units.la: CAPVT III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: Vestigia superioris historiae & veritatis.
units.tr: Traces of the earlier history and truth.

units.la: VESTIGIA superioris veritatis inue- stigaturus videor mihi iure illud Platonis ex ipsius Timaeo merito vsurpare posse, Ὦ Σόλων, Σόλων, Ἕλληνες ἀεὶ παῖδες ἐστέ, γέρων δ' Ἕλλην οὐχ ἔστι, [O Solon, Solon, Graeci semper pueri estis, Senex Graecorum est nullus.] Ita enim tum ipsi Graeci, tum qui ex eorum fontibus & monumentis hauserunt, omnia magna ambitione confuderunt (dum vetustissima quaeque ad suam vnam gentem reuocare studuerunt) vel tenebris inuoluerunt (dum vetera nomina immutarunt in sua quaedam, & sibi nota) vt paucas omnino antiquissimas istius, quam proxime declarauimus, historias, & tamen vera reliquias in illorum scriptis propterea reperiamus. Bene tamen est, quod summa Dei Opt. Max. prouidentia (ad refutandos aduersus homines, & obstinatos quosdam solis duntaxat Ethnicorum scriptis fidem habentes coincendos) factum est, vt in eorum libris nonnulla etiam illius velut tristissimi naufragii tabulae & fragmenta hodie extent post tot tenebras, & veritatis interpolationes. Praeclare enim Plato in eodem illo Dialogo docet non omnem rerum ante diluuium gestarum memoriam in Diluuio ipso fuisse deletam: sed partim memoria, partim literis quarundam gentium fuisse conseruatam. Ergo ecqua sint illa reliquia superstites expendamus. Ac primum quidem quod de Natiuitate Enoschi, & publica nominis Dei profanatione, quae sub eo contigit, scribit Moses, est eiusmodi, vt ex solis sacris literis repeti debeat. Nam vetustae illae priorum appellationes, velut {Enoschi, Chanochi, Mathusaleelis, Lemechi,} partim nouis nominibus repertis obliterata sunt (quia recentia vocabula magis placuerunt) partim vetustate ipsa, velut litura quadam, obsoleuerunt, & obscuriora facta sunt. Profanatio vero illa publica nominis Dei & cultus idcirco ab ipsdem Ethnicis obseruari non potuit, propterea quod semper eandem profanationem inter se vsurpatam viderunt: verum autem Dei cultum nunquam habuerunt. Nati enim ortiq; sunt & Graeci, & Romani praesertim: sed & alia quoq; gentes in terris disseminata & distincta sunt post linguarum confusionem, quae in extruenda turre Babylonica accidit, corrupto iam vero Dei cultu, vt apparet Genesi.
units.tr: I seem to myself to be searching for traces of the earlier truth, and I may fairly borrow that saying of Plato from his own Timaeus: "O Solon, Solon, you Greeks are always children; there is no old man among the Greeks" [Ὦ Σόλων, Σόλων, Ἕλληνες ἀεὶ παῖδες ἐστέ, γέρων δ' Ἕλλην οὐχ ἔστι]. For the Greeks themselves, and those who drew from their sources and records, have confused everything with great ambition, since they strove to claim every most ancient thing for their one nation alone; or they have wrapped it in darkness, since they changed the old names into certain names of their own that were familiar to them. So we find only a few of the most ancient histories of which I have just spoken, and even these true relics only in their writings. Yet it is well that, by the supreme providence of God, the Best and Greatest, some fragments and planks of that most sad shipwreck still survive in their books, after so much darkness and corruption of the truth. This was done to refute men who are obstinate, and to put to shame those who give credit only to the writings of the heathen. Plato in that same dialogue teaches admirably that the memory of all things done before the Flood was not wiped out by the Flood itself, but was preserved partly by memory and partly by the writings of certain nations. Let us therefore weigh what these surviving relics are. First, what Moses writes about the birth of Enos and the public profanation of the name of God that happened under him is of such a kind that it must be drawn from Holy Scripture alone. For those ancient names of the earlier men, such as Enos, Chanoch, Methuselah and Lamech, have partly been obliterated by newer names that were invented (since recent words pleased more), and partly have become worn and more obscure through age itself, like some erasure. Moreover, the heathen themselves could not observe that public profanation of the name and worship of God, because they always saw the same profanation practised among themselves, but never had the true worship of God. For the Greeks, and the Romans especially, were born and arose later; but other nations too were scattered over the lands and separated after the confusion of tongues that happened in building the tower of Babel, when the true worship of God was already corrupted, as appears from Genesis.

units.la: Ad II. Publica nominis Dei profanatio.
units.tr: On II. The public profanation of the name of God.

units.la: QVOD si tamen quaedam huius Publicae Prosanationis vestigia quaerutur, illud esse poterit, quod scribit, canitq; primum Hesiodus lib.1. Opera & Dies his versibus: Δεύτερον αὖτε γένος πολὺ χειρότερον μετόπισθεν Ἀργύρεον ποίησαν ὁλύμπια δώματ' ἔχοντες Ἀλλ' ὅταν ἥβησαι, χὴ ἥβησε μέτεσθ' ἵκοιτο. -- ὑβριν γὰρ ἀπαδάλον ἐκ ἐδωνάντο Ἀλλήλων ἀπέχειν· ἀλλ' ἀδάνατος δεχαπείναν Ἡσελον, ἐκ ἐξάνμαχάγου ἱερῆς ἐπ' ἑωμοῖς.
units.tr: But if we seek some traces of this public profanation, it may be what Hesiod first writes and sings in the first book of his Works and Days, in these verses: "Then came a second race, far worse than the first, the silver race, made by those who dwell in the Olympian houses. But when they came to youthful prime, they lived only a short time in grief, because of their folly; for they could not keep from wronging one another, nor would they serve the immortal gods or offer sacrifice on the holy altars of the blessed ones." [Δεύτερον αὖτε γένος πολὺ χειρότερον μετόπισθεν Ἀργύρεον ποίησαν ὁλύμπια δώματ' ἔχοντες Ἀλλ' ὅταν ἥβησαι, χὴ ἥβησε μέτεσθ' ἵκοιτο. -- ὑβριν γὰρ ἀπαδάλον ἐκ ἐδωνάντο Ἀλλήλων ἀπέχειν· ἀλλ' ἀδάνατος δεχαπείναν Ἡσελον, ἐκ ἐξάνμαχάγου ἱερῆς ἐπ' ἑωμοῖς.]

units.la: Ἡ Δίκη ἀνθρώποισι κατ' ἦδος. Τὴς αἰνῑξεταιτα
units.tr: "Justice is among men, according to custom..." [Ἡ Δίκη ἀνθρώποισι κατ' ἦδος. Τὴς αἰνῑξεταιτα]

units.la: Ζεὺς Κρονίδης ἐκφυ̃ξε χολώσεος ὕνεκα πυρός
units.tr: Zeus, son of Cronus, hid it in anger because of the fire.

units.la: Οὐκ ἐδίδου μαχάρεσι θεοῖς ὅ τ' Ολυμπον ἔχοντ.
units.tr: He did not grant it to the blessed gods who hold Olympus.

units.la: [Sed mortale genus successit proinde secundum,
units.tr: But a mortal race came next, second in order,

units.la: Quod simile Argenteo superi fecere potentes.
units.tr: Which the powerful gods of Olympus made, like the silver one.

units.la: Hoc, postquam ætatem potuit pertingere adultam,
units.tr: This race, when it had grown to adult age,

units.la: Peruersè vixit. Nec enim abstinuisse nefandis
units.tr: Lived perversely, for it could not refrain from unlawful wrongs

units.la: Inter se damnis potuit, quæ iniuria profert.
units.tr: Among themselves, which injustice brings forth.

units.la: Nec verò coluisse Deos, aut munera sacris
units.tr: Nor did those wretched men ever care to honour the gods,

units.la: Imposuisse aris, quæ ius pietásque iubebat,
units.tr: Or to lay offerings on the altars, as justice and piety required.

units.la: Curauère vnquam miseri. Quos Iuppiter atris
units.tr: Jupiter, angered at so great a crime,

units.la: Immersit tenebris iratus crimine tanto,
units.tr: Plunged them into dark shadows,

units.la: Tanto diuorum contemptu cunctipotentium.]
units.tr: For such great contempt of the all-powerful gods.

units.la: Huic consentit quod in Politico tradit ex vetustissima fama diuinus ille Plato, postquam homines ipsi sese, & Mundum ipsum regere cœpere, & male concupiuére (quod post prima mundi initia contigit) tantâ in iis intemperiem, tantâ insolentiam, tantam denique & tam fœdam libidinem tâdem extitisse, vt Deus curâ mundi pror sus abiecisse videretur, & res humana susq; deque temere ferri censerentur, quod inter homines summa licentia scelerum omnium, & maximè impietatis, impunitas tunc obtineret. Quod illius Publicæ nominis Dei profanationis proculdubio non obscurum vestigium est, quia in animis hominum ex veteri traditione remansit insculptū. Nec absimile huic est, quod lib. 2. Hist. scribit Herodotus, multis hominès vixisse seculis, quibus deos absq; humana forma ac idololatria colerent: postea verò eosdem sub specie hominis Deos adorare cœpisse : Vnde Profanatio horribilis & nefanda Nominis Dei sit exorta, & contemptum Dei (quemadmodū Au- gustino teste scribit Varro) in hunc mundum induĉtus. Quòd si Berosi istius (cuius fragmenta quædam extāt, nec enim iste Chaldæus esse putatur, cuius & Josephus, & Plinius sæpe meminerunt) sed si, vti dixi, testimoniū illius à quopiā admittitur, certè idem tradit de negle&ta statim à primi mundi temporibus Dei religione, ac proinde de Profanatione nominis Dei ante Diluuium, initio libri sui. Verùm pergamus, & ad tertium Historiæ sacræ caput accedamus.
units.tr: Divine Plato agrees with this, when in the Politicus he relates from the most ancient tradition that after men themselves began to rule themselves and the world (which happened after the first beginnings of the world) and grew wicked in desire, there arose such intemperance, such insolence, and finally such foul and shameless lust in them, that God seemed utterly to have cast off care of the world, and human affairs were thought to be carried along recklessly, since among men, in that age, full licence for all crimes, and above all for impiety, went unpunished. This is without doubt an unobscured trace of that public profanation of the name of God, since it remained engraved in men's minds through ancient tradition. Nor is it unlike this that Herodotus, in the second book of his Histories, writes that for many ages men lived who worshipped gods without human form and without idolatry, but afterwards began to adore the same gods under human appearance. From this the horrible and abominable profanation of the name of God arose, and contempt of God was brought into this world (as Varro, according to Augustine's report, writes). But if the testimony of that Berosus (some fragments of whom survive; for this man is not thought to be the Chaldean whom Josephus and Pliny often mention) is admitted by anyone, then he certainly also relates, at the beginning of his book, that the religion of God was neglected immediately from the first times of the world, and therefore the profanation of the name of God before the Flood. But let us press on, and come to the third chapter of sacred history.

units.la: Ad lII. Propagatio familiæ Sethi.
units.tr: To Chapter III. The propagation of Seth's family.

units.la: Hic de Setho Adami filio viro pio agitur, & de familia eius propagatione, seu illius posteris, qui fuerunt vsque ad Diluuium admodum longaevi, si cum nobis, nōstrisque annis comparentur. Certè quidem, quemadmodum antea monuimus, antiqua illa Patrum, & poste- rorum Sethi nomina (velut Cainam, Enosch, Chanoch, Mathusael, & reliqua) vel malitia hominū, vel quōd alia pro ys gratiora substituta suerint, inter Ethnicos obsoleuerunt. Ipsum verò Sethi nomen venerādum, & celebre, & notū semper inter homines perduranit. Inde enim voces hæ & appellationes propriæ tum Regum, tum Sacerdotum inter eos mansere, velut nomen Sethe, & rex Aegygti & sacerdos apud eos Vulcani seu Tubalcaini, de quo Herodot. scribit lib. 2. & cuius statuam lapideam in Aegypto à se visam esse affirmat. Qualis itē ille alius Setho Aegyptius, filius regis Amenophis, vt ipsa Aegyptiorum historiæ testantur; & ex ijs Josephus lib. 1. contra Appionem Grammat. Fuit autem Ame{*}Amenophis Pharao ille, sub quo Israelita ex Aegypto, Mose duce, sunt egressi, ut ex collatione historia sacra, & Aegyptiaca facile colligi potest. Ex eodem Sethi nomine est & nomen Seuthes (quod habuere multi & praeclari reges Thracum, sicut testatur Xenophon in Expeditione Cyri) & Sethas, qui idem & Typhon ab Aegyptiis dictus est, ut docet Plutarchus in Iside, & ab iis tanquam Deus vetustissimus, & ex primis unus ex antiqua traditione colebatur. Unde apud eosdem Aegyptios ῥωΘ ΣεΘεῖτις seu ΣεΘρεῖτις, id est, Praefectura seu pars Aegypti Sethetica, vel (ut alii describunt) Sethrenica dicta, in veneratione primi illius Sethi, qui fuit Adami filius, & ab Aegyptiis (qui ista nomina a Chamo primo parente suo filio Noachi, a quo & ipsi, & Pater Noachus oriundi erant, didicerat, fideliusque quam Graeci, conseruarunt integra, & propter cognationem cum lingua Hebraica maiorem illibata) summa laude cultus. De hac aute Aegypti Praefectura Sethetica scribit Strabo lib. 17. Hist. Denique & Seta seu Setha, & Sethia urbes dictae sunt: haec in Italia, illa in Bithynia, de quibus Plinius lib. 4, & Stephanus lib. de Urbibus. Quae omnia sunt certissima nominis Sethi, & viri ipsius pij, & Noachi filij amplissimaque vestigia, ac testimonia. Nunc de longaevitate vitae priscorum illorum hominum etiam reliquias (quales quidem extant apud eosdem Ethnicos) perquiramus. Ac primum quidem hominum alij sunt longioris vitae, quam alij, etiam in eadem gente, etiam in eadem familia, nedum in diuersis nationibus. Cuius rei rationem afferunt cum Medici ex temperamento vel ipsorum hominum, vel aeris & alimentorum, quibus
units.tr: Here the subject is Seth, the godly son of Adam, and the propagation of his family, that is, of his descendants, who were very long-lived up to the Flood, if they are compared with us and our years. Certainly, as we noted before, the ancient names of the patriarchs and of Seth's descendants (such as Cainan, Enos, Enoch, Methuselah and the rest), whether through human malice or because other names more pleasing to them were substituted, have fallen out of use among the Gentiles. But the name of Seth itself has remained venerable, famous, and always known among men. For from it these words and proper appellations, both of kings and of priests, have remained among them. Thus there is the name Sethe, and the king of Egypt, and the priest among them of Vulcan or Tubal-cain, of whom Herodotus writes in book 2, and whose stone statue he says he saw in Egypt. So too that other Seth of Egypt, son of King Amenophis, as the Egyptian histories attest, and from them Josephus in book 1 against Apion the grammarian. Now Amenophis was that Pharaoh under whom the Israelites went out of Egypt under Moses as their leader, as can easily be gathered by comparing sacred history with Egyptian history. From the same name Seth comes also the name Seuthes (which many famous kings of the Thracians bore, as Xenophon testifies in the Expedition of Cyrus), and Sethas, who was also called Typhon by the Egyptians, as Plutarch teaches in his book On Isis, and who was worshipped by them as a most ancient god, one of the very first, according to ancient tradition. Hence among the same Egyptians the Sethetic nome [νομὸς Σεθεῖτις], or Sethretic as others describe it, that is, the prefecture or part of Egypt called Sethetic, was held in the highest honour in veneration of that first Seth, who was Adam's son. The Egyptians had learned these names from Ham, their first parent, son of Noah, from whom both they and Father Noah had sprung; and they kept them more faithfully than the Greeks did, whole and, because of their kinship with the Hebrew language, unimpaired. Strabo writes of this Sethetic prefecture of Egypt in book 17 of his Histories. Finally, the towns called Seta or Setha and Sethia were also so named: the former in Italy, the latter in Bithynia, of which Pliny in book 4 and Stephanus in his book On Cities speak. All these are most certain and ample traces and testimonies of the name of Seth, that godly man and son of Noah. Now let us seek out the remnants also of the long life of those ancient men, such as indeed survive among the same Gentiles. And first, some men live longer than others, even within the same nation and the same family, and still more among different nations. Physicians give the reason for this partly from the temperament of the men themselves, and partly from the air and the foods on which they live,

units.la: vescuntur:tum imprimis Ariftoteles in libro illo aureo de Longitudine, & Breuitate vitæ. Nec ea vis, a diuersitas solum in hominibus animaduertitur: verum etiam in aliis animantium generibus. Nam non solum Cerui sunt reliquis animantibus terrenis viuaciores: & Corui ac Cornicula reliquis auibus, quemadmodum & experientia monstrat, & omnis ætas historia docet; & epigramma Aufonij ex Hesiodo sumptum, vt Plinius lib. 7. cap. 48. tradit, testatur:
units.tr: and especially Aristotle, in that golden book On the Length and Shortness of Life. Nor is this difference observed only among men, but also among other kinds of animals. For not only are stags longer-lived than other land animals, and ravens and crows longer-lived than other birds, as experience shows and all history teaches; and the epigram of Ausonius, taken from Hesiod, as Pliny reports in book 7, chapter 48, bears witness:

units.la: [Ter binos deciesque nouem super exit in annos, Iustaq; centum, quos implet vita virorum. Hos nouies superat viuendo garrula Cornix. Et quater egreditur Cornicis secula Ceruus: Alipedem Ceruum ter vincit Corvus.] Verumetiam inter ipsa mus cas, vt scribit Cicero, alia sunt magis longeua. Quædam enim ad Hypanin fluuiu Indiæ quam longissime viuunt: quædam vnum tantum diem viuunt. Ergo ex hominum etiam genere alia nationes sunt longæuiores aliis, velut Hyperborei reliquis Scythis Septentrionalibus vt refert Plinius lib. 4. Natur. Hist. cap. 12. Taprobanenses aliis Indis Orientalibus insulanis & maritimis: Idem lib. 7. cap. 2. Seres aliis Indis mediterraneis, vt scribit Strabo lib. 15. Geograph. quanquam tamen Indi omnes sunt cæteris mortalibus diuturniores: Æthiopes autem reliquis Africæ populis, vt vult Herodotus lib. 3. Qui in Macarorum insulis (quas Canaridas hodie vocant) habitant, ij omnibus Occidentalibus nationibus viuaciores censentur ex Homeri & Hesiodi testimonio. Verum inter ipsos eiusdem nationis homines alij longius, quam alij, viuunt. Nestor apud Homerum trecentos annos, & tres hominũ ætates in plesse dicitur inter reliquos Græcos: quod nunc si fieret pro miraculo crederetur, & à nonnullis ἀδύνατον iudicaretur. Sibylla plusquam trecentis annis vixerit, si vna duntaxat fuit, quod plerique existimant. Endymion in Asia Minore fuit longævus admodum: Masinissa rex Numidiæ, & Argantho nius Rex Tartessiorũ, vt scribunt Historici. Quid vero etiam nonnullos, ipsorum Ethnicorum testimonio, vixisse quingentos & nogentos annos accepimus, velut Dädonem quendam in Illyrico quingentos: Maritimorum regem, sexcentos: eius filiũ, octingentos, teste Xenophonte in Periplo. Arcadum reges plerosque, annos trecentos exegisse scribit Ephorus: Aetholos nonnullos in Epiro ducentos annos, testatur Hellanicus: Aegyptiorum reges multos, etiã penè mille totos annos singulos vixisse tradit Diodor. Sicul. lib. 1. cap. 2. Bibliothec. Quæ si vera non putat vir exigui pestoris, & Epicureæ sectæ professor C. Plinius lib. 7. cap. 48. sequiturne ea propterea falsa esse, & tot aliorum probatissimos autores fuisse mentitos? Neutiquam certè. Præclara igitur est hæc Iosephi lib. 1. Antiquit. cap. 8 sententia: [Nullum, ait, ad vitam modernam, & annorũ brevitatem quibus nunc vinimus, vitam comparans antiquorum, putes falsa, quæ de illis sunt dicta: Illi namque quum essent religiosi, & ab ipso Deo facti, quúmque eis vitæ opportunior ad maius tempus esset, tantorum annorũ curriculos vinebant. Deinde propter virtute & laude plenas vtilitates, quas ingiter perscrutabatur, id est, Astrologiam & Geometriam, Deus eis ampliora vivendi spatia condonauit, quas artes edisceere non potuissent, nisi fexcentis annis vixerent. Per tot enim curricula magnus annus impletur. Testes ante mei dicti sunt omnes, qui antiquitate apud Graecos & Barbaros conscripserunt. Nam & Manethon, qui descriptionem fecit Aegyptiorum, & Berosus, qui Chaldaica defloravit, & Mochus, & Estius, adhaec & Hieronymus Aegyptius, qui Phoenicia disposuerunt, concordant cum meis dictis. Isidorus quoq;, & Hecataeus, & Hellanicus, & inter hos Ephorus, & Nicolaus in historiis suis mentionem faciunt Antiquorum annis mille viventium.] Haec ille. Atque haec sunt veritatis nostrae de Longaevitate Patrum vestigia. Pergamus ad reliqua.
units.tr: [Thrice two and nine tens of years, and the just hundred, which a man's life fills. The chattering crow outlives these nine times over, and the stag exceeds the crow's centuries four times. The raven outdoes the swift-footed stag three times over.] Indeed, even among mice, as Cicero writes, some are longer-lived than others: some live as long as possible by the river Hypanis in India, while others live only a single day. So among the human race too, some nations are longer-lived than others. For example, the Hyperboreans are longer-lived than the other northern Scythians, as Pliny reports in book 4 of his Natural History, chapter 12; the Taprobanians than the other Indians who dwell on islands and by the sea, the same author in book 7, chapter 2; the Seres than the other inland Indians, as Strabo writes in book 15 of his Geography, although all Indians are longer-lived than other mortals; and the Ethiopians than the other peoples of Africa, as Herodotus holds in book 3. Those who live in the islands of the Macae (which today they call the Canaries) are judged more long-lived than all Western nations, on the testimony of Homer and Hesiod. But even among men of the same nation, some live longer than others. Nestor in Homer is said to have lived three hundred years and to have seen three generations of men among the other Greeks. If this happened now, it would be believed a miracle, and some would judge it impossible. The Sibyl lived more than three hundred years, if there was only one, as most think. Endymion in Asia Minor was very long-lived. Masinissa, king of Numidia, and Arganthonius, king of the Tartessians, lived long, as the historians write. But indeed, on the testimony of the Gentiles themselves, we have heard that some lived five hundred and nine hundred years: a certain Dardanus in Illyria five hundred, the king of the Maritimi six hundred, and his son eight hundred, according to Xenophon in the Periplus. Ephorus writes that many kings of the Arcadians spent three hundred years; Hellanicus attests that some Aetolians in Epirus lived two hundred years; Diodorus Siculus, in book 1, chapter 2 of his Library, relates that many kings of Egypt each lived almost a full thousand years. If Pliny the Elder, a man of small judgement and a professor of the Epicurean sect, does not think these true, does it follow that they are false and that so many other most approved authors lied? By no means. Excellent, therefore, is this opinion of Josephus in book 1 of the Antiquities, chapter 8: "Compare the life of the ancients with our present life and the brevity of the years in which we now live, and you would not think false what has been said of them. For they, being religious and made by God himself, and since a longer time was more suitable for their life, lived out such long courses of years. Then, because of the useful and praiseworthy things they continually investigated, namely astrology and geometry, God granted them longer spans of life, since they could not have learned these arts unless they lived six hundred years. For a great year is completed by so many cycles. All who have written of antiquity among the Greeks and barbarians are witnesses to my words. For both Manetho, who described the Egyptians, and Berosus, who gathered the Chaldean records, and Mochus, and Hestiaeus, and besides them Hieronymus the Egyptian, who arranged the Phoenician matters, agree with what I have said. Isidorus too, and Hecataeus, and Hellanicus, and among these Ephorus, and Nicolaus in their histories mention the ancients living a thousand years." So he. These are the traces of our truth concerning the long life of the patriarchs. Let us go on to the rest.

units.la: Ad IIII. Translatio visibilis Chanochi.
units.tr: On the fourth point: the visible translation of Enoch.

units.la: ET quidem quod ad translationem Enoschi vel Chanochi in coelum, illa vel neglecta, vel omnino intellecta ab iis non fuit, non autem non audita (quia fateantur primis Mundi temporibus homines cum Deo saepe collocutos) propterea quod distinctionem illam verae pietatis a falsa Ethnici homines neque intellexerunt, neque retinuerunt, utpote qui toti tenebris falsae religionis erant, immersi, & aliam, quam Idololatriam, non putarent esse veram religionem ullam. Ergo hanc veterem traditionem non conseruarunt illi: Et quum esset etiam hoc singulare quiddam, quod in uno solum, non autem in pluribus hominibus contigisset, eius singularis facti memoria facile fuit ex hominum animis postea obliterata, amissae. Quare vel nulla, vel omnino obscura huius Chanochi translationis vestigia extant, quae quidem reperire potuerim, nisi fortasse illud, Quod Ethnici fatentur homines mines pios, & bene de genere humano meritos in cœlum translatos, & in deorum numerum scriptos. Id quod proculdubio est istius Chanochi translationis, & ἀνάλη- ωσαις ꝑ visibiliter & in conspectu hominum facta vesti- gium, ac velut lineamentum quoddã, quanuis tenue, superstes tamen. Inde est illud M.T.Ciceronis lib.2.de Legibus, [Deos, & eos, qui cœlestes semper habiti, colunto, & ollos, quos in cœlum merita vocauerunt, Herculem, Liberum, Aesculapium, Castorem, Pollucem.] Quos Hesiodus post publicā nominis Dei profanatione supra à nobis descriptā (quam ille Argenteam ætatem appellat, cōparans eam cum sequentibus ætatibus mundi) extitisse scribit, & ἡρῶας, atque ἡμιθέος .i. heroas, & semideos appellat, qualem fuisse volunt illum Herculem qui Αλεξίκακος dictus est (nec enim omnes Hercules tales fuerunt, vt apparet ex Homeri lib.11 & 21 Odysseæ) De quo Diodor.Sicul lib.5.cap.2. Inde illud quoq; Platonis Heroas colendos esse, vtpote ex Diis natos, & in cœlum receptos, itaque ijs sacrificandū esse, lib 4 de Leg. Extat apud Augustin lib. 3.Ciuit.Dei cap 4.dictum Varronis vtile esse ciuitatibus, vt se viri fortes, etsi falsum est, Diis genitos putent, vt hac stirpis diuinæ fiducia res magnas gerant, & in cœlum se postea recipiendos existiment. Denique istius Canochi ex his terris in cœlum visibilis migrationis testimonii & vestigium est, quod Ethnici scribunt iustitiam, id est, ma- ximè iustum quempiam vltimum ex his terris in cœlū ad Deos euolasse. Ouidius lib.2.Metamor. [Vltima cœlestum terras Astræa reliquit.] Nec enim Iustitia ipsa, quæ est Res abstractla: sed Iustus aliquis, qui vltimus inter corruptissimi seculi homines vixit, translatus est à Deo, propter suam illam iustitiam è terris in coelum, idque conspicue. Id quod posteritas ad ipsam Iustitiam transtulit, dixitque [Ultima de superis illa reliquit humu.] Ergo hae sunt memoriae illius antiquissimae de Translatione Chanochi, reliquiae nobis, velut vetustissimi cuiusdam naufragii tabulae, salvae, & certe quidem colendae. Quod autem de piorum hominum connubio cum impiis mulieribus tradit Moses, minime fuit ab Ethnicis observatum, quoniam ipsi omnes impii erant, nec alios, quam se, pios censebant. Verum quod sequitur de Gigantibus, eorumque procreatione (fuerunt enim illius infausti coniugii effecta & fructus) factis, & moribus, velut saevitia in homines, impietate in Deum, crudeli audacia, & lascivia procacitate ac turpitudine in mulieres, illud manifesta apud Ethnicos testimonia, & infinita penè vestigia habet, quae extant in eorum scriptis.
units.tr: As for the translation of Enoch, or Chanochus, into heaven, they either neglected it or did not understand it at all; it was not that they had never heard of it, since they admit that in the earliest times of the world men often conversed with God. The reason is that the heathen neither grasped nor retained the distinction between true piety and false. Wholly immersed in the darkness of false religion, they did not think any true religion existed apart from idolatry. So they did not preserve this ancient tradition. And since this was also a singular event, one that happened to a single man and not to many, the memory of it was easily erased from men's minds afterwards. Hence either no traces of this translation of Chanochus survive, or only obscure ones, which I have been able to find. Perhaps the one exception is this: the heathen confess that pious men, who deserved well of the human race, were taken up into heaven and written among the gods. This is undoubtedly a trace of the translation of this Chanochus, which was made visibly and in the sight of men, and it survives as a kind of outline, though faint. From this comes that saying of Marcus Tullius Cicero in the second book of his De Legibus: "Let them worship the gods, both those who have always been held to be heavenly, and those whom their merits called to heaven: Hercules, Liber, Aesculapius, Castor and Pollux." Hesiod writes that these figures arose after the public profanation of the name of God that I have described above (which he calls the Silver Age, comparing it with the later ages of the world), and he calls them heroes and demigods [ἡρῶας, ἡμιθέους]. Such, they wished, was that Hercules who was called the Averter of Evils [Ἀλεξίκακος]. For not all the Hercules were such, as appears from Homer, Odyssey books 11 and 21; on him see Diodorus Siculus, book 5, chapter 2. From this too comes Plato's saying that heroes are to be honoured, as born of gods and received into heaven, and that sacrifices should therefore be made to them (Laws, book 4). In Augustine, City of God book 3, chapter 4, there is a saying of Varro that it is useful to states for brave men to think themselves born of gods, even if it is false, so that, trusting in this divine descent, they undertake great deeds and believe they will afterwards be received into heaven. Finally, there is a testimony and trace of Chanochus' visible migration from this earth into heaven in what the heathen write: that Justice, that is, some most just man, the last of the earthly race, flew up to the gods in heaven. Ovid, Metamorphoses book 2: "Astraea, the last of the heavenly beings, left the earth." For it is not Justice itself, which is an abstraction, but some just man, who lived last among the men of that most corrupt age, who was taken up from the earth into heaven by God on account of that justice, and visibly so. Posterity transferred this to Justice itself, and said: "She alone of the heavenly ones left the last of the earth." So these are the memories of that most ancient translation of Chanochus, remaining to us like the planks of some very ancient shipwreck: saved, and certainly to be cherished. As for what Moses relates about the marriage of pious men with impious women, the heathen did not observe it at all, since they were all impious themselves and thought none pious but themselves. But what follows about the Giants and their procreation (for they were the offspring and fruit of that unhappy marriage), and their deeds and morals, such as cruelty towards men, impiety towards God, savage audacity, and lust, shameless and foul towards women, that has clear testimony and almost countless traces among the heathen, which survive in their writings.

units.la: Ad VI. Gigantes, & eorum Procrea- tio, ac Mores.
units.tr: Ad VI. The Giants, their Offspring, and their Morals.

units.la: AC primum huiusmodi quosdam homines olim fuisse probant & scripta, & nomina, quae certis locis & regionibus diu manserunt, & inter Israelitas, & inter Ethnicos. Inter Israelitas quidem, quod vallis quaedam vicina Hierosolymis ad tempora usque Flavii Josephi dicta est Vallis Gigantum. Is autem vixit sub Vespasiano Imperatore Romano, idque scribit lib. 7. Antiquit. Iudaic. cap. 4. Inter Ethnicos autem, quod Arcadia ipsa Peloponnesi regio dicta fuit olim Gigantis, uti Stephanus in lib. de Vrbibus, & Eustathius in Dionysij Alexandr. lib. de Situ Orbis. Sic & Creta regio dicta quondam. Ergo quod nonnulli totam hanc historiam velut fabulosam repudiant, ineptum est, quemadmodū docet Augustinus lib. 15. Ciuit. Dei, cap. 23, [quasi vero, inquit, corpora hominum modum nostrum longè excedentia (quod etiam supra commemorauì) non etiam nostris temporibus nata sint. Nónne ante paucos annos, quū Romana vrbis, quod à Gothis factum est, appropinquaret excidiū, Roma fuit fœmina cum suo patre, & sua matre, quæ corpore quodammodo Giganteo longè cæteris præcelleret? Ad quam visenda mirabilis fiebat vndiq; concursus.] Tertullianus quoque lib. de resurrect. Carnis, [Nec Gigantum, ait, antiquissima corpora denorata consumabit, quorū crates adhuc viuunt. Sed & proximè in illa ciuitate, quū eo die fundamenta tot veterū sepulturarū sacrilega collocarentur, quingentorum fere annorum ossa adhuc succida, &c.] Plinius lib. 7. cap. 16. scribit in Creta insula terra motu inuentū esse Gigantis cuiusdā (siue is Orestes, siue Hercules, siue alius fuerit) corpus 47 cubitorum. Herculis corpus ex Olympico stadio in Achaia longè maximū, & nostra superare reperit Pythagoras, vt tradit A. Gellius lib. 1. Noct. Attic. cap. 1. Plutarchus, & Strabo idē. A Sertorio Romanorū duce Antei Gigantis corpus in sepulcro reteētū narrat Fulgosius, & ante eum Solinus, quòd sexaginta cubitos haberet. Typhœi Gigantis corpus iacens nonē iugera terræ continuisse scribit Virgilius, lib. 6. Aeneid. Hominis mortui sola ossa genuū magno disco similia viderūt Græci, teste Pausania lib. 8. Iosephi atate corpora immēsa magnitudine visa scribit ipse lib. 5. Antiquit.cap. 5. Sub Henrico II. Germano Impe-
units.tr: First, the writings and the names show that such men existed long ago, and these names remained for a long time in certain places and regions, both among the Israelites and among the Gentiles. Among the Israelites, a valley near Jerusalem was called the Valley of the Giants right down to the time of Flavius Josephus. He lived under the Roman emperor Vespasian, and he writes this in book 7 of the Jewish Antiquities, chapter 4. Among the Gentiles, the region of Arcadia in the Peloponnese was once called the land of the Giants, as Stephanus in his book on cities, and Eustathius on Dionysius of Alexandria's book on the description of the world record. Crete too was once called by this name. Therefore, that some people reject this whole story as fabulous is foolish, as Augustine teaches in book 15 of The City of God, chapter 23, [as if, he says, the bodies of men far exceeding our size (which I have also mentioned above) were not born in our own times as well. Did not, a few years ago, when the city of Rome was approaching destruction at the hands of the Goths, there live a woman in Rome with her father and her mother, who in body rose far above others, in a sort of giant stature? To see her, a remarkable crowd gathered from every side.] Tertullian also, in his book on the resurrection of the flesh, says: [Nor will the decay of time consume the most ancient bodies of the Giants, whose bones still survive. But also very recently in that city, when on a single day the foundations of so many old tombs were being laid by sacrilegious hands, the bones of nearly five hundred years, still moist, etc.] Pliny, in book 7, chapter 16, writes that in the island of Crete, after an earthquake, the body of a certain Giant was found, 47 cubits long (whether he was Orestes, or Hercules, or someone else). Pythagoras, as Aulus Gellius reports in book 1 of the Attic Nights, chapter 1, found the body of Hercules, far larger than any of ours, in the Olympic stadium in Achaia. Plutarch and Strabo say the same. Fulgosius narrates that the body of the Giant Antaeus was uncovered in a tomb by Sertorius, the Roman commander, and before him Solinus says it was sixty cubits long. Virgil, in book 6 of the Aeneid, writes that the lying body of the Giant Typhoeus covered nine acres of ground. The Greeks, according to Pausanias in book 8, saw only the knee-bones of a dead man, which resembled a great discus. In the time of Josephus, he himself writes in book 5 of the Antiquities, chapter 5, bodies of immense size were seen. Under Henry II, the German emperor, the body of Pallas was dug up, which matched the height of the walls of the city of Rome, in the year of the Lord 1171. Homi-

units.la: ratore, Pallantis corpus effossum est quod vrbis Romæ muros æquabat altitudine anno Domini 1171. Homi-
units.tr: The body of Pallas was dug up, which equalled the walls of the city of Rome in height, in the year of the Lord 1171.

units.la: nis solum caput in eadem Creta repertum, anno 1480, dolÿ magnitudine commemorat Sabellicus. In Anglia, corpus, cuius longitudo erat 50 pedum, Lycosthenes: In Drepano vrbe Sicilia corpus Erycis effossum, quod 200 cubitorum fuisse cõÿciebatur, Ioan. Boccatius. Denique in Gallia sub Carolo VII. Gallorum rege aliud visum, quod pedes 30 æquaret. Atque hæc omnia non Poetæ mendaces, qui omnia in maius tollunt: sed veraces Historici scriptis & literis prodiderunt partim à se visa: partim ab iis, qui viderant, accepta. Quamobrem olim Gigantes fuisse, & eos monstrosa, & immensa corporis statura, si cum nostra conferatur, dubitari non potest, nisi quis ea duntaxat credenda putet, quæ ipse vidit. Verum Poëtæ, præsertim Græci, multas fabulas isti veritati admiscuerunt: & quæ vetustissima erant, ea quasi recentia, & paulò ante suâ ætatem gesta descripserunt. Unde factum est, vt quicquid de Gigantibus narratur, falsum, fabulosum, ac tralatitium à plerisq; censeatur. Porrò Gigantes illos, qui popullariter, & magno in his terris numero erant, antiquissimos fuisse fatentur idem illi Ethnici: Eos enim Terræ filios esse dixerunt. Quicquid autem antiquissimum, & primo statim mundi seculo natum est, posterior ætas è Terra ortum, vel Tetræ filium, si homo erat, appellarunt, & esse censuerunt. Quamobrem eosdem Græci γηγενεῖς, id est è terra genitos: Latini verò Gigantes appellarunt, quos eosdem àpri-
units.tr: Only the skull of a man was found on this same Crete in the year 1480, of the size of a cask, Sabellicus records. In England a body whose length was 50 feet, Lycosthenes records; at Drepanum, a city in Sicily, the body of Eryx was dug up, which was reckoned to have been 200 cubits long, Giovanni Boccaccio records. Finally in Gaul, under Charles VII, king of the Gauls, another was seen that measured 30 feet. All these things were recorded in writing by truthful historians, not by lying poets who exaggerate everything. Some of the historians had seen these things themselves, and others had them from eyewitnesses. Therefore it cannot be doubted that the giants existed long ago, and that they were monstrous in size compared with our own, unless someone thinks that only what he has seen himself is to be believed. But the poets, especially the Greeks, mixed many fables with this truth. They described the most ancient things as if they were recent and had happened shortly before their own time. Hence it is that most people judge whatever is told of the giants to be false, fabulous and merely traditional. Moreover, those same heathen admit that the giants, who were common and existed in great number on these lands, were the most ancient, for they called them sons of the earth. Whatever is most ancient and was born in the very first age of the world, a later age called earth-born, or a son of the earth if it was a man, and they held that this was so. Therefore the Greeks called them gegenes, that is, earth-born, and the Latins called them giants, whom from their earliest ancestors

units.la: {·} primis parentibus & Titanas, & Aloidas quoque nominarunt, uti Virgil. lib. 6. Aeneid. Ergo Gigas terrigena .i. è terra genitus dicitur, ut ait Isidor. lib. 11. Etymolog. Unde Hesiodus in Theogonia eos vixisse primo mundi ævo canit, & terra filios fuisse, his versibus: Πάσας δ' ἐξ ατο Γαῖα, ἀϑεμπομένην δ' ἐνιαυτὸν Γίνατ' Ἐεννύσε κεγπεχές μεγάλες Τίγαι τυς Τεύχεσι λαμπομένυς, δ' ἰλιχ' ἑίχεα χερσὶν ἐχονλας. .I.
units.tr: {·} they also named Titans and Aloads, as Virgil says in book 6 of the Aeneid. Thus a giant is called earth-born, that is, born of the earth, as Isidore says in book 11 of the Etymologies. Hence Hesiod in the Theogony sings that they lived in the first age of the world and were sons of the earth, in these verses: [Πάσας δ' ἐξ ἀτοῦ Γαῖα, ἀϑεμπομένην δ' ἐνιαυτὸν Γίνατ' Ἐεννύσε κεγπεχές μεγάλες Τίγαι τυς Τεύχεσι λαμπομένυς, δ' ἰλιχ' ἑίχεα χερσὶν ἐχονλας.]

units.la: Omnes guttas sanguinis excepit Terra, & copletis annis Genuit postea Erinnyes fortes, magnosque Gigantes Armis lucentes, & manibus longa hastilia habentes.
units.tr: All the drops of blood the Earth received, and when the years were complete she bore afterwards the strong Erinyes and the great Giants, shining in arms and holding long spears in their hands.

units.la: Idem Diodor. Sicul. lib. 1. Biblioth. tradit, & in idem tempus collocat. Berosus quoque lib. 1. sect. 2. Imovero etiam Ethnici ipsi in eo cum Mose consentiunt, quod scribit eos ex Dei filijs natos. Nam cum fabulæ Poeticæ tradidissent Gigantes ex serpentum dentibus satis extitisse, hanc fabulam Palæphatus lib. de Fabul. Narrat. refutauit. Nam eos ex hominibus praestantissimis natos esse dixerunt. Pausanias lib. 8, [In Odyssea vero Homerus scripsit, ait, Lestrygonas impetum in Ulyssis navem fecisse Gigantibus, non viris similes. Item Phaeacensium rex apud eundem Homerum loquitur, atque Phaeaces, sicut & Cyclopes, & Gigantum vulgus, prope ad Deos accedere. His itaque locis declarat, non ex Deorum genere, sed mortales esse Gigantes: Id quod inde clarius intelligitur,
units.tr: Diodorus Siculus in book 1 of his Library teaches the same and places it in the same time. Berosus also, book 1, section 2. Indeed the heathen themselves agree with Moses in this, that they write that the giants were born of the sons of God. For when the poetic fables had said that the giants arose from serpents' teeth, Palaephatus refuted this fable in his book On Incredible Stories. For he said they were born of the most excellent men. Pausanias, book 8, says: [In the Odyssey, Homer wrote that the Laestrygonians attacked Ulysses' ship, being like giants and not like men. Likewise the king of the Phaeacians speaks in the same Homer, saying that the Phaeacians, like the Cyclopes and the common race of giants, come near to the gods. By these passages he shows that the giants were not of the race of the gods but were mortals. This is understood more clearly from the following:

units.la: Rex exit is immanes elata mente Gigantes,
units.tr: Rex exit is immanes elata mente Gigantes,

units.la: Perdidit & stultum populum: post occidit ipse.]
units.tr: He destroyed also the foolish people; afterwards he himself perished.]

units.la: Quamobrem recte à Cyrillo reprehensus est Julianus Imperator lib. 9. Operis adversus eum editi, sect. 1. qui
units.tr: Therefore Julian the Emperor was rightly rebuked by Cyril in book 9 of the work he published against him, section 1, who

units.la: Gigantes ex ipsis Daemonibus i. Dijs, eorumq; feminae procreatos putat: Neq; enim ex Dijs ipsis nati sunt, qui nullū feminę emittunt: sed ex hominibus heroibus. Porrò eosdem extitisse & in Deum impios, & in homines sui sęculi iniurios, ex ipsorum quoque Ethnicorum scriptis apparet. Scribunt enim illos contra deos pugnasse, eisq; honorem ac cultū omnem inter homines ademisse: Vnde Gigantomachia, & Theomachia nominata, quā Plato penitus ex hominum memoria delendam (ne tantum sceleris aliq; mortales imitentur) existimat lib. 2. de Rep. Et quod nonnulli locum huius pugnae definiunt, voluntque fuisse montes Peliam, Ossam, & Olympum in Thessalia: alij Phlegræos campos, vt Pomp. Mela lib. 2. cap. 3: alij Palenem in Macedonia, velut Eustathius in Dionysium Alexandrinum, leue est. Futilitas enim ista est hominum Gracorum, quam Poetę Latini posuerunt sunt secuti. Verum hoc ex omnium Ethnicorum scriptorum sententia manet immotum, Gigantes fuisse absq; cōtrouersia aduersus Deum ipsum impios, & blasphemos. Vnde dicuntur in cælum coniurasse. De hac pugna sic in Aetna Cornelius Severus,
units.tr: thinks that the giants were born of the demons themselves, that is, the gods, and their women. For they were not born of the gods themselves, who bear no women, but of heroic men. Moreover, that these same giants were both impious against God and injurious to men of their own age appears also from the writings of the heathen themselves. For they write that the giants fought against the gods and took from them all honour and worship among men, whence it is called the Gigantomachy and Theomachy, which Plato thinks should be wholly erased from human memory, lest mortals imitate such a crime, in book 2 of the Republic. And that some define the site of this battle and want it to have been the mountains Pelion, Ossa and Olympus in Thessaly, others the Phlegraean plains, as Pomponius Mela in book 2, chapter 3, others Pallene in Macedonia, as Eustathius on Dionysius of Alexandria, is trivial. For that is the futility of the Greek men, which the Latin poets followed. But this remains unshaken by the opinion of all the heathen writers: that the giants were beyond controversy impious and blasphemous against God himself. Hence they are said to have conspired against heaven. Cornelius Severus describes this battle thus in the Aetna:

units.la: [Tentauere (nefas) olim detrudere Mundo Sidera, captiniq; Iouis transferre Gigantes Imperium, & vitio leges imponere cœlo.] Hanc eandem describit Claudianus, vti & alij plerique. Caterum, eosdem in homines quoque fuisse iniurios, apparet ex eorundem scriptis. Berosus lib. 1. sed. 2. ait, [Scribit illis temporibus circa Libanum fuisse Enos vrbem maximam Gigantum, qui vniuerso orbi dominabantur ab occasu Solis ad ortum. Hi vastitate corporis, ac robore bore confisi,inuentis armis omnes opprimebat,libidinq; inseruientes inuenere papiliones, & instrumenta Musica,& omnes delitias. Manducabant homines,& procurabant abortus,in edulij nquè praeparabant,& commiscebantur matribus,filiabus,sororibus,& masculis, brutis:& nihil erat sceleris, quod non admitterent contemptores religionis,& Deorum.] Eusebius lib.1.Ecclesiast.Hist.cap.1, Nefarijs, ait, sceleribus hominis inter seipsos agentes sese corruperunt,& interemerunt, vsquequo procedente immanitate etiam inuicem alter alterum devorarunt. Hinc illæ, quæ mundo sceleris fabulas reliquerunt,Theomachia,& Gigantomachia exorta sunt. Idem quoque Eusebius lib.2 Præpar.Evang. cap.9 penè repetit,& lib.7 cap.3.eiusdem operis.Inde quoq; illud est,quod ydem illi Gigates ex sanguine nati scribuntur ab ysdem Ethnicis, velut Hesiodo in Theogonia,& Ouidio lib.1.Metamorph.qui sua ex Hesiodo sumpsit,quoniâ erant homines truculenti:Item quod ydem serpentinis pedibus fuisse dicuntur, quia dolosi veteratores,fraudulentiq; homines erat. Propter eorum scelera denique Sol,& Luna,& reliqua sidera sese loco mouisse feruntur, quòd tata eorum scelera etiam astra ipsa abhorreret,vti scribit Plutarchus lib.8.Sympos. quaest.9. In summa,Gigantum mortuorum poena in inferis tristissima,& acerbissima describitur à Virgilio, lib.6.Aeneidos. Et hæc quidem ostendunt magna esse nostra de Gigatibus,eorumq; turpissimis moribus inter Ethnicos vestigia. Quæ quum dixerimus, ad reliqua quoq; pergamus,velut ad Noachu,& eius liberos, qui ante Diluuiu illi nati sunt, nempe Iaphet,Sem,Cham.
units.tr: [Tentauere (nefas) olim detrudere Mundo Sidera, captiuumque Iouis transferre Gigantes Imperium, & vitio leges imponere cœlo.] This same battle is described by Claudian, and many others too. Moreover, that these same Giants were also harmful to men appears from their own writings. Berosus, in book 1, section 2, says: [He writes that in those times, near Libanus, there was Enos, a very great city of the Giants, who ruled the whole world from the setting of the sun to its rising. Trusting in the vastness of their bodies and their strength, they oppressed all by means of the arms they had found, and, serving their lust, they invented tents and musical instruments and every kind of pleasure. They ate men, they procured abortions, they prepared them as food, and they had intercourse with mothers, daughters, sisters, and males, like beasts; and there was no crime that these despisers of religion and of the gods did not commit.] Eusebius, in book 1, chapter 1 of the Ecclesiastical History, says: By wicked crimes, men among themselves corrupted and destroyed one another, until, as their savagery advanced, they devoured one another in turn. From this came those fables which left to the world the stories of crime, the Theomachy and the Gigantomachy. Eusebius also almost repeats the same in book 2, chapter 9, of the Preparation for the Gospel, and in book 7, chapter 3, of the same work. From this, too, comes the story that these same Giants are written about by the same Gentiles as born from blood, as in Hesiod's Theogony and in Ovid's Metamorphoses, book 1, who took it from Hesiod, because they were savage men. Likewise, they are said to have had serpent feet, because they were crafty deceivers and treacherous men. Finally, on account of their crimes, the sun, the moon, and the other stars are said to have moved from their places, because their great wickedness horrified even the stars themselves, as Plutarch writes in book 8 of the Symposiacs, question 9. In sum, the punishment of the dead Giants in the underworld is described most sadly and bitterly by Virgil in book 6 of the Aeneid. And these things indeed show that our account of the Giants and of their most shameful morals is supported by many traces among the Gentiles. Having said these things, let us go on to the rest, to Noah and his sons, who were born before the Flood, namely Japheth, Shem, and Ham.

units.la: Ad VII, & X. De Noacho, & eius filijs tribus.
units.tr: To VII and X. On Noah and his three sons.

units.la: AC primum quidem quod ad Noachum, dubitari non potest certissima de illo vestigia etiâ inter Ethnicos extare, non tantum quatenus Diluuiu illud vniuersale omnes pene fuisse agnoscunt, & vnum quendam hominem ex eo, summa Dei benignitate, fuisse seruatû, qui posteá genus humanû in Mundo propagarit (quem & Noam quoque nonnulli eorum appellant, quemadmodû à nobis suo loco docebitur) verum etiam quatenus Noachi & nomen, & inuentum seu beneficium in genus humanum agnouerunt, ac retinuerunt, nempe Vitis plantationem, & vini vsum, quem illi vni acceptû ferunt. Et certè clarissima totius veritatis iflius seu nostra testimonia fuperfuerunt inter omnes mortales, priusquam Graeci homines partim vani hanc veritatem suis fabulis inuoluisse[n]t, partim ambitiosi omnia (quae sunt egregia) sibi, suaeque genti, falsò tamen, tribuisset, atque aliis populis detraxisse, id est, omnia corrupisse, vti docet Lactantius lib.1.cap.13. Ergo Noachi nomen velut vetus & augustum ab Ethnicis retentum est. Extat enim & Noa ciuitas in sinu Troglodytico in Mari rubro, cuius meminit Plinius lib.6.Nat.Hist. & Noa in Sicilia insula, vti scribit Stephanus lib.de Vrbibus. Sed & Noas quoque fluuius Thraciae, sicut ait Herodot.lib.4. Hinc fit & Noarus nomen, quod est attributum Sordisconum flumini, testè Strabone lib.7, & viro quoq;. Sunt enim nonnulli Noari dicti, vti & Soemi, seu Semi, vt docet Iosephus lib.2.cap.20.de Bello Iudaico. Vnde vero? Nisi ex prisciis illis Noas & Sem nominibus, quæ Graeci imperitè, vel ad sui idiomatis formâ Noarum & Soëmü finxerunt. Id quod mecum sentit Iosephus lib. 1. Ant. cap. 12: [Aliter enim, ait, vltimas nominum syllabas declinant, & ad legentiū delectationem mutant Græci.] Pulcherrimus vero est in nostræ veritatis confirmationem ex Beroso lib. 1. Antiquit. locus, vbi ille sic scribit, [Unus inter Gigantes erat, qui Deorum veneratior & prudentior cunctis reliquus ex probis erat in Syria. Huic nomen erat Noa cum tribus filiis, Samo, Iapeto, Chem, & vxoribus Tythea magna, Pandora, Noela, Noegla.] Et lib. 3. [Chem semper magica & venefica studiosus, Zoroastt nomen consecutus est. Is patrem Noam odio habebat. Itaque nactus opportunitatem, quâ pater Noa madidus iaceret, illius virilia comprehendens, tacitè, submurmurans carmine magico patri illusit.] Consentit cum eo, quod, ut Mnaseas Phœnix, & Hieronymus Ægyptius tradunt, locus ille, in quē primùm in Armenia descendit ex Arca Noachus, dictus est ab incolis [Saleh Noah] id est, Egressus Noa, Græcè verò Ἀποβατήρια, quemadmodum ait Flavius Iosephus. Et hæc quidem de nomine ipso [Noachus] vestigia Ethnicorum superfuerunt. De re verò ista quoque restant. Nam hic Noachus est is, qui primus vitem plantauit, vinique vsum hominibus monstrauit, Gen. 9. 20. Ergo & Boachus primùm quasi Noachus: & per apharesin unius literæ postea Bachus ab Ethnicis dictus est primus vitis, ac vini inter mortales repertor & fator: Vnde & Lenæus genialis cognominatus est, vt scribit Ouidius lib. 4. Metamorphos. Nec
units.tr: And first, as regards Noah, there can be no doubt that very certain traces of him survive even among the heathen. This holds not only in that nearly all of them acknowledge that universal Flood and that one man was preserved from it by the great kindness of God, who afterwards propagated the human race in the world (some of them also call him Noam, as will be shown in its place). It holds also in that they recognised and kept the name of Noah and his discovery or benefit to the human race, namely the planting of the vine and the use of wine, which they credit to him alone. Indeed, clear testimonies to this whole truth survived among all mortals before the Greeks, some of them vain men, wrapped this truth in their fables, and others, ambitious, falsely claimed for themselves and their own nation everything that was excellent, and took it away from other peoples. In other words, they corrupted everything, as Lactantius teaches in book 1, chapter 13. So the name of Noah was retained by the heathen as an old and venerable one. For there is a city Noa in the Troglodyte bay of the Red Sea, which Pliny mentions in book 6 of the Natural History, and a Noa on the island of Sicily, as Stephanus writes in his book on cities. There is also a river Noas in Thrace, as Herodotus says in book 4. Hence also the name Noarus, which is applied to the river Sordiscus, according to Strabo in book 7, and also to a man. For some were called Noari, as also Soemi, or Semi, as Josephus teaches in book 2, chapter 20, of the Jewish War. But whence? Only from those ancient names Noas and Sem, which the Greeks, unskilfully or to suit the form of their own language, fashioned into Noarus and Soēmus. Josephus agrees with me on this in book 1 of the Antiquities, chapter 12: [For the Greeks, he says, alter the final syllables of names and change them for the pleasure of their readers.] Moreover, a most beautiful passage from Berossus, book 1 of the Antiquities, serves to confirm our truth, where he writes thus: [There was among the Giants one who was more reverent towards the gods and wiser than all the rest, and was one of the upright men in Syria. His name was Noa, with three sons, Samos, Iapetos, and Chem, and wives Tythea the Great, Pandora, Noela, and Noegla.] And in book 3: [Chem, always devoted to magic and sorcery, obtained the name Zoroastres. He hated his father Noa. So, seizing an opportunity when his father Noa lay drunk, he took hold of his private parts and, muttering quietly with a magic chant, mocked his father.] It agrees with this that, as Mnaseas the Phoenician and Hieronymus the Egyptian relate, the place where Noah first came down out of the Ark in Armenia was called by the inhabitants [Saleh Noah], that is, the Going Forth of Noah; in Greek it is Apobaterion, as Flavius Josephus says. These are the traces among the heathen of the name [Noachus] itself. But traces of the deed also remain. For this Noah is the one who first planted the vine and showed mortals the use of wine (Genesis 9:20). So Boachus, as it were Noachus at first, and later, by the dropping of one letter (apheresis), the heathen called him Bachus, the first planter and maker of the vine and the discoverer of wine among mortals. Hence also he was surnamed Lenaeus, the genial god, as Ovid writes in book 4 of the Metamorphoses. Nor

units.la: vero dubium mihi est, quin Bachi vox & nomen non à sono bacchantiu, vt nonnulli putât: sed à veteri Noachi appellatione fit deductum, & inde primum [Boachus, N, mutata in B,] deinde [Bachus] formatu, quod duplicata litera C, postea Bacchu ab ignaris huius etymologia hominibus sit pronuntiatum. Id quod ante me vere & acute G. Stuckius vir eruditissimus obseruauit in lib.Coniuualibus. Itaq; cum cantharo Bacchus pingebatur, vt ait Arnobius lib.6.contra Gentes: & vetustissimus Deorum censebatur, etiam ante Liberum & Vranium natus, quemadmodum lib.2 cap 2 commemorat Lactantius. Denique huius veritatis ignoratione multa de hoc antiquissimo Baccho fabula & allegoria inepta sunt ac commenta, vt tradit ac coqueritur Diod. Siculus lib.4 Biblioth.cap.5. Nec vero Bacchus iste est ille Dionysius Graecorum recens & Thebanus: sed vetus ille & Nysius ex Nysa monte India, de quo etiâ meminit Arnobius lib.5. Verum Graeci vetustissimum illum sua laude spoliarunt, vt ea huc suum sacrilege ornarent, ac commendarent. Nec vero Noachus, Boachus, & Bacchus solum: sed & Oenotrius quoque, Οἰνότροπος Graece, ἀπὸ τ οἶνος, appellatus est. Multis enim modis posteritas hoc tantum Noachi beneficium celebrare voluit. Itaque variis nominibus eum appellarunt. Idem enim est qui antiquissimus ἰνβτεος ἡ Βάχχος .i. [Oenotrius & Bacchus] & vinifer appellatur. Is ante Oenotrius, à quo Italia pars quaedam primùm: postea tota Italia Oenotria dicta est (quemadmodum ex Virgilio Marone, Strabone lib.5 & 6. Geograph. Dionysio Halicarnassaeus lib.1, & 2 Ἀρχαιολογίας sen de Origine
units.tr: am I in doubt that the word and name Bacchus is derived not from the sound of revellers (bacchantes), as some think, but from the old appellation Noachus. First it was formed as [Boachus, with N changed to B], and then as [Bachus]; and later, because the letter C was doubled, the ignorant, who did not know this etymology, pronounced it Bacchus. This was truly and acutely observed before me by G. Stuckius, a most learned man, in his book on the Convivial Matters. Accordingly, Bacchus was depicted with a drinking cup, as Arnobius says in book 6 Against the Gentiles, and he was regarded as the most ancient of the gods, born even before Liber and Uranus, as Lactantius records in book 2, chapter 2. Finally, through ignorance of this truth, many fables and allegories about this most ancient Bacchus have been foolishly invented, as Diodorus Siculus relates and laments in book 4 of the Library, chapter 5. Nor is this Bacchus that recent and Theban Dionysius of the Greeks, but that ancient one, the Nysian, from Mount Nysa in India, of whom Arnobius also speaks in book 5. But the Greeks despoiled that most ancient one of his praise, so that they might adorn and commend their own sacrilegious figure with it. Nor was he called only Noachus, Boachus, and Bacchus, but also Oenotrius, in Greek Oinotropos, from oinos (wine). For posterity wished to celebrate this single benefit of Noah in many ways, and so they called him by various names. The same is that most ancient [Oinotropos or Bacchus], also called vine-bearer. He is older than the Oenotrius from whom first a certain part of Italy, and later all of Italy, was called Oenotria, as appears from Virgil, from Strabo in books 5 and 6 of the Geography, from Dionysius of Halicarnassus in books 1 and 2 of the Roman Antiquities (or On the Origin of the Romans), and from Stephanus in his book on cities. That Oenotrius, I say, is more recent, an Arcadian, who afterwards falsely and arrogantly claimed for himself the name and discovery of that most ancient Oenotrius, that is, Noah, since he was a vain Greek, and wished to be held and worshipped as the first. Fabius Pictor in the fragments, and Myrsilus, whoever he was, write of this.

units.la: Romanorum, & Stephano de Vrbibus apparet) Is inquam, Oenotrius est recentior, & Arcas, qui postea no-men, & inuentū vetustissimi illius Oenotrij, nempe Noachi, falsò sibi & arrogantèr attribuit, vtpote vir Graecus & vanus, & pro primo illo haberi, coliqué voluit: de quo & Fabius Pictor in Fragmentis, & Myrsilus, quicunque idem fuit scriptor fit. Caeterum, quem Graeci & Latini Bacchum & Oenotrium vocant, eundem illi Syri, & Aramei omnes (qui lingua hebraea vel illi cognata viuuntur) appellant Ianum a voce [Iain] quae vinū significat, qui est Vitis ab eo vtpote Noacho sate fru-ctus, & eiusdem in homines beneficiū. Ex quo apparet Noachum dictum quoque esse Iainum, & postea Ianū: ac proinde eundem esse, qui & Noachus, & Ianus ille vetustissimus sit. Nam Iani quoque plures fuere, & recentiores omnes antiquo, qui tamen illius inuentum & nomen ambitiose sibi vendicarunt. De hoc antiquissimo Iano ac proinde Noacho Latini scriptores omnes Ethnici, ac vetustissimi quique meminerunt. Hic & Iane quoq; in libris ritualibus Saliorū dictus est, teste Tertulliano in Apologet. cap. 11, qui ante & Vranū, & Saturnū, & Iouem extitisse, quemadmodū dixi, ab omnibus conceditur, cuiq; propterea prius, quam alij cuiquā Deo sacrificabatur. De quo allegoria multa, vti monui, cofiétae fuere, quas omnes irridet Augustinus lib. 7. Ciuit. Dei, cap. 7 & 8. Sunt qui Ianum, tanquā Eanum (quod eat & redeat) dictum volunt, velut Cicero, propterea quod eum Annum esse existimant: vel Ianum nomen Latinū, non Syrum esse somniant à Ianua deductum, vt Ouidius lib. 1. Fast. sed ỹ certè quidem omnes hallucinantur toto cœlo. Ianus enim à Iain, id est, vino, deriuatur, estque nomen antiquissimum & Arameum, ante Latinos nedum Romanos natum. Cuius nominis vsus vel nullus, vel rarus semper fuit apud Graecos ve-tustatis contemptores, nisi quod [Ianassa] extat apud Higinū ex Graecis autoribus, & [Ianiscus] apud Pausaniam lib. 21: multum vero apud Latinos, qui fuerunt religiosiores quam Graeci: de quo Virgilius, & Ouid. toto lib. 1. Fastor. & Plutarchus in Quaest. Rom. & Varro, & Macrobius: imo loquuntur omnes. Mecum facit Ouidius lib. 1. Fastorum:
units.tr: Moreover, the one whom the Greeks and Latins call Bacchus and Oenotrius, all the Syrians and Arameans (who live in the Hebrew language or one akin to it) call Ianus, from the word [Iain], which means wine. He is the vine, the fruit sown by Noah himself, and the benefit of the same to men. From this it appears that Noah was also called Iainus, and afterwards Ianus; and therefore that he who is Noah and that most ancient Janus are the same. For there were also many Jani, and all the more recent ones were later than the ancient one, yet they ambitiously claimed for themselves his discovery and his name. All the Latin writers, heathen and the most ancient of them, speak of this most ancient Janus, and therefore of Noah. He is also called Janus in the ritual books of the Salii, as Tertullian witnesses in the Apology, chapter 11. It is granted by all that he existed before Uranus, Saturn, and Jupiter, as I have said, and for that reason he was sacrificed to before any other god. Many allegories have been invented about him, as I have pointed out, and Augustine mocks them all in book 7 of the City of God, chapters 7 and 8. Some want Janus to be named as if Eanus (from eo, to go, and redeo, to return), as Cicero does, because they think he is the Year. Others dream that the name Janus is Latin, not Syrian, derived from ianua (door), as Ovid does in book 1 of the Fasti. But all these are utterly mistaken. For Janus is derived from Iain, that is, wine, and is a most ancient Aramaic name, born long before the Latins, let alone the Romans. Use of this name was either absent or rare among the Greeks, who always despised antiquity, except that [Ianassa] appears in Hyginus from Greek authors, and [Ianiscus] in Pausanias, book 21. But among the Latins, who were more religious than the Greeks, it was very common. Concerning this, Virgil, and Ovid throughout book 1 of the Fasti, and Plutarch in the Roman Questions, and Varro, and Macrobius speak; indeed all of them do. Ovid in book 1 of the Fasti agrees with me:

units.la: [Quem tamen esse deum te dicam, Iane biformis? Nam tibi par nullum Graecia numen habet.] Verum Fabij Pictoris, Albrici, & Athenai tantum testimonia proferâ: Fabius Pictor in fragmentis, quae exstant, ait, [Iam at ite nulla erat Monarchia, quia mortalibus pectoribus nondum habferat ulla regnandi cupiditas. Principes, quia insti erat & religionibus dediti, iure habiti Dij, & dicti. Vinum & far primus populos docuit Ianus ad sacrificia & religionem magis, quam ad esum & potum. Primus etiam aras, & pomaria, & sacra docuit, & ob id illi in omni sacrificio perpetua praefatio praemittitur, farq; illi & vinum primo praelibatur.] Albricus de Deorum Imaginibus, [Ianus, inquit, in Deorum numerum acceptus est, cui omnis rei initium & finem tribuebat. Taliter figurabatur, Erat Rex homo sedens in throno fulgenti radijs: duas facies habebat, quarum vna ante se, altera post se respiciebat. In manu dextra habebat clauem: In sinistra vero habebat baculum, quo saxum percutere, & ex illo aquam producere videbatur.] quannis aliter Ouid.lib.1.Fast. Athenæus denique lib.15. Dipnosoph.ex Dracone Corcyrao in lib.de Lapidib. ait, [Ianum fama est bifrontem fuisse, altera facie posteriore, altera anteriore. Ianus flumen, Ianumque montem ab eo fuisse nominatum, quod in eo monte habitauerit (nimirum in Oriente & in India, vnde fortasse insula illa due in mari Indico vocata nimirum Iana seu Janna maior, & Iana minor) coronas illum reperisse, nauigia, rates: numum areum ab eo primum signatum: qua ratione ciuitates in Gracia multa, Italia & Sicilia monetam cudunt impressa bifronti facie & bicipiti: & ex altera parte vel rate, vel nauigio, vel corona. Sororem Camesen duxit.] Ergo bifrons tantum erat, & quidem primus non ante quadrifrons, quemadmodum sequens atas imperite finxit, eumque pinxit, quoniam vtrumque Mundum, nempe primum (qui per Diluuium a Deo deletus est) & hunc secundum, in quo post Diluuium viuimus, vidit, vt Arnobius lib 6 contra Gentes sentit. Nam quod Ouidius duas illas Iano facies ideo datas interpretatur, quod
units.tr: [And what god shall I say you are, two-faced Janus? For Greece has no god like you.] But I will cite only the testimonies of Fabius Pictor, Albricus and Athenaeus. Fabius Pictor, in the fragments that survive, says: [Now there was no monarchy at all, because human hearts had not yet developed any lust for ruling. Princes, because they were just and devoted to religion, were held and called gods by right. Janus first taught the peoples the use of wine and spelt, for sacrifices and religion rather than for eating and drinking. He also first taught altars, orchards and sacred rites, and for this reason a perpetual preface is placed before him in every sacrifice, and spelt and wine are first offered to him as a foretaste.] Albricus, in On the Images of the Gods: [Janus, he says, was received into the number of the gods, and to him he assigned the beginning and end of every thing. He was pictured thus: he was a king, a man seated on a throne shining with rays. He had two faces, one of which looked before him and the other behind. In his right hand he held a key, and in his left a staff, with which he seemed to strike a rock and bring water out of it.] Ovid, however, describes him differently in Fasti 1. Finally Athenaeus, in book 15 of the Deipnosophists, citing Dracon of Corcyra in his book On Stones, says: [It is said that Janus was two-faced, with one face at the back and the other at the front. The river Janus and the mount Janus were named after him, because he lived on that mountain (namely in the East and in India, whence perhaps the island called Diu in the Indian sea, namely Iana or Janna major and Iana minor). He discovered crowns, ships and rafts; he was the first to strike bronze coins, and for this reason many cities in Greece, Italy and Sicily mint coins stamped with a two-faced and double-headed figure, and on the other side a raft, a ship or a crown. He married Camese, his sister.] So Janus was only two-faced, and he was certainly not four-faced at first, as a later age foolishly imagined and painted him. He saw the two worlds, namely the first (which God destroyed by the Flood) and this second one in which we live after the Flood; this is what Arnobius thinks in book 6 of Against the Gentiles. For Ovid's explanation that Janus was given two faces for this reason, that

units.la: [Omnis habet geminas hinc, atque hinc Ianua frontes: E quibus hæc populum spectat, at illa Larem] puerile est: sed quod duplicem illum mundum, vt dixi, viderit, bifrons fuit. Ratis ei tribuebatur, & quadras moneta, qui illius ratem ex vna parte: ex altera bifrontem eiusdem Iani faciem habebat. Is quadras quadras [ratitum] a rate vocabatur, vt loquitur Ennius. Quare vera est de vno Iano hæc sententia eiusdem Ouidij. [Solus de superis, qui tua terga vides.]
units.tr: [Every door has two fronts, one on this side and one on that: of these, one looks upon the people, the other upon the household gods] is childish. But that he saw the double world, as I have said, is why he was two-faced. A raft was attributed to him, and a quadrans coin, which had a raft on one side and on the other the two-faced face of the same Janus. This quadrans was called ratitum, from the raft, as Ennius says. Hence this saying of Ovid is true of Janus alone: [You alone of the gods see the back of your own head.]

units.la: Atq; hæc ratio est, Cur Noachus ex vetustissimæ illius nostræ veritatis vestigys ab Ethnicis & Ianus dictus fit, & pingeretur bifrons, & ratis ei tribueretur. Quòd si quis eum a Ianua dictum quoque velit, is fortasse sua sententiam posset tueri, quod, ut Cyrillus lib. 1 contra Julian. ex Abydeno vetere scriptore tradit, Noachus Xisuthrus quoque a veteribus dictus est. Xisuthrus ante est a [Xuz] hebræo, per geminationem & epanalepsin primæ literæ z, sic [Zixuz] unde Xisuthrus nomen a Græcis factum. Est autem Xuz Hebræis, postis, porta, limen. Noachus igitur sic a dignitate fuerit olim appellatus. Porrò idem videtur quoq; nominatus ab ipsdem nonnunquam [Ogyges] lingua Aramea, ut Berosus vult: Græca verò, [Ogygus] ut convertere hac vocem Strabo lib. 8. Geographia, & Pausanias lib. 1. Sic Berosus lib. 2 [Primum, ait, dixerunt Noam Ogygisan Sagā, id est, Illustrem sacrorum Pontificem, & Difir.] Xenophon quidā in lib. de Aequinoctis, [Fuit verò, inquit, priscus Ogyges in prima inundatione terrarum: Alter verò Atticus, in tertia.] Idem tradit quoque Metasthenes. Certè [Sagan] vox principem Hebræis significat idem Assyriis, ut volunt, vocabulum [Ogyges] & Aegyptiis [Osiris] notat. Unde pulcherrimo, ac maximè honorifico nomine vocatum fuisse veterem illum seu primum Noachum vel Ianum Ogygen apparet. Sed posteri eius quendam se quoque ex prisci illius nomine appellarunt Ogyges, qualis is, de quo Eusebius lib. 10. cap. 3. Præparat. Euangel. & de quo Augustinus lib. 18. Ciuit. Dei, cap. 8, qui quando fuerit, ac Diluuium Ogygis ex eo dictum, ignoratur: qualis item ille alter Ogyges.
units.tr: And this is the reason why Noah, from the traces of that most ancient truth of ours, was also called Janus by the Gentiles, and was painted two-faced, and was given a raft. But if anyone wishes him to be called after a door (ianua), he might perhaps defend that view, since, as Cyril in book 1 Against Julian relates from the ancient writer Abydenus, Noah was also called Xisuthrus by the ancients. Xisuthrus comes from the Hebrew [Xuz], by doubling and repeating the first letter, z, thus [Zixuz], whence the name Xisuthrus was made by the Greeks. Now xuz in Hebrew means doorpost, gate, threshold. So Noah was called by this name of dignity long ago. Moreover he seems also to have been named by the same people at times [Ogyges], in the Aramaic language, as Berosus holds; but in Greek [Ogygus], as Strabo in book 8 of his Geography and Pausanias in book 1 translate this word. Thus Berosus in book 2: [First, he says, they called Noam Ogygisan Sagā, that is, the illustrious high priest of sacred rites, and Difir.] Xenophon, in his book On the Equinoxes, says: [There was, he says, an ancient Ogyges at the first flood of the lands; and another Attic one at the third.] Metasthenes also relates the same. Certainly the word [Sagan] means prince among the Hebrews, and the same among the Assyrians, as some hold; and the word [Ogyges] denotes [Osiris] among the Egyptians. Hence it is clear that the old, or first, Noah, or Janus Ogyges, was called by a most beautiful and most honourable name. But his descendants also called some of themselves Ogyges after the name of that ancient man, such as the one of whom Eusebius writes in book 10, chapter 3 of the Preparation for the Gospel, and of whom Augustine writes in book 18, chapter 8 of The City of God. When this Ogyges lived, and whether the Flood was named Ogygian after him, is not known; and likewise that other Ogyges.

units.la: Ogyges gyges Thebanus, à quo Thebarũ vrbis porta una Ogygia nominata est, quemadmodũ scribit Pausanias lib. 9: Imò tota ipsa Graecia Ogygia, honoris ergò sic olim vocata. Stephanus in lib. de Vrbibus. Sed isti Ogyges sunt recentiores: noster verò, qui idem & Noachus, & Bachus, & Ianus, vetustissimus est & primus. Hinc Ogygia quoque Insula ab Homero celebrata, sicque appellata propter vetustatẽ, Maris Ionici. Quicquid enim olim vetustũ erat, idem dicebatur, cõmendationis ergò, Ogygium, tanquã ex mundi totius concussione, & ruina (qualis in diluuio accidit) superstes, & saluum. [Gafgafch] enim Hebraïs mouere & concutere significat. Vnde Gyghes, & per epenthesin litera Hebraea h, Hogyges formatum est: unde postea Ogyges, id est, saluus ex Mundi excidio dictus, quicunque vetustissimus inter mortales censebatur: sic vocari fuit honorificũ. Caeterum, vt hoc ipsum quoque obiter dicam, Ogygia illa insula Homerica ponitur à Plinio lib. 3. cap. 10. in Mari Ionico, ex aduerso Locrorum Italicorũ: à Strabone lib. 6. in Mari Aegeo. At verò à Plutarcho lib. De facie Lunae in Oceano magno, & supra Britanniam, quae nunc Anglia, & fortassis est Mona insula, vbi primi dij fuerint. In summa, [Ogyges, & Ogygius] sunt voces, quibus antiquitas commendatur. Porro idem quoq; hic Noachus Xisuthus dictus, scribitur ex Alexandro Polyhistore à Cyrillo lib. 1. contra Iuliani, & Josepho lib. 1. contra Appionem. Et hac quidem de Noacho, & ijs, quae inter Ethnicos extiterunt, illius vestigijs, licet propter varietatem & immutationem nominum obscuris. Hic enim semper fuit astus Satanae, vt rebus verif. fimis & iam notis magnas tamen tenebras ex nominum, quibus primum appellabantur, mutatione vel interpolatione offunderet. Id quod diligenter obseruandum est. Iam vero ad Noachi filios accedamus, qui & tres tùc, id est, ante Diluuium fuisse dicuntur: & quorũ nomina hæc recitat Moses: Iaphet, Sem, & Cam vel Cham: vtroq; enim modo ab Ethnicis scribitur. Hac veritate quid ipsis adeo Ethnicis fuit notius, qui eadem dicunt? Tres enim Noachi filios fuisse nouerunt, scripserũtque, & sydem eos nominibus appellat. Ac primum quidem volunt, vti tres fuerũt primi, & præcipui Noachi filij: sic vniuersum mundum seu Orbem terrarum post diluuium à Noacho in tres partes diuisum fuisse, quarum Asia Sem fuerit assignata: Africa, Camo: Europa, Iapeto. Sic Berosus ille, quem iam citaui lib.4, [Designauit, inquit, illis Noachus tres partes Orbis, Asiam, Africam, & Europam, singulis his principibus partes, ad quas irent, partitus.] Verum hæc sententia nequaquam satis firma mihi videtur, refutatúrque primùm ex Dei verbo Gen.10. vbi posteri Iapeti etiam in Asia multas prouincias occupasse, & habitasse colliguntur. Deinde à Josepho lib.1. Antiquit. Iudaic. cap. 11: Scribit enim sic, [Iaphet filius Noë habuit filios septem, & habitarunt regionem à Tauro & Amano montibus incipientem, & pertingentem in Asiam usque ad flumen Tanaim.] Qua tota regio in Asia maiori & Septentrionem versus sita est, nequaquam autem in Europa. Josepho succinit Cedrenus lib. 1. Hist. Docet enim plerasque Ponti Polemoniaci prouincias, quæ sunt in Asia, primùm à Iapeto, eiusq; filiis habitatas fuisse. Nec certè ab ab hisce differentit Philo Iudaeus in Antiquit. Biblicis. Adio Viennensis in Aetate secunda scribit demum sub Heber, & longis post Diluuium seculis totum terrarum Orbem in tres quasdam partes, diuisum linguarum, sibi cognitarum diuisionem, partitum fuisse, quia tres erant Noe filij. Huic nepe ternario numero, & memoriae filiorum Noachi tantam reuerentiam posteri tribuerunt. Prima pars, ait, a Perside, Bactris, & India vsque ad Rhinocoruras (quae urbs Palaestinam ab Aegypto separat) extenditur, habuitque linguas 27 sibi similes: Prouincias autem & regiones 46. Hae fuit Sem: & est in Asia Maiore, ac Orientali. Secunda pars a Rhinocororis urbe ad Gadilah, Garamatas, & Aethiopas (qua tota regio seu terra tractus est Africa) continebat autem linguas 22, Regiones autem 393. Haec fuit Cam. Tertia pars Orbis pertingit a Gadilah ad Mediā vsque, habuit linguas 24, regiones penè mille. haec fuit Iaphet. Pertinet autem etiam haec ipsa ad Asiam quoque. Verum postea pro his partibus orbis posteritas Asiam, Africam, & Europam substituit, retinere que maluit. Sic autem hae tres continentes terras, & orbis partes primi Cares homines maritimi, quique ad eos accedebat, nominauere, mortuis iapridem tribus illis Noachi filijs, quemadmodum ex Strabonis lib. 1. Geograph. sub finem facile colligi potest. [Cares enim, ait, & Graeci non ad vniuersum terrarum orbem respicientes, sed ad suam duntaxat terram, & contra se positam Cariam, in qua nunc & Iones, & alij Graeci habitant, appellarunt Asiā, ab Asia palude, eam regionem, quam ipsi tunc incolebant.] Asia vero paludis (qua in eo tractu est .i. in Asia minore à Græcis habitata) meminit Virgil.lib.1.Georg. & imprimis lib.7. Aeneid. [& longa canoros
units.tr: Ogyges the Theban, after whom one gate of the city of Thebes was named Ogygian, as Pausanias writes in book 9. Indeed all Greece itself was called Ogygian of old, as a mark of honour; Stephanus writes this in his book On Cities. But those Ogyges are more recent; our Ogyges, who is the same as Noah, Bacchus and Janus, is the most ancient and the first. Hence also the Ogygian island celebrated by Homer, and so called because of its antiquity, in the Ionian Sea. For whatever was ancient in former times was called Ogygian, as a term of praise, as if it had survived and been saved from the shaking and ruin of the whole world (such as happened in the Flood). For [Gafgafch] in Hebrew means to shake and to agitate. Whence [Gyghes], and by the epenthesis of the Hebrew letter h, [Hogyges] was formed; from which afterwards came Ogyges, that is, one said to be saved from the destruction of the world, whoever was reckoned the most ancient among mortals: to be called thus was an honour. Moreover, to mention this in passing too, that Ogygian island of Homer is placed by Pliny in book 3, chapter 10, in the Ionian Sea, opposite the Italian Locri; by Strabo in book 6 in the Aegean Sea; but by Plutarch in On the Face of the Moon in the great Ocean, and above Britain, which is now England, and perhaps is the island of Mona, where the first gods were. In short, [Ogyges and Ogygius] are words by which antiquity is commended.
