Furthermore, this same Noah is also said to have been called Xisuthrus, as is written from Alexander Polyhistor by Cyril in book 1 Against Julian, and by Josephus in book 1 Against Apion. And so much for Noah, and for the things that existed among the Gentiles, traces of him, although obscure because of the variety and alteration of names. For Satan has always been crafty, so that he might cast great darkness over things that are most true and already known, by changing or distorting the names by which they were first called. This must be carefully observed. Now let us come to the sons of Noah, who are said to have been three before the Flood, and whose names Moses recites: Japheth, Shem, and Ham or Cham, for they are written in both forms by the Gentiles. What was more widely known even to the Gentiles than this truth, since they say the same things? For they knew that Noah had three sons, and they wrote about them and called them by the same names. And they first hold, just as the three were the first and principal sons of Noah, so that the whole world, or the orb of the lands, after the Flood, was divided by Noah into three parts, of which Asia was assigned to Shem, Africa to Ham, and Europe to Japheth. Thus that Berosus, whom I have already cited in book 4: [Noah, he says, assigned three parts of the world to them, Asia, Africa and Europe, dividing parts to each of these princes, to which they should go.] But this view does not seem to me firm enough at all, and it is refuted first by the word of God, Genesis 10, where the descendants of Japheth are gathered to have occupied and inhabited many provinces in Asia as well. Next by Josephus, book 1 of the Jewish Antiquities, chapter 11: for he writes thus: [Japheth, son of Noah, had seven sons, and they inhabited a region beginning at the mountains of Taurus and Amanus and reaching across into Asia as far as the river Tanais.] This whole region lies in Greater Asia towards the north, and certainly not in Europe. Cedrenus, in book 1 of his History, agrees with Josephus: for he teaches that most of the provinces of Pontus Polemoniacus, which are in Asia, were first inhabited by Japheth and his sons. Nor indeed does Philo the Jew, in his Biblical Antiquities, differ from these. Adio of Vienne, in the Second Age, writes that only under Heber, and many centuries after the Flood, was the whole orb of the lands divided into three parts by a division of languages that were known to them, because Noah had three sons. The posterity gave such great reverence to this ternary number and to the memory of Noah's sons. The first part, he says, extends from Persia, Bactria and India as far as Rhinocorura (a city which separates Palestine from Egypt), and it had 27 languages like one another, and 46 provinces and regions. This was Shem's, and it lies in Greater and Eastern Asia. The second part, from the city of Rhinocorura to Gadilah, the Garamantes and the Ethiopians (the whole of which region or tract is Africa), held 22 languages and 393 regions. This was Ham's. The third part of the orb extends from Gadilah as far as Media; it had 24 languages and nearly a thousand regions. This was Japheth's. This same part also extends into Asia. But later the posterity substituted Asia, Africa and Europe for these parts of the orb, and preferred to keep those names. Thus these three continents, and the parts of the orb, were named by the first Carians, maritime men, and by those who came to them, long after those three sons of Noah had died, as can easily be gathered from the end of Strabo's book 1 of the Geography. [For the Carians, he says, and the Greeks, looking not at the whole orb of the lands but only at their own land and Caria, which lies opposite and in which the Ionians and other Greeks now live, called it Asia, from the marsh of Asia, that region which they then inhabited.] The marsh of Asia (which is in that tract, that is, in Asia Minor, inhabited by the Greeks) is mentioned by Virgil in book 1 of the Georgics and especially in book 7 of the Aeneid: [and the long marsh of Asia, struck round about, gives song-birds their tunes along their necks, and sounds with their wings.] Therefore Asia was not named after a woman, as the widow-hunters think, but was known to the Greeks and Carians, who then frequented the sea, from that marsh; and at first that region alone was called so, and

units.la: Dant per colla modos, sonat armis, & Asia circum Pulsa palus.] Ergo Asia non a muliere, vt putat siduarum: sed ab ista palude Græcis hominibus, & Caribus tunc mare frequentantibus nota dicta est: & primum quidem solum ea regio, in qua ipsi Græci habitabant, id est, Asia minor: deinde vero tota reliqua continens, illiqúe adiuncta terra, vt scribit Strabo lib.12. quæ Asia Maior propterea cognominata est, ex comparatione ad Minorem illam. Europa autem ab ÿsdem Caribus, & Asianis Græcis appellata est ea regio, quæ ipsis Asiam minorem incolentibus erat obiecta, & in quam late liberéque ex suis littoribus prospiciebant, nimirum aperto Mari in ea mundi & Asiæ parte. Ergo Εὐρώπη dicta est tanquam εὐρὺ ὤπος, vel ἀνεῖνεν, id est, à lato libero que in eam partem & terra ex Asia minore prospectu non autè ab Europa nescioqua sorore Cadmi, quemadmodum nonnulli existimãt. Iustinus historicus Europam ab Europo rege Macedonia & Thracia vetustissimo nominata esse vult, qui cõsederit in ea Thracia regione, qua Asia opposita est. Sed verior est superior nominis ratio, ac notatio. Denique Africa abysdē Græcis Asianis dicta est ea regio, ex qua ad se ÿ, qui Afros sese vocabāt, veniebāt, & ex qua orbis parte mare agitatu maxime, erat procellosum, ac spumabat. Ἆϕεσν enim Græcis spuma est. Ergo sic Cares primi. Verum postea eadem hæc nomina & vocabula ab alys gentibus retenta sunt: nam ab istis Græcis Asianis in mari verfantibus communicata aliis sunt populis, postquam longius progressi essent, & navigando plures terra regiones & Orbis partes adiissent ac peragrassent. Ex quo tandem effectum est, ut uniuersum terrarum Orbis in istas tantum tres partes, non in plures a Græcis primum, post autem ab aliis Ethnicis hominibus diuideretur, nimirum in Asiam, Europam, & Africam. Id quod ab illis nequaquam factum est vel in memoriam, vel in respectu trium illorum Noachi filiorum, Iapheti videlicet, Semi, & Cami: sed quod ista nomina tria Terrarum a Caribus & Græcis Asianis didicissent, & accepissent. Et tamen tolerabilior est ista in numero trium Noachi liberorum subtilitas ac philosophia, quam illa prorsus allegorica, & certe quidem inepta Augustini rhetoricatio (pace tanti viri dictum sit) lib.16. Ciuit. Dei, cap.2, qui hic ternarium filiorum Noachi numerum refert ad Christum, fideles, & impios. Quod si quis significationem istorum nominum Hebraeorum quaerat (ex qua tantopere philosophatur Augustinus) haec est: [Iapheth] dictum est quasi pulcher facie, vel latis humeris esset. Sic a Græcis Plato appellatur. [Sem] vocatus videtur quasi fama celebris memorabilis futurus, vel positus a Deo, electusve: Sic Cleones Græce dicti. [Cham] autem vel Cami (nam sic promisceé a Latinis scribitur) nomen accepit quasi temperamento calidum, & niger esset colore. Sic Nigri multi a Latinis, & Mela Græcis, dicti. Quas ego nominum interpretationes sequi, quam inepta quaedam philosophamenta malo. Caeterum de Iapeto seu Iapheto primogenito Noachi filio extant plurima apud Ethnicos vestigia. Is enim est, quem ipsi Hebraam vocem ad suæ linguæ normam ac suauitatem inflēentes vocant Iapetum prisçum. Nam plures postea eodē hoc nomine sunt appellati. Prisçus verò ille Iapetus terra & cœli filius abys fuisse dicitur .i. hominum, post renouatum & receptum ex aquis hunc mundū, antiquissimus. Quod enim homines olim vetustissimos esse censebāt, eos terræ & cœli, velut primorū Mundi elementorum filios vocabāt. Ergo hic & ab Hesiod. in Theogon. & à Virgil. lib.1. Georgic. è terra ipsa natus scribitur, & ab Higino initio lib. De Fabul. Deniq; extitisse primus post diluuiū temporibus, cuius filius dicitur fuisse quidā Prometheus, non ille quidem antiquissimus (vt enim fuit Abel) sed recentior altus, qui tamen cum prisco illo confunditur ab Ethnicis hominibus, & Poetis, præsertim omnia miscentibus. De hoc igitur prisco Iapeto dixit Ouid. lib. 1. Metamorph. [Quam fatus Iapeto mistā fluuialibus vndis] de quo Cyrillus ex Ethnicorū scriptis lib. 3. contra Iulian. Hinc proverbiū etiam à Luciano Ethnico vsurpatum, ἰαπέτε ἀρχαιότερος, [Iapeto antiquior.] Hinc Iaphia nomen, Iof. 10, 2. Sam. & Japhie oppidum Zabulonis, Iof. 19: & fortasse Japodes populi vetustissimi inter Illyricos in Alpibus fiti, de quibus Appian. in Illyricis, & Strabo lib. 4. Geogr. Huius Iapeti Berosus lib. 1 & 4, diserte meminit. Semi verò (qui pius permansit, & à quo gēs Hebræorum orta) pauci scriptores Ethnici mentionem fecere, præter illum, quem iam dixi Berosum, cuius verba antea protuli ex lib. eius 1. Manent tamen etiam inter Ethnicos hæc nominis ipsius quædam vestigia, velut nomen [Soemus] de quo Iosephus lib. 2. de Bell. Iudaico cap. ἐap.20: & [Samos] infula, & [Samothracia] vbi dý Cabiri, seu dý Samothracum, quasi veriores, quam Dý Graecorum, qui religiosissime ab Ethnicis colebantur. Verùm Chami seu Cami lôgè plurima extát inter Ethnicos vestigia: fuit enim impius, & Ethnicis propterea notior, quàm Semus ille pius, & verè religiosus. Quem enim S. Scriptura vocat Chamum, eundem Ethnici nominát Camesen, quem Zoroastren quoque fuisse volunt. Sic igitur Berosus lib. 3 [Erat, inquit, Noacho filius ex tribus primis iunior Cham, qui semper Magica & Venefica studens, Zoroastr nomen consecutus erat. Is patrem Noachum odio habebat. Itaque nactus opportunitatem, quum Noa pater madidus iaceret, illius virilia comprehendens, tacitè, submurmurans carmine magico patri illusit, simul & illū sterilem atque castratum effecit. At verò Cham quum publicè corrumperet mortale genus, asserens, & re ipsa exequens congrediendum esse, ut ante exundationem, cū matribus, sororibus, filiabus, masculis, brutis, & quovis alio genere, ob hoc eiectus à Iano .i. Noa pyssimo, sortitus est nomen Chā esse nne, id est, Chem infamis & impudicus.] Unde nomen Camesēs formatū postea. Ex quo fit, ut vox [Ε-fenus seu Ezenus] proculdubio sit ab hebraeo verbo [Zanah] derivata, quod fornicari & animo, & corpore significat. Fabius Pictor lib. de Aureo saeculo docet sub finem aurei saeculi Camesen praefectum fuisse, seu imperasse Aboriginibus in Italia, siue is prisicus fuerit, de quo Berosus: siue recentior, quod magis puto. Multi enim postea fuerunt Camesēs. Cato in Fragm. [Italia (inquit) splendidissima origo fuit, tum tempore, tum origine gentis. Cœpit enim aureo seculo sub principibus diis, Iano, Camese, Saturno.] Et postea, [Italia à diis coplura sortita est nomina, à Iano Ianicula (quem quidam Oenotrii fuisse putant, quia inuenit vinũ & far) Camesena, à Camese: & à Saturno Saturnia.] Et mihi quidem dubium non est Italos primos potius à Camo, vel eius posteris propagatos esse, qui ex Africa in Graciam & Siciliam traiecerint, quam ex Iapeti posteris illis, qui in Asia vel Septentrionali Europa parte diu subsiterunt. Ergo illi Cami siue Camesis filij Noæ, velut primi autoris sua gentis & diutissime, & lubentissime memoriã conseruarunt, eámque posteris posteà tradiderunt. Ab eadem Cami voce videntur quoque & in Oriente quidem (vbi Camus cum patre Noa diu habitauit) hæc nomina velut illius vestigia formata reliquæque fuisse, Cambaia regio Orientalis, de qua Strabo lib.12 & Cambala, vbi sunt auri fodinæ, quæ nunc Cambalu vocatur: vnde Magnus Cham Tartariæ dictus, qui illis locis imperat. Hinc Cama & Camaca populi Scythiæ extremæ & Orientalis, vt docet Plinius lib.5.cap. 17: Camina Insula, lib.4 cap.12. Camina Ceres dicta apud Pausaniam lib.6. Camesis fluuius Oceani Indici & Orientalis: de quo Aethicus. Camesena oppidum in Italia, de qua M.Cato in Fragmentis. Cambysis quoq; regis Persiæ nomen honorificum inde natum, qui Cyro regi in imperio successit: à quo Cambysena regio Orientalis fuit appellata. Et hæ quidem tot appellationes videntur ab vno Cami nomine deductæ, & in hominum memoriã velut vestigia lucida, Camü renouasse. Quid quod nonnulli, velut Plesseius in lib.de Veritate Christi, scribunt? Hammon Iuppiter, aiunt, inter Afros est idem, qui & Cham filius Noachi: Scribitur enim per [Cheth] Hebraeum, quod per suum H, Latini, & Graeci per suam aspirationem pronuntiat. [Mon] autem syllaba addita fuit imperitè, vel ambitiosè à Gracis, vt ab arena nomen Ammonis tanquam suum & Gracum deducerent. Ἄμμος enim Graecè est arena: In arenosa vero Cyrenaica regionis parte situ est illius loius Ammonis templum. At Herodotus lib. 2. manult Ammonē quasi Amnonem, id est, arietinū vocatum Ἀμνὸς ἀμνὸς deductum, quòd facie arietina pingeretur. Vnde illud Nasonis, [Lybs est cum cornibus Aminon.]
units.tr: "They give their necks their rhythm, the Asian marsh resounds with arms and is struck all around." So Asia was named not after a woman, as the widows' tale would have it, but from that marsh, and it was known to the Greek men who then frequented the sea, the Carians among them. At first the name applied only to the region where the Greeks themselves lived, that is, Asia Minor; afterwards it came to cover the whole mainland beyond it, and was called Asia Major, as Strabo writes (Book 12), to distinguish it from the smaller one. Europe, too, was named by the same Carians and the Asian Greeks for the region that lay opposite those who inhabited Asia Minor, and which they looked out upon widely and freely from their shores, namely the open sea and that part of the world beyond. So Europe was called Εὐρώπη [Eurōpē], as if from εὐρὺ ὤψ [eurys ōps] or εὐρύ [eury], meaning broad and open, the land seen from Asia Minor, and not from some Europa, sister of Cadmus, as some suppose. The historian Justin wants Europe named after King Europus of Macedonia and Thrace, the most ancient of them, who settled in that part of Thrace which faces Asia. But the earlier explanation and derivation of the name is more likely. Finally, Africa was named by the same Asian Greeks for the region from which those who called themselves Afri came to them, and from the part of the world where the sea was most violently stirred and foamed. For ἀφρός [aphros] means foam in Greek. So the first Cares named them. Later, however, these same names and words were taken up by other peoples, since they were passed on to them by those Asian Greeks who sailed the sea, once those others had advanced further and, by voyaging, had reached and traversed more lands and parts of the world. In time it came about that the whole circle of the earth was divided, first by the Greeks and afterwards by other heathen peoples, into these three parts alone and not into more, namely Asia, Europe and Africa. This was in no way done with any thought or regard for the three sons of Noah, Japheth, Shem and Ham; rather, they had learned and received these three names of the lands from the Carians and the Asian Greeks. And yet that subtle philosophy about the number three of Noah's children is more tolerable than that wholly allegorical and certainly silly rhetoric of Augustine (with all due respect to so great a man), in Book 16 of The City of God, chapter 2, who refers this number of three sons of Noah to Christ, the faithful and the impious. But if anyone asks the meaning of these Hebrew names, on which Augustine philosophises so much, it is this: Japheth is said to mean, as it were, "beautiful of face" or "broad of shoulders." So Plato is called by the Greeks. Shem seems to be named as if he were to be famous and memorable, or appointed and chosen by God; so Cleones were called in Greek. Ham, or Cami (for so the Latins write it indiscriminately), received his name as if he were hot in temperament and dark in colour. So many Blacks are called by the Latins, and Melas by the Greeks. I prefer to follow these interpretations of the names rather than certain foolish philosophising. Moreover, there are very many traces among the heathen of Japhet or Iapetus, the firstborn son of Noah. For he is the one whom they, softening the Hebrew word to suit the sound and smoothness of their own tongue, call Iapetus the Elder. Later several were called by this same name. That ancient Iapetus is said to have been the son of Earth and Heaven, that is, of men, the most ancient after this world was renewed and brought back out of the waters. For because they once thought men were the most ancient, they called them sons of Earth and Heaven, as though they were the first elements of the world. So he is described by Hesiod in the Theogony, by Virgil in Book 1 of the Georgics, as born of the earth itself, and by Hyginus at the beginning of his Fabulae. Finally, he is said to have been the first to exist after the flood, and a certain Prometheus is said to have been his son, not the most ancient of all (for Abel was that), but a somewhat later one; yet the heathen and the poets, who especially mix everything together, confuse him with that ancient Iapetus. Of this ancient Iapetus Ovid spoke in Book 1 of the Metamorphoses: "Whom the son of Iapetus mixed with river waters." Cyril, drawing on the writings of the heathen, speaks of him in Book 3 against Julian. Hence the proverb, also used by the heathen Lucian, ἰαπέτε ἀρχαιότερος [iapete archaioteros], "older than Iapetus." Hence the name Japhia (Josh. 10; 2 Sam.) and Japhie, a town of Zebulun (Josh. 19), and perhaps the Japodes, a very ancient people among the Illyrians living in the Alps, of whom Appian speaks in his Illyrica and Strabo in Book 4 of the Geography. Berosus clearly mentions this Iapetus in Books 1 and 4. But Shem, who remained pious, and from whom the people of the Hebrews sprang, has been mentioned by few heathen writers, apart from Berosus, whom I have already cited, and whose words I quoted earlier from his first book. Yet some traces of this name survive even among the heathen, such as the name Soemus, of whom Josephus speaks in Book 2 of the Jewish War, chapter 20; and the island Samos, and Samothrace, where there are the Cabiri, or Samothracians, who are thought more genuine than the Greek gods, and who were worshipped most devoutly by the heathen. But of Ham, or Cam, there are by far the most traces among the heathen, for he was impious, and therefore better known to the heathen than that pious and truly religious Shem. For the one whom Holy Scripture calls Ham, the heathen name Camesen, and they want him also to have been Zoroaster. So Berosus says in Book 3: "There was, he says, a son of Noah, Ham, the youngest of the first three, who, always devoted to magic and sorcery, had acquired the name Zoroaster. He hated his father Noah. And so, when he found the opportunity, while Noah his father lay drunk, he seized his privy parts, and secretly, muttering a magic charm, mocked his father and at the same time made him barren and castrated. But Ham, publicly corrupting the mortal race and asserting and actually carrying out that men ought to mix, before the flood, with mothers, sisters, daughters, males, beasts and every other kind, was for this cast out by Janus, that is, the wicked Noah, and was given the name Chā esse nne, that is, Chem, infamous and shameless." From this the name Camesen was later formed. It follows that the word [Ε-fenus or Ezenus] is undoubtedly derived from the Hebrew verb [Zanah], which means to commit fornication both in mind and in body. Fabius Pictor, in his book on the Golden Age, teaches that at the end of the Golden Age Camesen was in command, or ruled the Aborigines in Italy, whether he was that ancient one of whom Berosus speaks, or a later one, which I think more likely. For there were many Camesi afterwards. Cato, in his fragments: "Italy, he says, had a most splendid origin, both in its time and in the origin of its people. For it began in the Golden Age under the divine princes, Janus, Camese, Saturn." And afterwards: "Italy received many names from the gods: from Janus, Janicula (whom some think were the Oenotrians, because he discovered wine and spelt), Camesena from Camese, and from Saturn, Saturnia." And to me there is no doubt that the first Italians were rather descended from Cam, or his posterity, who crossed from Africa into Greece and Sicily, than from those posterity of Japhet who long remained in Asia or the northern part of Europe. So those children of Cam, or Camesis, sons of Noah, as descendants of their first author, preserved his memory both for a very long time and most willingly, and afterwards handed it on to their posterity. From the same word Cam, these names also seem to have been formed in the East (where Cam dwelt for a long time with his father Noah) as traces of him, and the rest: the Eastern region of Cambaia, of which Strabo speaks in Book 12, and Cambala, where there are gold mines, now called Cambalu, whence the Great Cham of Tartary, who rules those places, is so named. From this come Cama and Camaca, peoples of far-eastern Scythia, as Pliny teaches in Book 5, chapter 17; the island Camina, Book 4, chapter 12; Camina, called Ceres by Pausanias in Book 6; the river Camesis of the Indian and Eastern Ocean, of which Aethicus speaks; Camesena, a town in Italy, of which Marcus Cato speaks in his fragments; and the honorific name of Cambyses, king of Persia, who succeeded Cyrus in the empire, from which the Eastern region of Cambysena was named. And all these appellations seem derived from the one name Cam, and, like bright traces preserved in human memory, to have renewed the memory of Cam. What of the fact that some, such as Plessis in his book On the Truth of Christ, write that Hammon, that is Jupiter, among the Africans, is the same as Ham the son of Noah? For it is written with the Hebrew [Cheth], which the Latins and Greeks pronounce with their own aspirate H. But the syllable [Mon] was added foolishly, or out of vanity, by the Greeks, so that they might derive the name Ammon from the sand (ἄμμος [ammos]) as if it were their own Greek word, for ἄμμος means sand in Greek. The temple of that Ammon stands in a sandy part of the Cyrenaic region. But Herodotus, in Book 2, says that Ammon was called as if Amnon, that is, the ram-god, derived from ἀμνός [amnos], a lamb, because he was painted with the face of a ram. Hence that line of Naso: "Libya is Ammon, with horns."

units.la: Sed errat omnes isti imperitia vere illius nominis etymologiæ. Chammon enim à Chamo dicitur. Est enim lingua & gens Aegyptia affinis Hebraea. Aegyptia igitur ab illa vocem Dei sui Chammonis desumpsit. Et hæc quidem de nominibus istis satis.
units.tr: But these men all err through ignorance of the true etymology of that name. For Chammon is so called from Cham. Indeed the Egyptian language and people is akin to the Hebrew. The Egyptians therefore took the word for their god Chammon from that root. And so much for these names.

units.la: Ad VIII. Corruptissimum vitæ genus.
units.tr: Chapter VIII. The most corrupt way of life.

units.la: Accedamus iam ad reliqua nostra Historia capita, nempe ad corruptissimum vitæ hominum genus, quod & post Gigantes natos, & tempore Noachi ante Diluuium à Deo immissum irrupit in orbem terrarum. Cuius rei hæc extant in Ethnicorum scriptis vestigia, quamquam obscurata ex eo, quòd illi etiam transtulerunt ad ætates Mundi, quæ secuta sunt Diluuium, ea, quæ ante diluuium contigerant, & facta fuerant, vel ignoratione temporis rerum gestarum: vel quòd eadem sæpius repetita fuisse putât, renouato sæpius mundo, quemadmodū illi autumant: Imprimis autem Plato in Timæo, & Po-
units.tr: Let us now come to the remaining chapters of our history, namely to the most corrupt way of life of men, which broke into the world both after the Giants were born and, in the time of Noah before the Flood, was sent in by God. Traces of this are found in the writings of the Gentiles, though they are obscured, partly because they transferred to the ages of the world that followed the Flood what had happened before it, either through ignorance of the timing of events or because they thought the same things were repeated often, the world being renewed again and again, as they maintain. Above all, Plato in the Timaeus and Polybius...

units.la: Ce litico, & lib.3.de Legibus. Ergo qua illi Ethnici de diuersis Mundi œtatibus aiunt, & præsertim de Ferrea tradunt, sunt istius morum corruptionis generalis, quae ante Diluuium accidit, certissima inter Ethnicos ipsos testimonia. Quamobrem Ouidius lib.1. Metamorph. docet Ferream illam Mundi ætatem (quæ fuit corruptissima, & depravatissima) & Gigantum aduersus deos pugnam præcepsisse, & terrarum inundationem. Nam de Ferrea illa, quæ diluuium proximè antecessit, hominum ætate sic scribit:
units.tr: Accordingly, what those Gentiles say about the different ages of the world, and especially what they relate about the Iron Age, are most certain testimonies among the Gentiles themselves to that general corruption of morals which happened before the Flood. Hence Ovid in the first book of the Metamorphoses teaches that this Iron Age of the world, which was the most corrupt and depraved, was followed by the war of the Giants against the gods and by the inundation of the lands. For about that Iron Age, which immediately preceded the Flood, he writes of the age of men thus:

units.la: [Viuitur ex rapto, non hospes ab hospite tutus: Non socer a genero: fratrum quoque gratia rara est: Vitia iacet pietas, & virgo cæde madentes Vltima cœlestum terras Astræa reliquit.] Atque hac ipsa ætate, ait idem Ouidius, Gigantes nati, qui in cœlum, & Deos ipsos coniurarunt, & belligerarunt: de quibus ille sic eodem loco:
units.tr: [They live by plunder; guest is not safe from guest, nor father-in-law from son-in-law; even brotherly affection is rare. Piety lies low, and the virgin Astraea, stained with slaughter, left the lands last of the heavenly beings.] And in this very age, says the same Ovid, the Giants were born, who conspired against heaven and the gods themselves and made war on them; of whom he says in the same place:

units.la: [Neve foret terris securior arduus æther, Assectasse ferunt regnum cœleste Gigantes:] ex quibus homines nati fuere & ipsi quoque in Deum impij, & in alios homines sæui.
units.tr: [Lest the lofty sky should be too safe for the lands, the Giants are said to have aspired to the heavenly kingdom:] from them men were born, who were themselves also impious toward God and savage toward other men.

units.la: -- [sed & illa propago (addit idem Poëta) Contemptrix superûm, sauaq; anidissima cædis Et violenta fuit.] Post quas & propter quas hominum impietates, crudelitates, libidines, & omne genus scelerû scribit idem Ouidius diluuium in terras vniuersas à Ioue .i. Deo effusum fuisse. Ergo subiycit
units.tr: -- [But that progeny too (the same poet adds) was scornful of the gods, and most savage, most eager for slaughter and violence.] After these, and on account of these human impieties, cruelties, lusts and every kind of crime, the same Ovid writes that a flood was poured by Jove, that is, by God, over all the lands. Therefore he adds:

units.la: [Jámque erat in totas sparsurus fulmina terras, Pœna placet diuersa, genus mortale sub vndis Perdere, & ex omni contrahere nubila cælo, Nec cœlo contenta suo est Iouis ira: sed illum Cæruleus frater iuuat auxiliaribus vndis.]
units.tr: [And now he was about to scatter lightning over all the lands; but a different punishment pleased him, to destroy the mortal race beneath the waves, and to draw all the clouds from the sky. Nor was Jove's anger content with his own heaven, but his brother of the blue sea helps him with his auxiliary waves.]

units.la: Quid vero aptius, & conuenientius nostra veritati dici & restare potest, siue series rerum, siue immanis corruptio hominum siue diluuij caussa spectetur, & quaratur? Ergo hoc est certissimum nostra veritatis vestigium. Hesiodus lib. 1. Opera & Dies, non procul ab iis abludit: docet enim tota Aerea ætate mundi (quæ secuta est Auream, & Argenteam) homines fuisse violentos & impios, prorsusque periisse: quibus Heroes successerint viri nempe meliores, quales qui ex Noacho post diluuium nati sunt, ac orti. Plato in Politico, post Saturni tempus & regnum tantà fuisse totius Mundi intemperiem ait, prauitatemq; hominum, vt Deus habenas regimenq; Mundi deseruisse censeretur. Itaque à Deo sublatam illam viuendi rationem, hominesque illos nempe per diluuium à Deo deletos: alios autem in eorum locum substitutos, & repositos. Diodorus Sicul. lib. 1. de Gigantibus (qui primo Mundi seculo vixerunt) loquens, ita scribit, [Multi existimant, quum y Iovi, Osiridiq; diys bellù intulissent (quod summa certe quidem impietatis indicium est) omnes peremptos esse.] Atque hac illi, quanuis Ethnici, nobisecum de corruptissimis hominum moribus ante Diluuium, punitúmque à Deo Mundum vniuersum consentientes tradunt. Ex eorundem etiam libris Lactantius plane affinia his scribit: Nam lib.
units.tr: What more fitting and more agreeable to our truth can be said or remain, whether one looks at the sequence of events, or at the monstrous corruption of men, or at the cause of the Flood, and seeks it out? Therefore this is the most certain trace of our truth. Hesiod in the first book of the Works and Days does not differ far from these; for he teaches that throughout the Bronze Age of the world (which followed the Golden and Silver Ages) men were violent and impious and utterly perished, and that heroes succeeded them, namely better men, such as those born and descended from Noah after the Flood. Plato in the Politicus says that after the time and reign of Saturn there was such great disorder of the whole world and such wickedness of men that God was thought to have abandoned the reins and government of the world. Thus that way of living was taken away by God, and those men were destroyed by God through the Flood, and others were put in their place and set down. Diodorus Siculus in the first book, speaking of the Giants (who lived in the first age of the world), writes thus: [Many think that when they made war on Jove and Osiris (which is certainly a sign of the greatest impiety) they were all destroyed.] These things, though they are Gentiles, relate in agreement with us the most corrupt morals of men before the Flood, and the whole world being punished by God. From the same authors Lactantius writes things entirely similar to these: for in the

units.la: 2. Institut. Christian. cap. 14, postquam homines quosdam à cæteris differentes ex coitu Angelorum & fœminarū natos dixit, eos ipsos totum mundū suis artibus & exemplis ante Diluuium depravasse vult: [Hi, ait, spiritus contaminati ac perditi per totā terram vagātur. Itaq; omnia insidiis, fraudibus, dolis, erroribus complent. Hi sibi Geniorū nomen assumunt.] Ergo isti primum mundum prorsus corrupēre. Sed & Berosus ait, Hi Gigantes libidinosissimi erant, impudici, & nihil non sceleris admittebant. Inde illa sunt, quae diis suis Ethnici attribuerunt scelera, quoniam illi Gigantes, & qui ex iis sunt procreati illo seculo, dicti sunt, quemadmodum docet Mosis, Fortes, dij, genij, heroes, & à posteris culti. Eusebius lib.2.cap.9. Praeparat.Evangel. [Quū primis illis ante Diluuium temporibus mores hominū, aist, stabiliti legibus non essent, nec supplicia peccatorū imminerent, adulteria, nefanda matrimonia, maribus ereptam pudicitiā, homicidia, parricidia, confecta scelere bella, quasi res pulcherrimē gestas, diis suis attribuebāt, & earum rerum memoriam, quasi perutilem, posteris tradiderunt.] Et hac ratione, ait idem, coluerunt eos, qui voluptatum inuenerunt genera, vel amplificarunt: itemq; maleficos & pestiferos viros, quasi Deos coluerunt. Idem Arnobius contra Gentes ex eorum tamen monumentis scribit. Sed hoc ipsum quoque confirmat idem Eusebius eiusdem operis, quod iam citaui, lib.7. cap.3.ex Ethnicorū quoque scriptis, vti ex Mosaicis sic scribens, [Et Gigantes illi, qui per ora omniū volitant impiys falsis (quod adhuc vsque praedicatur) Deo .i. virtuti & pietati bellum nō erubuerunt inferre. Et qui eos produxerunt siue immortales quidā, siue mortales, malefica quedam artificia, & magicam prauitatem primi excogitasse dicuntur.] Ex quibus omnibus apparet luce Meridiana clarius, & à Gigantibus, qui primi Mundi seculis fuerunt, summe corruptos fuisse hominum mores: & eam immanem corruptionem vsque ad Diluuium perseuerasse, propter quam illud immissum est à Deo.
units.tr: second book of the Institutes, chapter 14, after saying that certain men, different from the rest, were born from the intercourse of Angels and women, he holds that these same men by their arts and examples corrupted the whole world before the Flood: [These spirits, he says, polluted and lost, wander over the whole earth. And so they fill everything with snares, frauds, tricks, and errors. They assume for themselves the name of Genii.] Therefore these first utterly corrupted the world. But Berosus also says that these Giants were most lustful, shameless, and admitted nothing of wickedness. Hence come those crimes which the Gentiles attributed to their gods, since those Giants and those born of them in that age were called, as Moses teaches, Mighty ones, gods, genii, heroes, and were worshipped by posterity. Eusebius, Praeparatio Evangelica, book 2, chapter 9: [When in those first times before the Flood the morals of men were not established by laws, nor were punishments for sins hanging over them, they attributed to their gods adulteries, unspeakable marriages, the chastity of males snatched away, murders, parricides, and wars completed with crime, as if they were most beautifully accomplished deeds, and handed down the memory of such things to posterity as if it were very useful.] And in this way, says the same author, they worshipped as gods those who discovered or enlarged kinds of pleasures, and likewise wicked and destructive men. Arnobius writes the same against the Gentiles, drawing on their own monuments. But Eusebius himself confirms this same point in the same work, which I have already cited, book 7, chapter 3, from the writings of the Gentiles as well as the Mosaic ones, writing thus: [And those Giants, who fly through the mouths of all men with impious falsehoods (which is still proclaimed to this day), did not blush to make war on God, that is, on virtue and piety. And those who produced them, whether immortal or mortal, are said to have first devised certain magical arts and magical depravity.] From all these things it appears clearer than the noonday light that from the Giants, who were in the first ages of the world, the morals of men were utterly corrupted, and that this monstrous corruption persisted until the Flood, on account of which it was sent by God.

units.la: Ad XI. Denunciatio futuri Diluuij.
units.tr: Chapter XI. The announcement of the coming Flood.

units.la: SED iam ad ipsam Diluuij denuntiationem veniamus, cuius vestigia sunt à nobis in Ethnicorum libris quaerenda. Sunt autem haec, Primum, quod Iosephus lib. 1. cap. 4. Antiquit. Iudaic. scribit, Etiam ab Adamo ipso praedictum fuisse Diluuium Mundi propter hominum scelera: idque duabus columnis (quarum vna erat lapidea, altera lateritia) inscriptum: quarum vna etiam ad ipsius Iosephi tempora in Syria superfuerit, vt tunc sciebant omnes & ipse scribit. Deinde quod ante Iosephum M. T. Cicero lib. 1. de Diuinat. ex veteribus & Ethnicis scriptoribus docet ipsemet Ethnicum Assyrios & Babylonios habuisse monumenta rerum gestarum penè infinitorum annorum, in quibus quid Mundo esset euenturum, continebatur, ac praedictum erat. Consentit cum Cicerone Diodorus Siculus lib. 3 cap. 8. Biblioth. Scribit enim Chaldaeos rerum, quae futurae fuerant, & quae gesta sunt, longissimam memoriam scriptis tradita habuisse. Tertio loco C. Plinius lib. 7. Nat. Hist. cap. 56, [E diuerso, ait, Epigenes apud Babylonios DCCXX annorum obseruationes siderum coctilibus laterculis inscriptas docet, grauis autor imprimis. Qui minimum Berosus, & Critodemus CCCCLXXX annorum. Ex quo apparet aeternum literarum vsu.] Ea vero siderum obseruationes, rerum mutationes, & quae eluuiones mundi futura erant, praedicebant. Ergo ex veteri memoria & traditione Patrum hoc retinuerunt, sciuerunt q; Ethnici Diluuium & clades mundi à suis Maioribus, qui illis temporibus vixerunt, & priusquàm illa euenirent, cognitas fuisse: ac proinde ijdem fuisse a Deo denuntiatas. Sed quid tergiuersamur? Alexander Polyhistor apud Cyrillum lib. 1. contra Julian. narrat Saturnum praedixisse Xisuthro, id est, Noacho futurum Diluuiū, & quod fabricanda esset Arca, in qua ipse simul cum suis, reptilibus, & iumentis seruandus nauigare deberet. En denique ipsius Berosi, quem iam sapius citani, verba, qui, postquam de corruptissimis hominum illius primi seculi moribus, & praesertim Gigantum, locutus est, sic ait, [Tunc multi praedicabant, & vaticinabantur, & lapidibus incidebant de ea, quae ventura erat, Orbis perditione. Sed enim illi Gigantes malis assueti corridebant omnia, coelestiū illos ira atque ultione pergurgente pro impietate atque sceleribus.] Haec ipse, quicunq; tandem est, Berosus, certè Ethnicus, & vetus autor tradit. Finit enim suam historiam quemadmodum & vixit lōgè ante Romam conditam. Haec verò nonne sunt manifestissima denuntiati Diluuij vestigia etiam apud Ethnicos?
units.tr: But let us now come to the announcement of the Flood itself. Its traces must be sought by us in the books of the heathen. The first is that Josephus, in Antiquities of the Jews, book 1, chapter 4, writes that the Flood of the world was foretold even by Adam himself, because of the wickedness of men, and that this was inscribed on two pillars, one of stone and one of brick; and that one of them survived in Syria until Josephus's own time, as all people then knew, and he himself writes. Second, before Josephus, M. T. Cicero, in book 1 of On Divination, shows from ancient heathen writers that the Assyrians and Babylonians themselves had records of events covering almost infinite years, in which it was contained and foretold what was going to happen to the world. Diodorus Siculus, Library, book 3, chapter 8, agrees with Cicero. For he writes that the Chaldeans had a very long memory of things to come and of things done, handed down in writing. Third, C. Plinius, Natural History, book 7, chapter 56: [On the other hand, he says, Epigenes, a weighty author above all, reports that among the Babylonians observations of the stars for 720 years were inscribed on baked brick tablets. Berosus, at the least, and Critodemus, reckon 480 years. From this it appears that the use of letters is eternal.] Now these observations of the stars predicted changes in things and the coming floods of the world. Therefore, by old memory and the tradition of the Fathers, the heathen also retained this and knew that the Flood and the destruction of the world had been known from their ancestors, who lived in those times, before those events happened, and that therefore the same had been announced by God. But why do we hesitate? Alexander Polyhistor, in Cyril, Against Julian, book 1, relates that Saturn foretold to Xisuthrus, that is Noah, that a Flood would come, and that an ark must be built in which he, together with his own, and the creeping things and beasts, was to be saved by sailing. Lastly, here are the words of Berosus himself, whom I have cited often already. After speaking of the most corrupt morals of men in that first age, and especially of the Giants, he says: [Then many preached and prophesied, and carved on stones about the coming destruction of the world. But those Giants, accustomed to evils, mocked everything, while the wrath and vengeance of the heavenly beings overflowed upon their impiety and crimes.] These things are told by Berosus, whoever he finally was, certainly a heathen and an ancient author. For he ends his history in the same way he lived, long before Rome was founded. Are these not, then, the most manifest traces of the announced Flood, even among the heathen?

units.la: Ad XII. Diluuium vniuersale Mundi.
units.tr: Chapter XII. The universal Flood of the world.

units.la: Pergamus vero, & tandem ad vltimum nostra historia caput accedamus. Est autem de Diluuio ipso in vniuersum terrarum orbem immisso: cuius quot extent apud Ethnicos scriptores testimonia, vestigiaque, credi non potest, nedum dici. Quo magis miror quid Augustino stino in mentem venerit, vt lib. 18. Ciuitat. Dei, cap. 8 scriberet, huius vniuersalis & primi Diluuij nulla nec in Graca, nec in Latina historia factâ esse mentionem: sed tantum vel Ogigiani, vel Deucalionei diluuij, quod vtrumque primo illo longè posterius fuit. Refutatur vero Augustinus cum ex perpetuis Ethnicorum monumentis, quemadmodum mox docebimus: tum & Lactantij & Isidori scriptorum ecclesiasticorum testimonio, praterquam quod Augustini interpres eo loco Ioan. Vives vir eruditissimus hanc Augustini falsam esse sententiam, contra prolatis contrarijs, docet. Lactantius igitur lib. 2. cap. 10. non ex Christianorum modo, verum omnium Gentium consensu sic scribit, [Factum esse Diluuii ad perdendam, tollendamq; ex Orbe terra malitia constat inter omnes. Idem enim & Philosophi, Poeta, scriptoresque rerum antiquarum loquuntur: in eoque maxime cum Prophetarum sermone consentiunt.] Isidorus lib. 13. Etymolog. cap. 22. [Diluuium dictum est, ait, quod aquarum clade omnia, quae inundauerit, deleat. Primum diluuium extitit sub Noë, quando hominum sceleribus offensus Omnipotens, toto orbe contecto, deletis cunctis, vnum spatium cæli fuit & Pelagi. Cuius hastenus indicium videmus in lapidibus, quos in remotis montibus, conchis, & ostreis concretos, sepe etiam cauatos aquis visere solemus.] Hæc ille, qui docet omni mortalium generi superesse etiamnū hodie vetustissimi illius Diluuij memoriam ex lapidibus pretiosis, qui cernuiur in summis montium iugis, quos illic ex eo Diluuio reliƈtos ait Isidorus. Ex quibus apparet minimè Augustino assentiendum esse. Sed in eo decepti sunt Ethnici, quod ea, qua de primo illo & antiquissimo terrarum. Diluuio acceperant, imperitèvel ambitiosè ad quasdam aquarum eluuiones peculiares, quae in suis regionibus acciderant, transtulerunt, quemadmodum loco tam citato docet Lactantius. Ergo vera est illa Platonis lib. 3. Leg. sententia: multa quidem fuisse Diluuia: Vnum tamen inter catera celebre & maximum. Verba Platonis haec sunt ex Ioan. Serrani viri doctissimi versione. [ATH. Multas interneciones generis humani extitisse per Diluuia aquarum, & popularium morborum lues, aliasque huiusmodi noxas, eò quidem vsque vt paucula hominum reliquiae post illas vastitates superessent. CL. Omnino id cuilibet verisimile videtur. ATH. Age vero Vnā aliquam insignem consideremus e multis, eam videlicet, quae per celebre illud Diluuium quondam extitit.] Huius autem copiosius meminit idem Plato in Timaeo. Confuderunt igitur saepe Ethnici particularia illa diluuia, quae secuta sunt, cum illo Vniuersali, quod praecessit, non tamen semper, & vbique. Sed vt rem hanc totam perspicuè exponā, sic ex eorum scriptis colligo: Inundationes terrarum fuisse plures. Prima, aiunt illi, nouimestris sub prisco Ogyge. Haec sola fuit vniuersalis, & est Diluuiū à Mose Gen.6. & 7 descriptū vti postea, Deo fauente, demonstrabo. Secunda inundatio Niliaca, menstrua sub Aegyptijs Hercule, ac Prometheo. Tertia bimestris in Achaia sub Ogyge Attico, & recentiore. Quarta, trimestris in Thessalia sub Deucalione. Quinta in Pharo seu Aegypto, & ipsa trimestris (quae Pharaonica dicta est, vel à Pharaone, vel à Pharo insula, à qua tota Aegyptus, Pharos fuit olim appellata.) Quinta, inquam in Aegypto sub Proteo Aegyptio in raptu Helenæ. Eodem modo ex Eusebij Chronicis multoties diluuium exti-tisse constat, velut sub Noacho, Ogyge, Deucalione: de quibus etiam Isidorus lib. 13. cap. 22. Etymologic. sed etiā postea sub Mauricio Imperatore, anno salutis 586 item sub Carolo V. Imperatore Germano in Hollandia, & Zeelandia, anno Domini 1531: & alijs in locis sæpe. Verum Diluuium hoc vniuersale, & primum (quod Noachi temporibus fuit) κατ' ἐξοχὴν Terrarum inundationem vocarunt, à quo ad ortu Deucalionis volunt intercessisse annos septingentos, quemadmodu tradit Xenophon quidam in Æquinoctis. De hoc igitur prisca Ethnicorum testimonia querimus: nam de Ogygiano posteriore, quod in tota Attica & Achaia diuaxat fuit: vel Deucalioneo, quod solum in Thessalia, extant quaplurima reliquiae. Ogygiani istius posterioris (præter Eusebium, Xenophōtem istū, & superiores autores iam citatos) meminit etiā Varro in lib. de Pop. Rom. testle Augustin. lib. 18. Ciuit. Dei, cap. 8: & Berosus, & alij: quanquam eorum pleriq; sæpe primum illud Diluuium Ogygianum etiam vocant ab Ogyge prisco i. Noa, vti iam docuimus: non autem ab Ogyge Attico, homine omnino recente & nouo. Deucalionei diluuij mentione faciunt Virgilius, Ouidius, Pausanias variis in locis, qui Deucalionem solium Phthiotæ regionis (quæ est pars Thessaliæ) regem fuisse scribit, eiusq; sepulcrum in Attica extitisse affirmat lib. 1, & 5. Strabo lib. 9. Geogr. & alij pene infiniti. Illius vero, quod, vt sæpe dixi, & primum fuit, & vniuersale, & sub Noa contigit, infinita sunt in eorundem Ethnicorum libris vestigia. Ac primùm in libris Sibylla, cuius versus hi recitátur à Lactantio Firmiano lib.de Ira Dei, cap. 23.
units.tr: Let us proceed, and at last come to the final chapter of our history. It concerns the Flood itself, sent upon the whole orb of the earth. How many testimonies and traces of it exist among the heathen writers cannot be believed, let alone told. All the more do I wonder what came into the mind of Augustine, that in book 18 of The City of God, chapter 8, he wrote that no mention of this universal and first Flood was made in Greek or Latin history, but only of the Ogygian or Deucalionian flood, both of which were far later than the first. But Augustine is refuted both by the constant monuments of the heathen, as we shall soon show, and by the testimony of the ecclesiastical writers Lactantius and Isidore, besides which John Vives, a most learned man and the translator of Augustine in that passage, teaches that this opinion of Augustine is false, since contrary evidence has been brought forward. Lactantius, then, in book 2, chapter 10, writes thus, not only from the agreement of Christians but of all nations: [That a flood came to destroy and wipe out wickedness from the earth is agreed upon by all. For philosophers, poets, and writers of ancient history speak of the same thing, and in this especially they agree with the words of the Prophets.] Isidore, Etymologies, book 13, chapter 22: [The flood is so called, he says, because by the destruction of waters it blots out everything it has overflowed. The first flood happened under Noah, when the Almighty, offended by the crimes of men, covered the whole world, all being destroyed, and there was one expanse of sky and sea. Of this we still see evidence in the stones which we are accustomed to look upon in remote mountains, encrusted with shells and oysters, and often hollowed out by the waters.] So he writes, who teaches that the memory of that most ancient Flood still survives today for the whole human race, in the precious stones which are seen on the highest ridges of the mountains, which Isidore says were left there by that Flood. From these things it appears that Augustine must by no means be agreed with. But the heathen were deceived in this: that what they had received about that first and most ancient flood of the earth, they carelessly or ambitiously transferred to certain particular inundations of waters which had occurred in their own regions, as Lactantius teaches in the very passage cited. Therefore that saying of Plato in Laws, book 3, is true: that there were indeed many floods, but one among the rest was famous and greatest. The words of Plato are these, in the translation of John Serranus, a most learned man: [ATH. That there have been many destructions of the human race through floods of water, and plagues of diseases and other harms of this kind, to such an extent that only a few remnants of men survived those devastations. CL. Altogether that seems probable to anyone. ATH. Come then, let us consider one notable one out of many, namely that which once happened in that famous flood.] The same Plato speaks of this more fully in the Timaeus. Therefore the heathen often confused those particular floods which followed with that universal one which preceded, though not always and everywhere. But so that I may set out this whole matter clearly, I gather it thus from their writings: there were several inundations of the lands. The first, they say, was the ninth-month flood under the ancient Ogyges. This alone was universal, and it is the Flood described by Moses in Genesis 6 and 7, as I will afterwards show with God's help. The second was the Nilotic inundation, monthly, under the Egyptians Hercules and Prometheus. The third, lasting two months, was in Achaia under Ogyges of Attica, and under a more recent one. The fourth, lasting three months, was in Thessaly under Deucalion. The fifth was in Pharos or Egypt, itself lasting three months (which was called Pharaonic, either from Pharaoh or from the island of Pharos, from which all Egypt was once called Pharos). The fifth, I say, in Egypt under Proteus the Egyptian at the abduction of Helen. In the same way it is established from the Chronicles of Eusebius that floods occurred many times, as under Noah, Ogyges, and Deucalion, of which Isidore also speaks in Etymologies, book 13, chapter 22; but also afterwards under the Emperor Maurice, in the year of salvation 586; likewise under the German Emperor Charles V in Holland and Zeeland, in the year of the Lord 1531; and often in other places. But this universal and first flood (which was in the time of Noah) they called [by way of eminence] the inundation of the lands, from which they hold that seven hundred years passed until the birth of Deucalion, as a certain Xenophon writes in the Equinoxes. We therefore seek the ancient testimonies of the heathen concerning this one, for of the later Ogygian flood, which was only in all Attica and Achaia, or of the Deucalionian, which was only in Thessaly, there are very many remnants. Of this later Ogygian flood (besides Eusebius, this Xenophon, and the earlier authors already cited) Varro also makes mention in his book on the Roman people, as Augustine witnesses in The City of God, book 18, chapter 8; and Berosus and others also. Although most of them often call that first Ogygian flood by the name of the ancient Ogyges, that is Noah, as we have already shown, and not by the name of Ogyges of Attica, a man altogether recent and new. Virgil, Ovid, and Pausanias in various places make mention of the Deucalionian flood; Pausanias writes that Deucalion was king of the region of Phthiotis (which is part of Thessaly), and he affirms in books 1 and 5 that his tomb stood in Attica. Strabo, Geography, book 9, and almost infinitely many others do the same. But of that flood which, as I have often said, was both the first and universal, and happened under Noah, there are endless traces in the books of the same heathen. And first in the books of the Sibyl, whose verses are recited by Lactantius Firmianus, On the Anger of God, chapter 23.

units.la: Ἐξ οὐ ἀνίσαντ᾽ ἐπεςφνίς Θεοῖο Ἀ υταῖν πολίεσι, ἡ ἀνθρώποισιν ἄπαςι Τὴν ἐκάλυψε θάλασσα κ ταχκλυσμοῖο ςαγένλος, id est,
units.tr: Then, when God's anger fell upon the cities and upon all mankind, the sea covered the earth in a flood... [Ἐξ οὐ ἀνίσαντ᾽ ἐπεςφνίς Θεοῖο Ἀ υταῖν πολίεσι, ἡ ἀνθρώποισιν ἄπαςι Τὴν ἐκάλυψε θάλασσα κ ταχκλυσμοῖο ςαγένλος, id est,]

units.la: [Ergo excandescente Deo, qui sidera fecit, Vrbibus, & cunctis mortalibus isque scelestis, Diluuium terras magnum obruit & mare totas.]
units.tr: So, with God, who made the stars, enraged, he overwhelmed the lands and the sea entire with a great deluge, the cities and all mortals, and the wicked men.

units.la: Quod Cato quoq; in Fragm. Originum, quae extant, commemorat: [Chaldaei, ait, sempiternitatem Mundi sibi persuadent. Phoenicibus vero ac Sagis magis placet origo. Inter vtrosque conuenit ante Ninū circiter annis quinquaginta & ducentis (quibus durauit Aureum seculum] terras fuisse inūdatas, & in Scythia Saga renatum mortale genus.] Archilochus in lib. de Temporib. [Mnaseas Phoenix Damascenus, ait, lib. 97. hist. affeꝛit ante Ninum fermè 250 annis fuisse terrarum inundationem, & quendam (cui testimonium perhibet Moses antiquissimus Historicus) liberatum circa fluuium Araxin, ad montes Caspios.] Caeterum huius Mnaseas verba recitat Josephus lib. 1. Antiquit. Iudaic. cap. 5. Sunt autem haec, [Est & super Miniadā excelsus mōs in Armenia, qui Baris appellatur: in quo multos cōfugientes sermo est Diluuij tempore seruatos, & quendam simul in Arca deuectum (Is autem est Noa) in montis venisse summitatem, lignorumque reliquias multo tempore conseruatas. Fuit autem iste, quem etiam Moses legislator Iudaeorum scripsit.] Hec apud Fla. Josephū Mnaseas ille, quem citat Archilochus. Meminit huius ipsius magni Diluuij quoque Hieronymus Aegyptius, qui antiquitates Phœnicia literis mandarunt. Meminit & Berosus Chaldæus, teste eodem Flavio Iosepho, qui etiam Gordiæum montem nominat quoque, vt suo loco videbitur. Berosus ille, quem iã sæpius citauimus, lib. 1 de Noa scribens, hoc quoque diluuium commemorat. Ait enim, [Is Noë timens quam ex astris futuram prospectabat cladem, anno 78 ante inundationem nauim in tar Arcæ coopertam fabricare cœpit. Anno 78 ab incoata naui ex improuiso exundauit Oceanus, & omnia maria Mediterranea, fluminaq;, & fontes ab imo ebullientes exundauerunt supra omnes montes. Itaque omne humanum genus aquis suffocatum est, excepto Noa cum familia sua, quæ naui erepta est.] Hæc ille, quæ cum nostra veritate plane consentiunt. Quæ vero apud eundem Berosum sequuntur, omnia cum ys, quæ ex eodem refert Flauius Iosephus concordant. Huius quoq; diluuij meminerunt Alexander Polyhistor, & Abydenus. Alexander ait, Arto 3. Lamecho defuncto sub filio eius Xisuthro, id est Noa fuisse magnum Diluuium, quod predixisset ei Saturnus 3. Adamus futurum, & quòd fabricanda esset Arca, in qua ipse cum animalibus seruaretur. Abydenus vero vetustissimus autor sic scribit: [Post quæ & alij fuere, & Xisuthrus, cui Saturnus predixit futuram multitudinem imbrium. Itaq; Xisuthus statim ad Armenios nauigauit, subitoq; euenit diluuiu] Hæc ex Abydeno Cyrillus. Illa enim ex eorũ (qui scriptores sunt Ethnici) libris ipse lib. 1. contra Iulian. transcripsit, quæ sunt verissima historia Mosaice de Diluuio vestigia, vt videt omnes. Quid in Timæo Dialogo de eode diluuio scribat Plato, puto cuius homini docto notum esse, ut homines primi in eo perierint, ut Atlantica insula maxima tunc obruta fuerit, ut totius terrarum orbis facies inde immutata: qua omnia legat apud eum qui volet. Cato in fragmentis ante Ninum 250 annis terram totam inundatam fuisse tradit, ex Maiorii traditione. Ouidius lib. 1. Metamorph. Deucalioneis diluuium appellans illud, quod fuit vniuersale, ait:
units.tr: Cato also records this in the surviving fragments of his Origines: "The Chaldeans persuade themselves that the world is eternal. The Phoenicians and the Sagae prefer an account of its origin. They agree that about 250 years before Ninus (during which the Golden Age lasted) the lands were flooded, and that in Scythia the mortal race was reborn from a Saga." Archilochus, in his book on times, writes: "Mnaseas the Phoenician of Damascus, in book 97 of his history, states that about 250 years before Ninus there was a flooding of the lands, and that a certain man (to whom Moses, the most ancient historian, bears witness) was rescued near the river Araxes, at the Caspian mountains." Josephus, in book 1 of his Antiquities of the Jews, chapter 5, quotes Mnaseas's own words, which are these: "There is also a high mountain in Armenia above Miniadis, called Baris, on which, it is said, many who fled were saved at the time of the Deluge, and a certain man carried in an ark (this is Noah) came to the summit of the mountain, and remnants of the wood were preserved for a long time. This is the man whom Moses, the lawgiver of the Jews, also wrote about." So far Mnaseas, whom Archilochus cites, as quoted by Flavius Josephus. Hieronymus the Egyptian, who committed the antiquities of Phoenicia to writing, also mentions this same great Deluge. Berosus the Chaldean also mentions it, on the testimony of the same Flavius Josephus, and he names the mountain Gordyaeus too, as will be seen in its place. That Berosus, whom we have already cited several times, in book 1 on Noah, also records this flood. For he says: "Noah, fearing the disaster which he foresaw from the stars, began in the 78th year before the inundation to build a ship in the form of an ark, and to cover it over. In the 78th year after the ship was begun, the Ocean suddenly overflowed, and all the Mediterranean seas, rivers and springs, welling up from the depths, overflowed above all the mountains. So the whole human race was drowned by the waters, except Noah with his family, who was rescued in the ship." So he says, and these things entirely agree with our truth. What follows in the same Berosus also agrees in every respect with what Flavius Josephus reports from him. Alexander Polyhistor and Abydenus also mention this flood. Alexander says in book 3 that after Lamech died, under his son Xisuthrus (that is, Noah), there was a great Deluge, which Saturn, the third from Adam, had foretold to him, and that an ark was to be built in which he himself would be preserved with the animals. Abydenus, a very ancient author, writes thus: "After these there were others, and Xisuthrus, to whom Saturn foretold a coming multitude of rains. So Xisuthrus at once sailed to the Armenians, and suddenly the flood came." Cyril gives these words from Abydenus. For Cyril himself, in book 1 against Julian, copied these passages from the books of those writers who are Gentiles, and they are the most true traces of the Mosaic history of the Deluge, as everyone can see. It is known to any learned man, I think, what Plato writes about this same flood in his dialogue Timaeus: that the first men perished in it, that the great island of Atlantis was then overwhelmed, and that the face of the whole earth was thereby changed. Whoever wishes may read all of this in him. Cato, in the fragments, relates that 250 years before Ninus the whole earth was flooded, according to the tradition of our ancestors. Ovid, in book 1 of the Metamorphoses, calling that universal flood the Deucalionean one, says:

units.la: [Exspatiata ruunt per apertos flumina campos, Cumq; satis arbusta simul, pecudésque, virósque, Tectaq;, cumq; suis rapiunt penetralia sacris. Si qua domus mansit, potuitque resistere tanto Indeiecta malo: culmen tamen altior huius Vnda tegit, presséque latent sub gurgite turres. Iámque Mare, & Tellus nullum discrimen habebat: Omnia Pontus erant, deerant quoque littora Ponto. Occupat hic collem: cymba sedet alter adunca Et ducit remos illic, vbi nuper arárat: Ille super segetes, aut mersa culmina villæ Nauigat: hic summa piscem deprendit in vlmo: Et modo qua graciles gramen carpsére capella, Nunc ibi deformes ponunt sua corpora Phoca: Nat Lupus inter oues, sulnos vehit vnda Leones, Vnda vehit Tigris.
units.tr: They rush out, spreading across the open fields in flood, and sweep away together the crops, the trees, the flocks and the men, and the houses with their sacred shrines. If any house remained standing and could resist so great an evil, yet the water covers its highest roof, and the towers lie hidden under the deep flood. And now sea and land had no distinction: all was sea, and the sea had no shores. One man takes a hill; another sits in a curved boat and rows where lately he ploughed; another sails over the standing crops or over the submerged roof of a farmhouse; another catches a fish in the top of an elm. Where lately the nimble goats cropped the grass, now the ugly seals lay down their bodies; the wolf swims among the sheep; the waves carry lions; the waves carry tigers.

units.la: Obrnerat tumulos immensa licentia Ponti, Pulsabántque noui montana cacumina fluctus.]
units.tr: The unbridled license of the sea had covered the hills, and the new waves beat against the mountain peaks.

units.la: Hac Ouidius, quæ graphicè Diluuium illud Noeacum depingunt ex tradita vetustaq; memoria. Illud enim tunc euenit, quod Proba Falconia ex Virgilio collegit.
units.tr: These are the lines in which Ovid vividly portrays that Noachic Deluge, drawn from handed-down and ancient memory. For that is what then happened, which Proba Falconia gathered from Virgil.

units.la: [Tunc Pater omnipotens graviter commotus ab alto Aethere se mittit, tellurem & fundit in vndas, DiluDiluuium miscens, cœlúmque in tartara soluit. Sternit agros, sternit fata lata, boúmque labores, Et genus omne neci pecudum dedit, omne ferarum.] Et ne quid omittam ex illis Ethnicis scriptoribus, Plutarchus eius Diluuij quoq; meminit, quod ex Graecorū libris Deucalionem appellat in libro de Defectu oraculorum, & Plinius lib. 5. Nat. Hist. cap. 13. de Ioppe oppido loquens, [Ioppe, ait, Phœnicū antiquior terrarū inundatione, ut ferunt.] Solinus in Polyhist. cap. 37. Deinde Ioppe oppidū, inquit, antiquissimum Orbe toto, ante inundationem terrarum conditum.] Pomp. Mela lib. 1. de Situ Orbis cap. 11: Est Ioppe ante Diluuium (ut ferunt) condita.] Denique populi ipsi Indici nuper ab Hispanis reperti huius diluuij quoque memoriā adhuc inter se conseruant, quemadmodum in lib. de Veritate Christiana scripsit Plessieus, cap. 26. Et haec quidem tot & tanta pristina nostraque veritatis vestigia, testimoniáque certissima inter Ethnicos extant, ne ea fabula quadam esse, vel iucundum animi commentum censeatur.
units.tr: [Then the Father almighty, deeply stirred, sent himself from high heaven, and poured the earth into the waves, mixing the flood, and loosed the sky into the depths of hell. He levelled the fields, levelled the broad fates, the labours of the oxen, and gave every kind of cattle, every kind of wild beast, over to death.] And, to omit nothing from those Gentile writers, Plutarch also mentions this flood, which he calls the flood of Deucalion, in his book on the decline of oracles. Pliny, in book 5 of his Natural History, chapter 13, speaking of the town of Joppa, says: "Joppa, as they say, is older than the inundation of the Phoenician lands." Solinus, in his Polyhistor, chapter 37: "Then the town of Joppa, the most ancient in the whole world, was founded before the flood of the lands." Pomponius Mela, book 1 of On the Situation of the World, chapter 11: "Joppa, as they say, was founded before the Deluge." Finally, the native peoples of the Indies, recently discovered by the Spaniards, still preserve among themselves the memory of this flood, as Plessis wrote in his book On the Truth of Christianity, chapter 26. And so these many great traces and most certain testimonies of our ancient truth exist among the Gentiles, so that this may not be judged some fable or a pleasing invention of the mind.

units.la: CAPVT IIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: Qvæ Politia tum Ciuilis, tum Ecclesiastica fuerit toto illo seculo & tempore, quod habet à Profanatione publica Nominis Dei annos 1421.
units.tr: What the civil and the ecclesiastical polity was throughout that whole age and period, which runs from the public profanation of the Name of God for 1421 years.

units.la: ÆTERNUM, quæ toto eo tempore (quod longissimum fuit, continet enim annos 1421) Politia sive Civilis, sive Ecclesiastica inter homines fuerit, explicandum est. Utraque vero pene fuit eadem, quæ in proximo, superioreque sæculo, nisi quod omnia semper in peius ruebant, creuitque in immensum, præsertim hac ætate, hominum nequitia. Ergo quod ad Civilem Politiam (quæ in his quatuor posita est, Magistratu nempe, forma Reipub. Legibus, & Institutis seu Artibus, quæ tunc exercebantur) attinet, videtur hæc tunc fuisse: Magistratus proprie toto eo tempore nullus erat, etsi quidam in singulis familys ætatis ratione, utpote qui erant maximi natu, præerant: sed qui in Inuitos ius diceret, pluribus & diuersis familys summa autoritate imperaret, qui ius publicæ coercitionis haberet, qui facinora publicè puniret, vlla in Orbis regione nemo tunc fuit. Ergo tunc quoque scelera manebant impunita, violentia & libido effrenis in Mundo regnabat: nec vlla extant vel scribuntur illo sæculo exempla pœnarum sceleratis hominibus impositarum. Scribit quidem Iosephus eos, quos nominat mo commemorat Moses, alios alys post mortem velut in principatum succesisse, cui fenitia videtur quoque assentiri Augustinus lib. 15. Ciuit. Dei, cap. 20: Verum hic Principatus fuit duntaxat domesticum imperium, non autem regium, aut Pratorium: idque in suas cuiusq; solùm familias, nō in diuersas: in quo ipso Magistratus potestas à paterna differt. Ergo rectè Epiphanius lib. 1. contra Hæreses totum illud sæculum quantumuis lōgum appellat Barbarismum, vbi nempe nullum imperaret, ret, & iurisdictionem coërcitionemq; in inuitos, & alios haberet. Consentit cum Epiphanio Eusebius lib.2.cap. 9. Præparat. Euang. Docet enim totius illius aui mores fuisse insolentes, impios, & dissolutos. Quemadmodum autem nullus Magistratus publicus tunc fuit: sic neque Leges vlla communi eorum, qui tunc viuebant, consensu inter se constituta, vt idem Epiphanius, & recte, tradit. Nam sibi quisque lex erat: & quantum vel conscientiæ exiguus sanè tunc reliquis monebatur: vel saturata & expleta libidine tardabatur, tantum ab iniuria in alios & scelere, tantum à spurcitia, tantum à scortatione, intemperatia, impietate, caeterisq; vitijs abstinebat. Nullo vero legum vllarum & poenarum metu, vel vinculo quisquam constringebatur, quia nulla poena scelerum, & leges in ea vindicantes erant. Ex quo facilè euenit, vt omnis caro, id est, omnes homines, viam suam corrumperet. Sed quemadmodum Magistratus, necq; lex vlla publica, communiq;, sensu recepta, neque poena sancita tunc fuit: sic neque vlla Reipub. forma constitutioq; certa, vtpote quum nulla essent Respubl. id est, nullum hominum coetus communis iuris societate inter se vinctus: vrbes quidem & oppida iam habebant homines, in ijs propter metum vel belluarum, vel à seipsis habitabant: Politia tamen aut regimen certum tunc inter eos ipsos eiusdem vrbis incolas nullum erat: quanquam probabile est illos, qui simul in eodem oppido erant, ijsdemque mœnibus continebatur, fuisse in suos concives minus iniurios, propter viuendi consuetudinem. Propterea tamen neque communem totius vrbis Magistratum, qui scelera puniret, neque communem legem habebat: sed à primo ad vltimum sceleribus omnes & quidem impunè, dediti erant, ac liberè. Id quod etiâ post Dilunium Sodoma & Gabaoni oppidis, & eorum ciuibus accidit, Gen.19.4. Iudic.19.22: quia non erat, sit expresse textus, illo tempore Rex & Magistratus in Israel, Iud.19.1. Nullæ quoque tunc erant, vt nōnulli volunt agrorum diuisiones: sed erat terra communis possessio: nulla dominia: nulla regna: nulla Aristocratia, nulla Democratia: nulle propter fines regnorum tuendos, vel agros priuatorū finiendos & retinendos: nulla, inquâ, tunc lites inter homines erant, nullaque bella propterea. Id quod G. Stuckius ex Macrobio docet lib. 1. Conuiual. quæst. & ante eum Epiphanius grauis autor imprimis. Cedes nihilominus & homicidia tum armis & vi publica pluribus simul collectis: tum etiâ vi priuata à singulis vel etiam pugnis fiebant tunc quoque ab illis, sed aliis de causis nempe propter sortationes, vel iras & iurgia mutua, vel cibos, & omnis generis voluptates explicdas, quibus isti velut ventris serui addicti erant. Denique eas artes exercebant, quæ erant iam reperta: qualis Agricultura, & Pastoritia ad victum quæ rendum: Musica vocalis & organica ad voluptatem: Aeraria & ferraria ad arma, quibus se vindicarent, & vim aliis inferrent, fabricanda, & si quæ alia artes tunc notæ vel inuentæ erant, ab istis eximiè colebantur non ad communem Reipub. vel aliorū vtilitatem: sed ad priuatum cuiusque tantum vsum & commodum. Et hæc quidè de Ciuili, quæ tunc erat, Politia: quæ vel nulla, vel pessima dicenda est. Ecclesiastica verò iam exponenda, quæ in his quinque versatur, Verbo Dei externo, externo Dei cultu seu Sacramentis, Ministro, Loco, & Tempore conuenms ecclesiastici. Ac quidem Verbū Dei iam non tantum per manus ab Adamo traditum erat: vetnumetiā scriptis & literis ab Enoscho mandatū vt docet Iudas epist.verf. 14. Extabat enim iam liber Enoschi, seu Chanochi, qui postea translatus est à Deo. Quamobrem & promissio de Mediatore (qui futurus erat Semen mulieris) ab Adamo posteris denuntiata scripta erat ab Enoscho, ac proinde Misericordia Dei in pios: & Ira Dei quoque in impios literis commendata in Ecclesia, atque inter pios tunc sinabat, atq; annuntiabatur. Articuli quidem fidei Iustificantis (qua Iesum Christum Filium Dei Messiā & Mediatorem agnoscimus) tunc non tam pleni, distincti, atque perspicui erat, quam vel nunc sunt in Symbolo Apostolico, vel postea sub Abrahamo & posteris fuerunt (creuit enim explicatio cognitioq; fidei per momentū) fundamentū tamen ipsum salutis & remissionis peccatorum iam in Ecclesia notum erat, annuntiabatur, retinebatur, credebatur à pys hominibus, nempe Filiū Dei & eum (qui Satanæ & Serpentis caput .i. omnem potentiam Diaboli tollere & euertere posset) futurū Hominem ex solius mulieris femine pro nobis, & venturum in nostra cum Deo reconciliationem: cuius beneficij iam fructum ipsi pÿ sentiebant, & illius sacramenta, signa, ac sacrificia in viiis mis .i. umbras habebant. Ergo externus Dei cultus idem tunc vigebat in Ecclesia qui in superiore proximoque seculo, nempe Sacrificia victimarum, & ex ijs Sacra conuiuia: Discrimen mundorum & immundorum animalium tum ad immolādum, tum ad victum à Deo ipso institutum: Congressus singularum familiarum ad Dd ad Altare suum, ubi in memoriâ futuri Messiæ oblationes & victimæ (prout præceperat Deus Adamo, & Abeli) fiebant: Concionesde Dei Misericordia in suos, & Iustitia in peccatores annuntiabantur: Precationes publicæ concipiebantur, & Deus unus adorabatur: Mundi prima creatio, & eiusdem futura redemptio prædicabatur: Adventus Dei in extremum iudicium, Iudæ epist. verf. 14: & Resurrectio carnis, Heb. 6. Omnium Prophetia etiam in Ecclesia (velut in Chanocho, Lemecho pio, Noacho, & aliis quibusdam) tunc vigebat, ut ex ipsorum prædictionibus apparet. Denique Excommunicatione, eaque gravissima, quæ erat Maranatha, vtebatur Ecclesia contra homines Deo rebelles, Iud. epist. 14, & 1.Cor.16. Verùm Ministerisliius verbi, & Ecclesiæ publicus ecquis tunc esset, quaeritur. Respondeo vero, Eum fuisse, qui tunc in vnaquaque pia familia erat natu maximus ex eadem familia. Ergo Primogeniti munus Sacerdotum & Concionatorum verbi Dei in suis quisque familiis (patribus mortuis) obibant. Itaque Deus pro illis postea Levitas in Lege sua substituit. Quos autem pios recenset Moses ex familia Sethi, qui maioris tunc pietatis & probitatis laude inter hominesclarnerunt, atque illustriores fuerunt: non quòd tunc vi foli in Mundo pii fuerint, aut Sacerdotes, aut Ministri verbi Dei. Licet Iosephus lib. 1. cap. 5. Antiquitatum, vt dixi, putet eos alios aliis continua serie succedisse in administratione rerum Politicarum in familia: item in Prophetia, & cura regenda confernandæque Ecclesiæ: quod verò esse quantus ego concesserim, nego tamen eos solos tunc vixisse pios: verùm præcipuos fuisse
units.tr: What the polity among men was during that whole time, the longest of all since it covers 1421 years, whether civil or ecclesiastical, must now be explained. Both were almost the same as in the preceding and earlier age, except that everything kept sliding for the worse, and human wickedness grew without measure, especially in this period. As for civil polity, which consists in these four things (the magistracy, the form of the commonwealth, the laws, and the institutions or arts then practised), it seems that during this time there was no magistracy at all in the proper sense. Some men presided over individual families by reason of their age, as the eldest of each household, but there was no one in any region of the world who could pronounce judgment on unwilling persons, who held supreme authority over several and different families, who had the right of public restraint, and who punished crimes publicly. So in that age crimes went unpunished, violence and unbridled lust reigned in the world, and no examples of punishments imposed on wicked men survive or are recorded from that century. Josephus indeed writes that those whom Moses mentions succeeded one another after death, as if into a principate, and Augustine, in book 15 of The City of God, chapter 20, seems to agree. But this principate was only a domestic rule, not a royal or praetorian one, and it extended only over each man's own family, not over several. In this the power of the magistrate differs from paternal power. So Epiphanius, in book 1 of Against Heresies, rightly calls that whole long century a state of barbarism, in which no one ruled and held jurisdiction and power of restraint over unwilling and other persons. Eusebius agrees with Epiphanius in book 2, chapter 9, of the Preparation for the Gospel, for he teaches that the morals of that whole age were insolent, impious and dissolute. Just as there was no public magistrate then, so there were no laws agreed upon by the common consent of those who lived then, as Epiphanius also rightly reports. Each man was a law to himself, and each restrained himself only as far as his conscience, which was then slight indeed, urged him, or as far as his lust, once sated and satisfied, allowed. So he kept from injury to others and from crime, from filth, from fornication, intemperance, impiety and the other vices only to that extent. No one was bound by any fear of laws or penalties, because there were no punishments for crimes and no laws to avenge them. From this it easily came about that all flesh, that is, all men, corrupted their way. But just as there was no magistrate, no public law received by common consent, and no sanctioned penalty, so there was no fixed form or constitution of a commonwealth, since there were no commonwealths, that is, no assemblies of men bound together by the partnership of a common law. Men already had cities and towns, and in them they lived, partly out of fear of wild beasts and partly out of fear of one another. Yet there was no fixed polity or government among the very inhabitants of the same city. It is probable, however, that those who lived together in one town and were enclosed by the same walls were less unjust to their fellow citizens, on account of their habit of living together. Even so, they had no common magistrate of the whole city to punish crimes, and no common law. From first to last all of them were given over to crimes, and indeed with impunity and without restraint. This also happened after the Flood in the towns of Sodom and Gibeah and to their citizens (Gen. 19:4; Judg. 19:22), because at that time there was no king or magistrate in Israel, as the text expressly says (Judg. 19:1). Nor were there then, as some suppose, any divisions of fields, but the land was held in common. There were no lordships, no kingdoms, no aristocracy, no democracy; there were no wars over defending the borders of kingdoms or over marking and keeping the fields of private persons. Therefore, I say, there were no lawsuits among men at that time, and consequently no wars. G. Stuckius teaches this from Macrobius, in book 1 of the Saturnalia, and before him the weighty author Epiphanius above all. Nevertheless, slaughters and murders were committed then, both by armed force and public violence, with many gathered together, and also by private violence from single men, even by fists. These too were committed for other reasons: because of quarrels, or mutual anger and brawling, or to satisfy their food and every kind of pleasure, to which those men were given over like slaves of the belly. Finally, they practised those arts which had already been discovered: agriculture and herding to get food, vocal and instrumental music for pleasure, mining and smithing to make weapons with which they might avenge themselves and inflict violence on others, and whatever other arts were then known or invented. These men cultivated these arts with great zeal, not for the common benefit of the commonwealth or of others, but only for the private use and advantage of each one. So much for the civil polity of that time, which should be called either non-existent or the worst. Now the ecclesiastical polity must be set out, which consists in these five things: the external Word of God, the external worship of God or the sacraments, the minister, the place, and the fitting time of the church assembly. Indeed the Word of God was no longer handed down only by word of mouth from Adam, but had also been committed to writing and letters by Enoch, as Jude teaches in verse 14 of his epistle. For the book of Enoch, or Hanoch, which was afterwards taken up by God, was already in existence. Therefore the promise about the Mediator (who was to come as the Seed of the woman), announced to posterity by Adam, was also written down by Enoch. Accordingly, the mercy of God toward the godly and the wrath of God against the ungodly were commended in writing in the Church, and were then taught and proclaimed among the godly. The articles of justifying faith (by which we acknowledge Jesus Christ as the Son of God, the Messiah and the Mediator) were not then as full, distinct and clear as they are now in the Apostles' Creed, or as they were later under Abraham and his posterity, for the explanation and knowledge of faith grew little by little. Yet the very foundation of salvation and the forgiveness of sins was already known in the Church, was proclaimed, retained, and believed by the godly. This foundation was that the Son of God, who would be able to remove and overthrow the power of the devil (the head of Satan and of the Serpent), would become man from the seed of a woman alone, for us, and would come to effect our reconciliation with God. The godly already felt the fruit of this benefit, and had its sacraments, signs and sacrifices in their types, that is, in their shadows. Therefore the external worship of God then flourished in the Church just as it had in the preceding and neighbouring age: sacrifices of victims and sacred feasts made from them; the distinction between clean and unclean animals, both for sacrifice and for food, instituted by God himself; the gathering of each individual family at its own altar, where offerings and victims were made in memory of the Messiah to come, as God had commanded Adam and Abel; sermons on the mercy of God toward his own people and his justice toward sinners; public prayers offered up, and the one God adored; the first creation of the world and its future redemption were proclaimed; the coming of God to the last judgment (Jude, verse 14) and the resurrection of the flesh (Heb. 6) were preached. The gift of prophecy also flourished in the Church at that time, as in Enoch, the godly Lamech, Noah and certain others, as is clear from their predictions. Finally, the Church used excommunication, and that the most severe kind, which was called Maranatha, against men who rebelled against God (Jude, verse 14; 1 Cor. 16). But the question is raised as to who was then the public minister of the Word and of the Church. I answer that it was the eldest man in each godly family, who was then the head of that family.
