Therefore the firstborn of each family, after the fathers had died, performed the office of priest and preacher of the Word of God among his own household. Later God substituted the Levites for them in his law. Those godly men whom Moses lists from the family of Seth, who were then renowned for their great praise of piety and uprightness and were more illustrious among men, were not, I mean, the only godly men in the world at that time, nor the only priests or ministers of the Word of God. Although Josephus, in book 1, chapter 5, of the Antiquities, as I have said, thinks that they succeeded one another in an unbroken series in the administration of political affairs in the family, and likewise in prophecy and in the care of governing and preserving the Church, I grant as much as I have conceded, but I deny that they alone were godly in that age. Rather, I admit that they were the chief ones, and as it were the pillars, among the other godly men, and more sincere, until all flesh had corrupted its way.

units.la: ɣ Mark in left margin, not further transcribed. fuisse tantum, & tanquam inter caeteros pios columnas, ac sinceriores fateor, vsquequo omnis caro corrupisset viam suam. Caeterum vt putat Epiphanius, nulla tunc haereses fuere, sed manifestus in iis (qui py non erant) contemptus Dei, ac immanis publicaque profanitas elucebat. Idololatria vero vitrum tunc quoque coeperit, quaeritur. Fuisse autem, aut coepisse iam eo seculo volunt Patres, velut Iosephus, Philo, Tertullianus in libro de Idololatria: negat tamen vnus Epiphanius. Erectla tamen fuisse iam tunc Idola non existimo, etsi Deus immane sperneretur. Locus autem, in quo fiebat conuentus Ecclesiasticus in singulis familiis erat is, in quo Altare sibi tota familia exstruxerat. Sic enim censeo singulas familias (vbi vna ab alia se seiunxerat & separauerat) habuisse Altare suum peculiare, & locum in quem omnes ex hac vna familia conuenirent, & simul ad sacrificia preces, & audiendum Dei verbum solemniter congregarentur. Tempus denique istius solemnis coetus agendi in singulis familiis fuit Sabbatum seu diem septimam, in qua Deum post creationem Mundi cessasse ac quieuisse sciebant pij omnes: idque ab Adamo ipso per manus acceptum tenebant. Atque haec fuit totius illius aetatis seu seculi, nempe 1421 annis tum Civilis, tum Ecclesiastica Politia.
units.tr: [γ mark in left margin, not further transcribed.] I grant that they were only the pillars among the rest of the pious, and more sincere, until all flesh had corrupted its way. However, as Epiphanius thinks, there were no heresies then, but open contempt for God among those who were not pious, and a huge and public profanity stood out. Whether idolatry also began at that time is a question. The Fathers, such as Josephus, Philo and Tertullian in his book on idolatry, hold that it existed or began already in that age; Epiphanius alone denies it. I do not think idols had yet been set up at that time, although God was hugely despised. The place where the ecclesiastical assembly was held in each family was the one where the whole family had built its own altar. For I think that each family (where one had separated and set itself apart from another) had its own altar, and a place to which all from that one family came together, and where they gathered solemnly for sacrifices, prayers and hearing the word of God at the same time. Finally, the time for holding this solemn assembly in each family was the Sabbath, or seventh day, on which all the pious knew that God had rested and ceased after the creation of the world; and they held this from Adam himself, received by hand. And this was the whole state, both civil and ecclesiastical, of that age or period, namely 1421 years.

units.la: LIBER SEV SECTIO QVARTA PRIMAE MVN- DI AETATIS, QVAE CONTINET EA, qua in Anno Diluuij contigerunt, id est, ab Ingressu Noachi in Arcam, iussu Dei, vsque ad eiusdem ex eadem Arca exitum. Habet autem annum vnum, siue vnius anni res gestas, & spatium.
units.tr: THE FIRST BOOK OR FOURTH SECTION OF THE FIRST AGE OF THE WORLD, WHICH CONTAINS THE EVENTS OF THE YEAR OF THE FLOOD, THAT IS, FROM NOAH'S ENTRY INTO THE ARK, AT GOD'S COMMAND, UNTIL HIS EXIT FROM THAT SAME ARK. IT CONTAINS THE DEEDS AND THE SPAN OF ONE YEAR, OR OF ONE YEAR'S WORTH OF EVENTS.

units.la: VAE sequitur historia habet vnius solùm anni, vel paulò admodum plus, res gestas, & tempus: nimirum ab Ingressu Noachi in Arcā, iussu Dei, ad eiusdem exitum ex eadem illa Arca, Dei quoque mandato. Exiit autem Noachus ex Arca, Deo praecipiente, anno à Mundo condito 1657: anno vitae ipsius Noachi 601: Post illius in Arcam ingressum, anno toto revoluto, eóque solari: post publicam nominis Dei Profanationem, annis 1422. Habet autem hac postrema prima Mundi aetatis seculio & pars capita Historiae praecipua quatuor.
units.tr: The history that follows deals with the deeds and the time of only one year, or a little more: namely, from Noah's entry into the Ark, at God's command, to his exit from that same Ark, likewise by God's command. Noah came out of the Ark at God's direction in the year of the world 1657, in the 601st year of his own life. This was after his entry into the Ark, when a full year had run its course, a solar year; and 1422 years after the public profanation of God's name. This last section of the first age of the world contains four principal heads of history.

units.la: I. Incrementum aquarum Diluuij, quan- tum
units.tr: I. The rising of the waters of the Flood: how much

units.la: tum excreuerint, quandiu, & quan- tum temporis in ea inundatione permanserint Aquæ.
units.tr: they rose, how long, and how much time the waters remained in that inundation.

units.la: ERGO post ingressum in Arcam Noachum vnà cū vxore, tribus filys (Iapheto videlicet, Semo, & Chamo) eorúmq; vxoribus, & reliquis animalibus, quæ cum illis in Arca seruari Deus volebat (id quod mense 2. anni 600 vitæ Noachi contigit, die mensis eiusdem 17. quemadmodum diserté annotat Moses Gen. 7. 11) creuerunt in immensum Aquæ tum fontibus abyssi ruptis, tum etiam imbre copiosissimo è cœlo in terrâ decidente per totos quadraginta dies, & noctes continuas, Gen. 7. 12, adeo vt excelsissimos quosquis terræ montes totis 15. cubitis tandem aquæ illæ superarent, Gen. 7. 20, & omnia quæ in superficie terræ erant, quantumuis altè evolarent, aut scanderent, aut reperent (velut aues, bestiæ, & homines) aquæ illæ eadem mergerent, ac extinguerent partim ea suffocantes, partim victum illis eripientes. Durarunt autem aquæ illæ sic altæ diu, ac plusquâ per duos menses. Namquum 150 dies interceßerint inter initium istius immanis aquarum incrementi vsque quò eadem depressæ fuerint, ac ostenderentur & viderentur summa cacumina montium (illi verò 150 dies cõplent quinque menses totos) sic statuo duos menses cū dimidio isti incremento aquarū & earundem furenti altitudini & exundationi esse tribuendos. Quo temporis, & quidem longo spatio Arca per totū terrarum Orbem ferretur, ac iactaretur: deniquè fuerit omnis caro animal. ta deleta, quod aqua eam mergerent: & quod villum omnem, eiusque querendi rationem admeret (exceptis iis, qui erant, uti dixi, in arca) Gen. 7. 21. 22. Ergo itatum temporis, id est, per duos menses summus ille furor, & vis summa ac impetus aquarum duraverit, ut omnia ruerent, prosternerent extinguerent, & deiceret: atque ita Dei iustissima in mundum illum iudicia exerceret, impleretque. Verum postquam sic sanissent aqua, omniaque animantia in terra, & coelo deleuissent, Misericordissimus ille Pater, & Deus recordatus est Noachi & piorum, qui cum eo in Arca erant: & animalium quoque ipsorum, quanuis brutorum (quoniam ea quoque ad mundum instaurandum, servari Deus volebat) eorum, inquam, omnium recordatus est Dominus Deus, & Mundi conditor & Ecclesiae sua propagator ac custos. Ergo sontes abyssi (e quibus ebulliebant aqua illa immanes) repressit & occlusit: imbrem (qui plurimus e coelo ruebat ad eadem aquas semper augendas vel fovendas) sedavit, & continuit: ventum denique immisit, qui aquas illas immensas exsiccaret, donec intra centum illis quinquaginta dies a primo Diluvij die numerandos, prima, summaque montium iuga & cacumina conspicerentur, utpote iam aquae nudata, & aperta hominum oculis, Gen 8 1.2.3. Sic finiti sunt dies illi 150, quibus & creverunt aquae, & sedatae quoque fuerunt, Gen. 7.24, & 8 1. Quod dierum spatium efficit quinque menses, qui additi secundo menti anni 600 vitae Noachi, quo capit Diluuiun efficiunt eiusdem anni menses septem. Ergo septimo menee anni 600 vitae Noachi, eiusdem mensis die 17. vertices montium apparuerunt: imo ipsamet
units.tr: Therefore, after Noah had entered the Ark with his wife, his three sons (Japheth, Shem and Ham), their wives, and the other animals which God wished to be kept with them in the Ark (which happened in the second month of Noah's 600th year, on the 17th day of that month, as Moses expressly notes, Gen. 7.11), the waters increased immensely, both because the fountains of the deep were broken open and because very heavy rain fell from heaven upon the earth for forty days and forty continuous nights, Gen. 7.12. So the waters rose fifteen cubits above even the highest mountains of the earth, Gen. 7.20, and drowned everything that was on the surface of the earth, however high it flew, climbed or sought refuge (birds, beasts and men alike). Those waters submerged and extinguished them, partly suffocating them and partly taking away their food. The waters stayed so high for a long time, more than two months. For although 150 days passed between the beginning of this vast rise of the waters and the time when they subsided and the highest peaks of the mountains were uncovered and seen (and those 150 days make up five full months), I judge that two and a half months should be assigned to this rising of the waters and their raging height and overflow. During that time, and indeed for a long span, the Ark was carried and tossed about over the whole orb of the lands, until every creature of flesh was finally blotted out, since the waters drowned them, and every living thing and every means of seeking it was destroyed (except those who were, as I said, in the Ark), Gen. 7.21, 22. So for that space of time, that is, for two months, that supreme fury and greatest force and onrush of the waters lasted, so that everything was overthrown, laid low, extinguished and cast down; and thus God exercised and fulfilled his most just judgments upon that world. But after the waters had raged in this way and had destroyed all living things on earth and in heaven, that most merciful Father and God remembered Noah and the pious who were with him in the Ark, and the animals too, though brute beasts, since God wished them also to be preserved for restoring the world. The Lord God, the Creator of the world and the propagator and guardian of his Church, remembered all of them, I say. Therefore he restrained and shut the fountains of the deep from which those monstrous waters welled up; he quieted and checked the rain which poured from heaven in such quantity to keep those waters ever increasing or fed; and finally he sent a wind to dry up those immense waters, until within 150 days, counted from the first day of the Flood, the first and highest ridges and peaks of the mountains could be seen, now bared of water and open to human eyes, Gen. 8.1, 2, 3. So those 150 days, in which the waters both rose and were calmed, came to an end, Gen. 7.24 and 8.1. That span of days makes five months, which added to the second month of Noah's 600th year, when the Flood began, makes seven months of that year. So in the seventh month of Noah's 600th year, on the 17th day of that month, the peaks of the mountains appeared; indeed the Ark itself

units.la: Arca in vno quodam ex Armenys montibus, eoque altissimo & excelsissimo constitit, quum amplius non ferretur, aut eleuaretur ab aquis, illis vtpote ta infra iuga montium subsidentibus, & à Deo depressis, Gen.8.4. Atque hæc est mea de incremento aquarum, & earum exundatione, eiusque duratione: denique de earundem decremento sententia.
units.tr: came to rest on one of the Armenian mountains, and that the highest and loftiest, when it was no longer carried or lifted up by the waters, since those had subsided far below the mountain ranges and were depressed by God, Gen. 8.4. This is my opinion on the increase of the waters, their overflow and duration, and finally on their decrease.

units.la: II. Experimentum cessantis Diluuij, à Noacho factum.
units.tr: II. The experiment made by Noah of the receding and ceasing Flood.

units.la: Caeterum decrescentis cessantisque Diluuij habuit Noachus, etiam antequam vel exiret ipse, vel aues ex arca emitteret, multa testimonia. Ac quidem antequam Coruum emitteret, hac: Quod imber è cœlo decidere desiisset: Quod ventus aquas exsiccans flaret, isque & sentiretur, & audiretur, atque aquarum constrictio, crispatio, compactioque fieri cerneretur: Quod Arca ipsa ita non iactaretur huc & illuc fluctibus impetuque aquarum, vt antea: sed leniter primum in aquis ferretur, deinde in vno ex montibus Ararati constitisset: Denique quod summa montium cacumina consspici iam poterant vndiq; nudata, & exsiccata, Genes.8.1.2: & deinceps. Quæ omnia ante decimum mensem exactum anni 600 vitæ Noachi finitum contigerunt. Septimo enim illius anni mense cōstitit Arca in illo monte Armeniæ: decimi vero mensis eiusdem anni primo die conspecti sunt vertices montium, Gen.8.4.5. Postquam autem conspecti essent ex Arca illi vertices montium in terra, expectauit adhuc Noachus dies quadraginta, id est, à primo die mensis decimi vsque ad vndecimum diem mensis vn-decimi eodem illo 601 vitæ suæ anno patienter adhuc sustinuit sese Noachus in arca, licet ex ea iam cerneret suga montiū aperta, & aquis detecta probabiliter. prudenter, & vere cogiens non idcirco in inferioribus terra partibus, velut in conuallibus & locis planis exsiccatas esse aquas diluuij quod iam vertices montium ÿs destituerentur, ac conspicerentur nudati. Ergo post illos dies 40. .i. die vndecimo mensis vndecimi, Noachus emisit Coruum autem ex Arca, aperta illius fenestra, vt experiretur, Vtrum in locis terra imis subsedissent, ac exaruissent quoque aquæ. Verum Coruus ad eum redijt supra Arcam, & ex arca in agros iterum reuersus est: idque sæpe continuauit sic ire & redire Coruum, donec aquæ exsiccarentur, Gen. 8.7. Sed quum ex eo Coruus volatu, id est, siue in agros, & reditu ad se seu supra, non autem intra Arcam Noachus non posset satis notare, atque certò perspicere quantum aquæ subsedissent, ac defecissent (est enim Coruus volatus sublimior, deinde etiã Coruus subsidet in altiorum arborum ramis) idem Noachus septem post eductum Coruum diebus emittit Columbam. Hæc autem avis nec tam pernix est, quàm Coruus: nec tam alta petit. Ergo quū in conuallibus & planis locis nondum defecissent, aut exsiccatæ essent aquæ, & quum adhuc humiliores arbores exæquarent aquas illæ, redyt ad Noachum Columba, quod non inueniret, vbi plantam pedis poneret: Ipse autem eam ad se recepit, Gen.8 8. Septem vero postea diebus eadem Columba à Noacho emissa denuo fuit, quæ in ore folium olivæ (quod ex arbore ipsa defregerat, nõ autem in terra hu-mi iami iacens & positum reperierat, collegerátve) ad Noachum attulit. Hinc vero intellexit Noachum (quum sit Olea humilis arbor) aquas multùm subsedisse, & ipsi adeo superficiei terrā iā esse proximas, Gen. 8. 11. Redyt igitur ad Noachū Columba denuo, quæ fuerat denuo ab eo amissa. Post quod tempus interpositis iterum diebus septem Noachus non per impatientiam, sed Dei beneficium, & iram eius in Mundum placatam exploraturus, tertiò Columbam ex Arca emisit. Hæc autem tertium emissa non rediit amplius ad Noachū seu in Arcam, quòd in terris & locum, & pabulum sibi inueniret Columba, Genes. 8. 12. Atque inde Noachus coniecit placatum esse Deum in Mundum, & ergo genus humanū, ac proinde Diluuium finitū esse, & aquas in terra superficie esse exsiccatas. Nondū tamen egressus est: sed Dei iusum patienter expectauit. Nec enim adhuc erat exsiccata tota terra superficies, nedū vt esset sic firma & solida, vt & ipsum Noachum, aut eius liberos, & grádiora animalia sustinere aut ferre posset, eáque gressu firmo supra terram incedere quirent, vel auderent. Ergo totus adhuc mēsis duodecimus anni vitæ Noachi 600 interpositus fuit, & expectauit Noachus ipse totum illum adhuc mensem, post quem, nempe primo mense anni vitæ eiusdem 601 primo die eius mensis demum Noachus remouit tectum seu operculum arcæ, vt ex tecto vndiquaq; liberè iam circunspiceret, eequis esset terra status & facies. Vidit autem, & ex eo tecto animadvertit omnes aquas Diluuij esse planè iam exsiccatas, & ex tota superficie terra recessisse, Gen. 8. 12. Nondum tamen egressus est, quia nondum erat satis firma & arida terra superficies, vt supra illam infistere vel homines ipsi, vel bruta animantia possent. Isaac subsistit adhuc Noachus cum suis omnibus in Arca, Dei iussum de egrediendo ex monumento fide & patientia per duos pene menses totos expectarunt, Gen. 8. 15.
units.tr: Noah had many signs, even before he himself went out or sent the birds out of the ark, that the Flood was receding and ceasing. Before he sent out the raven, the signs were these: the rain had stopped falling from heaven; a wind was blowing to dry up the waters, and it could both be felt and be heard; the waters were seen to be checked, rippling, and settling; the ark itself no longer tossed here and there by the waves and the force of the waters as before, but was carried gently on the water at first and then came to rest on one of the mountains of Ararat; and finally the highest peaks of the mountains could now be seen on every side, bare and dry (Gen. 8:1, 2, and following). All these things happened before the tenth month of the six-hundredth year of Noah's life was over. For in the seventh month of that year the ark came to rest on that mountain of Armenia, and on the first day of the tenth month of the same year the tops of the mountains were seen (Gen. 8:4, 5). After those mountain tops had been seen from the ark, Noah still waited forty days, that is, from the first day of the tenth month until the eleventh day of the eleventh month of the six hundred and first year of his life. Noah remained patiently in the ark, although he could now see from it the summits of the mountains open and probably uncovered by the waters. He reasoned wisely and truly that the waters of the Flood had not dried up in the lower parts of the earth, such as the valleys and level places, merely because the tops of the mountains were now bare and visible. So after those forty days, on the eleventh day of the eleventh month, Noah sent out a raven, opening a window of the ark, to find out whether the waters had sunk down and dried up in the lower parts of the earth. But the raven came back to him above the ark, and went out again from the ark to the fields; and it kept on doing this often, going out and returning, until the waters dried up (Gen. 8:7). But because Noah could not clearly judge from the raven's flight, whether it went to the fields and returned to him above the ark, not inside it, how far the waters had sunk and withdrawn (for the raven flies rather high, and moreover settles on the branches of taller trees), Noah sent out a dove seven days after the raven. This bird is neither as swift as the raven nor does it seek such heights. Since the waters had not yet withdrawn and dried up in the valleys and level places, and the waters still covered the lower trees, the dove came back to Noah, because it found nowhere to set the sole of its foot; and he took it back to himself (Gen. 8:8, 9). Seven days later Noah sent the same dove out again, and it brought back to him in its beak a leaf of olive, which it had plucked from the tree itself, not gathered from something lying on the ground. From this Noah understood that the waters had greatly subsided, since the olive is a low tree, and that the surface of the earth was now very near (Gen. 8:11). So the dove returned to Noah again, having been lost by him once more. After this, with another seven days intervening, Noah sent the dove out of the ark a third time, wanting to learn not from impatience but from God's favour, and to see whether God's anger against the world had been appeased. This dove, sent out the third time, did not return to Noah or into the ark, because it found both a place and food for itself on the earth (Gen. 8:12). From this Noah guessed that God had been appeased toward the world, and therefore toward the human race, and that consequently the Flood had ended and the waters had dried up on the surface of the earth. Yet he did not go out, but patiently awaited God's command. For the whole surface of the earth was not yet dry, much less firm and solid enough to bear Noah himself, his children, or the larger animals, or to let them walk upon it with a steady step. So the whole of the twelfth month of the six-hundredth year of Noah's life passed, and Noah waited through that entire month. Then, on the first day of the first month of the six hundred and first year of his life, Noah at last removed the covering of the ark, so that he could now look around freely from above on every side and see what the state and appearance of the earth was. He saw, and perceived from that covering, that all the waters of the Flood had now clearly dried up and withdrawn from the whole surface of the earth (Gen. 8:13). Yet he did not go out, because the surface of the earth was not yet firm and dry enough for men or beasts to stand upon it. So Noah still remained with all his household in the ark; by faith and patience they waited nearly two whole months for God's command to come out of the ark (Gen. 8:15).

units.la: III. Noachi ex Arca egressus.
units.tr: III. Noah comes out of the Ark.

units.la: EGO subsistiterat Arca iam inde a 7. mense anni Noachi 600 in vno quodam, vt dixi, ex montibus Ararati, seu Assyriae vel Armeniae superioris, id est, post quinque menses a Diluuio coepto. Iam per dies 57 a die primo primi mensis anni 601 vitae Noachi ad 27 diem secundi mensis eiusdem anni Aquae Diluuij omnes exaruerant in tota superficie terrae, & se receperat mare, fontes, & flumina in suos alveos ordinarios: manebat tamen semper Noahus in Arca conclusus cum animalibus, in quam Dei iussu fuerat ingressus, & cuius ostium idem Deus, imminente diluuio, ipsemet clauserat. Dei enim iussum de egrediendo patienter in ea expectabat. Itaque die 27 secundi mensis anni 601 vitae suae Noachus subtur a Deo egredi ipse & liberi eius vna cum suis vxoribus, cumque omnibus animantibus, quae cum eo in Arca fuerant ingressa Gen 8. 14 15. 16. Sic autem egressi sunt omnes: Primum quidem ipse Noachus, deinde tres eius filij: postea vxor Noachi, post quam exierunt nurus eius: denique animalia bina egressa, nempe mas & foemina, quemadmodum primum fuerant in Arcam ingressa secundum genus suum, Gen. 8. 16. 18. 19. Nec vero perturbatè & confusè Noachus ea eduxit ex arca, sed placidè, commodè, & distinctè, postquam Deus ipse ipse Ὴοacho & illis ostium arca aperuisset finito diluuio, quemadmodum eo incipiente ostium clauserat.
units.tr: The Ark had come to rest from the 7th month of Noah's 600th year on one of the mountains of Ararat, as I said, or of Upper Assyria or Armenia; that is, five months after the Flood began. Now, over the 57 days from the first day of the first month of Noah's 601st year of life to the 27th day of the second month of that same year, the waters of the Flood had all dried up over the whole surface of the earth, and the sea, the springs and the rivers had returned to their ordinary channels. Yet Noah remained always shut in the Ark with the animals, into which he had entered at God's command, and whose door God himself had closed when the Flood was coming on. For he patiently awaited God's command to come out. So on the 27th day of the second month of the 601st year of his life, Noah was ordered by God to come out, he himself and his sons together with their wives, and with all the living creatures that had entered the Ark with him (Gen. 8. 14, 15, 16). They all came out in this order: first Noah himself, then his three sons; afterwards Noah's wife, after whom his daughters-in-law came out; finally the animals came out in pairs, male and female, just as they had first entered the Ark according to their kind (Gen. 8. 16, 18, 19). Noah did not lead them out of the Ark in a disordered and confused way, but calmly, conveniently and in good order, since God himself had opened the door of the Ark to Noah and them when the Flood was finished, just as he had closed it when it began.

units.la: IIII. Noachi ex Arca cum filijs, uxore, nuribus, & animalibus egressi Soteria, id est, Sacrificium, gratiarumque actio Deo reddita pro salute.
units.tr: Chapter IV. Noah's going out of the ark with his sons, wife, daughters-in-law and the animals; the Soteria, that is, the sacrifice and thanksgiving rendered to God for deliverance.

units.la: Egressus vero Noachus ex Arca cum filijs illis suis tribus, uxore tribus nuribus, & Animalibus, sacrificiū fide obtulit Deo. Obtulit vero ex animalibus quidem omnibus quæ fuerunt in Arca, sed puris duntaxat seu mundis nō etiā ex immundis. Obtulit autem illa omnia supra Altare quod in eum vsum ipse cum filijs post e-gressionem suā ex Arca exstruxerat. Gen. 8.20, Heb. 11.7. Fuit igitur ingens numerus victimarū ex omni animantium mundorum (quæ in Arca seruata fuerant) genere cæsarum atque mactatarum, quale sacrificium, támque solemne, & variūm, neque antea, neque postea vnquam fuisse commemoratur in S. Scriptura, quantūuis dies & copiosum fuerit Solomonis in dedicando Templo sacrificium, 1.Reg 8 5: Item Eʒechia regis infolemni illo Paschatis festo a se celebrato, 2.Chron. 30.24. Fuit vero hoc idem Noachi sacrificiū potiūs Eucharisticum, quàm pro peccatis Expiatorium. Gratias enim Deo de Mundo, & se, & liberis, & vxore, & nuribus, & animalibus ex tanta aquarū copia seruatis Noachus, quique cum eo erant omnes, agebant. Quanquàm eosdem pro placanda in posterum Dei ira in mu-
units.tr: Noah, having gone out of the ark with his three sons, his wife, his three daughters-in-law and the animals, offered a sacrifice to God in faith. He offered indeed of all the animals that had been in the ark, but only of the clean, that is, the pure, and not of the unclean. He offered all of them upon the altar which he and his sons had built for that purpose after their coming out of the ark. Gen. 8.20, Heb. 11.7. There was therefore an immense number of victims, of every kind of clean animal preserved in the ark, slain and sacrificed; such a sacrifice, so solemn and so varied, is not recorded in Holy Scripture either before or after, although the sacrifice of Solomon at the dedication of the Temple was great and abundant, 1 Kings 8.5; likewise that of King Hezekiah at the solemn Passover feast he celebrated, 2 Chron. 30.24. This sacrifice of Noah was rather a eucharistic one than an expiatory one for sins. For Noah and all who were with him were giving thanks to God for the world, for themselves, for their sons and wife and daughters-in-law, and for the animals, preserved from such a great abundance of waters. Yet that they offered them also to appease God's anger for the future, in this world, is also true; but the thanksgiving, as I have said, was chiefly the purpose of this sacrifice, and the sacrifice then offered to God was for the preservation of the things that remained.

units.la: dum hunc obtulisse eos quoque verum est: sed precipuè fuit Gratiarum, uti dixi, actio hoc sacrificium, & sutica tunc oblata Deo pro rerum, quæ supererant, conseruatione. Gratum autem fuit Deo sacrificium Noachi propter eius fidem, nō autem propter victimarum multitudinem (nec enim Deus rebus carnalibus per se delectatur, aut illum pinguedinis adusta tetrū odorem suauiter odoratur, Psal. 50. 13, Itaque acceptū ei fuit Gen.8.21. Nec verò hoc solùm: sed etiam amplißimas Noacho, totiq; futuro postea mūdo promissiones Deus addidit: de Mundi statu iterum instaurando: de condonandis hominum peccatis: de generali Diluuio in posterum non futuro: de iure hominum in bruta animantia restituendo: de hominibus tutis aduersus vim & impetum ferarum animantium præstādis: denique de hominibus ipsis inter se tutis futuris: ergo de pœna in homicidas grauissima exerenda, Genef.8.22.23,& 9.1,& deinceps. Quæ quanquam sunt locupletissima Dei in homines placati promissiones, quia tamen ad nouum (qui post diluuium à Deo institutus est) Mundum pertinet, suntque huius rerum status (quo in his terris fruuntur iam homines) fundamentum, ea prætermittemus. Fuit enim nobis propositum hoc tempus & seculū duntaxat explicare, & rerum in eo à Mose conscriptarum vestigia in Ethnicorum libris quærere, quod à Mundo condito ad egressum Noachi ex arca fluxit, ad pios in fide confirmandos, & ad Iudæos homines, qui hanc veritatem negant, refutandos, ac conuincendos. PATRI verò, Filio, & Spiritui sanćto, qui sunt vnus ille verus Deus in æternum, & vltra colendus ac benedicendus, sit laus
units.tr: The sacrifice of Noah was pleasing to God because of his faith, not because of the multitude of victims (for God does not delight in carnal things in themselves, nor does he savour with pleasure the foul odour of burnt fat, Psal. 50.13); and so it was acceptable to him, Gen. 8.21. Nor was this all: God also added most ample promises to Noah and to the whole world that was to come afterwards: concerning the renewal of the state of the world, concerning the forgiveness of men's sins, concerning a general deluge not to come in future, concerning the restoration of man's dominion over the brute animals, concerning men being secured against the violence and attack of wild beasts, and finally concerning men being secure among themselves; and therefore concerning the most severe punishment to be inflicted on murderers, Gen. 8.22, 23, and 9.1 and following. Although these are the most abundant promises of God to men who have been appeased, because they pertain to the new world (which God established after the flood), and are the foundation of the present state of things in which men now enjoy this earth, we shall pass them over. For it was our purpose to explain only this time and age, and to seek out in the books of the Gentiles the traces of the things recorded by Moses in that period, which flowed from the creation of the world to Noah's coming out of the ark, both to confirm the faithful in faith and to refute and convict those Jews who deny this truth. To the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, who are that one true God, to be worshipped and blessed for ever and beyond, be praise

units.la: { } laus, & gloria in secula seculorum. Amen.
units.tr: and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: ¶ Disputata, & agitata quædam in his quatuor superioribus Historiæ capitibus.
units.tr: ¶ Some matters disputed and discussed in the four preceding chapters of this History.

units.la: ABET autem & hæc pars quoque Historiæ suæ quasdam quæstiones obscuras, quas, quantum quidem poterimus, facilè tum explicabuntur, tum illustrabuntur. Ac primùm quidem de Incremento Aquarum.
units.tr: This part of the History also contains some obscure questions, which we shall, as far as we can, explain and clarify without difficulty. First, concerning the increase of the waters.

units.la: Ad I. De Incremento Aquarum.
units.tr: On I. The Increase of the Waters.

units.la: Quaeritur, Quomodo & quadraginta, & centum illi quinquaginta dies, quibus aquæ primùm creuisse, postea verò defecisse & decreuisse dicuntur, sunt numerandi? utrum in illo maiori numero nempe 150 diebus, minor videlicet dies 40 continentur: an seorsim sunt sumendi, & post dies 40 supputandi præterea dies illi 150, Gen. 7.17.24. R. Et ratio temporis, quo duravit diluvium: & verba ipsa Mosis suadent in maiori illo 150. dierum numero dies 40 contineri. Nam totum illud Diluuij & immissi & exsiccati negotium, Dei judicium perstitit dūtaxat annum unum solarem ac plenum, qui constat 365 diebus, Genes.8. At verò si quis 40 illos dies, quibus creverunt aquæ, supra 150 addat, excresceret numerus dierum omnium collectorum, & à Mose postea commemoratorum annum illum Solarem constantem 365 diebus. Quamobrem in 150 diebus illi 40 sunt proculdubio comprehendendi. Id quod & Math. Beroaldus libro 3. Chron. cap. 1, & Iosephus Scaliger lib. 3. de Emend. Temp. cap. vltimo, & lib. 5. cap. de Diluuio viri summi doctissimique probant ac confirmant. Verba vero Mosis idem sibi volunt. Nam recapitulas Moses Gen. 7. 24 totum illud, quod eodem capite de aquis primum excrescentibus, postea Arcam subleuantibus, deinde omnes homines omniaq; animatia in terra superficie extinguentibus, & denique subsistentibus dixerat, & uno tanquam temporis spatio colligens, addit omne illud temporis spatium fuisse ac comprehendisse dies solum 150, quemadmodum idem ipse quoque, Gen. 8. 1. 2. statim explicat. Nam ait Arcam quieuisse (nimirum subsidentibus aquis Diluuij) post exactos praecise 150 dies ab eo, quo primum coeperat Diluuium in terris fieri, & aqua coeperant excrescere tum imbre e coelo cadente, tum fontibus Abyssi erumpentibus, Gen. 8 3: qui dies, quodve spatium fuit, mensis septimus a capite anni 600 vitae Noachi, cuius mensè 2, die 17 coeperat diluuium in terris existere. Ergo in his verbis Mosis Gen. 7. 24 [Praevaluerunt aquae illae super terram 150 dies] inest ἀναχεφαλαίωσις totius superioris historiae, illiq; dies 40 (quibus aquae creuerant) continentur. Atq; hoc ipsum, quamuis obscure & intricate, voluit, censuitque Augustinus lib. Quaest. in Gen. cap. 12. Dies autem illi sine 40, sine 150 sunt a primo die Diluuij immissi sumendi .i. a die 17, mensis 2 anni 1656, & Noachi vitae 600 quemadmodum & Sacra Historia, & Iosephus lib. 1. AntiVirum totis illis 150 diebus Aquæ Diluuij creuerint, quum dicantur toto illo spatio pranulußfe super terrâ, totámque eam cooperuisse. Sic initio creandi Mundi Psal.104.6, Gen.1.2 fecerant eámque texerant aquæ. De hoc ipso quærit Augustinus lib.quæst.in Gen. cap.11: sed suam sententiam perspicuè non exponit. Apparet autem ex Mose Gen.8.1, & deinceps aquas euâ intra illud 150 dierum spatium decreuisse adeo, vt statim post 150 dies capita montium aquis nudata cernerentur, quæ eadem antea ab aquis mersa fuerat, & cooperta, superatáque totis quindecim cubitis. Ergo aquæ Diluuy per 40 tantum dies crescunt, & Arcam sublevant, montium quorumvis altissimorum summa cacumina cubitis 15 superant & excedunt, denique omnia deiciunt, mergunt, suffocant vi, & impetu suo. Manent autem vsque ad 150 diem, à primo die Diluuij sic superiores & terra & montibus: die denique 151 verticos montium apparuerunt Gen.8. Ergo omnino necesse est aquas eas decreuisse intra illud idem 150 dierum spatium: & inferiores, quam prius fuerant, euasisse 15 totis cubitis, atq; tanta mensura fuisse exsiccatas per ventum à Deo immissum, cohibita cœlesti pluuia, & fontibus abyssi clausis. Quod 150 dierum spatium quum 5. mensis compleat, sic eos diuidamus, vt dicamus per 40 dies .i. per mensem totum, nempe primum diluuij, cum sequentis mensis tritente seu tertia parte (quæ decem dies habet) creuisse aquas illas, & ad summum illud fastigium suum (quo superabant montes 15. cubitis) peruenisse. Quod spatiû si a quinque mensibus detraxeris, restant
units.tr: Question: how are the forty days and the hundred and fifty days, during which the waters are said first to have risen and afterwards to have fallen and subsided, to be counted? Are the forty days contained within the larger number of one hundred and fifty days, or are they to be taken separately, so that the hundred and fifty days are reckoned as well as the forty days after them? Gen. 7.17.24. A. The length of time the flood lasted, and the words of Moses themselves, suggest that the forty days are contained within the larger total of one hundred and fifty. For the whole business of the flood, its coming and its drying up, under God's judgment, lasted only one full solar year, which consists of 365 days (Gen. 8). If anyone added those forty days, during which the waters rose, to the hundred and fifty, the total of all the days counted together would exceed that solar year of 365 days which Moses records afterwards. Therefore the forty days are undoubtedly included in the hundred and fifty. Matthaeus Beroaldus (Chronicle, book 3, ch. 1), and Joseph Scaliger (On the Emendation of Time, book 3, last chapter, and book 5, chapter on the Flood), great and very learned men, prove and confirm this. Moreover, the words of Moses mean the same thing. For in Gen. 7.24 Moses sums up everything he had said in that chapter about the waters first rising, then lifting the ark, then destroying all men and all living things on the surface of the earth, and finally subsiding; gathering it into one span of time, he adds that the whole period was only one hundred and fifty days, as he himself at once explains in Gen. 8.1, 2. For he says that the ark rested (namely when the waters of the flood subsided) after exactly one hundred and fifty days from the day on which the flood first began on the earth and the waters began to rise, both from the rain falling from heaven and from the fountains of the deep breaking forth (Gen. 8.3). This day, or span, was the seventh month, on the seventeenth day of the second month of the six hundredth year of Noah's life, when the flood had begun on the earth. Therefore in these words of Moses, Gen. 7.24 [The waters prevailed upon the earth for one hundred and fifty days], there is a recapitulation [ἀνακεφαλαίωσις] of the whole preceding history, and the forty days (during which the waters rose) are included in it. Augustine also, though obscurely and intricately, meant this and held it (Questions on Genesis, ch. 12). Those days, whether forty or one hundred and fifty, are to be counted from the first day of the flood's coming, that is, from the seventeenth day of the second month of the year 1656 and of Noah's life, 600, as both Sacred History and Josephus (Antiquities, book 1) show.

units.la: {Q} Antiquit. & Beroaldus lib. 3. Chron. testantur. menses tres cum diebus 20, qui efficiunt in summa dies 110. Iam vero dies istos 110 sic partiamur, ut ex iis 46 decremento aquarum tribuamus (ut totidem diebus postea decreuerint aquae, per quot antea creuerant) restabunt dies 70 .i. menses duo cum triente quo toto tempo-ris spatio aqua in illa sua altitudine permanere potuerunt, ac Mundum euerterunt, terraque animantia omnia viuentia delerunt. Q. Vtrum Arca per duos illos menses & triente, id est, per 70 dies (quibus sic alte permanserunt aquae, ut montium vertices 15 cubitis excederent) in vno tantum terra seu orbis loco subsiteterit, an per vniuersum terrarum Orbem iactata, & impetu aquarum, procellisque ventorum delata fuerit.
units.tr: {Q} Antiquities, and Beroaldus in book 3 of the Chronicle, bear witness. The months are three, together with twenty days, which make up in sum 110 days. Now let us divide these 110 days so that from them we assign 40 days to the decrease of the waters (so that the waters decreased in as many days as they had risen before), which leaves 70 days, that is, two months and a third, during which the waters could remain at that height, overturn the world, and destroy all the living creatures on earth. Q. Did the ark, during those two months and a third, that is, during the 70 days when the waters stood so high that they exceeded the peaks of the mountains by fifteen cubits, rest in only one place on the earth or on the globe, or was it tossed about over the whole orb of the lands and carried along by the force of the waters and the storms of the winds?

units.la: R. Quum manifeste Moses annotet Gen. 8.4. Arca demum postquam ab aquis ex superficie terra fuerat exaltata, & elevata, quieuisse, quando in vno ex montibus Armeniacis subsistit, & 7. demum mensis anni illius die 17 id contigisse scribat, satis intelligi potest eandem Arcam & antea iactatam, & ventis procellisque delatam in varia terrarum loca, atque agitatam fuisse. Vtrum vero per vniuersum terrarum orbem interea vagata fuerit, non explicat S. Scriptura: neque nos definire posumus.
units.tr: A. Since Moses clearly notes in Gen. 8.4 that the ark finally rested, after it had been lifted and raised up from the surface of the earth by the waters, when it settled on one of the Armenian mountains, and that this happened in the seventh month of that year on the seventeenth day, it can well be understood that the same ark, before that, was thrown about and carried by the winds and storms to various places on the earth and was tossed about. Whether it wandered meanwhile over the whole orb of the lands, Holy Scripture does not explain, and we cannot determine it.

units.la: Q. Quomodo Arca illa tatis, tamq; immanibus ventis pulsa, & fluctibus aquarum, & impetu vndarum tam saeuo totiesque percussa, tamen soluta, quasi sata, disruptaq; tandem non fuerit: sed salua & incolumis, nullo latere, aut aflere, tabulaeve eius amissa, vel etiam fracta permanserit: quum nullum nauigium, quantumuis robustum, benéque compactum, & tandiu, & tot fluctus sustinere queat, neque tot vndarum impetus infractum & saluum ferre possit, eisque obsistere. R. Aliam esse aliorum nauigiorum rationem: aliam verò huius arca verum est. Illa enim ab hominibus gubernantur: haec verò ab ipso Deo, & quidem modo extraordinario, & miraculoso regebatur. Ergo firma & incolumis, infractaque aduersus omnem vim aquarum & procellarum (Deo sic eam tuente) Arca mansit. Quum enim illius ostium Deus ipse clausisset, Gen. 7. 16. hoc (velut manus sua) peculiari sigillo appositio, arca haec tuta aduersus omnes cæli, maris qu iniurias reddita est, ac perstitit. Quamobrem immediatè à Deo seruabatur, ne fluctibus ventisve collideretur. In medijs enim illis aquarum tempestatibus Deus & Arca ipsius, & Noachi, & omnium, quæ in Arca erant, tàquam custos & pater meminerat Gen. 8.1. Q. Utrum montes ante Diluuium fuerint, quum dicantur aquæ eorum capita 15 cubitis superasse, Gen. 7.20: Nonnulli enim existimant Montes demum post diluuium ex aquis defluentibus extitisse, prius autem minimè in toto terrarum orbe fuisse. R. Ex Psal. 104.6, vbi de prima terra creatione disseritur, apparet etiam montes à Deo conditos fuisse, quum primum (i. multis ante diluuiū seculis) terra creata fuit, non autem ex solo aquarum diluuij decursu enatos. Id quod verissimum est. Nec enim aquæ adhuc defluxerant, quum Arca subsitit in Ararati monte, Gen. 8.4: & tamen iam montes, iique maximi erant, vt docet Moses, i. ipsa veritas. Q. Utrum verisimile sit aquas Diluuij potuisse superare summa excelsissimorum montium cacumina totis quindecim cubitis, Gen. 7.20: quum nonnulli montes (velut
units.tr: Q. How was that ark, so large and tossed by such huge winds, struck so fiercely and so many times by the waves of the waters and the force of the billows, not broken up and shattered like a chaff-sheaf, but kept safe and sound, without any side, plank or beam lost or even broken? For no ship, however sturdy and well built, can endure so long and so many waves, nor bear the assaults of so many waves unbroken and unharmed, nor withstand them. A. It is true that the manner of other ships is one thing, and that of this ark another. For those are steered by men, but this one was governed by God himself, and that in an extraordinary and miraculous way. Therefore the ark remained firm, sound and unbroken against every force of the waters and storms, God thus keeping it safe. For when God himself had shut its door (Gen. 7.16), this ark, sealed with his own special seal as with his own hand, was made and remained safe against all the injuries of heaven and sea. Therefore it was preserved immediately by God, lest it be dashed by the waves or winds. For in the midst of those storms of the waters God remembered both the ark itself and Noah and everything that was in the ark, as a guardian and father (Gen. 8.1). Q. Did mountains exist before the flood, since the waters are said to have exceeded their peaks by fifteen cubits (Gen. 7.20)? For some think that mountains only came into being after the flood, from the waters flowing down, and were not at all present in the whole orb of the earth before. A. From Psalm 104.6, where the first creation of the earth is discussed, it appears that mountains too were founded by God when the earth was first created (that is, many centuries before the flood), and were not produced merely by the flowing away of the flood waters. This is most true. For the waters had not yet drained away when the ark rested on Mount Ararat (Gen. 8.4), and yet the mountains already existed, and very great ones, as Moses, that is, the truth itself, teaches. Q. Is it likely that the waters of the flood could have risen above the summits of the very highest mountains by a full fifteen cubits (Gen. 7.20), since some mountains (such as Olympus in Thessaly and Athos in Greece) are found which rise above the winds, the rains, and the whole middle region of the air, as Solinus the Polyhistor relates in chapter 17? A. Augustine often treated this question, as in the Questions on Genesis, ch. 10, and in book 15 of the City of God…

units.la: Olympus in Thessalia, & Athos in Gracia) reperiantur, qui ventos, & pluvias, totámque mediam aëris regionem altitudine superet, quemadmodum Solinus Polyhistor cap. 17. tradit. R. Hanc quaestionem sæpè tractavit Augustinus, velut lib. quaest. in Genes. cap. 10: lib. 15. Civit. Dei, cap. 27: & lib. 20. eiusdem operis, cap. 18, quo in loco sic ait, [Ergo verum est illo tempore perîsse, qui tunc erat, Mundum: nec solum Orbem terrae, verum etiam cœlos, quos utique istos aëreos intelligimus, quorum locum & spatiū tunc aqua crescendo superaverat. Ergo totus, aut penè totus aër iste vetosus (quod cœlum, vel potius cœlos vocat Petrus, sed istos utique imos, non illos supremos, ubi Sol, & Luna, & sydera constituta sunt) conversus fuerat in humidam qualitatem, atque hoc modo cum terra perierat, cuius terra utique prior facies fuerat deleta Diluvio.] Et quod affertur de Olympi summa altitudine, sic idem Augustinus retorquet, [Si enim, inquit, Olympus mons (qui est terra) potuit innuadere spatium tranquilli illius aëris, ubi dicitur nec nubes videri, nec vetos sentiri, cur non & aqua crescendo eò penetrare in Diluvio potuit? Cur igitur usque ad illa cœli spatia terris exaltari licuisse, & aquis exaltari non licuisse contendunt, quum isti mensores & penfores elementorum aquas terris perhibeant superiores, atque leviores?] Ex quibus colligitur aquas Diluvij vertices superasse montium Olympi, Athos, & caeterorum omnium, quum inga Armeniorum montium, qui sunt omnium altissimi, eadem aqua excesserint. Cuius rei testimonium affert Tertullianus in lib. de Pallio, quod in summis montibus etiamnum suo tempore pore, velut & hodie, concha & buccina maris peregrinentur & reperiantur nimirum aduentitia, & extra suam elementum. Quod argumentu & Isidorus in Etymol. lib. 13. cap. 22: & Solinus cap. 15. proferunt quoque. Ex quo falsa apparet Thalmudistarum sententia, qui scribunt Aquas diluuij non peruenisse vsque ad cacumen montis Sion. Id enim falsum est. Namillud saltem 15 cubitis superarunt, imo pluribus. Q. Utrum annus, & menses, quibus vtitur ante Diluuium Moses, quos in eodem describendo & supputando commemorat, fuerint Solares, an Lunares. Sunt autem menses Solares singuli inter se æquales, & tricenum dierum. Annus Solaris est 365. dierum. Menses vero Lunares sunt inter se inæquales, & partim caui, partim pleni. Pleni menses habent dies 30. Caui menses sunt duntaxat 29 dierum. Ergo Lunaris annus habet tantum dies 354. Atque ita diuersa omnino erit Anni, & mensium Diluuij supputandi ratio, magni, interest ad illius loci intelligentiam quæ sententia probetur, vel vera fit. Math. Beroaldus scribit Mosem vti quidem in supputando Diluuio anno Solari: sed de Mensibus aliter statuit, & Lunares esse definit, quibus idem Moses annum illum numeret: Ergo vult idem vndecim dies ex menses secundo anni vitæ Noachi 601, velut epactas, additas à Mose fuisse. Sic ille lib. 3. Chron. cap. 1, vt annus ille Solaris, quem refert Moses, completus effet, alioqui plenus ex illis 12 mensibus, quos enumerat Moses, non futurus, nisi epactæ ac vndecim illi dies adiungerentur. Hac sentit ille, quemadmodum & I yranus, id est, Mosem vti mensibus Lunaribus. Sic enim Beroaldus, [Caterum, ait, 12 menstrua spatia diebus cô- stant 354: quæ alternis, singuli menses 30:alternis 29, dies cõpleant. Itaque à 17 die mensis 2, anni 600 vitæ Noachi ad 17 diem mensis 2. insequétis anni, qui fuit vitæ Noæ 601, annū Lunarem expletū habemus constantem 12 Lunaribus mensibus, quibus desunt dies undecim ad Solarem annum conficiendum, qui diebus cōficitur 365.] At verò hac sententiam minimè probat Iosephus Scaliger grauis autor imprimis, ac eruditus, qui cõtendit & Annum, & Menses esse Solares, quibus non modò Moses, & qui eũ ætate præcesserunt, vsi sunt: sed etiam post Mosem Israelitæ temporibus, & Iosua, & Iudicum, & Regum quoque ipsorum. Sic igitur ille totidem verbis lib. 3. de Emend. Temp. cap. vlt. De anno prisco rum Hebræorum scribit, [Ne quid tergiuersemur amplius, Annus (prisco rum nempe) Hebræorum non fuit Lunaris. Fuit ergo Chaldaicus, ant (si manus) Ægyptiacus annus duodecim æqualibus mensibus cum quinque appendicibus dierum. Quis melius hoc nos docuerit, quam Moses ipse? Is igitur scribit Diluuiu cœpisse 17. mensis secundi: 150 dies aquas inualuisse, & diem proximum à 150, hoc est, 151 fuisse 17. mensis septimi. 46 dies ante diluuium fluxerant. Nam 46. cœpit diluuium, nempe 17. mensis secundi. Iunge 150 cum 46, fiunt manifestè dies 197: qui per 30 diuisi relinquunt menses exactos sex, & 17 diem septimi, in quo Arcam quieuisse scribit Moses. Ergo nemo refragari posssit, quum fateatur menses Hebræorum veterum tricenis diebus descriptos fuisse. Nullum locum hic habet Luna.] Hæc ille, quæ etiam eiusdem operis lib. 5. cap. De Diluuio repetit. Et certè quidem nos in Iosephi Scaligeri viri nobis charissimi sententiâ pedibus imus, & annum, & menses (quos in vsu habuit Moses) solares, non lunares fuisse perspicimus, quanquam non diffiteor Beroaldi sententiam in summa anni supputanda locum habere posse, & rationem eam numerandi non improbabilem, absurdámve videri. Q. Quo mense anni Romani (quo nos iam vtimur) haec singula contigerint, quae Moses commemorat de aquis crescentibus, decrescentibus, de Arca in monte Armeniae quiescente, de emisso Coruo, & Columba, & exitu Noachi. R. Vt huic quaestioni facillimè, verissimeq; respondeatur, imprimis hæc duo constare oportet: Primum, Ecquis annus, Ciuilis-ne, an Sacer sit hoc toto in libro Genesis sumendus. Alterum, Ecquis anni Romani mensis Hebrai huius anni primo mensi respondeat. Et quidè à nobis antea demonstratum est, Annum eum, quo & in mundi, & Patriarcharum aetate supputanda Moses vitiur, esse Ciuilem Hebræorum annum, non autem Sacrum. Sacer verò à mense Nisan incipit, quod omnes sciunt. Ciuilis autem à mense Tisri. Quare hoc velut à nobis abundè probatum, hoc loco sumatur velut concessum. Iam verò mensis Tisri, qui est Primus mensis Anni prisci, & Ciuilis Hebrai, vt vult Beroaldus, mensi ei respondet, qui in anno Romano September vocatur: Vt verò mauult Scaliger, mensi Octobri. Nos verò Beroaldum sequamur. Ergo Tisri mensis primus anni Ciuilis Hebrai, qui fuit etiam caput anni vitae Noachi 600, esto noster mensis September.
units.tr: Olympus in Thessaly and Athos in Greece are found to rise higher than the winds and rains and the whole middle region of the air, as Solinus the Polyhistor relates in chapter 17. R. Augustine often treated this question, as in the book of Questions on Genesis, chapter 10; in book 15 of The City of God, chapter 27; and in book 20 of the same work, chapter 18, where he says: [Therefore it is true that the world which then existed perished at that time, not only the orb of the earth but also the heavens, which we certainly understand to be those airy heavens, whose place and extent the water had then surpassed by rising. Therefore the whole, or nearly the whole, of that tempestuous air (which Peter calls heaven, or rather heavens, but certainly the lower ones, not those highest ones where the Sun, Moon and stars are set) was turned into a watery condition, and in this way perished along with the earth, whose former face had certainly been destroyed by the Flood.] And as for the claim about the great height of Olympus, Augustine turns it back in this way: [For if, he says, Mount Olympus (which is earth) was able to penetrate the space of that calm air, where it is said that neither clouds are seen nor winds felt, why could water, by rising, not also have penetrated there in the Flood? Why, then, do they contend that it was permitted for earth to be raised up to those spaces of the heavens, but not permitted for water to be raised up, since these surveyors and weighers of the elements declare that water is higher than and lighter than earth?] From these things it is gathered that the waters of the Flood surpassed the peaks of Olympus, Athos and all the others, since the same water rose above the peaks of the Armenian mountains, which are the highest of all. Tertullian, in his book On the Cloak, offers evidence for this, that on the highest mountains even in his own time, as also today, shells and trumpet-shells of the sea are found wandering about, plainly brought there from elsewhere and outside their own element. Isidore in his Etymologies book 13, chapter 22, and Solinus, chapter 15, also put forward this argument. From this the opinion of the Talmudists is shown to be false, who write that the waters of the Flood did not reach as far as the summit of Mount Zion. For that is false. Indeed they surpassed that height by at least fifteen cubits, and even by more. Q. Whether the year and the months which Moses uses before the Flood, which he mentions in describing and reckoning it, were solar or lunar. Now the solar months are each equal to one another and of thirty days, and the solar year has 365 days. But lunar months are unequal to one another, some hollow and some full: full months have 30 days, hollow months only 29 days. So the lunar year has only 354 days. And thus the method of reckoning the years and months of the Flood will be entirely different, and it matters greatly for understanding that passage which view is approved or is true. Matthaeus Beroaldus writes that Moses did indeed use the solar year in reckoning the Flood, but he decided otherwise about the months, and holds that they were lunar, by which same Moses counts that year. Therefore he thinks that eleven days were added by Moses to the second month of Noah's 601st year of life, like epacts. So he says in book 3 of his Chronicle, chapter 1: that solar year which Moses reports would not have been complete, otherwise, if it were full of those twelve months which Moses lists, unless the epacts and those eleven days were added. He holds this view, as does Iyranus, that is, that Moses used lunar months. For Beroaldus says: [Moreover, he says, twelve months' spans amount to 354 days, in which alternately single months have 30 and alternately 29 days. So from the 17th day of the 2nd month of the 600th year of Noah's life to the 17th day of the 2nd month of the following year, which was Noah's 601st year, we have a completed lunar year made up of twelve lunar months, which lack eleven days for completing the solar year, which is made up of 365 days.] But Joseph Scaliger, a weighty and learned author above all, by no means approves this opinion. He contends that both the year and the months are solar, and these were used not only by Moses and those who preceded him in time, but also by the Israelites after Moses, and by Joshua, and by the Judges and the Kings themselves. So he writes in the same words in book 3 of On the Emendation of Time, last chapter: [Lest we dodge the issue any further: the year of the ancient Hebrews was not lunar. It was therefore a Chaldean, or (if you prefer) Egyptian, year of twelve equal months with five added days. Who could teach us this better than Moses himself? He therefore writes that the Flood began on the 17th day of the second month, that the waters prevailed for 150 days, and that the day following the 150th, that is the 151st, was the 17th day of the seventh month. 46 days had passed before the Flood, for the Flood began on the 17th day of the second month, as we said. Add 150 to 46, and clearly you get 197 days, which divided by 30 leave six full months and the 17th day of the seventh month, on which Moses writes that the Ark rested. Therefore no one can gainsay this, since he admits that the months of the ancient Hebrews were described by thirty days each. The moon has no place here.] So he says, and he repeats this in book 5 of the same work, the chapter on the Flood. And indeed we, following the opinion of Joseph Scaliger, a man very dear to us, see that both the year and the months (which Moses used) were solar, not lunar, although I do not deny that Beroaldus's opinion may have a place in the total reckoning of the year, and that his method of counting does not seem improbable or absurd. Q. In what month of our Roman year (which we now use) each of these events which Moses records happened: the waters rising and falling, the Ark resting on a mountain of Armenia, the raven and dove being sent out, and the going out of Noah. R. To answer this question most easily and most truly, two points must first be established: first, whether the year to be taken in this whole book of Genesis is the civil or the sacred year; second, to which month of our Roman year the first month of this Hebrew year corresponds. Indeed we have demonstrated earlier that the year which Moses uses in reckoning the age of the world and of the Patriarchs is the civil year of the Hebrews, not the sacred one. The sacred year begins in the month of Nisan, as everyone knows; the civil year begins in the month of Tishri. Therefore, since this has been sufficiently proved by us, let it be taken here as granted. Now the month of Tishri, which is the first month of the ancient and civil Hebrew year, as Beroaldus holds, corresponds to the month which in the Roman year is called September; but as Scaliger prefers, to October. Let us follow Beroaldus. Therefore the month of Tishri, the first month of the civil Hebrew year, which was also the beginning of the 600th year of Noah's life, let it be our September.

units.la: 1. Tisri, September, primus mensis anni Noachi 600
units.tr: 1. Tishri, September, the first month of Noah's 600th year

units.la: II. Marhesvan, Octob er, mensis secundus, cuius die 17 cœpit Diluuiu̅ esse in terris. Iam vero ab eo die per totos dies 40 pluit e cœlo, & fontes abyssi rupti sunt .i. usque ad 27 mensis sequentis, qui Casleu, seu Nouember dicitur.
units.tr: II. Marheshvan, October, the second month, on whose 17th day the Flood began on the earth. From that day for forty days it rained from heaven, and the fountains of the deep were broken up, that is, until the 27th day of the following month, which is called Kislev or November.

units.la: III. Casleu, Nouember, tertius mensis, ad 27. diem cuius a die 17 Octobris mensis continui imbres e cœlo fuere. Iam vero ab eo die usque ad 17 diem mensis Nisan, id est, Martij (qui fuit mensis illius anni septimus, ac proinde dies 150 a cœpto Diluuio) iastata semper fuit Arca. Die vero illa 17 mensis septimi demum substitit in montibus Armenia, ac quieuit.
units.tr: III. Marheshvan, or Cheshvan, which the Latins call November, the third month, to the 27th day of which there were continuous rains from heaven from the 17th day of October. From that day until the 17th day of the month Nisan, that is, March (which was the seventh month of that year, and therefore the 150th day from the beginning of the Flood), the Ark was always tossed about. On that 17th day of the seventh month it at last came to rest on the mountains of Armenia and settled.

units.la: IIII. Thebeth, December, mensis quartus.
units.tr: IV. Tevet, December, the fourth month.

units.la: V. Sebath, Ianuarius, mensis quintus.
units.tr: V. Shevat, January, the fifth month.

units.la: VI. Adar, Februarius, mensis sextus. Videntur Aquæ cœpisse decrescere die septimo Februarij, id est, 40 diebus antequam Arca subsisteret.
units.tr: VI. Adar, February, the sixth month. The waters seem to have begun to decrease on the seventh day of February, that is, forty days before the Ark came to rest.

units.la: VII. Nisan, Martius, mensis septimus. Huius mensis Martij die 17 Arca in Armenia quieuit seu substitit. Decimo vero mense (qui fuit Tamuz, Iunius Latinus) montium capita apparuere, aquis diluuij subsidentibus ac multum exsiccatis.
units.tr: VII. Nisan, March, the seventh month. On the 17th day of this month of March the Ark rested, or settled, in Armenia. In the tenth month (which was Tammuz, June in Latin), the tops of the mountains appeared, the waters of the Flood having subsided and largely dried up.

units.la: VIII. Iar, Aprilis, mensis octauus.
units.tr: VIII. Iyar, April, the eighth month.

units.la: IX. Siran, Maius, mensis nonus.
units.tr: IX. Sivan, May, the ninth month.

units.la: X. Tamuz, Iunius, mensis decimus: cuius primo die cacumina montium apparuerunt nudata aquis, uti dixi, atque aperta: Post quem diem expectat Noachus adhuc 40 dies 1. usque ad 10. diem mensis sequentis, qui est Ab, vel Iullius, quo die primùm emisit Coruum ex Arca.
units.tr: X. Tammuz, June, the tenth month, on the first day of which the summits of the mountains appeared, bared of water and open, as I have said. After that day Noah waited a further forty days, from the 1st to the 10th day of the following month, which is Av, or July, on which day he first sent out the raven from the Ark.

units.la: XI. Ab, Iulius, mensis vndecimus, cuius vndecimo die Noachus, vt demonstrauit, emisit ex Arca Coruum. It Coruus, & redit, sed quanto tempore non desinat Moses. Finge totis 7. diebus id fecisse Coruū, id est, vsque ad diem 17 mensis illius vndecimi: post quē diem bis emisit Columbam Noachus, interpositis septē diebus inter singulas emissiones, qui dies efficiunt dies 14: sed dempto die emissionis erunt dies 13. qui cōplent totum vndecimum mensem. si cum 17 diebus superioribus coniungantur. Ergo toto hoc mense emittitur semel Coruus, & Columba bis. Tertio quidem emittitur eadē Columba: sed non rediit ex tertia dimissione.
units.tr: XI. Av, July, the eleventh month, on whose eleventh day Noah, as he has shown, sent the raven out of the Ark. The raven went out and returned, but Moses does not say for how long. Suppose the raven did this for seven whole days, that is, until the 17th day of that eleventh month. After that day Noah sent out the dove twice, with seven days intervening between each sending. These days make fourteen days, but if the day of sending is subtracted there are thirteen, which complete the whole eleventh month if they are joined to the 17 earlier days. So in this whole month the raven was sent out once and the dove twice. The same dove was indeed sent out a third time, but it did not return from the third sending.

units.la: XII. Elul, Augustus. Hic fuit postremus, & duodecimus mensis anni Mundi 1656, anni Noachi 600, quo toto mense post tertiō dimissam Columbam, & iam non redeuntem, expectabat tamen Noachus in Arca vsquequo magis adhuc aquæ desiccarētur .i. ex tota superficie terræ deficerent. Sed Mense primo anni Mundi 1657, anni vero vitæ Noachi 601 (qui fuit September Latinis, & Tisri Hebræis, vt docuimus) primo die eius mensis, & Anni, vt dixi, 601 vitæ suæ Noachus totum superius Operculum Arcæ remouit, omnibus aquis Diluuij vbique iam etiam in superficie terræ exsiccatis, Gen. 8.13.
units.tr: XII. Elul, August. This was the last and twelfth month of the year of the world 1656, the year of Noah 600. Throughout this month, after the dove had been sent out for the third time and no longer returned, Noah nevertheless waited in the Ark until the waters should dry up further, that is, should disappear from the whole surface of the earth. But in the first month of the year of the world 1657, and in the 601st year of Noah's life (which was September for the Latins and Tishri for the Hebrews, as we have shown), on the first day of that month, and of that year, which as I said was the 601st of his life, Noah removed the whole upper covering of the Ark, all the waters of the Flood having now dried up everywhere on the surface of the earth, Gen. 8.13.

units.la: Mense secundo eiusdem anni vitæ Noachi 601, (qui fuit Hebræis Marhesuan, Latinis October) eius mensis die 27 Noachus, iussu Dei, ex Arca egreditur. Ex his autem omnibus apparet, quo tempore & mense singula contigerint, quæ Moses in Diluuio (& dum in Arca Noachus versatur) gesta narrat, Gen.7, & 8.
units.tr: In the second month of the same year of Noah's life, the 601st (which was Marheshvan for the Hebrews, October for the Latins), on the 27th day of that month Noah went out of the Ark by God's command. From all this it appears at what time and in what month each event occurred that Moses relates concerning the Flood, while Noah was in the Ark, Gen. 7 and 8.

units.la: De his ipsis paulò aliter Iosephus Scalig.lib. 5. Emend. Temp.cap. De Diluuio. Tribuit enim mensi Nouébri, quæ nos Octobri. Sed alij, quos nos hoc loco sequimur, mensem Marhefuan (qui Macedonibus Dios est) Septembrem esse volunt. Hoc verò mense Diluuium accidisse tradit etiã Iosephus lib. 1. Antiquit. Judaic. cap. 5: sed Tisri potius est nominandus, si menses Hebræos cum Latinis comparamus. Quibus, vt potuimus, expositis, ad reliqua nostra .i. Mosis historia capita pergamus. Sequuntur autem quæ in experimentis de Diluuio cessante à Noacho factis controuerti & possunt, & solent.
units.tr: Josephus differs somewhat from these dates, in the fifth book of Scaliger's Emendatio Temporum, chapter "On the Flood": he assigns it to the month of November, which we call October. But others, whom we follow in this place, wish the month Marheshvan (which among the Macedonians is Dius) to be September. Josephus also records that the Flood happened in this month, in the first book of the Antiquities of the Jews, chapter 5; but if we compare the Hebrew months with the Latin, it ought rather to be called Tishri. Having explained these matters as well as we could, let us proceed to the remaining chapters of our history, that is, of Moses. What follows are the questions that can be and commonly are raised about the experiments made by Noah when the Flood ceased.

units.la: Ad II. Experimentũ cessantis Diluuij.
units.tr: Concerning the second experiment: of the Flood ceasing

units.la: Quæritur, Vtrum Noachus ex impatientia quadã animi Coruũ & Columbam emisit ex Arca quasi tanta in Arca mora tedio affectus, in qua velut in sepulcro iacebat, & tanto sterquilinio rum ac sordium (quæ ex animalibus egrediebantur) tamq; tetro odore, & tædiû tolerato fatigatus vixerat, quasi statim ex ea tam insucunda sede sese proripere & liberare cuperet. Q. uũ sidei nomine maximè laudetur, & à Spiritufanto comendetur Noachus, Heb. 11.7, dicaturq; ex fide præparasse Arcam: Impatientia verò ex infidelitate nascatur (quæ fidei repugnat) minimè propter impatientiam Noachus emisit Corvum & Columbam ex Arca sed potius ex fide. Quum enim se seruandũ esse ex Diluuio sciret, & reliqua omnia quæ in eadem illa Arca tunc erat, vt illius Dei beneficij gustum aliquem præsentiret, & oculis fidei prauideret, emisit ex Arca aues illas futuras indices & nuntias deficientium ac recedentium aquarū. Caeterum ex fide, non ex animi praecipiti quodam desiderio Noachum id fecisse, apparet, quod etiam aqua ex tota terra superficie iam exsiccatus, non exuit tamen ex arca ante Dei iussum Noachus: sed diu patienter Dei mandatum in ea expectauit, Gen. 8. 13. 14, vt quemadmodum Deo praecipiente fuerat Arcam ingressus, sic eodem iubente ex ea quoque egrederetur.
units.tr: The question is whether Noah, out of a certain impatience of mind, sent the raven and the dove out of the ark, as though he were so wearied by the tedium of so long a stay in the ark, where he lay as if in a tomb, and so exhausted by the endurance of such a dunghill and filth (which came out of the animals) and such a foul odour and weariness, that he wished to hurry out of that most unpleasant dwelling and be freed from it at once. Since Noah is especially praised for his faith, and commended by the Holy Spirit, Heb. 11.7, and it is said that by faith he prepared the ark, while impatience arises from unbelief (which is opposed to faith), Noah by no means sent the raven and the dove out of the ark on account of impatience, but rather from faith. For since he knew that he was to be saved from the Flood, and since all the other things which were then in that same ark were to be preserved, he sent out of the ark those birds, future indicators and messengers of the receding and subsiding waters, so that he might have some foretaste of that benefit of God and foresee it with the eyes of faith. Moreover, that Noah did this from faith, and not from some headlong desire of mind, is clear from the fact that, even when the water had already dried from the whole surface of the earth, Noah did not leave the ark before God's command, but patiently waited in it for God's order, Gen. 8.13, 14, so that just as he had entered the ark at God's command, so at the same command he would also come out of it.

units.la: Q. Cur Coruum potius ex arca Noachus emisit, quam auem aliam quampiam, quum multa alia aquis gaudeant, velut Ardea, Gracculi, Anates, Cornices, & Mergi: ex quibus potuit idem iudicium fieri de aquis subsidentibus, vt ex Coruo aue. Nam in Pelago grauissimam esse tempestatem conflat, quū Mergi aues ad littora confugiunt inquit Isidorus lib. 12. Etymolog. R. Alij censent Coruū praesertim emissum a Noacho, propterea quod sit vilis quadā auis Coruus prae alijs. Ergo propter vilitatem selectū putant, quasi eo amisso, minor esset futura iactura. Verum Noachus minime vile existimauit quicquid Deus voluerat esse secum in Arca illa seruatum. Praeterea multis in locis corui, velut auis (quae sit testis benignissima Dei de suis creaturis prouidentia) sit mentio in S. Scriptura, sicut Iob. 39. Psal. 147. 9, Luc. 12. 24. Itaq; Greg. Magnus lib 3. Moral. cap. 15. sic scribit, [Coruns professo est quisque doctus praedicator, qui magna voce clamat, dum peccatorum suorum memoriā, atque cognitionem infirmitatis propriae, quasi quandam nigredinem coloris, portat.] Id quo idem Gregorius lib. 18. eiusdem operis, cap. 18. repetit. Sed & quanti a profanis scri-
units.tr: Q. Why did Noah send out the raven from the ark rather than some other bird? Many other birds delight in water, such as the heron, jackdaws, ducks, crows and gulls, from which the same judgment about the subsiding waters could have been made as from the raven. For it is clear that in the open sea the storm is most severe when gulls flee to the shores, says Isidore, lib. 12, Etymologies. R. Others think that the raven was especially sent out by Noah for this reason: that the raven is a rather worthless bird compared with the others. They therefore think it was chosen for its worthlessness, as if, if it were lost, the loss would be smaller. But Noah did not in the least regard as worthless whatever God had willed to be preserved with him in that ark. Moreover, the raven is mentioned in many places in Holy Scripture as a bird (which is a most faithful witness of God's providence over his creatures), as in Job 39, Ps. 147.9, Luke 12.24. Therefore Gregory the Great, lib. 3, Moralia, ch. 15, writes thus: [Every learned preacher is rightly called a raven, who with a loud voice cries out, while he bears the memory of his sins and the knowledge of his own weakness, as it were a certain blackness of colour.] The same Gregory repeats this in lib. 18 of the same work, ch. 18. But how highly it is esteemed by the profane writers

units.la: • ptoribus fiat, apparet ex Aeliani lib. 15. Hist. Anim. cap. 39: quantiç à populo ipso Romano ostendit Plinius lib. 10. Natur. Hist. cap. 43. Ipse ego sum testis quàti fiat Leydæ ab Hollandris seu Batauis. Eos enim ex vicis & publicis plateis ne quidem abigere licet: uti nec aues Ciconiae ex domorum tectis, nedum eos occidere. Ergo nequaquam propter utilitatem emissus est Coruus. Alij malunt eum contrà propter diminutatem potissimum ex omnibus auibus deleētum, ac emissum. Coruum enim auem esse maximè & diuinam & intelligentem, prasertim in auspiciis capiendis putant. Plinius lib. 10. Nat. Hist. cap. 12, [Corui, ait, in auspiciis soli videntur intelleētum habere significationum suarum. Nam quum Media hospites occisi sunt, omnes è Peloponeso, & Attica volauerunt.] Aelianus lib. 15. Hist. Animal. cap. 40. sic ait, [Si Coruus quid agit, quod pertineat ad Deum, hic tibi sacrum quippiam, & diuinationis plenum loquitur.] Verum hæc ratio est inepta. Nam ex superstitione Gentili nascitur, quæ statuit fouetque auspicia ex auium garritu vel volatu: quod obseruationis rerum genus prorsus verbo Dei damnatum est, Isa. 47. Itaque nec ex ea caussa Coruum emisit Noachus. Ego verò iudico deleētum à Noacho præsertim Coruum, propter eius naturam, ac volatum: Naturam quidem, quòd & aquis non terretur, & ex sordibus (si quas in aquis, vel alibi piscari potest) vescitur: Volatu autem, quoniam in cacuminibus arborum sidere solent, neque pernices alas habent Corui, ut longè latèue uno tractu volare possint, sed subsistunt, & quiescunt statim. Ut igitur experiretur Noachus, Verum aqua Diluuij iam infra summa vesti.
units.tr: How highly it is esteemed by the profane writers appears from Aelian, lib. 15, Hist. Anim. cap. 39: and how highly it is esteemed by the Roman people itself Pliny, lib. 10, Nat. Hist. cap. 43. I myself am a witness how highly it is esteemed at Leiden by the Hollanders, or Batavians. For they do not even allow it to be driven away from the villages and public squares, just as they do not allow storks to be driven from the roofs of houses, much less killed. Therefore the raven was by no means sent out on account of its usefulness. Others prefer to think that it was chosen and sent out from among all the birds chiefly because of its divinity. For they think the raven is above all a bird both divine and intelligent, especially in taking auspices. Pliny, lib. 10, Nat. Hist. ch. 12, says: [Ravens alone seem, in the taking of auspices, to have an understanding of their meaning. For when the guests were killed in Media, all the birds flew from the Peloponnese and Attica.] Aelian, lib. 15, Hist. Animal. ch. 40, says thus: [If a raven does anything that pertains to God, it speaks to you something sacred and full of divination.] But this reason is foolish. For it arises from Gentile superstition, which establishes and fosters auspices from the chattering or flight of birds; a kind of observation which is utterly condemned by the Word of God, Isa. 47. Therefore Noah did not send out the raven for that reason either. But I judge that Noah chose the raven especially on account of its nature and its flight: its nature, because it is not terrified by water, and feeds on filth (if it can fish for any in the water or elsewhere); its flight, because ravens are accustomed to settle on the tops of trees, and they do not have swift wings, so that they cannot fly far and wide in one stretch, but stop and rest at once. Therefore, so that Noah might test whether the water of the Flood had already sunk below the tops of the trees, as the traces of trees (such as oaks, elms, walnuts and other similar trees) would have shown, as it had also sunk below the peaks of the mountains 40 days earlier, he sent out chiefly the raven, from whose nature and flight Noah could recognise that. For if there were no trees, or their tops above the waters…

units.la: • vestigia arborum (velut quercuum, ulmorum, nucum, & caeterarū similium) subsedissent, quemadmodū infra cacum na montium erat etiam ante 40. dies, emisit potissimum Coruū ex cuius natura & volatu id agnoscere potuit Noachus. Nam si nullas arbores, earūmve vertices aquis superiores coruus reperiret, nondū aquis nudata erant arbores: at si quas reperiret superiores aquis Coruum, in ijs sideret, subsisteret, ac volaret: ex quo facile erat conijciendi aquas iam esse arboribus inferiores in superficie terrae. Quamobrem aptissime Corvum ad id conijciendum, deprehendendumve delegit primum Noachus potius, quam vllam aliam auem. Caeterum praetermitto illas allegorias, quas in Corno, & Columba quarit Augustinus lib. 12. contra Manichaeum, cap. 20 & 21. Legat apud eum, qui volet. Nec enim ipse eas probo. Quid haec verba significat Gen. 8. 7: [Et Coruus ibat, & redibat, vsquedum exsiccarentur aquae e superficie terrae:] quum etiam Columba ierit, & redierit ad Noachum, donec exsiccatis aquis potuit consistere in terrae superficie. His verbis notari differentiam dico inter Coruum, & Columbam a Noacho emissam. Coruus enim semel ex Arca emissus nunquam in eam postea se conclusi passus est, nec se voluit aut suit manu comprehendi iterum a Noacho. Ergo Coruus ille volabat, subsistebatque modo supra tectum arcae, modo supra arboris alicuius verticem aquis nudatam: quod ipsum seu quia vicissitudinem vocat Mosis [Ire, & redire.] Nunquam tamen in ipsam Arcam fenestram, ex qua semel emissus evolarat, rediit, ut se a Noacho sineret iterum manu prehendi. At Columba non tantum in Arcam redijt: sed etiam ad fenestram eam ipsam unde primùm dimissa fuerat, & à Noacho bis emissa, se bis manu quoque comprehendi, retrahiq; in Arcam passa est, Gen.8.9. Ergo docilior, timidiorve fuit Columba, quàm Coruus. Hic enim Coruus intrepidus extra Arcam remansit, etsi terra superficies nondum erat planè levata aquis, modò in tecto Arcæ: modò, uti dixi, in cacumine arboris alicuius subsistens. Illa autem Columba trepida revertsa est, & intravit intra Arcâ ipsam, quia totius terræ superficies nòdum erat exsiccata. Ex quibus duo colliguntur: Unum, Arbores videlicet nequaquam omnes fuisse aquis Diluuij radicitùs euulsas, sed quasdam fixas in terra etiam post diluuium remansisse, quemadmodum & exitu reditúque Corui, & ex Oliua (cuius folium defregit Columba) manifestè colligitur. Alterum, Non periisse Coruum illum, quem Noachus ex Arca emiserat (quod tamen putat Augustinus lib. quæst. in Genef. cap. 13) sed vixisse ex morticinio, putredine, & ex iis quisquilijs, quas vel in montibus, vel in arboribus inueniebat, partim in Arca operculo, partim in cacumine arborum manens, uti demonstrauimus. Q. Quandiu post Coruum emissa est à Noacho primùm Columba ex Arca. Iosephus Scaliger lib. 5. de Emend. Temp. cap. De Diluuio sentit, scribitque totos 40 dies intercessisse inter Corui, & Columbæ primam emissionem. Alij verò, velut Franciscus Junius in annotationculis illis eruditissimis in Genef. interponit septem duntaxat dies inter Coruum emissum ex Arca, & Columbam. Etsi uterq; rationibus nititur, ego tamen Iunij sententiam ampleßor. Q. Cur Columbam potissimum post Corvu Noachus emisit ex Arca? R. Nonnulli in ys aenibus quærunt allegorias. Aly alias eius fasti rationes afferunt, Ergo quidam potissimum Columbam electam à Noacho propter prudentiam seu intellectu existimant. Plinius lib. 10. cap. 36, [Columbis inest, ait, quidam & gloria intellectus. Nolle credas suos colores, varietatemque dispositam: quin etiam ex volatu quaeritur (alias creditur) plaudere in cœlo, varieque sulcare.] Quin & meditatio Columbæ tribuitur à Bernardo sicut clamor pulli hirundinis, Serm. de Cantico Ezech. Columba vero prudentia à Gregorio Magno pulchrè explicatur in Cant. Cant. c. cap. 5.
