[Ad hoc, ait, Columba iuxta fluenta residere solent, ut volantium animum vmbram in aqua videant, super quam se proiicientes vngues rapacium animalium sic effugiant.] Aly malunt à Noacho delestam Columbam tanquam Deo gratiorem auem, quam esset Corvus. Est enim Columba animal & castum, & innocens. Castum quidem animal, quoniam, vt scribit Plinius lib. 10. Nat. Histor. cap. 34, neque Columba, neque Perdices Coniugij fidem violant: nisi enim cœlebs, aut vidua Columba, non relinquit domum. Aelianus lib. 15. Hist. Animal. cap. 31, [Columbæ, ait, ex auibus maxima esse pudicitia, ab omni, adulterio castissimas esse percepi. Nunquam enim ex societate inter se instituta, neque mas nisi morte vxoris distrahitur: neque fœmina dissociatur, nisi vidua fuerit.] Innocens verò animal est Columba, vel teste Christo [Estote, ait, simplices, vt Columba, Math. 10. 16.] Itaque Ecclesia Dei comparatur Columbæ, Cantico Cantic. cap. 5. Gregorius Magnus Homil. 5. in Euangel. [Columba, ait, simplex est animal, atque à malitia fellis alienû. Quasi Columba ergo ad suas fenestras sunt, qui nihil in hoc Mundo concupiscunt, qui omnia simpliciter aspiciunt.] Bernardus Serm 2. de Epiph. Domini, [Quod agnus in animalibus, Columba inter animalibus est, inquit. Summa vtriusque innocentia, summa simplicitas. Quid enim sic alienum ab omni malitia, sicut Agnus, & Columba? Nocere cuiquâ nesciunt, ladere non nouerunt.] Et hæc quidem illi. Ego verò sic sentio, Noachum Columbam post Coruum ex Arca emisisse præsertim, quod illius & naturam, & volatum consideraret, & quod Corui non patientis se in Arcam retrahi contumacia fuerat offensus. Volebat igitur iam Noachus periculum facere, Virum ipsa terra superficies esset aquis leuata (Nam maiorum arborum, quæ erant in terra superficie, cacuminā iam aquis nudata esse deprehenderat ex Corui volatu, qui in illis subsidebat, remanebatque, nec in arcam iam ingrediebatur) & Virum humiliorum arborum inhærentiū in ista terra superficie vertices essent quoq; aquis liberati, exoneratiq;. Itaque auem Noachus delegit, cuius non esset pernix, & lō inquus volatus: sed humilis, lenis, & circa vicina tantum loca. Deinde auē eiusmodi emisit, quæ non esset contumax, vt Coruus: sed quæ se retrahi in Arcam, & tractari, capiq; manu hominum facile pateretur: id quod non sinebat de se fieri Coruus. Est autē Columba eiusmodi anis, nempe lenis, placida, & tractabilis, quæ etiam hominum est amantissima, quemadmodum Physici tradunt. Aelianus lib. 15. Hist. Animal. cap. 31, [In vrbibus, inquit, Columba cum hominibus frequenter habitant, seque ad pedes horum huc & illuc magna mansuetudine, & facilitate versantes: In locis autem, vbi ab hominum frequentia solitudo est, propinquitatem hominum minime expectantes, anfugiunt: In multitudine hominum confidentiores sunt, seq; nihil ibi grave passuras plane sciunt.] Hac ille, qua demonstrant Noachum virum & prudentissimum, & optimum physicum Columbam rectissimè delegisse, quæ capi postea comprehendiq; posset ac retrahi: & humiles arbores peteret. Q. Virum eandem Columbam sapius ex Arca Noachus emisit, an diuersam & aliam. R. Eandem omnino, non autem diuersam Columbam ter emisit Noachus. Eandem enim fuisse, non aliam, atque aliam ostendit [He Haiedia] prepositum vbique voci [Ionah] quæ Columbam significat, Gen.8.10.11.12. He vero Haiedia certâ, eandemq; rem, de qua supra actum est, notat, ac designat. Q. Quomodo Noachus ex folio Oliuæ decerpto (quod in ore Columba ferebat) collegit aquas Diluuij subsidisse plurimum, & terræ superficiem illius prope totam esse liberatam, ac lenatam. R. Olea est arbor humilis, non excelsa vel ardua, quemadmodum Pinus, Nux, Quercus, Acer, reliquæque similes arbores. Ergo quiè ex Oliua, id est, depressa, & terra superficiei vicina arbore folium decerptum videret in ore Columba Noachus, optimè coniecit, prope iam aquas omnes Diluuij recessisse, & terra superficiem iam esse liberatam. Hanc coiecturam & doctissimè, & verissimè explicauit Ioannes Calvinus. Porro folium illud Oliuæ (quod in ore Columba gestabat, atque ad Noachū afferebat) non humi iacens & positū Columba inuenerat, sed ex arbore ipsa dezerpferat, anulferatque. Nam si humi iaceret, aquæ Diluuij prorsus iam defecisset, quæ tamen postea & demum post aliquot dies exsiccata, & prorsus ex terræ superficie recessisse dicuntur, Gen 8.13. Ergo terræ superficiem quæ operiebant adhuc aquæ: sed non magna altitudine. Itaque cacumen Oliuæ arboris (quæ est humilis) iam non superabant: imo illud aquis nudatum erat. Cæterum virum viride fuerit adhuc illud Oliuæ folium, an marcidum & mortuum, non exponit Moses: utcunque certe valde tenax & in ipsa arbore firmum & inhærens fuit folium, illud, quod toi procellæ, & tantis aquarum impetus illud euellere, & deycere ex suo trunco & arbore non potuerunt. Quod denique scribunt Physici, velut Gyllius apud Aelianum, Columbas ramulos lauri, non oleæ pertinentes colligere solere, tanquam amuletum & remedium ad propulsationem fascini, altò pertinet, quam ad scopum Noachi. Item quod tradit Plinius lib.8.cap 27. eas leuare, & purgare annuum fastidium & morbum herbâ, quæ vocatur Helxine, non habet quicquam cum isto Oliuæ folio commune. Q. Cur Columba denuo ex Arca emissa redierit tamen ad Noachum: quum & locum, vbi consisteret, in terra inueniret, nempe Oleam arborem, & moticulos seu colles, & folium in ore haberet. R. Propterea quod pabulum, unde viueret, nondum in terra superficie adhuc aquis operta reperire poterat Columba. Nec enim illa, quemadmodum & coruus, sordibus, & putredine vesci potuit. Ergo reuersa est ad Arcam, vbi à Noacho pascebatur, & cibum reperiebat. Quod autem Augustinus lib.quæst.in Gen.cap.14 quæsrit, quomodo Columba dicatur eatur, quū primùm ex Arca fuit emissa,non habuisse, nec inuenijse locum,vbi plantam pedis poneret,quum tamen iam montium capita nudata essent aquis, habet facilem hanc responsionem, nempe Columbas non solere cacumina montium petere, & tam altè ac sublimè volare:sed subsistere in locis inferioribus terra & humilioribus,quàm sint montes. Illa verò loca adhuc tecta manebant aquis Diluuij. Ergo locum, vbi subsisteret, nondum reperiebat Columba,quum esset primùm emissa & reuersa. Q. Vtrum tùc primùm Noachus Arcæ fenestras aperuit,Gen.8.6,quum Corummex ea emisit: annon etiam priùs & sæpiùs id fecerit. R. Equidem non dubito,quin vsus fenestrarum earum, quæ erant in Arca ( plures enim quàm vnam fuisse, non dubito, & illic singularem numerum pro plurali sumi dico,quemadmodum eodem libr.Gen.2.10. [Fluuius exibat ex Hedene] quin, inquam, vsus earum præcipuus fuerit, vt lumen Solis per eas Noachus,quæq; in Arca cum eo erant animalia viderent ac reciperent:ne in Arca tanquam in perpetuis tenebris versarentur: sed diem illic à noƈte distinguebat Noachus,Gen.6.16. Tamen fuerunt quoque alij earundem fenestrarum in Arca vsus, ac commoditates, veluti,si quid sordium domesticarū erat ex Arca proijciendum,si quid aquæ hauriendum ad vsus familiæ Noachi domesticos,& necessarios:aut si quidpiam eiusmodi emittendum, aut admittendum, fenestra aliqua aperiebatur.. Q uanquā enim non erat in Arca Noachus,velut in regio spatioso, aliquo patlatio,vbi cōmodè distinctas cœnationes,deambulationes, & cameras plures ad voluptatem dispositas haberet:
units.tr: ...the tops of the trees (such as oaks, elms, walnuts and other similar trees) had settled, as they were also on the mountain peaks about forty days earlier, Noah chiefly sent out the raven, and from its nature and flight Noah could recognise this. For if the raven found no trees, or their tops above the waters, the trees were not yet uncovered by the waters. But if the raven found any trees with their tops above the waters, it would settle there, rest, and fly about, and from this it was easy to conjecture that the waters were now lower than the trees on the surface of the earth. For this reason Noah chose the raven first, rather than any other bird, to make this conjecture or test. I pass over those allegories which Augustine seeks in the raven and the dove, Book 12 against the Manichaeans, chapters 20 and 21. Let whoever wishes read them there; for I do not myself approve of them. What do these words of Genesis 8:7 mean: "And the raven went out, and returned, until the waters were dried up from the earth"? Since the dove also went out and returned to Noah, until the waters had dried up and it could settle on the surface of the earth. By these words, I say, a difference is marked between the raven and the dove sent out by Noah. For the raven, once sent out of the ark, never allowed itself to be shut in there again, nor would it be caught by Noah's hand again. So that raven flew, and rested now on the roof of the ark, now, as I said, on the top of some tree uncovered by the waters; and Moses calls this a going out and returning, yet it never returned to the window of the ark itself from which it had once flown out, so as to let Noah take hold of it again. But the dove not only returned to the ark, but also to that very window from which it had first been let go, and when Noah sent it out a second time it allowed itself to be taken by hand and drawn back into the ark, twice (Genesis 8:9). So the dove was more tame and timid than the raven. For the raven remained boldly outside the ark, though the surface of the earth was not yet fully lifted above the waters, now on the roof of the ark, now, as I said, resting on the top of some tree. But the dove, trembling, came back and entered the ark itself, because the whole surface of the earth was not yet dry. From these things two conclusions are drawn. First, that not all the trees had been torn up by the roots by the waters of the Flood, but some remained fixed in the earth even after the Flood, as is clearly gathered both from the going out and returning of the raven and from the olive tree (whose leaf the dove plucked). Second, that that raven which Noah had sent out from the ark did not perish (though Augustine thinks so, Book of Questions on Genesis, chapter 13), but lived on carrion, rotting flesh and those scraps which it found either on the mountains or in the trees, remaining partly on the ark's covering and partly on the tops of trees, as we have shown. Q. How long after the raven was the dove first sent out of the ark by Noah? Joseph Scaliger, Book 5 of On the Emendation of Time, chapter On the Flood, thinks and writes that a full forty days passed between the first sending out of the raven and of the dove. But others, such as Franciscus Junius in his most learned little notes on Genesis, allow only seven days between the raven sent out of the ark and the dove. Although both rest on arguments, I prefer the opinion of Junius, as the more ample. Q. Why did Noah send out the dove after the raven, rather than some other bird? R. Some seek allegories in these matters; others give other reasons for this. Some therefore think that the dove was chosen by Noah above all for its prudence or intelligence. Pliny, Book 10, chapter 36: "Doves have, he says, a certain glory of intelligence. You would not believe their colours and their ordered variety; indeed, from their flight it is sought (or rather believed) that they clap in the sky and plough the air in varied patterns." Indeed Bernard also attributes meditation to the dove, as to the cry of the swallow's chick, in his sermon on the Song of Songs. The prudence of the dove is finely explained by Gregory the Great on the Song of Songs, chapter 5: "For this reason, he says, doves are wont to sit beside streams, so that they may see the shadow of the flying bird in the water, and, throwing themselves upon it, thus escape the claws of the rapacious animals." Others prefer that the dove was chosen by Noah as a bird more pleasing to God than the raven. For the dove is a chaste and innocent animal. It is chaste, since, as Pliny writes in Book 10 of the Natural History, chapter 34, neither doves nor partridges violate the faith of marriage: a dove, unless it is unmarried or a widow, does not leave the home. Aelian, Book 15 of On the Nature of Animals, chapter 31: "Among birds, he says, doves have the greatest chastity; I have learned that they are most pure from all adultery. For once their partnership is established, the male is never parted from the female except by the death of his wife, nor is the female separated unless she is a widow." Moreover, the dove is an innocent animal, by the testimony of Christ himself: "Be simple, he says, as doves (Matthew 10:16)." Thus the Church of God is compared to a dove (Song of Songs 5). Gregory the Great, Homily 5 on the Gospel: "The dove, he says, is a simple animal, and free from the malice of gall. Those, therefore, who desire nothing in this world, who look at all things simply, are like doves at their windows." Bernard, Sermon 2 on the Epiphany of the Lord: "As the lamb is among animals, so the dove is among animals, he says. Both are the sum of innocence, the sum of simplicity. For what is so far removed from all malice as the lamb and the dove? They know not how to harm anyone, they have not learned to injure." And so far those writers. But I think this: Noah sent out the dove after the raven, especially because he considered its nature and its flight, and because he was offended by the raven's obstinacy in not allowing itself to be drawn back into the ark. Noah therefore wished now to make a trial, whether the surface of the earth itself had been lifted above the waters (for from the raven's flight, which settled and remained on the tops of the larger trees standing on the surface of the earth, and no longer entered the ark, he had perceived that the tops of those trees were now uncovered by the waters), and whether the tops of the lower trees fixed in this surface of the earth were also freed and relieved of the waters. And so Noah chose a bird whose flight was not swift and far-ranging, but low, gentle, and confined to nearby places. Then he sent out a bird of such a kind as would not be stubborn like the raven, but would easily allow itself to be drawn back into the ark, handled and taken in a man's hand; which the raven did not permit to be done to itself. Now the dove is such a bird, namely gentle, placid, and tractable, and also most fond of human beings, as the naturalists teach. Aelian, Book 15 of On the Nature of Animals, chapter 31: "In cities, he says, doves live frequently among men, moving about at people's feet with great tameness and ease. But in places where there is solitude, away from the crowds of men, they do not at all expect the nearness of men, but flee. Among crowds of men they are more confident, and they know full well that nothing grave will befall them there." So far Aelian; these things show that Noah, a most prudent man and an excellent natural philosopher, rightly chose the dove, which could afterwards be caught, grasped, and drawn back, and which would seek the low trees. Q. Did Noah send the same dove out of the ark several times, or different doves? R. Noah sent out the same dove three times, not different doves. For the expression ["He Haiedia"], the particle "he" placed before the word Ionah [יוֹנָה], which means dove, everywhere shows that it was the same and not another and another (Genesis 8:10, 11, 12). And this "He Haiedia" marks and designates the same thing as was discussed above. Q. How did Noah, from the olive leaf plucked (which the dove carried in its mouth), gather that the waters of the Flood had largely subsided and that the surface of the earth was almost wholly free and relieved? R. The olive is a low tree, not tall or lofty, like the pine, walnut, oak, maple and the other similar trees. Therefore Noah, seeing in the dove's mouth a leaf plucked from an olive, that is, from a low tree near the surface of the earth, rightly conjectured that the waters of the Flood had almost all withdrawn and that the surface of the earth was now free. John Calvin explained this conjecture most learnedly and most truly. Moreover, that olive leaf which the dove carried in its mouth and brought to Noah the dove had not found lying on the ground, but had plucked and carried off from the tree itself. For if it had been lying on the ground, the waters of the Flood would already have quite gone, whereas they are said to have dried up and withdrawn entirely from the surface of the earth only after some days more (Genesis 8:13). Therefore the waters still covered the surface of the earth, but not to a great height; so they no longer covered the top of the olive tree (which is low), indeed it was uncovered by the waters. But whether that olive leaf was still green, or withered and dead, Moses does not state; in any case the leaf was very tenacious and firmly fixed and clinging to the tree itself, since neither the storm nor such great rushes of waters could tear it off and throw it down from its stalk and tree. As for what the naturalists write, for example Gyllius, cited by Aelian, that doves are wont to gather sprigs of laurel, not of olive, as an amulet and remedy for averting the evil eye, this pertains far less to Noah's purpose. Likewise what Pliny, Book 8, chapter 27, relates, that they relieve and purge their annual distaste and sickness with an herb called helxine, has nothing in common with this olive leaf. Q. Why, when the dove was sent out again from the ark, did it nevertheless return to Noah, since it could find a place in the earth where it might settle, namely the olive tree and the little hills, and had a leaf in its mouth? R. Because the Dove could not yet find food on the surface of the earth, which was still covered by the waters, on which to live. For it could not, like the raven, feed on filth and rottenness. Therefore it returned to the ark, where it was fed by Noah and found its food. As for what Augustine, in Book of Questions on Genesis, chapter 14, asks, namely how the dove is said to have found no place where it could set the sole of its foot when first sent out of the ark, although the tops of the mountains were already uncovered by the waters, he has this easy answer: that doves are not wont to seek the tops of mountains and fly so high and lofty, but to settle in places lower on the earth and humbler than the mountains. But those places still remained covered by the waters of the Flood. Therefore the dove, when first sent out and returning, did not yet find a place where it might settle. Q. Did Noah then first open the windows of the ark (Genesis 8:6), when he sent the raven out of it, or did he do so earlier and more often? R. I certainly do not doubt that the use of those windows, which were in the ark (for I do not doubt there were more than one, and I say that the singular is here used for the plural, just as in the same book, Genesis 2:10, "a river went out from Eden"), that, I say, their chief use was so that Noah and the animals with him in the ark might see and receive the light of the sun through them, lest they dwell in the ark as in perpetual darkness; and Noah distinguished day from night there (Genesis 6:16). Yet there were also other uses and conveniences of these same windows in the ark: for example, if any household refuse had to be thrown out of the ark, or if water had to be drawn for the domestic and necessary uses of Noah's family, or if anything of that kind had to be sent out or let in, some window was opened. For although Noah was not in the ark as in some spacious royal palace, where he might have conveniently separated dining rooms, walking halls and several chambers arranged for pleasure,

units.la: Ff sed in ea velut in sepulcro, cum putore, fœtore, & sor- dibus animalium iacebat: Ea tamen, quae ad vitam erant ipsi animalibusque in Arca necessaria vel secum habebat Noachus in Arca, vel quaerebat quantum poterat, quemadmodum aquam ad potum suum, & eorum ani- malium, quae Deus in Arca seruari volebat. Ergo et ta fenestris illis ad eiusmodi commoditates, vti dixi, poterat vti Noachus: ac proinde verum est ijs vsum quoque fuisse. Quare iudico eu fenestras Arcae, videlicet hanc tantum vel illa (prout necesse aut opus erat) aperuisse, & quidem saepius, & priusquam Coruum emitteret ex Arca. Nam quomodo idem Noachus videre ac dignoscere potuit ex Arca capita montium esse inundata aquis, nisi arca fenestras aperuisset? Nec enim illae erant vitreae, vti nostrae, per transfuersum & medium quarum cerni quidpiam posset, nisi aperirentur: sed erant lignea fenestrae. Ergo eas aperuit 40, diebus ante Coruum emisssum, quia nimirum aspexit, viditque Noachus inga montium aperta, & aquis liberata, Gen. 8.5. Verum quum Coruu emisit, dicitur Noachus diserte fenestra Arca aperuisse, quoniam tunc non vnam, aut alteram dûtaxat ex illis fenestris remouit, & aperuit: sed simul omnes, vt intromitteret iam liberiorem aerem in Arca, utpote plane tunc sedatum & quietum ab omnibus procellis, & pluuys, & sese, eosque omnes (qui secum vna in Arca versabantur) luce illa maiore, & copiosiore recrearet, ac consolaretur. Sic enim & seipsum & vxorem, liberos suos, & nurus suas ad Dei beneficium agnoscendum vehementius excitauit, & spem optimam de sua ex aquis Diluuij liberatione, propinquoque ex Arca egressu suo concepit. Ergo tunc aperuit Noachus fenestram Arcæ Gen.8.6,id est,omnes fenestras,quas ad clarum lumen in ea suscipiendum idem priùs fecerat, iussu Dei,exstruxeratque:non autem vnam tantum,aut alteram,vt antea. Nonnulli verò sic tunc Noachum fenestras aperuisse volunt, vt eas postea non clauserit. Nec enim quia Columbam ad se recipiit in Arcâ Noachus,manúmque ex arca extendit Gen.8.9,dicitur aperiuisse tunc fenestram Arcæ,quum tamen id,non nisi aliqua fenestra aperta,facere potuerit. Ergo, aiunt, mansit semper aperta. Q. Cur vento aquas diluuij exsiccauit & dispulit Deus,Gen.8.1. R. Ersi absq; vento id facere Deus potuit:voluit tamen,quemadmodum ad diluuium in terras immittendum,& ventis, & pluuijs vsus fuerat:sic ad idem illud siniendum vti contrario vento, vt intelligamus omnia voluntati Dei inseruire,eúmque vetis caterìsque rebus omnibus pro suo arbitratu vti posse ad nostrum exitium, vel salutem. Ergo sicut Notum madidosq; ventos induxerat ad Diluuij aquas iniciedas:sic Boream,vrentésq; ventos Subsolanos immisit calidos & sudos, quibus aquas Diluuij velut hauriret,& siccaret. Q. Virum statim post emissam tertio Columbam ex Arca Noachus eius operculum remouerit,quoniam Gen.8.12.13, continuatur vtrumque nullo interietlo temporis, vt videtur spatio, quo post non redeuntem in Arcam Columbâ expestarit Noachus,vt testum illius auferret. R. Ratio temporis,supputatióque Anni Diluuij requirit omnino, vt Noachus post emissam tertiò Columbâ expestarit totû mensem duodecimum, antequam operculum Arcæ remoueret. Sic enim expletus intelligetur annus Mundi 1656, & vitae Noachi 600. Nam 40 dies illi, quos ab initio decimi mensis (considerlu motum nudatis capitibus) expectauit Noachus, donec Corvum ex Arca emitteret, quadraginta, inquam, illi dies incidunt in decimum mensis undecimi seu sequentis: ad cuius complementum addendi sunt dies viginti, quibus Corvus, & Columba emissa fuerit, & ad Noachi redierit, nempe septem dies post Corvi emissionem: deinde dies 14 quibus Columba denuo fuit ex Arca dimissa. Ergo dies illi 10, & 20 isti ex emissione avium, efficiunt dies integros 30, quibus completur annus vitae Noachi 600 mensis undecimus. A quo usque ad mensem primum anni 601 vitae Noachi (quo operculum Arcae primum detractum est) interiungitur mensis eiusdem 600 vitae Noachi unus nempe duodecimus. Nam Anni veteres seu prisci, quemadmodum docuimus, & duodecim mensibus constabant & Solares erant. Ergo ad implementum illius 600 anni restat mensis ille duodecimus, qui totum expectauit, ac praeterfluere fuit Noachus, antequam operculum Arcae remouteret. In quo summa Noachi patientia apparet, minimeq; praeceps de egrediendo ex Arca desiderium. Q. Cur Noachus operculum Arcae tandem remouit. R. Hoc ut commodius intelligatur primum explicandum est, Ecquod & quale Arcae operculum fuerit illud, quod primo die primi mensis anni vitae Noachi 601 fuit abeo sublatum. Sciendum est igitur Nauigium illud, in quo Noachus cum familia sua, & animalibus introgressis seruatus est ex aquis Diluuij, fuisse quadrangula forma exstructum ad modum Arca,ac propterea Arcam non Nauim appellatum. Ergo tectum primum,& quod vere fuit pars su-perior istius Arcæ, fuit & planum & quadrangulum, eadem longitudine,& latitudine constans,qua fundum seu imum Arcæ,quod fuit infima pars Arcæ Sic olim erant tecta domuum inter Hebræos quadrangula. Non fuit quidem Arca ista, velut Cubus,æquilatera, sed tamen fuit quadrāgula:nam illius longitudo maior erat, quàm eiusdem latitudo. Porrò huic Arcæ tecto plano & quadrangulo fuit aliud impositum quod operculum hîc nominat Moses. Erat autem hoc operculum non planum,ut tectum ipsum: sed fastigiatum,& assurgens in altitudinem cubiti in angulum,Gen.6.16. vbi fiebat coaxatio asserum, & ex eo fastigio paulatim hoc idem operculum deorsum deprimebatur:cuius suggrunda & latera proÿciebantur omnes ex parte extra Arcam, vt velut stiriæ quædam aquæ pluuias exciperent,& emitterent extra Arcam. Hoc autem operculum erat primi tecti Arcæ velut integumentum. Ergo simillima fuit in eo huius Arcæ Noachi cum Arca fœderis Dei (quam postea iussu est Moses exstruere) similitudo,quòd quèadmodum Arca fœderis habebat operculū, quod Propitiatorium vocabatur,Exod 25: sic hæc arca Noachi habuit & ipsa quoque operculū ad sui tecti primi custodiam,& pluuias ab eo arcendas, denique vt eo desuper tegeretur. Itaque [Cefeh] à tegendo dicitur. Nec verò operculum illud fuit pars Arcæ,uti nec Propitiatoriū erat pars Arcæ fœderis, sed tegmen tantum, et à tecti ipsius Arcæ primi: alioqui illud auelli & remoueri ab Arca non potuisset,quin ipsam Arcam rupisset ac fregisset Noachus: & quidem temerè, quum eius rei mandatum à Deo non accepisset. Deinde fe, & suos iniurijs cœli, & frigoribus noctis exponeret fi ipsum arcæ tectum primum auferret. Quare hoc est operculum, quod Arcæ detraxit Noachus, & quo detracto mansit nihilominus Arca adhuc & tota, & perfecta, & omnibus suis partibus constans. Cur autem illud remouit ratio est, Quod quum ad eum neque Corvus, neque Columba iam redirent, unde conjiceret quantùm aquæ diluuij à tempore emissæ tertium Columba defecissent: nec ipse quoque ex arca (Deo nondum præcipiente) egredi adhuc vel vellet, vel posset: fuit necesse vt in aliquem ⌂Arcæ locum ascenderet ipse, unde iam vndique intueretur ac conspiceret quæ effet terræ facies, quantum aquæ depressæ & exsiccatæ effent, vt ea ratione tum seipsum, tum alios Noachus infide beneficij Dei confirmaret, & ipfem suturi propediem ex Arca egressus, instaurandi mundi conciperet: denique fe, & omnes, qui in Arca secum erant, ad deum immensè laudandi excitaret. Nec verò dubito, quinetiam Noachi filij, vxor, & nurus, remoto illo Arcæ operculo, in tectum arcæ ipsi quoque confcenderint, vt tale Dei miraculum ipsis oculis suis intuerentur & viderent, ac Deum eximiè ex eiusmodi aspectu collaudarent, illi gratias agerent, ac suam salutem propediem sperarent. Quare non frustra, neque de nihilo Noachus Arcæ operculum remouit: non temerè, nonv pracipiti desiderio: sed omnia legitima suæ, suorumque fidei confirmandæ subsidia quærens & captans. Omnes tamen, quantumuis ex tecto arcæ cernerent aquas omnes diluuij in tota terra superficie exsiccatas, manserunt tamen
units.tr: But Noah lay in it as if in a tomb, amid the stench, the foulness and the filth of the animals. Still, Noah kept with him in the ark, or sought as far as he could, whatever was needed for life, both for himself and for the animals, which God wished to be preserved in the ark, such as water for drinking for himself and for those animals. So Noah could use those windows for such purposes, as I have said, and it is therefore true that he did use them. Hence I judge that he opened the windows of the ark, this one or that (as need or occasion required), and indeed often, and before he sent the Raven out of the ark. For how could Noah have seen and recognised from the ark that the tops of the mountains were covered with water, unless he had opened the windows of the ark? Those windows were not glazed like ours, through which something could be seen across and through the middle unless they were opened; they were wooden windows. So he opened them forty days before the Raven was sent out, because he indeed looked and saw that the peaks of the mountains were visible and freed from the waters (Gen. 8.5). But when he sent out the Raven, Noah is expressly said to have opened the window of the ark, because then he did not remove and open just one or two of those windows, but all of them at once, so that he might let a freer air into the ark, since it was then plainly calm and quiet from all storms and rains, and might refresh and comfort himself and all those who lived with him in the ark with that greater and fuller light. For in this way he more strongly stirred up himself, his wife, his sons and his daughters-in-law to acknowledge God's benefit, and conceived the best hope of his deliverance from the waters of the Flood and of his coming exit from the ark. So then Noah opened the window of the ark (Gen. 8.6), that is, all the windows which he had earlier made, by God's command, for receiving clear light into it, and not just one or two, as before. Some, however, want Noah to have opened the windows at that time in such a way that he did not afterwards close them. For they say that when Noah took the Dove back into the ark and stretched out his hand from the ark (Gen. 8.9), it is not said that he then opened the window of the ark, although he could not have done that without some window being open. Therefore, they say, it always remained open. Q. Why did God dry up and drive away the waters of the Flood by a wind (Gen. 8.1)? A. Although God could have done this without a wind, he nevertheless chose, just as he had used both winds and rains to bring the Flood upon the earth, so to use a contrary wind to end it, so that we may understand that all things serve the will of God, and that he can use the winds and all other things at his discretion for our destruction or our salvation. Therefore, just as he had brought on the moist south and west winds to pour out the waters of the Flood, so he sent the north wind and the scorching east winds, hot and dry, by which he would, as it were, draw off and dry up the waters of the Flood. Q. Since the Dove was sent out a third time, why did Noah remove the cover of the ark immediately afterwards? For Gen. 8.12-13 joins the two together with no interval of time, as it seems, in which Noah might have waited, after the Dove did not return to the ark, before he removed its covering. A. The reckoning of time and the calculation of the year of the Flood require altogether that Noah waited the whole twelfth month after the third sending out of the Dove before he removed the cover of the ark. For in this way the year 1656 of the world and the six hundredth year of Noah's life will be understood as complete. For those forty days which Noah waited from the beginning of the tenth month (with his head uncovered, as he considered the movement of the waters) until he sent the Raven out of the ark, those forty days, I say, fall into the tenth day of the eleventh month, or the following one; to complete them must be added the twenty days in which the Raven and the Dove were sent out and returned to Noah, namely seven days after the sending out of the Raven, and then fourteen days, after which the Dove was let out of the ark again. Those ten days and these twenty days of the sending out of the birds make up thirty full days, by which the six hundredth year of Noah's life is completed, in the eleventh month. From this point until the first month of the six hundred and first year of Noah's life (when the cover of the ark was first taken off), there intervenes the twelfth month of that six hundredth year of Noah's life. For the ancient or early years, as we have taught, consisted of twelve months and were solar. So to complete that six hundredth year the twelfth month remains, which Noah waited out entirely, and let pass by, before he removed the cover of the ark. In this the great patience of Noah appears, and his desire to leave the ark was in no way hasty. Q. Why did Noah finally remove the cover of the ark? A. So that this may be understood more conveniently, we must first explain what kind of cover that was, and of what sort, which was taken off the ark on the first day of the first month of Noah's six hundred and first year. It must be known, then, that the vessel in which Noah with his family and the animals that had entered was saved from the waters of the Flood was built in a quadrangular shape, in the manner of a box, and so was called an ark and not a ship. So the first roof, which was truly the upper part of that ark, was both flat and quadrangular, of the same length and breadth as the bottom or lowest part of the ark. In this way, too, the roofs of houses among the Hebrews were formerly quadrangular. Indeed this ark was not like a cube, equal on every side, but it was quadrangular, for its length was greater than its breadth. Moreover, another thing was placed upon this flat, quadrangular roof of the ark, which Moses here calls the cover. This cover was not flat, like the roof itself, but was pointed, rising to a height of one cubit into a ridge (Gen. 6.16), where the beams were joined together, and from that ridge this same cover was gradually lowered downward; its eaves and sides all projected outside the ark, so that, like gutters, they might catch the rains and carry them away from the ark. This cover, then, was like a covering over the first roof of the ark. In this respect there is a very close resemblance between this ark of Noah and the ark of God's covenant (which Moses was afterwards commanded to build): just as the ark of the covenant had a cover, which was called the mercy seat (Exod. 25), so this ark of Noah also had its own cover, to guard its first roof and to keep off the rains, and finally to shelter it from above. Thus [כפה] is so called from covering. Yet that cover was not a part of the ark, any more than the mercy seat was a part of the ark of the covenant, but merely a covering of the first roof of the ark itself. Otherwise it could not have been pulled off and removed from the ark without Noah breaking and shattering the ark itself, and that rashly, since he had not received a command from God for this. Then he would have exposed himself and his people to the injuries of the sky and the cold of the night, if he had taken away the first roof of the ark itself. Therefore this is the cover which Noah took off the ark, and with it removed the ark nevertheless remained whole and complete, consisting of all its parts. The reason why he removed it is this: since neither the Raven nor the Dove was yet returning to him, from which he might conjecture how much the waters of the Flood had sunk since the third sending out of the Dove; and since he himself, God not yet commanding it, did not yet wish or was not able to leave the ark, it was necessary for him to climb to some place in the ark from which he could now look and see on every side what the face of the earth was like, how much the waters had sunk and dried up; so that by this means Noah might strengthen both himself and others in the sure faith of God's benefit, and might conceive, for the restoring of the world, the hope of soon leaving the ark, and finally might rouse himself and all who were with him in the ark to praise God immensely. Nor do I doubt that Noah's sons, his wife and his daughters-in-law, once that cover of the ark was removed, also climbed onto the roof of the ark itself, so that they might see with their own eyes such a miracle of God, and might greatly praise God from such a sight, give thanks to him and hope for their salvation before long. Therefore Noah did not remove the cover of the ark without reason or for no purpose; he did not do it rashly or from a hasty desire, but in seeking and grasping at all the lawful aids for strengthening his own faith and that of his family. Yet all of them, however much they saw from the roof of the ark that all the waters of the Flood had been dried up over the whole surface of the earth, nevertheless remained in the ark without moving

units.la: tamen men patienter in Arca, vsquequo à Deo ipso inberentur ex ea egredi, & Mundum instaurare. Quæ quæ de secundo nostræ historiæ capite dicta sint, iam ad tertium accedamus. Continet autem Noachi, & eorum omnium, qui in Arca erant, etiam animalium ipsorum egressum ex eadem arca iussu Dei factum 27 die mensis secundi anni Noachi 601.
units.tr: Yet they waited patiently in the ark until God himself should command them to leave it and restore the world. Having said what needs saying about the second chapter of our history, let us now come to the third. It contains the departure of Noah, and of all who were in the ark, together with the animals themselves, from the same ark, made by the command of God on the 27th day of the second month of Noah's 601st year.

units.la: Ad III. Noachi ex Arca egressus.
units.tr: On III. Noah's coming out of the Ark.

units.la: Quaritur, Quinam sint montes Ararati, in quorum uno, quemadmodum Moses scribit Gen. 8. 4, Arca subsitit aquis subsidentibus. R. Isti montes sint sunt in ea Assyriæ parte, quæ Armenia Maior à scriptoribus Græcis & Latinis dicta est. Fit quidem à Strabone lib. 16. mentio Ararenæ regionis, quæ Arabicæ Petræ pars est: sed illa nequaquam ad hoc pertinet loci. Nam in Oriente, non in Meridie subsistit Arca illa; & qui montes omnium altissimi esse scribuntur, illi in Armenia, non in Arabia statuuntur, velut à Strabone lib. 11. & Dionysio Alexand. de Situ Orbis. Arachosiam appellatse videtur Am. Marcellinus lib. 23 Hist. eam ipsam regionem, quam Moses vocat Ararat. Sed quid verbis opus est? Huius ipsius regionis meminit alibi quoque S. Scriptura, veluti 2. Reg. 19. 37, Isa. 37 38, Hierem. 51. 27. Ex quibus locis eam regionem Armeniæ Maioris partem esse constat. Id quod verum esse confirmat quoque Plinius, qui lib. 6 Natur. Hist. cap. 13. populos Aratiaticos (melius autem Araratiaticos) in illa Armenia collocat. Hos autem quis ab Ararati dictos neget? Sed & in Itinerario Antonini in descriptione Armeniæ commemoratur Araratbia oppidum, quod est a Mosaica voce Ararati proculdubio nominatum. Hanc quoque vocem in descriptione Assyriæ seu Armeniæ restituit apud Aethicum veteris satis autorem Iosias Simlerus. Denique huius Ararath & Epiphanius lib. 1. Tomo 1. haresi 18, & Isidorus lib. 14. Etymolog. cap. 8. meminêre graves autores. Iosephus lib. 1. Antiquit. cap. 5. Montem huc vocat ex veteri autore Mnasea Damasceno [Barin] quem etiam consultuit in Armenia Maiore supra Minniadam, id est, Armeniam Minorem. Minnij enim vel Minniau, ut apparet ex Hierem. 51. 27, est Armenia Minor, dicta Armenia tàquam Aram Minnim, ut etiam scribit Franciscus Iunius, quae notior fuit Græcis & Latinis: ac propterea Armenia Maior tribuitur ab ijs Assyriæ. Q. Quis egres-furo ex Arca Noacho, caeterisque, offtiū illum aperuit, quum extrorsum, non autem introrsum post ingressum Noachum a Deo clausum fuisset, quemadmodum facile ex verbis Moisis colligitur, Gen. 7. 16. R. Deus ipse ostium Arcæ aperuit, quum praecepit Noacho, ut exiret ipse, uxor eius, liberi, nurus, & animalia, quæ cum eo erant. Genes. 8. 13. 14. Nam ad Dei iussum Noachus & in Arcâ ingressus est, & ex eadem exiit. Itaque uti Deus illi clauserat ostium Arcæ, sic aperuit. Q. Utrum omnia, quæ in arca erant, aperto ostio sint simul & confusè egressa, velut homines ipsi cum animalibus: an potius ordinatim: & utrum homines prius egressi, quàm animalia. R. Apparet cùm ex Dei praecepto de egrediendo, quod extat Gen. 8. 15. 16 & 17. & 17: tùm etiam ex eius implemento, quod secutum est, primùm homines ipsos egressos ex Arca:tum postea animalia. Iubetur enim Noachus exire primùm ex arca:tùm uxor & liberi,& nurus:& postea educere animalia ex eadem arca, quemadmodù idem illa primùm in Arcam admiserat. Ergo neque confuse ruerunt & proripuerunt se ex arca Bestiæ,sed prout à Noacho educebantur,apertis cellularù (in quibus singula bestiarum genera conclusa fuerant in Arca) ostiys : neque illæ primæ sunt ex Arca egressæ,neque primæ in Arcam ingressæ,verùm vtrobique post homines & ingressos,& egressos,iussu Dei,quemadmodù apparet Gen.7.14.15.
units.tr: Question: Which are the mountains of Ararat, on one of which, as Moses writes in Gen. 8. 4, the Ark rested when the waters subsided? Answer: These mountains lie in that part of Assyria which the Greek and Latin writers call Greater Armenia. Strabo, book 16, does mention the region of Ararene, which is part of Arabia Petraea, but that has nothing to do with this place. For the Ark rested in the East, not the South, and the mountains which are said to be the highest of all are placed in Armenia, not Arabia, as Strabo (book 11) and Dionysius of Alexandria in On the Description of the World state. Ammianus Marcellinus (book 23 of his History) seems to call by the name Arachosia that very region which Moses calls Ararat. But why use many words? Holy Scripture mentions this same region elsewhere too, as in 2 Kings 19:37, Isa. 37:38 and Jer. 51:27, and from these passages it is clear that the region is part of Greater Armenia. Pliny confirms that this is true: in book 6, chapter 13 of his Natural History he places the Aratiaci (or better, Araratiaci) peoples in that Armenia. And who would deny that these were named after Ararat? Moreover, in the description of Armenia in the Itinerary of Antoninus the town of Araratbia is mentioned, which is certainly named from the Mosaic word Ararat. Josias Simlerus also restores this same word in the description of Assyria or Armenia in Aethicus, a fairly ancient author. Finally, the serious authors Epiphanius (book 1, tome 1, heresy 18) and Isidore (Etymologies, book 14, chapter 8) also mention this Ararat. Josephus (Antiquities, book 1, chapter 5), citing the ancient author Mnaseas of Damascus, calls the mountain here [Barin], which he also places in Greater Armenia, above Minniadas, that is, Lesser Armenia. For Minni or Minniu, as appears from Jer. 51:27, is Lesser Armenia, called Armenia as if it were Aram Minnim, as Francis Junius also writes; this was better known to Greeks and Latins, and for that reason the Assyrians attribute Greater Armenia to these places. Question: Who opened the door of the Ark for Noah and the others, since it had been shut from the outside, not from the inside, after Noah entered, as is easily gathered from the words of Moses in Gen. 7:16? Answer: God himself opened the door of the Ark when he commanded Noah to go out, himself, his wife, sons, daughters-in-law and the animals that were with him (Gen. 8:13-14). For Noah both entered the Ark and came out of it at God's command. Therefore, just as God had shut the door of the Ark for him, so he opened it. Question: Did everything that was in the Ark come out together and in confusion when the door was opened, the humans along with the animals, or rather in order; and did the humans come out before the animals? Answer: This is clear both from God's command about going out, which stands in Gen. 8:15, 16 and 17, and from its fulfilment that followed: first the humans themselves came out of the Ark, and afterwards the animals. For Noah is commanded to go out first from the Ark, then his wife and sons and daughters-in-law, and afterwards to lead the animals out of the same Ark, just as he had earlier admitted them first into the Ark. So the beasts did not rush out of the Ark in confusion and throw themselves out, but were brought out by Noah, the doors of their compartments (in which each kind of beast had been shut up in the Ark) being opened. So they neither came out of the Ark first, nor entered it first, but in both cases came after the humans, both entering and leaving, by God's command, as appears from Gen. 7:14-15.

units.la: Q. Vtrum omnia,quæ fuerant in Arca sint egressa vno die. R. Id quidè manifestè non declarat S.Scriptura:Si quis tamen cóieɛluris locus est,censuerim ipse quod,quemadmodum & quanto tempore illa in arcam ingressa sunt,sic & tanto spatio ex eadem exiuisse. Apparet autem ex Gen.7.4. penè dies totos septem Noachum in Arcam introisse,priusquam omnia animalia in eandem confluxissent, & interim dum illa in Arcam recipit ipse. Ergo totidem diebus, nempe septem, post egressum Noachum,& eius familiam(quam ex Gen.7 13 statuo eodem die totam ex Arca exisse, vti in eam intrauerat)animalia bruta ex eadem arca secundù sua genera sunt ordinatim emissa. Tantum igitur temporis spatium nimirum septimanam dierum totam tribuo illi rei,quâ sumpsit sibi Noachus ad animalia extrahenda seriatim & producenda, & in diuersas Mundi partes ex Arca dimittenda. Q. Quo ordine Noachus,& eius familia sit ex Arca egressa, Vtrum mares omnes coniunctim & prius: & postea fœmina. R. Hoc vbi- que in tota hac egressione ex arca statuo, sumo, Eodem ordine omnia in egredie lo gesta esse, quo in ingrediendo fuerant. Quare quum viri seu mares, nempe Noachus & tres eius filij Sem, Cam, & Iaphet primi fuerint ingressi in arcam, & quidem ante mulieres omnes, adeoante matrem suam id est, vxorem Noachi, Gen. 7. 7 13: sic ex eadem Arca viri & mares primi, & ante fœminas omnes exierunt, Gen. 8. 18 (quanquam tamen omnes eodem die Gen. 7. 13) etiam filij ante matrem suam & Noachi vxorem. Ergo quod Gen. 8. 16 videtur vxor Noachi suberi prius egredi, & ante filios suos, accipi debet quasi in globo dictum & præceptum, vt omnes ex arca exirent, velut Gen. 7 1: non vt ordo exeundi præscriptus illic fuerit, qui, quema modum supra demonstraui, cum ex verf. 18. eiusdem cap intelligi: tum ex ordine & ratione ingrediendi colligi debet. Neque tamen quod liberi ante matrem suam ingrediuntur, vel egrediuntur ex Arca, id ab iis factum est ex vllo cotemptu, aut irreuerentia matris: sed vt patri Noacho adiutores essent ad omnia parandi, quæ ad introitum vel exitum omnium erant necessaria, etiam mulierum ipsarum. Quamobrem quum scribit Augustinus lib. 12. contra Faustum Manich. cap. 21, Homines de Arca coniunctos exijse, qui disiuncti in eam intrauerant, meo quidem iudicio fallitur. Eodem enim prorsus modo digressi sunt ex Arca, quo fuerant in eam prius ingressi, nempe primum Noachus, dein Sem, Cam, & Iaphet. Vtrobiq, viri seorsim, & seorsim fœminæ siue in intrando, siue in exeundo. Cessent igitur omnes, quas in ista di- neruerfitate ( quam falso esse putat Augustinus) quærit, allegoriæ: nihil enim diuersum gestū est in exitu à primo introitu. Q. Q uomodo animalia ex Arca e- grefla sint,vel educta à Noacho. R. Primùm per genera quæ, sua, non confuse, velut Cerui,& Leones: Lupi,& Oues: Volatilia,& Canes, seu terrestria animalia:item Munda & Immunda simul, Genef.8.19. Ergo quum Leones emitti à Noacho ex cellulis & stabulis suis coepissent omnes emissi sunt ex arca, priusquā Cerui, vel aliud aliquod animalium genus quadrupes & terrestre ab eodem Noacho educeretur. Sic de reliquis animalibus terrestribus. Deinde ad Volatilia dimittenda ventum est, quæ ipsa quoque vnumquodq; secundum genus suū emissa sunt,velut Accipitres omnes, deinde Columbæ:& sic de cæteris volatilibus. Bina verò simul emittebantur à Noacho & filiis eius ex suis nidis & cellulis,nempe ex vnoquoque genere mas & fœmina, vti bina in Arcam fuerant, ingressa, Gen.7.9,& 16. Ergo Leo vnus,& Leæna vna simul educebatur ex arca: deinde Leo adhuc vnus,& Leæna adhuc vna,donec huius generis omnes ex suo stabulo educti fuissent. Sic ex Coruis,Coruus vnus mas,& Coruus vnus fœmina si- mul:deinde Coruus adhuc vnus mas, & Coruus adhuc vnus fœmina, vsquequo Corui omnes ex suo nido fuifsent dimissi: & sic de omnibus bestiis,nisi si quas ad sacerisicium Soteriorum reseruauit Noachus,vti quasdā conseruauit. Ex quo apparet bestias quantumuis feras & nobis hodie crudeles & intractabiles, fuisse tamen tunc & in ingressu in arcā, & in exitu ex arca Noacho filiis eius subiectas,tractabiles,domitas,Domino Deo ferociam earum sic dom inte, & contundente. Q. Verum prius Immunda animalia sint in arca & ingressa & egressa ex ea quam Munda: an potius contra, Mun-da prius, Immunda posterius. R. Quanquam id dif-ferte non explicat Moses, tamen quia quum de eorum in Arcam intromissu agit, prius semper Munda quam Immunda commemorat, & appellat: Idcirco Munda prius in Arcam intrasse crediderim, posteaque vero Immunda. Ergo & eadem Munda animalia prius egressa fuerint i. ante Immunda. Q uum autem Munda emisit Noachus ex vnoquoque eorum genere bina, nempe marem & foeminam in cellulis vel nidis suis in sacrificium Soteriorum Deo efferenda retinuit. Ad quod sacrificium quia tandem peruentum est, estque quartum & vltimum historia nostra caput, de eo paucis agamus.
units.tr: Question: Did all that had been in the Ark come out in one day? Answer: Holy Scripture does not clearly declare this. If, however, there is any place for conjecture, I would suppose that they came out over the same length of time in which they went in. It appears from Gen. 7:4 that Noah took almost seven whole days to enter the Ark before all the animals had flowed into it, and meanwhile he was receiving them into the Ark. Therefore for as many days, namely seven, after Noah and his family came out (which, from Gen. 7:13, I hold came out of the Ark all on the same day, as they had gone in), the brute animals were sent out of the Ark in order, according to their kinds. So I assign to that task the whole length of time, a full week of days, which Noah took to bring out and lead forth the animals one by one, and to release them from the Ark into the various parts of the world. Question: In what order did Noah and his family come out of the Ark: were all the males together and first, and afterwards the females? Answer: I hold and assume that throughout this whole going out of the Ark, everything was done in the same order as when they went in. For since the men, that is Noah and his three sons Shem, Ham and Japheth, went into the Ark first, and indeed before all the women, even before their mother, that is Noah's wife (Gen. 7:7, 13), so from the same Ark the men and males came out first, before all the females (Gen. 8:18), although all on the same day (Gen. 7:13), and the sons came out before their mother, Noah's wife. Therefore what appears in Gen. 8:16, that Noah's wife seems to come out before her sons, should be understood as a general statement and command that all should come out of the Ark, as in Gen. 7:1, and not as if an order of going out were prescribed there. This, as I have shown above from verse 18 of the same chapter, must be understood, and also gathered from the order and manner of going in. Nor did the sons go in or come out before their mother out of any contempt or disrespect for her; rather, they were helpers to their father Noah in preparing everything needful for the entry and exit of all, the women included. Therefore when Augustine writes (book 12 against Faustus the Manichaean, chapter 21) that men came out of the Ark joined together, though they had gone in separately, I think he is mistaken. For they went out in exactly the same way as they had earlier gone in: first Noah, then Shem, Ham and Japheth. In each case the men went separately and the women separately, whether entering or leaving. Therefore let all the allegories cease which he seeks in this supposed difference (which Augustine wrongly thinks exists), for nothing was done differently in the exit from what was done at the first entry. Question: In what way were the animals brought out or led forth from the Ark by Noah? Answer: First, by their kinds, not in confusion, such as the stags and lions, wolves and sheep, birds and dogs, or land animals; likewise clean and unclean together (Gen. 8:19). So when the lions had begun to be released by Noah from their cells and stalls, they were all brought out of the Ark before the stags, or any other kind of four-footed land animal, was led out by the same Noah. So it was with the other land animals. Then it came to the release of the birds, and these too were sent out each according to its own kind: for example all the hawks, then the doves, and so with the other birds. Two at a time were released by Noah and his sons from their nests and cells, namely a male and a female of each kind, just as two of each had gone into the Ark (Gen. 7:9, 16). So one male lion and one female lion were led out of the Ark together; then again one male lion and one female lion, until all of this kind had been led out of their stall. Likewise with the crows: one male crow and one female crow together, then again one male crow and one female crow, until all the crows had been released from their nest. And so with all the beasts, except any which Noah kept back for the sacrifice of the peace offerings, as he kept some back. From this it appears that the beasts, however fierce and now cruel and untractable to us, were then, both in entering the Ark and in leaving it, subject to Noah and his sons, tractable and tamed, their ferocity being so tempered and broken by the Lord God. Question: Did the unclean animals enter the Ark and leave it before the clean, or rather the reverse: clean first, unclean afterwards? Answer: Although Moses does not explain this in detail, yet, since when he speaks of their being admitted into the Ark he always mentions and names the clean before the unclean, I would believe that the clean entered the Ark first and the unclean afterwards. So the same clean animals also came out first, that is, before the unclean. And when Noah released the clean from each of their kinds, two at a time, namely a male and a female, he kept back from their nests or cells those to be offered to God in the sacrifice of the peace offerings. Since we have now come to that sacrifice, which is the fourth and last chapter of our history, let us deal with it briefly.

units.la: Ad III. Sacrificium Soteriorum a Noa-cho factum.
units.tr: On III. The Sacrifice of Salvation Made by Noah.

units.la: Quaeritur, Quot ex vnoquoque mundorum animalium genere capita Noachus obtulerit Deo Soteriorum i. salutis recepta nomine posteaque egressum. R. Bina tantum, nempe marem & foeminam ex vnaquaque mundorum animalium specie Noachus tunc sacrificauit, vt totum eorum genus, hoc velut primitiuum in mysculo & foemina Deo consecraret, esseque Deo sancto & gratum quicquid ex iis animalibus postea in perpetuum nascerentur. Ergo septem paria, id est, impari numero ex Mundis animalibus in Arcam ingressa fuerant, Gen. 7. 3. vt ex eo numero par vnum i. marem & foeminam Deo postea Noachus in sacrificium offerret, ac totum Mundum futurum eidem dedicaret. Dicitur autem hoc sacrificiū fuisse Deo boni odoris, Gen.8.21. Cuius etiā sacrificij & Cinerum eius, & Altaris reliquias extitisse adhuc suo seculo in mōtibus Armeniæ scribit Epiphanius lib. 1.Tom.1.hæresi 18. Q. Quod sacrificij genus fuerit illud, quod primum Deo Noachus post suū ex arca egressum obtulit, Vtrum expiatorium, quemadmodum scribit Flavius Iosephus lib.1.Antiq.Iudaic.cap.6:an verò potiùs Eucharisticum, vt putant ȳ, qui illud Σωτηρια vocant. R. Partim Expiatorium, partim etiā Eucharisticum fuit. Ac quidem Expiatorium, quatenus pro pace Mundi in futurum à Deo exquirenda, & Deo ipsò propter hominū peccata irato placando fuit oblatum: Eucharisticum autem, quatenus idem Sacrificium Sotericum est, id est, pro salute Mundo à Deo data offerebatur, & gratiarum actio erat, quam Deo Noachus pro femine Mundi futuri conseruato agebat. Itaque missum fuit hoc sacrificium, magneq; vtilitatis.
units.tr: Question: How many animals of each clean kind did Noah offer to God of Salvation, that is, to God under the name of the salvation received, after he came out of the ark? Answer: Noah then sacrificed only two, a male and a female, from each species of clean animal, so that the whole kind would be consecrated to God in this firstfruits pair, and whatever was afterwards born of those animals in perpetuity would be holy and pleasing to God. For seven pairs, that is an odd number, of the clean animals had entered the ark (Gen. 7.3), so that from that number Noah might offer one pair, a male and a female, to God, and dedicate the whole future clean stock to him. This sacrifice is said to have been a sweet-smelling savour to God (Gen. 8.21). Epiphanius, in book 1, volume 1, heresy 18, writes that remains of this sacrifice, its ashes and the altar, were still to be seen in his own time on the mountains of Armenia. Question: What kind of sacrifice was it that Noah first offered to God after coming out of the ark? Was it an expiatory sacrifice, as Flavius Josephus writes (Jewish Antiquities, book 1, chapter 6), or rather a eucharistic sacrifice, as those think who call it the sacrifice of salvation [Σωτηρια]? Answer: It was partly expiatory and partly eucharistic. It was expiatory insofar as it was offered to seek from God peace for the world in the future, and to appease God himself, who was angry because of men's sins. It was eucharistic insofar as it was a sacrifice of salvation, that is, it was offered for the salvation given by God to the world, and it was an act of thanksgiving which Noah rendered to God for the preservation of the seed of the future world. So this sacrifice was a welcome one and of great use.

units.la: Q. Cur hoc Noachi sacrificiū Deo gratum fuerit, Vtrum propter hostiarum seu victimarum multitudinem: an potiùs propter ipsius Noachi illud offerentis fidem in Deum. R. Quum Deus victimarum neque sanguine, neque numero per se deleceretur, Psal.50: non potuit propter victimarū numerum gratū esse Deo Noachi sacrificium. Etsi enim propter hostiarum illarum varietatem (Nam ex omni Mundorum animalium sive terrestrium sive volatilium genere par obtulit Noachus) fuit singulare ac unicum hoc sacrificium, quale neque antea, neque postea vllum fuisse cõmemoratur: multitudine tamen bestiarum non est vel cum illo Solomonis conferendum, vbi viginti duo millia boum casa dicuntur, & centum viginti millia ovium mactata, 1. Reg. 8.64: vel cum illo Ezechiæ regis, in quo mille tauri occisi sunt, & ones decies mille, 2. Chron. 30.24: vel etiam cum illo Josia, vbi oblata fuere tria boum millia, ovium autem agnorum, & hædorum triginta millia, 2. Chron. 35.7. Sed neque cum illis Ethnicorum Imperatorum, velut Alexandri Magni, & Marci Philosophi Imperatoris Romani Hecatombis, in quibus apud Ammian. Marcellinū extat hæc Boum querimonia, lib. 25: Οἱ ἀλλοι ... Albi boues Marco Cæsari, Si tu viceris, nos perymus, tam fuit profusa, & immanis stlorum hominum Ethnicorum in sacrificiado prodigalitas, & mactatio boum, vt pene ad edendū boves deficerent, tam furiose, tantoq; numero eos Ethnici sisti diis suis offerebant. Ergo & Alexandri, & Marci hominū infidelium sacrificia Deo placuissent, quod nemo pius vnquam dixerit, senseritve. Quid igitur? Cur Noachi sacrificiū odoratus est Deus bona flagrantia, & habuit gratum? Nimirum propter fidem Noachi, quā habuit ille quidem primum in vniuersum in Deū ipsum, in quem velut omnipotentem & Deum verum & solum Noachus credidit: Postea in eius peculiare promissum de se, & ýs (quæ in Arca erant) omnibus ad futuri mundi propagationem conseruādis: Denique de Messia futuro, & semine illo mulieris, quod caput Serpentis cōtereret: quem & venturū credidit, & per propterque eum Messiam se, piosque futuros Deo gratos fore Noachus credidit, nec Mundum hunc prius esse omnino delendum, quàm Deus hoc suum promissum praestitisset, ac impleuisset. Ex quibus apparet Noachum uti isthuc fidei sua in Arca collocatum fuisse cum omnibus cœlis, marisque periculis & procellis, cum ipso terrore mortis totties ante oculos versantis, cum impatientia carnis, & cæteris eiusmodi ac pene infinitis tentationibus. Denique ut fidei illius etiam in Arca tanquam in sepulcro Noachum eundem vitâ tamen sperasse, & patienter suam liberationem à Deo & petysse, & exspectasse. Postquam egressum igitur suum in illa fide sua confirmatus, & Dei promissionum erga se & suos implementum cernens Noachus maiori adhuc cum fide in Deum egressus est, quàm ingressus fuerat, Deóque sacrificat. Ergo propter illam Noachi fidem gratum fuit Deo illius sacrificium, Heb. 11.7, Gen. 8.21. Illa enim est, quæ nos nostrasque actiones Deo commendat, & acceptas reddit, Heb. 11.6, Habac. 2.4, Rom. 5.1.2.3.
units.tr: Question: Why was this sacrifice of Noah pleasing to God? Was it because of the multitude of the victims, or rather because of the faith in God of Noah himself, who offered it? Answer: Since God is not delighted in himself by the blood or the number of victims (Ps. 50), the sacrifice of Noah could not have been pleasing to God because of the number of victims. For although, because of the variety of those victims (for Noah offered a pair from every kind of clean animal, both land and winged), this sacrifice was singular and unique, such as is recorded to have been neither before nor after, yet the multitude of beasts is not to be compared even with that of Solomon, where twenty-two thousand oxen and a hundred and twenty thousand sheep are said to have been slaughtered (1 Kings 8.64); nor with that of King Hezekiah, where a thousand bulls and ten thousand sheep were killed (2 Chron. 30.24); nor even with that of Josiah, where three thousand oxen and thirty thousand lambs and kids were offered (2 Chron. 35.7). Nor is it to be compared with the hecatombs of the heathen emperors, such as Alexander the Great and Marcus the philosopher, Roman emperor, in which, according to Ammianus Marcellinus (book 25), this lament of the oxen is found: "The others..." [Οἱ ἀλλοι ...] "White oxen to Caesar Marcus: if you win, we perish." So lavish and monstrous was the prodigality of the heathen in sacrificing, and the slaughter of oxen, that they nearly ran short of oxen to eat, so furiously and in such numbers did the heathen offer them to their gods. Therefore, if the sacrifices of Alexander and Marcus, unbelieving men, had pleased God, no pious man would ever have said or thought so. What then? Why did God smell the sacrifice of Noah as a sweet fragrance and find it pleasing? Surely because of the faith of Noah, which he first held in God in general, believing in him as almighty, the true and only God; afterwards in God's particular promise concerning himself and all those in the ark, that they would be preserved for the propagation of the future world; and finally in the future Messiah, and that seed of the woman who would crush the serpent's head. Noah believed both that he would come, and that through him and for his sake Noah and the pious who would follow would be pleasing to God, and that this world was not to be utterly destroyed before God had fulfilled and accomplished his promise. From this it appears that Noah exercised his faith in the ark, placed there amid all the dangers of storms and waves, with the very terror of death constantly before his eyes, with the impatience of the flesh, and with other such and almost countless temptations. Finally, Noah, while in the ark, hoped for life as if in a tomb, and patiently sought and awaited his deliverance from God. Therefore, when Noah came out, confirmed in that faith, and saw God's promises to himself and his family fulfilled, he came out with an even greater faith in God than he had when he went in, and sacrificed to God. Therefore it was because of that faith of Noah that his sacrifice was pleasing to God (Heb. 11.7; Gen. 8.21). For it is faith that commends us and our actions to God and makes them acceptable (Heb. 11.6; Hab. 2.4; Rom. 5.1–3).

units.la: Q. Utrum uno & eodem die Noachus omnes illas victimas, id est, par unum ex omnibus mundis animalibus occiderit, quum solus esset cum tribus duntaxat filiis reliquis ad tantum bestiarum numerum ingulandum.
units.tr: Question: Did Noah slaughter all those victims, that is, a pair from every clean animal, on one and the same day, since he was alone with only his three remaining sons to slaughter so great a number of beasts?

units.la: R. Non definit quidem S. Scriptura Verum uno die tot victimæ fuerint mactatæ: verùm quum omnium earum oblatarum velut unius duntaxat sacrificij, & femel oblati meminerit Moses, uno & eodem die, uno eodem sacrificio victimas illas omnes oblatas fuisse Deo iudico sentiô. Fuit autem Holocaustum Sacrificium illud, quemadmodum docet Moses, Gen. 8.20, in quo tota hostiæ cremabantur: nihil autem ex ys ad conuiuium
units.tr: Answer: Holy Scripture indeed does not state that so many victims were slain on one day. But since Moses mentions all of them as one sacrifice, offered once, I judge and think that all those victims were offered to God on one and the same day, in one and the same sacrifice. That sacrifice was a burnt offering, as Moses teaches (Gen. 8.20), in which the whole victim was burned; none of it was reserved for a later sacred feast.

units.la: {y} sacrum postea peragendum referu ibatur. Et hæc quidem hactenus. Nunc ad perscrutandas istius veritatis reliquias accedamus, In quo maxima huius Historia vtilitas confirmatiõ, aduersus ἀθεους ἁμπακτους homines continetur.
units.tr: {y} And so far, indeed, for this. Now let us turn to examining the remaining traces of this truth, in which the greatest usefulness of this history lies, namely its confirmation against atheists, the most shameless men [ἀθεους ἁμπακτους].

units.la: CAPVT III.
units.tr: CAPVT III.

units.la: Vestigia superioris historię, & veritatis.
units.tr: The traces of the earlier history, and of the truth.

units.la: NON est verò futura nobis, vel cuiquam alij dubia superior historia etiam ex ipsis Ethnicorum hominum scriptis, si modò eorum (quae supra de Diluuio Vniuersali ex isdem probauimus) memoria prorsus non excidit. Cohærent enim haec cum illis, vt qui illa superiora vera, & tradita ab illis concesserit, hæc iam negare nō possit. Verùm ne qua dubitatio cuiusquam vel obstinatissimi hominis animo inhæreat, peculiariter & huius quoq; historia vestigia ex eorundem Ethnicorum libris ac traditionibus inuestigemus, à primo capite exorsi, quod est Aquarū Diluuij supra quosuis montes exundatio, & incrementum.
units.tr: The earlier history will not be doubtful to us, or to anyone else, even from the writings of the Gentiles themselves, provided that their testimony, which we have already set out above concerning the Universal Flood, has not entirely faded from memory. For these things cohere with those. Whoever has granted that the earlier accounts are true and handed down by them cannot now deny these. But so that no doubt may cling to anyone's mind, even of the most obstinate man, let us also specifically trace the vestiges of this history in the books and traditions of the same Gentiles, beginning from the first point, which is the overflowing and rising of the waters above every mountain.

units.la: Ad I. De Incremento Aquarum.
units.tr: I. On the Rising of the Waters.

units.la: Primùm quidem certo certius est omnes, qui Diluuia scripserūt, dixerúntve fuisse, idcircò ea vocasse Diluuia, quòd tunc Aqua totam terrā eius superficiem (in qua illa extiterunt) mersit, & inundauit, etiam montes ipsos, qui in eadem illa regione siti, & alti appareret. Sic enim Ouidius lib. 1. Metamorph. etiam de Deucalionis Diluuio: Obruerat tumulos immensa licentia Ponti, Pulsabantq; noui montana cacumina fluctus.
units.tr: First of all, it is quite certain that all who have written or spoken of floods have said that they were called floods because at that time the water covered and inundated the whole surface of the land in which they occurred, even the mountains themselves, which were situated and appeared high in that same region. Thus Ovid, in Metamorphoses book 1, speaks even of Deucalion's flood: "The immense licence of the sea had overwhelmed the hills, and the waves beat against the mountain peaks."

units.la: Horatius item lib. 1. Carm. Ode 2. de Inundatione Tyberis, & de eo ipso Deucalionis diluuio agens, docet iptes ipsos tunc aquis fuisse obrutos. Sic enim canit: Terruit gentes, graue ne redirent Seculum Pyrrhæ nova monstra quæstæ, Omne quum Protheus pecus egit altos Visere montes. Piscium & summa genus haesit vlmo. (Nota quæ sedes fuerat Columbæ) Et superiecto pauidi natarint Aequore Dama.
units.tr: Horace too, in the first book of Odes, Ode 2, speaking of the flooding of the Tiber and of that very flood of Deucalion, shows that the mountain peaks themselves were then overwhelmed by the waters. For he sings: "He terrified the nations, lest the grievous age of Pyrrha return, complaining of new portents, when Proteus drove his whole flock to visit the high mountains. The fish of the sea clung to the top of the elm (which had once been the dove's nest), and the frightened deer swam across the water that had covered the plain."

units.la: Ergo quod scribit Pausanias lib. 1. Megarum quendam tempore Deucalionei diluuij sese recepisse in montem Megara regionis nomine Geraniam, vbi sernatus fuerit, quod diluuij illius aquæ in cacumen istius montis non peruenissent, merè est fabulosum: quemadmodū & illud, quod Ouidius eodem libro 1 Metamorph. & idē Pausanias lib. 10. volunt Parnassū montem aquis illis minimè tunc obrutū fuisse, sed superiorem. quum idem hic Pausanias fateatur oppidū, quod in cacumine Parnassi situm erat, aquis tunc fuisse mersum. Quod accidere certe quidem non potuit, nisi diluuij istius aquæ ad caput ipsum montis ascendissent illúdque etiam ipsum texissent. Sed quum rationem, qua Deucalion cum
units.tr: So what Pausanias writes in book 1 is pure fable: that a certain Megarian, at the time of Deucalion's flood, took refuge on a mountain in the Megarid called Geranea, and was saved there because the waters of that flood did not reach the summit of that mountain. Likewise the claim that Ovid in the first book of the Metamorphoses, and Pausanias in book 10, say that Mount Parnassus was not covered at all by those waters but rose above them. Yet this same Pausanias admits that a town which stood on the summit of Parnassus was then submerged by the waters. Certainly this could not have happened unless the waters of that flood had risen to the very top of the mountain and covered it entirely.

units.la: Pyrrha vxore seruatus esset ex illis aquis, non reperireni (fuit autem in Noacho Arca: & nauigiū in Deucalione isto recentiore.) finxerunt Parnassum montem superiorem illis aquis manssisse, in quem Deucalion, & Pyrrha soli confugissent. Sed cur non etiam aliy in eandem se quoque recepissent? Ergo Diluuij cuiusuis quonis tempore definitio in eo est, quod tota terra illius, in qua diluuiū euenit. superficies tecta fuit aquis: ac proinde montes quoq; ipsi illius loci. Sunt enim pars superficiei terrae. Quamobrem hoc ipsum multo magis in hoc Vniuersali Diluuio accidit. Sed ne cuiquam vel minimum eius rei scrupulus resteret, en ex ipsis Ethnicorum libris testimonia manifesta, quae sunt certissima nostrae veritatis vestigia: Ac primum Abydeni testimonium veteris scriptoris, quod extat apud Cyrillum, lib. 1. contra Iulianū, qui tempore istius diluuij nullibi terras aquis nudatas & immunes fuisse scribit, ex vetustissima traditione, ac memoria. Idem Mnaseas Damascen. apud Iosephum lib. 1. Antiquit. cap. 5. tradit, nimirum in illo Diluuio omnes Orbis montes summersos fuisse, praeter unum omnium excelsissimum, qui situs est supra Miniadam. id est, supra Minorem Armeniam in maiore Armenia, qui mons, ait, Baris dicitur, in quo se cum Arca pius quidam vir seruauit. Berosus lib. 1. de eodem diluuio loquens, ait, [Fluminaq; & fontes ab imo ebullientes supra omnes montes excessisse, accedentibus & impetuosissimè ac praeter naturā e coelo per multos dies corruentibus copiosissimis imbribus.] Idē Cato in frag. & Archilochus de Temporibus. Sed & Tertullianus licet autor Christianus, tamen ex Ethnicorum & scriptis ptis & consensu in lib.de Pallio: & Isidorus lib.13.cap. 22. Etymologic.idem prodiderunt, in illo diluuio omnes terræ montes aquis obrutos fuisse. Solinus quoque, sed autor Ethnicus in Polyhist cap.15, etsi ipse illud Diluuium Deucalioneum vocat. Nam quod de Noe, seu veteris Deucalionis Diluuio tradit Moses, Graci homines ambitiosi ad suum & iunioris Deucalionis diluuium transtulerunt. Ex quibus, uti etiam iam annotaui, omnino falsa ineptaque apparet Iudæorum Thalmudistarum sententia, qui negant aquas illius Diluuij usque ad verticem montis Sionis (ubi postea Templum Dei positum fuit) peruenisse, vel ascendisse: Imo eum vel falsè cubitis totis quindecim superarunt, nedum ut eo inferiores fuisse censeantur. Sed ad secundum caput nostræ Historiæ pergamus, ubi de Coruo & Columba emissis à Noacho agitur, & loco ubi substitit Arca Noachi, illiusque etiam reliquijs, quæ diu in eo loco permansere. Iam verò quæ rerum istarum apud Ethnicos scriptores extent vestigia, videamus.
units.tr: Being saved from those waters with his wife Pyrrha, they could not find him (there was an Ark in Noah's case, and a ship in this later Deucalion). They invented that Mount Parnassus stayed above those waters, into which Deucalion and Pyrrha alone had fled. But why did no others also take refuge there? So the defining mark of any flood at any time is that the whole surface of the land where the flood happened was covered by waters, and consequently also the mountains of that place, since they are part of the earth's surface. Much more, then, does this apply to this Universal Flood. But lest anyone have the slightest scruple about this matter, here are clear testimonies from the books of the Gentiles themselves, which are most certain traces of our truth. First, the testimony of the ancient writer Abydenus, extant in Cyril, book 1 against Julian, who writes that at the time of that flood no lands anywhere were bared of water or free from it, according to the most ancient tradition and memory. The same Mnaseas of Damascus, in Josephus, Antiquities book 1 chapter 5, relates that in that Flood all the mountains of the world were submerged except one, the highest of all, which lies above Miniadis, that is, above Lesser Armenia in Greater Armenia; this mountain, he says, is called Baris, where a certain pious man saved himself with the Ark. Berosus, speaking of the same flood in book 1, says: [Rivers and springs welling up from the depths rose above all the mountains, and with most abundant rains falling from heaven violently and beyond nature for many days.] Likewise Cato in a fragment, and Archilochus in On Times. But also Tertullian, though a Christian author, nonetheless drawing from the Gentile writings and their consensus, in his book On the Pallium, and Isidore, Etymologies book 13 chapter 22, have handed down the same: that in that flood all the mountains of the earth were overwhelmed by waters. Solinus too, though a Gentile author, in Polyhistor chapter 15, even though he himself calls that flood the Deucalionean flood. For what Moses hands down about Noah, or the flood of the older Deucalion, the ambitious Greeks transferred to their own flood and to that of the younger Deucalion. From these things, as I have already noted, the opinion of the Jewish Talmudists appears entirely false and foolish, who deny that the waters of that flood reached or rose up to the summit of Mount Zion (where the Temple of God was later placed). Indeed, they falsely put the water fifteen full cubits above it, let alone think it was lower than that. But let us proceed to the second chapter of our History, where the Raven and the Dove sent out by Noah are discussed, and the place where Noah's Ark came to rest, and also its remains, which long stayed in that place. Now let us see what traces of these things survive in the writings of the Gentiles.

units.la: Ad II. De Diluuio cessante, & Coruo, & Columba.
units.tr: On the Flood Ceasing, and on the Raven and the Dove.

units.la: AC primum quidem de Coruo & Columba certè auspicia & auguria, id est, prædictiones rerum futurarum (quales est euentus belli, felicitas vel infelicitas inceptorum nostrorum, cæteraque huiusmodi) ex isto Noachi facto male abEthnicis postea interpretato natas esse non dubito, quòd hominum memoria inhæreret primum illu noui huius Mundi parentem Noachum anibus ad explorandas Diluuij aquas vsum esse, & ad iram Dei (sedatáne iam profsus esset, an nondum placata) perscrutandam. Nonquid eas aues quas emisit Noachus, facerent voluntatis Dei interpretes, & internuntias sicut Ethnici illi censuerunt, sed quod ex Corui & Columbæ volatu coniecerent, Utrum aquæ Diluuij adhuc aliæ essent in terræ superficie, necne. Quamobrem illi abusi hac prudenti Noachi coniectura & consilio Ethnici, ex avibus auguria auspiciaque ad res futuras prædicendas, Deíq; voluntatem expiscandam (quasi illæ essent Dei internuntiæ) postea instituerunt: quæ quanquam sunt illæ quidè superstitiosa, sunt tamen vestigia emissi à Noacho ex Arca Corui, Columbæq; ad tentandas explorandasve Diluuij aquas. Quemadmodum autem Corvum emisit Noachus. Sic autem hanc Ethnici homines in auspiciis suis potissimum sequuntur. Corvum enim autem maximè & intelligetem, & aptam ad res futuras prænuntiandas esse volunt. Plinius lib. 10 Nat. Hist. cap. 12, [Corui, inquit, in auspiciis soli videntur intellectum habere significationum suarum. Nam quum Media hostium occisi sunt, omnes è Peloponneso, & Attica (ubi propterea insignissima bella fuere) volarunt. Aelianus lib. 15 Hist. Animal. cap 40: [Si quod ad Deum pertinet, ait, Corvus agit, sacrum quippiam & divinationis plenum loquitur.] Et cap. 42: [Coruum, ait, Apollinis sacrum esse, eumque pedisequum esse dicunt (qui Deus Apollo divinationibus præest ex sententia Ethnicorum) & idcirco Corvum auscultandi facultate præditum fatentur, eiusque clamorem observant, qui augurem sedes, & clangere, & volatus ipsarum à dextra & à sinistra cognocognosciunt] id est, qui auspicia observant. Huic consentit Plutarchus, qui in lib. de Ifide ex omnium Graecorum Ethnicorum sententia recepta sic scribit: [Graeci reste, quum dicunt & sentiunt Columbam esse animal sacrum Veneri, Draconem Minervae, Corvum Apollinis, Canem Dianae. Fulgentius lib. 1. Mythologic. [In Apollinis tutela Corvum ponunt] ait. Cuius rei causa afferre varias, sed tum ex Anaximandro, tum ex Pindaro hanc probat, quod solus Corvus & res futuras, & vocum significationes inter omnes aves novit. Huius virtusque summae pra ceteris avibus Corvi sapientiae testimonium proferunt. Ac quidem quod res futuras Corvus praesagit, exemplum testatum extat, ut scribit Pausanias lib. 10, praeter illa Plinij supra commemorata, quod quum Athenienses infelicissimam illam in Siciliam navigationem suscepissent, statuam aurum detraxit Corvus, quia in Delphis collocarant Athenienses. Quod autem idem Corvus aliis humanas voces & intelligit, & fingit, prodidit Plinius lib. 10. cap. 43. De Cornorum intellig. Scribit Aelianus lib. 15. cap. 40. esse talem ut ad hominis imitationem alia sit vox Corvi ludentis, alia serio agentis. Plutarchus item in libro, Utrum animalia ratione vestria, quam aquatilia plus rationis habeant, ex experientia ipsa probat hoc ipsum. Sed hoc superstitiose in Corvo notatum est, quod de Augurijs istis, & rerum futurarum praedictione Ethnici tradunt: Est tamen, ut dixi, illius emissionis Corvi ex Arca ad indicandam aquarum Diluvii altitudinem vestigium obscurum & depravatum. Illud vero & recte, & conuenienter eius naturae fuit observatum, Corvum nempe pluviae futuræ e prasagam esse auem, ac pranuntiam, quod quum sit teperamento siccissimo, facile aeris mutationem, & pluuia aduentum sentiat. Id quod vary prodiderunt, & res ipsa docet. Aratus in fine Φαυουέναν sic ait, -- Καί τε Κόρακες δὶς καλαγμές Φαυῆ ἐωμιήσαντο σωὸ ὑς ἀτ' ἐχομένοιο Ἠποτε ἢ κέρκα τε βαρείᾳ δασάκι φαυῇ Μακρὸν ἔπ' ποιζεῦσι πνασζομένοι τῆς τυχρά.
