units.tr: First, as to the raven and the dove: I do not doubt that the auspices and auguries, that is, predictions of future events (such as the outcome of a war, the success or failure of our undertakings, and other things of this kind), arose from this act of Noah's, which the heathens later misinterpreted. The memory of men clung to the fact that Noah, the first parent of this new world, had used birds to explore the waters of the Flood and to find out whether God's anger had fully subsided or was not yet appeased. The birds Noah sent out were not, as those heathens supposed, interpreters and messengers of God's will; rather, from the flight of the raven and the dove he would conjecture whether the waters of the Flood were still on the surface of the earth. The heathens therefore abused this prudent conjecture and counsel of Noah, and afterwards established auguries and auspices from birds for foretelling future events and for discovering the will of God (as if the birds were God's messengers). Although these practices are superstitious, they are nevertheless traces of the raven and dove that Noah sent out of the Ark to test and explore the waters of the Flood. Now, the way Noah sent out the raven is exactly the way the heathens chiefly follow in their auspices. For they hold that the raven is especially intelligent and fit to foretell the future. Pliny, Natural History, Book 10, chapter 12: "Ravens," he says, "alone seem in auspices to understand the meaning of their signs. For when the Medes were slain, all of them flew out of the Peloponnese and Attica (where for that reason there had been the most notable wars)." Aelian, Animal History, Book 15, chapter 40: "If the raven does something that pertains to God," he says, "it utters something sacred and full of divination." And chapter 42: "They say that the raven is sacred to Apollo, and that it is his attendant (the god Apollo presides over divinations, according to the opinion of the heathens); and so they declare that the raven is endowed with the faculty of listening, and they observe its cry, and by its seat, its croaking, and the flights of the birds on the right and on the left they know," that is, they observe the auspices. Plutarch agrees with this; in his book On Isis, following the accepted opinion of all the Greek heathens, he writes thus: "The Greeks rightly say and think that the dove is the animal sacred to Venus, the dragon to Minerva, the raven to Apollo, the dog to Diana." Fulgentius, Mythology, Book 1: "They place the raven under the protection of Apollo," he says. For the reason for this he gives various accounts, but he proves it, from Anaximander and also from Pindar, by the fact that the raven alone among all birds knows both future events and the meanings of voices. They bring forward, as evidence of the highest wisdom of the raven above other birds, this twofold virtue. And indeed that the raven foretells future events is attested by an example, as Pausanias writes in Book 10, besides those mentioned above by Pliny: when the Athenians undertook that most unlucky voyage to Sicily, a raven tore off a golden statue, because the Athenians had placed it in Delphi. That the same raven both understands and imitates human voices, Pliny has reported in Book 10, chapter 43, on the understanding of ravens. Aelian writes in Book 15, chapter 40, that the raven's voice is such that, in imitation of man, it has one voice when it plays and another when it is serious. Plutarch likewise, in his book On Whether Land Animals Have More Reason than Water Animals, proves this very thing from experience. But this, which the heathens hand down about the auguries and the prediction of future events, is superstition attached to the raven; yet, as I have said, there remains an obscure and corrupted trace of the raven's release from the Ark to indicate the depth of the Flood's waters. That the raven was rightly and fittingly observed to be by nature a forerunner and herald of future rain is also true, because being of a very dry temperament it easily senses a change in the air and the approach of rain. Many have reported this, and the thing itself teaches it. Aratus, at the end of the Phaenomena, says thus: "And the ravens, in the cries they make, foretell the rain to come, when, with their wings beating, they drink the air and ... with the heavy tail ..." [Καί τε Κόρακες δὶς καλαγμές Φαυῆ ἐωμιήσαντο σωὸ ὑς ἀτ' ἐχομένοιο Ἠποτε ἢ κέρκα τε βαρείᾳ δασάκι φαυῇ Μακρὸν ἔπ' ποιζεῦσι πνασζομένοι τῆς τυχρά.]

units.la: Quae sic interpretatus est Virgilius lib. 1. Georgicon:
units.tr: Virgil interpreted these things thus, in Book 1 of the Georgics:

units.la: [Tum liquidas Corui presso ter gutture voces, Aut quater ingeminant: & sepe cubilibus altis Nescio qua praeter solitum dulcedine laeti Inter se folys strepitant.] Plinius lib. 18. cap. 35: [Corui, ait, singultu quodam latrantes, seq; concutientes, si continuabunt, ventos praesagiunt: si vero raptim voce reforbebut, ventosum imbrem.] Omitto cetera, quae de Corui indutiria in siti, in petenda stipe seu cibo a viatoribus Physici scripsere: itemque Proverbia illa, [Ex malo Coruo malum ouum:] & [Corum cibum habens captat umbram] ut docet Epiphanius, Haeresi 66. nam ad Grammaticos pertinent. Quod autem addit Moses, Non redyt ad Noachu ipsum Corum ab eo semel emissum ex Arca, licet iret & rediret, hoc retentum est, ac memoria conseruatum ab Ethnicis, sed fabulis obscuratum, & interpolatum a stu Satanae, ut veritas S. Scripturae deleretur. Aiunt enim, quum Corus ab Apolline sacrificii fatturo dimissus esset ad aquas petendas, quibus Apollo in eo vteretur, Corum non rediisse. Higinus lib 2. Astronomicon, cap. De Hydra. Ouidius lib. 2. Fastorum: [ I, mea, dixit, anis, ne quid pia sacra moretur;
units.tr: [Then the ravens, three or four times, with a pressed throat repeat their clear voices, and often in their high nests, glad with a sweetness unknown beyond their custom, they chatter among themselves.] Pliny, Book 18, chapter 35: "Ravens," he says, "croaking with a kind of hiccup and shaking themselves, if they keep it up, foretell winds; but if they swallow back their voice quickly, a windy rain." "Go, my bird," he said, "lest anything delay the pious rites;" Ovid, Fasti, Book 2. I omit the rest, which the natural historians have written about the ravens' industry in thirst, in begging alms or food from travellers; likewise the proverbs, "A bad egg from a bad raven," and "The raven, having food, seeks shade," as Epiphanius teaches in Heresy 66; for these belong to the grammarians. But as for what Moses adds, that the raven, though it went out and came back, never returned to Noah, this was retained and preserved in memory by the heathens, but obscured by fables and corrupted at the instigation of Satan, so that the truth of Holy Scripture might be erased. For they say that when the raven was sent by Apollo to fetch water for a sacrifice he was about to make, and that he used it, the raven did not return. Hyginus, Astronomy, Book 2, chapter on the Hydra. Ovid, Fasti, Book 2: "Go, my bird," he said, "lest anything delay the pious rites,

units.la: Et tenuem è vinis fontibus affer aquam.
units.tr: And bring thin water from the living springs."

units.tr: Forgetful of his command, he is said to have sat down under the tree

units.la: Vnde volunt ydem hanc Coruo pœnam impositam, ut quandiu ficus maturescunt, de nullo fonte, nullâve aqua bibat, quòd tunc habeat guttur fitis & ariditate perseratum. Et hæc quidem de Coruo. De Columba verò à Noacho emissa hæc apud eosdem Ethnicos extât veftigia: Primum id genus anis pro Deo à Syrii cultum est, ut tradit Higinus in Fabul. cap. 197. non quidem ex ea caussa, quam Græci homines vani fingunt, Quod omnium eximia magnitudinis quedam Columba olim apud Euphratis fluuij ripam inuenerit, quod postea excluserit (ecquæ enim ista, & quàm friuola σπονδαις & deificationis Columbæ caussa?) sed quoniam Syri memoriæ operæ à Columba in Diluuio præstita Noacho retinebant, quum illa fuit aquarum maxime decrescentium nuntia, ac proinde Columbæ à Syris velut pacis erga homines diuinæ precones, & præsagæ coleb antur. Erant enim Syri, ut cæteri homines, superstitiosi. Vnde etiam eas in vexillis Babyloniorum depictas fuisse volunt nonnulli, suisseque eorum exercitus signa, quemadmodum Aquilæ Romanorum, Luna Byzantinorum, Noctua Atheniensium, nimirum propter ifius beneficij Columbæ memoriam. Erant enim Babylonij & Chaldæi Assyrijs,vbi Arca subsedit,vicini,à quibus id inaudierant, ac didicerant factum. Multa de Columbis,earúmque diuerso genere (sunt enim illius quinq; species) ingenio, moribus scribit Athenæus lib. 9. Dipnosoph. sed hoc imprimis eas vocem hyeme non emittere, nisi sereno & tranquillo die. Sunt enim serenitatis nuntiæ. Plutarchus libro, Vtrum Terrestria Animalia plus rationis habeant, ait, Columbas crudeles esse propter nimiam coitus cupiditatem: [Proruunt enim, ait, earum mares oua fœminarum, & fœminas perdunt, quòd, dum oua incubata fouent, coitum non admittunt.] Vnde ex ea parte sunt infames. Epiphanius Hæresi 73 contra Ophitas, [Quanquàm Columbæ genus, inquit, non laudatur in multis (petulans enim est Columbarum genus, & à multiplici mixtione non alienum la sciuiumque, & per omne tempus voluptati dediti.] Vnde Veneri eas homines profani sacras esse dixerunt.) [Ad hæc verò debile, & infirmum est. Sed (addit idem) propter innocentiam, patientiam, & mali facilem oblivionem Columbæ laudantur.] Verùm istis Columbarum laudibus, vel vituperationibus omissis, videamus ecquæ restent nobis ex scriptis Ethnicorum reliquiæ & manifestissimæ. Emisse à Noacho ex Arca Columbæ testimonia, præter illud, quod iam demonstraui, de ea à Syriis adorata, & à Chaldæis sumpta in signum Militiæ, Plutarchus in libro, Vtrum Terrestria animalia plus rationis habeat, sic aperte scribit, Versionem enim Latinam afferam: [Poëtæ igitur, ait, Columbam Deucalionis scribunt Arcâ emissam, quantisper remearet, & eodem continuò se reciperet, tempestatis: postquam autem anolasset. serenitatis argumentum dedisse.] Hanc eandem Deucalionis Columbam volunt in Molossis, Epiri populo, futse, ac manifse postea, & ex quercubus in sylua Dodonea respõnsa dedisse: imo quum in quercubus illa sederet, eas arbores vocales fuisse, & futura prædixisse ydem Ethnici scribunt. Pausanias libro 7. [Confugiunt,inquit ad oraculum Dodonæum. Hanc enim terra continentem qui incolebant, & Acetoli,& eis finitimi Acarnanes, ac Epirotæ, Columbas existimarunt, & è quercu editum oraculum omnium verissimum.] Nam & veterem Deucalionem & Pyrrham, sub quibus fuit vniuersale Diluuium, fabulantur Græci (postquam vterque ex aquis euasisset) sese in Epiri regionem recepisse, eam Columbam secum adduxisse, & Dodonei souis templum ibi ædificasse, quod Templum Græci primum omnium summè coluisse dicuntur, & ex eo ipso loco natam esse totam Gracia fabulositatem tenere quoque Plinius lib. 4. Hist. Nat. in Proœmio. Ergo huius templi velut sanctissimi, & in quo ex illa Columba oracula prima reddita sunt, meminère religiosissimè postea optimi quiq; Scriptores Ethnici, Strabo lib.7. Pausanias lib.7. & 9. Pomponius Mela lib. 2.cap.3. Solinus Polyhistor cap.13. Cur verò hæc? Quod antiquissima huius Historia nostræ de Columba à Noacho (quem, vt diximus, veterem Deucalionem nominarunt) ex Arca in Diluuio emissa memoriam conseruabant quidem: eam autem fabulis & mendacijs suis homines vani & ambitiosi Græci interpolabant, vt eam laudem sibi tribuerent, & arrogarent, quasi hæc in sua Gente, non in Armenia primùm cõtigissent. Quid, quod Oliuam, eiusque ramum ydem illi Ethnici dicunt esse signum, testimoniúmque pacis (unde illud est Virgi. ly [R]amum pretendit oliua] de missis fœderu contrahendi caussa legatis) unde sumpserunt, obsecro? Nónne ex eo, quod sedatarum aquarum, & proinde Dei erga homines placati testimonium, & velut symbolum Columba à Noacho emissa attulit ramum Oliua, vt scribit Moses? Ifidorus lib. 17. Etymolog. cap. 9. ex Ethnicis, [Est, inquit, Olea arbor pacis insigne.] Virgilius libro vndecimo Aeneidos:
units.tr: Whence they hold that this punishment was laid on the raven: that as long as the figs ripen, he should drink from no spring and no water, because his throat then is parched with thirst and dryness. And these are the things about the raven. Concerning the dove sent out by Noah, these traces remain among the same heathens. First, this kind of bird was worshipped as a god by the Syrians, as Hyginus relates in Fable 197; not for the reason that the foolish Greeks invent, that a dove of unusual size once found a place on the bank of the Euphrates and afterwards hatched an egg (for what kind of tale is that, and how trivial is the reason for libations and the deification of the dove?), but because the Syrians kept in memory the service the dove performed for Noah in the Flood, when it was the messenger that the waters were greatly subsiding; and therefore the Syrians worshipped doves as heralds and omens of divine peace towards men. For the Syrians, like other men, were superstitious. Hence some hold that doves were painted on the standards of the Babylonians and were their military emblem, just as the eagle was for the Romans, the moon for the Byzantines, and the owl for the Athenians, no doubt in memory of that benefit of the dove. For the Babylonians and Chaldeans were neighbours of the Assyrians, where the Ark came to rest, and so they had heard of and learned the event from them. Athenaeus, Book 9 of the Deipnosophists, writes much about doves and their varied kinds (for there are five species of them), their nature and habits; but above all he notes that in winter they do not utter their voice except on a clear and calm day, for they are heralds of fair weather. Plutarch, in his book On Whether Land Animals Have More Reason, says that doves are cruel because of their excessive lust for mating: "For their males," he says, "destroy the eggs of the females, and kill the females, because the females do not admit mating while they are sitting on their eggs." Hence in this respect they are infamous. Epiphanius, in Heresy 73 against the Ophites: "Although the kind of dove," he says, "is not praised in many respects (for the tribe of doves is wanton, and not free from manifold mixing and pollution, and always given over to pleasure)," for which reason profane men said they were sacred to Venus. "Moreover, it is weak and feeble. But," he adds, "because of their innocence, patience, and easy forgetfulness of injury, doves are praised." But, leaving aside these praises or censures of doves, let us see what remains to us from the writings of the heathens, and those most manifest. That the dove was sent out of the Ark by Noah, apart from what I have already shown (that it was worshipped by the Syrians and adopted by the Chaldeans as a military sign), Plutarch in his book On Whether Land Animals Have More Reason writes plainly, and I will give the Latin version: "The poets therefore," he says, "write that the dove of Deucalion was sent out of the Ark, and that it returned at once to the same place as long as the storm lasted; but after it had flown away, it gave a sign of fair weather." This same dove of Deucalion they hold also gave later, in Molossia, a people of Epirus, certain and manifest responses from the oaks in the grove of Dodona; indeed, while it was sitting in the oaks, the same heathens write that those trees were vocal and foretold the future. Pausanias, Book 7: "They take refuge," he says, "at the oracle of Dodona. For those who inhabited the mainland, and the Acetolians, and the Acarnanians neighbouring them, and the Epirotes, believed the doves, and the oracle uttered from the oak to be the most true of all." For the Greeks also tell the fable that old Deucalion and Pyrrha, under whom there was the universal Flood, after both had escaped from the waters, withdrew to the region of Epirus, brought the dove with them, and built there the temple of Dodonaean Zeus, which the Greeks are said to have honoured most highly of all, and from this very place all Greek fabulousness is said to have arisen; Pliny too mentions this in the Preface to Book 4 of the Natural History. Therefore the best heathen writers afterwards recalled this temple, as it were most holy, and the place where the first oracles were given by that dove: Strabo, Book 7; Pausanias, Books 7 and 9; Pomponius Mela, Book 2, chapter 3; Solinus, Polyhistor, chapter 13. But why these things? Because the very ancient history of the dove sent out of the Ark by Noah in the Flood (whom, as we have said, they named old Deucalion) was indeed kept in memory; but vain and ambitious Greeks corrupted it with their fables and lies, so that they might claim and arrogate this praise to themselves, as if these things had happened first in their own nation and not in Armenia. And what of the olive and its branch, which those same heathens say is a sign and token of peace (whence comes that line of Virgil, "The olive holds out its branch," about envoys sent to make a treaty)? Whence, I beg you, did they derive this? Did they not derive it from the fact that the dove sent out by Noah brought back an olive branch, as Moses writes, a sign and as it were a symbol of the waters being calmed, and therefore of God's favour towards men appeased? Isidore, Etymologies, Book 17, chapter 9, from the heathens: "The olive," he says, "is a tree that is the emblem of peace." Virgil, Aeneid, Book 11:

units.la: [Iámque oratores aderant ex vrbe Latina Velati ramis oleæ, veniámque petentes.
units.tr: And now the envoys had come from the Latin city, wrapped in olive branches, asking for pardon.

units.la: Plinius lib. 15. cap. vlt. [In profanis vsibus, ait, pollui Laurum, & Oleam fa non est, vt ne propitiandis quidem numinibus accendi ex his altaria, arave soleant,] & cap. 4. Olea honorem Romani Maiestas mutuum præbuit, turmæ Equitum Idibus Iullijs ex ea coronando. Athenæ victores olea coronant. Denique Augustinus lib. 83. quæst. cap 59. typicè lætitiam per oleam significari docet. Verùm de eo pluribus agere minimè necesse est, propterea quòd vary tum veterum, tum recentes scriptores hoc ipsum docent, qui bonos Oliuæ tributum ab Ethnicis esse illius nostra historia & de Oliua ramo ad Noachum à Columba, tanquam pacis Dei erga homines nuntia, ad ito certissimum, antiquissimumq; testimonium, & vestigium. Pergamus ad reliqua eiusdem veritatis capita.
units.tr: Pliny, Natural History book 15, last chapter: "In profane uses, it is not lawful for the laurel and the olive to be burned, nor are altars or hearths usually kindled from them even to propitiate the gods." And chapter 4: "The majesty of Rome has lent honour to the olive in return, since squadrons of knights are crowned with it on the Ides of July. The Athenians crown their victors with olive." Finally, Augustine, Eighty-Three Questions, question 59, teaches that joy is signified typologically by the olive. But there is no need to dwell on this at length, since various writers, both ancient and recent, teach this very point, that the olive was held in honour by the heathen. Our history of the olive branch brought to Noah by the dove, as a messenger of God's peace toward men, is a most certain and most ancient testimony and trace of this. Let us proceed to the remaining heads of this same truth.

units.la: Ad III. De exitu Noachi, & Loco, vbi Arca constitit.
units.tr: On the Third Point: Noah's Exit from the Ark, and the Place Where the Ark Came to Rest.

units.la: Incidit autem tertium, quod est de exitu Noachi ex Arca: & de loco, vbi illa constitit. Sunt autem hæ duæ quæstiones coniunctæ. Nam & ibi subsitit Arca, vbi Noachus ex ea egressus est: & ibi egressus est, vbi illa conquieuit a fluctibus & tactatione aquarum Diluuij.
units.tr: The third point that follows concerns Noah's exit from the Ark and the place where the Ark came to rest. These two questions are linked. The Ark came to rest in the very place from which Noah went out, and he went out where it settled after the waters of the Flood had receded and ceased to toss it.

units.la: In quo primum explodenda sunt Græcorum hominum ambitiosorum, & planè nouorum ac recentium scriptorum, quemadmodum docet Plato in Timæo, commenta, qui Nanigiũ (in quo homines ex Diluuio seruati sunt) in sua Græcia, & in monte Parnasso subsistisse tradunt.
units.tr: First, the fictions of those ambitious Greeks, and of plainly new and recent writers, must be exploded. As Plato teaches in the Timaeus, they report that the vessel in which men were saved from the Flood came to rest in their own Greece, on Mount Parnassus.

units.la: Illud enim Diluuium omnino recens est, & multis, post vniuersalem seu Noachi inundationem, seculis contigit: denique fuit peculiare illi duntaxat Phocidis & Thessaliæ regioni. Nos vero de eo quærimus Diluuio, quod & primum omnium fuit, & vniuersale, & sub primo vetustissimoque Deucalione (qui idem & Noachus, & Xisuthrus, & Ianus dictus est) euenit terrarum Orbi, omnesque mortales, imo viuentia omnia, quæ vbiq; gentium erant, consumpsit, præter ea quæ in vna illa Noachi Arca continebantur. Ergo & de exitu huius Noachi: & de loco, vbi Arca illa subsiitit, quæritur. Respondet Moses, [In montibus Ararati.] Iam vero ex ipsis Ethnicorum scriptis velut Plinio, & Itinerario Antonini demonstrauimus, & populos Araratiaticos, & vrbem Ariarathiam in Armenia Maiore (quæ Assyriæ pars est) sitam fuisse.. Isidorus lib. 14. cap. 8 [Ararath mons Armeniæ, in quo Arcam post Diluuium resedisse testantur. Vnde & vsque hodie ibidem lignorum eius videntur vestigia.] Ariarathi regis Cappadociæ meminit Iustinus Historicus, quod nomen procul dubio ex illis vetustissimis vestigiis restat. Imò & Ammianus Marcellinus lib. 23. non solum eas regiones omnes scribit habere montes maximae celsitudinis: verùm etiam Coronum montem inter eos ipsos altissimum esse tradit, & nominat: cuius partem habitantes occiduam frumentarijs agris affluunt, & vinarijs pingui fœcunditate latissimis. Quamobrem ex eiusmodi ethnicorum scriptis apparent vestigia nostrae veritatis, quae descensum seu exitum Noachi ex Arca in montibus Ararati, id est Assyria seu Armenia maiore collocat. Sed maiora adhuc, amplioraque eius rei testimonia ex ipsdem Ethnicis proferamus. Abydenus apud Cyrillum sapius iam à nobis citatus scribit pium quendam virum in Armenia monte quodam altissimo ex Diluuio seruatum fuisse. Hunc locum Armenij ipsi etiam tempore Flauij Josephi illius liberationis memoriam à Maioribus traditam pie seruantes, vocarunt Καταβατήριον, vt idem Josephus tradit lib. 1. Antiquitat. cap. 5. Mnaseas Damascenus apud eundem Josephum sic ait, [Est & super Mynniada excelsus mons in Armenia, qui Baris appellatur, in quem multos confugientes fama est Diluuij tempore liberatos, & quendam simul in Arca deuectum in montis venisse summitatem, lignorumque Arca reliquias multo tempore conseruatas. Fuit autem iste quem etiam Moses Iudeorum legislator scripsit.] Est autem Minnius, seu Minnium, vt Curtius nominat lib. 5. Vrbs celebris in Armenia, à quo oppido, & à voce [Aram] Arminia tanquam [Aram Minnij] vel Aram Minnia] primùm dicta est. Hier. 51. 27: deinde à Græcis & Latinis, maioris suauitatis gratia, ArmeArmenia nuncupata, nominatáq;. Quid si Minyæ populi Thessalia (quorum princeps fuit Iason, qui Colchos innauigit) ab ijs Minnijs Armenijs orti sunt? Sed redeo ad Arcam in Armenia relictam vestigia. Hieronymus Ægyptius, qui Phœnicum historiam literis mandauit, cum superioribus, nimirum Abydeno, & Mnaseas consentit, vt docet idem Iosephus. Epiphanius lib. 1. Hæresi 18 contra Nazaræos [Adhuc hodie, inquit, reliquiæ Arcæ Noæ ostenduntur in Carduersum montibus, & regione.] Berosus noster lib. 1. [Eleuata ab aquis Arca, ait, in Gordiei montis vertice quiescit, cuius adhuc dicitur pars aliqua esse, & homines exinde bitumen tollere, quo maximè vtuntur ad expiationes.] Hæc eadem ex Beroso habet quoque Iosephus loco tam citato, id est, lib. 1. Antiquit. cap. 5. Ex quibus apparet eundem esse montem, quem Mnaseas [Barin,] & Berosus [Gordieū] vocat, & Epiphanius [Carduensem:] alij verò etiam Kardeum, & Chardiacum nominant, prout diuersa idiomata rem eandem & idem vocabulum varie nimirum pronuntiant. Baris igitur fuit is ipse mons appellatus, in quo peculiariter Arca Noæ subsistit. Regio ipsa, & pars Mundi, in qua Mons ille situs est ab Hebræis & Mose dicitur Ararath, vnde Araratha vibs: à Græcis & Latinis modò Assyria, modò Maior Armenia: à Chaldæis & Babylonijs, vt ait Franciscus Iunius in Genes. cap. 8, Kardu Vnde Karduena vel Korduena regio apud Ammianum Marcellinum lib. 25. transligritana, vicina Zabdicena, & Medieiu Cassijs montibus, & ad Caucasum montem sita, quem appellant Græci, scilicet vnisque esse montium omnium altissimum, & ad flumen Niphaten. Has ab Aethico Cosmographo vocatur Cordubenna. In Karduena regione habitat Kardi, quorum idem Ammianus meminit in descriptione totius Caspiani tractus, & regionum, quae sunt ad mare Caspium, libr. 23. Histor. In eadem autem Karduena vel Korduena regione sunt Kardyenses vel Karduenses, vel Kardiei, vel Karduai (sunt enim omnes isti ipsi montes, e quibus unus est nomine Baris, ille videlicet ipse, in quo Noachus cum Arca, deficientibus aquis Diluvii, substitit. Hos montes, qui tam varie ex voce Chaldaea describuntur, Graeci nonnulli, Latini primum Chardiaos: deinde Cardiaos & Cordiaos, demptā h, aspirationis nota, vocarunt: denique alii ex Cardiaos vel Cordiaos scripserunt, effecerunt, dixerunt Gordiaos. Unde vulgo & passim inualuit postea, ut hi Assyria seu Masorus Armeniae Montes celsissimi scriberentur, pronunciaretúrque montes Gordiaei, quorum pars & unus est mons ille celebris Caucasus, seu Baris. Iam vero montium istorum Gordiaeorum meminerunt Ethnici Scriptores pene innumeri, velut Ptolemaeus, Strabo lib. 16, Plutarchus in Alexandro, & Lucullo: Q. Curtius in libr. de Rebus gestis Alexandri Magni lib. 5, quos etiam (uti & populum eorum incolam Medis vicinum) Gordienum & Gordienos vocat, quemadmodum eosdem Plinius lib. 6. cap. 15. Gordyaos quoque, velut eiusdē lib. cap. 11, & 26. Quanquam Strabo lib. 16, videtur distinguere Gordyos populos à Karduchis vel Karduenis: sed parum fidei in his vocabulis habendum est Graecis autoribus, vel eorum Latinorumve descriptioni credendum. dendum quum in ysdem vocabulis pronuntiandis mirè varient, & errent isti omnes. Constat verò Armeniam, vbi montes isti collocantur, dici derivarið à voce Hebræa [Aram] quæ excelsum significat, quod sit ea regio excelsa: & Dionysius Alexandrinus excelsissimos in eadem regione montes esse tradit, quos, vt dixi, Gordiæos Græci vocant & Gordyæos, vti & Stephanus libr. De vrbibus in voce Gordyæa. Huic nostræ sententiæ consentit quod M. Cato in Fragm. scribit his verbis [Ante Ninum circiter annis 250 (quibus duravit aureum seculum) terras fuisse inundatas constat, & in Scythia Saga renatū mortale genus.] Dicta verò est Assyria, seu Armenia Maior Scythia Saga vel ab oppido & flumine Saga (quod vtrumque in Assyria est) vel à verbo Hebræo [Schagah,] unde regio & pars illa Mundi Saga dicta est prisci seculis tanquam populosa, multiplicata, & cæterarum Gentium fons & mater, qualis fuit. Ex quo controversia illa, quæ est apud tum Platonem in Timæo, tum Iustinum Historicum lib. 1, quæstio facilè deciditur, Vtrum Scythæ, an Ægyptij primi hominum in hoc mundo extitére. Vindicia enim pro Scythis sunt pronuntianda, & illi priores esse censendi non modo, quàm Ægyptij, sed etiá quàm Phryges, & Arcades, contraquàm tamen (sed falsò) sentit Herodotus, & quam vlli alij mortales, qui quidem in hoc terrarum Orbe sint, fuerintve post vniuersale terrarum Diluuium. Denique quod scribit Higinus in Fab. cap. 153. ex Ouidio, aliisque Poetis, post diluuium illud nates esse homines ex lapidibus à Deucalione & Pyrrha post tergum in humum & terrā iactatis (unde Populi Λαοὶ ἐκ τῆς λαδὸς, id est, lapide, vocantur à Græcis) hoc quoq; falsum est & ineptum. Procreati sunt enim etiam post Diluuium homines ex hominibus naturali propagatione, & ex femine coitu𝔮 maris & fœminæ hominis, uti ante diluuiū: nam illud totum, quod hodie in terræ superficie extitit, extátve, hominū genus, quantumuis sparsū & diffusum ex illis tamē ôtto personis emanauit, quæ in Arca seruata sunt, nimirum ex Noacho, & eius uxore, tribus eius filys Sem, Cam, & Iapheto, & eorum uxoribus. Et hæc quidem de tertio nostræ Historiæ capite hactenus dicta sunto.
units.tr: That flood is altogether recent, and happened many centuries after the universal inundation of Noah; it was, in short, peculiar to the region of Phocis and Thessaly alone. We, however, are inquiring about the Flood that was both the first of all and universal, which befell the orb of the earth under the first and most ancient Deucalion (who is also called Noah, Xisuthrus, and Janus), and which destroyed all mortals, indeed all living things wherever they were found among the nations, except those contained in that one Ark of Noah. So we are asking about the exit of this Noah, and about the place where that Ark came to rest. Moses answers: [On the mountains of Ararat.] Now from the writings of the pagans themselves, as from Pliny and the Itinerary of Antoninus, we have already shown that the Araratian peoples and the city of Ariarathia were situated in Greater Armenia, which is part of Assyria. Isidore, book 14, chapter 8: [Ararath is a mountain of Armenia, on which they testify the Ark settled after the Flood. Hence even today traces of its timber are seen in that place.] The historian Justin mentions Ariarathes, king of Cappadocia, and that name undoubtedly survives from those most ancient traces. Moreover Ammianus Marcellinus, book 23, not only writes that all those regions have mountains of very great height, but also names Mount Coronus as the highest among them, and says that the inhabitants of its western side abound in grain fields and, in the broadest parts, in vineyards of rich fertility. Therefore the traces of our truth appear in such pagan writings, which place Noah's descent or exit from the Ark on the mountains of Ararat, that is, in Assyria or Greater Armenia. But let us bring forward still greater and fuller testimonies to this matter from the same pagans. Abydenus, cited often by us already in Cyril, writes that a certain pious man was saved from the Flood on a very high mountain in Armenia. The Armenians themselves, in the time of Flavius Josephus, devoutly preserving the memory of that deliverance handed down by their ancestors, called the place Katabaterion [Καταβατήριον], as Josephus himself reports in book 1 of the Antiquities, chapter 5. Mnaseas of Damascus, in the same Josephus, says: [There is also, above Mynniad, a lofty mountain in Armenia called Baris, to which, it is said, many fled and were saved at the time of the Flood, and one man carried in the Ark came to the summit of the mountain; and remains of the Ark's timber were preserved for a long time. This is the mountain that Moses, the lawgiver of the Jews, also wrote about.] Now Minnius, or Minnium, as Curtius calls it in book 5, is a famous city in Armenia, from which town and from the word [Aram] Armenia was first called, as if [Aram Minnij] or [Aram Minnia]. Then from Greeks and Latins, for the sake of a smoother sound, it was named and called Armenia (Jeremiah 51:27). What if the Minyae of Thessaly (whose leader was Jason, who sailed to Colchis) sprang from those Minnii of Armenia? But I return to the traces of the Ark left in Armenia. Hieronymus the Egyptian, who committed the history of the Phoenicians to writing, agrees with the earlier writers, namely Abydenus and Mnaseas, as Josephus also reports. Epiphanius, book 1, heresy 18, against the Nazarenes: [Even today, he says, remains of Noah's Ark are shown on the mountains and in the region of Carduersum.] Our Berosus, book 1: [The Ark, lifted up by the waters, rests on the peak of Mount Gordiaeus, and it is said that some part of it still remains there, and that men take bitumen from it, which they chiefly use for purifications.] Josephus also has the same account from Berosus in the passage just cited, that is, book 1 of the Antiquities, chapter 5. From these it appears that it is the same mountain which Mnaseas calls [Baris], Berosus [Gordiaeus], and Epiphanius [Carduensis]; others call it Kardeus and Chardiacus, since different languages pronounce the same thing and the same word in various ways. Baris, then, was the very mountain so called, on which the Ark of Noah came to rest in a particular way. The region itself, and the part of the world in which that mountain lies, is called Ararat by the Hebrews and Moses, whence the city of Araratha; by the Greeks and Latins it is now called Assyria, now Greater Armenia; by the Chaldeans and Babylonians, as Franciscus Junius says on Genesis 8, Kardu. Hence the region of Karduena or Korduena, mentioned by Ammianus Marcellinus in book 25, lies across the Tigris, near Zabdicena and the Medes, at the Cassian mountains, and by the Caucasus, which the Greeks name, that is, the highest of all mountains, and by the river Niphates. The Ethiopian cosmographer calls this region Cordubenna. In the region of Karduena dwell the Kardi, whom the same Ammianus mentions in his description of the whole Caspian tract and the regions that lie by the Caspian Sea, in book 23 of the Histories. In that same region of Karduena or Korduena are the Kardyenses, Karduenses, Kardiei, or Karduai (for all these are the same mountains, one of which bears the name Baris, that very one on which Noah with the Ark came to rest when the waters of the Flood receded). These mountains, which are described in so many different ways from the Chaldean word, some Greeks and Latins first called Chardiaei; then Cardiaei and Cordiaei, with the h removed as the mark of aspiration; finally others, writing Cardiaei or Cordiaei, made and said Gordiaei. Hence it later became common and widespread that these highest mountains of Assyria, or of Armenia Masorus, were written and pronounced the Gordiaean mountains, of which one part, and indeed that famous mountain, is the Caucasus, or Baris. Now innumerable pagan writers have mentioned these Gordiaean mountains: Ptolemy, Strabo in book 16, Plutarch in the lives of Alexander and Lucullus, and Quintus Curtius in his book on the deeds of Alexander the Great, book 5, who also calls them, and their people who dwell near the Medes, Gordienus and Gordienoi; Pliny likewise calls them in book 6, chapter 15; Gordyaei too, in the same book, chapters 11 and 26. Although Strabo in book 16 seems to distinguish the Gordyaean peoples from the Carduchi or Carduenes, little trust is to be placed in these names in Greek authors, nor is their description or that of the Latins to be believed, since all of them vary wildly and err in pronouncing these same words.

units.la: Ad IIII. Sacrificium Noachi Deo factū.
units.tr: Concerning the Fourth: the Sacrifice Offered to God by Noah.

units.la: Iam igitur ad quartum & vltimū accedamus. Est autem Sacrificium pro salute & sua, & caeterarum rerum, quæ erant in Arca à Noacho factum, & oblatum à Deo. Huius quoque etiam quædam apud Ethnicos vestigia restant: Primum fatentur, & scribunt Græci Deucalionem priscum nempe (sed quod de prisco scriptum est, ipsi ad suum & iuniorem quoque transferunt ambitiose, quemadmodum sæpe demonstrau.) Ergo fatentur illum Deucalionem, qui & Noachus fuit, & pium in Deum fuisse, & moderatissimum sanctissimumq; virum, cæterósque mortales vitam honestam docuisse. Ouidius lib. 1. Metamorphos. de eo, & Pyrrha eius uxore loquens, ait,
units.tr: Let us now come to the fourth and last point. The sacrifice that Noah offered to God after the flood, for the safety of himself and of the other creatures that were in the ark, also has some traces among the Gentiles. First, the Greeks admit and write that Deucalion, the ancient one (though what is written of the ancient man they ambitiously transfer to their own, later figure, as I have often shown), was a pious man toward God, a most moderate and holy man, who taught the other mortals an honest way of life. Ovid, speaking of him and of his wife Pyrrha in the first book of the Metamorphoses, says:

units.la: [Non illo melior quisquam, nec amantior aqui Vir fuit: aut illa reuerentior ulla deorum.]
units.tr: No man was better than he, or more devoted to what is right; no woman was more reverent toward the gods.

units.la: Plutarchus lib. 2. contra Coloten, [Deucalion, inquit, Græciam uniuersam (imò terrarū orbem) imbuit sanctè, qua Sie, quasi expiauit precationibus, ieiunando, eraculis, elogiis propositis, mortales ita erga numen animauit, vt eos tum spes bona, tum metus in officio contineret. Deinde eundem post Diluuium religiosissime Deo sacrificasse tradunt Ouidius lib. 1. am citato, & Higinus in fabulis cap. 154. Denique vero eius altaris, quod ad eiusmodi pro salute sua sacrificium offerendum idem edificauit, reliquias extitisse etiam suo seculo tradit ex Ethnicorum, & Armeniorum ipsorum testimonio & literis Epiphanius lib. 1. Tom. 1. Haresi 18. Ex quibus omnibus manifestissima etiam istius sacrificij à Noacho post Diluuium oblati Deo vestigia, sed alieno, id est, Deucalionis nomine (altu Satanæ & Diaboli) interpolata reliqua esse colliguntur etiā inter ipsos Ethnicos. Quæ obrem & ex ea parte idem & veritatem nostram confirmant, & atheos homines confutant. Sequitur vero vltimum totum huius operis caput.
units.tr: Plutarch, in the second book against Colotes, says: Deucalion, he says, imbued all Greece (indeed the whole orb of the earth) with holiness, which he atoned for with prayers, fasting, and oracles, and by proposing sayings, he animated mortals toward the divinity so that hope of good and fear kept them in their duty. Then, that the same man after the flood most devoutly sacrificed to God, is related by Ovid in the book already cited, and by Hyginus in the Fables, chapter 154. Finally, Epiphanius, in the first book, first volume, heresy 18, reports from the testimony and writings of the Gentiles and of the Armenians themselves that remains of the altar which the same man built for offering this sacrifice for his safety still existed in his own age. From all of these things, it is gathered that the very clear traces of this sacrifice offered to God by Noah after the flood remain, though they have been corrupted by another name, that of Deucalion (by the deceit of Satan and the Devil), even among the Gentiles themselves. For this reason they both confirm our truth on this point and refute atheists. The last chapter of this whole work now follows.

units.la: CAPVT IIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: Quæ Politia tum Ciuilis, tum Ecclesiastica toto illo Diluuij vniuersalis anno fuerit.
units.tr: What the civil and ecclesiastical polity was during the whole year of the universal Flood.

units.la: QVANQVAM non multum discrepauit Politia tum Ciuilis, tum Ecclesiastica, quæ fuit toto illo Diluuij vniuersalis anno ab ea, quae ante Diluuium in Mundo fuisse demonstrata est: tamen quoniam habuit hic ipse annus aliquid in utroque à superiori ae- tate diuersum, neque huic quoque nostri operis & laboris parti sua coronis detrahenda videtur, explicemus, quae, qualisve fuerit illo, quanuis breui, tempore vtraq; ista Politia. Ac quidem Ciuilis pcsita est in Magistratu, Legibus, Forma Reipubl. Artibus, quae tunc exercebantur, & Moribus tum publicis, tum priuatim receptis. Quod ad Magistratum, illud fuit singulare illo Diluuij anno, quod Vnus duntaxat esset totim Orbis terrarum tunc Magistratus, non plures: ne sine Magistratu summo essent illo anno homines, quo tamen tota superiore Mundi aetate, id est per 1656 annos. Is autem Vnus & summus Magistratus, fuit Noachus. Fuit autem eius potestas non quidem propriè Regia, sed Regiæ proximè accedens, nempe Paterna, seu Patris in Liberos & Nurus. Nam quemadmodum in Ethicis & Politicis eas comparat inter se Aristoteles, sunt similima illa potestates. Ergo Noachus habebat tunc Paternum, ac proinde proximum Regio imperiû in omnes, qui tunc restabant homines, nempe vxorem, & liberos, nurusque suas: quod minimè tyrannicè, sed moderatè, ciuiliter, sanctè, piè, vtpote vir Dei timens, exercebat. Leges autem Politicae, nulla huic à quoquam homine scriptæ erant: Conscientia tamen reliquum ex naturali luce per peccatum deperdita testimonium, fide, verboque Dei renelato, corroboratum in Noachø, & filijs eius pro legibus audiebatur, & hominum superstitum actiones salitem in Arca illa, & tempore Di- luuij luniy regebat, eásque moderabatur: non intemperans libido, & effrænis audacia. Nam omnes in Arca modestè, moderatéq;, proculdubio vixerunt. Noachus enim familiam suam & pie prius instruxerat: & in Arca in Dei metu seuerè regebat. Forma Reipubl. fuit Domestica potius, quam Regia, & Aristocratica. Parebant enim filij Noacho velut Patri suo. Et tamen ea regiminis ratio fuit & Regis, & Aristocratica persimilis. Non erat verò regia. Nec enim familijs ex diuerso stirpe propagatis imperabat Noachus, quiî quæ restabant omnes ex se uno & uxore sua, nata procreataque essent. Nó erat etiam verè Aristocratica: Vnus enim nempe Pater, non plures, in reliquos nempe filios imperium, & quidem summum, tunc obtinebat, sed velut Pater: non autem tanquam Rex. Omnes autem homines tunc in vna Arca erant conclusi. Nulli verò toto illo Diluuij anno nati narrantur, & in Arca suscepti sine ab hominibus liberi: siue ab animalibus, quæ in ea erant, fœtus & pulli. Tunc generis humani procreatio conquieuit, quòd Deus Arcam iudicijs suis exercendis, non hominum voluptatibus explendis praparasset. Artes autem quæ tunc erat, sciebantúrque, fuerunt eædem illæ, quas superior ætas, & homines ante Diluuium didicerant, atque repererant, qualis Agricultura, Pastoritia, Musica, Ferraria, Aerariáque, & cetera, quæ hominum usus pepererat. Husciebant & Noachus, & illius filij: & quum in Arca minimè essent otiosi, eas exercuerunt, quas tunc & in eo loco administrare potuerunt. Mores denique hominum in illa Arca versantium tum publici, tum priuati, fuerunt quod ad exteruam speciem sancti, moderati, & laudabiles, licèt iam tunc Cam minimus natu esset hypocrita: sed ingenium suum Patrem celabat: Verùm postea se suúmque illum animum silium prodidit. Et hæc quidem tunc, totúque illo Diluuij anno fuit Politia Mundi Ciuilis. Ecclesiastica vero iam explicanda, quæ consistit in Verbo Dei ecquod tunc fuerit: In Ministro: Cultu Dei externo: Loco, & Tempore illius cultus concelebrandi. Verbum Dei, quod tunc erat, quum Noachus & quàdiu in Arca vixit, erat quidem nō scriptum, à Deo tamen ipso renelatum (si libros Enoschi exceperu: in quibus aliqua pars Verbi diuini scriptis tradita erat, velut de Diluuio, & punitione sceleratorū continebatur.) Ergo verbum Dei, quod tunc Noachus cum liberis habuit, fuit duplex: Vnum Generale, nempe de Semine Mulieris, id est, Messia venturo, & contrituro caput Serpentis. Hoc fuit fundamentū Ecclesiæ Dei, & Electionis piorum. Quod verbum ab Adamo per manus traditum Noachus liberiq; eius & animo, & mente, & memoria illibatum conseruabant. Deinde habebant idē Verbum Dei peculiare, nempe de se ex hac tanta mundi clade, & aquis Diluuij eripiendis ac conseruandis, cui credidit Noachus, Hebr. 11.7. filiiq; eius, qui idem illud sæpè ex Patre suo audierant, ipse ex Deo. Ergo hoc Dei promissum animis infixum illi sæpè in Arca repetebant. Minister illius Verbi, & in vniuersum totius externi cultus Diuini in illa Arca fuit Noachus, qui vtrumque illud Dei Verbum sæpe suis iugiter predicabat, repetebatq;, vt se suosq; in Dei promissionibus confirmaret, ac consolaretur: præsertim dumin medyt medijs illis aëris & Maris tempestatibus, & procellis Arca grauissime tàctaretur, ac ijs feriretur. Sustenandæ enim mètes filiorum Noachi, vxoris, & nurum suarum fuerunt recitatione, & inculcatione tum genealium, tum peculiarium Dei promissionum. Id quod proculdubio sedulò & diligenter, & sæpe fecit Noachus. Ergo fuit ille Minister Ecclesiæ in Arca, & prædicator diuini verbi. Cultus exterior Dei fuit in eadem Arca idem, qui & ante Diluuium, excepto quod toto illo Diluuij anno non fuit sacrificatum Deo: sed demum postquam ex Arca fuit egressus Noachus. Verùm coniones de Verbo Dei, Preces ad Deum & publicæ, & priuatæ propter Mediatorem fuerunt in Arca concepte: Publicæ per Noachum: Priuatæ, per singulos, qui illic erant, preces, inquam, & mentales, & vocales, quibus se & suam salutem Deo commendabant. Disciplinam verò Ecclesiasticam etiam tunc fuisse non dubito, quandiu in Arca simul illi vixerunt, vt Noachus reprehenderet non tantum velut Pater: sed etiam velut Pastor & Propheta Dei, si quid reprehensione dignum in suis cerneret, & dictu, factuve turpe ac fœdum. Prophetia denique in eadem Arca retenta est, & sæpe inculcata de venturo Messia, & futura ipsorum omnium, qui in Arca erant, etiam animalium ex aquis Diluuij liberatione, & novi postea Mundi instauratione. Quæ omnia suis fore prædixit ex Dei verbo Noachus. Locus exercitij diuini cultus toto illo anno fuit Arca ipsa, in qua non puto fuisse vllum altare: sed tamen certo loco in ea Arca conueniebat tota Noachi familia, & ad audiendum Noachum, & ad preces Deo publicè fundendas. dus, in quocunq; Arce tabulato locus ille fuerit. Postquam vero ex Arca Noachus exijt, & Altare exstruxit, ubi Deo sacrificaret, non dubito quin posteri eius, qui in ijs locis manserunt, quàdiu illius & Arcae, & Altaris in ijs motibus reliquiae fuerunt, sæpe in eum ipsum locum concurrerint, & convenerint ad eas Arcae vel Altaris reliquias superstites videndas, partim religiosè & pie, partim superstitiosè. Religiosè, velut si qui fidei suæ de Dei iudicijs in homines sceleratos, & de eiusdem misericordia in Noachum & pios confirmandæ gratiâ eò confluerent: Superstitiosè, si qui Deum ibi propter Arcam illam, & ligna illius reliqua sanctius soli existimabant, & credebant. Qui mos est superstitiosorum hominum certis locis potestatem præsentiamque Dei extra ipsius verbum adstringere, & affigere.
units.tr: Although the civil and ecclesiastical polity during the whole year of the universal Flood did not differ much from that which, as has been shown, existed in the world before the Flood, still, since this very year had something in both that differed from the earlier age, and since this part of our work and labour should not be left without its crown, let us explain what that polity was, both civil and ecclesiastical, and what sort it was, though it lasted only a short time. The civil polity consists in the magistracy, the laws, the form of the commonwealth, the arts then practised, and the customs, both public and private, that were received. As for the magistracy, it was peculiar to that year of the Flood that there was only one magistrate in the whole world at that time, not several; yet men were not left without a supreme magistrate that year, whereas throughout the whole earlier age of the world, that is, for 1656 years, there had been such. This one and supreme magistrate was Noah. His power was not strictly royal, but came very near to royal, namely paternal, that is, the power of a father over his children and daughters-in-law. For as Aristotle compares them with each other in his Ethics and Politics, these powers are very similar. So Noah then held paternal authority, and therefore authority close to royal, over all the men who then remained, namely his wife, his children, and his daughters-in-law; and he exercised it not tyrannically but moderately, civilly, holily and piously, as a man who feared God. Political laws, however, had been written for him by no man. Yet the conscience, which retained a remnant of the natural light lost through sin, strengthened by faith and by the word of God revealed, was heeded in Noah and his sons as law. It alone governed the actions of the surviving men in that Ark and during the time of the Flood, and moderated them, so that there was no unrestrained lust or unbridled boldness. For all lived modestly and temperately in the Ark, without doubt. Noah had first trained his household piously, and in the Ark he ruled them strictly in the fear of God. The form of the commonwealth was more domestic than royal or aristocratic. For the sons obeyed Noah as their father. Yet this manner of government was very like that of a king and also of an aristocracy. It was not truly royal, for Noah did not rule over families sprung from different stocks, since all who remained had been born and begotten from him alone and his wife. Nor was it truly aristocratic, for there was one father, not several, who then held the rule over the remaining sons, and indeed supreme rule, but as a father, not as a king. Now all men were then shut up together in one Ark. And no children are said to have been born during the whole year of the Flood, nor taken into the Ark either from men or from the animals that were in it, whether offspring or young. Then the propagation of the human race came to rest, because God had prepared the Ark for carrying out his judgements, not for satisfying human pleasures. The arts that then existed and were known were the same as those which the earlier age and men before the Flood had learned and discovered, such as agriculture, herding, music, ironworking and bronzeworking, and the other things which human need had produced. Noah and his sons practised them too; and since they were by no means idle in the Ark, they pursued those arts which they could carry on in that place. Finally, the morals of the men dwelling in that Ark, both public and private, were, as far as outward appearance went, holy, moderate and praiseworthy, although even then Ham, the youngest, was a hypocrite; but he concealed his disposition from his father, though later he revealed that wicked mind of his. So much for the civil polity of the world during the whole year of the Flood. Now the ecclesiastical polity must be explained, which consists in the word of God, the minister, the external worship of God, and the place and time for celebrating that worship. The word of God that existed when Noah lived in the Ark, and for as long as he lived there, was indeed unwritten but revealed by God himself (excepting the books of Enoch, in which some part of the divine word was handed down in writing, such as what concerned the Flood and the punishment of the wicked). So the word of God which Noah then had with his children was twofold. One was general, namely concerning the Seed of the Woman, that is, the Messiah who was to come and crush the head of the Serpent. This was the foundation of the Church of God and of the election of the pious. Noah and his children preserved this word, handed down from Adam, unimpaired in their spirit, mind and memory. Then they had another, peculiar word of God, namely concerning the rescue and preservation of himself from such great destruction of the world and from the waters of the Flood, in which Noah believed (Heb. 11:7), and which his sons, who had often heard the same thing from their father, had heard from God himself. So they often repeated this promise of God, fixed in their minds, while in the Ark. The minister of that word, and in general of all the outward worship of God in that Ark, was Noah, who constantly preached and repeated both words of God to his family, so that he and they might be confirmed and comforted in the promises of God, especially when the Ark was struck very hard amid the storms and tempests of air and sea and was battered by them. For the minds of Noah's sons, his wife and his daughters-in-law were sustained by the recital and inculcation of both general and particular promises of God. Noah certainly did this diligently and often. Thus he was the minister of the Church in the Ark and the preacher of the divine word. The outward worship of God in the same Ark was the same as before the Flood, except that during the whole year of the Flood no sacrifice was offered to God, but only after Noah had come out of the Ark. Yet sermons on the word of God, and prayers to God, both public and private, for the sake of the Mediator, were conducted in the Ark: public prayers by Noah, private prayers by each one who was there, both silent and spoken, by which they commended themselves and their salvation to God. I do not doubt that church discipline also existed then, as long as they lived together in the Ark, so that Noah might rebuke not only as a father but also as a minister and prophet of God whatever in his household he saw worthy of rebuke, whether in word or deed, base and foul. Finally, prophecy was kept alive in the same Ark, and often inculcated: concerning the coming Messiah, and the future rescue from the waters of the Flood of all those who were in the Ark, including the animals, and the later restoration of a new world. Noah foretold all these things to them from the word of God. The place for the exercise of divine worship during the whole year was the Ark itself, in which I do not think there was any altar; yet the whole family of Noah gathered at a certain spot in the Ark, both to hear Noah and to pour out public prayers to God. Whatever place that was, on whatever deck of the Ark it lay. But after Noah came out of the Ark and built an altar on which to sacrifice to God, I do not doubt that his descendants, who remained in those places, as long as remains of both the Ark and the altar survived in those regions, often gathered and came together at that very spot to see the surviving remnants of the Ark or the altar, partly religiously and piously, partly superstitiously. Religiously, as those who flocked there to confirm their faith in God's judgements on wicked men and in his mercy toward Noah and the pious; superstitiously, if some believed and thought that God was holier and more present there because of that Ark and its remaining wood. This is the custom of superstitious men: to bind and fasten the power and presence of God to certain places, apart from his word.

units.la: Denique Tempus publicorum & ecclesiasticorum congressuum etiam in Arca ipsa, & toto anno & spatio diluuij, fuit Dies septima, quam Deus ab initio Mundi peculiariter ad sui ultimum, meditandáque opera sua instituerat, Gen. 1, & 2. Ergo non dubito quin die cuiusque Hebdomadis septima, tota familia Noachi solemniùs convenerit ad audiendum Noachum concionantem, & ad precandum Deum. Tunc enim suos omnes maximè consolabatur, instruebatque Noachus, non solùm quà Pater: sed etiam, uti dixi, quà Pastor, & Propheta Dei. Reliquis verò septimana diebus quisque se in Arca ijs, quas illic potuit, Artibus exercuit, nec otiosus fuit: Septima verò ex Dei præcepto quisque ab ijs etiam in Arca conquieuit. Et hæc quidem, quæ qualisuè toto illo anno Politia & status Ecclesia in Mundo fuerit, ostendunt. Qua quoniam sunt à nobis explicata, & opus ipsum institutum ad finem iam & umbilicum perductum, expositaq; sunt à nobis veterissimi Mundi Antiquitates, laudem Deo Opt. Max. (tanquam nauta, qui ex longa navigatione portum tandem attigerunt) canamus, & infinitam illius in primi Mundi administratione Sapientiam, Potentiam, Iustitiam, ac Misericordiâ agnoscamus, admiremur, celebremus, quæ elucet, vti demonstravimus.
units.tr: Finally, the time for public and ecclesiastical assemblies, even within the Ark itself, throughout the whole year and the span of the Flood, was the seventh day, which God from the beginning of the world had specially appointed for his own rest and for pondering his works (Gen. 1 and 2). Therefore I do not doubt that on the seventh day of each week the whole household of Noah gathered more solemnly to hear Noah preaching and to pray to God. For then Noah especially comforted and instructed all of them, not only as a father but also, as I said, as their minister and prophet of God. On the remaining days of the week each person occupied himself in the Ark with whatever crafts he could practise, and was not idle; but on the seventh day, by God's command, each rested from these as well. These things show what sort of polity and state the Church was in throughout that whole year in the world. Since these matters have now been explained by us, and the work itself has been brought to its end and crown, and the most ancient antiquities of the world have been set forth by us, let us sing praise to God Most Good and Greatest (like sailors who at last reach harbour after a long voyage), and let us acknowledge, marvel at and celebrate his infinite wisdom, power, justice and mercy in the governance of the first world, which shines forth, as we have demonstrated.

units.la: Patri vero, & Filio, & Spiritui Sancto, qui sunt vnus ille Deus, laus, & gloria in æternum, & vltra. Amen.
units.tr: To the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit, who are that one God, be praise and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

units.la: FINIS.
units.tr: THE END.
